There is not a single day that passes over the face of the earth that does not see ordinary, uncelebrated men and women perform great deeds, speak words that ring through ages, and bear noble, quiet sorrows. Most of these unheralded heroes, philosophers, and martyrs will never be known until that final hour when the great of the world are brought low and the low are lifted high—but for others, the world’s knowledge of them only sleeps. Their lives are locked away in the dry, curt annals that record them, too cold and compressed to stir the average reader’s heart: they are not breathing stories that pull at the chest, but little hard pebbles of fact that glance off a person’s understanding before they can catch hold. Epitomes are not narratives, any more than bare skeletons are living, breathing human beings.
And so these records of profound, human truths remain dead letters to plain folk, because old chronicle writers left all the color and feeling to the imagination—and imagination is a rare gift, indeed. This is where the storyteller may serve the world, as a gentle interpreter between those long-gone lives and the hearts that have not yet met them.
There exists a tattered, musty old chronicle written in harsh, unforgiving Latin, every single sentence of its hidden chapter holding a true fact. It tells, in sharp, unflinching brevity, the strange story of two people who lived untrumpeted, died unsung, four hundred years ago, and lie still now in that stern page as unhonored as fossils trapped in rock. Fate was unjust to them, living and dead—but if I can only show you the beating, messy, brave humanity hidden under that dry chronicler’s words, I think you will make up for centuries of indifference, and give these two sorely tried souls a small, warm place in your heart, if only for a day.
It was the middle of the fifteenth century. Louis XI sat on the throne of France; Edward IV held the crown of England by force rather than right; and Philip “the Good,” who had dispossessed his cousin Jacqueline through brute cunning and outright force and broken her heart in the process, reigned undisturbed for decades over Holland, where our tale begins.
Elias, a cloth and leather merchant, and his wife Catherine lived in the small, quiet town of Tergou. He traded wholesale and retail in fine cloth, silk, coarse brown holland, and most of all in thick curried leather: a material prized by the middling folk of the time, for it could stand twenty years of hard wear, and turn the blade of an ordinary knife—no small virtue for a jerkin in that century, when people were far too free with their steel. It was not unheard of for a man to set down his dinner spoon mid-meal to carve his neighbor over the pettiest difference of opinion.
The couple were comfortable enough in their trade, and would have had no earthly cares to weigh on them, if not for their nine children. The babes came one a year, and each was greeted with loud rejoicing, and prayers of thanks to the saints, no complaints offered at all. When the whole family was young together, the children seemed like delightful little playthings Heaven had sent to make the long, busy workdays and quiet evenings soft and joyful for hardworking burghers.
But as the “olive branches” shot tall, and Elias and Catherine grew older, and saw firsthand how hard life could be for large families, tender love was tangled tight with quiet worry. They were part of a remarkably careful, provident people: in fifteenth century Holland, reckless parents were as rare as disobedient children. So when the enormous household loaf was set down on its giant wooden trencher, looking like a small fortress sitting in its moat of crumbs, and made the round of the table only to vanish almost entirely, Elias and Catherine would lock eyes and say softly, “Who will find bread for all of them when we are gone?”
The younger children had to work very hard to keep their stolid little Dutch faces straight at these words, for to them dinner and supper arrived as naturally as sunrise and sunset, and the great brown loaf would circle the family table for ever, to rest in their bellies only to rise again fresh from the oven next day. But the remark stirred the thrifty national thoughtfulness in the elder boys, and said often enough, it set them all to thinking: some of the thoughts were kind, some were self-serving, according to the character of each boy.
“Kate, the children are growing so fast this table will soon be too small for all of them,” Elias said one evening.
“We cannot afford it, Eli,” Catherine replied, answering not his words but the unspoken fear behind them, as wives so often do.
Their worry for the future sometimes shifted from grim to sharp with pride. The free burghers of Holland held their station as dear as any noble held his title, and the pair could not bear to think any of their blood would fall in the town’s social ranks after they were gone.
By prudence and small, steady self-denial, they managed to clothe all nine small bodies, feed all nine hungry mouths, and still tuck a small hoard away for the days ahead. As that little pile of coins grew, they felt a joy no miser hoarding gold for himself could ever know.
One day, their second-oldest son Richart, nineteen years old, came to his mother with the quiet, unshakable composure that so often tricked outsiders into underestimating the Dutch temperament, and begged her to plead with his father to send him to Amsterdam, to apprentice under a wealthy merchant. “That is the life I want for myself. I am quick with numbers, and merchants grow rich. Please, good mother, take my part in this, and I will be your grateful debtor for the rest of my days.”
Catherine threw up her hands in shock and disbelief.
“What? Leave Tergou? Leave all the streets you have known since you were a babe?”
“What is one street more or less to me? If I can leave the people I love here, I can surely leave the stones.”
“What? Quit your poor father now that he is no longer young?”
“Mother, if I can leave you, I can leave him too.”
“What? Leave your little brothers and sisters that love you so dearly?”
“There are enough mouths in this house to feed, without mine.”
“What do you mean, Richart? No one is more loved than you. Wait—have I spoken sharp to you? Have I been unkind?”
“Never that I can remember. And if you had been, I would never have breathed a word of it to anyone. Mother,” Richart said gravely, though a tear glistened in his eye, “it all comes down to one simple thing, and nothing will change my mind: there will be one less mouth for you to feed.”
“There now, look what my foolish tongue has done,” Catherine cried, and burst into tears. She could see her first young fledgling perched on the edge of the nest, beating his wings hard enough to fly out into the wide world. Richart had a steady, unbreakable will, and she knew he never wasted a single word.
It ended as all such goodbyes must end: young Richart left for Amsterdam with a face as long and sad as anyone had ever seen on him, and a will as unyielding as granite.
That afternoon at supper, there was one empty chair. Catherine stared at Richart’s vacant spot and wept bitterly, until Elias shouted roughly at the rest of the children, “Sit wider, can’t you? Sit wider!” then turned his face over the back of his wooden chair, and went silent for a long while.
Richart never cost his parents a penny again, but kitting him out and placing him in the household of the merchant Vander Stegen had drained all their small hoard, save for one single gold crown. They started saving again, ants hoarding crumb by crumb. Two years later, Richart found a spot for his brother Jacob in a firm, and Jacob left Tergou right after the eleven o’clock midday dinner. That supper, Elias remembered the last goodbye, and whispered softly, “Sit wider, dears.” Up until that moment, Catherine had refused to see the empty gap at the table, for her oldest daughter Catherine had begged her not to grieve, and she had promised she would not, for the sake of the rest of her children. But when Elias whispered “Sit wider!” she said, voice thick with forced calm, “Aye, soon the table will be too big for the children, and you thought it would be too small.” The next moment she pressed her apron to her face and wept hard.
“It is the best of our children that leave us first,” she sobbed. “That is the cruel part.”
“Nay, nay,” Elias said. “All our children are good, and all are equally dear to us. Heed her not! What God takes from us always seems sweeter than what He leaves behind—if only because men are naturally unthankful, and women are naturally silly,” he added gruffly to hide his own tear.
“And I say Richart and Jacob are the flower of the flock,” Catherine sobbed.
Their little iron-bound money coffer was empty again, and they set to refilling it, saving every penny that was not spent on the shop and their bare necessities, giving up even the smallest small luxuries, then catching each other’s eye across the table and smiling, with a joy far warmer than any self-indulgence could bring. Three years later, they had gleaned enough to set their fourth son up as a master tailor, and their oldest daughter as a ropemaker, right there in Tergou. They could send work their way from their own shop, and set them up for life. The coffer was drained completely dry, this time even the shop gave up a little stock instead of coin to fund their new ventures.
Alas, there were still four children left at home: two who could not earn their own bread, and two who would not. The two unable ones were first Giles, a dwarf of the worst sort: half dull-witted, half malicious, all big head, sharp claws, and booming voice, whom dogs and every unprejudiced local woman ran from, and whom only his mother defended through every mischief. Second was Little Catherine, a soft-spoken little girl who could only move on crutches, who lived with constant quiet pain, but never let it show on her marble-pale face with its violet eyes and long silky lashes, who never spoke a single fretful or complaining word to anyone. The two unwilling ones were Sybrandt, the youngest, a ne’er-do-well who loved playing games far more than he loved working, and Cornelis, the oldest of all the boys, who had run the numbers in his head and decided to huddle by the hearth waiting for distant relatives to die and leave him their fortunes.
Almost worn out by all their efforts, and disheartened by the physical and moral frailties of the four children still in their care, the anxious couple would still find themselves sighing, “What will become of all of them when we are no longer here to look after them?” But they said it more and more mechanically, until one day their domestic horizon cleared, and they added the bright, cheerful coda without fail: “But thanks to Saint Bavon and all the saints, we have Gerard.”
Young Gerard was a son apart, destined for the Church. In those days, the Church could always support her children, one way or another, and his family did not hold out grand hopes for him—they had no powerful connections to pull strings for a wealthy benefice. His frivolous habits, the ones that would have made his father furious in any son not marked for the clergy, were reading and calligraphy, and he was so wrapped up in them he often had to be physically dragged away from his desk to come eat. The day was never long enough for him; he carried a tinderbox and brimstone matches everywhere, begged stub ends of candles off all the neighbors so he could light his lamp at ridiculous hours—even eight o’clock at night in winter, long after the burgomaster of the town had gone to bed. His odd habits were tolerated at home, and actively encouraged by the monks of the nearby monastery. They had taught him calligraphy, and continued teaching him until one day, halfway through a lesson, they realized to their shock he was teaching them.
They told him this with good humor, and he hung his head and blushed. He had suspected it himself, but had never dared trust his own judgment on such a delicate matter. “But my son,” an elderly monk said to him, “God has given you an eye so true, a hand so subtle yet firm, and a heart that loves these beautiful crafts—why do you not paint and illuminate as well as you write? A scroll of words is bare and barren, unless it is surrounded by a border of fruit, leaves, and rich swirling arabesques that delight the eye as the words delight the soul and understanding. You can paint holy men and women on the pages, pictures of saints in glory, that will not only soothe the eye with rich, blended colors, but lift the reader’s heart high. Why not try?”
Gerard was flustered, and mumbled that he had tried illuminating several times, but never got it right. The matter rested there, until a fellow enthusiast soon arrived, in the unexpected form of an old woman. Margaret Van Eyck, the last surviving sister of the famous Van Eyck painter brothers, had left Flanders to return to her native land to spend her last days. She bought a small house near Tergou, heard of Gerard’s skill, saw a sample of his handwriting, and liked it so much she sent her servant Reicht Heynes to invite him over. It was an instant, warm acquaintance: tiny Tergou had never held two people as passionate about art as the two of them. At first, the old painter damped Gerard’s courage terribly—every time he visited, she pulled out drawings and paintings from nooks and crannies, some of them her own work, that seemed to him far beyond anything he could ever hope to make. But if the artist in her overwhelmed him, the kind woman in her kept his heart up. She and Reicht soon drew every secret out of him, including the one the monks never learned: the reason he had never been able to make illuminating work, was that he could not afford the expensive gold, ultramarine blue, and vermilion red, only cheap earth pigments, and he was too shy to ask his mother for the costly paints, certain she would say no.
Margaret Van Eyck gave him a small brush full of fine gold leaf, little pots of vermilion and ultramarine, and a sheet of perfect smooth vellum to paint on. He almost worshipped her. As he left the house, Reicht ran after him with a spare candle and a couple of small coin bits, and he kissed her hand gratefully. Even better than the rare paints was the sympathy for a young, isolated enthusiast that no one else in town had ever given him. Their shared love of art sparked a deep affection between the old painter and the young calligrapher, very typical of that century, when fine art and skilled craftsmanship had no hard line drawn between them, and artists sought each other out and loved one another with no petty jealousy—back when even the early Christians still loved one another, too.
Backed by such a venerable mentor and warmed by their kindness, Gerard advanced fast in skill and learning. His spirits rose visibly: he would still glance back longingly at his half-finished letter when he was dragged away to dinner mid-sentence, but once seated, he showed a bright, lively sense of humor that no one had ever seen in him before, and often made the whole table roar with laughter, telling old jokes from ancient Roman stories that were perfectly new to his stolid Dutch family. As a thank you to the monks who had taught him to write, he made them perfect, exquisite copies of their two most precious manuscripts: the life of their order’s founder, and their rare copy of Terence’s comedies, with the monastery supplying the fine vellum.
The high and puissant Prince Philip “the Good,” Duke of Burgundy, Luxemburg, and Brabant, Earl of Holland and Zealand, Lord of Friesland, Count of Flanders, Artois, and Hainault, Lord of Salins and Macklyn, was a man of many contradictions. He could fight as well as any king alive, and lie almost as well as the King of France. He was a mighty hunter, and he could read and write. He loved jewels as dearly as any noble lady, and gorgeous rich apparel. He was fond of his maids of honor, and of paintings generally—proof of which he had ennobled Jan Van Eyck, elevating a mere artist to noble rank. He also had a rabid passion for giants, dwarfs, and Turks. These last he lured from Istanbul with fair promises, then forced to baptize in a giant tub the moment they arrived at his court, then let them squat facing Mecca and pray to Mahound as much as they pleased, laughing up his sleeve at them for thinking they were still infidels. He kept lions in cages, and fleet leopards trained by Oriental handlers to run down hares and deer. He loved every strange, rare thing in the world except the plain, humdrum virtues. The best part of him was that he was openhanded to the poor; the second best part was that he fostered the arts with real, earnest commitment.
That year he gave dramatic proof of that commitment. He announced grand prizes for the finest examples of several crafts: for the finest religious and secular gold work, for the best oil, egg-tempera, and white lead painting on panel, silk, or metal, for the finest stained glass transparent painting, for the best illumination and border work on vellum, and for the fairest calligraphy on vellum. He ordered the burgomasters of every town to help all poor competitors by collecting their entries and sending them at the town’s expense to Rotterdam for the contest.
When the town crier rang his bell and shouted this news through the streets of Tergou, a thousand mouths gaped and chattered—but only one heart beat fast enough to feel like it would burst out of someone’s chest: Gerard’s. He told his family shyly that he wanted to enter two of the contests. They stared in stunned silence, too shocked at his audacity to breathe, until a horrid loud laugh exploded on the floor like a petard. Gerard looked down, and there was the dwarf Giles, grinning from ear to ear at his expense, laughing as loud as a lion. When Nature made Giles tiny and deformed, she had given him the biggest, deepest voice on record: even his whisper rumbled like a bassoon, making him look like one of those stubby, wide-mouthed little cannons perched on old fortifications, that look like a flower pot until they bellow loud enough to shake the

“The soup is hot,” said Gerard, leaning in to where the old scholar huddled stiff and shivering by the little roadside fire.

The senior man sighed, his shoulders slumping despondently. “But how are we to reach it without burning ourselves? My bones ache too much to kneel, not with these short straws, and the flask sits too close to the flame.”

“Father, the young man has brought us straws already,” Margaret put in, a tiny, sly, warm smile tugging at the corner of her mouth.

“Ay, ay!” the old man nodded, “but my poor limbs are too creaky to bend that far. St. John the Baptist, but this lad is quick!”
Even as he spoke of his difficulty, Gerard had already solved it. He undid the small knot fastened at his breast in a heartbeat, pulled off his soft felt hat, tucked a smooth river stone into each of its four corners, wrapped his jerkin’s tail around his hand to shield it, and plucked the bubbling flask straight off the fire. He wedged it snug between the weighted stones in the crown of his hat, then held it right under the old man’s nose with a merry, crinkling smile. The elder tremulously slipped one of the rye straws into the soup and sipped. Slowly his wan, drawn face lightened, glowing brighter and brighter until it was almost radiant, and he drew a long, deep breath of pure delight.

“Hippocrates and Galen!” he cried. “‘Tis soupe au vin — the restorative of all restoratives! Blessed be the nation that invented it, the woman who stirred it, and the young man who brought it to fainting folk. Have a sip, girl, while I tell our young host the full history and virtues of this sovereign draught. This elixir, sir, was unknown to the ancients: you will find no mention of it in their medical treatises, nor even in the popular tales that leak so many of their chirurgery and home remedy secrets. Hector, in the *Iliad*, if my memory does not fail me —”
“— was offered a cup of pure wine by one of the poem’s ladies, but he refused, saying he was off to battle and would not drink anything that might weaken his strength. Why, if soupe au vin had existed at Troy, he would have added a line in that very hexameter to say ‘But madam, I will gladly taste your soupe au vin.’ Not only would that have been common courtesy, no perfect commander lacks that — but to refuse it would have marked him as shallow and unfit to lead an entire war! Men going into battle need sustenance, as all history proves: foolish generals who march hungry troops against well-fed enemies are beaten every time, even when they outnumber their foe. The Romans lost a great battle in northern Italy to Hannibal the Carthaginian for that very folly alone. This divine cordial puts new strength in the limbs and fire in the spirits in a single sip — had Hector drunk it at the right moment, with Phoebus, Venus, and all the blessed saints looking on, the Greeks would almost certainly have lost that war! Look at me: a minute ago I was faint, weary, and heartsick, and now? I am brave as Achilles, and strong as an eagle.”

“Oh father, an eagle? Don’t exaggerate so!” Margaret laughed.

“Girl, I defy you and anyone else! I could run all the way to Rotterdam right now, and fight every ill life throws at me — even poverty and old age, which philosophers call the greatest of all evils. Negatur! That is only true if a man has wasted his life, which, to be fair, far too many do. Now for the moderns —”

“Father, dearest father, drink more soup first before it cools!” Margaret held the hat out to him imploringly with both hands, and he slipped the straw back between his lips, spared from launching into another long string of historical anecdotes.

Gerard took the chance to tell Margaret how proud his mother would be to know her soup had helped a man of such learning.

“Ay, but” Margaret said, her eyes glinting playfully, “it would grieve her to see her son give all of his own food away and take none for himself. Why did you only cut two straws?”

“Fair mistress, I hoped you would let me share your straw,” Gerard smiled. “There were only two, after all.”

Margaret blushed and grinned. “Never beg what you may command. The straw is not mine, it is yours — you cut it in the yonder field.”

“I cut it, so it was mine. But then your lips touched it, so it became yours.”

“Did it now? Then I will lend it back to you. There — now it is yours again, your lips have touched it.”

“No, it belongs to both of us now. Let us split it.”

“By all means, you have a knife.”

“I will not cut it — that would be bad luck. I’ll bite it in half. I will keep my half. I dare say you will burn yours as soon as you get home.”

“You do not know me. I waste nothing. Ten to one I turn it into a hairpin, or some other little trinket.”

Her answer made Gerard fall quiet, soft and flustered rather than teased, his heart thrumming. Once the bread and soup were all gone, the old scholar gathered his things to continue their journey. Only then did the quick, clever Gerard find himself stuck: he could not retie the little silk ribbon around his neck, the one his mother Catherine had tied for him so neatly at home. Margaret watched him fumble with it slyly for a while, then offered to help — at her age, girls love to play at being coy and tender, saucy and gentle by turns, and she had seen she had made him flustered just a little earlier. Her fair head, crowned with stately auburn hair that glowed like polished copper through its silver threads, bowed sweetly towards him, and his eyes drank in the sight of her. Two soft, white, supple hands worked delicately at the stubborn ribbon, molding the ends into a neat, perfect knot with light, airy touches. A heavenly thrill shot through the innocent young man, and vague, beautiful glimpses of an entire new world of feeling opened up before him. Margaret prolonged that sweet moment unwittingly — no woman hurries a task that touches the gentle, small rituals of adornment. When her taper fingers finally had the knot fastened tight, she still was not quite satisfied: she curved her palm, pressed it soft and warm to the very center of the ribbon knot, a little coaxing hand-kiss as if to say “now be a good knot, and stay tied.” The palm-kiss was meant for the ribbon, but Gerard’s heart leaped up to meet it.

“There, that is exactly how it was,” Margaret said, drawing back to admire her work, then looked up to wait for his approval. She met his gaze full on — his eyes were burning with such ardent, adoring longing that she dropped her own eyes at once, her face flushing bright scarlet. An indescribable tremor ran through her, and she stepped back quickly, took her father’s arm on the other side of him, her lashes lowered and her cheeks betraying every bit of her flustered feeling. Gerard, blushing that he had scared her away with his stare, took the old man’s other arm. And so the two young things walked side by side, both downcast and acutely aware of each other, propping up their “eagle” of a scholar in soft, silent peace.

They entered Rotterdam through the Schiedamze Poort. Gerard did not know the town, so Peter pointed him the way to Hooch Straet, where the Stadthouse stood. He and Margaret were bound for his cousin’s house in Ooster-Waagen Straet, so almost as soon as they passed through the gate their paths split. They bid each other a friendly farewell, and Gerard stepped into the bustle of the great city. A heavy, profound loneliness settled over him even in the crowded streets. He kicked himself, far too late, for being too shy to ask their names, or where they lived.

“Curse my foolish shamefacedness!” he muttered to himself. “But their speech and their breeding were far finer than their worn clothes would suggest, and something whispered me they did not wish to be recognized by strangers. I will never see her again. Oh, weary world, I hate you and your ways! To meet such beauty, goodness, and learning — three priceless pearls — and lose them forever before I even know their names.”

Lost in that sad reverie, he let his feet carry him wherever they would, and soon found himself completely turned around. He spotted a crowd of people all heading the same way, and joined them, assuming they must be bound for the Stadthouse. But the noisy troop led him not to the town hall, but to a wide meadow on the banks of the Maas. All sorts of games were underway: wrestling, palm-ball, quintain, legerdemain, archery, tumbling — and the crowd roared with delight as men and women alike flipped and somersaulted for their amusement. There was a trained bear that stood on his head, marched upright, and bowed with great gravity to his master, a hare that beat a tiny drum, and a cock that strutted about on little stilts with a haughty air. The sights made Gerard laugh now and then, but the gaiety could not truly reach him — his heart was too sad and out of tune with the fun. When he heard a young man say to his friend that the Duke had been at the meadow, but had left for the Stadthouse to feast the burgomasters, aldermen, art competition prize competitors and all their guests, he suddenly realized he was ravenously hungry, and very much wanted to sup at the prince’s table. He turned away from the river, and this time found Hooch Straet, which led him straight to the Stadthouse.

But when he arrived, he was turned away at every small door, until he reached the great main courtyard gate. It was guarded by soldiers, overseen by a pompous major-domo glittering with an embroidered collar, a heavy gold chain of office, and a white staff with a gilded knob. A whole crowd of people clustered at the gate, trying to wheedle their way past the official, who stood as immovable as a rock. They came up to him one by one like ripples on water, and were turned away just as easily. Gerard struggled to push through the crowd, and when he was only four heads away from the gate, his heart leapt: there was Peter, Margaret on his arm, humbly begging for entrance.

“My cousin the alderman is not at home,” the old man said. “The servants told us he is here at the feast. If you will not let us in to see him, at least carry this slip of paper with his name on it to him — he will come out to meet us.”

“What is that to me, old man?” the porter snapped. “I carry no messages. I only keep the gate.”

He then roared in a stentorian, unyielding voice: “No strangers enter here but the competitors and their invited companies!”

“Step aside old man, you got your answer,” someone in the crowd called.

Margaret turned half around, her eyes imploring. “Good people, we have traveled a very long way. My father is old, and my cousin has a new servant who does not know us, and turned us away from his own house before we could explain.”

The crowd laughed hoarsely. Margaret shrank back as if they had struck her. At that moment, a hand wrapped around hers — a warm, firm grasp that felt like heart meeting heart, like magnet drawing steel. She spun around, and there was Gerard. A little cry of joy and relief burst from her, and she began to sniffle softly, prettily. The crowd had jostled and frightened her, her cousin’s thoughtlessness to forget to tell his new servants they were coming was cruel, and the servant’s caution, however loyal to his master, had humiliated her and her father terribly. To her, sore, anxious, and jostled, Gerard’s kind face and hand felt like a miracle.

“Ah, all’s well now,” jeered a coarse voice in the crowd. “She’s found her sweetheart!”

“Haw haw haw!” the rest of the crowd roared.

Margaret dropped Gerard’s hand at once, and spun around, her eyes bright and flashing through her tears. “I have no sweetheart, you rude men. But I am friendless in your boorish town, and this is a friend — one who knows, as you do not, how to treat the aged and the weak.”

The crowd fell dead silent. They had only been thoughtless, and now they knew her sharp rebuke was entirely just. The quiet let Gerard turn to the porter.

“I am a competitor, sir.”

“What is your name?” the man squinted at him suspiciously.

“Gerard, son of Elias.”

The janitor checked the slip of parchment he held. “Gerard Eliassoen may enter.”

“With my company, these two?” Gerard asked.

“Nay. They are not your company. They came before you.”

“What does that matter? They are my friends, and I will not go in without them.”

“Then stay outside.”

“That I will not.”

“That we shall see.”

“Speedily, then.” Gerard drew a breath, and shouted at the top of his powerful, ringing voice, so loud the whole street echoed: “HO, PHILIP, EARL OF HOLLAND!”

“Are you mad?” the porter gasped.

“HERE IS ONE OF YOUR SERVANTS WHO DEFIES YOU!” Gerard roared on.

“Hush! Hush, man!”

“Murder! The Duke is right there! I am dead!” the janitor quaked, panicking. He yelled as loud as he could, to drown out Gerard’s voice: “OPEN THE GATE, YE KNAVES! WAY THERE FOR GERARD ELIASSOEN AND HIS COMPANY! (The fiends go with him!)”

The gate swung open as if by magic. Eight soldiers lowered their pikes halfway, making an arch the three of them walked under, triumphant, past the portal. The moment they were through, the pikes clashed together horizontally to bar the gate, almost spearing a greedy townsman who tried to slip in after them.

A few steps past the gate, they found themselves in a scene of almost Oriental luxury. The courtyard was lined with tables heaped with rich meats and glowing, ornate silver plate. Guests in rich, varied costumes sat beneath a canopy of fresh cut boughs strung from golden, silver, and blue silken cords strung across the space. Fruits of every hue — even artificial ones made of gold, silver, and wax — hung from the plane and lime trees, peeking out like bright eyes through the green leaves. The Duke’s minstrels swept their lutes at intervals, and a fountain played red Burgundy wine in six jets that met and danced in the air. The evening sun shot its golden fire through the purple wine spouts, turning them into cascades of molten rubies. The red-gold light spilled over fair faces, snowy beards, velvet, satin, jeweled sword hilts, glowing gold, gleaming silver, and sparkling glass. Gerard and his two friends stood dazzled, spellbound. A whisper buzzed around them: “Salute the Duke! Salute the Duke!” They looked up, and there on the dais high above them their sovereign stood, waving a kind welcome down to them. The men bowed low, Margaret curtsied with a deep, graceful obeisance. The Duke, his hand still raised, pointed the new arrivals out to a group of valets. Instantly seven of his servants rushed over, seated the three of them at a table, and set fifteen different colored soups down in little silver bowls before them, and as many fine wines in crystal vases.

“Nay father, let us not eat until we thank our good friend,” Margaret said, only now recovering from all the bustle.

“Child, he is our guardian angel.”

Gerard covered his face with his hands. “Tell me when you have finished thanking me, and I will look up and have my supper, for I am very hungry. I know which of us three is the happiest to have met again.”

“Me?” Margaret asked.

“No. Guess again.”

“Father?”

“No.”

“Then I have no guess at all!” Margaret laughed, a bright little crow of pure happiness.

They sipped the soup, which vanished quickly, and then fish arrived in a dozen different preparations, lobster and almond patties, almond and cream patties, and a huge variety of savory rissoles. Next came a whole wild boar, that smelled divine — until Margaret sprang back from it with two shrieks of dismay, and pinched Gerard’s arm hard. The Duke’s chef had been far too clever: he had restored the boar’s bristles and fur with burnt sugar and edible dyes, its great tusks still in its jaw, and two bright, colored sugar eyes that seemed to follow every movement of knife and spoon across the table.

“What is all that noise?” the Duke called, hearing Margaret’s cry. Seven servants hurried to tell him, and he laughed. “Give her some of the beef-stuffing then, and bring me Sir Boar!” That beef-stuffing was the Duke’s own private favorite dish: on grand occasions, he had an entire ox roasted whole, and all the venison, hare, lamb, and poultry stuffed into the big cavity in its side cooked to absolute perfection, soaking up all the ox’s rich juices. The Duke sent his servants over, who drove silver tridents straight into the steaming ox and fished out a kid, a cygnet, and a whole flock of wildfowl, which were set smoking hot before Gerard and his friends. Old Peter’s face, which had fallen a little glum at missing out on the wild boar, lit up with joy. After that came twenty different fruit and herb tarts, and last of all confectionery on a grand scale: cathedrals of sugar, gilded and painted along the bas-reliefs, castles with imitated moats and ditches, sugar elephants, camels, toads, knights on horseback jousting, kings and princesses watching, trumpeters blowing — all the sweet statues filled with scented sugary syrup, works of art made only to be eaten. The guests bit through sugar bastions, crunched crusaders and their horses whole, and cracked sugar bishops, cope, crosier and all, as unthinkingly as we crunch a caraway comfit

A grave, white-haired seneschal picked his way through the noisy, torch-lit banquet hall, and halted respectfully at Gerard’s party’s table to ask if the young man Gerard Eliassoen was of their company. When Gerard affirmed his identity, the seneschal bowed courteously. “The Princess Marie would confer with you, young sir. I am to conduct you to her presence.”
Every head within earshot snapped round at the news, all eyes fixed on the young man summoned to a royal audience, bright with unmasked curiosity and green-edged envy. Gerard rose at once to obey.
“I wager we shall not see you again,” Margaret said calmly, though a faint pink rose high on her cheeks.
“That you most certainly will,” Gerard smiled back, then leaned in to whisper in her ear, “This is my good princess, aye – but you are my queen.” Straightening, he added aloud, “Wait for me, I pray you. I shall return before you know it.”
“Ay, ay!” grunted Peter, jolting awake as if he had been called by name.
The moment Gerard was gone, Margaret and her father, plain and roughly clad as they were, became the unmissable centre of every gaze in the hall. Spotting their sudden prominence, William Johnson sauntered over, feigning delighted surprise, and claimed kinship with them.
“To think I was standing right at your backs this whole while, and you never saw me!” he cried.
“Nay, cousin Johnson,” Margaret said coolly, “I spotted you long syne.”
“You saw me, and spoke not a word?”
“Cousin, it was for you to welcome us to Rotterdam, just as it falls to us to welcome you to Sevenbergen. Your own servant turned us away from your door, would not even grant us a bench to sit on.”
“The addle-pated idiot!”
“I had half a mind to test the old proverb, see if it was true ‘like maid like master’ – and sayings do not lie, after all.”
William Johnson blushed so deep a purple his ears went dark. He saw Margaret was sharp, and knew she suspected he had snubbed them on purpose. The wisest course was to outrun his mistake with actions, not words: he insisted they come home with him immediately, that he would prove beyond doubt they were welcome in his house.
“Who doubts it, cousin? Who doubts it?” the scholar Peter chuckled.
Margaret thanked him graciously, but demurred at leaving just then. She said she wanted to listen to the wandering minstrels a while longer. A quarter of an hour later, when most of the other guests had begun to drift away, Johnson renewed his plea, and Margaret admitted her real reason.
“It would be rude to our friend Gerard, would it not? He has no idea where we lodge in this great city, and we have already lost each other once on the road from Sevenbergen.”
“Oh, that is easily remedied!” Johnson said. “My young man – ahem, my secretary – shall sit right here and wait for him, and bring him straight to my house on Ooster-Waagen Straat. He shall lodge with us, and no other, you have my word.”
“Cousin, we shall be far too burdensome,” Margaret protested.
“Nay, nay! You shall see exactly how welcome you are, you and your father and your friend, no questions asked. I, for one, am dying to hear what the Princess could possibly want with a young scholar from the countryside.”
Margaret felt a little jolt of joy at the thought that Gerard would be staying under the same roof as them, before a faint flicker of misgiving crossed her face. “But what if your young man is thoughtless, slips off to play at dice, and Gerard misses him?”
“Play? Leave the spot I order him to stand? Ho! Hans Cloterman, step forward!”
A solemn figure clad in plain black serge and dark violet hose rose from a far bench, took two stiff, even steps, and planted himself before them without moving a single muscle. He was the very statue of gravity, prim, precise, starched to the very bone. Margaret, giddy with happiness, could barely keep a straight face at the sight of him, and leaned over to whisper to Johnson, “I would put my hand in the fire for that man. We are at your command, cousin, as soon as you have given him his orders.”
Hans was instructed to sit at their vacated table, wait for Gerard’s return, and lead him straight to Johnson’s house. He made no verbal reply at all, only calmly lowered himself onto the indicated bench, and Margaret, Peter, and William Johnson left the hall together. “Indeed, father, it is high time you were abed after all that travel,” Margaret said gently – that had been her quiet priority all along.
Hans Cloterman sat waiting for Gerard, solemn and businesslike, as the minutes ticked by, never growing the least bit impatient. Johnson had not exaggerated when he laughed at the idea of his perfect secretary abandoning his post to chase sport or youthful frivolity. But with no one’s eye on him, the model clerk decided to improve the empty time by sipping, at short, perfectly measured intervals, goblets of strong Corsican wine. The wine was heady, but Cloterman’s head was sturdier still: it was a full hour after Gerard had left the banquet hall before the notion dawned on him that the whole of Creation was expecting him to drink a toast to all good fellows, and most especially to the Duke of Burgundy, then in attendance at the feast.
With great gingerly solemnity, he filled his ninth bumper, and rose slowly to his full height. The next instant, he rolled straight backward onto the grass, goblet still clutched in his hand, spilling cold wine over the ankles of several nearby passersby who yelped and frisked away – not a single muscle in his long, rigid face shifting, even as he lost all reason, for his features retained their full gravity, primness, and air of unshakable infallibility all the while.

Back at the royal pavilion, the seneschal led Gerard through winding torchlit passages to the door of the pavilion, where a cluster of young noblemen, all embroidered silk and towering plumes, sat guard over the heir apparent, playing cards by the red guttering light of servants’ torches. A single whisper from the seneschal, and one of them rose reluctantly, stared at Gerard with haughty surprise, and ducked inside to announce him. He returned moments later, beckoned the pair on, and led them through two more passages to an antechamber where three more fine gentlemen, furred and gem-studded like fancy tapestries, were deep in a raucous game of dice.
“You can’t see the Princess, it’s far too late,” one grumbled without looking up.
“Aye, she passed through here but now with her nurse,” a second added. “She’s gone straight to bed, doll and all. Deuce-ace again!”
Gerard turned to leave, but the seneschal smiled incredulously. “This young man is here by the Countess’s direct orders. Be so good as to conduct him to her ladies.”
At that, a superb foppish Adonis rose to his feet with an injured look, and led Gerard into a sunlit chamber where eleven ladies lolled and chattered like a flock of magpies. Two of the more industrious ones were playing cat’s cradle, their fingers as nimble as their tongues. At the sight of a stranger, every single tongue fell silent as if pulled by one shared string, and every pair of eyes turned fixed on Gerard, as if that same string had wrenched all their gazes toward him. Gerard had been ill at ease before, but this full battery of curious stares disconcerted him so thoroughly his own eyes dropped to stare hard at the floor.
The young court ladies, giddy to find a creature they could fluster after being hectored by courtiers all day, giggled openly and revelled in their small triumph – until a stern duenna rapped her fan and said severely, “Mesdames!” They all went abashed in an instant, as if someone had pulled a hidden “modesty string” to hush them. The duenna then took Gerard by the arm, and marched him ahead in solemn silence.
Gerard’s heart sank, and he half wanted to turn and run for the door. What must princes be, he thought, if even their courtiers are so cold and stiff? They must learn all their icy breeding from the royal household they serve.
His reflections were cut short when the duenna suddenly showed him into a smaller inner chamber, where three ladies sat working at embroidery, and a pretty little twelve-year-old girl was tuning a lute. The ladies were richly but modestly dressed, no gaudy trimmings, and the duenna went up to the one hemming a linen kerchief, and whispered a few low words. That lady turned toward Gerard with a soft smile, and beckoned him closer. She did not rise, but laid her work aside, and the small, gentle movement was full of grace, ease, and quiet courtesy.
“Margaret Van Eyck is an old, dear friend of mine, sir,” she began at once, “and I was overjoyed to receive a letter from her hand. I owe you no small thanks for bringing it to me safely. Marie, my love, this is the gentleman who brought you that pretty miniature you admired so much.”
“Sir, I thank you a thousand times over,” the young princess said warmly.
“I am glad you feel in her debt, sweetheart,” the Countess of Charolois continued, “for our old friend has asked us to do this young gentleman a small service in return.”
“I will do anything on earth for him,” the little girl replied with unfeigned ardour.
“Anything on earth is hardly enough for a favour from Margaret Van Eyck,” the Countess said quietly. “Well then – what would you have us do for you, sir?”
Gerard had just realised exactly how exalted the company he stood in was. “My sovereign demoiselle,” he said, gently, a little tremulous, “where no pains have been taken, no reward is needed.”
“But we must obey mamma, you know,” the princess put in. “All the world must.”
“That is true,” Gerard smiled. “Then, demoiselle, reward me if you will by letting me hear the stave you were about to sing before I interrupted you.”
“What! You love music, sir?”
“I adore it.”
The little princess glanced inquiringly at her mother, received a smiling nod of assent, and picked up her lute to sing a popular romaunt of the day. Though only twelve, she was a well-taught, painstaking musician. Her small hand swept the chords with courage and precision, striking every note of the arpeggio clear and distinct, bright as twinkling stars on a frosty night – but the true charm was her voice. It was not loud, but it was round, clear, full, and ringing like a well-tuned bell. She sang with a quiet, modest eloquence, no over-the-top theatrical tricks, no forced sentiment: every note gushed pure and unfeigned from her throat, as if Nature herself was singing through her. The ditty was as unadulterated as its singer, no whining slurs, no trite, turgid flourishes, no frothy musical tricks that drowned out melody and meaning.
As the soft, tender strain flowed from that young pure throat, Gerard’s eyes filled with tears. The Countess watched him with quiet interest: most guests applauded the princess loudly, but few of them cried, their cheeks wet with unfeigned emotion. When the last note faded, and the lute strings stopped ringing, she asked him demurely, “Are you content?”
Gerard started a little, the sound of her voice breaking the spell and dragging him back to earth. “Oh, madam!” he cried. “Surely this is how cherubs and seraphs sing, to charm the saints in heaven.”
“I am much of your opinion, my young friend,” the Countess said, moved. She turned a look of soft, loving, proud affection on her daughter – a heavenly look, the kind that old tales say only a mother’s eye can hold, resting on the child she cherishes.
The Countess resumed her conversation. “My old friend Margaret has asked me to be of service to you. This is the first favour she has ever seen fit to ask of us, and her request is sacred. You are in holy orders, sir?”
Gerard bowed.
“I fear you are no priest, though – you look far too young.”
“Oh no, madam. I am not even a sub-deacon. I am only a lector, but next month I shall be made an exorcist, and before long an acolyte.”
“Well, Monsieur Gerard, with your gifts and accomplishments you will pass through the minor orders in no time. And let me beg you to do so quickly: the day after you say your first mass, I shall have the pleasure of appointing you to a wealthy, comfortable benefice.”
“Oh, madam!”
“And Marie, remember I make this promise in your name as well as my own.”
“Fear not, mamma, I will not forget!” the little princess piped up. “But if you take my advice, what you will be is Bishop of Liege. The Bishop of Liege is the grandest bishop who ever lived! Do you not remember him, mamma, the day we visited Liege? He was braver than grandpapa himself! He wore a tall crown cut right down the middle, stuffed full of the most beautiful jewels you ever saw, and his gown was stiff all over with gold thread, and his mantle had a broad border stitched all over with painted pictures – and above all, his gloves! You have no gloves like them, mamma. They were embroidered all over with jewels, and scented with the sweetest perfume, I could smell it the whole time he laid his hands on my head to give me his blessing. Dear old man! I dare say he will die soon, most old people do, and then sir – you can be bishop, and wear all those grand things –”
“Gently, Marie, gently,” the Countess laughed. “Bishoprics are for old gentlemen, and this is still a very young one.”
“Mamma! He is not that young!”
“Not compared to you, Marie, eh?”
“He is of good birth, dear mamma, and I am certain he is good enough for a bishop.”
“Alas! mademoiselle, you are mistaken,” Gerard said, flustered.
“I do not know that, Monsieur Gerard,” the Countess said, smiling, “but I am a little puzzled to know on what grounds my daughter pronounces on your character so boldly.”
“Alas, mamma!” the princess said, raising her eyebrows at her mother’s supposed simplicity, “have you not looked at his face, then?”
“I beg your pardon – I have,” the Countess said, turning back to Gerard. “Well, sir, if I cannot move quite as fast as my daughter, attribute that to my old age, not to a lack of interest in your welfare. A benefice will do to start your career. And I shall make sure it is not far from – what do you call the place you are from? Tergou? A priest gives up much,” she continued, her gentle woman’s eye resting on him for a moment with mild pity, half-surprised that he would choose to give up the company of women, all the joy and love they bring, the great happiness of raising a family. “At least you shall be near your friends. Have you a mother?”
“Yes, madam, thanks be to God!”
“Good. You shall have a church close to Tergou. She will thank me for that. And now, sir, we must not detain you any longer from those who have a better claim on your society than we do. Duchess, oblige me by bidding one of the pages conduct him back to the banquet hall – the way is hard to find.”
Gerard bowed low to the Countess and the Princess, and backed toward the door.
“I hope it will be a very nice benefice,” the Princess called after him with a pretty smile, as he reached the threshold, then shook her head with a solemn, mock-serious air. “But you really would have been better off as Bishop of Liege, you know.”
Gerard followed his new guide, his heart warm with gratitude – but before he reached the banquet hall, a cold weight settled over him. He was a young man who had lived a quiet, uneventful life in the countryside, unused to holding contradictory feelings in his head at once, balancing joy and grief. The excitement of the royal audience, the unlooked-for promise of a good living, the joy it would bring his family at home – that had possessed him wholly while he was in the Countess’s chamber. But now, the voice of his own passion spoke up loud and clear. What! Give up Margaret, whose soft hand he could still feel in his, whose deep eyes he still saw before him? Resign her, and all the world of love and joy she had opened up for him that very day?
The revulsion was so strong he hastily resolved to say nothing at all about the offered benefice when he got home. The Countess is so kind, he thought, she must have a hundred ways to aid a young man’s fortune. She will not force me to take holy orders when she learns I love a girl – one would almost think she already suspects it, for she looked at me so strangely just now, and said “A priest gives up much, too much.” I dare say she will give me a post at the palace, instead. His mind eased by that hopeful thought, he reached the entrance to the banqueting hall, thanked his guide, and ran in, eyes bright and eager, looking for Margaret.
He came in sight of their table – and it was empty. Margaret was gone, Peter was gone. No one was sitting there at all. Only a soberly dressed citizen of Rotterdam had just tumbled headfirst under the table dead drunk, and several passersby were hauling him up to carry him away. Gerard never guessed how important that solemn drunkard was to his fate: he was looking for Beauty, and left the Beast to lie.
He ran wildly round the hall, which was now nearly empty. She was nowhere to be found. He left the palace, and found a crowd outside gawking at two great new lanterns lit over the gate, turning night almost into day. He asked them earnestly if they had seen an old man in a scholar’s gown, and a lovely young girl pass out of the gates. They laughed at his question: they had been staring at the new lights, not bothering to glance at ordinary old men and young

It was close on four o’clock in the afternoon, when low golden light slanted through Tergou’s cobblestone lanes. Eli the hosier was busy in his shop at the front of the house, his two eldest sons out running errands for the day. Catherine and her little crippled daughter Kate had fretted over their missing son Gerard for hours, and had wandered a little way down the high road, craning their necks for any glimpse of him coming over the distant hill. Left entirely alone in the family sitting room was Giles, whose odd form and favourite trick of the moment we will pause to sketch in full.

The Dutch have long been an innovative, leading people—they lay claim to inventing woodblock printing, oil painting, modern liberty, banking, formal gardening, and above all, a famously rigorous standard of cleanliness long before the rest of Europe caught on. Where across the Channel, English gentry in velvet jerkins and pointed-toed shoes trod over floor rushes that sat unchanged for months, crusted with gnawed bones, rotting scraps, spittle, eggshells and all manner of foul refuse, this humble hosier’s sitting room was floored with bright, glazed Dutch tile, washed so often and carefully that you could eat a meal straight off its surface. One large leaded window took up most of the far wall, its central cross-shaped stone mullion carved so bold and raised that the whole household crossed themselves and murmured a short prayer whenever they caught sight of it. Its small lozenge-shaped panes were soldered together with thin strips of lead, the same design you can still spot in rural Dutch cottages to this day. All the chairs in the room were simple, rough-hewn pieces, save for one towering oak armchair: its back stood so perfectly perpendicular to its seat that the sitter’s head would stop a full two feet short of its intricately carved acanthus crest. Beside it sat a waisted copper pail of holy water, with a small hand aspergillum for sprinkling it over the household and its goods, and a long, heavy oak dining table.

It was this table that little Giles clung to now, his jaws clamped tight around its rim, his eyes bulging, his stubby claw-like hands flailing in the air like a vampire mid-leap. Nature, it seemed, had not made Giles a dwarf out of deliberate cruelty: she had crafted his head and torso with all her usual care, only to be distracted halfway through shaping his lower half, leaving the rest to random chance. The result was a human wedge, an inverted cone, that made no sense by any ordinary rule of proportion. Bisected at the waist, the top half of Giles would have outweighed the three times the lower half. That very disproportion, though, let him pull off feats that would have stumped even the legendary strongman Milo. His powerfully brawny arms had almost no lower body weight to drag behind them, so he could shin up a vertical pole like a squirrel, and hang for hours from a bough by one hand like a cherry dangling from its stalk. If he could have created a vacuum with his palms the way lizards supposedly do with their toes, he would have been able to walk across the ceiling. This pocket-sized athlete’s greatest joy, lately, had been to grip the edge of the dining table and swing back and forth, then—at the peak of delight—he would release his hands and hang suspended by nothing but his strong, sharp teeth.

All pleasures, though, are prone to interruption. Little Kate hobbled into the room and caught Sampsonet mid-swing, and stood aghast. She was every inch her mother’s daughter, her heart set on protecting the fine furniture, not on marvelling at a twelve-inch gymnast’s tricks.
“Oh Giles! How can you do that? Mother will be home any minute. You’ll dent the table edge for good.”
“Go on then, run tell her, you little tale-bearer,” Giles snarled, not bothering to release his grip. “You’re the biggest mischief-maker in all Tergou, everyone knows it.”
“Am I?” Kate asked calmly. “That is new to me.”
“Biggest there is,” he growled, chomping down harder on the oak.
“Oh, indeed,” she said drily.

That sally of unusual satire landed, and Giles was still very much unblasted, so Kate simply sat down on a plain wooden chair and began to cry. Her mother stepped through the door at that very moment, and Giles scrambled to hurl himself under the table, where he glared out from the shadows.
“What on earth is the matter now?” Catherine said sharply. She glanced from Kate’s tear-streaked face to the telltale shadow under the table, and lifted a threatening hand to hint at cuffed ears.
“Nay, mother,” Kate said quickly. “Giles only spoke a foolish word. I would not have noticed it on any other day, but I am tired, and I have been so worried for Gerard, you know.”
“Let no one waste their worry on me,” a faint, dusty voice called from the doorway. Gerard tottered in, pale, caked in road dust, and worn thin, and before anyone could speak he dropped exhausted into the nearest chair, surrounded by a storm of half-shouted cries of delight, curiosity, and relief.
He had combed every corner of Rotterdam for Margaret, beating through the city like it was a thick game covert, and the long, unbroken walk home had completely drained him. But youth is elastic, and within minutes he was bright again, the eager centre of his whole family’s circle. First they badgered him to tell every last detail of the prize competition.
“Oh mother, oh Kate,” he gushed, “when I walked into the great hall where all the competitors’ work was laid out before the judges, I nearly fainted where I stood at the goldsmiths’ displays. I did not think all the goldsmiths in the world could ever gather so much gold, silver, gemstone, and sheer clever, beautiful craftsmanship. Every art, truly, is divine.” He went on to describe the gleaming reliquaries, feretories, chalices, croziers, monstrances, fine jewelled goblets, pocket clocks, chains and brooches, until his mother and sister sat transfixed, their mouths soft with wonder. “But when I reached the illuminated manuscripts from Ghent and Bruges, my heart sank. My own little submission looked like smudged dirt beside them. For a minute I thought I would cry, but I prayed for a better spirit, and soon enough I could only feel grateful, awed by those patient, skilful craftsmen I count as my masters. I was so lost in the beauty of the coloured pages I quite forgot all about the plain black and white writing entries. But the next day, after every other prize had been handed out, they came around to the writing category, and whose name do you think the herald shouted first?”
“Yours!” Kate cried immediately.
The rest of the family laughed at her certainty.
“You may laugh all you like,” Gerard said, grinning, “but it was Gerard Eliassoen of Tergou he called. I stood there stupid, frozen, until they pushed me forward. Everything swam before my eyes, until I found myself kneeling on a velvet cushion at the feet of the Duke. He spoke some kind words to me, but I was so flustered I could not answer a single one. Then he reached to his side, and instead of drawing his dagger to cut off my dull, stammering head, he hung a heavy gold medal around my neck. Here it is.”
A roar of excitement went up, and the whole family crowded close to see it. “And then he gave me fifteen bright, heavy gold angel coins. I had seen one of those before, but I never once got to hold one. Here they are.”
“Oh Gerard! Oh our Gerard!”
“I’ve split them all fair,” he said, sorting them out. “One for you, Cornelis, one for you Sybrandt, one for you, Giles the Little Mischief. Two for you, my little crippled Lily, because God has laid that burden on you. One for myself, to buy the best vellum and the brightest new coloured inks. The last nine are for you, mother, who nursed all of us, and risked two whole crowns to fund my trip when no one else would.”
The gold pulled every quirk of their characters right to the surface. Cornelis and Sybrandt snatched their coins, their faces tight with greed, then glowered at Kate out of the corners of their eyes, furious that she had been given two pieces. Giles grabbed his, rolled it across the gleaming tile floor, and went whooping after it. Kate set down her crutches, sat soft and slow, and held out her little arms to Gerard in a gesture brimming with tender, uncomplicated love. Catherine, who had been half stunned at first by the shower of gold spilling into her apron, suddenly cried out, “Stop kissing him a minute, Kate, he is my son first! Ah Gerard, my brave boy, I never thought you would grow to be half so worthy.”
Gerard knelt down beside her, and she wound her arms around his neck and wept there, half for joy, half for pride.
“Good lad! Good, steady lad!” Eli the hosier cried, his voice thick with emotion. “I’m off to tell all the neighbours. Lend me that medal a minute, Gerard, I’ll go show my old friend Peter Buyskens. He’s forever badgering me with stories about how his son Jorian won a cheap tin mug at the archery butts.”
“Aye, go show him,” Gerard laughed. “Take one of the angels to show off too. Tell him there’s fourteen more just like it where that came from. But mind you bring it straight back!”
“Wait, father,” Gerard said, flushing bright with joy at the delight he had already brought them. “There is far better news still to come.”
“Better? Better than winning a Duke’s prize and all this gold?”
Gerard told them then of his audience with the Countess, who had secured a fine, well-paid benefice for him to take up once he was ordained. The whole house rang with cheers. “God bless that good lady, and bless the old dame Van Eyck too!” Catherine cried. “A benefice for our son! All my old cares are gone. Eli, my old love, we two can die happy whenever our time comes now. This dear boy will be the mainstay of the family, none of the people we love will ever go wanting for a home or a friend.”
From that hour on, Gerard was regarded as the undisputed pillar of the family. He was a son set apart, always in the right, and nothing was considered too good for him. Cornelis and Sybrandt’s jealousy curdled deeper, and they began counting the days until he left to take up his post at the benefice, certain their favourite brother’s priest’s purse would be wide open to fund all their whims. Gerard, for his part, had no objection to speeding his ordination. The sharp pain of Margaret’s supposed ingratitude he had carried back from Rotterdam throbbed fainter and fainter. His public success, and the open adoration of his parents, made him hold his head higher, and he resented more sharply still the slight he believed Margaret had dealt him. Even so, no other woman could hold a candle to her in his mind, and for every reason he was eager to take holy orders as quickly as he could, moving through the required ranks step by step. He already knew the Vulgate better than most of the local parish clergy, and studied the Church’s rubrics and dogma every evening with his friends the local monastery monks. The very next time the bishop made his visitation to Tergou, Gerard petitioned to be admitted to the order of exorcist, the third of the minor holy orders. The bishop quizzed him at length, astonished at his depth of learning, and ordained him on the spot. Gerard knelt, the bishop said a short blessing prayer, then handed him a small handwritten manuscript full of exorcism rites. “Take this, Gerard,” he said, “and receive power to lay hands on the possessed, whether they be baptized or catechumen.” Gerard took the little book reverently, walking home with the formal authority of the Church to cast out demons settled soft and weighty on his shoulders.
He had barely stepped over his own threshold when little Kate hobbled up to him on her crutches, breathless.
“Oh Gerard! Guess who has been to the house looking for you? The burgomaster himself.”
“Ghysbrecht Van Swieten? What could he possibly want with me?”
“I do not know, Gerard. But he is most urgent to see you. He says you are to come to his house at once.”
“He is the burgomaster, so I will go,” Gerard said, his face darkening. “But I do not like this. I have seen him cast a look at me no friend would ever wear. No matter. Such looks are a warning to the wise. Though I suspect—”
“Suspect what, Gerard?”
“Nothing,” he said, shaking his head. “Nothing at all. Come, little one. I will go.”

Ghysbrecht Van Swieten was a man whose every word was a carefully laid snare, never moving straight toward the mark he hunted, always circling first to throw his prey completely off guard. That afternoon, he sat across from the young novice Gerard, his face draped in feigned benevolence, and led far from the real errand that had drawn the boy to his chambers.
“The town’s ancient records,” he purred, tapping a stack of yellowed, crabbed manuscripts stacked on his scarred oak desk, “are scrawled in a script no modern clerk can parse, their ink turned rust-brown and brittle by a hundred years of damp and sun. I thought you, with your fine scholar’s hand, might do the town the great honour of transcribing all of them fair, neat enough that future generations might read our history without squinting.”
Gerard leaned forward, practical even in his eagerness for honest work. “What wage would you offer for the task, burgomaster?”
Ghysbrecht named a sum so small it would scarcely cover the cost of the new quills, iron-gall ink, and fine parchment the work would demand, not a penny left over for the hours of labour it would require.
Gerard’s brow furrowed. “That would barely pay for the supplies, sir. This is near a full year’s steady work, sitting late by candlelight every night.”
“Your labour?” Ghysbrecht scoffed, leaning back in his carved chair, feigning utter disbelief. “Call tracing marks on smooth parchment labour? I’d wager not a single drop of sweat would bead on your brow the whole time you’re at it.”
“It is labour, and skilled labour at that,” Gerard returned, steady, unflinching. “Every trade pays more for a craftsman’s trained skill than it does for common unskilled toil, sweat or no. And beyond that, it takes my whole time—time I might spend earning coin at some other work.”
“Your time?” Ghysbrecht laughed, sharp as a shard of broken glass, then fixed his sharp, fox-like eyes straight on Gerard’s face, watching for every flicker of expression. “What on earth is time to a bright lad of two and twenty? Truth be told, I think you’ve grown idle, no purpose to you at all these days. You’re in love. Your body might be here among the chanting brother monks of the cloister, but your heart’s off with Peter Brandt and his wild red-haired daughter, is it not?”
Gerard’s face went blank, cold. “I know no Peter Brandt.”
That quick, flat denial only confirmed Ghysbrecht’s long-held suspicion that the young exorcist was hiding a far deeper game than anyone guessed. “Ye lie!” he roared, slamming a fist down on the desk so that the ink horn rattled. “Did I not spot you lingering at her very elbow on the high road to Rotterdam only last week?”
Gerard’s head tilted, just a little. “Ah.”
“Ah, and you were seen at Sevenbergen no more than three days past!”
“Was I?” Gerard said, quiet.
“Aye, and inside Peter Brandt’s very own house!”
“At Sevenbergen?” Gerard asked, his voice rising just a fraction.
“Ay, at Sevenbergen.”
This, in later ages, would be called a bluff: a wild guess spoken loud and certain as proven fact, designed to drag a confession out of the suspect by the very strength of its boldness. But the result of the trick caught the crafty old burgomaster completely off guard.
Gerard shot to his feet, every nerve strung tight, his hands trembling where they rested on the edge of the desk. “Burgomaster,” he said, his voice shaking with a strange, bright excitement, “I have not set foot in Sevenbergen for three whole years. I do not know the names of the people you claim to have seen me with, nor where they dwell. But as you hold my time so cheap, I will waste no more of it here. Good day to you.”
He turned and darted out of the chamber, his eyes glowing like lit embers, before Ghysbrecht could even speak another word.
Ghysbrecht leaped to his feet, roaring with rage, then sank right back into his heavy chair, his chest heaving. “He does not fear me. He knows something—if not the whole of my plot.”
He called out sharply to his most trusted servant, all but yanking the man by the collar over to the casement window that looked out over the town square. “See that lad there, walking fast down the cobbles?” he hissed. “Run! Follow him. But do not let him catch so much as a glimpse of you. He is young, but he is sharp, crafty beyond his years. Dog his heels the whole day. Come back and tell me exactly where he goes, and every single thing he does.”
It was long past sundown, the sky pitch black and the streets all lit by guttering torches, when the servant stumbled back into the burgomaster’s house.
“Well?” Van Swieten cried, leaning forward, hungry for the news. “What did you find?”
“Master,” the servant panted, “the young man went straight from your doors all the way to Sevenbergen. Right to the house of Peter the Magician.”
Ghysbrecht groaned loud, his head falling back against the chair’s back.

“Peer into your own heart and write!” thundered Herr Cant, and every scribbling poet and prattling self-styled philosopher across the Low Countries took up the cry like cuckoo birds echoing one another’s call. They bade folk sink their buckets in the deepest eddies of the Rhine, the murkiest bends of the Thames, and dredge up the unvarnished truth at the very bottom. Lower a pail into a well of self-deception, they swore, and what you haul back can be nothing less than immortal truth, can it? But the plain fact of the matter is: no child of Adam can read his own heart at all until he has spent years poring over the hearts of other men, learning their secrets, their lies, their quiet buried joys and griefs. Even then, with all that borrowed light and hard-won wisdom, he can only spell out his own soul letter by letter, deciphering it slow, never reading it smooth and unhesitating.

Halfway down the sun-dappled road to Sevenbergen, Gerard did exactly what that popular maxim bade him: he peered deep into his own breast, and asked why he was tramping all that way to see Margaret Brandt. His heart replied at once, no stutter, no hesitation. “We go out of simple curiosity, to learn why she cast us off so suddenly, to show her our hearts never broke. We are perfectly content with our new honours, our promised benefice, and we want no part of her, nor any other of that fickle, inconstant sex.”

He found Peter Brandt’s cottage soon enough, its thatch glowing gold in the late afternoon light. There in the doorway sat Margaret, plying her needle through a length of fine linen, while a broad, stalwart figure leaned on a war-worn yew longbow, chatting away at her. A sharp, unaccountable pang twisted in Gerard’s chest at the sight of the stranger. Then he breathed easy: the man was well past fifty, an old veteran who had shot at the village butts a hundred times, and Gerard had seen him split a willow wand at a hundred paces more than once.

A minute later, the young scribe stood before them. Margaret looked up, dropped her needlework with a soft thud, and let out a faint, breathless cry. Her face flushed bright red then drained white in the space of a heartbeat. She stamped that flutter of emotion down fast, though, turning far chillier and more indifferent than she would have needed to be, had she not already betrayed how much his sudden appearance had shaken her.

“Is that you, Master Gerard? What in the world brings you tramping all this way out here, I wonder?”
“I was passing by the lane, saw you sitting in the door, so I thought I would stop and bid you good day, and ask after your father.”
“My father is well. He will be home before sundown.”
“Then I may as well wait here until he comes back.”
“Please yourself. Martin, step down to the village and tell my father an old friend of his is waiting for him.”
“And not a friend of yours?”
“My father’s friends are my friends.”
“That is a doubtful claim, Margaret. A friend does not promise to wait, then vanish the very moment a man turns his back. Cruel girl, you have no idea how I tore through every street in Rotterdam searching for you, how nothing on earth felt the least bit pleasant, once I found you gone.”
“Empty words, all of them. If you had truly wanted my company, or my father’s, you would have come back for us. I laid a bed out for you at my cousin’s house, sir. He would have fussed over you, fed you the best he had, and who knows? I might have fussed over you too, that day. I was in just the humour to forgive you any foolish slight. You will never catch me in that soft a temper again, not you, nor any other young man, I swear it.”
“Margaret, I came back the very second the Countess let me leave! But you were all gone, the whole house empty.”
“No, that is not true. If you had come back that day, you would have found Hans Cloterman sitting at our table—we left him behind to wait for you, to bring you after us.”
“I saw no one at that table but a drunken lout, who had just tumbled face down on the floorboards.”
“By our table? What sort of clothes was he wearing?”
“I did not stop to look close. Dull, sad-coloured garb, nothing remarkable.”

Slowly the flush crept back into Margaret’s cheeks, warm and soft. She fixed him with a mock-severe, incredulous stare, and fired off a dozen sharp, shrewd little questions, one after another. Gerard answered every last one of them honestly, no evasions, no falsehoods, and little by little the clouds of misunderstanding cleared completely away. At last they both saw how that stupid, harmless mix-up had torn them apart for weeks.

A great rush of tenderness flooded them both, sharper and sweeter for the wrongs they had each done the other, all unknowing. And then came something far more dangerous than soft looks: they confessed, freely, that neither of them had known a single happy day since they parted, that they would have gone on half-miserable forever, if they had not stumbled into this meeting.

Then Gerard’s eye fell on a hand-copied Vulgate, lying open on the rough wooden table. He pounced on it like a hawk after a sparrow—illuminated manuscripts were his dearest delight. But before he could glance at the text, two small white hands slammed flat down on the page, a bright red face leaning over them.
“Nay, Margaret, take your hands away. Let me see what passage you are reading now, and I will read that very same verse at home tonight. So our two souls may meet, side by side, on that sacred page. You will not move your hands? Then I shall have to kiss them off of there.”
He pressed his lips to her knuckles, over and over, until she grew so flustered and shamefaced she could not hold them down any longer, and pulled them away. There the sacred book lay open, the line glowing ink-black on vellum: *“An apple of gold in a network of silver.”*
“There!” she cried, half laughing, half exasperated. “I have been hunting that exact proverb for weeks, only found it a moment before you knocked on the door. And you caught me at it!” Even as she complained, she pointed to the line with the tip of her white finger.
“Aye,” said he, grinning. “Though it is all hidden under that great plain linen cap you are wearing now.”
“It is a handsome cap, so some folk tell me.”
“Maybe. But what it hides beneath it is far more beautiful than any cap could ever be.”
“That is not true. My hair is plain and ugly.”
“Well, it was not ugly that day in Rotterdam.”
“Aye,” she sighed soft, “everything was beautiful that day.”

Just then old Peter trundled through the gate, and welcomed Gerard like a long-lost son, insisting he stay for supper. Margaret slipped away quietly, and Gerard sat for an hour chatting with the old weaver about old books, Latin verse, and the new printing presses that were just starting to creep across the border from Mainz. Then Margaret came back, her pale fair hair twisted up and caught in that fine silver wire net the proverb spoke of, glinting in the candlelight, her glance half arch, half coy. She glided soft around the room, laying out rye bread, spiced butter, a bowl of steaming hare stew, mugs of home-brewed ale, and the whole room seemed to glow with her quiet gaiety and bright happiness.

Later, when the air turned cool, and the dusk smelled of clover and new-mown hay, Gerard coaxed her outside. She pretended to protest, but came all the same. He coaxed her further, down the lane leading toward Tergou. She said no, no, she could not go so far, but walked beside him anyway. Up and down that quiet stretch of road they wandered, hand in hand, with no one to see them. When it came time for Gerard to go home, they pledged to one another that they would never let stupid misunderstandings, or other people’s meddling, ever drive a wedge between them again. They sealed that promise with a long, sweet, lingering kiss, and Gerard tramped all the way back to Tergou walking on wings, his feet barely touching the dirt road.

From that day on, Gerard spent almost every evening he could steal out at Sevenbergen. Their love deepened, week by week, until the hours they spent together were the only hours they truly lived. All the rest of the time, apart, was just empty waiting, a chore they endured. At the start of that great, consuming affection, everything ran smooth. There were obstacles on the horizon, of course, but to the eyes of youth, hope, and foolish young love, they looked tiny, distant, easy to step around. None of the many people whose lives this attachment would thwart gave so much as a wisp of warning smoke to hint at the volcanic, fiery fury they would soon unleash. The course of their true love ran placid, smooth as a mill pond, drawing both their young hearts deep into its current, until there was no turning back.

And then—

One bright spring morning in Tergou, the cobblestones glinted under a parade of sights the townsfolk rarely saw: rich velvet liveries, plumes of exotic bobbing over riding helmets, and horse hooves striking sparks as the French ambassador rode through the streets bound for a hunt in the neighbouring royal forest. Every window and balcony was crammed with curious faces: old women set their spindles aside, children scrambled atop railings, and even the most dour blacksmith paused mid-blow at his anvil to gawk. Alongside the ambassador’s own retinue, the Duke of Burgundy had lent a cohort of his most peculiar household staff to honour the guest and amuse him.

First in the procession rode the Duke’s tumbler, sitting his horse with such absurdly grave, almost regal dignity that all the actual noble lords beside him seemed frivolous and flighty by comparison. But the second the crowd’s awe threatened to turn uncomfortable, he rolled clean off his mount in a silly, undignified somersault that even the stony-faced ambassador burst out laughing at. He then proceeded to scramble back up over the horse’s tail in a further fit of buffoonery, and the crowd roared.

Far more eyes turned to the figure riding further back: the Duke’s own hunting leopard.
