A giant huntsman, mounted on a Flemish dray-horse so large his boots nearly brushed the ground, had a long wooden box strapped to his saddle, and on it crouched the sleek, spotted beast, chained fast to the man’s wrist. Villagers pressed close to marvel at her glossy pelt, more than one bold soul reaching out to stroke her, even pluck at her tail, until the huntsman bellowed so loud the crowd jumped back: “Beware! In Antwerp last month a fool threw a handful of dust at her, and the Duke turned him to dust for it. Locked him in a sunken cell where the rats stripped his bones bare in a single night. Serves any man right who molests the poor creature.” A murmur of fear rippled through the onlookers, and no one dared tease their sovereign’s leopard after that.

Bringing up the very rear was the Duke’s Hungarian giant, seven feet four inches tall, with a soft, fluting treble voice so small it was absurd coming from such a mountain of flesh. Vain and completely unaware of his ridiculous speaking voice, he spotted little Giles perched right on the top rail of a front balcony, and called out in that high squeak: “Hallo, brother! I almost rode past without seeing thee!”
“You’re big enough for a blind mole to spot,” Giles boomed back in his deep, rumbling bass.
“Come up on my shoulder, little brother,” the giant piped up, holding out a fist the size of a leg of mutton to help him down.
“If I do I’ll box your ears so hard you’ll hear bells in Brussels for a month,” roared the dwarf.

The crowd shrieked with laughter, not at the giant’s terrible jokes, but at the sublime absurdity of the pair: the giant, all bulk, emitting a tiny squeak like a sparrow, and the tiny dwarf, all fire, spitting thunder like a storm cloud. The giant mistook the mirth for approval, and teased Giles further, until the little man snapped entirely. Fearless, and blazing with rage, he leaped clean off the balcony right onto the giant’s neck, one hand fisting his hair, the other pummeling his skull as fast and hard as he could. The giant started laughing at first, but the force of the blows quickly sobered him.
“Hey! Stop! Help! Holy saints, the imp will knock my brains out! I’ll dash his skull against that balcony–” he charged backwards full tilt at the stone balustrade. Giles saw the crack coming, grabbed the balcony top with both hands, and flung himself over the edge just as the giant’s head slammed into the stone with a resounding, echoing crack. The crowd cheered so loud the windowpanes rattled. Furious, the giant grabbed two random bystanders, knocked their heads together like wooden dumbbells, and flung them flat on the cobblestones. Catherine shrieked and yanked her apron over Giles to hide him, and the giant, nursing his throbbing head, stomped off to catch up with the rest of the hunting party.

The incident had unforeseen soft consequences: overnight the whole town was proud of their plucky little Giles, and everyone happily gave him the scraps of parchment he begged for to trade to his brother Gerard for copper pennies, running his tiny side trade smoothly for weeks.

Later that same afternoon, Catherine and her daughter Kate sat gossiping by the hearth, their favourite topic of conversation the bright future ahead for their family, now that Gerard was set to take the prestigious benefice the Countess Charolois herself had promised him. They thrilled at the thought of having a holy priest in their own home: he would officiate Cornelis and Sybrandt’s weddings, hear their confessions instead of a stranger priest, anoint them with sacred oil, and close their eyes when their time came. Kate shivered and begged her mother not to speak of dying any time soon; her chronic leg pain was gone that day, she felt light as air, and she had a secret to show her, something beautiful Gerard had been hiding to surprise them. She hobbled over on her crutches, fetched a cloth-wrapped wooden panel, and unwrapped it to reveal a stunning painting of the Virgin, a jeweled tiara sitting atop great cascades of burnished red-gold hair spilling loose over her shoulders, her eyes lifted soft and serene to heaven. Catherine crossed herself in awe, swearing it looked like the Queen of Heaven had stepped right onto the wood.

Before they had finished exclaiming over it, the cottage door creaked open. In stepped Ghysbrecht Van Swieten, the burgomaster, who had not set foot in their home for ten years, since the old land dispute that pitted his interests against Eli’s. The two women stared, stupefied. He claimed to have come to atone for that old unfriendly visit, for their sake, not his own, and that his news concerned their son Gerard. Catherine assumed he wanted Gerard to paint for the town for free, but he shook his head and dropped his bombshell: Gerard was falling into bad hands, spending every waking hour with Margaret Brandt, Peter the magician’s red-haired daughter, so deep in love he would never take holy orders if they did not part the two soon.

Catherine and Kate burst out laughing at first, certain he was lying, that their pious Gerard would never look at a woman that way. But doubt crept over Catherine’s face; she remembered how foolish and headstrong she had been in her own youth. Indignant, Kate held the painted Virgin high, declaring that if Gerard’s heart was tangled up in earthly love, he could never have rendered the Holy Mother with such pure, unworldly grace.

Ghysbrecht gaped at the panel, his eyes going wide. “That is no Virgin!” he gasped. “That is Margaret Brandt! Every painter paints his sweetheart’s face that beautifully, man has done since paint was invented.” The women reeled in horror, arguing that the figure wore a crown, she could not be a mortal girl. The burgomaster snorted: “Crown? Look at that bright red hair! The Holy Virgin would never be painted with red hair, that is Margaret, sure as the sun rises.”

Just then their neighbour Peter Buyskens poked his head in the door, saying the whole street could hear them shouting, and asked what the ruckus was about. Ghysbrecht dragged him over to the panel and demanded he name the woman in the painting. Peter squinted, grinned, and said it was Margaret Brandt, as natural as life, though he had never seen her wearing a crown before. Catherine and Kate immediately flung their aprons over their faces, rocking back and forth in silent, heartbroken sobs.

Eli walked in from his shop moments later, and went white as a sheet, convinced someone was dead. When the story was laid out before him, he huffed in relief at first, saying boys will be boys, he would grow out of the silly infatuation. But when Ghysbrecht pointed out the two youngsters were clearly already talking marriage, his face hardened. “Marriage? That shall never be,” he swore. “I will stop it, even by force if need be, as I would stop his hand raised to cut his own throat. I will do what old John Koestein did not long ago.” The burgomaster filled in the rest: Koestein had made him lock his son Albert in the Stadthouse prison for forty-eight hours, on bread and water, until the boy forgot all about his girl and begged to see the sun again. Catherine sighed at the cruelty, but Eli insisted a father had every right by law to keep his son from throwing his whole life away.

Supper passed in gloomy silence. Evening fell, eight o'clock struck, and Gerard still had not come home. Eli sent everyone else to bed, took Catherine’s hand, and said they would walk out to the road to Sevenbergen to meet him, talk this through that very night, no putting it off till tomorrow. The night was clear and balmy, the moon bright over the fields, and the old couple walked hand in hand – the custom of linking elbows while walking would not reach Europe for centuries yet – reminiscing about their own courting days, and how happy they had been together through every hardship, the old proverb proving true: shared joy is doubled, shared trouble is halved.

And then around the curve of the road, they saw him. Gerard was walking home, singing soft under his breath in the moonlight, his face glowing bright, like he trod on air.

While the burgomaster of Tergou railed against Gerard to the town council, far off in the quiet village of Sevenbergen, Margaret nursed a quiet, heavy distress of her own. It was a housewife’s grief, stoked by love, deeper than modern sensibilities can easily grasp.
She found old Martin Wittenhaagen, the weathered ex-soldier of the Duke’s wars, with bright tears glistening in her eyes. “Martin, there’s not a crumb left in the larder, and Gerard will step through that door any hour now. The lad is so thoughtless when he’s deep in his copying work he forgets to break his fast half the day. The second he lays down his pen he runs straight here, no stopping for a bite, and half the time he stumbles over the threshold faint as a lamb. I’ve nothing warm to set before the dear soul that loves me so.”
Martin scratched his grizzled head, calloused from decades of pulling bowstrings. “What’s an old fellow like me to do about that, mistress?”
“Today’s Thursday,” she said, brightening a little. “It’s your licensed day to shoot, after all. Truth be told, I was counting on you to bring home game today.”
“Nay now,” Martin shook his head, digging a crumpled parchment out of his leather pouch, its great wax seal cracked and stained with years of use. “I can’t loose an arrow in the Duke’s woods if his grace or his lords are out on the chase—see for yourself, though I can’t read a line of it.”
That parchment was the lifetime reward Philip, Duke of Burgundy, had granted the old archer for taking a crossbow bolt meant for the Duke right in the thigh on a French battlefield. It promised him four merks a year in stipend, and the rare right to shoot three arrows, one single day a week—Thursday, and no other—anywhere in the Duke’s Holland forests, so long as he did not harm a seven-year-old buck or a doe heavy with fawn. The fine for breaking that rule? Forfeit his salary, his good name, and very likely his head, plus a penny administrative fee. It explicitly banned hunting on any day the Duke or his noble party was out chasing game.
Margaret’s shoulders slumped, and she fell quiet, sighing soft.
“Cheer up now, lass,” Martin said, patting her arm gently. “For your sake I’ll risk the Duke’s displeasure. I’ve thrown my life on the line for folks not worth the tip of your finger before, and this is no great danger at all. I’ll just slip to the very edge of the forest, not ten minutes’ walk from here. Likely enough the beaters will drive a hare or a young fawn right within arrow range before anyone notices me.”
“Very well,” Margaret said, but her voice was tight with worry. “But you must promise me you won’t go far, and you won’t let a soul spot you. Far better Gerard eats a dry crust tonight than any harm comes to you, faithful old Martin.”
He gave his word, slung his six-foot English yew bow over his shoulder, took his three permitted arrows, and slipped silent as a shadow into the treeline, barely a furlong from the village cottages. The faint, winding blare of hunting horns drifted on the wind from deep in the woods, and every beast of the field was already up and running for cover. “Easy now,” Martin thought, grinning to himself. “I’ll have the pot boiling before anyone’s the wiser.”
He tucked himself behind the thick gnarled trunk of an ancient oak, which gave him a clear line of sight across an open sun-dappled glade, and strung his bow. It was a legendary weapon, six feet two inches of solid yew, carved thick enough to stop a light blow from a broadsword. Martin, broad-chested, his arms hard as forged iron wrapped in sinew, had been drawing bows since he was a small boy, and he could pull a three-foot war arrow all the way back to his ear. When that arrow flew it moved so fast the human eye could barely track it, and the twang of the bowstring sang out as clear as a plucked harp string. That very bow had sent dozens of armed men tumbling from their saddles in the brutal civil wars between the Hoecks and the Cabbeljaws, back when battlefields were thick with men rather than gunsmoke: every archer saw exactly where his arrow landed, and far fewer shots went to waste than the lead bullets of later days.
A hare came cantering out into the glade, then stopped stock still, her long ears pricked up to make a perfect sharp V. Martin levelled his great bow, loosed his arrow in a hurry. It missed her by a bare inch, hissed right across the short grass under her belly, and vanished into the underbrush. The hare jumped three feet straight in the air before bolting off at top speed. “Clumsy oaf,” Martin muttered to himself—sure proof he was no habitual bad shot, else he’d have blamed the hare for moving.
He had barely nocked his second arrow when a fat wood pigeon fluttered down to perch right on the lowest bough of the oak he was hiding behind. “Aha,” he thought, smiling. “Small, but sweet eating, roasted over a fire.” This time he took his time, drew the arrow slow and steady, loosed it smooth. It looked to fly straight through the bird, sending feathers floating up like dust into the air. But the pigeon was only torn in the breast, not killed outright. It fluttered feebly up over the treetops, flew fifty yards, and dropped out of sight behind the thick foliage, where he could not reach it.
“Luck’s turned against me today,” he grumbled, nocking his third and last permitted arrow. He peered sharp across the glade, and a few minutes later he heard a crash of brush behind him. He spun around just in time to see a magnificent full-grown buck leap across the open clearing, gone before he could even draw his bow. He threw his bow down on the turf with a vicious curse.
Just then a long, spotted tawny shape slithered past him after the deer, its belly almost brushing the ground as it ran. Martin snatched his bow back up instantly. That was the Duke’s own trained hunting leopard. The hunters could not be more than a few hundred yards behind her. “Best get out of here,” he thought. “Gerard will go supperless tonight.”
He plunged deeper into the trees, heading for home, following the path the buck and leopard had taken. He had not gone far when he heard a terrible commotion up ahead: leaves rustling wildly, the ground trampled under heavy hooves. He ran toward the noise, and found the leopard perched on the buck’s back, tearing at his neck with claws and fangs. The buck was bounding in wild, convulsive circles, blood pouring down his flanks.
Martin made a desperate, foolhardy decision. He would take that buck home to Margaret. He drew his third arrow all the way back to his head, and buried it deep in the deer’s heart. The buck, still carrying the leopard on his back, leapt high into the air, then dropped stone dead. The leopard did not even pause, just kept tearing at the buck’s throat as if nothing had happened.
Martin waited, hoping the big cat would gorge itself so full of blood it would let him drag the carcass away unmolested. After a few minutes he stepped forward bold as brass, and laid his hand on the buck’s front leg. The leopard let out a roar that shook the leaves off the branches, and fixed him with a savage glare. Old tales said no wild beast could bear to meet a man’s unblinking gaze. So Martin stood tall, stared the beast straight in the eyes. The leopard stared right back, never breaking eye contact for a second. Brutally ignorant of that old bit of folk wisdom, the creature let out a shriek and launched itself straight at his face, jaws stretched wide.
He barely had time to clamp one calloused hand around its throat before its fangs could crush his skull. One of its front claws tore straight through his jerkin, raking deep gashes into his shoulder. The other claw, aimed straight for his cheek, got caught fast in the thick leather scapulary he wore over his head instead of a hat, the same tough material as his tunic. Martin squeezed its throat harder, his iron arms never slackening, as the cat’s claws ripped deeper and deeper into his shoulder, the pain like blunt reaping hooks grinding into his flesh. The agony did not cow the old soldier—it lit his blood on fire. His teeth were bared in a snarl just as ferocious as the leopard’s, and the two pairs of eyes blazed at each other in the dim wood.
The leopard realized it was being throttled, and thrashed wildly to break free. It dragged Martin’s leather cowl right over his eyes, blinding him, and tore its claw out of his shoulder leaving a ragged trail of flesh behind. But Martin never loosened his iron grip, squeezing harder and harder. First the leopard’s long tail, held high in the air, went limp. “That’s it!” Martin gasped, grinning through the pain, and squeezed like death. Soon the big cat’s body lost all its tension, then stopped moving entirely. He dashed it against the ground, then tore the cowl off his face, panting for breath. The Duke’s prized hunting leopard lay dead at his feet, tongue lolling out, one paw caked in his blood. For the first time, a cold wave of terror washed over Martin. I’m a dead man, he thought. I’ve killed the Duke’s own leopard.
He grabbed a handful of leaves and tossed them over the cat’s body to hide it, then slung the heavy buck’s carcass over his shoulders and staggered home, leaving a winding trail of blood behind him—half the deer’s, half his own. He burst through the door of Peter’s cottage a sight to stop a man’s breath, covered in gore from head to toe, and dropped the buck on the floor with a heavy thud. “There,” he panted. “No questions now, just broil me a thick steak of that venison, for I’m about to faint dead away.”
Margaret did not notice his wounds at first, assuming all the blood belonged to the deer. She hurried to stoke the hearth fire, and Martin slipped off to the corner to tear strips from his undershirt to stanch and bind the ragged cuts on his shoulder. By the time Gerard walked through the door, the three of them were sitting down to a feast of juicy broiled venison. Gerard, to everyone’s surprise, had brought a full flask of strong Schiedam gin, and the drink soon warmed old Martin up enough to tell them the whole wild story of how he’d gotten the meat. They laughed loud over his mad exploit, all three of them light and happy around the fire.
Their merriment died sudden and cold. Margaret’s eyes went wide and fixed, her face blanched pure white with terror. She gasped for breath, too stunned to speak, and pointed a trembling finger toward the window. The two men followed her gaze, and there in the twilight, crouched just outside the glass, was a dark spotted shape, its two eyes glowing bright green like smouldering embers.
It was the leopard.
They all stood frozen in place, transfixed by those eyes of fire, when a single deep, baying cry echoed out from the woods. Martin shook like a leaf. “They missed her trail, and have set their muzzled bloodhounds on her scent. They’ll track her right here, find her and the buck. Goodbye, my friends. Martin Wittenhaagen’s life ends tonight.”
Gerard snatched Martin’s bow from the wall and pushed it into his hands. “Be a man!” he shouted. “Shoot the beast dead, drag her back into the woods before the hunters get here. No one will ever know.”
More hound voices joined the first, louder and closer by the second. “Curse that brute!” Martin roared, nocking an arrow. “I spared her once, now either she dies or I do, and likely both of us otherwise.” He drew the arrow all the way back, ready to loose.
“Nay! Stop!” Margaret screamed, lunging forward to grab the arrow. It snapped clean in two, the two halves clattering to the floor on either side of the bow. The baying of the hounds filled the whole house now, they were so close, hot on the scent.
“What have you done, girl?” Martin groaned. “You’ve put the hangman’s noose straight around my neck.”
“No!” Margaret cried, snatching his long hunting knife from his belt, yanking it almost out of its sheath. “I’ve saved you. Both of you, stand back from the window right now!” She darted out of the room, even as the hunters’ shouts and the baying of the hounds surrounded the little cottage, and the glowing green eyes of the wounded leopard never moved from the dark glass.

Margaret hacked off a great heaving slab of venison, flew to the casement, and tossed it out to the pair of fire-green eyes glinting in the dark. The leopard sprang upon the meat with a ravening snarl, and the quiet of the night was rent by the sound of tearing fur and crunching bone. At that very instant, a hound bayed so near, so loud, the reverberations shook the timbers of the little cottage. The three huddled at the window shrank back as one.
The leopard, fearing its supper would be stolen, grabbed the half-eaten venison in its jaws and slipped away swift and silent for the dark line of the woods. Barely a heartbeat later, the whole hunt thundered past the window: horses’ hooves drumming the rutted mud, halloos ringing out, the whole pack of hounds baying full cry on the leopard’s trail. Martin and his companions let out a long, shared breath. The beast was fleet of foot; no hound alive would run it to ground within a league of their house. They clasped hands tight in relief. Margaret, the rush of adrenaline draining away all at once, burst into quiet tears, and Gerard kissed the salt from her cheeks.
They returned to the table, and Gerard raised his cup to toast Margaret. “A woman’s wit is stronger than any man’s brute force,” he said.
“Ay,” she replied, smiling through damp eyelashes, “only when those she loves are in danger. Never otherwise.”
That night Gerard stayed far later than he usually dared, and walked home prouder of Margaret than he had ever been, light of heart as any crowned prince. A short stretch from his own lane, under the shadow of the gnarled oak trees that lined the road, two figures stepped out and all but barred his path. It was his father and mother. Out so late? A cold dread settled in his bones. He stopped, and stared at them. They stood grim, silent, no light of welcome on their faces.
He stammered out a question of what brought them there.
“Why ask?” his father said gruffly. “You know full well why we are here.”
“Oh, Gerard,” his mother wept, her voice thick with reproach and brimming over with old affection.
Gerard’s heart quailed. He could not speak. Then his father, seeing his utter confusion, softened a little. “Nay, you need not hang your head. You are not the first young fool to be led astray by a red cheek and a pair of bright blue eyes.”
“Nay, nay!” Catherine cut in quickly. “It was witchcraft. Everyone knows Peter the Magician of Sevenbergen casts such spells.”
“Come, you would-be priest,” his father went on, “you know you have no business meddling with women. Swear to us now you will never go to Sevenbergen again, and all is forgiven. We will not be hard on you for this one foolish mistake.”
“I cannot promise that, father.”
“Not promise, you young hypocrite!”
“Nay, father, do not call me such names,” Gerard said. “I lacked the courage to tell you something I knew would grieve you, and I am grateful to the friend who has let you hear the truth at last – it is a weight off my mind. I love Margaret. Call me no priest, for a priest I will never be. I would die first.”
“That we shall see,” his father snapped. “Do not defy me again. You will learn what it means to disrespect your own father.”
Gerard held his peace. The three of them walked home in heavy, gloomy silence, broken only by Catherine’s soft, catching sighs.
From that hour, the little house in Tergou was no longer a home of peace. The very next day, Gerard was called to account before the whole family, and every voice was raised against him – save little Kate’s, and the dwarf’s, who copied her lead without even understanding why he did. Cornelis and Sybrandt, his two older brothers, were far more bitter than their own father had ever been. Gerard, dismayed to find so many turned against him, looked wistfully at his little sister’s face. Her eyes were brimming with tears at the harsh words they hurled at the boy who had once been the family’s universal pet. But she gave him no comfort. She turned her head away, and said, “Dear, dear Gerard, pray Heaven to cure you of this folly.”
“Even you are against me?” Gerard said, his voice heavy with sadness. He rose with a deep sigh, left the house, and walked all the way to Sevenbergen.
When quarrels break out between people bound by love even as they are divided by opposing desires, the first sparks are almost innocent. Both sides might even start out half right. At such a time, a calm, wise friend who can see both perspectives is a gift from Heaven. But the longer the rift drags on, the wider and deeper it grows, stoked by human fallibility and hot tempers on both sides. There is no side that does no wrong, until at last both are in the wrong equally.
The fight was unfairly matched: Elias was furious, Cornelis and Sybrandt were spiteful and petty, but Gerard, with his wider, more cultivated mind, saw both sides where they saw only one, and was wracked with fits of irresolution. He was not angry, only unhappy. And he was utterly alone in his struggle. He could not unburden his heart to anyone. Margaret was high-spirited, and he dared not tell her the abuse he endured at home, for she would no doubt choose to renounce him to spare him pain, even if it broke her own heart. Margaret Van Eyck had been a great comfort to him once before, but he dared not confide in her now. Everyone knew her story: in her youth she had refused every marriage offer to dedicate herself to art, a calling that left no time for the duties of a wife and mother. How could he tell her he was turning down the fine benefice she had worked to secure for him, and rejecting the very life of art she had sacrificed all love for, for the sake of the love she had thrown away so lightly?
Gerard was on the verge of breaking. But his mother, kind-hearted but uneducated, rash and inconsistent, was an unexpected, terrible ally on his side. She could not act with quiet, steady purpose like her daughter, nor hold to a single plan, and she irritated Gerard so often that anger gave him the very courage he was losing. At other times, she turned on her own family mid-argument without warning. One day, when the whole household was gathered, Cornelis sneered, “Our Gerard wed Margaret Brandt? Why, that’s hunger marrying thirst.”
“And what will it be when you marry?” Catherine roared back at him. “Gerard can paint, Gerard can write – what can you do to keep a wife, you lazy loon? Nothing but wait for your father to die so you can wear his boots. We all see why you and Sybrandt do not want the poor boy to marry. You are afraid he will ask for his share of the family property. And even if he did, it is not yours to give away – it may never be yours at all!”
On days like that, Gerard would smile to himself, pick up his courage, and leave his father and brothers floundering in sudden confusion.
But after six months of this constant, grinding irritation, the climax came. Elias stood before the whole family and told his son he had already ordered the burgomaster to lock Gerard in the Stadthouse prison before he would ever let him marry Margaret Brandt. Gerard paled with hot anger, but with a great effort held his peace.
“And you will be a priest before the year is out, willing or not,” his father finished.
“Is that so?” Gerard cried. “Then hear me, all of you. By God and Saint Bavon, I swear I will never be a priest while Margaret lives. If force is to decide this, not love and duty, then try force, father. But force will not serve you. The very day the burgomaster comes to drag me away, I will leave Tergou forever, leave Holland too, and this house where I have lived for years valued not for myself, but for what profit others could wring out of me.”
He flung out of the room, white with anger and desperation.
“There!” Catherine cried. “That is what comes of driving young folk too hard. Men are crueller than tigers, even to their own flesh and blood. Heaven forbid he should ever leave us, married or unmarried.”
As Gerard stepped out of the house, his cheeks pale and his heart pounding, he met Reicht Heynes. She had a message for him: Margaret Van Eyck wished to see him. He found the old painter lady seated as grim as a judge. She wasted no time on pleasantries, and asked coldly why he had not visited her for so long. Before he could answer, she spoke in a sharp, sarcastic tone: “I thought we were friends, young sir.”
Gerard looked utterly lost and confused.
“He never dared tell her he was in love,” Reicht said, taking pity on his stricken face.
“Silence, wench!” the old lady snapped. “Why should he tell us his affairs? We are not his friends, we have not earned his confidence.”
“Alas, my second mother,” Gerard said, “I did not dare tell you of my folly.”
“What folly? Is it folly to love?”
“I am told so every day of my life.”
“You had no cause to fear telling me,” Margaret Van Eyck said, softening. “I have always been kind to true lovers.”
“Madam – Reicht – I was told that in your youth you scorned love, and chose art instead.”
“I did, boy. And look what came of it. Here I am, a barren stock, while all the girls I grew up with have children at their sides and grandchildren at their knees. I gave up the sweet joys of wifehood and motherhood for what? For my dear brothers, who left this world long ago. For my art – which has almost left me too. I still have all the knowledge, but what use is it when my hands shake so I cannot hold a brush steady? No, Gerard. I look on you as my own son. You are good, you are handsome, you are a painter – though not half as good as the masters I learned from. I will not let you throw your youth away as I did mine. You shall marry this Margaret. I have made inquiries, and she is a good, honest daughter. Reicht here is a gossip, she has told me every last detail. But that is no reason you should not tell me your side of the story.”
Overjoyed, Gerard poured out his heart, and praised Margaret aloud to someone who could understand exactly what he loved in her. Soon there were two pairs of wet eyes listening to his story, and when Gerard saw that, his own eyes overflowed too.
Women are brimful of a peculiar courage of their own: it is vicarious, the kind of courage that makes them sit unflinching through a bullfight while the men beside them tremble for the fighters, that makes them send their men off to battle with far more resolution than any man could muster on his own. And Gerard profited from that trait that day. Margaret and Reicht were both of one mind: the only sensible thing to do was to marry Margaret Brandt at once, offhand. Once the deed was done, the old people would come around in time, and all the bickering that dragged on would only grow worse the longer they waited.
“See how pale and thin they have made him,” Reicht said. “It makes my heart ache to see a young man so worn down. When I met him on the street today, I almost burst out crying, he has changed so.”
“And I will wager Cornelis and Sybrandt still keep their coarse, ruddy colour, no doubt,” the old painter said. “We painters are no match for boors. We are glass, they are stone. We cannot stand the endless, petty nagging of small minds – and it is no good to anyone that we should be exposed to it. It is hard enough to design and paint a masterpiece, without being stung to death by gnats and flies all day long.”
Gerard was still reeling from his father’s threat to throw him in prison, and he listened eagerly to these friendly voices telling him that rebellion was the wisest course. But he was not yet fully convinced. “I do not fear my father’s prison,” he said. “But I fear his curse. He will not jail me, he will disown me. I would take Margaret away from her father, and give her a poor husband who will never thrive, weighed down by his own parent’s hatred. Madam, I have thought sometimes that if I could marry her in secret, then take her away to some country where my craft is better paid than it is here. After a year or two, when the storm has blown over, I could come back with a purse full of money, and say ‘My dear parents, we do not ask for your property, we only ask that you love us once more as you used, for we have never ceased to love you.’ But I suppose these are only the foolish dreams of an inexperienced young man.”
The old lady’s eyes sparkled. “It is no dream, it is the most sensible thing any boy has ever said to me. The only question is whether you have the courage to carry it out. There is a land waiting for you, Gerard, where certain fortune is yours if you are bold enough. Here the arts freeze, but there they flourish as no art has ever flourished in any age.”
“It is Italy!” Gerard cried. “It must be Italy!”
“Ay, Italy! There painters are honoured like princes, and scribes are paid three hundred crowns for copying a single manuscript. Do you not know the Holy Father the Pope has sent letters to every land, seeking skilled scribes to copy the hundreds of precious manuscripts pouring into Rome from Constantinople, where barbarian Turks are driving out all learning and all learned men?”
“I never knew that,” Gerard said, “but visiting Italy, the queen of all the arts, has been the dream of my whole life. But the journey… we are all so poor.”
“If you have the heart to go, I will find the means. I have ten golden angels set aside, enough to take you both to Rome, if the girl loves you as she ought.”
They sat talking long past midnight. After that day, Gerard’s spirits came back, and he carried a secret talisman against all the jeers and harsh words his brothers hurled at him at home. Beyond the money for the journey, Margaret Van Eyck gave him something far more precious. “I will tell you secrets the old masters taught me, secrets no living soul knows now. Even the Italians have never heard them, and what I tell you here in Tergou you will be able to sell for a fortune in Florence. Look at my brother Jan’s paintings. Time, which fades every other painter’s colours, leaves his as bright as the day they left the easel. He never trusted a hireling to grind his colours, he did it himself, or stood over the work to make sure it was done right. He prepared his panels, again and again, a whole year before he ever laid a single brushstroke. No lazy painter bothers to do that. Above all, Gerard, never use much oil, and never boil it. Boiling oil melts the vegetable dross deep into its heart, when your whole aim should be to wash that dross away. Pour your oil into a bottle of clear water. In two days the water will turn muddy – that is all the muck leaching out of the oil. Pour the dirty water away, add fresh water. You will think the oil is clear then, but you are wrong.” She nodded to Reicht, who fetched a glass trough with a tight-fitting glass lid. “Pour your washed oil into this trough with fresh water, set it in the sun all day. The water will turn turbid again. Do not go too far, or the sun will turn your oil to varnish. When it is as clear as crystal, drain it carefully, cork it up tight. Grind your finest colours by hand, lay them on with this pure oil, and they will last forever. Jan Van Eyck was never in a hurry. That is why the world will never forget him in a hurry.”
With these secrets of the Van Eyck at his fingertips, and the ten golden angels tucked safe away, Gerard decided he would marry Margaret, and flee with her to Italy. All that was left was to tell Margaret Brandt his plan, and arrange to publish the banns as quietly as possible. He went to Sevenbergen earlier than usual, and told her all that Margaret Van Eyck had done for him, and his new plan to run away.
Margaret refused outright. “No, Gerard. You and I have never spoken of your family, but when it comes to marriage… I do not believe your father bears me any special ill will. He told Peter Buyskens as much, and Peter told me. But so long as he is determined you should be a priest – you ought to have told me this, not I you – I cannot marry you, dearly as I love you.”
Gerard argued with her in vain. It was easy to make her cry, but impossible to make her yield. At last, hot with impatience, he cried, “Very well! You are on their side. You will drive me to be a priest, for this must end one way or another. My parents hate me in earnest, but my lover only loves me in jest.” He stormed off, leaving Margaret weeping.
But when a man a girl truly loves misbehaves out of misery, she does not grow angry – she pities him. Less than an hour and a half after Gerard left, he came running back to her, the broken fragments of his half-finished portrait of her in his hands, panting with rage and grief.
“There, Margaret! Look! The wretches! They have cut your portrait to pieces.”
Margaret stared. Some spiteful hand had hacked the portrait into five jagged pieces, cutting straight through the face he had spent six months painting. She flushed bright red to the very top of her forehead. “Who did this?”
“I do not know,” Gerard said. “I dared not ask, for I would have hated the hand that did it till my dying day. Six months of my work, gone for nothing. They have cut right through your sweet face, that everyone who sees it loves. Oh, heartless, cruel vipers!”
“Never mind, Gerard,” Margaret said, her breath coming fast. “Since this is how they treat you for my sake – they rob you of my portrait, do they? Well, then, you shall have the face itself, such as it is. Forgive me for refusing you. I will be

The banns of matrimony, much as they are read in our own day, required three proclamations—with one stark 15th century difference: they were almost always read on week days, and the eager young lovers Gerard and Margaret had no trouble persuading their new, untested parish curate to perform all three readings in the space of twenty-four short hours. Their soft, pleading faces spoke louder than any formal entreaty, and the curate could not find it in his heart to refuse.

The first two banns were cried at Monday matins and vespers, and to their giddy delight, not a single soul from the distant village of Tergou had turned up to the Sevenbergen church to spoil their plan. They arrived at dawn the next day, hearts hammering so hard they could barely breathe—only to freeze in horror as a complete stranger rose from the pews, and forbade the banns outright on the grounds that both parties were underage, and their parents had given no consent.

Trembling and half broken with despair, Margaret and Gerard huddled just outside the church door to confer, before the man who had ruined their quiet joy strolled over to them, all false sympathy. He claimed he hated to meddle in young love, but that forbidding banns was his only steady living: all they had to do was hand over one crown, and he would go straight back to the curate, admit he had been entirely misinformed, and clear the way for their marriage.

“A crown? I will give you a golden angel to do this,” Gerard cried, fumbling for his purse. The man agreed as quickly, and followed Gerard back to the curate to spin his story of a ridiculous, easily corrected mistake. The curate, none the wiser, promised to marry them the following morning at ten, and the professional bliss-obstructor trundled off with his golden angel in his pocket.

Like most petty, clever knaves, he was a fool. He headed straight for a Tergou tavern whose back green was given over to archery contests and village sports, and proceeded to drink the full value of his angel in ale. Drunk and bragging of his easy earnings, he spilled every detail of his scheme—right within earshot of Sybrandt, Gerard’s idle, ne’er-do-well brother, who haunted the tavern green every day. Sybrandt ran straight home to tell his father, only to find the old man had travelled to Rotterdam to buy cloth from merchant traders. He waved his older brother Cornelis out of the house, and spilled the whole story.

The two were Gerard’s black sheep siblings. Idleness rots the soul, and the greedy, years-long wait for their father’s inheritance had turned their hearts vicious; they would tear apart anyone who dared to interfere with the fortune they lusted after day and night, their parents’ hardworking, loving parsimony twisted in their selfish minds into ravenous avarice, the root of a hundred future crimes. They agreed not to tell their soft, uncertain mother, and instead headed straight for the burgomaster, Ghysbrecht Van Swieten. They were clever enough to guess he hated the match, even if they could not fathom why.

Ghysbrecht saw through the two lazy schemers in an instant, but kept his cards close to his chest. Drawing on his full magisterial dignity, he told them: “Since your father is not here, his duty falls to me, as father of this town. I know his mind perfectly. Leave all this to me, and above all, do not breathe a word of this to any woman in your household—chattering tongues unravel even the wisest plans.” He dismissed them a little superciliously, half ashamed to count two such oafs as his confederates.

When they trundled home, they found Gerard sitting on a low stool at his mother’s knee, her hand carding gently through his hair, speaking soft words to him and promising to take his part against his father, to thwart his love no more. Her change of heart was entirely characteristic: it was she who had torn Margaret’s portrait to bits in a fit of sharp female temper, only to watch Gerard turn deathly pale, sit motionless holding the scraps till tears blurred his eyes. She had been terrified of what she had done, her heart stung with bitter guilt, and though she would never admit what she had done out loud, she swore silently she would make it up to him. Her anger melted, and she had turned fully to Gerard’s side just as the two black sheep walked in.

Gerard, naive to the twists of feminine temper, was so overjoyed by her kindness he forgot he had ever suspected her of destroying the portrait, kissed her again and again, and went to bed as happy as a prince, convinced his mother was on his side at the very peak of his fate.

The next morning at ten, Gerard and Margaret stood in the Sevenbergen church, him radiant, her cheeks flushed bright red with blushes. Only Peter Brandt, Martin Wittenhaagen, and no other friends were with them—secrecy was their only protection. Margaret had refused the plan to flee to Italy; she could not leave her gentle, learned, helpless father alone. The pair had agreed they would retire to a quiet corner of Flanders for a few weeks till the storm of Tergou’s anger blew over.

The curate did not keep them waiting long. He stepped to the altar, called them forward hand in hand, the two happiest people in all of Holland, and opened his prayer book.

But before he could utter a single word of the sacred marriage rite, a harsh, rough voice roared “FORBEAR!” The constables of Tergou marched up the aisle and seized Gerard in the name of the law. Martin’s long hunting knife flashed out instantly.

“Hold, man!” the priest shouted. “You will not draw steel in the house of God! And you who interrupt this holy sacrament—what impiety is this?”

“There is no impiety, father,” the lead constable said respectfully. “This young man seeks to marry against his father’s explicit will, and his father has begged our burgomaster to deal with him according to the law. Let him deny it if he can.”

Gerard hung his head, he could not deny the truth.

“We take him to Rotterdam to abide the sentence of the Duke.”

Margaret cried out in utter despair. The two lovers, who had been on the brink of joy a moment before, sobbed clinging to each other so piteously that even the hardened constables stepped back, ashamed. One of the kinder ones leaned in, pretending to separate them, and whispered in her ear: “Rotterdam? It is a lie. We are taking him straight to our Tergou Stadthouse prison.”

They set Gerard on horseback, rode off as if heading for Rotterdam, but after a dozen sly detours and hidden halts, they circled back to Tergou. Just outside the town, a rickety canvas-covered cart was waiting for him. They thrust him inside, and by five that evening, he was smuggled secretly up the flights of the Stadthouse tower, and thrown into a tiny cell lit only by a narrow, slitted window crisscrossed with a single vertical iron bar. The only furniture in the whole room was a massive, heavy oak chest.

Prison in that brutal century was one of the surest roads to an early grave. Even at its mildest it was a horror: here, it meant unbroken solitude, cold, starvation, very often poison. Gerard knew he was in the hands of an enemy. “That look the burgomaster gave me on the road,” he thought. “This is more than my father’s wrath. I doubt I will ever see the light of day again.” He knelt, and commended his soul to God.

He stood up a moment later, lunged for the iron bar in the window, wrenched it loose from its rusty nails, and propped his knees against the wall to peer out. For only a minute he saw the sight no captive ever takes for granted: Martin Wittenhaagen’s broad back, sitting quiet by the brook at the foot of the tower, pretending to fish.

Gerard whistled sharp and soft. Martin turned in an instant, far more alert than any man who was really fishing, spotted Gerard’s face at the slit window, made a quick reassuring signal, grabbed his line and his bow, and vanished. Gerard’s heart lifted—his friends had not abandoned him. As he fell back from the window, the cell door creaked stealthily open, and Ghysbrecht Van Swieten stepped inside. His eyes flicked straight to the wrenched iron bar, then to the open window. He did not say a word. A hundred feet below the ground, if Gerard wanted to jump, why stop him? He set a brown loaf of bread and a pitcher of water down on the oak chest in dead silence.

Gerard’s first impulse was to bash the burgomaster’s skull in with the iron bar and run for the stairs, but Ghysbrecht gave a tiny, deliberate cough. Three armed, burly guards stepped into the doorway immediately.

“My orders,” the burgomaster said coldly, “are to keep you locked in here until you swear an oath to abandon Margaret Brandt, and return to the Church you were baptized into from your cradle.”

“Death sooner,” Gerard spat back.

“With all my heart,” the burgomaster said, and left him alone.

Martin ran straight to Sevenbergen, where he found Margaret pale, agitated, but sharp and full of fire, just finishing a letter to the Countess Charolois, begging her to intervene against Ghysbrecht’s cruelty and treachery.

“Courage!” Martin called as he burst in. “I found him. He’s locked in the top of the so-called Haunted Tower. Aye, I know that place—many a poor soul went up those stairs walking, and came down feet first.”

Margaret gasped, “Oh Martin! How did he look?”

“Just like Gerard Eliassoen, what else?”

“Was he pale? Did he look doomed?”

“Nay, nay, he was bright as a new pewter tankard when he saw me. He’s counting on us.”

Margaret shook her head, full of despair, and handed Martin the sealed letter for Rotterdam. But old Peter Brandt, who had sat quiet pondering the whole time, spoke up. “Put not your trust in princes,” he said.

“Alas, what else have we left to trust?” Margaret cried.

“Knowledge.”

“Your learning cannot help us here, father,” she sighed. “There is no ladder in all Holland high enough to reach that hundred foot window.”

“I need no ladder. All I need is one gold crown.”

Margaret had nine golden angels Gerard had left in her keeping, but she knew they could not bribe the burgomaster to let Gerard go free. But Peter spoke with such absolute confidence that he made them listen: he told them the old story of a Florentine knight locked in a tower higher than Gerard’s in Brescia, whose faithful squire had pulled him out with nothing more than a bow, a ball of silk, and a few pennies’ worth of rope. The trick was so simple, once he explained it, they could not believe they had ever thought it impossible. Margaret tore up the letter to the countess. They would trust to Peter’s old learning, and their own dexterity.

While they made their plans, two more figures crept through the dark streets of Tergou. Gerard’s sister Kate had overheard Cornelis and Sybrandt muttering about their brother, and snuck to the door of their room to listen, learning the terrible truth of Gerard’s imprisonment. She fetched their little hunchback brother Giles, woken him from his bed, and persuaded him to walk with her to the foot of the Haunted Tower to bring Gerard word that their father was still away in Rotterdam, and would surely set him free the moment he came home. “I would go alone,” she told him, “but I am afraid of the spirits men say haunt this tower. With you beside me, I have nothing to fear.”

Giles, who had never seen a ghost in his whole life, grabbed his lantern, and the two slipped out into the bright moonlit night.

Up in the tower cell, Gerard’s hope had faded with the setting sun. He was faint with hunger, too afraid to eat the bread the burgomaster had left him lest it be poisoned. He sat huddled on the oak chest, head drooped, a perfect picture of despair—until something thudded sharp against the wall behind him, and clattered to the floor at his feet.

It was an arrow, fletched with white feathers, no iron head on its tip. Gerard froze, thinking they meant to assassinate him through the window—until he spotted the soft skein of silk tied around its shaft. He pulled his tinderbox from his pocket, struck a tiny flame, and read the words scrawled on the arrow’s shaft, his heart leaping for joy: *Well beloved, make fast the silk to thy knife and lower to us: but hold thine end fast: then count an hundred and draw up.*

With almost superhuman strength he dragged the massive oak chest across the cell to sit under the window. He tied the silk to his knife, lowered it out the slit until it tugged tight, counted out one hundred slow beats, and began to pull the silk back up. It grew heavier, until at last he drew a thick knot through the window, with a length of stout whipcord tied to it. He pulled that up next, and it gave way to a heavy, thick hemp rope.

Margaret’s soft voice drifted up to him on the night air: “Draw up, Gerard, till you see liberty.”

He pulled till sweat streamed down his face, until the thick end of the new hemp rope slipped into his hands. He tied it fast through both handles of the oak chest, then jumped on it with all his weight to test its strength. On the third jump, the chest’s side popped open, spilling a whole mess of ancient parchments out across the stone floor. Gerard grabbed the iron bar he had wrenched from the window, lashed it across the rope and the window sill for extra bracing, then climbed up on the chest, pushed his legs out through the narrow window, and hung half over the drop, his heart thudding loud enough to hear in the still night.

He prayed a short, quiet prayer, then gripped the rope tight, hand over hand, lowering himself down the hundred foot stone wall. His palms burned, his fingers ached, he dared not look down for fear of dizziness, until at last his feet touched two warm, outstretched hands, and Margaret and Martin caught him before he hit the ground. All three clung together, sobbing quiet, overjoyed.

“Hush,” Martin hissed. “Away in silence, dears.”

They had barely gone a dozen steps, when a stream of lantern light burst out from the tower’s angle, cutting across their path like a bar of fire, followed by soft whispers and approaching footsteps.

“Back!” Martin breathed. “Keep in the shadows.” They scurried back past the dangling loose end of the escape rope, and pressed around the small side turret of the tower. The lantern light flickered past them, bobbing off into the distance.

“Someone’s hunting us,” Martin groaned. He slung his crossbow off his shoulder, strung it, and nocked an arrow. “I will drop two of them before they know where the shot came from.” He slipped around the turret’s corner, ready to loose.

A moment later, he staggered back, the bow wobbling in his hands, his face deathly pale, the arrow clattering to the ground. He grabbed Gerard’s arm, gasping so hard he could barely speak. “Let me feel flesh and blood. The haunted tower! The haunted tower! There it goes, climbing up the wall, its head all on fire, walking straight up the stone like it’s grass. Say your prayers if you know them—hell is loose in Tergou tonight.”

Gerard, trembling, straightened his shoulders. “I have power to exorcise spirits,” he said. “I will go and look.”

“Go alone then,” Martin whimpered. “I’ve seen it once, and I’ll never forget it as long as I live.”

The bitter, unmasked glint of hatred the burgomaster Ghysbrecht had fixed on him, fresh on the heels of his weeks of unjust imprisonment, had settled deep in Gerard’s bones: he knew the man would never rest until he was destroyed. So when he slipped around the shadowed corner of the old tower, he did not half-expect ghosts or wraiths. He expected cruel, hidden traps, laid by a treacherous foe to finish him off while his escape had barely been discovered by the town watch.

As he stole forward, a hand slipped soft but steady, brave as any soldier’s, into his own. Margaret was at his side, silent, ready to share whatever new peril waited for them.

The moment the full bulk of the haunted tower came into view, they froze, every limb turning leaden. Halfway up the stone face, a creature with a blazing fiery head, no smaller than an enormous overfed glowworm, crawled steadily up the wall. Its body was dark, but the outline blazed clear against the bright glow spilling from its head, and the whole thing stretched nearly four feet long. At the foot of the tower, a tall figure draped in pure white stood perfectly still, its silhouette exactly matching the shape of a robed woman. They both gasped, their hearts hammering hard enough to burst.
“The rope!” Gerard hissed, hoarse with awe. “It’s climbing the rope.”

Before their eyes, the fiery “worm” vanished through the gap of his old prison cell window. Its light flooded the small room within, painting the dusty window glass a deep, bloody red. The white figure at the base of the tower never stirred an inch.

Folks who do not collapse completely into hysterics when faced with what they believe is supernatural horror often fall prey to a very specific, strange madness: the wild, overwhelming urge to fling themselves directly at the terrifying object that transfixes them, the way a mesmerized bird hurls itself at the coiled snake. The great tragedian Macready used to play this beat masterfully in *Macbeth*, when Banquo’s ghost appears the second time: he would lunge, eyes averted, right at the shadow on the stage. That same wild impulse seized Margaret now. She gently set Gerard’s hand aside, stood dazed for half a breath, then let out a sharp, wild cry and darted straight for the spectre.

Gerard, ignorant of the common human quirk that drove her, was convinced the devil himself was luring her to eternal damnation. He dropped to his knees so hard his knuckles scraped the mossy turf, screaming his exorcism at the top of his terror-stricken lungs: “Exorcizo vos. In nomine beatae Mariae, exorcizo vos.”

Even as he shrieked the Latin prayers, he heard a thin, feeble cry of fear rise from the supposed spectre below. To learn that even hell’s minions could whimper with fright was the most reassuring shock of his life. He redoubled his chants, and soon spotted the ghastly white figure sinking to its knees at Margaret’s feet, blubbering and begging piteously for mercy.

A few minutes later, Kate and Giles trundled up to the tower, and stopped dead at the sight of the brand new rope dangling all the way from Gerard’s former cell window down to the grass at their feet.
“Ah, I see how it is,” Giles said, his plain, practical wits cutting straight through every superstition. “Gerard climbed down this rope. He’s free. I’m going up to check.”
“No, Giles, no!” Kate cried, her mind clouded by old, deep-seated superstition. “Can’t you see this is glamour? The evil one cast that rope out to trick you to your death! He knows how you love clambering up every high thing you see. Where would Gerard get a rope long enough to reach all this way, tied fast to a prison bar? That is not natural. Holy saints protect us tonight, for hell walks abroad in the dark.”
“Stuff and nonsense,” the dwarf hooted. “The road to hell goes downward. This rope leads up. I may live a hundred years and never get a chance at a climb this perfect again. I’d as soon break my neck and get it over with as spend my whole life wondering what was up there.” He launched himself at the rope with a cry of pure delight, light as a cat leaping for a table piled high with fresh fish. Every muscle in his gymnast’s body burned with excitement. The only concession he let Kate talk him into was tying her small lantern around the nape of his neck. “A light scares ill spirits away,” she insisted. With his broad, powerful arms hauling him upward and his short legs kicking light as feathers, Giles climbed the rope faster than Gerard had ever climbed down it. The lantern glowing on his neck turned him into that very same fiery glowworm Gerard and Margaret had spotted from the shadows. Kate watched him go, trembling all over with fear.

Then a figure burst out from behind the solid stonework of the tower, sprinting at her with a speed no mortal woman should ever be able to reach. Kate let out a thin, breathless cry that was all she could manage, her tongue sticking fast to the roof of her mouth with terror. She dropped her crutches, sank to her knees, hid her face in her hands and sobbed: “Take my body, but spare my soul!”
Margaret skidded to a halt, panting hard: “Wait, I’m just a woman!”
Kate, shaking so hard her teeth chattered, lifted her head: “Why, I am just a woman too! You scared half the wits clean out of me.”
They stared at each other, bewildered, Margaret laughing breathless: “And you scared me half to death, creeping up like that! But what of that fiery-headed thing? It was you, wasn’t it? You’re no harm. What are you doing out here at this hour of the night?”
“Nay, what are you doing out here?” Kate shot back. The realization dawned on them both at once: they had both come looking for Gerard. “You’re Margaret Brandt,” Kate breathed, and Margaret nodded. “That is all the better. You love him. Then Giles was right – he’s escaped.”

Gerard stepped forward then, and all doubt was gone. Before any more explanations could spill out, a horrible, unearthly roar boomed down from the tower, echoing like a tomb speaking:
The volume rose with every repetition. They looked up, and there was the dwarf, his arms stuffed full of old legal parchments, his face lit with feral glee, his skin glowing lurid red in the lantern light tied to his neck, the spitting image of some grinning hell imp. He hurled the parchments down at their astonished heads. Documents fluttered down like wounded wild ducks: some crumpled the second they hit the grass, some flapped hard mid-fall, others spread wide and wheeled slow, lazy circles through the night air. They had barely settled when the roar boomed out again, and another flood of parchments pattered down, until the whole lawn at the foot of the tower was whitened like fresh driven snow. Finally, the fire-headed little imp slid down the rope fast as a falling star, landed light as a feather, and held out his claw-like hand to his brother, ready to collect payment for the stolen stash of documents he had just delivered.

“Hush, speak quieter,” Gerard said, “Gather them all up, and follow us far away from this tower, somewhere safer.”
“Will you come home with me, Gerard?” Kate asked softly.
“I have no home,” he said grimly.
“You will not say that,” she protested. “After this cruel wrong, there is no one more welcome at your father’s house than you.”
“Father?” Gerard’s voice went hard as flint. “The man who was my father has turned my gaoler. I escaped from his hands, and I will never come within reach of them again.”
“It was not our father who did this,” Kate told him, and relayed every word she had overheard their brothers Cornelis and Sybrandt plotting, to frame him and hand him over to the burgomaster. But the wound was still too fresh to soothe. Gerard’s anger, raw and sharp, was fiercer than anyone had ever seen it. “Cornelis and Sybrandt are two mangy curs that have bared their fangs at me for years, but they never had the power to hurt me this bad. It was our father that gave the burgomaster leave to touch me – a free burgher of this town – or he would never have dared lay a finger on me. So be it. I was his son, he made me his prisoner. He has played his part. Now I will play mine. Farewell to Tergou, the burgh where I was born, where I lived honest, and where they threw me in a dungeon. As long as there is a single other town left in the world, I will never set foot in you again.”
“Gerard, Gerard!” Margaret whispered to Kate, “Do not argue with him now. Give his rage time to cool.” Kate turned to her, asked to look at her face, and the inspection pleased her. “That is a comely face,” she whispered back, “and no mischief-maker’s.”
“Fear me not,” Margaret smiled back. “I could never be happy without your love, just as I could never be happy without Gerard’s.”
“Those are sweet words,” Kate sobbed. “I never thought I would come to love you so fast. My heart wants to embrace you, but my lame legs will not let me.” Margaret leaned in, wrapped her arms gentle around Gerard’s sister, and kissed her warm. Gerard kissed Kate goodbye too, and she hobbled off on her crutches, the soft, patient sound of her last sigh drifting back to them across the grass. Margaret’s eyes filled thick with tears, but Gerard, caught up in the hard, bright edge of his resolve, did not notice.

As they turned toward the road to Sevenbergen, Giles nudged Gerard in the side with his armful of stolen parchments, and held out his open palm. Margaret tried to talk Gerard out of paying for the stolen goods. “Why take property that does not belong to us?”
“Why not? Spoil your enemy any way you can,” Gerard laughed.
“But might they not use this as an excuse to hunt you down and hurt you all over again?”
“What can they do? Do you think I am staying in Tergou after tonight? The burgomaster stole my liberty. If I could, I would take his life in return. What – is a man’s life worth more than his freedom? I cannot take his life, so I will take the first thing of his I can lay my hands on.” He pressed a handful of small silver coins into the dwarf’s palm, and the little man, overjoyed, shuffled off after his sister. Before long, their old friend Martin joined them, and the three of them set off fast down the dark road to Sevenbergen, leaving Tergou and all its treacheries far behind them.

Ghysbrecht Van Swieten, burgomaster of Tergou, kept the iron key to Gerard Eliassoen’s cell tucked deep in the fur-lined pouch at his belt, and bided his time until the town steeple tolled ten full chimes before he made his way to the prison stairs. “A little hunger softens even the stiffest-necked lad,” he’d muttered to his trusted armed servant Dierich Brower, certain a half-day on nothing but cold cell air would have broken the young scholar’s stubborn resolve.
He crept up the winding damp stone steps, paused to press his ear to the oak cell door, and heard no sound at all: no huffed complaints, no shuffling of feet, no plea for water. A grim, satisfied smirk tugged at his jowly, weathered face. “By now he will be as down-hearted as Albert Koestein was,” he thought, recalling the man who’d once dared contest Ghysbrecht’s land claims, and broken in that very same cell.
He turned the key in the lock, swung the door open, and stood stock-still.
The cell was empty.
For a long breath he did not move at all, his heavy wool cloak still swirled half-around his legs, then a violent tremor wracked his frame so hard his silver signet ring clattered against the door latch. Dierich, alarmed, pressed close to peer over his shoulder, and gaped at the sight before him: no Gerard, only a frayed rope braided from torn blanket strands dangling from the outer window ledge, and the iron bar that had once barred the window wrenched clean out of its mortar. He yelped in loud surprise, but his master paid him no heed at all. Ghysbrecht flung himself on his knees before the heavy iron-bound oaken chest that sat in the cell’s far corner, his quivering hands patting every inch of its surface wildly, as if refusing to trust his eyes that the secret lock he’d guarded for twenty years had been sprung, and the chest gaped wide, completely empty.
“Master, what ails you?” Dierich asked, bewildered. “The lad’s not in that box, look—see the rogue’s cunning? He pried the bar free and climbed out—”
“GONE. GONE. GONE,” Ghysbrecht gasped, his pale lips working but barely forming sound.
“Gone? Holy saints, the man’s planet-struck!”
“STOP THIEF!” Ghysbrecht shrieked suddenly, spinning to grab Dierich by the collar of his doublet and shaking him so hard his wool cap tumbled off his head. “D’ye stand there gawping while your master is robbed? Run! Fly! A hundred crowns to the man who brings it back to me! No—no, it’s too late. Oh, fool, fool that I was, to leave that chest in the same room with him. No soul ever found its secret spring before. None ever would have, but him. It was fated. Lost! All lost!”
Age and his chronic wheezing caught up with his short-lived frenzy then, and he sank heavily down onto the edge of the empty chest, muttering the word “lost” over and over under his breath.
“What is lost, master?” Dierich asked, half-sympathetic, half-curious.
The sharp, eager tone of the question cut through Ghysbrecht’s haze of despair, and his natural cunning snapped back to him. He darted a sidelong, furtive glance at his servant, like a fox caught mid-sneak near a henhouse, and stammered out a lie. “The town’s official record parchments. That is what I lost.”
“Oh, is that all?” Dierich huffed, relieved.
“Is that not enough?” Ghysbrecht snapped, regaining his bluster. “What will the burghers say? What will they do to me? A hundred crowns, mind you, for every last scrap of parchment that was in this chest. If even one is missing, you get nothing.”
“Then the crowns are as good as mine,” Dierich grinned. “Wherever Gerard Eliassoen is, those scuffed sheepskins you value so high will be too. I’ll round up four constables this instant, march to his father the hosier’s house, and seize him for the theft.”
“Theft!” Ghysbrecht’s eyes lit up, the perfect excuse no one would dare question. “Aye, theft! That’s the charge. Drag him down to the lowest dungeon, the one where the toads creep and the rats breed. That man will never see daylight again. It is his own fault, for prying where he had no business. Be quick, before he has time to talk, before he can tell anyone what he found.”
Less than half an hour later, Dierich and his four constables were pounding on the door of the hosier’s cottage, and demanded the boy Gerard be handed over. Gerard’s mother Catherine, white-faced and trembling, cried out that the boy would break her heart, that no one had seen him since he was taken to the prison.
Dierich softened his tone into a smooth, patronizing lie to calm her. “Nay, dame, it is nothing but a foolish prank of youth. He ran off with a handful of old town parchments for a lark, no doubt. The burgomaster is only anxious to get them back, that is all. The lad will get no worse than a sharp reprimand, you may rest easy.”
Catherine bought the story entirely, but Gerard’s lame little sister Kate, sharpened by years of loving and protecting her brother, saw the hungry, greedy glint in Dierich’s eyes, and her suspicion spiked higher still when he flew into a violent, frustrated rage the moment he confirmed Gerard had not been home all night, was nowhere in the house.
“Come on then,” he snarled at his men. “We are wasting time. I will hunt that boy down if he is still breathing above ground.”
As he turned to leave, Kate signaled to him that she wished to speak in private. He sent his constables ahead out the gate, and waited for her by the lintel.
“Hush,” she whispered, glancing back over her shoulder to make sure her mother could not hear. “Gerard has fled Tergou for good. I saw him at the foot of the old haunted tower last night. He swore once they locked him in that cell, he would never set foot in this town again. He is many leagues across the border by now. The burgomaster got his wish: he imprisoned the boy, drove him from his birthplace. What need have you now to drag our good name through the mud for a handful of worthless old skins?”
Dierich was too mortified at the loss of his hundred crowns to pause and see the sense in her words. “Worthless trash?” he snapped back. “Then likely enough the little thief tossed them straight in the nearest brook or pigsty before he left, eh? The sheepskins you scorn are worth more to me than the skin of any fool in Tergou.” He turned on his heel and stormed off, chasing the false scent that Gerard had fled Holland entirely.
Kate hurried back inside, pulled her hunchback brother Giles aside, and whispered her secret. “I lied to Dirk. Gerard is no leagues away. He has gone to Sevenbergen, to the girl he loves. The men chasing him mean him harm, not just a scolding, and I am lame, I cannot run there to warn him. Giles, dear Giles, you are strong. Will you not go for me?”
Giles grumbled that he hated to travel on foot, but when she pressed him if he loved Gerard, who had always been kindest to him of all their siblings, he puffed out his broad chest. “Aye, I like him best of the lot. I will borrow Peter Buyskens’ mule. I will ride out the west gate first, so all the gossips think I am heading for the northern market, and not turn the mule’s head south for Sevenbergen until I am well clear of the town walls.”
Kate made him repeat her warning message over and over, word for word, until he had it memorized perfectly, then saw him mount the mule and set off down the road. When he was out of sight, she sank to her knees beside the cottage hearth, and prayed long and earnestly for her brother’s safety, until the last of the peat embers burned low.

Gerard and Margaret walked the road to Sevenbergen light as thistledown, giddy on the first breath of freedom after his narrow escape from the Tergou prison, their recent bold adventure still thrumming warm in their veins. But that bright glow soon faded to heavy, cold dread: Gerard was an escaped fugitive, liable to be dragged back in irons at any moment, no matter that the charge against him was a lie. They would have to part, if only for a little while, and he had already come to loathe the narrow, spiteful bounds of his hometown.

Margaret begged him to flee the country for a spell, but the very thought of him crossing the brutal Alps to Italy made her heart feel as if it would split in two. Gerard, for his part, could only reconcile himself to leaving her by clinging to the dream of that same Italy: a place where his skill as an illuminator and carver would be valued, where he could earn gold and renown fast enough to sweep away every petty obstacle that stood between them and marriage. He told her again all that the noble Van Eyck had counseled him, reminded her the demoiselle’s gold coins had been given him expressly for that Italian journey. This boorish, small-minded village would never nurture his talent, he said. In the south, artists were revered. The unselfish girl gave her consent at last, but not before hot, tender tears streamed down her cheeks. Young and wild with love himself, Gerard wept bitter tears right alongside her, and they clung to each other, over and over asking what wrong they had ever done to earn so many secret enemies, all bent on tearing them apart.

They sat hand in hand long past midnight, now bemoaning their cruel fate, now painting glowing, sunlit pictures of the little home they would share one day, with a wide window for his workbench and a garden full of herbs. Midway through his grandest, most hopeful description of their future, Margaret’s tears would start flowing afresh, and all his grand eloquence would dissolve into a soft, shaking sigh. By dawn they had resigned themselves to parting, but neither had the courage to name the hour. No doubt they would have lingered in that soft, suspended limbo for weeks if fate had not crashed down upon them.

It was three o’clock in the afternoon when Giles came thudding up the lane on horseback, having ridden a dozen miles out of his way to shake off any eyes that might be following him. The pair ran out to meet him, curiosity bright on their faces, but his grim tone struck them cold.
“Brother Gerard,” he boomed, his deep voice rough with urgency, “Kate bids you run for your very life. They have laid a false theft charge at your feet, to give them a pretense to seize you. Do not waste a breath trying to explain. There is no justice for you in Tergou. Those parchments you took from Ghysbrecht? They are but a blind. Kate has seen the murderous look in the men they’ve sent after you. There is a price on your head. Fly! For Margaret’s sake, and for every soul that loves you, do not loiter another second. Fly!”

It hit them like a thunderclap, leaving two white, stunned faces staring first at each other, then at the grim messenger. Up until that moment Giles had only spoken the lines Catherine had bade him carry, but now he added a word of his own, gruff and earnest. “All the constables of Tergou were tramping through our cottage an hour after you vanished, and Dirk Brower at their head. Kate is no fool, Gerard. Listen to her, and run now.”

“Oh yes, Gerard!” Margaret cried, wild with terror. “Fly this instant! Those parchments—my heart misgave me the day you took them, why did I ever let you?”

“Nay, Margaret, Giles says those parchments are nothing but a ruse,” Gerard said firmly. “But that old caitiff Ghysbrecht will never lay eyes on them again. I will not leave until I hide his hoard where he shall never dig it up.” He thanked Giles warmly, bade him farewell, and told him to ride back fast and tell Catherine he was already gone. “For I shall be leagues away before you reach Tergou,” he promised.

He called for old Martin the hunter, told him what had befallen them, and begged him to walk a little way down the Tergou road to keep watch. “Aye,” Martin nodded, testing the tip of his arrow. “If I spot Dirk Brower or any of his men, I will shoot a single arrow straight into the gnarled old oak that grows in your garden. The second you see it, run hard for the forest edge, make for the weird hunter’s spring, and I will guide you through the hidden paths no townsman has ever known.”

Now that the warning had been made plain, Gerard breathed a little easier. He went back out with Margaret, who trembled by the oak tree, every rustle of its leaves making her flinch, while he dug a deep pit in the soft loam under the hawthorn hedge. He tossed the parchments in one by one—most were ancient town charters and burgh records, but one folded deed bore the names of Floris Brandt, Margaret’s father, and Ghysbrecht. “Why, this is as much yours as his,” Gerard said, reaching for it to read.

“Oh not now, Gerard, not now!” Margaret pleaded, clutching his arm. “Every second you waste fills me with fear. See? Heavy drops of rain are starting to fall, and the clouds hang low enough to touch the tops of the trees.” Gerard yielded, tucking that single deed into the breast of his tunic, then shoveled the dirt back over the rest of the parchments and stamped it flat with his boot.

Just then a flash of lightning split the sky, followed by a low roll of distant thunder, and the rain came lashing down hard. Margaret and Gerard ran back to the cottage, and Martin stumbled through the door soon after, his cloak soaked through. “The road is clear for now,” he said, “but a right heavy storm is coming.” His words proved true. The thunder rolled closer and closer until it crashed overhead, lightning flashes coming so fast they looked like the cracks of a whip, and rain falling in torrents that lashed the thatch so hard it sounded like thousands of tiny footsteps. Margaret hid her face against Gerard’s shoulder to avoid seeing the blue-white glare of the lightning. Gerard pushed the rough wooden shutter closed and lit a tallow candle, and the two lovers huddled together, blessing the storm that had stolen them a few more precious hours alone.

The sun set unmarked by either of them, the thunder still pealing, the lightning still flaring, the rain still pouring down. Supper was set on the table, but neither could swallow a bite: the thought that this was the last meal they would share for months, maybe years, choked them. When the storm lulled a little, old Peter retired to his bed. Gerard meant to slip away at peep of day, and neither he nor Margaret would waste a single minute of their remaining time asleep. Martin sat close by the door, fitting a new string to his bow, a task he was always particular about, while the lovers murmured all their sorrows and all their quiet vows over the faint glow of the hearth.

Suddenly the old hunter held up one gnarled hand, signaling for silence. They stilled at once, listening, and for a long moment heard nothing. Then came a faint, soft crunch of autumn leaves strewn across the garden path at the back door: a footstep, trying so hard to be noiseless it made the hair on the back of their necks stand straight up. Martin nocked an arrow to his bowstring in a single fluid motion, and blew the candle out. At that exact moment, they heard more than one set of footsteps creep up to the front of the cottage, not quite as silent as the first, but stealthy as a pack of wolves closing in on prey. Then came a dead, heavy pause.

Their blood turned to ice in their veins.
“Oh Catherine, oh Catherine!” Margaret moaned under her breath, wringing her hands in wild remorse. “You said to fly the instant the warning came.”

“Hush, girl,” Martin hissed in a sharp, stern whisper.

A heavy, booming knock fell on the oak door.
And it hit their terrified hearts harder than a fist.

The sharp, rude thud against the cottage back door hit the hush of the storm-wracked night like a prearranged signal. They were trapped, hemmed in on all sides. At the alarming sound, Margaret’s rigid panic shattered long enough for her to grab Gerard’s arm, her voice a frantic, breathless whisper against his ear: “Tell them he was here, but already gone.” She all but dragged him up the rough, splintered wooden steps leading to her father Peter’s garret sleeping chamber, her own small bedroom just a little further down the narrow upper landing.

The blows on the lower door came again, harder, rattling the oaken planks in their frames.
“Who knocks at this ungodly hour?” Martin Wittenhaagen called, from his seat by the peat fire.
“Open the door, and you’ll see well enough!” the voice boomed back.
“I do not throw my door open to thieves. All honest folk are abed and asleep at this hour.”
“Open in the name of the law, Martin Wittenhaagen, or you’ll rue your stubbornness before dawn.”
Martin grunted, recognition pricking through his feigned confusion. “Why, if that isn’t Dirk Brower’s voice all the way from Tergou! What brings you tramping so far out of your jurisdiction on a night fit to drown a duck?”
“Open the door, and I’ll explain all your questions soon enough.”
