Martin drew back the bolt slow as molasses, and Dierich Brower burst through the threshold with four hard-faced men at his heels. They waved their waiting companion in from the back path to join them.
“Right then, Martin. Where is Gerard Eliassoen?” Dierich demanded, planting his boots on the packed earthen floor by the fire.
“Gerard Eliassoen? Why, he was here not half an hour ago!” Martin said, feigning wide, innocent surprise.
“Was here?” Dierich’s face fell. “And where has he run off to now?”
“Folks say he’s bound for Italy. What’s all the ruckus about, man?”
“Don’t play the fool with me. You’ll not make me believe he tramped off through that lashing gale, out in the pitch dark.”

Martin huffed, feigning scorn at the whole commotion, lit a tallow candle, and settled himself coolly back by the hearth, winding fine silk thread around the nicked section of his bowstring where arrow fletchings wore thin. “I’ll tell you the whole truth, then. You know that rascal of his brother Giles? The little misbegotten imp, all head and gangling arms? He came tearing over here on a stolen mule, yelling at the top of his lungs the whole ride. I was out by the byre and too far off to make out his squawking, but there was no mistaking he was raising a terrible ruckus. No sooner had he galloped off than there was all this crying and clinging, and off Gerard went. The girls round here say he’s heading for Italy—mayhap you’ve a better idea where that far-off country lies than I do.”

Dierich’s face darkened further and further the longer Martin spoke, and he could find no flaw in the tale. A cleverer, more cunning man might have overplayed his hand, added extra lies that would rouse suspicion, but Martin stuck strictly to the single falsehood he and the others had agreed on, inventing no extra tales of his own.
“Mates,” Dierich said, turning to his men, “I think he’s telling the truth. I warned the burgomaster this is exactly how it would go. I saw that dwarf Giles galloping past on Peter Buyskens’s mule from Sevenbergen an hour back, and I said straight off, ‘That little imp’s been sent to warn Gerard, so Gerard’s at Sevenbergen.’ But did they listen? No! They wasted half the night rummaging every ratty corner of Tergou hunting for those cursed parchments, and forgot all about Sevenbergen till that imp had time to give the whole game away. Gerard’s leagues away by now, long gone before we even set foot on this path. That chalk-faced girl Margaret’s outwitted all of us bearded men, and I told the burgomaster we’d get nothing for this errand but wet jerkins and cold shoulders.” Martin grinned slow and smug right in Dierich’s face.

“Still,” Dierich added, sighing, “to satisfy the old burgomaster when we get back, we’ll search the whole house top to bottom.”
Martin’s grin vanished instantly, his face turning grave. Dierich spotted the shift in his expression at once, and paused to think. “Two of you, stand guard outside, one on each side of the cottage. No one jumps out an upper window and slips past us. The rest, come on with me.” He snatched the tallow candle from the table and started up the stairs, three of his men tramping heavy at his heels.

Left alone at the foot of the stair, Martin’s broad soldier’s shoulders slumped. Everything had gone so perfectly up till that moment, and now this fatal, terrible turn. Then a wild idea struck him—all was not lost yet. Gerard was hiding in one of the two upper chambers, not far off the ground. He’d leap for the window the second the men found him, Dierich had posted only one man down below to catch him. For half a minute, that would make Martin and Gerard two against one, and in that small window of time, anything could happen.
He propped the back door ajar and waited, watching. The light of the candle glowed bright in Peter’s bedroom. “Curse the fool,” Martin growled under his breath, “is he going to let them march him off like a frightened milkmaid?”
The light moved past the landing and into Margaret’s bedroom, and still no window sash was thrown open. Martin saw at once Gerard would never have waited till the men were in the room to make his escape out the glass. He’d begun to creep to the foot of the stair, half convinced Gerard had already slipped out a window while all the law men were crowded inside the lower cottage—until a faint, trembling cry drifted down from Margaret’s bedroom.
“They’ve got him,” Martin groaned, “they’ve caught him for sure.”

The thought flashed through his mind like a lightning bolt: if they dragged Gerard off to Tergou, his life wasn’t worth a brass farthing. And if Gerard was killed, Margaret’s heart would break right in her chest. He glanced wildly around the little room, like a cornered wild boar hunting a way out, and in an instant settled on a resolution as fierce and unyielding as the iron men of his day, a soldier driven straight to bay. He stepped to the front door, then the back, mimicked Dierich Brower’s sharp, commanding voice perfectly, and called “Watch the windows, don’t leave your posts!” Then he quietly slid the bolts home on both doors, locking the four law men inside the cottage with him.
He grabbed his old war bow and six arrows, nocked one tight to the string, slipped the rest in his quiver. He set his hunting knife on the chair behind him, hilt turned outward for easy grabbing, and settled himself at the foot of the stairs, calm as stone, determined to kill all four men before they could take Gerard, or die trying. He knew he could put two arrows through their chests before they could reach him, then he and Gerard would fight the remaining two hand to hand. He’d seen men break and run in sudden, unexpected ambushes. If Brower and his men hesitated even a single heartbeat before rushing him, he could bring down three with his arrows, and the fight would be on his side.

He didn’t have long to wait. Heavy boots thudded down the upper landing, coming closer and closer. The glow of the tallow candle drew near, and the murmur of loud voices. Martin’s stout soldier’s heart thudded hard against his ribs, thinking he was about to send four men to their graves on no more than the chance to save his friend. But this same man who’d trembled at the sight of Giles prancing in a lanthorn mask never wavered for a second in that awful, breathless moment. He stood braced, eye glowing bright, ready to take lives and lose his own if need be. It was a desperate game: win, and he’d be exiled for life instantly. Lose, and he’d drop dead on that very earthen floor before the hour was out.

Upstairs, Dierich and his men had first stumbled into Peter’s room while the old man was deep in his first sleep. They rummaged through every cupboard, ran their daggers through the stuffed alligator pelt Peter had nailed to his wall as a curio, poked under the bed, but the large room, full of crannies and nooks, held no sign of Gerard.
They moved on to Margaret’s bedroom, and the sight of it gave them pause: small, bare, not a single cupboard in sight, nothing to hide a full grown man. Only a wide fireplace and tall stone chimney. Dierich’s eyes locked on the chimney straight away. There lay Margaret, the beauty of Sevenbergen, pretending to sleep on a low old oak chest bed no more than a foot off the ground, her linen sheets snow white, her shift peeking out equally bright, looking for all the world like a pure white lily that had fallen into the muddy rut of their rough, uninvited intrusion.
She woke after a moment, sat up in the bed like a woman dazed from a deep dream, spotted the four armed men looming over her, and began to scream soft, trembling pleas for mercy. Her distress shamed Dierich Brower right out of his bluster.
“Easy now, lass, we’re not here to hurt you,” he said, flustered. “Lie still, shut those pretty eyes, and dream of your wedding night while I poke up this chimney to see if Master Gerard is hiding there.”
“Gerard? In my bedroom?” Margaret cried, her voice rising. “Cruel men! You all know full well they drove him away from me, drove him out of his own native land! This is nothing but a lie. You’re thieves, you’re wicked brutes, you’re no men of Sevenbergen, or you’d know Margaret Brandt better than to dare look for her lover in this room of all places in the world. Oh, brave, brave thing! Four great hulking armed men tramping in at midnight to insult one poor honest girl! The women in your own houses must be good for nothing, or you’d respect your own wives and daughters too much to dare shame a girl of good name like this.”
“Right, come away, lads, before she gives us an earful we’ll never live down,” Dierich said, hastily beating a retreat from the bedroom. “He’s not hiding in the chimney, that’s plain. You can plaster over a crack a cudgel makes easy, but a woman’s sharp tongue is a double-edged dagger, and a girl that young still has her mother’s milk in her bones, and she’ll carve you to shreds before you know what hit you. I told the burgomaster this whole fool’s errand would come to nothing.”

Show me the woman who cannot play a part when the man she loves hangs in the balance. Show me the one who will not throw every scrap of her native wit to the task, and play it better than any court actor, to shield the heart that is dearer to her than her own life. On these desperate, fateful occasions, even the simplest, most unassuming girl finds herself gifted with a cleverness that outwits the wisest of men—Solomon himself could be led astray by the softest of the sex, when love gives her the lead.

No sooner had the last of the search party’s footsteps vanished over the threshold than Margaret slipped off the long oak chest where she had been lying, fully clad in her skirt, petticoat, and woolen stockings, with her linen nightgown pulled on over all. She heaved the heavy lid, bedclothes and all, propped it flush against the wall, then glided barefoot to the door, her breath catching in her throat, to listen. The tramp of heavy boots echoed slow past her father’s bedchamber, then faded step by step down the creaking wooden stairs to the ground floor.

That old chest held a secret no stranger on earth could ever spot. A section of the room’s floorboards had rotted through some months prior, and when Gerard had been called in to patch the damage, short of coin for new lumber, he had sawed a narrow slot in the chest’s base just wide enough to fit snugly over the gap, then used the discarded rotted boarding to mend the rest of the floor. The chest now rested fully on the rafters a full foot below the visible floorboards, making its true hidden depth a full two feet—though to any casual eye, it looked no deeper than a common clothes chest, barely a foot high, far too shallow to ever hide a man.

All was still in the quiet house. Margaret sank to her knees on the cold planks, breathed a quick, tearful prayer of thanks to the Virgin and all the saints, then leaned over the chest’s dark opening, whispering soft as a lullaby: “Gerard.”
No answer came.
She whispered a little louder, her voice thrumming with hard-won relief: “Gerard, all danger is past, thank the good Lord. You may rise now—only do be careful, make no noise.”
Still no reply.

A prickle of icy dread ran down her spine. She laid her hand on what she thought was his shoulder, and found it stone cold and utterly still. “Gerard!”
No movement.
“Oh, what is this?” she cried, and her hands flew wild over his face, his chest, his neck. She seized him by the shoulders, shook him hard, hauled him up half out of the chest—only for his heavy, limp form to slip right out of her trembling grasp and fall back into the dark wood, not like a living man, but like a dead weight.

A paralyzing horror settled over her. The lid had been shut tight the whole time. She had lain her full weight upon it for the long minutes the men searched the room. With a strength born of frenzy that no one would have thought the slight, quiet girl possessed, she hauled his full limp body out of the chest, dragged him across the floor to the casement window, and flung it wide open. The cool, sweet night air flooded in, silver moonlight spilling over their faces. She laid him there, face upturned to the wind and the moon.

His skin was the pale, ashen grey of ash left on a hearth after the last embers have died. His limbs were loose, utterly motionless. She pressed her fingers to the pulse in his neck, then to his heart. Horror of horrors. It was still. She had smothered him, trapped in that narrow dark space, under the weight of her own body on the closed lid.

The human mind reels from a calamity so sudden, so monstrous, it cannot grasp it at first. Gerard, who had climbed alive and laughing into that chest not five minutes before—how could he be dead? She called him every endearing name her heart had ever dared to whisper to itself, names she had never breathed aloud to any living soul. She kissed his cold cheeks, stroked his hair, pleaded, coaxed, begged him to open his eyes, to speak one word to her. No answer. Not a flicker of movement.

Then the poor girl, shaking so hard her teeth chattered, began to babble soft, foolish, broken little phrases over his ashy face, half pitying, half distraught. “Oh Gerard, I am so sorry you are dead. I am so sorry I killed you. Forgive me for not letting those wicked men take you. That would have been a thousand times better than this. Oh Gerard, I am so, so sorry for what I have done.”

Then her grief snapped, and she raved, half mad with the injustice of it. “No! No! This cannot be. If this is true, there is no God in heaven. It cannot be. My Gerard cannot be dead. I, Margaret, who love him more than my own life—how could I kill him? You see all this, O Lord. You know how I love him. He never even knew. I never told him how deep my love runs. If he did, he would speak to me now. He would not be so cruel, so deaf to his own Margaret. This is just a trick, is it not? A game to make me cry out and give you away to the men downstairs? But I will not. I love you too much to betray you. I will choke on my own screams before I make a sound that gives you away.” She seized her own throat hard, nails digging into her flesh, to choke back the wild, ragged scream clawing its way up her throat.

“Only speak one word, Gerard. Do not die without a word. Have mercy on me. Scold me. Curse me if you are angry. I deserve it. I am the idiot, the fool who killed the man she loved better than her own soul. I am a murderess. The worst wretch in all the world. Help! Help! I have murdered him!”

The shrieks tore out of her, wild, piercing, unearthly, ringing through the silent house like the tolling of a funeral bell. Downstairs, Dierich Brower and his men, just rising to take their leave, heard the sound. Every man froze, and stared at one another, wide-eyed.

Martin Wittenhaagen braced at the foot of the cottage stairs, his yew bow drawn nearly to the arrowhead, a sharp hunting knife tucked out of sight behind his back, went utterly still with shock when the raiding party tramped back through the door without Gerard. He let the bowstring slack unbidden, his jaw hanging agape as he stared at the sodden, mud-caked men.

For their part, the bandits were equally confused to catch the old farmer in that obvious combat stance.
"Hey, mates, was the old sod about to put a bolt through us before we even crossed the threshold?"

Martin shook himself, his stolid, weathered composure snapping back into place fast. "Stuff and nonsense. I was just testing out my new bowstring, that's all. There, see? I'll unstring the whole thing if you're so nervous about it."

Dierich, the party’s surly leader, narrowed his eyes suspiciously. "Hmph. There’s more going on with you than I can puzzle out. Go heave a good log on that hearth – we’ll dry our hides a bit before we head out again."

A roaring blaze caught fast, and the men clustered around it, their heavy wool cloaks and matted uncut hair wisping steam as they thawed from the chill of the moor. That was when the high, sharp, terrified shrieks rang out from Margaret’s bedchamber at the top of the stairs. The whole group jumped to their feet at once, one man snatching up the sputtering tallow candle to go bounding up the bedroom steps.

Martin lurched up in a panic, his wits reeling from the sudden screams. Terrified the man would harm the girl he’d sworn to protect, he threw himself forward to block the path. Dierich lunged at him from behind, wrapping both arms tight around his chest and yelling for the others to hold the old brute down. The man with the candle slipped past the scuffle and vanished up the stairs, and the rest of the gang piled onto Martin all at once. The struggle was long and brutal: over and over, the whole heaving knot of men rolled across the packed earthen floor with Martin at its center, the old countryman strong as a grizzled Samson even against four younger men. At last they managed to overpower him, and bind his hands and feet tight with the thick hemp rope they had brought along specifically to tie up Gerard.

Martin groaned aloud. He knew the intruder had reached Margaret’s room while they were all distracted by the fight, and now he was completely helpless to stop whatever might happen to her.

"Go on, grind your teeth all you want, you old rogue," Dierich panted, red and sweating from the brawl. "You won’t be sinking them into any of us now. I swear mates, our lives weren’t even safe a minute while this old fellow’s bones were free to move."

"Wait a minute," another bandit put in, frowning. "Makes me think that Gerard we were chasing can’t be far off, hiding somewhere nearby."

"No such luck for us, or him," Dierich scoffed. Then he tilted his head, frowning. "Hallo, lads. Jorian Ketel’s been up in that girl’s bedroom an awful long time. Some of you go see what’s keeping him, won’t you?"

The crude, leering laugh that rippled through the gang barely died away before they heard rapid, thudding footsteps sprinting across the upper floorboards.
"Oh, here he comes at last! Well, Jorian – what the devil is going on up there?"

Jorian Ketel’s heavy boots thudded across Margaret’s oak chamber planks, and he rounded the doorframe fully expecting to hunt his fugitive through every nook of the small house. What he found there stopped him dead, tallow candle shaking in his calloused fist so that wax dripped hot onto his jerkin: the very man he’d been chasing, Gerard, pale as a bleached funeral shroud, motionless, his head resting in Margaret’s lap. She knelt over him, frozen to stone, eyes blown wide yet glazed over, seeing neither the thin moonbeam slanting through the leaded glass pane nor Jorian’s sharp intake of breath, every thread of her being fixed solely on the white, still face pressed to her linen apron.

Jorian stood awestruck for a long minute, then crept over to the empty oak chest they had stashed the boy in, prodded the crumpled discarded cloak at its bottom, and the whole tale unspooled in his head. The girl’s dumb, frozen despair twisted something soft in the rough workman’s chest. “A sorry sight, this,” he muttered under his breath. “A black night’s work, all for a few miserable deerskins. Better he’d run off with us than end like this. She’s past hearing a word from me, poor wench—wait, though.”

He fished a tiny hand-mirror no bigger than his palm out of his pocket, held it to Gerard’s nostrils and mouth, and withdrew it. The polished glass was fogged, faint and sure, with breath. “There’s life in him!” he breathed to himself.

Though the words were no louder than a sigh, Margaret caught them instantly. It was as if a carved stone statue had burst open into warm, wild life. She sprang to her feet and flung her arms around Jorian’s neck, clinging to his broad shoulders almost fiercely, over and over, sobbing half-laughing blessings on the rough tongue that had brought her that single scrap of hope.

“There, there, lass, let’s lay him warm,” Jorian rumbled, and he hefted Gerard up gentle as a lamb, laid him on the piled wool blankets of the truckle bed. He pulled his flask of Schiedam gin from his belt, filled his cupped palm twice, and flung the sharp, pungent liquor hard across Gerard’s pale cheeks. The fumes bit through the fog of his unconsciousness, and he drew a faint, trembling sigh. No sound that ever fell on human ears was half so sweet to Margaret. She flew toward him, then skidded to a halt, quivering, too scared even to brush his hair back lest she snuff out his returning breath.

“That’s right, leave him be,” Jorian ordered, gruff but kind. “Don’t smother him the way you clung to me, or you’ll drive his breath right back out. He’s young, not some old grandad tottering at death’s door—he’ll come round of his own accord.”

Gerard sighed deeper still, a faint pink tinge stealing back to his colourless lips. Jorian turned for the door, and had barely crossed the threshold when something coiled tight around his ankles. It was Margaret, curled round his knees like a soft little eel, kissing his calloused work-worn hands, begging him not to drag Gerard back to the grave he had just pulled him from, not to undo the good he’d done.

“Never you fear, lass,” Jorian said. “This ain’t the first time I’ve done you two a good turn, remember? I slipped you the warning in the church before the chase ever began. Dierich Brower’s no friend of mine—I’d see him strung up before I breathe a word of this. Though truth be told, I’d be lying if I said the hundred crowns reward for those missing parchments don’t tempt me. That’d feed my Joan and our three bairns for years, no more scraping to make rent.”

“Those hundred crowns are yours,” Margaret swore at once. “I know exactly where they’re hidden. On my faith, and on St. Bavon’s bones, I’ll hand every last parchment over to you tomorrow—come alone, and no one else gets a penny of that gold.”

“Couldn’t pay me to share it with that weasel Brower,” Jorian grunted, and swore on his own bones he’d not breathe a soul that Gerard was under this roof, then slipped off fast, lest his long loitering rouse the rest of the bailiffs’ suspicions.

Margaret sank to her knees beside the bed then, shaking from head to toe, and prayed long and hard for Gerard, beside Gerard. When Dierich Brower demanded to know where on earth they’d got to, Jorian shrugged easy, told him the girl had worked herself into a dead faint, he’d roused her old doctor father Peter to tend to her, and the last thing they needed was a crowd of loud men tramping in to scare her straight to the churchyard. His offhand, unconcerned tone disarmed every last flicker of suspicion. The rest of the party quickly agreed the kitchen of the Three Kings tavern was far warmer than Peter’s cold, draughty parlour, trundled off, and untied the bound servant Martin on their way out. At the door, Dierich Brower even smirked at his men, muttering he’d told the burgomaster they’d be too late to catch the boy, and sure enough, he’d been right.

So in one single terrible night, Gerard had brushed the iron bars of a prison cell and the cold dark of the grave both. He owed his escape not to his cleverly conceived hiding spot, nor to Margaret’s quick wits, but to a small, unlooked-for spark of humanity in a rough, reckless man, tangled up with that same man’s quiet hunger for the gold that would feed his family. Human motives are always mixed, messy, seemingly contradictory; even the shrewdest, best laid plans go astray, and the paths out of disaster are rarely the ones we mapped out for ourselves.

Folks whose lives run gentle, unshaken by the fiercest heights of joy and depths of anguish the human heart can bear, are the luckiest of us all—but no quiet, untested soul could ever fathom the unnameable, overwhelming bliss that wrapped around Margaret and Gerard now. To sit and watch the face you love drift back from the edge of death, see roses bloom on his once death-pale cheek, light spark back in his eyes, words return to his lips, was a joy great enough to balance years of sorrow for Margaret. For Gerard, to wake from that trance and find his head pillowed on Margaret’s soft arm, to hear the woman he adored murmur words of love he’d never dared hope to hear, to feel her warm tears drop on his forehead and her gentle kisses brush his hands—he had never guessed just how fiercely, how tenderly she loved him. For half a second he almost thanked the men who had chased him to the grave’s edge, for gifting him this moment.

They wove their arms around each other, called each other husband and wife, and why not? They were solemnly betrothed, they had stood before the altar together, had received the Holy Church’s blessing on their union, and her curse on any soul who dared tear them apart.

But no woman’s nerves can bear a strain that sharp without breaking. Presently Margaret’s strength gave out, and she sank against Gerard’s shoulder, smiling faint and soft, completely unstrung. Gerard panicked and tried to rise to fetch help, but she held him with a gentle, unyielding grasp, begging him not to leave her for a single second. “While my hand is on you, I know you are safe, dearest. Nothing ails me—only that I am weak, and happy, so very happy.”

It was Gerard’s turn to cradle that dear head, her great waves of loose hair spilling over his chest, to soothe the trembling out of her, to whisper soft, quiet words of love. There is no charm in a woman’s heart sweeter to a man who loves her than that soft, unguarded vulnerability. They were poor, hunted, fugitives, but for those hours they were happy beyond measure. They knew they must part on the morrow, but that seemed nothing next to the grave they had just stood beside. A year or two apart, when they were so young? It was light as dandelion fluff. While there is life there is hope, they told themselves, and while there is hope there is joy. The future glowed bright as a sunrise, and the present was heaven itself.

Alas, their innocence held other risks they did not see, far greater than prison or the chase. Now that all visible danger had faded, they were in the gravest peril of all from their own full hearts, and their own inexperience.

All through the wild thunderstorm that raged over medieval Sevenbergen, Ghysbrecht Van Swieten tossed on his bed, too gnawed by anxious, greedy dread to sleep a single wink. He was a man whose nerve always crumpled at the roar of thunder and flash of lightning, else he would have marched at the head of the party sent to ransack Peter’s cottage the night before. No sooner had the last distant rumble of the tempest died away entirely, and the first pale streaks of dawn bleached the storm clouds thin, than he crept down his creaking oak stairs without rousing his household, saddled his own stubborn mule, and rode hard for the sign of the Three Kings at the edge of the village.

When he pushed open the tavern door, the reek of stale ale and smoldering peat hit him, and there were his men, dead to the world: some splayed across the rough wooden chairs, some draped over the table tops with half-empty tankards still clutched loose in their fists, others curled atop the dirty rush-strewn earthen floor. He kicked the nearest man hard in the ribs to rouse them all, snarling in a frothing fury, and listened to their bungled tale of the failed search, every line larded with their own inflated praise for their supposed zeal and diligence.

“Fools! To think I ever sent you off without me!” the burgomaster roared. “I’d stake every penny I own the man we hunt was hiding right under your noses the whole time. Did ye think to look under the girl Margaret’s bed?”

“Pah,” grunted one of the men, yawning and rubbing the fresh bruise on his side. “There’s not space enough under there for a small child, let alone a full grown man.”

“How dare ye speak of what ye do not know, when ye never stooped to look?” Ghysbrecht snapped, his round face purpling with rage. “Ye should have looked under her bed, pried apart the very frame of it if need be, and tapped every last panel in the house with your knives to seek out hollow hiding spots. Up with you now, the whole lot of you, and I will show you how a proper search is done.”

The burly Dierich Brower climbed to his feet, shaking straw off his breeches and cracking his thick knuckles. “If that man is still hiding in that little hovel when we get there, you may call me a plough horse and no man for the rest of my days.”

Within minutes, Peter’s cottage was ringed by the whole party. The fiery old burgomaster tossed his mule’s reins to Jorian Ketel, and stormed into the house with Dierich Brower and the rest of his men at his heels. The place was utterly empty. Not a living soul to be seen, not even old Peter himself. They tramped up the narrow creaking stair, when suddenly one of the men gave a sharp shout, and pointed through Peter’s wide-open casement window. The rest crowded to look, and there, a short way off, walking calmly across the dew-damp fields side by side with Margaret and Martin, was the very man they had torn the house apart to find.

Ghysbrecht let out a yell of ferocious triumph, stumbled headlong back down the stairs, and flung himself astride his mule. In moments he and his whole band were galloping across the pasture, thundering in hot pursuit of their quarry.

Still reeling from last night’s narrow brush with capture, Gerard roused long before the first streaks of grey gilded the cottage thatch, and shook old Martin awake. The veteran soldier blinked in utter astonishment, half-convinced the lad had already slipped out the window under cover of dark. When Gerard asked for the surest path to slip out of the country and shake off pursuit, Martin did not hesitate: there was only one safe road. “I’ll guide you through the great old forest to a hidden bridle track no traveler uses but me. It will carry you straight to a wayside hostelry where they’ll lend you a swift horse, and a full day’s gallop will put all of Holland behind you before any hue and cry can spread. But we must leave before the villagers drag themselves out of their beds at dawn.”
Peter’s cottage stood barely a furlong and a half from the forest edge. They set out at once: Martin slung his well-worn war bow over his shoulder and slipped three extra arrows in his belt, a old soldier’s habit he never broke on a Thursday, while Gerard carried nothing but the stout knotted oak staff Peter had pressed into his hands that morning, worn smooth from years of prodding turnip rows and fending off stray hounds. Margaret hitched her wool kirtle and farthingale up above her ankles, for the grass was still soaked and muddied from last night’s rain. Peter walked them all the way to his garden hedge, his usual stolid face softening with a rare surge of emotion, and pressed a father’s blessing to Gerard’s head.
The sun was just peeking its red rim over the low horizon as they tramped across the stony fallow fields, making straight for the wood. They were halfway across the open stretch when Margaret, who had been craning her neck backward every few steps, let out a sharp terrified cry. Her instinct took over before she could think: she sprinted for the trees, screaming all the way. Ghysbrecht and his men were hot on their heels.
To fight a whole band of pursuers would be madness, so Martin and Gerard ran after her. The men on foot gained ground little by little, but Martin shouted over the wind, “Only win the wood! Just reach the first trees, lads!” Their head start was still good, and hope swelled in their chests: the great oak boughs seemed to stretch out like open friendly arms, the thick underbrush a ready screen to hide them from sight.
But an unforeseen danger tore from the flank. Fiery old Burgomaster Ghysbrecht had hurled himself onto his sturdy mule, spurring the poor beast to a flat gallop, outpacing not just his own men but the fugitives themselves. He traced a wide semicircle, his only goal to cut Gerard off before he could reach cover. The old man came thundering around the curve, and suddenly he was right on the edge of the wood, dead in front of Gerard. The rest of the runaways he did not care about at all. Margaret shrieked, throwing her arms around Gerard to shield him, but he shoved her aside none too gently.
Ghysbrecht, drunk on rage, forgot that hunted animals turn on their hunter, that two men who have hated each other for months, who have both longed for the other’s ruin, will not run. Instead of ducking out of the way as the burgomaster fully expected, Gerard flew at him with a savage, wild cry, and swung that oak staff with every ounce of his fear, his fury, his pent-up strength. The stick crashed down on Ghysbrecht’s face with a sickening thunderous crack, and the old man went flying off his mule, landing in the mud under its tail, heels kicking wildly, blood streaming down his face and soaking his linen collar. The very next second, all three were diving into the shelter of the trees.
A roar of dismay and vengeance burst from Ghysbrecht’s men when they saw their leader felled, and the fugitives knew now it was a race for life or death.
“Why run?” Gerard panted, stopping short and shaking his bloodied staff. “You have your bow, I have this—we can stand and fight.”
“Boy, are you mad?” Martin roared back. “The gallows are waiting for us if they catch us! Follow me!” He bolted deeper into the undergrowth.
Soon they heard a sound like hounds baying when they catch sight of their quarry: the men were in the wood now, and had spotted their three figures darting between the trunks. Margaret whimpered and panted as she ran, Gerard clenched his teeth so hard his jaw ached, his grip on the staff so tight his knuckles blanched. A minute later they hit a thick dense hazel coppice. Martin burst right through it, shoving thin young saplings aside as if they were dry standing corn. They did not make fifty yards before they hit four overgrown blind paths snaking off in every direction. Martin dived down one, hissing “Bend low” and they half-crawled, half-scuttled along the soft leaf litter. Soon the path forked again into more tiny winding trails. They picked one that seemed to loop back on itself, then twisted sharply, leading them to a thick stand of old pines where the ground was hard and carpeted with pine needles, no paths at all. The young firs grew so close here you could not see three feet in front of your own face.
When they were well inside the pine grove, Martin dropped onto a fallen log. The old campaigner, long trained to shed all fear the second immediate danger passed, pulled a hunk of black bread and a slice of ham from his wallet and began calmly eating his breakfast, as if no hue and cry hunted them down. The two younger ones stared at him in dismay, and he met their looks with a dry grin.
“Not a soul in all Sevenbergen could find you lot here. And Gerard—you’re going to lose your purse long before you get to Italy, if you carry it hanging loose like that.”
Gerard glanced down, and there was a large triangular purse, tangled by its chain fast to the buckle of his wallet strap. “That’s none of mine,” he said, confused, fumbling to untangle it. “Wonder what’s inside?” It was stuck inextricably in the leather, so he had to pull his knife to cut it free. When they emptied it out, it was full of silver coins of every size, half its bloated bulk made of crumpled folded brown paper, stuffed in to make it look far fatter than it was.
Gerard laughed out loud. “Why, this must belong to that old thief Ghysbrecht! He stuffed it with paper to fool the world into thinking he carried twice the coin he did!”
They puzzled over how it got there, before the truth clicked: the purse had hung from Ghysbrecht’s saddle bow, and when Gerard charged at him, he had torn it free without even noticing, felling his enemy and robbing him in the exact same wild, single gesture. Gerard was giddy over the absurd lucky feat, but Margaret was uneasy.
“Throw it away, Gerard. Or let Martin take it back to him. They already call you a thief. I cannot bear them to have even more cause to speak ill of you.”
“Throw it away? Give it back? Not a single stiver!” Gerard crowed. “This is plunder fairly won in open fight against an enemy, isn’t it, Martin?”
“Aye, that’s the truth,” Martin said, chewing. “Send him his crumpled brown paper scraps back if you like, but the coin? Giving that back’d be a sin.”
“Oh Gerard,” Margaret said, soft and worried, “you are going to a far country. We need Heaven’s goodwill on our side. How can we hope for that if we take something that is not ours?”
But Gerard saw it differently, bright with pious delight. “Heaven handed it to me by a miracle, that’s what it is. The chosen people of Israel spoiled the Egyptians, did they not? And they were blessed for it.”
“Take your own way,” Margaret said humbly, bowing her head. “You are wiser than I. You are my husband,” she added in a low murmur, “it is not my place to gainsay you.”
Those soft meek words from Margaret, who had always led their little dynamic before that day, surprised Martin for a moment, and the thought tucked itself away in his head, to puzzle over later. Gerard kissed her tenderly in return, and they walked hand in hand deeper into the vast forest, Martin leading the way. The further they went, the safer they felt: no villager from Sevenbergen ever dared venture this far into the trackless heart of the wood.
Impetuous natures repent fast, and Gerard’s hot temper cooled as soon as the last echo of pursuit faded. His conscience pricked him sharp.
“Martin, I wish I had not struck quite so hard.”
“Whom? Oh, let that pass, he got off cheap.”
“I saw his grey hairs the second my stick fell. I doubt that sight will leave my eyes for many a day.”
Martin grunted with contempt. “Who spares a badger for his grey hairs? The greyer your enemy is, the older he is, the craftier he is. And the craftier the better for a little killing.”
“Killing? Killing, Martin? Speak not of killing!” Gerard shook all over. “I never meant that.”
“I am much mistaken if you have not done it,” Martin said cheerfully. “That old vagabond’s skull cracked like a ripe walnut, mark my words.”
“Heaven and the saints forbid it!”
“He rolled off his mule like a stone shot out of a cart. Said I to myself, there’s one old scoundrel wiped right off the map,” the iron old soldier grinned ruthlessly.
Gerard fell to his knees and began to pray for his enemy’s life. Martin lost his patience.
“What mummery is this? You that set up for learning, know you not a wise man never strikes his enemy but to kill him? And what is all this coil over killing an old man? If it had been a young fellow, with wine, women, and plage waiting for him, that’d be a tragedy. But an old greybeard tottering right on the edge of the grave—why not shove him in? Go he must, today or tomorrow. If I ever live to be as broken down as Ghysbrecht, riding a mule instead of walking on my own legs, with a back as stiff as my bow wood instead of as flexible as my bowstring? I’ll thank any young man that knocks me on the head, same as you did that old shopkeeper. Malison on his memory.”
“Oh, my fault! My great fault!” Gerard cried, smiting his breast.
“Look there!” Martin said to Margaret scornfully. “He is a priest at heart still—when he is not in a rage, what a milksop!”
“Tush, Martin!” Margaret chided him, then she wreathed her arms round Gerard, and comforted him with the soft dual magic of a woman’s gentle sense and a woman’s warm voice. “Sweetheart,” she murmured, “you forget: you went not a step out of your way to harm him, who hunted you to your death. You fled from him. He it was who spurred straight at you. Then did you strike, but in self-defence, a single blow, with that which was in your hand. If malice had ruled you, you would have drawn a knife, or struck again and again. Men are smitten with staves many blows over, and yet live! If your enemy has fallen, it is through his own malice, not yours, and by the will of God.”
“Bless you, Margaret, bless you for thinking so!”
“Aye, but beloved one, if you have had the misfortune to harm that wicked man, the more need there is that you fly with haste from Holland. Oh, let us on.”
“Nay, Margaret,” said Gerard. “I fear not man’s vengeance, thanks to Martin and this thick wood. Only Him I fear whose eye pierces the forest and reads the heart of man. If I but struck in self-defence, ’tis well. But if in hate, He may bid the avenger of blood follow me to Italy—ay, to earth’s remotest bounds.”
“Hush!” said Martin peevishly. “Your chatter’s drowning out the sound.”
“What is it?”
“Do you hear nothing, Margaret? My ears are getting old.”
Margaret listened, and presently she caught a tuneful sound, like a single stroke upon a deep ringing bell. She described it, and Martin nodded grimly.
“I heard it,” he said.
“So did I,” said Gerard. “It is beautiful. Ah, there it is again! How sweetly it blends with the air. It is a long way off. It is before us, is it not?”
“No, no! The echoes of this wood confound the ear of a stranger. It comes from the pine grove.”
“What! The one we passed? Martin, is this anything? You look pale.”
“Wonderful!” said Martin, with a sickly sneer. “He asks me is it anything? Come, on, on! At any rate, let us reach a better place than this.”
“A better place—for what?”
“To stand at bay, Gerard,” said Martin gravely. “And die like soldiers, killing three for one.”
“What’s that sound?”
“It is the Avenger of Blood.”
“Oh, Martin, save him! Oh Heaven be merciful! What new mysterious peril is this?”
“Girl,” Martin said, his voice tight with dread, “it’s a bloodhound.”

The courage of ordinary men, much like their natural talent, runs within a narrow, well-worn groove. Drag them but an inch outside the bounds of what they know, and it curdles into nothing.
Martin Wittenhaagen’s courage had never failed him before, not in all his rough life. He had faced down wild boars in the thicket, outwitted river pirates on the Meuse, stood frostbitten and hungry through a three-day blizzard in the dunes, and every familiar danger he met he bore with Spartan fortitude, almost unflinching indifference. But he had never been hunted by a bloodhound. He had never seen that brute’s unerring, unshakable instinct outrun man’s cleverest trickery. Now, novelty tangled with a creeping, unspoken sense of the supernatural, and the iron in his chest turned soft. He stumbled to a halt a few paces into the trees, leaned his weight on his gnarled yew bow, and felt all his energy, all his hope, seep out of him like water through a sieve.

Gerard, for his part, had thought the danger small for as long as it stayed distant, and he urged the older man to run, to put more miles between them and the hunt.
“What use is running?” Martin said, his voice heavy with despair. “If we break for the open fields, they’ll cut us down like stray dogs before we’ve run a mile. But here, close by, I know a spot where we’ll sell our lives dear, not cheap.”
“Ah, good Martin, don’t give up so fast!” Gerard cried. “There has to be some way out of this.”
“Wait,” Margaret cut in, her mind sharp while the two men hung limp with dread. “What if we split apart? It’s only Gerard’s life they want. Can we not draw the hound after the two of us, and let him slip away safe?”
“Girl, you do not know the nature of a bloodhound,” Martin sighed, not lifting his head from where it hung over his bow. “He does not track a man’s face, or his clothes. He tracks blood. I’d stake my life they took that cur straight to the spot where Ghysbrecht fell. From the old man’s spilt blood, that hound will follow the man who shed it, no matter if Gerard runs through a whole army or swims the full breadth of the Meuse.”

The hound’s deep, mellow bay rolled through the wood then, clear as a bell. No hunter’s horn in Crete, Sparta, or Thessaly ever called a pack to heel so sweetly. It was strange, was it not? that something so beautiful could be so deadly? The boa constrictor’s eyes, when it fascinates its prey, glow like no jewel in any royal crown: ruby red shot through with emerald green, and the deer that meets that gaze loses all power to move, trembling as it waits for death. Just so, that soft, ringing bay seemed to wrap around Martin, to freeze his limbs. He stood bewildered, unstrung, all his hard-won nerve gone to nothing.
Gerard was little better. Martin’s words had daunted him. He had struck an old man, shed his blood, and now that very blood had summoned a four-footed avenger on his heels. Could this not be the hand of Heaven, reaching out to punish him?

While the two men stood benumbed, Margaret’s brain raced faster than it ever had. The man she loved was marked for death.
“Give me your knife,” she said to Martin, quiet as a shadow.
He passed it over, half careless. “Twill do you no good, lass, soft as your hands are.”
Margaret turned her back to them both before they could see, drew the sharp blade across the soft flesh of her upper arm, and let the blood flow freely. She stooped, smeared the warm, dark liquid all over her wool hose, her leather shoes, dabbing at the grass beneath her heels to leave a strong, fresh scent trail, and never once let the two men notice what she did. When she was done, she seized Martin’s arm, hard.
“Come on, be a man!” she snapped. “Lead us to the thickest part of the wood, the kind that swallows numbers whole. There our foes’ numbers won’t do them any good.”
“I’m going,” Martin said, sullen as a man tramping to the gallows. “Hurry does no good. We can’t outrun the hound, and the place is but a furlong off.” He turned left, leading the way, and soon brought them to a dense hazel coppice, thick with thin, springy shoots, very like the thicket that had hidden them from the patrol earlier that morning.
“This is it,” he said. “It’s no more than a furlong across, but it’ll serve.”
“What’s the plan?” Gerard asked.
“Push through to the other side, wait there. When they come straggling out after us, I’ll shoot three with my bow, you’ll crack two heads with your cudgel, and the rest will swarm us and kill us dead.”
“That’s all you can think of?” Gerard said, shaking his head. “Then I’m taking the lead, for you’ve lost your wits. Can you obey a boy half your age, Martin Wittenhaagen?”
“Oh yes, do as he says!” Margaret put in at once. “He’s wiser than his years.”
Martin gave a sullen, grudging nod.
“Then copy exactly what I do,” Gerard said, drawing his big hunting knife. At every step he took, he cut one or two hazel shoots clean off at the root, then twisted the loose ends up breast-high through the standing, living stems, weaving a tangled, invisible barrier that would catch at clothes and slow a man’s steps to a crawl. Martin followed suit, moving slow, dogged, still convinced they were all going to die.

Halfway through the coppice, the hound’s bay grew louder, closer, no longer sweet and mellow, but sharp, harsh, thunderous. Margaret trembled so hard her teeth chattered. Martin dropped flat to the leaf litter, pressing his ear to the ground.
“I hear horse hooves,” he muttered.
“Not a horse,” Gerard said. “A mule. That cursed Ghysbrecht isn’t dead at all. No one else would hound me this hard.”
“Never strike an enemy unless you mean to kill him,” Martin growled.
“I’ll hit far harder this time, if Heaven lets me get close enough,” Gerard swore.

At last they pushed through the last of the hazel, and came out into an open stretch of old wood, with great gnarled oaks standing far apart, no cover worth the name. Now the hound’s bay was tangled up with a dozen voices, shouting and hallooing, the whole village out to hunt them down.
“The entire parish is on our trail,” Martin said.
“I don’t care,” Gerard whispered. “Listen. The path we wove will be smooth as silk for the hound’s nose, but tangled as a thorn bush for the men chasing him. The dog will outrun all the rest, and we will kill him the second he steps out of the coppice.”
“Kill the hound?” Martin said. “There’s more than one.”
“I only hear the one barking.”
“Aye, only the lead hound gives tongue. The rest run silent. If he loses the scent, the next will start baying. There’s at least two dogs here, devils in dog fur.”
“Then we kill two,” Gerard said. “The second they are dead, we dive back into the coppice, and run the whole length of it back the way we came, right past the men following the hound.”
Martin’s eyes flashed, a flicker of his old courage coming back. “That’s a sharp thought, lad.”
“Hush. The men are in the coppice now.”

Gerard gave his orders in a whisper. “You take your bow and hide in that ditch right at the edge of the trees. I’ll go a dozen paces out to that big oak, and hide behind it. The dogs will be straight on my scent. When they come bursting out, you shoot as many as you can, and I’ll bash the rest’s heads in before they know what’s happening.”
Martin nocked an arrow, his old sharp self again. The shouts drew closer, the rustle of young hazel stems crackling, and every few seconds the bloodhound gave a short, sharp bay, a death knell ringing minute by minute.
A trembling hand fell on Gerard’s shoulder, making him jump half out of his skin. “Martin says if we have to split, make for the tall ash tree at the edge of the wood where we first came in.”
“Go back, for Heaven’s sake!” Gerard hissed. “Don’t stay out here in the open!”

Margaret turned to run back to Martin, but before she could reach him, a great brindled hound burst out of the coppice. It stood stock still for a heartbeat, nose down, and then gave a deafening snarl and launched itself straight at Gerard’s oak. Before it could cover half the distance, Martin’s bow twanged, and the arrow caught it full in the chest, spitting it clean through. The hound rolled head over heels and dropped dead on the spot.
The second hound came bounding out right after, nosed its dead comrade, and Gerard charged at it with his cudgel. He didn’t get there in time: a streak of white movement, and the hound crumpled to the dust, screaming piteously, a knife wound deep in its flank. But before Gerard could finish it off, the coppice exploded with noise. Three men, who had outpaced the rest of the hunt, burst out of the hazel, and Gerard barely had time to gesture wildly at Martin to go back, before he turned and scrambled back into the tangled thicket on all fours. Margaret and Martin, their wits sharp now, followed the same path, crawling back along the line of the trail they had woven. The pursuers and the pursued passed within a few yards of each other, moving in opposite directions through the brush.
A loud cry went up, as the hunters spotted the dead and dying hounds. Voices babbled, swelling as more and more villagers piled onto the scene, all crowding around, exclaiming, wasting precious minutes.
“I don’t hear any more hounds,” Martin whispered to Margaret. His nerve was fully back now.
It was Margaret’s turn to tremble, to feel despair closing over her. “Oh, why did we leave Gerard? They will kill my Gerard, and I will not be there to help him.”
“Nay, nay, those fools haven’t the wit to catch him. You told him to meet us at the ash tree, aye?”
“I did,” Margaret said, brightening. “Bless you for remembering. To the ash tree, then!”
“Softly, no noise.”

They were almost at the edge of the coppice, when they heard shouts and hallooing behind them. The hunters had worked out the fugitives were still in the thicket, and were beating their way back across it.
“No matter,” Martin whispered to his trembling companion. “We can break for the far treeline, run hard, and lose them in the open fields before they see us.” He tensed to burst out of the brush, then froze.
Seated on his mule at the edge of the wood was Ghysbrecht Van Swieten. A bloody bandage was tied across his broken nose, his eyes sharp and alert above it, and he had clearly heard their rustle, craning his neck to spot them. Martin muttered a vicious oath, strung his bow slow, nocked his last arrow. Margaret pressed her hands to her face, but did not make a sound. She knew one of them had to die, the burgomaster or Gerard. She peered through her fingers, her heart hammering so hard she could hear it in her ears.
Martin drew the bowstring back, the arrowhead level with his eye, ready to loose, when a figure launched itself at Ghysbrecht out of the trees behind him, fast as a hawk stooping on a pigeon. A kerchief whipped over the burgomaster’s face, his head was muffled tight in an instant, and he was hauled off his mule, crashing hard to the dirt, groaning in terror. Gerard jumped down after him.
“Hist! Martin! Margaret! Over here!”
They stumbled out of the coppice, Martin gaping. “Run! Now, while they’re all busy in the thicket! We’re saved!”

But the rush of the fight, the loss of blood from the cut on her arm, caught up to Margaret all at once. She swayed on her feet, gasping. “Oh my love, go on without me. Leave me, I’m too faint to run.”
“Not a step without you,” Gerard said, catching her as she fell. “We live together or die together. The mule! Put her on the mule, Martin, I’ll run at her side.”
Martin swung himself up on the mule’s back in an instant, Gerard lifted the fainting girl, settled her safe in the saddle, and grabbed Martin’s bow from him.
“Treason! Murder! Help!” Ghysbrecht shrieked, rearing up off the ground.
“Silence, you cur!” Gerard roared, shoving his boot down hard on the burgomaster’s throat, the way a man crushes an adder under his heel. “You hold on tight there, Margaret! Ride for your life!”
The mule lurched forward, its hooves kicking up sparks from the flints as it broke into a canter. Gerard lifted his boot off Ghysbrecht’s throat to run, and that very second, Dierich Brower and his five men, who had circled back for new orders, came bursting roaring out of the coppice, straight at them.

Speech is the easy, familiar outlet for all the tangled, mundane thoughts humans carry in their heads, but there are emotions so raw, uncomplicated, and overpowering that they burst forth not as formed words, but as rough, wordless cries that carry more weight than any carefully turned speech ever could. At those moments, a man sheds every last trace of the civility that sets him apart from the beasts, and becomes nothing more than a creature of raw, urgent impulse—for even the highest of animals, when pushed to the edge of great triumph or great terror, will cry out without having the words to name what moves them.

That unthinking, almost feral quality hung thick in the forest air that day: it blazed in the roar of brutal triumph that tore from Dierich and his men’s throats the moment they burst from the thicket straight onto the heels of the two fugitives and their mule, and it seared through the sharp, piercing cry of terror that burst from Margaret and Gerard as they darted away so fast their pursuers’ outstretched hands closed on nothing but empty air, scarce two feet behind their backs.

Stunned for a split second, like lions that miss their pounce mid-spring, Dierich and his crew gave Gerard and the mule a full ten yards of head start before they collected themselves, and flew after them with cudgels and daggers raised high over their heads. They were certain they would catch their prey, too—this was not the first time they had raced one another that morning. Out on the open moorland earlier, the hunters had been visibly gaining on the three, and now, at last, there were no more brambles to trip them, no winding tree roots to slow them: it was a fair, unobstructed race, to be decided by nothing but raw speed.

They ate up a hundred yards in the blink of an eye, but that ten-yard gap between pursuers and pursued never shrank. Dierich Brower could not make sense of it—why were the three fugitives suddenly running twice as fast as they had all morning? The answer was simple: when three people run side by side, the whole group can only go as fast as the slowest one. All the way from Peter’s cottage to the edge of the forest, Gerard had held his pace back to match Margaret’s, but now he was running full tilt at his own natural speed: the mule beneath Martin was fleet of foot enough to outrun all of them if she wished, and the young lovers’ unspent youth and sober, unburdened bodies gave them a stamina none of the hard-drinking middle-aged pursuers could match.

Bit by bit, almost imperceptibly, daylight widened between the hunters and the hunted. Dierich threw every last bit of strength he had into one desperate burst, and cut the gap down by two whole yards—but before he could catch his breath, Gerard had quietly pulled that distance back again. The men behind him began to snarl and curse in frustration.

Martin, perched steady on the mule’s back, heard them, and his worn face lit up with hope. “Courage, Gerard! Courage, brave lad! They’re breaking, they’re falling away from each other!”

He was right. Dierich, already winded, was soon overtaken by one of his own men, while another straggled so far behind he was barely visible to the rest. The path ahead sloped up a long, gentle rise, and here the stamina of youth, grit, and a lifetime of clean living told more than ever. Before Dierich even reached the crest of the hill, his forty years of heavy drinking and rough living weighed on him like forty lead bullets. “Our hunt’s done,” he gasped, doubling over, too winded to take another step. “If you can’t take them alive, shoot them dead!” He dropped out of the chase right there, and staggered along after the rest at a slow walking pace.

Jorian Ketel fell out of the run next, then another man, and one by one, Gerard ran every last one of the pursuers to a standstill—all except one, who stuck to the chase as steadfast as a bloodhound, even if he lost a little ground with every stride. If old local tales are to be trusted, his name was Eric Wouverman.

Pursued only by Eric now, the trio rounded a bend in the wood, and came to a second hill, shorter than the last but far steeper. “Hand on her mane!” Martin shouted to Gerard, who was running beside the mule. Gerard obeyed immediately, and the sure-footed creature hauled both him and Martin up the sharp slope faster than they had been running on the flat.

When he saw that trick, the last remaining pursuer lost his nerve. He was now a full eighty yards behind Gerard, and more than that far ahead of his nearest straggling comrade, so he skidded to a sudden halt. Following Dierich’s last order, he unslung his crossbow from his shoulder, drew the bolt back and levelled it slow and deliberate, and just as the three fugitives sank over the crest of the hill, out of sight, he loosed. The bolt whistled through the air, straight at them.

There was a sharp cry of dismay, and the next instant, as if a thunderbolt had struck the whole group, every last one of them—Gerard, Margaret, Martin, and the mule—tumbled together to the ground in a heap.

The shock of what followed was so sudden, so unearthly in its speed, that the man who had loosed the crossbow stood frozen, stupefied, for a full heartbeat. Then he roared for his comrades to rally to him and help seize their quarry, and started scrambling up the grassy slope himself. But before he had covered half the distance, a broad, grim figure stepped out from behind the gnarled trunk of an ancient oak: Martin Wittenhaagen, his yew bow bent to full draw, a sharp, broad-headed arrow aimed dead straight down the path.

Eric Wouverman spotted him in that stance and darted behind the thickest tree he could reach, pressing himself flat to the bark as if he meant to melt right into it. Martin’s legendary skill with the bow was known across every village for ten miles around, and the dead bloodhound they had left lying at the edge of the wood was a keen, fresh reminder of what that skill could do. Wouverman poked one cautious eye around the edge of the bark, and there it was: the glint of the arrow’s point, still locked straight on where he huddled. He did not dare shift an inch, not even to brush the stinging nettles off his bare ankle.

He huddled there peeking out for minutes that stretched like hours, until the rest of his band came trampling up the hill in a noisy, grumbling crowd, clubs and crossbows raised, four deep. At that, Martin let out a short, scornful laugh that echoed off the treetops, and vanished into the underbrush. A moment later, they heard the clatter of hooves, and he was riding off at a gallop on the burgomaster’s own mule.

All the hunters pelted up to the hill crest together, and the high ground gave them an unobstructed view down a narrow, seemingly endless glade that stretched for miles ahead. Far, far below, they spotted Gerard and Margaret running for all they were worth, so tiny against the green grass they looked no bigger than dancing gnats, and Martin galloping after them, heels dug into the mule’s flanks, riding as if the hounds of hell were nipping at his heels. The hunters had been outwitted before they even realized they had fallen for a trick, and they would soon be outrun too.

A few simple words explain exactly how Martin’s gambit came together. We are all apt to chase clear causes behind coincidences, but coincidences are often deceptive. Everyone has seen a hare stumble over a bramble the very moment a musket goes off, raising a hunter’s hopes that he has struck his mark, only to dash them as the animal leaps up and streaks away unharmed. That is exactly what played out here: the burgomaster’s stubborn mule put her hoof straight down a rabbit burrow the very same instant the crossbow bolt whizzed harmlessly over the top of her head. She stumbled, reared, and fell hard, throwing both her riders clear. Gerard caught Margaret mid-fall to break her impact, but her weight and momentum dragged him right down beside her, and suddenly the whole party was sprawling winded in the dirt.

The docile mule was back on her feet in a trice, trembling all over. Martin staggered upright next, and glanced back to see only one lone hunter had crested the path behind them, far out of bowshot. That was when he sent the young lovers sprinting ahead on foot, while he hung back to check their pursuers exactly as we saw.

He galloped after them now, and when he finally caught up to the breathless pair after what felt like an endless chase, he boosted both Gerard and Margaret up onto the mule’s back at once, then loped along beside them until his own lungs burned too hard to keep the pace. Then he took his turn riding, letting the two of them run alongside to catch their breath. They rotated like that, so whoever was on their feet stayed fresh, and long before they even thought to slacken their speed, every sound of Dierich and his men, every trace of their hunt, had vanished hopelessly behind them. The crestfallen band of hunters trundled back through the woods eventually, to tend to their injured chief and mourn their prized dead bloodhound, their entire manhunt gone up in smoke.

Life and liberty are things we scarcely notice when they run smooth, as natural as breath itself. Only when the shadow of peril wraps around them do men grasp their true weight, and treasure every beat of unshackled hearts. This truth holds as true for them as it does for the sun—whose noon blaze is so familiar we barely pause to mark it, until dusk dips its light in topaz and spills it across the boughs of shadowed elms. The light is fainter then, yes, but the gloom gathered at its edge throws every spark into sharp, glowing relief.

So it was for Gerard and Margaret, creeping soft as shadows through the tangled woodland, every rustle of dry leaves making them flinch, every distant snap of twigs sending a jolt up their spines. The memory of baying hounds and the brutal shouts of their pursuers still hummed in their ears, but every step they took deeper into the quiet, sheltering trees wrapped them in a warm, throbbing joy they had never known in all their days of ease.

Presently Gerard spotted dark streaks of blood on Margaret’s bare ankles, and his blood ran cold. “Martin! Martin, quick—she’s hurt! The crossbow bolt struck her!” he cried, fumbling to steady her as she swayed. Margaret laughed soft to calm him, her cheeks flushed pink. “No, no, my love, not a scratch on me, I swear it.” Gerard’s hands trembled as he knelt to examine the stain. “Then what in God’s name is this red mark on your skin?”

Margaret blushed bright, twisting her hands together. “Don’t scold me, then,” she murmured. Gerard stared, bewildered. “When have I ever scolded you?” “Never, dearest Gerard. Well then—Martin said the hounds were tracking us by the scent of blood. I thought, if I smeared a little on my shoes, the hounds would follow my trail instead, and let you slip away free. So I took Martin’s knife and scratched my arm. Forgive me! Whose else could I use? Not yours, Gerard, never yours. You’ll forgive me, won’t you?” she pleaded, leaning into him, her voice soft and warm as a summer wind.

Gerard’s throat tightened so he could barely speak. “Let me see that scratch first,” he managed. He pulled back her sleeve, and his breath caught. “A scratch? This is a deep, cruel gash—you might have drained yourself for me!” He shuddered, his eyes swimming. The rough soldier Martin huffed a laugh from a few paces off: “Milksop, over a little nick and a drop of blood? Sicken at the sight of that, would you?” “Not a sea of blood,” Gerard gasped, “only hers. Oh Margaret, how could you be so reckless with your own life for me?”

Margaret smiled, her face soft with a love too big for words. “Silly Gerard,” she whispered, wrapping her cut arm tight around his neck. “As if I would not pour every drop of blood in my heart out for you, never mind a few from my arm.” The shock of how close they had come to being torn apart hit her then, and she wept into his shoulder, hot tears soaking his tunic, and he wept right there with her, clinging to her like he would never let go.

“And I must part from her,” he sobbed. “We two who love so dear—one to be in Holland, one in Italy. Ah me! Ah me!” Margaret cried fresh then, but silent, patient; her instinct for unselfishness kept her from voicing the grief that would only weigh heavier on Gerard when he had to leave.

Suddenly they stepped out onto a beaten bridle path, and Martin halted, hanging his head. “This is the road I told you of,” he said, nodding ahead. “The little hostelry is just over that rise.” Margaret and Gerard exchanged a terrified, heartbroken glance. Gerard drew Martin aside, his voice cracking. “Good Martin, watch over her for me. She is my wife, though I leave her behind. Here, take this gold—all the coin I set aside for my journey. She will never take it from me, but she will take it from you, won’t she? God, is that all I have to give her? Money? But poverty is a curse I will not let her bear. You will not let her want for anything, dear Martin? The burgomaster’s silver is all I need for the road.”

Martin clapped him on the shoulder, his gruff face softening. “Thou art a good lad, Gerard. No harm shall come to her, no want shall touch her. I care more for her little finger than the whole rest of the world, and even if she was nothing to me, I would be a father to her for your sake. Go with a stout heart, and God go with you, coming and going.” He turned his head away, no longer hiding how much the moment moved him.

Gerard stopped him before he could step back to Margaret. “Stay here, behind this thicket, I beg you. Turn your head away. I cannot bear anyone to see how I grieve to leave her.” And so Martin did not see the two young lovers kneel in the dust, renewing the sacred vows that cruel men had tried to tear asunder before Heaven. He did not see them cling together as if their two bodies were one, then try to step apart and fail, then cling again, like two drowning men clutching the last floating plank. But he heard Gerard sob, again and again, and Margaret let out soft, broken moans.

At last there was a hoarse, tearing cry, and the sound of boots pattering hard on the packed dirt road. Martin looked up. Gerard was running wild, both hands clasped over his head in desperate prayer, and Margaret tottered after him, palms outstretched as if begging for him not to go, her cheeks ashen, her eyes fixed on nothing. Martin caught her as she swayed, his arms around her, and spoke soft, comforting words—but her grief was too sharp to take them in, she only clung to his tunic tight, trembling all over at the sound of his voice. He lifted her onto the mule, wrapped his arm around her to hold her up, her once strong, boyish frame gone all soft and limp with grief, and led her slow and sad back home. She did not shed a tear, did not speak a single word. At the edge of the wood he helped her down, and bade her go across to her father’s cottage. She obeyed, numb as a statue. Martin set off for Rotterdam next—Sevenbergen was far too dangerous for him now.

Gerard, torn away from the woman he loved, moved like a man in a dream. He hired a horse and guide at the little wayside inn, and rode fast towards the German border. All his movements were mechanical, his senses blunted: trees, cottages, peasants passing by drifted past him like shapes seen through a thick veil. His guide spoke to him twice, and he did not answer. Only once he cried out, hoarse and raw: “Will we never be free of this hateful country?”

After hours of hard riding, they reached the brow of a steep hill, a small silver brook glinting at its foot. “Halt!” the guide called out, pointing across the valley. “That there is Germany, sir.” “Where?” “T’other side of that brook. No need to ride down, I reckon.”

Gerard dismounted without a word, and pulled the burgomaster’s purse from his girdle. As he fumbled to open it, the guide muttered, half-sulky: “Soon you’ll be out of that hateful country, like you said. Mind, the one you’re going to might not like you no better. But whatever you ran from, they can’t touch you once you cross that little brook.” A month before, those words would have earned him a sharp rebuke, maybe a cuff to the ear. Now they were idle wind to Gerard. He paid the guide in silence, and walked down the hill alone.

The brook babbled soft over glinting pebbles, varnished clear by the running water. He sat down, staring at them stupidly for a long minute, then cupped his hands and drank the cold water, then laved his hot, throbbing feet and hands in it. The cold woke him, sharp. He stood up, took a running leap, and cleared the brook, landing on German soil. The moment his boots touched the strange ground, he spun around to look back. “Farewell, ungrateful country!” he cried out. “But for her, I would leave you without a second thought—all my kin, my mother that bore me, my childhood playmates, my little home town. Farewell, fatherland! Welcome the wide world! Omne solum forti patria—every land is a home to the brave.” But the brave words died in his throat, his arms and legs turned weak as water, and he sank down on the foreign soil and sobbed bitter, tearing sobs.

When he had sat there bowed for a long while, he stood up, dashed the tears from his eyes like a man, and did not glance back once more to weaken his resolve. He stepped out onto the long road south. His great love, his heavy grief, left no room in his heart for small, petty fears. Compared to the agony of tearing himself away from Margaret, the thousand-mile walk to Italy in that rough, hard age felt like a small, trivial thing. He knew all nations welcomed strangers in their convents; thanks to his monk friends back home, and his own hunger for learning, he could speak almost every language he would need on that long journey. He told himself, “I will reach Rome soon, the sooner the better now.”

After he had walked a good league, he came to a crossroads, four country lanes winding and serpentine, that had confused many a local villager before. Gerard pulled out the small pocket dial Peter had given him, set it to the autumn sun, and steered straight for Rome, unhesitating, inexperienced as a young swallow flying south for the first time—only unlike the swallow, he was flying there all alone.

He had not travelled far along the sun-dappled rural lane when he rounded a hedge and came upon a small curious group. Two men in plain, sober wool suits leaned lazily on either side of a grazing horse, chatting idly to each other, while their master, clad in a glossy silk doublet, bright English green jerkin and hose that shone as smooth as a mole’s pelt, lay flat on his stomach in the warm afternoon sun, looking for all the world like some overgrown iridescent lizard. His flaming yellow velvet cloak had been carefully spread out over the horse’s loins, as if the steed was far more precious than the man sprawled unguarded in the dust.

“Is aught amiss here?” Gerard called out, pausing beside them.
“None that I know of,” one of the servants replied without shifting his weight.
“But your master lies there as still as a corpse. Are you not ashamed to let him grovel in the bare dirt?”
“Go on now, hard ground is the best cure for his sort of disorder,” the man laughed. “Sober up in a soft bed and you wake with a splitting headache. But leap up off cold packed earth and you’re as spry as a lark in spring. Eh, Ulric?”
“He speaks true, young man,” Ulric agreed warmly.
The simplicity of Gerard’s next question made the two servants snort out hoarse, rough laughter. “What? The gentleman is drunk?”
Ulric suddenly stopped laughing, narrowed his eyes, and stared Gerard up and down from head to toe very gravely. “Who are you, and where were you born, that you don’t know the Count is always dead drunk at this hour?” In an instant, Gerard found himself eyed as a suspicious stranger.
“I am a traveller, new to these parts,” Gerard said quickly. “But an honest man, who loves to learn what he does not know. I ask out of curiosity, not prying.”
“If you’re an honest man,” Ulric said shrewdly, “then pay us trinkgeld for the knowledge we’ve just given you.”
Gerard’s face fell blank for a moment, but he put on a brave face. “You shall have what little my lean purse can spare, if you will first tell me why you’ve taken his fine cloak off the man and laid it across the horse’s back.”
At the promise of coming coin, the two men immediately offered two competing explanations. The first was practical: if the Count woke suddenly (and he was a seasoned toper, apt to come to his senses in a single sharp jolt) to find his horse standing out in the cold sweating, while a good cloak lay unused nearby, he’d fly into a cursing rage and likely lay about him with his staff. The second was far more grand: a horse was a soft milksop that drank nothing but cold water, so it needed to be warmed from the outside. But a nobleman, full of good beer, carried a fire of inward heat that kept his skin warm, making a cloak nothing but useless, silly vanity.

Each man grew fiercely attached to his own theory, and since both had shared more than a little of their master’s drink that day, their voices rose higher and higher until the green-clad Count on the ground stopped snoring and began to growl. Neither noticed. Soon the argument turned physical, as most arguments did in that rough age. Hans, holding the bridle in his right hand, cuffed Ulric hard across the ear with his left. Ulric returned the blow twice over, his own right hand free, and the two banged away at each other over the horse’s mane, jostling and poking the poor beast until it reared backwards and brought its iron-shod hoof down right on the fleshy backside of the prostrate nobleman. The Count started up howling like a toad pricked by an angel’s spear, one hand clamped to his smarting rear, the other fumbling to draw his sword. The terrified servants dropped the bridle, the horse galloped off whinnying down the lane, the two men pelted after it screaming, and the green-clad nobleman chased after all three, stark raving mad, naked sword in his hand, bouncing from hedge to hedge in his zigzag headlong rush down the narrow road.

Gerard turned his back on the whole ridiculous scene and walked calmly south, glad he had no need to hand over the four tin farthings he’d pulled out ready for trinkgeld. His heart was too heavy, though, to even smile at the absurd drunken chaos he’d left behind.

The sun was already dipping low, and Gerard had been hoping in vain for hours to spot an inn along the road. Black heavy clouds rolled across the sky, and he quickened his pace almost to a run. It was no use: the rain burst down in torrents, drenching him to the skin, seeming to snuff out the last fading rays of the sun. He trudged on through the dark, unfamiliar land, shivering. “Fool that I was, to leave Margaret,” he murmured to himself.

The dark thickened fast as he entered a vast, ancient wood. Huge gnarled branches stretched across the narrow track, turning the path into an endless, pitch-black cave with a rugged, stony floor that made him stumble again and again. On he went, shivering, his stomach empty, his heart faint, until the wolves roused from their lairs and bayed all around the edges of the wood. His hair bristled on his scalp, but he tightened his grip on his oak cudgel, ready to sell his life dearly. There was no wind, and his straining ears caught the soft patter of light paws across fallen leaves, and the rustle of low branches as unseen creatures glided past him in the dark.

Then, in that sea of inky black, he spotted a bright fiery star bobbing close to the ground. He hailed it like he would his patron saint. “A candle! A candle!” he shouted, trying to run towards it, though the rough uneven ground slowed him down. At last, deep in the heart of the forest, he found a low cottage, candles glowing behind the windows, loud voices ringing from inside. He looked for a signboard, but there was none. “Not an inn, after all,” he thought sadly. “But what Christian would turn a dog out into this wood on a night like this?” He pushed the door open slowly and stuck his head in, then jerked it back as if he’d been slapped in the face, recoiling back into the rain and dark.

He’d peeked into a large, low-ceilinged room, dominated by a huge round clay stove that stretched all the way up to the rafters. Wet clothes hung drying on lines strung across the room, and even more were draped straight over the backs of the rustics huddled around the heat. Their garments, soaked through from the day’s rain and caked with years of accumulated grime, steamed thickly, belching out rank, unnameable odours. In one corner a large travelling family huddled, giving off the faint sickly smell of neglected, unwashed children. Garlic hung thick in every gap of the air, all the windows were closed, the central furnace blazed hot, and the breath of at least forty people filled the small space to bursting. They had just finished supper.

Gerard, like most artists, had sensitive senses, and the potent stench filled him with dismay. But the rain lashed him outside, and the light and heat were too tempting to resist. He crept back to the door again and again, like a moth singed by flame, until he realized the different smells did not fully mix: the sour family stench ruled two corners, the reeking odour of unwashed peasants hung thickest around the stove, and the sharp tang of garlic clustered around the loud group by the window. He slipped into a small corner right beside the door, the farthest possible from the thickest clouds of stench, but even there the heat and damp vapours circulated until the walls dripped. The soft home-raised novice felt something like a cold snake wind around his legs, his head grew heavy as lead, and he felt half choked, half drifting off to faint, all at once.
