He nearly swooned, but recovered, and resolved to turn back for Holland at the first peep of dawn. Faint with hunger, he asked the garlic-eating group if the house was not, after all, an inn.

“Whence do you come that you do not know the Star of the Forest?” the man replied, bewildered.
“I am a stranger. In my country, every inn has a sign hanging out front.”
“Droll country yours! Who needs a sign for a public house, when every soul for twenty miles round knows it?”

Too tired and faint to argue, Gerard asked for the landlord. The native’s contempt at his ignorance rose too high for words, and he just pointed to a middle-aged woman sitting on the other side of the oven, before turning to his friends to tell them what a strange outlandish animal had wandered in. All the loud voices in the room fell silent one by one, and every eye turned to stare at Gerard, studying him like a new, exotic specimen. The landlady sat on a chair a few inches higher than everyone else, picking plumes out of a huge heap of feathers, littering the floor ankle-deep with loose quills that added a stuffy, drowsy haze to the already thick air.

Gerard asked if he could have something to eat. She stared at him in astonishment. “Supper ended more than an hour ago.”
“But I had no supper at all, good dame.”
“Is that my fault? You were welcome to show up for it same as anyone else.”
“I was lost in the dark, a stranger, forced to linger on the road against my will.”
“What have I to do with that? Everyone knows the Star of the Forest serves supper from six till eight. Show up before six, you eat well. Show up before eight, you get whatever Heaven sends. Show up after eight, you get a clean bed, a stirrup cup, or a horn of cow’s milk at dawn.”

Gerard’s face fell. “Then may I go to bed at once, dame?” he said grumpily. “It does no good to sit up wet and fasting, and the old saying goes ‘he who sleeps, sups well enough’.”
“The beds are not here yet,” she replied. “You will sleep when the rest do. Inns are not built for just one man.”

Gerard was stunned. What on earth did she mean, the beds were not here yet? He dared not ask, every word he had spoken so far had the whole room staring at him like a freak. He leaned against the wall and sighed loudly, and a ripple of quiet titter went around the watching company. “So this is Germany,” he thought. “A great big country right next to Holland. Give me small nations, any day.” He consoled himself that this would be his first and last night in the land.

An elbow jabbed sharply into his ribs. He turned, and saw a woman in the far corner beckoning him over. He walked towards her gingerly, as if her outstretched finger was pulling him across the floor with a gut-string. “Hold the child a moment,” she said cheerfully, and plopped her squalling bairn right into Gerard’s arms. He stood frozen, the child a heavy lump of lead in his hands, his face stretched in perfect comical horror. The whole room burst into loud, long laughter at his expression.

“Never mind them,” the woman said, still smiling. “They know no better, how should they, bred and born in the middle of a wood?” She rummaged through her bundle of clothes, and pulled out a small tin plate and a dried, pressed pudding, taking her child back with one arm and holding the food out to Gerard with the other. “Go set it by the stove to warm. You’re too young to go to bed fasting.”

Gerard thanked her warmly, but hesitated when he saw the group of unwashed rustics blocking the stove door. The landlady noticed, calmly set down her pile of feathers, and came over to move the men out of the way as easily as someone shifting furniture, her face completely impassive. “Turn about is fair play,” she said. “You’ve been dry for ten minutes now.” The men, who had gone from steaming to baking hot by the fire, trundled away grumbling, and Gerard set his pudding to warm, standing so close to the stove his damp clothes burst into steam.

The door flew open, and a farmhand hurled a bundle of straw into the room with his pitchfork. Another, and another, followed, until the whole floor was strewn like a clean farmyard. They layered the straw in rings around the stove, like seats in an arena, and in a moment every single person in the room had laid down to sleep. The beds had arrived.

Gerard pulled his warm pudding off the stove, and found it absolutely delicious. The woman who had given it to him, already curled up on her straw bed, beckoned him over again. He went to her side, and she whispered that the landlady had waited to let him warm his food. He hurried to finish the rest of his meal, then went over and knelt to help her pick up the loose feathers scattered all over the floor. “I do not know where you come from,” she said, her distrust fading into warmth, “but you were well brought up. I’ll wager you had a good mother.” She said a quick blessing over the whole house before she vanished to her own bed, and Gerard dragged his straw to the very edge of the room, right by the door, the best spot he could get, reserved for the last arrival. It was a blessing, not a punishment: he lay right on the shore of the thick stench and heat, instead of drowning in its middle by the stove.

He was just drifting off to sleep when the farmhand woke him, striding over all the sleeping bodies to press a huge oaken mug of beer under his nose. “She bade me say one good turn deserves another. Here is your nightcap.” Gerard took a deep drink, and made a wry face: the beer was muddy, with a strange sharp medicinal tang he had never tasted before in Holland. “Drink it all!” the farmhand reproached him.
“Enough is as good as a feast,” Gerard said. The farmhand pitied the strange traveller who would leave good liquor in his mug, took the mug from him, and drained the rest to the dregs.

Gerard turned his face to the wall, pulled up two handfuls of clean straw, bored a little hollow in it with his finger, and sheathed his nose deep inside to block out the smell. Soon the whole room was asleep: men, maids, wives, and children all higgledy-piggledy, snoring in a dozen different keys like an orchestra slowly tuning its instruments. His body lay on straw in the German forest, but his spirit was already miles away, back in Sevenbergen with Margaret.

When he woke at dawn, most of the guests had already left. He paid the landlady her asking price of two pfenning, barely an English halfpenny, and gave the farmhand a small extra trinkgeld. The man saw Gerard staring longingly at a foaming milk pail he had just brought fresh from the cow, and hoisted it straight to his lips. “Drink your fill, man,” he said, refusing Gerard’s offer of payment, saying no man should have to pay for a skinful of fresh milk. At the door, Gerard found his kind benefactress and her broad-chested artisan husband, and tried to press a small creutzer coin into her hand for the pudding. She pushed his hand away gently, colouring faintly. “What do you take me for? We are travellers and strangers, same as you. We owe kindness to anyone in the same plight.” Gerard blushed and stammered his apologies. The big husband grinned, and said “Give the vixen a kiss for her pudding, and call it even.” Gerard obeyed, kissed her cheek softly, and the two wished him God speed. He never saw them again for the rest of his life.

The sun had just risen, raindrops on the leaves glinting like diamonds, the air fresh and sharp. Gerard strode south, and completely forgot his half-hearted resolve to turn back for Holland. He walked eight leagues that day, and in the afternoon spotted a huge stone building with an enormous arched gateway and a smaller postern gate set in its side. “A monastery!” he cried joyfully. “I will go no further, lest I fare worse.” He knocked at the postern, stated where he came from and where he was bound, and was admitted at once, led to the spacious high-walled guest chamber where pilgrims and travellers were fed and lodged free of charge by the monks’ charity.

Soon the chapel bell tinkled for vespers. Gerard stepped into the convent church, and heard the service sung so exquisitely it sounded like the choir of heaven itself. The only thing that marred his rapture was the thought that Margaret was not there beside him to hear it, and he sighed bitterly mid-hymn. Supper was plain but wholesome, abundant food and good home-brewed convent beer laid out for him and his fellow travellers. At an early hour they were ushered into a large dormitory, and since the number of guests was small, each had a proper truckle bed, covered in soft sheepskins tanned with the fleece still on. A monk, struck by Gerard’s youth and earnest face, questioned him, and soon drew out all his plans to travel to Rome alone. When the monks learned he had been raised in a cloister himself, he became a favoured guest. The next morning they showed him the whole convent, made him stay for dinner in the refectory, pricked out a safe route for him on a slip of parchment, and the prior gave him a silver guilder to help him on his way. “Join the first honest group of travellers you meet,” he advised. “Do not face all the manifold perils of the road alone.”
“Perils?” Gerard thought to himself, surprised.

That evening he reached a small straggling town, and found its only inn. It had no sign hanging out, but he was now wise to local customs, and spotted it at once by the old coats of arms painted on its walls, left there by generations of distinguished nobles who had stopped to sleep there over the centuries. The place looked more like a mausoleum than an inn: nothing moved, no sound came from inside. Gerard hammered on the great oak main door, no answer. He shouted, no reply. He shouted louder, and at last a small round hole in the wall opened, a man’s head poked out cautiously like a tortoise from its shell, stared at Gerard stolidly, and said not a single word.
“Is this an inn?” Gerard asked, half smirking.

Denys lunged to catch Gerard mid-fall from the tree bough, slowing his plunge just enough that he didn’t crack his skull against the hard packed dirt—but what truly saved the young clerk from breaking a neck or limb was the great shaggy she-bear, still gasping out her last breaths, whose furry carcass caught his head and shoulders full force. Denys hauled him off the creature in a panic, but it was unnecessary: the bear’s limbs quivered and her chest heaved, but she was as harmless as a startled leveret, and within a minute she breathed her last. The practical old soldier propped Gerard against her warm, pelted flank for a soft cushion, fanning his pale face with his wool cap till color seeped back into his cheeks.

Gerard roused slowly, disoriented, and when his bleary senses registered thick bear fur pressing all around him, he scrambled yelling behind the nearest oak, gasping for air.
“Courage!” Denys called, cackling. “Le diable est mort—the devil himself is dead and gone.”
“Is it dead? Quite dead?” Gerard peeked out from behind the trunk, his courage frayed thin, the cold shiver of delayed shock still racing through his bones.
“Behold!” Denys plucked the brute’s ear playfully, pried her slack jaws wide to stick his whole head inside, and pulled half a dozen more ridiculous, taunting antics—until Gerard doubled over and retched, the iron tang of bear’s blood in the air turning his stomach.
Denys roared with laughter. “What ails you now? And why did you tumble off your perch the very second we’d won the fight?”
“I swooned, I think.”
“And for what cause? Green girls faint at the sight of a man’s wink, but they choose a soft parlor to do it in. Did you ever hear of a woman fainting halfway up an oak tree?”
“She splattered her nasty blood all over me! The smell overpowered me, I swear—faugh, I cannot stand the sight of blood.”
“I’ll not doubt that for a moment.”
“Look what a mess she’s made of my tunic!”
“A mess of her blood, not yours. I pity any foe foolish enough to try to put you to the test of spilling yours.”
“Brave talk, Maitre Denys! I saw you pale as your own linen shirt cowering at the foot of that tree before we struck.”
“Let us make distinctions!” Denys flushed, prickling a little. “It is permitted to tremble for the sake of a friend, is it not?”

Gerard said nothing in reply, but flung his arms tight around Denys’s neck, the rush of relief and gratitude spilling over into unmanly tears. The gruff soldier squirmed, flustered. “There now—was ever a creature so soft as a green youth? I love thee, little milksop, but enough of that—wait, what new folly is this, kneeling in the dirt?”
“Denys, ought we not give thanks to God, who spared both our lives against such terrible odds?” Gerard bowed his head, praying aloud, and before he had finished his petition Denys was kneeling quiet beside him, hands crossed over his chest the way his Breton mother had taught him at mass, his face solemn and long. When they stood, Gerard was glowing.
“Good Denys, Heaven will reward that piety of yours.”
“Bah! I did it out of politeness, to please thee, little one,” Denys huffed, though his eyes crinkled. “It was a fine, orderly prayer, too—scarcely a bishop could have delivered it better. Our evensong is sung, the saints are on our side—marchons, let’s be off.”
They’d barely taken two steps when Denys stopped short. “Wait—the cub!”
“Oh no, never mind the cub!” Gerard groaned.
“You are right. It’s late, we’ve wasted hours climbing trees, tumbling off them, swooning, heaving up our dinners, and praying—and the she-bear is far too heavy to haul. Besides, her mate will be coming looking for that cub soon enough, and we’ve no taste for another fight. Wait—what is this? You are wounded! You are bleeding, man, miserable fool that I am!”
“Not I,” Gerard protested.
“You are! You feel no pain for yourself, you soft thing,” Denys gasped, his eyes glistening, dropping to his knees to yank up Gerard’s hose and see the deep, gory gash the bear’s claw had raked across his calf. “Quick, quick, before the muscle stiffens!” He hauled Gerard upright to hurry him along.
“Who is making a great coil over nothing now?” Gerard asked, calm as you please.
Denys didn’t reply directly. “Mark this: I have a bad heart, and a worse tongue. You saved my life back there, and I sneered at you for a novice in war, called you a milksop when you fainted from the pain of that gash and I thought you’d swooned from fear. I was a fool, once, too, just like you.”
“Denys, you lie,” Gerard said softly.
“Thank you for saying so, little one,” Denys mumbled, remorseful.

They hadn’t walked more than a few furlongs before the wound in Gerard’s leg seized up, stiff and burning, until he could barely put his toe to the ground without screaming. At last he sank helpless in the dirt, groaning. “Let me lie down and die, this pain is intolerable.”
Denys argued that it was afternoon, the frosty autumn night was coming on fast, and cold and hunger were far worse companions than a sore leg—besides, the bear that had threatened them was well and truly dead. Gerard leaned his whole weight on his axe to hobble onward, but soon his strength gave out entirely. Denys dragged him into the thick of the trees, pressed his crossbow and a handful of bolts into his hands, and bade him lie quiet. “Shoot any ill-looking fellow that comes within twenty paces without calling out, do not parley. Honest men stay to the road; only fools stop to talk to knaves in the woods.” He snatched up Gerard’s axe and ran off—not toward Dusseldorf, as Gerard expected, but back the way they had come.

Gerard lay there aching, his thoughts drifting first to Rome, the distant city that had felt so near when he left Sevenbergen, now leagues and leagues away, then to Margaret. The thought of her face, of holding her hand one day and telling her all the wild adventures he’d survived just to get to her, soothed the pain till he lay smiling faint and soft, despite the stinging wound. He’d been there more than two hours when shouts broke out through the trees, and a thud sent an arrow quivering into the oak trunk not three feet from his head.
More missiles rattled through the branches, battle-cries echoed off the wood’s high boughs, then he heard thunderous hoofbeats, fiercer shouts mingling with shrieks and groans, and strange, thunderous cracking booms that died away in echoing pops, red flames spitting through the leaves, and thick sulphur smoke drifting over his face. Then all went silent.
Gerard shuddered. “What has become of Denys? Oh, my friend, my friend, why did you leave me?”

Just before sunset, Denys stumbled back, almost collapsing under the weight of the full heavy bear pelt slung over his shoulders. Gerard greeted him with a burst of joy that made the gruff soldier blink.
“I thought I would never see you again, Denys! Were you in that terrible battle that raged through the wood just now?”
“Battle? What battle?”
“The fight of men or fiends, with arrows and thunderous booms and smoke!” Gerard described every last detail, vivid as a painted manuscript.
Denys patted his back indulgently. “You are a fine storyteller, and fever makes the imagination run wild. Once I lay in a cart shed with a cracked skull, and saw two whole armies maneuver and fight for an hour on a patch of ground no bigger than my boot. It was the fever, nothing more.”
“You do not believe me? The arrows whizzed over my head—look!” Gerard pointed to the long arrow stuck in the oak.
Denys peered at it, and whistled. “That is an English longbow shaft, three feet long. No other archers draw their bow all the way to their ear, only the English. That is no fever dream. There was a battle, right enough. But my duke has no quarrel hereabouts, it is none of our business. Let us make our bed.” He scraped up a great heap of dry leaves, laid Gerard on it, draped the thick bear skin over both of them fur-side in, and they were soon as warm as fresh bread, fast asleep.

Long before dawn, Gerard shook Denys awake. “I am starving, I will die of hunger.”
“Go back to sleep! Who sleeps, dines, they say.”
“I am far too hungry to sleep,” Gerard snapped.
“Then we march,” Denys said, yawning indulgently. He cut the bear’s two ears off, rolled them in a scrap of the pelt, and they set off down the road, Gerard leaning on his axe, Denys propping him up on the other side, limping slow.
Soon the moon rose, and they saw the end of the wood not far ahead, with Dusseldorf only a league beyond. At the treeline they halted, staring at a sight that made their skin prickle. Two tall white wooden pillars stood a few paces apart, with a dark crossbeam strung between them, and dozens of dark figures dangling from ropes tied to the beam, swaying slowly in the breeze.
“I will not go a step further till I know what this is,” Gerard whispered, terrified. “Saints’ effigies? Or robbers lying in wait? They do not stand on anything, Denys—let us turn back till daylight, this is no natural sight.”
Denys peered long and hard. “They are men. But men that will never hurt us. Don’t look at their feet—look above their heads.”
Gerard lifted his eyes, and saw the crossbeam, the thick snake-like ropes, the hanged corpses dangling from them, their ropes creaking soft in the wind. A small fire burned right under the gibbet, and a lone man in a countryman’s clothes, a stiff Brunswick three-cornered hat on his head, was huddled asleep beside it, his axe glinting red in the firelight.
Denys heaped more wood on the fire. Gerard seized the sleeping man’s axe and sat tight on it, his own weapon in hand, while Denys ran two sticks through the bear’s ears and held them over the flame to toast. “The burgomaster of Dusseldorf would give us a rix-dollar for these ears to prove the bear is dead,” he said. “But a lean purse is better than an empty stomach.”
“Unhappy man!” Gerard gasped, shuddering as one of the corpses swayed and the rope creaked loud. “How can you eat here, under these poor wretches?”
“Where the fire burns, the meat roasts, and where the meat roasts, you eat it—roast meat travels worse than any other food.”

The sleeping man woke up, stared at them, and made a move to run for the bushes. Denys levelled his crossbow at his head, and the man fell to his knees. He crawled back to the fire slowly, pale as a sheet, and shared his bread, his roasted kid, and a full two-gallon leather bottle of rich Rhenish wine with the two travellers, too scared to protest. He got drunk fast, and babbled out the whole story: the hanged men were his old robber band, who had ambushed what they thought was a group of rich merchants from Dusseldorf, only to find they were Archbishop of Cologne’s soldiers in disguise, wearing hidden armor under their gowns, armed with the new fire-spitting handguns that shot lead balls. The soldiers had ambushed them, killed half the band in seconds, hanged the rest on this gibbet, and left him behind to watch the bodies so the crows would not peck them apart before dawn.

Denys told him to support Gerard’s weight as they walked toward Dusseldorf, and the man obeyed, too scared to argue. When the distant outline of Dusseldorf’s watchtower loomed on the horizon, the robber halted, and said he would rather they killed him right there than drag him inside the town gates, where the hangman would be waiting for him. Denys let him go, gave him back his axe, and even tossed him a few silver groshen. But the robber still lingered, and begged Gerard, the clerk, to say a prayer for him, for he did not know a single one by heart.
Gerard frowned, sharp and irritable from the pain of his wound, and asked him if it was true that Rhenish thieves murdered innocent travellers just to avoid being caught. The robber shrugged, and said the harsh laws were to blame: if a thief was hanged for stealing a purse, he had no choice but to cut the traveller’s throat, for dead men tell no tales.
Gerard doffed his bonnet, and recited a loud, blunt Latin prayer that the man be hanged soon and quickly, alongside his former companions, for the public good, to the glory of the just God, amen. The robber, who did not know a word of Latin, thanked him warmly, satisfied he had received a fine, powerful holy prayer, and wandered back into the woods.

The two friends limped onward in silence, till Gerard spoke at last, soft and thoughtful.
“That dying she-bear saved both our lives, back there in the wood. By God’s own grace.”

The afternoon light slanted thin and gold through the leaded panes of the northern inn room the next day. Gerard’s fevered lightheadedness had burned off, leaving him sharp-tempered, thrumming with odd, restless fancies, until at last he begged Denys to fetch him a lemon to suck. The rough old soldier, softened by weeks of tender care for his friend into something as fussy and doting as a grey-haired grandparent, sprang to his feet at once. “Set thy mind at rest,” he laughed, “thou shalt have a lemon faster than a quart pot of ale can be drained dry,” and off he trotted to ransack every shop in the town for the rare southern fruit.

Lemons were not half so common in 15th century northern climes as they are now, and Denys was gone far longer than Gerard expected. He was growing thoroughly impatient when the door at last creaked open — but it was no Denys on the threshold.

A stately, imposing figure stepped softly into the room: an old gentleman clad in a long, sober gown trimmed with rich sable fur, cherry-red hose, and sharp-pointed poulaine shoes, a slender sword at his hip sheathed in tooled morocco leather. A starched ruff bit deep into his neck, held stiff in sharp furrows by a hidden wooden rebato framework, a four-cornered fur-bordered cap sat square on his head, and a majestic flowing white beard spilled over his chest. Gerard needed no telling his trade, save for the sword at his side this was the full formal dress of a leading physician, and a small boy trailed at his heels hefting a wide wicker basket where glass phials, lint, and sharp surgical tools peeped openly over the rim. The old man glided to the bedside, and murmured soft and sotto voce, “How fares it with thee, my son?”

Gerard thanked him, and told him his wound ached very little now, but his throat was parched dry and his head felt heavy as lead.

“A wound? No one spoke to me of a wound. Let me see it, then. Aye, aye — a fine clean bite. That mastiff had sound, sharp teeth to tear this out, I’ll warrant.” The doctor’s sympathy seemed to drift straight past Gerard to the imaginary dog he had invented on the spot. “This must be cauterized at once, or else thou’lt soon start shrinking from water, and kicking and thrashing under our hands in fever. This is a terrible year for raving curs, and one has done thee harm — but we shall outwit him yet. Boy, go heat the iron!”

“Wait, sir,” Gerard cut in gently, “it was no dog that hurt me, it was a bear.”

“A bear! Young man,” the doctor rebuked him severely, “think what thou sayest. It is no jest to mock a man of art who brings grey hairs and forty years of study to heal thee. A bear, quotha! Hadst thou dissected a tenth as many bears as I have, drawn their teeth just to keep my hand steady, thou wouldst know no bear’s jaw could ever leave such a silly, trifling wound. I tell thee it was a dog — and since thou pressest me on the point, it was no great large hound, neither, but one of those rabid little curs that plague every street these days, snatching at every man’s leg and felling their victims — were it not for me and my learned brethren, who stop the mischief dead with knife and hot iron.”

“Alas, sir, I never said it was a bear’s jaw that bit me,” Gerard protested. “I said it was a bear — it was his paw that scratched me.”

“And why didst thou not tell me that at once?”

“Because thou wouldst not stop talking long enough to let me.”

“Never hide anything from your leech, young man,” the doctor continued, a great lover of the sound of his own voice and one of the very worst listeners in all of Europe. “Well, this is bad business. All hard, horny growths on animals — the claws of tigers, panthers, badgers, cats, bears, the antlers of deer, even the nails of humans, especially little children — are steeped in the direst poison. Thou wouldst far rather have been bitten by a common cur than gored by a bull, or struck by a stag’s antler, or scratched by a bear. Still, I shall make thee a drawing poultice for thy leg. Meantime, we must cool thy whole body: put out thy tongue! Good. Fever. Let me feel thy pulse — good. Fever. I ordain bloodletting, and at once.”

“Flebotomy? That is bloodletting, is it not?” Gerard hummed. “Well, no matter, if it will surely cure me, for I will not lie idle stuck here in this bed.” The doctor assured him bloodletting was infallible, especially for his condition.

“Hans, go fetch all the things we need, and I will entertain the patient meantime with sound reasoning.”

The man of art then explained to Gerard that when the body fell ill, the blood grew hot, distempered, and more or less poisonous; draw off a portion of that bad fluid, and Nature would be forced to make new, purer blood to fill its place. Bleeding, he declared, was both a cooler and a purifier, a specific cure for every disease that existed — for all diseases were febrile, no matter what quack empirics might claim otherwise.

“Think not,” he added warmly, “that any fool barber can do this right, just because he can open a vein (though not all of them can close it again after). The art is to know exactly which vein to open for which illness. Only last week they brought me a man tormented with earache. I bled him in the right thigh, and his earache vanished straight away. By the by, he died a few days later. Another man came to me with toothache. I bled him behind the ear, and relieved him in the blink of an eye. He too, as it happens, died not long after. I bled our town bailiff between thumb and forefinger for his rheumatism. Next week he came back to me with a raging headache and drumming in his ears, held his hand out over the basin ready to be bled again — but I laughed at his folly, and bled him in the left ankle sore against his will, and made his head as light as a dried nut.”

Wandering off from his immediate subject, as all men passionate about their art will, the learned physician went on to hold forth:
“Know, young man, that two great schools of medicine are fighting for mastery across all of Europe right now. The Arabian school, whose ancient oracles are Avicenna, Rhazes, Albucazis, and whose modern revivers are Chauliac and Lanfranc. And then the Greek school, whose modern champions are Bessarion, Platinus, and Marsilius Ficinus, but whose first great masters were the very gods of healing themselves: Phoebus, Chiron, Aesculapius and his sons Podalinus and Machaon, Pythagoras, Democritus, Praxagoras who first named the arteries, and Dioctes, ‘who first gave his full attention to the reading of urine.’ All these taught their pupils by word of mouth. Then came Hippocrates, eighteenth in direct line from Aesculapius, and we have his writings still. To him we owe the very idea of the vital principle. He invented the bandage, and first tapped the chest to drain fluid from dropsy. Above all else, he dissected — though only quadrupeds, for the brutal prejudices of pagan common folk would never let a human body fall under the knife of science. Then came Aristotle, who gave us the aorta, the largest blood vessel in the human body.”

“Surely, sir,” Gerard objected humbly, “the Almighty made every part inside our bodies, not Aristotle, nor any pagan Greek man.”

“Child, of course He made the thing itself! But Aristotle did far more: he gave us the name for it, showed us where it was, told us what it did. But young men will always argue. The next great light was Galen, who studied at Alexandria, then the very home of all science. He grew frustrated with only dissecting quadrupeds, so he dissected apes, for they are closer to man, and bled them as freely as a Trojan warrior. Then came Theophilus, who gave us the nerves, the lacteal vessels, and the pia mater.”

This was too much for Gerard. “I cannot lie still and hear it said that mortal man gave us parts of the body that Adam our father received straight from the Lord, who made him from clay, and us his sons.”

“Did ever you hear such perversity?” The doctor’s face flushed bright red. “Who is the true giver of a thing to man? He who hides it deep in the dark recesses of the flesh where no man can see it, or the learned sage who reveals it to your understanding, so that your mind is enriched with knowledge of it? True possession is nothing but comprehension. Art thou answered?”

“I am silenced, sir.”

“And that is all for the better, for garrulous fevered patients are impossible to cure. I say then that Eristratus gave us the cerebral nerves and the milk vessels — nay, more, he invented the operation for cutting bladder stones, whatever you may say. Then came another whose name I forget, you have perturbed me so with your petty little objections. Then came Ammonius, the man who invented crushing stones in the bladder without cutting. And here comes Hans with the basin, to stop your tongue. Blow on your chafing dish, boy, and hand me the basin. Good. The Arabians? What are they, but a new sect who stumbled on the old Greek writings around the year 1000, and read them all wrong, having no light of their own? Their false prophet Mahound, an impostor in science as he was in religion, strictly forbade them to dissect even the lowliest animals — and he who takes anatomy from medicine ‘takes the sun from the world,’ as Cicero well said. Do not wonder at my passion, good youth: when the public good is at stake, a little anger is civic, humane, and honorable. Only lately a pestilent Arabist empiric has settled in this very town, no knowledge of anatomy, can scarce tell Greek from Hebrew, and he has stolen half my patients already, and I tremble for the rest. Stretch out thy ankle. And thou, Hans, breathe on the coals.”

It was at this exact moment that Denys burst through the door, the lemons in his hand, and stopped short, staring. “What sport is this?” he asked, lifting his eyebrows high.

Gerard flushed a little, and told him the learned doctor was planning to bleed him, then cauterize the wound. That was all.

“Aye, indeed — and what is that urchin over there blowing hot coals for?”

“What else can it be,” the doctor said to Gerard, “but to cauterize the vein once we open it and let the poisoned blood out? It is the only safe way. Avicenna does recommend tying the vein shut with a ligature, but he never once explains how it is to be done — I doubt he knew himself, nor any of the spawn of Ishmael. For my part, I put no faith in such tricky, half-baked tricks. Remember this for a certainty: whatever an Arab or Arabist claims is right, must of necessity be wrong.”

“Oh, I see what the coals are for now,” Denys said. “Art thou fool enough to let him press hot iron to thy living flesh? Hast thou ever held thy little finger in a candle flame for ten seconds? This will go on for minutes. Art not content to burn in purgatory after thou art dead? Must thou needs taste its torments ahead of time, right here?”

“I never thought of that,” Gerard said gravely. “The good doctor spoke of cautery, not burning — it is all the same, I suppose, but cautery does not sound nearly so fearful a word.”

“Imbecile! That is their whole trick, to wrap plain men up in dark, fancy words until hissing flesh teaches them what they really meant. Now listen to what I have seen with my own eyes. When a soldier bleeds from a wound on the battlefield, these leeches say, ‘Fever. Bleed him!’ and so they drain the blood that the wound spared him, the blood he needs to fight the coming weakness. Hundreds of tall, strong fellows I have seen bled and pricked right out of the world. But if by luck they are wounded where no surgeon can reach them? Then they live. I should never have outlived that battle in Brabant if it had not been for the lucky mischance that no chirurgeon found me before the frost clotted my bleeding wounds. A surgeon would have pricked one more hole in my body with his lance, drained my last drop of blood out, and my soul right after it. That is why I place no trust in them: what can kill a hardened veteran can certainly kill a soft, gentle clerk like thee.”

“That sounds like plain common sense,” Gerard sighed languidly. “But there is no need to shout so loud. I was not born deaf, and my ears are sharp enough just now.”

“Common sense? A very brute common sense indeed!” the bad-listening doctor shouted. “Why, this is a soldier, a man whose trade is to kill, not cure!” He switched to fluent, harsh French. “Woe to you, unlearned oaf, if you stand between a physician and his patient! And woe to you, misguided youth, if you listen to that man of blood.”

“Much obliged to you for the compliment,” Denys bowed with mock politeness. “But I am an honest man, and I will not rob thee of thy trade name. I kill a man now and then, it is true — but you slay a score for every one of mine. I spill a spoonful of blood, you spill a whole tubful. The world is always fooled by fine shows. We soldiers rattle about with long swords, making noise, and make two enemies for every man we kill — but you smooth gownsmen, with soft phrases and hidden lancets, you are the ones who thin out the human race.”

“A sick chamber is no place for foolery,” the physician cried.

“No, nor is it a place for bawling at the top of your lungs,” Gerard peevishly corrected him.

“Come, young man,” the doctor said, softening his tone to be kind, “be reasonable. Every man must be trusted in his own art. My whole life has been given over to healing. I studied at Montpellier, the greatest school in all France, and therefore all of Europe. There I learned divination by pulse, divination by excrement, pathology, therapeutics, and greater than all of them, anatomy. As disciples of Hippocrates and Galen, we had opportunities those ancient men never dreamed of. Goodbye to quadrupeds, apes, pagan ignorance, and Mohammedan nonsense! We paid the churchwardens, shook down the gallows, snuck into graveyards at dead of night, driven by nothing but love of science and our fellow man. The Paris authorities all had orders to wink at our work, and wink they did! The good king himself helped us: twice a year he sent us a living criminal condemned to death, and told us ‘do with him as science requires, dissect him alive if you think fit.’”

“By Herod’s liver and Nero’s bowels, he will make me ashamed of the land that bore me if he praises it one second more!” Denys roared at the top of his voice.

Gerard yelped a little, clapped his fingers over his ears — then pulled them right out again, and shouted back just as loud, “Thou great roaring blaspheming bull of Bashan, hold thy noisy tongue!”

Denys’s face softened at once, he looked properly contrite.

“Tush, petty fellow,” the doctor waved a hand over Denys as if he was training a pointer dog to lie down, completely unruffled. “We very seldom dissected the living criminal all the way through, only bits and pieces. Mostly we inoculated them with whatever interesting diseases were going around at the time, of course picking the most fascinating ones.”

“Which means the filthiest,” Denys whispered meekly.

“Then we watched every stage of the disease right through to its natural end.”

“Which means until the poor rogue died,” Denys whispered again, still meek.

“And now, my poor suffering lad, who deserves thy confidence more? This honest soldier with his youthful ignorance and silly prejudices, or a greybeard loaded with the gathered wisdom of hundreds of years?”

“That means,” Denys burst out impatiently, “wilt thou believe what a jackdaw in a long gown heard from a starling in a long gown, who heard it from a jay, who heard it from a magpie, who heard it from a popinjay — or wilt thou believe what I, a man with nothing to gain from lying, have seen with my own two eyes? That fevered men who get bled die, and fevered men left to rest live? Wait — who sent for this bloodsucking leech? Didst thou?”

“Not I. I thought thou hadst.”

“Nay,” the doctor explained, “the innkeeper told me a stranger was lying sick in his house, so I said to myself ‘a poor soul who needs my art’ and came at once.”

“That was the act of a good Christian, sir,” Gerard said gently.

“Act of a good bloodhound!” Denys snorted contemptuously. “Art thou so green thou dost not know all innkeepers are in league with these leeches, who pay them a toll for every patient they trick? Whatever thou payest this old man for stealing thy lifeblood, the innkeeper takes a third of it for betraying thee to him. And no sooner does thy blood run down the stairs in that basin than he will smell or see it, and send straight for the undertaker to get another third of that fee too. He dare not wait for the doctor to go down and bespeak the undertaker first, or he would lose his cut. Am I not right, old Red and Black? Say it!”

“Denys, Denys, who taught thee to think so ill of all mankind?” Gerard sighed.

“Mine own eyes, that never let themselves be gulled by fine words, watching what men actually do across every land I have ever traveled.”

The doctor cleverly ducked the personal insult to turn the conversation back to his credibility. “

The good physician trundled home and told his housekeeper he was in agonies from “a bad burn.” Those were his exact words. For as in all matters of phlogistic humours, so in every other small cruelty of human nature: we do not hesitate to cauterize our neighbour’s fingers for petty gain, but how we wail and coddle our own burnt ones. His housekeeper slathered him with soft, mild old wives’ salve gentle as new milk, and he submitted meek as a lamb to her care—for his only priority in this hour was to be cured quickly enough to carry out his schemes. He scribbled out a full bill for every phial Gerard had shattered on his floor, then marched straight to the local magistrate to swear an oath: the two strange travellers, strangers to the township and deeply indebted to him, planned to flee before the sun set that very day.

Alas, it was his unluckiest hour. His sincere, carefully laid plan to perjure himself to lock the pair away failed, baffled by a circumstance he had never foreseen, nor even thought possible. He had spoken nothing but the unvarnished, absolute truth. On a sworn affidavit.

The officers arrived at The Silver Lion to find the birds had already flown. They picked up a tip from the wharf workers at the river, and set off hot-foot up the east bank in close pursuit.

The friends had escaped this fate thanks entirely to Denys’s sharp wits. He had laughed so hard at the quack’s discomfiture his sides ached, shouted his favourite battle-cry three times as a charm, then suddenly went stone sober and told Gerard Dusseldorf was no place to linger. “That old babbler went far too unnaturally quiet for a man who wouldn’t stop yammering ten minutes prior,” he pointed out. “We’re strangers here, the bailiff is his old drinking buddy, and we’ll be locked in a stinking dungeon for assaulting a Dusseldorf dignitary before five more minutes pass. Are you strong enough to hobble the short way to the water’s edge? Once there, we need only lie down in a boat instead of a bed—what odds is that to us?”

“Odds, Denys? Untold, all in favour of the boat. I burn for Rome, for Rome is my road back to Sevenbergen. We’ll lie in that boat, but *on* the Rhine, the famous, cool, refreshing Rhine. I can already feel its breezes on my face; the very sight will cure this silly little hop-o’-my-thumb fever of mine. Away, away at once!”

Seeing his excitable friend so fired up, Denys settled their bill with the landlord in two quick shakes, and they hurried to the wharf. To their dismay, they learned the public passage barge had left half an hour prior, and no other would sail for the rest of the afternoon. But after pestering a dozen passersby and drawing a small curious crowd, they secured a private passage offer from an old boatman and his two strapping sons.

A bystander snickered at the small craft. “The Rhine current runs far too strong for three oars alone to fight.”

“Then my comrade and I will help row,” put in the feverish invalid Gerard.

“No need, lad,” the old boatman chuckled. “Bless your soft silly heart, look at that fine fair wind blowing straight at our stern.”

They hoisted a broad, heavy sail, added a few steady strokes of their oars, and the little craft flew up the Rhine at a spanking pace.

“Feeling better for the river breeze, eh?” Denys asked.
“Much better. And truth be told, that doctor did me far more good than harm.”
“The doctor? But you refused every single one of his potions, didn’t you?”
“Aye, but what I mean—you’ll think me a brute, I know—knocking that old fool flat somehow soothed the fever right out of me.”
“My amiable dove!” Denys cackled, eyes glinting. “How your little character unfurls more every day, soft as a rosebud. I read you all wrong at first, when I thought you nothing but a pious quiet clerk.”
“Nay, Denys, do not mistake me,” Gerard protested. “I would have borne his idle threats well enough, even if his grating voice did go straight through my poor aching ears. But he was an infidel, or next door to one, and such I have been taught to abhor. Did he not all but say our bodies were formed by long-dead Greek men with hard names, not by Him whose name is but a single syllable, whose hand holds all the world in its palm? Pagan!”
“So you knocked him flat forthwith, like a good pious Christian.”
“Now Denys, you will still jest at me. Do not take that wicked old man’s part. Had a thunderbolt struck him from heaven he would have met no more than his due, and all he got was a sorry soft blow from this weak arm.”

“What weak arm?” Denys cried, laughing. “I have lived among fighting men my whole life, and by Samson’s hairy old head, I never saw an arm more like a man-catapult. That bolster wrapped right around the quack’s nose till the two ends kissed behind his head, his forehead rang like a blacksmith’s anvil, and had he been Goliath or Julius Caesar instead of a doddering old fraud, he would have gone down just as hard. St. Denys guard me from such feeble opposites as you! And above all, from their so-called weak arms, thou diabolical young hypocrite.”

The river curved again and again, and at times the wind slipped from dead astern to blow at their side. All the men crowded to the weather rail to shift their weight and stop the boat heeling over too far—all save a five-year-old urchin, the boatman’s petted grandson, who had snuck on board at the very moment of departure, too light to affect the craft’s trim, completely above and beyond all the laws of navigation.

They sailed merrily on, entirely unaware a whole posse of constables armed with the bailiff’s writ was tramping along the bank behind them, drawing ever closer. The wind was strong, but the Rhine’s current was swifter.

It was then Gerard suddenly remembered this course would take him to Rome, but nowhere near Burgundy, Denys’s home. “Oh Denys!” he said, looking half panicked. “This is not your road.”
“I know it,” Denys said, quiet and unconcerned. “But what can I do? I will not leave your side till that fever breaks, and it still hangs on you—your cheeks flare red then go deathly white by turns, I have been watching you. I suppose I will sail all the way to Cologne with you first, then strike cross country east to Burgundy.”

“Thank Heaven!” Gerard cried, overjoyed. He added a little eagerly, with a soft touch of self-deception, “It would be a sin to be this close to Cologne and not see it. Oh man, it is a vast ancient city, the kind I have dreamed of a hundred times but never had the luck to visit. It is old enough to have been founded by a Roman lady in the first century of grace, sacked by Attila the Hun, then sorely defaced by the Norman Lothaire. It holds a church for every week of the year, on top of innumerable chapels and convent churches, and above all the stupendous unfinished minster. In its own chapel rest the three kings who brought gifts to the Christ child: Melchior with gold, Gaspar with frankincense, and Balthazar the black king who brought myrrh. Over their bones stands the shrine, the wonder of the whole world: made of ever-shining brass brighter than gold, studded with carved images, inlaid with fine devices, brave with bright colours, and strung with two broad bands of jewels so large and rare each could adorn a king’s crown or ransom a captive’s whole life. On top stand the three kings carved in fine detail, two in solid silver gilded bright, bareheaded, and the Ethiop king carved of ebony wearing a golden crown. In their midst stands the blessed Virgin in virgin silver, holding the Christ child, and at the four corners golden candle branches hold four great wax tapers that burn night and day. Holy hands have watched and renewed that unceasing light for ages, and holy eyes will tend them for all eternity. The oldest Flemish and German legends found them burning, and they will burn till the earth itself dies. And then there is St. Ursula’s church, dedicated to that British saint, where her bones and the bones of her eleven thousand virgin followers rest. They all died for the faith, struck down by barbarian Moors on the 23rd of October in the year 238. Their bones are piled in the vaults, and many of their skulls are displayed in the church. St. Ursula’s own skull rests in a thin golden case on the high altar, only shown to humble worshippers on the highest holy days.”

“Eleven thousand virgins!” Denys exclaimed. “What lily-livered babies German men must have been in days of yore. Well, would all their bones might turn flesh again and their skulls sweet young faces, just as we pass through the city gates. It’s good odds at least a few of them are tired of being dead by now.”
“Tush, Denys!” Gerard huffed. “Why, for all your goodness, do you still make yourself seem wicked? If your wishing cap is on, pray that we meet the humblest of all those wise virgins in the next world, and to that end let us reverence their holy dust in this one. There is also the church of the Maccabees, and the great cauldron where they and their mother Solomona were boiled by a wicked king for refusing to eat swine’s flesh.”
“Oh, stubborn king, and pig-headed Maccabees!” Denys laughed. “I’d have eaten bacon alongside my pork meal before I’d change places with it in a boiling cauldron.”
“Such scurvy words! It was their sacred faith.”
“Nay, bridle your choler,” Denys said, grinning. “Tell me, is there nothing but churches in this so-vaunted city of yours? I care far more for the knight than the priest, you know.”
“Aye, there is a university nearly a hundred years old, a market square no fairer anywhere in the world, lined with houses great as palaces, a stupendous senate house covered top to bottom with carved images. At the very front of them all stands the statue of stout Herman Gryn, a soldier just like you, lad.”
“Ah! Tell me of him! What feat of arms earned him that niche?”
“A rare one. He slew a lion in fair single combat, armed with nothing but his cloak and a short sword. He thrust the cloak straight down the brute’s throat, then cut its spine clean in two. His effigy and the lion’s stand there to prove it. Only three other men in all history ever did the like: Samson was one, Lysimachus of Macedon another, and Benaiah, one of King David’s captains.”
“Marry! Three tall, formidable fellows. I’d love to sit down to supper with all three of them tonight.”
“Not I,” Gerard said drily.

Denys blinked at him, surprised. “And when wast thou ever in Cologne, then?”
“Never but in the spirit. I talk to all the good wandering monks on the road, and they tell me every notable thing old and new.”
“Aye, aye, I’ve seen you with your nose buried in their cowls, badgering them for stories. When I talk of things out of sight my words are small and the thing they describe is big, but your words are as big or bigger than the wonders themselves. You are a fine painter with your tongue, that I’ll say. And for a supposed pious clerk, you are as quick with hand, steel, or a bolster as any poor sinner alive. So shall I tell you which of all these fine things you described draws me to Cologne?”
“Aye, Denys.”
“You. And you only. No dead saint, no ancient wonder, but my living friend and true comrade. ‘Tis thou alone draws Denys of Burgundy to Cologne.”

Gerard hung his head, flustered.

At that very moment, one of the younger boatmen suddenly frowned and asked what was amiss with “little turnip-face?” His tiny nephew, the urchin who snuck on board, had just wandered aft looking grave as a hanging judge, and burst out wailing without a single word of warning. They plied him with questions, some coaxing, some sharp: had he hurt himself? Eaten too much? Was he cold? Sick? Frightened? An idiot? To every last one he just wailed, oh! oh! oh! and refused to say another word.

“Who can tell what ails this peevish little brat?” the young boatman snarled, impatient. “Rather look this way and tell me who those are after us!”

The old man and his other son looked up, and saw four men tramping along the east bank of the Rhine, staring hard directly at their craft. They left off rowing for a moment, gathered in the stern whispering, casting glances alternately at their two passengers and the pursuers on the bank. They would have spent their time far better trying to unravel the mystery of the wailing turnip-face, that deep unknowable mind of dauntless infancy.

“If it’s who I think it is,” whispered one of the young men, “why don’t we slip for the west bank and give them the slip?”
The old man objected stoutly. “What, risk running into trouble for two total strangers? Are ye mad? Nay, we’ll cross to the east side. Stand always on the side of the strong arm, that’s my rule. What say you, Werter?”
“Please yourselves.”

What age and youth could not decide, a sudden puff of squall settled with perfect impartiality. A hard gust hit the little craft full on, it heeled over sharply, and the men jumped for the weather rail to trim it—only to see a ditch of dark river water rush from stem to stern across their boat’s bottom. The next moment they saw nothing at all, but felt the cold, rushing Rhine close over their heads.

Turnip-face had pulled the boat’s drain plug.

The constables on the bank unwound the thick ropes from their waists. Gerard could swim like a duck, but even the strongest swimmer canted out of a capsizing boat will sink a few feet before he can right himself. The dark water bubbled loud over his head, and he popped back up, half blind and half deaf for a moment. He shook his head like a water dog, saw the overturned black hull of the boat bobbing nearby, figures clinging to its keel, and made unthinkingly for it—until he heard a quiet cry behind him, not loud, but ringing with deep manly despair: “Adieu, comrade, adieu!”

He spun around. There was poor Denys, sinking, sinking fast, weighed down by the heavy arbalest he always slung across his back. His face was ashen, his eyes wide and staring, turned in utter despair on his dearest friend. Gerard uttered a wild cry of love and terror, and cleaved through the water madly towards him—but the next moment Denys slipped under the surface.

The next, Gerard dove straight in after him.

The officers knotted a heavy rope and hurled the weighted end far out into the churning dark river.

The good and ill of this world balance with near-universal, almost miraculous precision – and on that rain-swollen Rhine afternoon, that rule held perfectly true. The heavy steel bow fixed to the arbalest slung over Denys’s back, hoisted high above his head as he floundered under the waves, had dragged him half-drowning beneath the surface. That very same bow, held high as it was, landed straight in Gerard’s outstretched grasp: one hand clamped hard to the steel frame, the other slipped neatly between the curved wood and its taut cord, a hold no drenching could break. The next instant, Denys was hauled upwards with such a sharp, eager jerk that half his torso bobbed clean out of the frigid water.
“Not a choke hold! Don’t make that fatal mistake!” Gerard shouted, his voice tight with mortal terror that the panicking soldier would drag him under too.
“Not fool enough for that,” Denys gurgled back through sputters of river water.
Seeing his companion still had his wits about him, Gerard calmed at once, hope blooming sharp in his chest. “Lie flat on thy back,” he commanded sharply, seizing the arbalest to stroke hard against the current and help Denys shift into position. “One hand on my shoulder. Slap the water hard with the other – no, downward, like so. Do naught else but what I bid thee.”
Gerard curled his fist in Denys’s long tangled hair, twisted it tight, and clamped the end between his side teeth. The strong muscles of his young, straining neck kept Denys’s head well above the waves without wasting a hand on the task, and he struck out lustily across the racing current. For a heartbeat he hesitated which bank to make for, never guessing how much hung on that trivial split-second choice; then he spotted the western shore was a hair closer, and struck out for it instead of swimming meekly back to Dusseldorf jail like an obedient citizen, a choice that would rewrite the rest of their days.
The current swept them far sideways as they swam, and after nearly a hundred yards of labour, Denys murmured uneasily through chattering teeth, “How much farther?”
“Courage,” Gerard mumbled around the lock of hair still between his teeth. “What any duck can do, a Dutchman can do better. Thou art safer than thou wouldst be tucked in thy own bed.”
The next moment, to their utter shock, their feet scraped pebbled riverbed, and they found themselves wading through thigh-deep shallow water onto the bank. Once on solid land, they stared at each other from head to toe as if their eyes might devour the other whole, then on the same impulse slung an arm round one another’s necks, panting there with hearts so full no words could come. At that sacred, breathless moment, life tasted sweeter than heaven to both of them – sweeter still, perhaps, for the exiled young lover who had just dragged his dearest friend back from the cold dark of the Rhine. What poet has ever climbed the height of that joy, or even dared to try? To save a human life – and that life, the one you love best? Moments like that are worth living three score and ten years for, a hundred times over.
When their pulses slowed at last, they took each other’s hands, and walked along the riverbank hand in hand like two sweethearts, hardly noticing or caring where their steps led them.
Back on the water, the boat’s party were all huddled safe on what had been a concave hull, now flipped convex like a turned tortoise shell, with Herr Turnip-Face, the so-called “Inverter of All Things,” wedged right in the middle. The whole chaos of capsizing had barely disrupted his habits: he had been mid-greeting when he shot Gerard and Denys into the Rhine, and mid-greeting still when they waded out again far down the bank.
“Shall we wait for them to right the boat?” Denys asked.
“Nay,” Gerard replied. “Our fare is paid. We owe them not a farthing. Let us press on, and quickly.”
Denys agreed, pointing out they could walk all the way to Cologne on this very bank.
“I am not bound for Cologne,” Gerard said calmly.
“What? Whither then?”
“Burgundy.”
“Burgundy? Ah no, that is far too good to be true.”
“Tis true, and sensible too. What does it matter to me what road I take to Rome?”
“Nay, you only say that to please me. The change is far too sudden. Do not think me so hard-hearted as to take you at your word. And did I not see your eyes sparkle at all the wonders of Cologne, the great churches, the painted statues, the holy relics?”
“How dull art thou, Denys,” Gerard laughed, soft and warm. “That was when we were to see them together. Churches? I shall pass a hundred of them, go what road I will to Rome. The bones of saints and martyrs? The world is full of them, heaven knows – but a friend like thee? Where on all God’s green earth shall I ever find another? I will not drag thee farther from the road that leads to thy home, and the lass that pines for thee there. Nor will I rob myself of thee by going our separate ways. Since I fished thee out of the Rhine, I love thee better than I ever did before. Thou art my pearl: I pulled thee from the water, and I mean to keep thee. Do not gainsay me, or thou wilt bring my old fever back – but cry courage, and lead on. Hey for Burgundy!”
Denys gave a wild, joyful caper. “Courage! To Burgundy! Oh, rest easy – that rogue of a fever is dead and buried for good this time.” And they turned their backs on the glinting Rhine.
No sooner had that decision settled than a commotion broke out on the far eastern bank, where the four officers had been watching them talk. They had not gone twenty paces before a voice boomed across the water. “HALT!”
Gerard turned, and saw one of the men holding up a silver badge of office and a rolled parchment warrant. His heart sank: he was a law-abiding citizen, bred to obey the call of the state that bade him turn back for Dusseldorf jail.
Denys shared no such scruples. He was a French soldier, who held every other nation, their laws, customs, and inhabitants all in equal contempt. He saw the situation for what it was, through a campaigner’s eye: superior force stuck on the opposite bank, no boats to hand, their own rear completely clear. A retreat could not be easier. He glanced back, saw the capsized barge still drifting in mid-stream, and no ferry for miles short of Dusseldorf.
“I shall beat a quick retreat up that yonder hill,” he said. “Once we are out of their sight, we can make tracks at full speed.”
They sauntered casually away, no sign of haste.
“Halt! In the bailiff’s name!” the voice shouted from the far shore.
Denys turned, ostentatiously snapped his fingers in the direction of the bailiff, and kept walking.
“Halt! In the archbishop’s name!”
Denys snapped his fingers at his grace, and kept walking.
“Halt! In the emperor’s name!”
Denys snapped his fingers at his imperial majesty, and kept walking.
Gerard watched this silly, useless pantomime with regret, and the moment they were over the brow of the hill out of sight of the river, said “There is only one path left us now: we run to Burgundy, not walk.” He set off at a full sprint, and ran nearly a full league without stopping to draw breath.
Denys was gasping for air by the end of it, and asked dryly what had become of Gerard’s famous fever. “I begin to miss the rascal sorely,” he panted.
“I dropped it in the Rhine, I think,” Gerard grinned back.
Presently they came to a tiny village, where Denys bought a crusty loaf of rye bread and a huge stone bottle of heady Rhenish wine. “We must sleep in some hidden hole or corner tonight,” he explained. “If we lie at an inn, they will clap us in our beds before dawn.” That was no more than the old soldier’s common prudence. The official network for catching lawbreakers, especially poor common ones, was woven tight as a fisherman’s net in that 15th century: the public rarely troubled themselves to interfere, but innkeepers everywhere were kept under strict surveillance, held even more accountable for the actions of their guests than for any harm that might befall them.
The friends rejoiced when the sun dipped below the horizon, and tramped on for miles under the stars – the moon, if memory serves, did not rise till three that morning – until they stumbled on a great barn belonging to a manor house set some way back from the road. Barley had been threshed there that very week: the heap of dry straw on one side of the threshing floor rose almost as high as the stacks of unthreshed grain on the other.
“Two royal beds, right here,” Denys declared. “Which shall we choose? The mow of unthreshed grain, or the soft straw heap?”
“Straw for me,” said Gerard.
They sat on the heap, tore at their brown bread and passed the wine bottle back and forth, before Denys proceeded to pile straw high over Gerard, leaving only a tiny gap for him to breathe through. “Folks say cold water kills fevered men,” he said. “I’ll make sure thou art warm as toast under this lot, no chill can touch thee.”
Gerard laughed and bade him set his mind at rest. “Those few drops of Rhine water can never chill me. I have heat enough in my bones now to parch a whole kennel of hounds, or boil a cloud right out of the sky.” The words were barely out of his mouth before his eyes fluttered shut, and he dropped straight into a deep sleep.
Denys lay awake for a little while, when he heard something that made him nestle deeper into his own patch of straw. The clatter of horses’ hooves came ringing up the road from Dusseldorf, and the wooden barn shook as a troop of riders thundered past, howling a war cry that was all too familiar in the 1400s, and as unknown in modern Europe as a red Indian’s battle whoop. Denys shook where he lay, but Gerard slept as sound as a top. The troop swept by, and the cries died away into the dark distance. The stout soldier drew a long, shaky breath, whistled soft as a whisper, closed his own eyes, and slept just as soundly.
When he woke at dawn, he reached out to shake Gerard, and his hand landed on the young man’s forehead, damp with sweat. Being an old campaigner who knew fever, he forbore to wake him. “Never rouse a sick man from sleep, nor break his sweat,” he muttered. “That much I know, even if I never tended a caged ape nor a gallows bird.”
He waited a full hour, till he was so ravenous with hunger he could bear it no longer, and rolled over to fall back asleep – a trick he had learned a hundred times in his hard wandering life, to outwait empty bellies. He woke again at high noon, prodded by Gerard moving beside him, to find the young man sitting up, straw clinging to him like smoke rising from a dung hill. The heat of his body had steamed all the damp out of the straw piled over him.
Gerard called him a lazy loon, and Denys just grinned.
They set out at once, and the first thing Denys did was hand Gerard his arbalest and his gear, before scrambling up a tall roadside oak to scout the road ahead. “Coast is clear all the way to the next village,” he reported when he climbed down, and they set off again.
Just before they reached the village, Denys halted all of a sudden, and turned to Gerard. “How dost thou feel, lad?”
“See for thyself!” Gerard laughed. “I feel as if Rome is no farther than that little hamlet yonder.”
“But thy body? Thy skin? No chills, no burning heat?”
“Neither one nor the other. Yesterday I was hot one minute, shivering the next. The only thing that plagues me is this tiresome old leg wound.”
“Le grand malheur,” Denys groaned, mock solemn. “Many of my comrades never found any trouble at all getting over wounds far worse than that.”
“Ah, there it goes again, itching fit to drive me mad.”
“Unhappy youth,” Denys said, deadpan, “the sum of all thy troubles is this: thy fever is gone, and thy wound is at last healing. Since that is so,” he added, more gently, “I shall tell thee a piece of news I had meant to keep hidden from thee.”
“What is it?” Gerard asked, eyes sparkling with curiosity.
“The hue and cry is out after us. And they are mounted on the fleetest horses in the district.”
“Oh!”

The sudden, unwelcome news hit Gerard like a physical blow, and the colour drained then flooded back to his cheeks in rapid, unsteady waves. His jaw clamped tight with rising ire a moment later. For any man of spirit is much like the wild boar that roams the Rhineland woodlands: he will retreat before an overwhelming superior force, not out of cowardice, but simple good sense, not being the foolhardy ass that stands its ground to be butchered for no gain. But hound him too long, press too close at his heels, wear him past the point of patience, and he will whirl with a snarl, charge straight through a whole pack of hunters, and very well may turn his own fury on you before any of them can strike.

Gerard squared his shoulders, eyes blazing, face set for battle. But the fire drained right out of him a heartbeat later, and his whole frame sagged. “And my axe,” he said, voice soft and plaintive, “lies at the bottom of the Rhine.”

The two men huddled to weigh their options. Prudence whispered sharp and urgent that they must avoid the nearby village entirely, where their enemies were no doubt lying in wait. But hunger gnawed at their bellies so fiercely it roared louder than all caution, demanding they find food. In the end the two impulses struck a careful truce, and they settled to cut across the open farm fields well away from the village paths rather than risk the main high road.

They halted behind a thick, well-stacked haystack, pulled two armfuls of dry straw to pad an overgrown dry ditch hidden from prying eyes, and hunkered down there, their thin travelling clothes prickled by the nettles that grew thick along its banks. They took turns sneaking out one at a time, and returned with pockets full of raw turnips dug from a nearby patch, munching on the coarse, earthy roots in slow, careful intervals in their hidden nook until the sun dipped fully below the horizon.

Presently they crept out shivering, into the lashing cold rain and total darkness, and slipped onto the high road on the far side of the village. It was a dismal, wretched night: dark as pitch, the gale blew so hard it drowned out every other sound. They could not see three paces before their faces, could not hear a thing over the howling wind, and so were as invisible and unheard as phantoms. For aught they knew, they drifted close enough to brush shoulders with their pursuing foes that very night, undetected. The raw horrors of the black tempest soon drove all thought of their hunters clean out of their heads: they stumbled forward groping, fighting the gale every step, as if they were hewing their way through solid slabs of black marble.

When the thin moon finally broke through the roiling storm clouds, they had put many long leagues between themselves and Düsseldorf. Still they trudged on, boots caked in mud, their bodies aching with cold and exhaustion. Presently a massive stone building loomed out of the dark before them.

“Courage!” cried Denys, his hoarse voice bright with sudden relief. “I know this convent. Aye, it is. We are in the see of Juliers now. Cologne has no power here.”

The next moment the heavy oak gates swung open, and they were safe within its sheltering walls.

It was on this stretch of the road that Gerard fell in with a most ingenious brother at the abbey: the very monk who had carved the great precision sundial in the prior’s herb garden, built the water wheel that hauled full buckets up the deep well without a single hand to heft them, and crafted a winnowing machine that sifted chaff from grain faster than ten farmwives working side by side with hand sieves. Some clever new mechanism was always in progress in his cell. He had already turned half a dozen psalteries and two sweet-toned dulcimers, and was halfway through building a set of regalles: a tiny, portable organ for the abbey choir.

Gerard had only ever dabbled a little at the humble psaltery, but this old brother drew music from its strings so fine it felt like angels were humming the tune through the wood, and showed him gently just how much of a novice he was to the craft. His illuminated manuscripts were lovely, too, but he openly admitted he could never match Gerard’s sharp, elegant script. In that earnest, unpretentious age where any skill was a marker of true natural bent, the two clicked like old friends: youth and age bound by shared love of beauty and making, and the monk would not hear of Gerard and Denys travelling another mile that night. Gerard glanced at Denys, who shrugged ruefully, clearly preferring a dry straw pallet indoors to huddling in a frost-kissed hedgerow, and agreed to stay.

He told his new friend where they were bound, and recounted all their recent adventures, softening the ridiculous detail of whacking a rogue over the head with a feather bolster. “Alack,” the old monk sighed, “I travelled half the known world in my youth, and never a soul molested me. Mark my words: avoid all roadside inns. They swarm with thieves and brawlers, and you risk your soul there even if you escape unharmed in body. Plan every day’s march so you end it at a quiet, peaceful monastery.” He broke off abruptly, squinting as sharp as a needle at Gerard. “How long has it been since you were last shriven?”

Gerard flushed bright hot, and mumbled weakly that it was more than a fortnight. “You, a man who carries the right to perform exorcisms? No wonder peril hounds you! You must be absolved at once.”

“Gladly, father, with all my heart,” Gerard said, and sank to his knees, hands clasped to confess right there—only for the monk to wave him off half-fretfully.
“Not to me! Not to me! My whole fool soul is tangled up in these wooden pipes and dinky leather stops that will rot in a few years’ time right alongside me. I am as full of worldly vanity as any layman walking the roads. I am no fit confessor for you.”

“Dear father,” Gerard protested, “these organs are built for the use of the Church—surely that sanctifies the work you put into them?”

“That is exactly the line the devil has been whispering in my ear these past months!” the monk laughed, shaking a finger half-playful, half-threatening at him. “He even quoted Scripture, ever so thoughtful, to remind me that Solomon built the Lord a temple with fine carvings and rich hangings, and that counted as piety, no sin. Oh, he can quote the Bible like a trained preacher. But I am not as simple as I look, lad,” he suddenly declared, all defiance, speaking not to Gerard but to the empty air of the corridor. “The second I finish this tiny organ, it will be nothing but vigils, fasts, and prayers for me. Prayers standing in the drafty chapel aisle, prayers flat on my face on the cold stone floor, prayers sat right in a tub of icy water. Nothing the devil hates more than seeing a monk praying half-submerged in cold water—for water tames the flesh, after all. Off you go, then, confess your silly little pardonable youthful secular sins, and leave me to mine: sins that taste sweeter than honey, for which I will have to atone ten times over.”

They had come to the row of monks’ cells lining the corridor. “Any of these cells holds a worthy confessor,” the monk said simply. “Go to Brother Anselm, yonder.”

Gerard walked toward the first door he saw, about to rap on the wood, when he heard his new friend hissing at him in a state of wild panic: “Nay! Nay! Nay!” He turned, and saw the old monk pacing back and forth outside his own cell, waving both hands like a sawyer working a two-man pit saw, so twisted up with anxiety Gerard half assumed that first cell must hold a raving wild beast, if not the very fiend they had just been speaking of. He nodded apologetically, and moved to the next door. The monk’s face instantly softened into relief, he nodded rapidly, scurried back into his own cell, flipped his hourglass over, and dived back to work on his regalles, muttering to himself every few minutes: “Well-a-day, how fast the sands run when a man is bent over worldly toys.”

Father Anselm was a venerable old brother, broad of forehead, his face lined with equal parts dignity and gentle love. As Gerard knelt to confess, and answered his soft but searching questions, he could not help staring at that wise, kind face, and thinking *Oh, I do hope he will let me draw his portrait once we are done*—and mid-distraction, he forgot a couple of tiny, trivial sins. But he did not downplay the bolster brawl, nor was he dishonest about the roguish character of the man he had hit.

His penance was light: go into the abbey church, prostrate yourself, kiss the lowest step of the altar three times, then kneel on the bare floor to say three paternosters and a credo. “When you are done, come back to me at once.”

Gerard finished his small mortification and returned to find Father Anselm spreading thick, cool plaster on a linen cloth. “Tend the soul first, then the body,” he said. “I am the abbey chirurgeon here, for want of a better. This plaster will go on your sore leg: it will cool the ache, not burn it, the saints forbid I should harm you.”

As he wrapped the bandage, the monastic leech, who had taken a quiet interest in Gerard’s tales of his journey from Dusseldorf, sided openly with Denys on the matter of bloodletting. “We Dominicans seldom draw blood these days; lay surgeons call us cowardly and unskilled, but in truth we have long known that simples and herbs cure most ills that can be cured at all. And in capable hands, they never kill a patient—unlike harsher, sharper remedies that slay a man as fast as a lightning bolt. The Vulgate says explicitly that blood is the life of a man, and in medicine, law, or divinity, to think yourself wiser than the All-wise is pure foolishness. Besides, the lowliest creatures know the power of healing herbs: the four-footed weasel, bitten by a venomous snake, will seek out a herb to draw the poison out. We learned that trick from the beasts, and from our old traditions, and still we test the virtues of all the plants good God scattered across the earth: some to feed men, some to heal them. Only for the most dire, desperate ills do we steep a sliver of a saint’s hair or bone in the draught, and work marvellous cures that way.”

“Think you those cures work because of the relics?” Gerard asked. “For Peter a Floris, that learned lay leech, swears stoutly that it is all nonsense.”

“What does Peter a Floris know? What do any of us know?” Anselm smiled. “I do not pretend we can command the saints, and draw virtue from their blessed remains against their will. But I have seen a sick man drink that draught in perfect faith and get better, as if by charm. Doubtless the faith of the patient counts for much, as it always did. The sick woman whom all the Jewish leeches could not cure touched only the hem of Christ’s garment, and was healed on the instant. If she had not had faith, she could have worn that scrap of cloth to her grave and gained no good from it. It does not do to pry too deeply into these secrets. All around us the world calls for faith. So I, your confessor for this hour, strictly forbid you, on pain of your soul’s health, to listen to arrogant learned laymen picking holes in matters of religion. Arrogance is their curse, and with it they shut heaven’s door in their own faces. The unlearned simple folk have often been my masters in humility, and may yet be yours. Your wound is cared for; in three days it will be nothing but a faint scar. Now God speed you, and the saints make you as good and happy as you are thoughtful and gracious.”

Gerard had hoped they might talk longer, but Anselm told him, with only the faintest trace of regret, that he did not leave his cell all that week, as he was observing a personal penance. He took Gerard’s face gently in both hands, kissed him on the brow, and was back at his devotions before the cell door had even clicked shut behind Gerard. The young traveller walked away chilled at heart, saddened by the quiet isolation of the monastic life. “Alas,” he thought, “here is a kind face I shall never see again on this earth, a kind voice gone from my ears forever. There is nothing but meeting and parting in this sorrowful world.”

A young monk soon interrupted his pensive mood, to lead him to the refectory. There Gerard found Denys standing stiff as a poker, being grilled by the assembled brothers on every town he planned to pass through. The friars pooled all their knowledge, mapped out a safe route for the two travellers, and marked down every hospitable religious house along the way, to save them ever needing to stop at a rogue’s inn. After supper, the old mechanical monk carried Gerard back to his cell for a long, eager chat, and finally explained the ridiculous agitated pantomime he had put on in the corridor earlier.

“You had nearly walked straight into Brother Jerome’s clutches! That first cell you were about to knock on was his.”

“Is Father Jerome an ill man, then?” Gerard asked.

“An ill man!” the friar crossed himself devoutly. “He is a saint, an anchorite, the very pillar of this house! He would have set you penance to walk barefoot all the way to Loretto—nay, since you are bound for Italy, that spiteful old earthly saint would have sent you hundreds of miles out of your way on detour pilgrimage to Canterbury or Compostella. Jerome was born old, and born wearing a cowl. Anselm and I were boys once, wild and sinful far more than you can imagine,” he added, at Gerard’s faintly incredulous look, “and that memory keeps us humble, and lenient to hot-blooded youth.” At Gerard’s earnest request, he played one last heavenly strain on the psaltery, before they turned in for the night: Gerard’s jangled, travel-worn spirits were calmed, his sore leg soothed, and his mind light.

I have described this quiet, contrasting day in full—this day that fell like oil on storm-tossed waves after so many passions and perils—because it stands as a representative for the many such peaceful days that followed it. Most readers will recognize this pattern from their own lives: stirring events never spread evenly across the whole journey, but come in clusters, by fits and starts, linked by subtle threads, or just happening as life wills it. Life is an intermittent fever, after all.
