Most narrators, of history or fiction, skip over these quiet barren stretches of time entirely, or pad them out with unnecessary detail, and that practice often gives readers a false sense that no time passes at all between grand adventures. I ask you to fill in the gaps with me, then: for weeks on end, one day’s steady march followed another, one monastery after another fed and lodged the pair free of charge, with welcome that was always charitable and often genial. The only foes they faced were cold winter winds and rough slushy roads, antagonists no less stubborn for not bearing swords. By the time they had tramped over hundreds of miles of that quiet, uneventful countryside, Gerard was tanned deep by sun and frost, dust-stained from head to toe, Denys’s boots were falling to tatters, and both of them were stiff, footsore, and drawing near the Burgundian frontier.

Gerard was nearly as giddy to reach the fabled promised land of Burgundy as Denys himself. The soldier never ceased singing his homeland’s praises: at every petty travel mishap, every grumpy innkeeper, every scratchy blanket, he would gesture broadly and declare “they do all this far better in Burgundy.” Most of all, he had perfectly preyed on Gerard’s greatest soft spot, vowing that every inn in that polished, civilized nation provided clean, fresh-laundered bed linens. “I ask no more than that,” the Dutchman would sigh. “Think of it— I haven’t once slept in a bare, clean bed since I left home. The linen at these wayside taverns is so foul that when I look at it, I don’t want to strip off my tunic and hose, I want to shut both my eyes and my nose tight so I never have to touch the stuff.”

Denys’s love for his country ran so deep he once walked twenty full leagues in shoes that had split wide open, soles flapping loose from uppers, rather than spend a single coin on a surly German cobbler who would drag his feet, invent a dozen petty obstacles to serving a customer, pause mid-work to finish his dinner, even lumber his fat body across the shop slow as molasses just to make a traveler wait.

As the sun dipped low over the hills, they found themselves exactly halfway between a tiny walled town and a remote monastery, the abbey’s stone roofs visible a short walk off the main road. Denys voted at once for the town inn; Gerard was set on taking shelter at the convent. Denys caved, but only on one strict condition: the very second they crossed the Burgundian border, they would stop at inns every night after that, no exceptions. Gerard agreed readily, for his little travel pamphlet listing all hospitable monasteries along their route ended right at this spot.

They turned off the main track, and Gerard asked, confused, where this sudden aversion to the monasteries that had fed and lodged them for free so many times had come from. Denys hemmed and hawed at first, dancing around the answer, until all his pent-up frustrations burst free. This was no new dislike, it turned out: it was a deep, long-buried horror he had forced himself to suppress the whole trip, purely out of politeness. “I saw how delighted you were to chat with every grey old shaven-headed monk we met,” he explained, “so I bit my tongue. But this is the last one, so why not unburden my mind? I’ve been like a fish dragged out of water in every one of those great gloomy stone dungeons you dragged me to. You’re off gabbing with some old priest the second we step through the gate, so you never see the personal purgatory I’m stuck in.”

“Forgive me,” Gerard said, stricken. “I’ve been entirely selfish, never stopping to ask how you were faring.”

“Ay, ay, I forgive you, little comrade,” Denys waved it off. “It’s no fault of yours. You’re far from the first fool to be priest-ridden and monk-beguiled. But I’ll never forgive those monks for the utter misery they put me through.”

A full century before Henry VIII’s royal commissioners would come to audit every abbey in the realm, Denys delivered his full, roaring indictment. Those gloomy stone piles were all identical, no variation at all, unlike the ever-unique inns scattered across the countryside. Every one had a grand main gate, a tiny postern gate, the same number of weathered stone steps leading into a shadowed cloister walk. Over here the drafty dormitory, over there the great ice-cold refectory, where you had to sit dead silent, not a peep out of you—an agony for a man like Denys, who loved to speak his mind loud and clear whenever he pleased.

“And then,” he ranted on, “no one there is a proper man. We’re all slaves to what? A peevish little tinkling bell that never, ever sleeps. If it were a blaring battle trumpet, sounding alarms, it wouldn’t freeze a man’s blood in his veins half so bad. Tinkle, tinkle, tinkle—you’re supposed to sit down to a meal you might not even have an appetite for. Before that food’s even settled in your stomach, tinkle, tinkle! Now you’ve got to troop off to church to pray, when you don’t have an ounce of devotion in you. I’m no hog that chews through his prayers half-asleep, for one. Tinkle, tinkle—now you’ve got to climb into your hard straw bed, eyes wide awake. You finally drift off? Some miserable little imp of a monk is yanking the bell rope, tinkle, tinkle, you’ve got to mumble a prayer in the pitch dark whether you know a single one or not. If they ever heard the sort of grumbling half-cussed prayers I mutter when they wake me up mid-sleep, they’d toss me out on my ear before I could blink. You drop off again, get barely a handful of actual sleep? Tinkle, tinkle, it’s matins time.”

“I suppose the only clapper you’d ever listen to gladly is a woman’s tongue,” Gerard put in, half amused, half contemptuous.

“At least a woman’s scolding has music in it, even when she’s nagging you half to death,” Denys shot back unapologetically.

“And every tiny thing you do gets you scolded. If I so much as dip my finger in the salt cellar to grab a pinch, right away someone’s squawking, ‘Have you no knife to handle the salt with, that you use your filthy fingers?’ If I wipe my knife quick on the tablecloth to save time, then it’s ‘Wipe your dirty knife on the bread, and the clean part on the cloth!’ Oh, small-souled lot! All those petty, nitpicking little rules land on a man trying to be friendly like tiny icicles dripping off the edge of a thatched straw roof, cold and sharp and annoying.”

“I don’t think being clean is any petty pedantry,” Gerard argued. “You ought to learn proper manners once and for all.”

“Nay, they’re the ones with no manners. They stop a man’s mouth every other word out of his head.”

“Every other obscene or blasphemous word, you mean,” Gerard corrected him.

“Exaggerator, go on with you! Why, just at the very last of those dungeons, I saw a whole crowd of poor travelers sitting shivering and dead silent around one shaven old monk, like a bunch of thieves waiting in line to be dragged up to the gallows. So I tried to cheer them up, right? I just yelled out ‘Courage, everyone, the dev--’”

“Whoa, I can guess what happened next!” Gerard cut in.

“Marry, this. ‘Do not blaspheme!’ the lout snarled at me. ‘Pardon?’ says I. Wouldn’t you know it, he spins around and starts yelling at me in that terrible Alsatian French of his, where he turns every P sound into a B. I almost laughed right in his face, I did.”

“Says the man who can’t speak ten words of proper French without making a mistake himself,” Gerard teased.

“Pfft, everyone in the whole world ought to speak proper French. What’s the point of all these silly different jargons, except to build walls between men’s hearts?”

“Well what did he actually say to you?”

“What does it matter what a fool says?”

“Oh, not every word a fool speaks is folly, or I wouldn’t bother listening to you ramble on,” Gerard grinned.

“Fine, fine. He says ‘Those who start throwing the devil's name around for fun always end by taking the Lord's name in vain too.’ ‘Father,’ I says, ‘I’m a soldier, that’s just my watchword, my consigne.’ ‘Oh, so it's just a silly habit?’ he says. I didn’t see the old fox’s trick, and I tried to clear my name, so I said ‘Aye, it is.’ ‘Then that’s ten times worse,’ he says. ‘He’ll come sniffing around you one of these days, when he hears his name called over and over again.’ Not a single bit of gratitude that I was telling him a bit of news he never got from his missal or his breviary, mind you. Then he has the gall to tell me that soldiers go around committing all the crimes that get regular men broken on the wheel—murder, rape, pillage, the whole list.”

“And isn’t that often true?” Gerard asked.

“True or not, it was damned rude of him to say it to my face,” Denys replied, suddenly wary of agreeing. “And this so-called courteous host of mine goes on, ‘You men are enemies to all mankind, why would you go making enemies of all the good spirits too, by shouting the names of evil ones?’ Blah blah blah, a whole lot more of that tedious stuff.”

“Well Denys, whether you take his advice or ignore it, why blame a man for trying to raise his voice to save your soul?”

“How the devil is he supposed to save my soul when he can’t even say the words right, turning every P into a B?”

Gerard was so stunned by that absurd Gallic quip he couldn’t think of a reply for a full second. Before he could recover, Denys was already off on a new tangent, ranting that every last monk was a hypocrite. “Just look at them, creeping around the halls, never able to meet your eye like an honest man would.”

“Nay,” Gerard said eagerly, jumping to defend them, “that modest downcast gaze is part of their discipline! It’s called custodia oculorum, the guarding of the eyes.”

“Cussed toads, muttering their Latin hocus-pocus? That's no custom, that's exactly how a cutpurse looks, when he can't meet an honest man's eye. Take off a monk's cowl, and there's a thief. Stick a cowl on a thief, and suddenly he's a monk. Don't tell me they'll ever be able to look God Almighty in the face up in heaven, when they can't even look a regular honest man in the eye down here on earth. Ah, there's the gates, black as pitch! Let's head on in, comrade. Mercy me, there's that tinkle already! Though this one's the best tinkle of all—it's for dinner. Listen, hear that? The wolf howling in my stomach just said Amen!” He swore two loud, hearty oaths to confirm that last statement, and marched into the convent like a victorious gamecock, assuming from Gerard's quiet silence that he had won the argument, and never dreaming how deeply his crude, unfair rant had disgusted the pious young Dutchman.

The thick, warm air of the monastery refectory reeked of spiced ale, crusty rye bread, and roasting game when talk rippled across Gerard’s table of Brother Werter, the scribe who had dropped dead suddenly only days before, leaving the work of transcribing the abbey’s ancient royal charter half finished. Gerard leaned forward, listening intently, before he spoke up timidly to offer his own services. The monks hesitated, and he misread their quiet doubt as hesitation to accept work for nothing. “Nay, I ask no hire, my lords,” he assured them. “I do this for love, a small token of thanks for the many safe nights your order has granted a poor wandering wayfarer like me.”
One older monk smiled approvingly, but gently pointed out that the late Brother Werter was a master penman, his flowing script nearly impossible for any amateur to match. Trepidatious, Gerard pulled a scrap of cleaned vellum from his wallet: the back of an old deed he’d polished smooth and filled with illuminated calligraphy as a practice sample on the road. The monk’s eyes went wide at first glance, and he hurried up the length of the hall to the high table, genuflecting just enough to brush the fifth and tenth steps as custom dictated, before handing the sample to the prior with a flurry of excited comments. A dozen pairs of knowing eyes fixed on the vellum at once, a low buzz of astonishment rippling out. Soon the first monk returned, grinning as proud as a peacock, carrying a spiced, gravied game crustade for Gerard, and a silver grace cup brimming with rich, honeyed piment wine. Gerard bowed low first to the distant prior, then to his own table, drank deep, and passed the cup to the rest of the company.
To his shock, the whole table cheered him at once, calling him a fellow convent-bred lad. “You cannot hide it!” they laughed. When Gerard blinked and asked how they had guessed, two monks spoke at once, pointing out he had lifted the grace cup to his lips with both hands, an old lifelong habit he had never unlearned.
For some time, the far end of the refectory had been loud with rowdy banter, before a burst of unruly, prolonged laughter rang out so loud the prior dispatched the sub-prior at once to march down the hall and dole out penance to every last monk at that table. Gerard’s face burned hot with shame: he had picked out Denys of Burgundy’s booming trumpet tone dead center of the ruckus, and the rough shout of “Courage!” that had cut through the din.
By mid-afternoon, Gerard was settled in old Werter’s empty cell, supplied with beeswax tapers, a tiltable writing frame that could be adjusted to any angle, and every ink, pigment, and sheet of vellum a scribe could ask for. The charter work was far too great for one evening, and Gerard fretted over how to ask his openly monk-hating friend Denys to linger a day longer. To his great surprise, Denys agreed graciously. “A day’s rest will do neither of us harm,” he shrugged. “Write thou, and I will find some way to pass the time.”
By the time Gerard finished the transcription, the whole monastery sang his praises: they openly agreed the finished charter was far more beautiful than any work the late Werter could have produced. The sub-prior pressed a silver rix-dollar into his palm, plus a handful of fine sable brushes and rare imported pigments pulled from the abbey’s vast, well-stocked scriptorium stores. They set out on the road again soon after, Gerard’s chest light with hope: this was a good omen, the pen he relied on to make his fortune and win back his beloved Margaret had already proven its worth. He nudged Denys playfully, holding up his new gifts. “Do try to be fairer to these good men,” he said. “To be plain with you, it chilled my friendship for you a little when I heard you call my benefactors hypocrites.”
Denys laughed, holding up his hands. “I recant. I was a scurrilous vagabond, no more. We soldiers are rude and hasty, that is all. I give myself the lie, and offer all these men I misjudged my full esteem. It is unjust to slander thousands for the hypocrisy of a few.”
Gerard preened, happy to be proven right, and leaned in to hear exactly what had changed Denys’s mind.
Denys told the tale gaily: the first night at dinner, a broad-shouldered young monk next to him had laughed out loud, bright and unforced, and Denys had thought at last he had found a man, not a shorn ape. He clapped the monk on the back and delivered his usual crude soldier’s jest, only for the monk to look as deadpan sorrowful as King Solomon, and point out that war obviously did nothing to sharpen wits. “What are monks for but to fight the foul fiend?” he had said. “If the fiend is dead, the friars are sped. We will have nothing left to do but turn soldiers, and bring him back to life.” The whole table roared at Denys’s expense, and he hit it off with the lot of them at once.
After dinner, they led him to a private cell instead of the crowded shared dormitory, strictly forbidding him from sleeping. They handed him a bound book of ribald illustrations depicting monks chasing lay women, then marched him barefoot down to a private parlour where a feast fit for a duke was laid out, attended by a dozen of the jolliest, rowdiest monks Denys had ever met, even on campaign. They swapped war stories, toasted, jested, and played cards with a gilded deck where Saint Theresa and Saint Catherine stood in for queens, and the four orders of friars were the knaves. They bet their very rosaries, swearing like troopers when they lost. Around midnight, one sly monk snuck out, and the rest followed him quiet as cats to the garden, to watch him pull a rope ladder from the ivy and scramble up the ten-foot abbey wall—only for a girl in a russet kirtle to pop up on the other side just as fast, the two of them clinging to each other to kiss and cuddle on the wall’s top. Denys mewed like a cat at them, the rest of the monks joined in the caterwauling chorus, and the girl shrieked in surprise. The monk on the wall yelled back that they would pay for it, he would dress every last one of them in a fardingale the next night. The whole lot of them danced in a circle mewing, gave the couple on the wall a mock solemn benediction, and trundled back to the parlour to find two of their brothers dead drunk on the table, two more blubbering over old drinking tales. They hauled the unconscious men off to their cells, dragged the crying ones after, and kicked every last one through their cell doors to sleep it off.
Gerard groaned in disgust as Denys cackled through the tale. The next day, Denys went on, he and the young monks drained the fish ponds, stashing away huge piles of pike, carp, tench, and eel to eat in secret. That night, they led him barefoot down twisted dark paths to the chapel, then down cold stone steps into the crypt under the chapel floor, and suddenly the whole place blazed with light, like paradise itself had opened up.
“The holy fathers retire down there to pray,” Gerard put in, shocked.
“Not that night,” Denys snickered. “Dozens of beeswax candles lit, princely cheer laid out: fifteen ‘Lenten’ soups all secretly laced with venison, grouse, and hare, twenty different artfully cooked fish for the Friday fast. Every monk seated between two buxom local girls, every girl between two hooded lads—except me. I had to court through a translator, who definitely stole three quarters of my lines for himself. The wine flagons were carved to look like breviaries, a monk plucked at a cittern and sang ribald little ballads that turned the girls’ cheeks bright red at first, before they laughed and settled right in.”
Gerard exploded. “Miserable wretches! Corrupters of youth! Perverters of innocence! But for you being there, Denys, who has been taught no better, I wish the whole church had fallen on the entire gang. Impious, abominable hypocrites!”
“Hypocrites?” Denys echoed, genuinely confused. “That is what I called them before I knew them, and you withstood me. Nay, they are sinners—all good fellows are, that—but by Saint Denys’s helmeted skull, they are no hypocrites. No pretense about them at all, just right jolly roaring blades.”
Gerard leaned in, his voice dropping to a spooky, hushed whisper. “Denys, you little know the peril you ran that night. That crypt is haunted. I had it from one of the elder monks. The dead walk there, their light feet pattering soft over the cold stones. Heavenly, unearthly sounds drift out of those vaults at midnight: voices of the dead holding ghostly communion that chill the listener to the bone, chords played by no mortal finger, swept by no mortal hand, ringing faint as echoes deep among the tombs.”
Denys’s face went pale. “Misericorde! If I had known that, no team of mules and wain ropes would have hauled me down there—though,” he sighed, “I would have missed the merriest time of my whole life.”
Before they could argue further, a bearded lay brother from the abbey came spurring up on a mule, waving a scrap of vellum. It was the old lost deed between Ghysbrecht and Floris Brandt, Gerard’s precious memento of home. Gerard turned pale with relief, so overjoyed he not only pressed a coin into the brother’s hand, he leaned down and kissed the mule’s soft nose. He pulled out a needle and thread, sewed the precious deed to the lining of his doublet with neat, deft, almost feminine stitches, his heart and mind drifting all the way back to Sevenbergen, to Margaret.
They kept walking, soon crossing over into Burgundy. Denys was in high spirits, doffing his cap to every woman they passed, firing off his crude soldier’s greeting to every man, before finally leading Gerard to the long-promised inn: Les Trois Poissons, The Three Fishes. “It is small, but I have known it for years, it is a good one,” he said, squinting at the huge new inscription painted across the whole front of the building, sounding the letters out slowly before puffing out his chest. “Ah, there we go: ‘Ici on loge a pied et a cheval’—Here we lodge travelers on foot and on horse.”
Gerard leaned over to read the actual words, and snorted. The full inscription ran: *ON NE LOGE CEANS A CREDIT; CE BONHOMME EST MORT, LES MAUVAIS PAIEURS L'ONT TUE*. No credit given here; the good old innkeeper died, and his bad-paying customers killed him.

“Where be the true men?”
“Here be we! God bless you all! God bless you!”

A roar of warm, rough voices rose above the reek of smoke and blood still hanging heavy in the inn’s upper chamber. The archers crowded the stairs, half a dozen hard, calloused hands outstretched to grip Denys and Gerard’s own, firm as oak. “Ye’ve saved our lives, lads,” Denys cried, grinning through a fleck of drying blood on his brow, “ye’ve plucked us from the gallows this very night.”

A wild, stark sight met the two rescued men’s eyes: torches guttered against the dark rafters, gilding the polished steel breastplates of the bowmen, painting their sun-browned faces a ruddy bronze. Bound and disarmed, the captured thieves huddled against the far wall, their cheeks drained of all color, while the carcass of the massive robber Denys had hurled over the banister lay splayed half in its own dark gore on the stone flags.

Gerard walked slow from archer to archer, pressing each calloused hand in his own, tears glistening bright in his eyes, until the rough soldiers crowded in to kiss his cheeks in the old custom of battle-brothers. This time he did not flinch, but returned their kisses, worn thin as he was by the night’s terror. Turning to a handsome archer near his own age, he said, half slurring with sudden, bone-deep exhaustion: “Prithee, good soldier, keep an eye on me. A strange drowsiness is swallowing me whole. Do not let any soul cut my throat while I sleep, for pity’s sake.”

The archer laughed aloud, thinking the young clerk was jesting, and swore to stand guard. No sooner had the promise left his lips than Gerard slid down against the wall, and sank into a deep, dreamless slumber.

Denys blinked in surprise, but did not wake him—for the chance to claim credit for that impossible throw of his suited his purposes perfectly. A pair of archers were prodding the dead abbot of the thieves with their boot toes, marveling aloud what man could have hurled the 20-stone brute down from the upper landing, and begging to learn the trick of that arm. At first Denys made a show of downplaying the feat, but he dared not risk bragging loud while Gerard was awake—for he knew the pious lad would no doubt pipe up and swear the brute was cast down by the finger of Heaven, and make Denys look a fool for his boasting. Now that he saw Gerard dead to the world, he leaned in and gave the story full voice.

“Well then, comrades, I ran my sword through that rogue up to the hilt, and two more of his pack came buzzing at my throat. I had no choice but keep my grip on my blade or die, so I planted my boot firm against his stomach, heaved with all my might, and gave a great spring with my foot, and sent him flying straight to kingdom come! Died mid-air, he did, and his carrion rolled right in amongst you unannounced—made you all jump, I warrant. But what’s the use prattling of such trifles now they’re past? Buvons, camarades, buvons! *Drink*, lads, drink!”

The archers laughed and pointed out it was easy to cry for wine when there was not a bottle in sight. “Nay!” Denys clapped a hand to his chest. “My nose hath a natural knack for sniffing out good wine even through three feet of stone. Follow me, and follow my nose—bring a torch!”

They tramped down a short flight of slimy stone steps into a large, low, damp cellar. The air hung thick and mildewed, the walls crusted all over with what looked like thick cobwebs, until you touched it and found it was saltpetre, oozed slow from the wet stones and crystallized glistening white. “Ah, that fine mouldy smell!” Denys sniffed with delight. “Good casks always hide in places like this. Hold thy torch higher. Diable! What’s that huddled in the corner? A pile of rags? No—’tis a man.”

They crowded round the torchlight, and found a figure crouched on a heap of dirt, pale as ash and shivering so hard his teeth chattered. “Why, it’s the landlord!” Denys said, grabbing him by the collar to yank him to his feet. “Up with thee, craven heart!” shouted one archer. “The thieves are all bound, and we’re parched dry from fighting them. Show us thy wine, man—we see no bottles here.”

“Wh-what? The rascals are bound?” the landlord stammered. “That is good news. W-wine? I’ll show ye that this instant, honest sirs.” His joints wobbled as he rose, and he offered to lead them to the next cellar where he kept his stock. But Denys held him back, sharp as a knife. “Ye are all fools, comrades. This man is in league with the thieves.”

“Alack, good soldier, me in league with the accursed robbers! Is that reasonable?” the landlord wailed.

“The girl said so anyway.”

“The girl! What girl? Ah, curse her, that traitress!”

“Now hold,” the other archer put in. “The girl’s already gone to fetch the bailiff. Let the burghers judge if he’s guilty or no, since we did not catch him with a blade in his hand. Make him fetch us the wine.”

“One moment,” Denys said, shrewd as a fox. “Why curse the girl? If he were an honest man, he’d be blessing her the same as we do, for ridding the roads of these robbers.”

“Alas, sirs!” the landlord whimpered. “My good name is all I have left to live by. I cursed her only because ye told me she had belied me, and I thought to prove I was angry at the lie.”

“Humph!” Denys grunted. “I trow thou art a thief, and every thief can lie smooth-faced as a saint. Hold him, lads—even a prisoner can draw wine, so long as his hands are not tied too tight.”

The landlord made no objection. He said he would gladly show them his small stock, only begged they pay for what they drank, for his rent was two months overdue. The archers smiled grimly at what they took for his naivete, one setting a firm but quiet hand on his shoulder, the other leading the way with the torch. They had almost reached the next cellar’s threshold when Denys roared “Halt!”

“What is it?”

“Bottles in this corner, sure. Bring the torch hither.” The torchbearer—Philippe by name—stepped toward him. Denys had slipped his sword from its scabbard, and was probing the loose heap the landlord had been crouched on just moments before.

“Nay, nay!” the landlord cried, panic flaring in his voice. “The wine is in the next cellar. There is nothing there.”

“Nothing is mighty hard, then,” Denys said, and fished something out of the heap with his hand. It clattered on the stone floor, a bone. “Naught there but the bones of the house,” the landlord said quickly.

“Just now ’twas nothing. Now we found something, and ’tis nothing but bones?” Denys dug out a second, and held it out to Philippe. “Look at that, mate. Bring our smooth-faced knave over too, to look at it.”

Philippe turned the bone over in the torchlight. “Well?” said Denys. “Well, if this were a battlefield, I’d swear it’s a man’s shin bone, no more, no less. But this is no battlefield, nor a churchyard—it’s an inn.”

“True, mate. But yon knave’s ashy face is a better light to me than any battlefield could be. Bring yon face nearer, I say. When the chine of the house is missing, and the house dog can’t look at you without tucking his tail between his legs, who’s the thief? Good brothers, my flesh creeps. The deeper I dig, the more bones I find. Mayhap if they could speak, they’d make every honest man’s blood run cold.”

“Alas! Young man, what hideous fancies are these!” the landlord wailed. “They are bones of beeves, and sheep, and kids, not men and women, as ye think. Holy saints preserve us!”

“Hold thy peace. Thou dost not speak to burghers who can’t tell a veal knuckle from their grandsire’s ribs. Thou speakest to soldiers—men who have gone out to look for their dead comrades, and found their bones picked clean by crows, just as these have been by thee and thy pack. Men and women, saidst thou? Prithee, when did I ever utter a word of women’s bones? Thou wouldst make even a child suspect thee. Drag him close. Now what is this, thou knave?” Denys thrust a small, pale object suddenly under his nose.

“Alas, I know not!”

“I’d not swear to it either, but it looks far too like the thumb bone of a man’s hand. Mates, my flesh is crawling. How know we this is not a hidden charnel house, not a cellar at all?” He drew his sword full from its sheath, and began raking the heap of dirt, broken crockery and bones out across the floor.

The landlord babbled that he was wasting his time. “We poor innkeepers are sinners, to be sure—we give short measure, we water the wine, we must do such things for the laws are cruel to us. But we are no assassins. How could we afford to kill our customers? May Heaven’s lightning strike me dead if there is a single human bone here! These are all kitchen scraps the wench tossed aside. I swear by the Holy Mother, by Saint Paul, by Saint Dominic, and by Denys my patron saint—ah!”

Denys held a full, bare human skull up before his eyes, dead silent. No man, no matter how ignorant or how lying, could mistake it for the skull of a sheep or ox. The sight of it clamped the landlord’s lying lips shut, and palsied his cowardly heart. His hair rose straight up on his head like sharp spikes, and his knees gave way as if someone had struck his legs out from under him. The archers dragged him back up by the arms, held him pinned under the torchlight, staring face to face with the white skull, as pale as his own terror-stricken cheek, its empty eye sockets glaring back at the man who had pried the eyes from the head it once belonged to. The landlord’s mouth gaped open and open, but no sound would come out.

“Ah!” Denys spoke, solemn now, trembling with rage. “Look on those sockets thou robbed of sight. Let them blast thine own eyes, that the crows shall pick out before the week is out. Now hold that while I search on. Hold it, I say, or here I will rob the gallows of its due!” He threatened the quaking wretch with his naked sword, until the landlord took the cold skull in his shaking hands, and almost fainted dead away.

Soon the whole heap was scattered, and not one or two, but dozens of skulls glinted in the torchlight, the murderer whimpering at every new discovery.

Suddenly Denys uttered a sharp, strange cry of pain, the sort no one would expect from so bold and hard a man. He held up a great tangled mass of long, glossy golden human hair. At the sight of it the archers shook the craven landlord hard in their grasp, and he whined like a kicked dog.

“I have a little sister back home with hair just this fair and shining,” Denys gulped, thick with rage. “Jesu! What if this was hers? Quick, lads—take my sword and my dagger, keep them far from my hand, lest I strike him dead and cheat the wheel of its rightful work. Thou poor innocent soul, whose head this beautiful hair once grew on, hear me swear on bended knee: I will never leave this man’s side till I see him broken to pieces on the wheel, even for thy sake.”

He rose to his feet, fire in his eyes. “Aye, had he as many lives as there are hairs in that lock, I’d take every last one, by God.” He tucked the golden hair safe into his tunic, then seized the landlord by the throat, forced him face down into the thickest pile of his victims’ bones, grinding his face savagely into the shards of human remains until the wretch first yelled, then whimpered, then sniveled like a dog whose nose has been rubbed in the innocent creature he killed.

“Lend me thy bowstring, Philippe!” He threaded the cord alternately through the two empty sockets of a skull, hung the ghastly relic round the man’s neck, then dragged him up by the scruff of his neck and kicked him steadily all the way into the inn’s kitchen. There, an alderman of the town had just arrived with his constables, and was taking a deposition from one of the archers. The grave burgher started up in shock at the sight of the bleeding innkeeper, his face crisscrossed with shallow cuts from the shards of bone, wearing his horrible skull collar.

Denys panted in after him, and told the full, fiery story in a dozen short, blazing words. “Bind him like the rest of the thieves,” the alderman said sternly. “I count him the blackest villain of the whole gang.” As his hands were bound tight behind his back, the wretch begged piteously that the skull might be taken off his neck. “Humph!” the alderman said. “Certes I would never have ordered such a thing done to a mortal man. But since it hangs there already, I will not lift a finger to take it off. Methinks it fits thee perfectly, thou bloody dog. ’Tis thy true ensign, and it hangs well above a heart so foul as thine.”

He asked Denys if they had secured the entire gang, or only a part. “Your worship,” Denys said, “there are seven robbers in the band, plus this landlord. One we slew upstairs, one we trundled down dead, the rest are all bound before you.”

“Good. Go fetch the dead one from upstairs, and lay him beside the other corpse I had my men remove earlier.”

A shrill, peevish voice cut in then, like a guinea fowl squawking. “Now, now, now! Where is the severed hand? That is what I want to see!” The speaker was a small, pettifogging little clerk, giddy with the chance to collect high-profile evidence. He whispered in his master’s ear that the pieces de conviction would make a very fine show for the court, and then scribbled them down one by one in a high squeak: Skulls, Bones, A woman’s golden hair, 1 severed thief’s hand, 1 axe, 2 carcasses, 1 crossbow bolt.

When he was done writing, he ached to search the cellar himself for more priceless bits of evidence—maybe a severed ear, even a gold earring. The alderman gave his assent, and the clerk grabbed a torch and hurried toward the cellar stairs—only to be stopped short by a most ridiculous accident.

The constables had gone up the upper stairs in single file. No sooner did the head constable catch sight of the phosphorescent corpse of the dead robber propped by the bed, than he froze, stupefied. Then he began to shake like a man in the grip of a bad ague, terror swallowing him whole, and he let out a wild howl, recoiling backward as fast as his legs could carry him. He forgot the steps were there, and tumbled over right on top of the constable behind him, who, already startled by the shout and catching a glimpse of the horrible glowing corpse, was already staggering back, and could not support the ponderous head constable’s weight. The two knocked over the third, the three knocked over the fourth, and they all streamed back into the kitchen, piling up on the floor in a tangled, overlapping heap like cards laid out on a table. The clerk, hurrying along with his torch, ran full tilt into the last man in the heap, and went flying flat on his back, the torch waving in the air as if in triumph—though he was really quite unconscious, the breath driven clean out of his lungs by the impact.

“What in Heaven’s name is happening now?” the alderman cried, jumping up in alarm. But Denys laughed and explained the sight of the glowing corpse had spooked the entire lot, and offered to escort his worship upstairs to see for himself. The alderman agreed, his rueful men picked themselves up off the floor, and the whole party searched the premises top to bottom. The prisoners’ formal interrogation was put off until the serving girl could return from the town to confront them.

Before the first streaks of dawn painted the sky gray, all the thieves, dead and alive, and every grim relic of their decades of hidden murder had been swept away into the custody of the town law. The inn fell silent, almost deserted. Only one single constable remained on guard, along with Denys and Gerard—who still slept on, heavily, unaware of all the horror and hard justice that had unfolded around him while he lay lost to the world.

Gerard stirred at last, slow to drag his eyes open after a night that had unspooled into blood and terror before they found the rough, reed-thatched hovel that had sheltered them till dawn. Denys the archer crouched beside him, his weathered face lined with uncharacteristic worry, a half-carved arrow shaft idle in his calloused, bow-string hardened hand.
“By all the saints, you can sleep,” Denys chided, nodding toward the slant of honeyed noon light spilling through the cracks in the hut’s mud wall. “It is full midday, man. The town criers have done three rounds of the streets already.”
Gerard drew a long, deep breath, his chest still tight with the half-memory of glinting daggers and the roar of bandits in the dark treeline. “That sleep was a blessed gift sent from Heaven,” he murmured softly. “It hangs like a soft, kind veil between me and that awful night. To think we sit here whole, unharmed—half the time I can almost convince myself the whole bloody struggle was nothing more than a fever dream.”
“Aye, lad, that’s the only sensible way to look on such things once they are done,” Denys grunted, clapping him gently on the shoulder, hard enough to make the young man wince faintly at the bruise hidden under his tunic. “They’re shadows, no more, once the sun’s up. Eat a bite to break your fast, and you’ll scarce think of it again. Besides, I swore I’d have you into the town by noon, to stand before his worship the alderman as we are bound to.”
Gerard reached for the hunk of hard rye bread they’d stashed in their pack the day before, sopping the crust deep in the sour, spiced red wine they’d scavenged from a roadside tavern the prior afternoon, and ate slowly, his gaze drifting now and then to the dark treeline beyond the hut’s door. When he was done, the two men tramped back out to the stretch of forest clearing where the fight had unfolded, and Gerard flinched, shuddering, at the sight of discarded daggers, torn scraps of bandit tunic, and dark, crusted stains seeping into the fallen autumn leaves. He did not linger there, hurrying after Denys as they took the rutted road toward the small walled town, his eyes darting between every hedge and thicket, half-expecting a hidden attacker to leap out at them with every step.
They passed through the town gates at last, and Denys led him straight to *The White Hart*, a stout timber inn with a swinging sign painted with the white hart of Burgundy’s royal arms. “No cut-throats will touch you here,” Denys promised, shoving the door open to the warm, yeasty smell of spiced ale. “I’ve known the landlord nigh on ten years. He’s a burgess of good standing, and halfway to being named bailiff by the town council. This was where I was heading for yestereve, but we lost too much time fending off the rogues, and night overtook us before we could make the walls, and—”
“And you would not listen to the woman at the cottage door, would you?” Gerard put in, a faint, wobbly laugh breaking through his frayed nerves. “You thought you knew better than old Jeanneton, who warned us the woods were full of thieves.”
Denys huffed, not affronted. “Aye, and who was it that saved our lives in the end, if not a woman? Risked her own skin to slip out in the dark and carry word of the ambush right to the alderman, so the patrol came in time to haul those villains off before they cut our throats.”
“That is the very truth of it,” Gerard said warmly, his face softening. “Women have never been aught to me, not since—” He paused, thinking of Margaret far away in their native Holland, and his voice steadied. “But I would give half the coins in my purse right now to find that lass, to thank her, to reward her for what she did. Do you not feel the same?”
“Parbleu, of course,” Denys nodded.
“Where are we to find her, then?” Gerard asked.
“The alderman will surely know where she lives,” Denys told him. “We have to go and speak to him first, anyway.”
When they were shown into the alderman’s panelled parlour, the town worthy regarded them for a long, strange, unreadable moment, his bushy brows drawn together. Then a grim, slow smile spread across his face, and he leaned forward to fire question after question at Gerard, scribbling down every word of their account of the ambush with a sharp goose quill. When he had finished, he set down the quill and fixed them with a stern look.
“You two will remain in this town until the bandits are brought to trial,” he said, “and you will be on hand to give your testimony. Fail to appear, and you face heavy fines, even a turn in the town jail.”
Both men’s faces fell, their shoulders slumping.
“Do not look so glum,” the alderman added. “It will not be long. The rogues were taken red-handed, still with their daggers drawn, no way to deny their crimes. And besides—” he added, with a thin little smile “—you could not leave this town at all this week, in any case.”
Denys blinked, confused, but Gerard almost laughed, thinking the old man must be daft to imagine a tiny provincial Burgundy town could hold him back from Rome, from the Margaret he ached to return to. He leaned forward, speaking before either of them could press the alderman on his odd remark.
“Your worship,” he said, “the thing that weighs most on both our hearts right now—we cannot find the lass who saved our lives anywhere in the town.”
The alderman tilted his head. “Your benefactress? Who do you mean?”
“Why, the good girl who slipped out in the dead of night to come to you, who risked being caught by the bandits to carry word that we were about to be murdered out on the west road,” Gerard said, his voice earnest and warm. “Sir, our hearts burn within us to thank her, to bless her, to make sure she is repaid for her kindness. Where is she?”

“In prison, sir? Good lack, what wickedness could she have committed?”

“Ah, she’s a witness. A necessary one, at that.”

“Now, Messire Bailiff,” Denys cut in, grinning, “you don’t clap every last witness in irons, I’d wager?”

The alderman, flattered to be given the courtesy title of bailiff, grew far more talkative. “In a case of blood, we detain any soul that’s like to give us leg bail and cheat justice — that’s why we’ve held all the womenfolk connected to this band. A man might hide a secret in his own mind for a week, off and on, but a woman? If she does her duty to the realm on a Friday, she’ll undo the whole of it before Sunday, mark me. If you saw that girl Manon now, you’d find her blubbering her eyes out, guilty that she betrayed five men to the gallows. Had they been other women, we’d have trusted a simple subpoena — they despise one another, and that shows no small share of sense. But now I think on it, there’s more reason than that to lock her up. Hand me those depositions, young man.” He slid his spectacles on, flipping through the pages. “Aye, here it is. She was mixed up in the lot of them, part of the band.”

Denys and Gerard both burst out in loud, immediate denial.

“Save your breath, no need to din my ears,” the alderman waved them off. “It’s all here in black and white. ‘Jean Hardy, one of the thieves, under questioning, confessed that — humph, aye, here it is. And that the girl Manon was their decoy, and her sweetheart was Georges Vipont, one of the band, hanged last month; that she’s been dejected ever since, and openly blamed the rest of the band for his death, swearing if they hadn’t been rank cowards he’d never have been taken, and it is his opinion she only betrayed them out of pure spite, and—’”

“His opinion?” Gerard cried, indignant. “What value has the word of a cutthroat burning to revenge himself on the woman who delivered him to justice? Why should his testimony count? Is a thief ever anything but a liar? And here he has the strongest motive in the world to lie: revenge, the most ungovernable of all human passions. Oh sir, what madness to question a caught felon, and take his word over an innocent life — as if he were an honest man swearing in open court, his true hand laid on the Gospel!”

“Young man,” the alderman said, frowning, “restrain that heat in front of authority! Your tone tells me you are a stranger here. Know that in this land we question everyone. We are not so foolish as to hope to find truth by stopping up either our left or our right ear.”

“So you would listen to Satan himself slandering the saints!”

“Tush, tush! The law only deals with men and women, and no man alive can spin a tale that is all lies, no matter how hard he tries. We do not bar the barn door against any man’s grain, as the saying goes. Once we’ve taken it in, we winnow it, and sift it clean. And who told you I swallowed that thief’s story whole like plain spring water? I only credited the parts of it that were borne out by far better proof.”

“Better proof?” Gerard stared, bewildered. “Why, who but the thieves would breathe a word against her?”

“Marry — herself.”

“Herself, sir? You questioned her too?”

“I told you, we question everyone. Here is her deposition. Can you read? Then read it for yourself.”

Gerard glanced at Denys, and read the simple, trembling words in Manon’s own hand:
“I am a native of Epinal. I left my home two years ago because I was unfortunate: I could not bear the man my father bade me marry. He beat me for it, so I ran away. I went into service, but left when my mistress grew jealous of me, and turned me out for being saucy. Last year I stood in the marketplace to be hired with the other girls, and the landlord of The Fair Star inn took me on. I stayed eleven months with him. A young man courted me, and I fell in love with him. Then I found out that travellers who came to the inn never left again. I told my lover, and he bade me hold my peace, threatened me when I would not. I learned my lover was one of the band of thieves. When travellers were meant to be robbed, the landlord would slip out and call the band in. I wept, and prayed for the travellers’ souls, but I never spoke a word. A month ago, my lover died.
“The soldier [Denys] reminded me of him — he wore a beard just like the one my love had. I do not know if I would have run for help if that soldier had not had a beard. I am sorry I told now.”

The paper nearly slipped out of Gerard’s fingers. For the first time, he saw that Manon’s life hung by a thread, that the stubborn, unyielding local law would hang her without a second thought. He dropped hard on his knees at the alderman’s feet. “Oh, sir! Think of the difference between those brutal men and this poor weak girl! Could you find it in your heart to send her to the same death as the thieves? Could you condemn us to stand and watch her slaughtered — when she risked her own life to save ours, and would never be in any danger at all if not for that? Show Denys and me pity, at least, if you have none for her, poor soul. We are both honest men, and you will break our hearts if you kill that simple, helpless girl. What else could we do but cut our own throats at the foot of her gallows?”

The alderman was tough, but he was still human. Gerard’s desperate pleas first stunned him, then softened him, in his own gruff way. He grew peevish, waving a hand. “There, get up off the floor, will you. I doubt anyone would waste half that many words begging for me. Daniel! Go fetch the town clerk at once.” When the clerk stepped in from the next room, he nodded at Gerard. “This foolish lad is fretting himself ill over that Manon girl. Can we stretch the rules a little? Let her be admitted as a witness, question her gently, no harshness.”

The town clerk was one of those men whose whole job is to find impossibilities. “Nay sir, we cannot do that. She was not party to the attack on your two travellers. If she had been an accessory, we could legally offer her a pardon in return for giving evidence.”

Gerard burst in, “But she did far better than being an accessory! She stopped the murder from happening, and ran all the way here to report the crime of her own free will!”

“Tush, young man, this is a matter of written law.” The alderman and the clerk bickered for a long while, the first arguing that Manon’s actions put her in the exact same legal position as if she had been an accessory, the other repeating that every step was against the rules. That was Manon’s luck: irritated past endurance at the clerk’s endless list of things he “could not” do, the alderman thundered that he would show him he could do whatever he chose in this case. He had Manon brought out, arranged for the landlord of The White Hart to stand as her bondsman, and Denys deposited five gold pieces with the court to guarantee she would appear when summoned. The alderman set her free, but eased his own conscience by explaining his “leniency” bluntly: “The town has to buy a new rope for every hanged man, and give it to the hangman, or pay him the cost in coin. She is not worth that municipal expense, not like the hardened rogues she once ran with.”

So Denys and Gerard led her away, Gerard dancing around her for joy, Denys cheering her up by telling her all her old bad acquaintances were soon to be dead, while she wept weakly. On the walk back to The White Hart, the crowd spotted her — the archers had already spread the full story, praising her for her courage, and the public followed them cheering, shouting words of encouragement, until Manon, finding herself surrounded by well-wishers, plucked up her courage. The inn landlord saw at a glance that her presence would draw crowds of curious customers, and welcomed her politely, giving her a private upper chamber. She shut herself inside, and as soon as she was alone, the tears came pouring down again. Poor little soul, her spirits were as unsteady as a ripple on water, rising and falling, falling and rising, no stillness at all. Gerard and Denys bade the landlord treat her gently, keep her effectively “prisoner” but never let her feel confined, and then stepped out into the street.

Right in front of them, two processions were coming from opposite directions. One was huge, noisy, full of howls and the wild, raw cries rude folk give voice to when they let the beast beneath their civilized manners show itself. The other was small, quiet, attended only by a handful of nuns and friars, moving slow and silent.

The thieves were being paraded on a cart to the marketplace, to be put on public display before hanging. The bones of their murdered victims were being carried to the churchyard, for Christian burial.

The two groups met in the narrow street, right at the door of the inn, and could not pass one another for a long time. The bier holding the mortal remains of the dead travellers wedged tight against the cart that carried the men who had murdered them — men who would themselves be dead before the sun set. The mob did not grasp the grim poetry of the moment at first, but then a woman screamed out, “Look at your work, you dogs!” and the crowd took up the cry like wildfire, a horrible yell that made the culprits groan, trying to hide their faces against their chests, though their bound hands would not let them. There they stood, pale, hollow-eyed, images of utter despair, staring at the bier, envying the men they had sent ahead down the dark road they were about to walk themselves. Even Manon, hearing the commotion, crept to the window, hid half her face, and peeped trembling through her fingers, as women so often do.

That strange, stark meeting parted Denys and Gerard. Denys, drawn by curiosity and quiet revenge, drifted off to follow the thieves’ cart to the marketplace. Gerard pulled his bonnet off his head, and piously followed the bier carrying the poor souls whose fate he and Denys had so narrowly escaped. For a while he was the only lay mourner, but when they reached the suburbs, far away from the bigger spectacle the gallows promised, more than one artisan dropped his tools, more than one shopkeeper left his shop, touched by pity and common humanity, and drawn in no small part by Gerard’s bareheaded example. They followed the bones, uncovered, until the priests laid them in hallowed ground with the full prayers of the Church.

When the funeral rites were done, Gerard stepped respectfully up to the cure, and offered to pay for a mass to be said for the dead travellers’ souls. Gerard, son of Catherine, always looked at both sides of a penny, and he tried to haggle the price down a little, citing the pitiable circumstances of the deaths. But the good cure gently, adroitly parried his every attempt at a discount, and blandly pushed him to pay the full standard market price.

As they talked, they realized they shared a striking similarity of sentiment. Piety and worldly prudence are not rare companions, but it is uncommon to see both carried so far as these two men carried them. Their little collision in the “prayer market” sparked a mutual respect, like two knights meeting in the lists, each finding the other a worthy opponent. The cure loved a good bit of gossip, and when he learned his customer was one of the two men who had fought off the thieves at Domfront, he dragged Gerard back to his parlour to hear the whole story from his own lips. His heart warmed to Gerard. “God was good to you,” he said. “I thank Him for that, with all my soul. You are a good lad.” He added drily, “You should have told me that tale in the churchyard. I doubt I would have charged you a sou for the mass, out of affection. But” — his tone cooled sharply — “it is bad luck to go back on a bargain once struck. But I will broach a bottle of my very oldest Medoc for you. Few guests in this world get that honour.” He rummaged in his cupboard for the precious bottle, and muttered under his breath, “At their old tricks again!”

“Pardon, your reverence?” Gerard said.

“I said nothing. Aye, here it is.”

“Nay, you spoke. You said, ‘At their old tricks again!’”

“Did I, in truth?” The cure smiled. He poured them each a full cup, tossed an extra log on the fire — for Burgundy had no stoves, back then — and leaned back. “So I said ‘At their old tricks’? Come, sip the good wine, and while it lasts, story for story. I will not deny you a little tale of my own.”

Gerard’s eyes sparkled. “I love a good story more than life itself.”

“Do not raise your hopes too high, mind you. It is but a silly trifle, next to your own adventures.”

---
“Once upon a time, in the kingdom of France, in the duchy of Burgundy, less than a day’s ride from the very town where we sit sipping this old Medoc, there lived a cure. I say he ‘lived’ — he barely scraped by. His parish was small, the parishioners were greedy, and never gave their cure a single doit more than he could force them to pay. The closer they starved him to a disembodied ghost, the holier they believed his prayers for them would be. I do not know if that was their exact creed, but their behaviour certainly made it look that way.

“At last, the cure thought up a trick to teach them a lesson. One fine day, the richest farmer in the parish had twins to baptize. The cure was invited to the christening feast, as was customary — but before he would baptize the children, he demanded not just the standard christening fee, but their burial fees, too. ‘Saints defend us, parson!’ the new mother cried. ‘Do not talk of burying! I never saw two healthier children more likely to live long lives.’ ‘Nor did I,’ the cure said. ‘Praise be to God. But none the less, they are sons of Adam, same as you and I, and they will die one day. Whenever that day comes, their burial will cost them nothing — the fees are paid already, and written down in my book.’ ‘Nay, that will cost them something else,’ the miller cut in, the biggest joker and the biggest rogue in the parish. The whole parish laughed loud at his jest, and in the middle of all the merriment, they paid the fees, and the twins were baptized.

“But soon every new child born in the parish had their burial fee paid at christening too, or they could not be entered in the parish register, making them ineligible for heaven. Resentment simmered, secret, through the whole village. One day they met in secret, and sent their churchwarden to the bishop with a formal complaint. A summons arrived for the cure at dinnertime: he was to bring all his parish books to the episcopal palace, and answer the charges against him. His appetite vanished instantly. He left his half-eaten food on the table, took the books, and rode to the palace, quaking.

“The bishop greeted him with a frown, laid the complaint out on the table. ‘Monseigneur,’ the cure said, humbly, ‘does the parish lay many charges against me, or just this one?’ ‘Only this one,’ the bishop said, softening a little. ‘First, monseigneur, I admit the facts are true.’ ‘Good,’ the bishop said. ‘That saves us time. Now, give me your excuse, if you have one.’ ‘Monseigneur,’ the cure said, ‘I have been cure of that parish seven years. In that time, I baptized fifty children, and buried fewer than five. At first I thought “Heaven be praised, the air of this village is so healthy!” But when I checked the registers, I saw that it had always been that way. I dug into the matter, and found that almost every child born in Domfront left the village, went to Aix, and got himself hanged. They did that not just to cheat their own cure of fees, but the whole Church — for hanged men are buried out in the open air, and never pay funeral dues. Knowing how greedy my parishioners are, how they grudge the Church every single sou, I laid that little trap for them. Greed against greed, you see. I knew that rather than pay the Church nothing for their funeral, they would stay home, die peacefully in their beds, like honest men.’

“The bishop laughed so hard the tears ran down his face. He called in the churchwarden, who had to admit that far too many of the parish’s young men did indeed end up hanged at Aix. ‘I approve your action,’ the bishop told the cure. ‘I will make sure all my successors approve it too — until your parishioners mend their ways, and start dying in their beds like decent folk.’ The next day, the ringleaders of the complaint came to the cure, crestfallen. ‘Parson, you have always been good to us, save for this one silly quarrel. Let there be no hard feelings between us, over nothing.’ And the cure said, ‘My children, I would not be worthy to be your pastor if I could not forgive a small wrong. Go in peace. Now go and have as many children as you possibly can, so that between the double fees, the cure you love will not starve to death.’

“The bishop told that story for years, and never forgot that cure. At last he moved him to a decent, generous parish, where that cure can offer a bottle of his old Medoc to any guest worthy of it. And worthy guests, as you can guess, are few and far between.”

A light dawned on Gerard’s face. “Aye,” the cure grinned. “That cure is me. Now you know why I muttered ‘At their old tricks.’ I would wager my life

The band of captured highwaymen were sentenced to stand pinioned in the Neufchasteau market square for two full hours, a public display meant to give any unrecognized victims time to come forward and name them for other unproven crimes.
The whole two hours passed with no accuser stepping forth, little surprise given these were night-roving vampires of the road, who preyed almost exclusively on weary, far-travelling strangers who had no local kin to speak for them. But the moment the officers moved to cut them down and march them back to gaol, a woman in the crowd let out a scream so raw it cut over every other murmur, and pointed shaking at one of the prisoners, her eyes bulging almost out of her head. She did not get a single word out before she fainted dead away.
The crowd swarmed her, half to offer aid, half gawking. As she came to, they bickered over which man she had pointed at — no one could agree, until the woman flew upright like a lioness springing for her cub before any could stop her. “My child!” she shrieked at the burly innkeeper turned robber, “Man, man, give me back my child!” She tore the glossy golden child’s hair strung as a trophy around his neck, kissed it over and over, and then the fog cleared from her grief-muddled mind. She knew instantly by that very hair that her little girl was long dead, and sank back wailing, sobbing so hard over the locks that the whole crowd roared as one, surging for the thief to tear him limb from limb.
His life would have ended that minute, swift and brutal, in an age where every man carried a knife at his belt — but Denys the archer drew his sword in a single fluid motion, shouting, “To me, comrades!” and planted himself between the mob and the prisoner, steel glinting. “Who lays a finger on him dies.” His fellow archers stepped up behind him, and they held the crowd back by main force while Denys called out to the roaring throng: “What fool’s vengeance is this? Would you rob the public wheel of its due, and give this vermin an easy, quick death before the sentence even passes?”
The mob was held back less by his words than the edge of the archers’ drawn blades, growling and baring their teeth all the while, until the town’s municipal guards clustered round the prisoners to form a living shield, and marched them prudently back to gaol, the crowd hooting and jeering at both guards and robbers all the way.
Denys made sure the prisoners were locked safely away before heading for the White Hart inn, where he expected to meet Gerard. On the short walk, he spotted two pretty girls leaning out a first-floor window, working at their needlework. He tipped his hat, they smiled, he stopped to chat. Their manners were easy, their cheeks flushed bright, and when he invited them back to the White Hart for a feast of wine and spiced pastries, they demurred at first, then he playfully accepted their refusal, and they laughed and agreed instead. Lost in their company, he forgot all about Gerard, who at that very moment was being dragged off to gaol by two constables.
Gerard, still dazed from the chaos of the square, snapped back to his senses mid-journey, and stopped short, demanding to know by what authority he was being arrested.
“By the vice-bailiff’s,” the constable grunted.
“The vice-bailiff? Alas, what could a stranger far from home possibly have done to offend him? This charge of sorcery must be a blind — I am no magician, only a poor honest lad far from his village.”
The constable scoffed at the vague plea. “Show him the writ, Jacques,” he said. Jacques held the warrant out a full yard and a half from Gerard’s face, and the other constable pinned his arms tight at the same time: both men were on tenterhooks, scared the prisoner would lunge to tear the document up, for they held all official writs in superstitious awe.
But Gerard had no such thought. He would not have touched the cursed paper with a pair of tongs, for all the fear he was in. He just craned his neck, squinted, and read it. To his utter shock, the vice-bailiff who had signed the order was none other than the friendly alderman he had sat and drunk with not two days before. He begged the constables there was some terrible mistake, offered each of them an ecu if they would detour and take him to the alderman first, not straight to the dark gaol cell.
The two men bickered. “We have no orders to take him before his worship,” Jacques said.
“But — we also have no orders *not* to,” his partner pointed out, squinting at the fine print on the writ. They agreed, took the coins, and made a great show of doing Gerard a huge favour. He was too tense to feign the gratitude they wanted, but he tried, for fear they would change their minds.
He walked into the alderman’s parlour with his heart hammering in his throat, stammering that he had done no wrong since he left this very room alongside Manon and Denys a day prior.
“Nought that I know of,” the alderman said, confused, until the writ was handed to him. He sighed. “I signed this at dawn. I am old, my memory slips. I got to talking about that poor dead child the robber had murdered, and quite forgot I had ordered your arrest, you sorcerer. All is well, now I recall. Before you go to gaol, you will hear what your accuser says — run and fetch him, you.”
The servant could not find the accuser right away, and the impatient alderman explained to Gerard what the charge actually was: “They say you lit a dead man’s face with devil’s fire, that flames bright but never burns flesh. If that is true, lad, I grieve for you — you will burn alive on good pine logs in the Neufchasteau market square, no reprieve.”
“Sir, for pity’s sake, let me speak to the cure, our parish priest!” Gerard begged.
The alderman warned him against it: the Church was far harsher on accused sorcerers than the town council could ever be.
“But sir, I am innocent!” Gerard cried, half indignant, half desperate.
“If you truly think that — officer, go with him to the cure, but mind he does not escape. Innocent, indeed!”
They found the cure in his linen doublet, out in his yard nailing a broken wheelbarrow back together. Gerard spilled the whole tale, about the white chemical he had used only to scare the bandits off, no magic at all, and the shrewd priest, who had already heard the full story from Gerard the day before, knew exactly what was what. He told the constable to wait outside the private room, guard the door, and not come in no matter what sounds he heard. The big constable stood outside trembling, half expecting the walls to blow open in a puff of brimstone at any second.
The moment the door clicked shut behind the guard, the cure dropped his grave clerical face and grinned, curious as a boy. “Show me the trick,” he said.
“I cannot, unless the room is fully dark,” Gerard said. The cure slammed the wooden shutters closed, blocking every sliver of daylight. “But what can I put it on?” Gerard said. “There is no dead face here to make the glow look eerie.” The cure groped along the shelf, and fished out a small wooden statue of his patron saint.
“Good, use that.”
“Heaven forbid! That would be profanation,” Gerard protested.
“Pshaw, it will rub right off, will it not?” the cure laughed.
Thus encouraged, Gerard daubed the phosphorus on the statue’s eyes, nostrils, then streaked it through the wood-carved curls of its hair, until the whole face glowed like a live glow-worm in the pitch black. The cure yelped and jumped back in surprise.
“By Our Lady!” he shouted. “No wonder every soul who saw that dead robber’s face lit up like that thought you were a magician! Come, we go see the alderman now.”
He pulled on his grey clerical gown and big wide-brimmed hat, and they were back in the alderman’s parlour in minutes. Standing at the alderman’s side, whispering poison in his ear, was Gerard’s accuser: a gaunt, odd figure in bright red hose, red shoes, a black gown stitched with blue bands, and a lopsided cocked hat.
The cure smiled at the man, whose name was Mangis, and said, “So, Mangis, you are at your old tricks again, babbling honest men to their deaths! This is the same old game: two sorcerers will never agree. This man Mangis claims to be a white sorcerer, who would sell his soul to the devil tonight if Satan was fool enough to buy what he can take for free. This quack, who fancies himself a magician but is only a con man, accuses this innocent lad of black magic, when the boy only used a simple chemical secret well known to all learned churchmen to defend himself against robbers.”
“But he is no churchman, to dabble in such mysteries,” the alderman objected.
“He is more churchman than layman, raised in a convent, and ordained in the lesser orders,” the cure said smoothly. “Therefore, sorcerer, withdraw your complaint now.”
“Not I,” Mangis blustered. “I am a white sorcerer, I make no pact with the devil. I battle his black arts lawfully, I detect hidden black magicians — as I did that whole coven we burned at Dol last year!”
“Ay, Mangis,” the cure said, his voice turning sharp. “And what came of that famous fire you lit? Dijon’s parliament investigated last month, found they were all peaceful, innocent citizens, and ordered high masses said for their souls, and expiatory mystery plays performed for them across seven Burgundian towns. We do not blame our own credulous ears for burning the innocent — we blame the lying tongue that tricked us. If you do not drop this charge, I will send word to my lord bishop this very hour, and you will smell burning pine far closer than any man has ever lived through. The very word ‘devil’ in our Latin means ‘false accuser’ — and you wear his colours of red and black for all to see.”
The alderman nodded. “That is truth, now I look at him. Red and black are the fiend’s own livery.”
Mangis’s face bleached as pale as his gown was bright, stammered that he respected Holy Church, dropped the complaint immediately, and scurried out of the room as fast as his legs could carry him.
The cure turned back to the alderman, and told him that Gerard had already given over every last bit of the phosphorus to him, the Church, so no harm had been done. The alderman laughed, signed Gerard’s release papers instantly, and the two men struck a bargain over the town’s unpaid four silver francs owed to the cure for parish work.
The moment they stepped out into the street, Gerard knelt and kissed the cure’s hand. “Sir, you have saved me from the fire! How can I ever thank you?”
“Nought, foolish lad. Bounty rewards itself. Though — humph — I had to tell a small lie just now, that you gave me all the phosphorus. That falsehood will earn me a full fortnight of penance, no less,” the cure sighed, his eyes twinkling mischievously.
“Falsehood? But that was no lie!” Gerard cried, shoving the sealed glass bottle of phosphorus right into the priest’s palm. “It is yours, every last drop. And take this purse of mine, for the poor of the church!”
The cure stepped back, waved it away, gruff as ever. “Not a single denier. Fie, you are a pauper and an exile, you need it far more than the church. Come to my house every noon, instead, and eat your midday meal with me. I have taken a liking to you.” He turned and walked off abruptly, his hands stuffed behind his back, itching to take the purse far more than he would ever admit.
Gerard hurried to the White Hart to find Denys, and walked in on him happily rattling dice in a cup, playing for coin with the two pretty girls Denys had stopped to chat with that morning.
Gerard’s face flushed hot. “Do you forget Jeanneton’s proverb?” he said sharply. “Le peu que sont les femmes — women are nothing but trouble.”
Denys laughed, rattling the dice. “What say you to that, mesdemoiselles?” he asked the girls.
They tittered. “No man runs down women save one too old, too ugly, or too witless to please them,” they teased.
“Witless? Wise men do not have the folly to please you, nor the madness to want to,” Gerard said loftily. “I do not speak to you, brazen hussies who make free with a man the first time you meet him — I speak to my comrade.”
“Go on, preach away,” Denys said, grinning. “He is very Solomon of old proverbs, this one, lads, fed on nothing but wise sayings from the cradle.”
“Your friendship is a byword, then!” Gerard snapped. “Friendship that melts to nothing the second you see a farthingale.”
“Unhappy wretch!” Denys cried, laughing. “I only spout pellets of fun, and you answer with daggers.”
“Would that I could,” Gerard said, and turned to storm out. He paused in the doorway, glowered back, and shouted his new proverb at them:
“Qui hante femmes et dez
Il mourra en pauvretez.”
He slammed the door so hard the windows rattled, having delivered his thunderbolt of old wisdom.
Drained by all the day’s terror, he wandered to the inn bar for a crust of bread and a cup of wine. The landlord handed him a “pint” bottle that was unnaturally thick and heavy at the bottom, holding barely half the measure it claimed. Gerard pointed out the cheat at once, and threatened to carry the short-measure bottle straight to the vice-bailiff.
The landlord turned white, begged him not to, offered to sell him two of the “pints” for the price of one, and then launched into a long, passionate rant about how impossible it was to run an honest inn in Burgundy. Soldiers quartered on him were paid two sous a day and ate ten times that in food, pilgrims and black and grey friars ate like wolves and paid nothing but empty prayers, the local gentry were allowed to sell wine by the cup in the market square for half his price, excise men from three different layers of government showed up every week demanding free food and drink to “overlook” his measures, and the law forbade him from buying more than three bushels of meal at a time when market day only came once a week. He swore he did not cut travellers’ throats like the other road inns, he only cheated a little on the wine measures just to keep a roof over his head.
Mid-rant, Denys burst through the door, swearing so loud the whole bar went quiet. The two girls had snuck out one after the other, and stolen his entire purse, fifteen gold crowns. He roared that he hated the law, did not want to chase them, but Gerard dragged him to the provost marshal anyway. The official only shrugged, said these girls were respectable needleworkers most days, who only robbed gullible drunks when the chance came, and they were long gone over the town walls by now.
Denys stormed back out, fuming, but eventually calmed down enough to admit he had left five gold crowns with the alderman and ten more with Manon for safekeeping, so he was not completely ruined. Then he paused, and admitted sheepishly: “I — well. I asked her to marry me. Manon.”
Gerard stared at him, completely dumbfounded. “What? You offered marriage to a strange girl you met on the road, passing through?”
“Nay, I was not such a fool as that,” Denys grinned. “I knew she would never go off on the road with me otherwise. ‘Mademoiselle,’ I said, ‘marriage is not one of my usual habits, but struck by your great qualities, I make an exception. Deign to bestow your hand on me.’”
“And did she bestow her answer on your ear, with a slap?” Gerard said, gaping.

The crisp snow outside the town gate was crisscrossed paw to print by a thousand wolves, every yard of the winding road stitched with their fresh, heavy tracks. “We were wise to heed that old innkeeper’s warning, Denys,” Gerard said, his breath pluming white in the frosty air.

Denys grunted, shifting the weight of his crossbow over his shoulder. “Aye, wise enough. Only last night I heard the beasts scurrying right beneath our inn window, howling and whimpering for warm man’s flesh out in the market square. Not a single fat burgher leaned out to toss the poor vagabones a scrap, more’s the pity.”

Gerard smiled, but his gaze was distant, as if he was looking far past the drifts piling at the roadside. They tramped on in silence for a stretch, their boots crunching through frozen crust.

“What’s got you so deep in thought, lad?” Denys asked at last, prodding him gently in the ribs with an elbow.
“Your goodness,” Gerard said softly.

Denys’s face hardened instantly, all good humour gone in a flash. The veteran could stand a world of playful impertinence, his temper was as warm and easygoing as any man’s, but he would flare up over the silliest, smallest slight no one else even noticed. “A civil question deserves a civil answer,” he said drily, not looking at Gerard.
“Alas, I meant no offence,” Gerard protested.
“Then why pretend you were thinking on my goodness? There’s no such thing under my old leather skin.”
“Had any other man said that, I’d have called him a liar to his face,” Gerard said, half laughing. “But to you I say: you’ve no eye for your own virtues, only for women’s. And I defy your unreasonable choler right now – I was thinking of what you did last night, how you nearly married me off to the Golden Head tavern lass, and sent yourself off alone on the road, so I wouldn’t have to go back to Rome.”

“Ah, so that’s what’s got you moping!” Denys’s good humour flooded back as fast as it had vanished. “Truth be told, that wasn’t goodness, that was plain old friendship, no more. Though my conscience pricks me even now, that I didn’t hamstring you then and there, like a good true friend should. You’d have lain a month nursing the sore leg up at the *Tete d’Or*, that skittish pretty lass would have waited on you hand and foot, and you’d have stayed there fat and happy, no more tramping off to Rome after a girl you haven’t seen in months. I had my blade out all ready to do it, but then I remembered how you hate even the tiniest scratch, and my craven old heart failed me at the last minute.” He wore a look of genuine humble remorse, as if he’d failed a most sacred duty by not maiming his best friend.

Gerard gaped at him, astonished at the monstrous, utterly characteristic admission – but they never got a chance to argue the ethics of whether a true friend ought to cut their companion’s Achilles tendon out of love, for a shout cut across the wintry quiet.
“Look out behind us! Some fool is riding hell for leather on his neighbour’s mule!” Denys yelled.

Gerard spun around. “How can you tell it’s not his own?”
“Blind as a bat! No man rides his own mule like that, half out of his wits.”

Sure enough, a rustic came galloping at them full tilt, and when he reached the two travellers, his eyes went round as saucers, and he hauled so hard on the reins that the mule planted her forelegs and slid forward across the packed snow like a four-legged table on castors.
“Ye’re the two that stayed at the *Tete d’Or* inn, aye?” he panted.
They nodded.
“Which of ye’s the younger one?”
“The one born later,” Denys winked at Gerard.

“Cheers for that, genius,” the rustic said, unimpressed. “Right, then, youngster. You left this behind at the inn, our mistress sent me after you with it.” He held out a crumpled paper packet.
“Nay, good man, I didn’t leave aught behind,” Gerard said, patting his leather pouch.
“D’ye want to call our burgess’s wife a liar?” the man said, reproachful. “And where’s my pourboire? I rode all the way here ventre a terre, stomach to the earth, like.”

Gerard fished out a small copper coin and handed it over. The clown’s face lit up so bright he looked ready to dance. “God bless ye both! The Virgin ride with ye! Come on, Jenny!” He wheeled the mule around and galloped back the way he’d come.

Gerard untied the packet. It was six inches square, and inside was another wrapped packet, then another, then a fourth, until he got so impatient he nearly hurled the whole mess into the snow. Denys snatched it out of the drift and chided him for his petulance.
“O for Herodias’s little daughter’s big toe, that’s no affectation, that’s woman’s wit!” Denys said. “She’d not let her servants see what she’s giving a young unmarried man, out of modesty. Likely it’s your garter she found last night.”
“I don’t wear garters,” Gerard said.
“Then it’s hers! Or a lock of her hair. Wait, what’s this? Raw silk, soft as down. Saints and pikestaves, there’s something hard hiding in here!”

He fished it out: a great gold ring set with a deep purple amethyst, glowing like crushed wine, clear as crystal.
“Lovely,” Gerard said, blushing.
“And there’s a scrap of paper with writing on it! Read it, lad, I can’t read the fancy script when I don’t know what it’s about.”
