Gerard took the paper, and his face burned bright red as a girl’s as he read the lines, naive and soft as the girl who wrote them:

“The little dove!” Denys cooed.
“The great silly owl,” Gerard said, shaking his head. “Risking her good name for a foolish prank like this. Thank heaven she gave it to an honest lad who’d never spread word of it to shame her. But why on earth didn’t she bestow this on you? You’re far more ripe for foolish romance than I am.”

Denys sighed and shrugged, he had to admit the boy was right – it was absurd that a pretty lass would pass over a seasoned soldier like him to dote on a green lad barely out of his teens. He handed the ring back to Gerard, insisting he go back to the *Tete d’Or* right that minute to return it, but Gerard refused, saying the tiny pewter ring Margaret had given him was worth more than all the rubies in the world, and he kissed the dented base metal like it was a holy relic. Denys finally convinced him to tuck the amethyst ring inside the lining of his bonnet, where it could act as a protective talisman, as folks said amethysts had power to ward off drunkenness and danger.

Gerard then begged Denys not to talk of women any more: every word of it made him ache so bad for Margaret he could barely stand, it felt like every step they took was pulling him farther and farther away from her. “There’s only room in my heart for one sweetheart, and one friend, Denys. Let me drink our friendship pure, no silly female nonsense to dilute it, while I still have it.”
“Sure thing, honey-pot, sure thing,” Denys said, clapping him on the shoulder. “And forget any idea I’m leaving you at Remiremont! I’ll go with you all the way to Rome. The Pope’s always got a little merry war going, and Burgundian soldiers are always welcome in his ranks. Hand on it, lad!”

Gerard’s heart swelled so full he could barely speak. He ran twice circles around Denys where he walked, danced backwards in front of him, then took his hand, and they tramped on hand in hand like two sweethearts, until they spotted a band of fifty mounted soldiers crested over the brow of the hill, the banner of Burgundy flying bright in the sun.
“Glorious,” Gerard said, staring at their velvet coats, their plumed helmets, their steel breastplates polished like mirrors. But Denys’s smile dropped the second he recognised the commander.
“That’s the Bastard of Burgundy himself! He’s out, which means there’s fighting up north in Flanders. That’s no man to trifle with.”

The troop rode right up to them. “Halt!” a stentorian voice roared.
The Bastard glared at Denys. “Arbalestrier, what are you doing heading south, when every loyal man in the duchy is hurrying north to put down the rebellion?”
Denys bowed respectfully, explained he was on leave after three years of service, on his way home to Remiremont to see his family.
“No leave now. Get on that spare mule, you’re coming north with us to Flanders.”
“Begging your highness’s pardon, I cannot,” Denys said, standing firm. “My home is close by, I haven’t seen my kin in three years, and I am in charge of this young man, I cannot leave him until I see him safe shipped to Rome.”

“You dare bandy words with me?” The Bastard’s face turned purple with rage. “Jarnac! Dismount six archers, shoot this white-livered cur dead for an example! Strip him, put his arms on the spare mule, we’ll find some man worthier to wear them.”
“NO!” Gerard screamed, waking from the stunned stupor the tyrant’s order had thrown him into. “He’ll go with you! I’d lose him for ever before I let a hair on his head be harmed. Just give me one minute to say goodbye, please!”

The Bastard nodded coldly, then rode off with the rest of the troop, leaving Count de Jarnac and six archers behind. The two friends stared at each other, haggard, their faces streaked with tears. “Go to Rotterdam,” Denys gasped. “Margaret is there. I’ll break away at the first chance, meet you there, we’ll all be together.”

The archers hauled Denys up onto the mule, gentle as they could, even rough soldiers had respect for comrades who loved each other that deep. They spurred after the Bastard, and Gerard ran as fast as he could after them, until he saw Denys leaning over the mule’s neck, tearing his hair out in grief, and Gerard’s throat closed up so tight he couldn’t breathe, and he collapsed against a thorn hedge, the thorns piercing his hand unnoticed.

When he got his breath back, he staggered on alone. The whole world was nothing but white snow, silent, desolate, not a living soul in sight. He was friendless now, and soon, a band of servants riding with a wealthy nobleman galloped back, surrounded him, and bade him stand and deliver. The nobleman sat his horse a hundred yards off, watching, too proud to do his own robbing, but happy to take the coin. Gerard didn’t fight, he didn’t want to throw his life away for a few coins, that would break Margaret’s heart. He tossed them his purse, and they rode off laughing.

Penniless, friendless, exhausted to the bone, Gerard stumbled to the edge of a wood. He couldn’t get to Rome now, he couldn’t even get to Strasbourg. The lass’s words echoed in his head: *If the world prove harsh and cold, come back to the Hedde of Gold.* But he’d never go back there as her servant, he was Margaret’s, body and soul. He was so tired, he crawled to the snow at the roadside, stretched out his limbs, and his eyes closed. He’d barely noticed the thorns in his hand, barely felt the cold seep into his bones. The last thing he thought of was Margaret’s face, and Denys’s laugh, before the darkness closed over him, alone in the wintry drift, half way to Rome, with no one to help him.

Some men turn hard and old at forty, while others carry the fire of youth right through their eightieth year. Margaret Van Eyck’s heart was an evergreen. She loved her young namesake, Margaret Brandt, with all the ardour of a girl half her age, and this fondness was no fleeting fancy: she had a sharp eye for character, and saw in the younger Margaret that rarest of qualities, that which wins the regard of an intelligent woman most of all in another of her sex: unshakable genuineness. But even beyond Margaret Brandt’s own sterling nature, there was a force in the old artist’s bosom pulling her close that neither she nor the girl ever spoke of out loud.

Human nature.

It is a truth that surprises most folk who never stop to observe their own hearts: we warm far faster to the people we have benefited than we ever do to the people who benefit us. Greek philosophers noted this thousands of years back, and the old British balladeer stamped it into immortal verse, when he wrote of the soldier who could not bring himself to kill his old comrade, not for any kindness the comrade had done him, but for all the kindness he had given the man:
“I heard, and thought how side by side
We two had stemmed the battle's tide
In many a well-debated field,
Where Bertram's breast was Philip's shield.
I thought on Darien's deserts pale,
Where Death bestrides the evening gale,
How o'er my friend my cloak I threw,
And fenceless faced the deadly dew.
I thought on Quariana's cliff,
Where, rescued from our foundering skiff,
Through the white breakers' wrath I bore
Exhausted Bertram to the shore:
And when his side an arrow found, I sucked the Indian's venom'd wound.
These thoughts like torrents rushed along
To sweep away my purpose strong.”

The assassin’s hand was stayed not by memories of favours received, but favours he had given.

Margaret Van Eyck had lavished care on Margaret Brandt: she had broken all her usual quiet routines to make the journey out to Sevenbergen to visit her, nursed her through the worst of her grief-stricken fever, soothed her, petted her, and pulled her through far better than any apothecary’s medicine could have done. No wonder her heart opened wide to the girl on the receiving end of all that goodness, till she loved her far more tenderly than she had ever loved Gerard, even though she had first gone to visit the girl purely out of fondness for him.

So when she saw the rose colour creep back into Margaret Brandt’s cheeks, and read the scrap of parchment that had proven Gerard was alive and on his way to Italy, she set aside her own long-laid plans without a single murmur.

“Sweetheart,” she said, “I had hoped he might stay in Italy five or six years, come back rich, and above all come back a master painter. But your happiness stands above all that, and I can see plain as day you cannot live a full life without him. So we will send for him home as fast as we possibly can.”

“Ah, madam! You see my very thoughts,” the young woman breathed, and hung her head, blushing deep. “But how do we get word to him? That is far beyond my wits. He has gone to Italy, but I do not know what part. Wait! He named the cities he planned to visit: Florence was one, Rome the next. But—” She paused, and the sensible girl in her quickly realised a letter addressed to “My Gerard, Italy” would almost certainly go astray, and she looked to her older friend with desperate, imploring eyes.

“You have come to exactly the right person, at exactly the right time,” the old lady smiled. “Hans Memling was with me only this morning. He is off to Italy no later than next week, he says, ‘to improve his hand’. And it could not come a moment too soon, I can tell you.”

“But how will he find my Gerard?” Margaret frowned.

“Why, he knows your Gerard, child! They have supped at my table together more than once, thick as thieves. Their work is the same, after all: he will visit every church, every artist’s workshop Gerard planned to see, and he is bound to cross paths with him sooner or later. So sit down and write him a long letter, copy out that pardon of ours that proves you are well and waiting for him, and I will answer for the messenger. In six months at the very farthest, Gerard will hold it in his hands. And when he does, you know he will kiss it, tuck it next to his heart, and fly home to you. What are you smiling at? And why are your cheeks so bright red, and why are you smothering me in hugs, silly thing? Happy days are coming to my little pearl at last.”

Down in the kitchen meanwhile, Martin Wittenhaagen sat by the fire with a black jack of ale before him, while Reicht Heynes spun at her wheel beside him, and pestered every last scrap of gossip out of him that night.

For all Margaret Van Eyck’s light gibe at his “need to improve his hand”, Hans Memling was a genuine painter, an old pupil of Jan Van Eyck and his sister, a good soul at heart who had only one real fault: he loved a draught of brown ale far more than it deserved. That soft spot kept him from ever amassing wealth, and he was forever popping back to Margaret Van Eyck’s door for a free meal, or a few small coins to tide him over. That meant she had a firm hold on his loyalty, and she knew full well he would never trifle with any commission she entrusted to him.

The letter was duly written, and left in Margaret Van Eyck’s care. The following week, Hans Memling turned up fresh from a trip through Flanders, and she pressed the letter into his hands, plus a piece of gold to cover his travel expenses. He was in such a tearing hurry to set off, she thought it a good sign: he would be in Italy all the faster, to deliver their news.

But horses that snort and rage to bolt before the start often slow to a crawl the second they are out of the gate. No sooner had Hans got as far as the main inn in Tergou, than he spotted two of his favourite drinking buddies sitting in the bay window. He stepped in for one parting glass, and before he knew what was happening, his friends insisted on treating him, then the landlord insisted on buying the next round, and by the end of the night his tongue was as loose as if the wine had been oil. He bragged to the whole convivial crowd that he was off to Italy to show the Italians how to paint, sang stories of his battles with a pike, recounted his romantic conquests (none of the women in question were there to contradict him), and spilled every little secret he had in no time at all. Before he knew it, he was blabbing that he was carrying a letter to a local lad, a good fellow named Gerard. He slapped Sybrandt, Gerard’s own brother, on the back so hard he nearly knocked the breath out of him.

Sybrandt slipped around the table to avoid the blow, and drank in every single word. It was the first time he had learned Gerard was in Italy at all. To make sure he had not misheard, he pretended to doubt it.

“My brother Gerard is never in Italy,” he lied.

“You lie, you cur!” Hans roared, instantly irascible from the ale, too far gone to realise the man he had just praised and whacked was the same one he was arguing with. “If he is ten times your brother, he is in Italy. Look here! Read that address!” He flung the letter down on the table.

Sybrandt picked it up, pretended to examine it gravely, then shrugged and said he could not read. But one man in the crowd, proud of his rare skill with letters, picked it up and read it out loud for all to hear: “To Gerard Eliassoen, of Tergou. These by the hand of the trusty Hans Memling, with all speed.”

“Beautifully written,” the reader marvelled, tracing each letter with his finger.

“Ay!” Hans declared, grandiloquent. “Small wonder! That writing comes from a famous hand: Margaret Van Eyck herself. Blessed be Jan Van Eyck’s memory! She is an old, old friend of mine.” He rambled off into forty different unrelated topics after that, none of them worth remembering.

Sybrandt slipped out of the tavern quietly, and ran to find his brother Cornelis. The two leant their heads together over the news. Italy was thousands of miles away. If they could just keep Gerard there forever?

“Nothing would keep him away from his Margaret for long,” Cornelis said, frowning.

“Curse her!” Sybrandt spat. “Why did she not die when she was so close to it?”

“She would outlive the plague just to spite us,” Cornelis grumbled, furious that the girl had the selfishness to refuse to die just to make their lives easier. The two black sheep of the Eliassoen family put their heads together, tainting each other’s malice more and more, until they hatched a plot: if Gerard stayed in Italy for good, they would never have to give him his fair share of their father’s inheritance. But for all their scheming, they had no idea how to pull it off, until it felt like Satan himself whispered an idea into both their ears at the same moment.

“THE BURGOMASTER!” they both shouted, at once.

They went straight to Ghysbrecht Van Swieten, who received them instantly. A man in the throes of torturous suspense will grab at any scrap of information, for certainty may be painful, but it is never half as unbearable as waiting.

“You have news of Gerard?” he asked, leaning forward, eager.

They told him all about the letter, and Hans Memling, off to Italy. His eyes darted restlessly as he listened. “Who wrote the letter?”

“Margaret Van Eyck,” they said, assuming the handwriting on the address must match the writing inside.

“Are you sure?” He pulled open a drawer, and drew out an old document Margaret Van Eyck had written when she was negotiating to buy property from the town. “Did it look like this?”

“Exactly the same writing,” Sybrandt lied boldly.

“Good. And what do you want of me?” the burgomaster said, his heart racing, but his manner so carefully careless it made the two brothers stagger. They fumbled with their bonnets, stammered, beat around the bush, and finally confessed they wanted him to write a false letter, something that would make Gerard stay in Italy, to swap it for the real one in Hans’s wallet.

While they hemmed and hawed, torn between respect for the burgomaster and the sneaking suspicion he was just as big a rogue as they were, thoughts raced through the old man’s sharp head: Vengeance said let Gerard come home, so he can feel the full weight of the law. Prudence said keep him a thousand miles away. Then prudence added: why do this dirty work for a gamble? Why let these two fools have the power to ruin your reputation? But the overpowering certainty that Gerard was holding a secret that could destroy him, mixed with his native caution, made him speak at last.

“It is my duty to help townsfolk who cannot write. But I will take no responsibility for what the letter says. Tell me what to write.”

“Something about that Margaret,” Sybrandt said.

“Ay! That she is false, that she has married another man, I’ll warrant you,” Ghysbrecht said, dry.

“Nay, burgomaster, nay! Not for all the world!” Sybrandt cried. “Gerard would never believe it, or only half believe it, and he would sail straight home to find out the truth. No. Tell him she is dead.”

“Dead? At her age? He will never credit it.”

“He will far sooner credit that than the other. She was at death’s door not long ago. So it is barely even a lie, after all.”

“Hmph. And you think that will keep him in Italy?”

“We are sure of it, are we not, Cornelis?”

“Ay,” Cornelis put in. “Gerard’s whole dream was to go to Italy. He would only ever come back for his Margaret, not for the likes of us. He despises his own family, always has.”

“It will be a bitter pill for him to swallow,” the old hypocrite said, his eyes glinting with hidden pleasure.

“It will be for his own good in the end,” Cornelis shrugged. “Famine does not care to wed Thirst, and Gerard will not bother coming back for us.”

“And the grief you two are planning for him, so coolly?” Ghysbrecht spoke sarcastically, but he was already tasting his own long-awaited vengeance.

“Oh, a lie is not like a blow from a battle axe,” Sybrandt said. “It cuts no flesh, breaks no bones.” He snuck a venomous little glance at the burgomaster’s famously broken nose.

Ghysbrecht’s face darkened with rage when the adder’s tongue struck that old, unhealed wound. It worked exactly as the brothers hoped: the old man bristled with hate.

“Very well,” he snapped. “Tell me what you want written, and I will write it. But mark this: you bear all the blame if anything goes wrong. It is not the hand that writes that commits the deed, it is the tongue that dictates it.” The brothers agreed eagerly, sneering behind their backs at how easy he was to manipulate. Ghysbrecht drew his inkhorn towards him, set the sample of Margaret Van Eyck’s handwriting in front of him, and asked a few questions about the size and shape of the real letter—when the door burst open.

Jorian Ketel stumbled into the room, looking furious that the burgomaster was not alone.

“Thou seest I have serious business on hand,” Ghysbrecht said, annoyed.

“Ay, but this is graver. I bring good news, but it is not for every pair of ears.”

The burgomaster stood, and pulled Jorian aside into the deep window embrasure, leaving the two brothers to hear the low, urgent hum of their conversation. Before long, Ghysbrecht sent Jorian out to saddle his mule. He turned back to the two brothers, his manner suddenly cold enough to make them shiver. “I prize the peace of households, but this is no business to rush into. We will see about it later. We will see.”

“But burgomaster! The man will leave any minute now! It will be too late!” Sybrandt protested.

“Where is he now?”

“At the inn, still drinking.”

“Then keep him drinking. We will see. We will see.” He sent the two confused, disheartened brothers on their way.

To understand why he changed his tune so abruptly, we must step back a few hours. That very same morning, young Margaret Brandt had run into Jorian Ketel outside her front door. He had scowled and tried to walk past her, but she had stopped him.

“Wait! You are the good man who saved Gerard’s life, are you not? Why have you never come to see me since? And why never came to collect the parchments? Was it not true about the hundred crowns I promised you?”

Jorian snorted, but when he saw her candid, open face, he realised there had been a terrible mistake. He told her how he had come to her house, and Martin had turned him away, and he had thought she was lying.

“Alas,” she said, “I knew nothing of that. I was lying at death’s door. Come, follow me.” She led him out into the garden, and showed him the spot where the parchments Gerard had hidden were buried. “Martin wanted to dig them up, but I would not let him. Gerard put them there, and I swore no one would move them but you, who earned them so well.”

“Give me a spade!” Jorian cried, overjoyed. “Wait—are you sure they are still there? He is a suspicious man, that burgomaster.”

“I will take full blame if any human hand has touched them,” Margaret swore.

“Then leave them just two more hours, I beg you, good Margaret!” Jorian yelped, and ran all the way to the Tergou Stadthouse a happy man.

Ghysbrecht rode along the road towards Sevenbergen, Jorian striding beside him, promising that in an hour’s time all the missing town parchments would be safely in his hands.

“Ah, master!” Jorian said. “Lucky for us it was not a thief who stole them.”

“Not a thief? What else would you call him?” Ghysbrecht grumbled.

“With all respect, I call him a jackdaw. This is jackdaw’s work, through and through: steal the thing you need least, and hide it away. I should know—I was raised side by side with a tame chough. We were born the same year, but he cut his teeth long before me, and for years my life was pure misery. If there was a hole in your hose no bigger than a groat, he would stick his beak in it like a gimlet. He would steal whatever the household needed most, even if he had no use for it at all. My mother lost her thimble every time she turned her back. My father, a cobbler, lost his awl, his wax, his twine every single morning. One day my mother told him to his face he would corrupt half a dozen children, and he cocked his eye at her, then stole the baby’s shoe right off its foot. That Gerard is exactly the same. Those parchments were no more use to him than a thimble is to a bird. He stole them for pure mischief, and hid them, and you would never have found them but for me.”

“I believe you are right,” Ghysbrecht said, relaxing. “I have fretted over this far more than I needed to.”

When they reached Peter Brandt’s gate, though, he grew uneasy. “I wish the parchments had been buried anywhere but here.”

Jorian reassured him. “The girl is honest and kind. She had nothing to do with stealing them, I swear.” He led the burgomaster into the garden. “There, master, if a face can be trusted, that is the spot. Look, the mould on top is still loose.” He ran to get a spade stuck in the hedge, and began digging. Within seconds,

Hemmed in tight between his comrades to stamp out any mad impulse to flee, Denys was borne away in a storm of grief and gnawing remorse. Gerard had cast aside the safer German route to Rome purely for his sake, and this was the reward: left adrift, all alone, in the vast wilds of Burgundy. That thought was the maddest sting of all, making him rave at heaven and earth one moment, then sink into a savage, brooding silence so dark and menacing his guards judged it only prudent to strip him of his weapons.

They caught up to their troop leader just outside the town gates, and the whole cavalcade drew rein at the sign of the *Tete d’Or* to bait their horses and rest. The young landlady, harried half out of her wits tending to the count and more so to the bastard leading the raiding party, caught sight of Denys and leaned in anxiously to ask what had become of his quiet young travelling companion. Denys burst out in a flood of raw grief, told her every last detail of the separation, and begged her to send a rider after Gerard at once. “Now he is parted from me, he may yet listen to good sense,” he wept. “The poor wretch cannot bear to be alone.”

The landlady tossed her head, a flush rising high on her cheeks. “I think I have already been far too over-kind to the pair of you,” she said, and turned sharply away.
“You will not go?”
“Not I.”

At that denial, Denys loosed a whole torrent of curses and abuse at her. She turned her back sniffling, huffing that no one had ever dared speak to her in such a fashion, and ordered her stable hand to saddle two mules immediately. Denys rode north with his troop after that, hunched silent and drooping over his saddle bow, never guessing that that sharp-tongued young woman had slipped into a riding habit in only forty minutes (for she was truly in a hurry) and was spurring hard south with her servant, straight the way Gerard had wandered.

By dark, after a long day of hard marching, the bastard and his men trundled into the *White Hart*. Their arrival threw the whole inn into a roar of bustle, and it was some time before Manon spotted her old acquaintance Denys in the press of armed men. When she did, she betrayed the recognition only by a heightened flush to her cheeks — she made no move to claim their old familiarity. The poor soul had already begun to scorn the low, humble stations by which she had climbed to respectability. Denys saw the quiet slight, but he could not even summon a smile. Every corner of the inn stung, thick with memories of Gerard.

Before full dark fell, the wind shifted. Manon poked her head into the great room and beckoned him over with a single finger. He stood up sullen, his two guards trailing close at his heels. “Nay,” she said, “I would speak a word to thee in private.” She tugged him to a shadowed corner of the room, and whispered under her breath to ask if he would do her a small kindness. He answered loud and rough, “No, I will not. I am in no vein to do favours for man or woman this day. The only thing I would waste a kindness on is a dog, and even that I would skip if I could help it.”

“Alas, good archer,” Manon said humbly, “I did you one kindness once before, you and your pretty young comrade.”
“You did, dame, you did,” Denys softened at once. “Well then, for his sake — what is it you need?”
“Thou knowest my story. I fell on hard times once, made mistakes, but now I am worshipful, respected by all the village. But this very day a woman cast that old past sin right in my teeth, and it will haunt me every waking hour so long as that wretch hangs gibbeted by the road. I would have him taken down. Well-a-day!”
“With all my heart.”
“And none dare I ask but thee. Wilt do’t?”
“Not I, even if I were not a prisoner under guard.”

At that stern refusal, the tender Manon sighed and clasped her palms together in helpless despair. Denys told her not to fret: there were soldiers of a coarser, less scrupulous stamp who would not hesitate at such trivial work. It was nothing but a matter of coin. If she could lay hands on two gold angels, he could find two men to do that dirty work right there at the White Hart.

The thought was not exactly palatable, but Manon reflected that soldiers were birds of passage — they would be gone drinking in some far-off town by the next night, or knocked on the head in some border skirmish before the week was out. She murmured soft, “Send them out to me. But prithee, tell them ’tis for a friend of mine; let them not think ’tis me that asks. I should sink into the earth with shame — times are changed for me now.”

Denys had no trouble finding two warriors glad to earn a whole angel apiece for work so light. He sent them out to her, then dismissed the whole sordid matter from his mind immediately, sinking back into brooding over his lost friend. Manon and the two soldiers soon hammered out the rest of the plan — except for what to do with the body once it was cut down. She murmured, “The river runs nigh that very spot.”
“Fling him in, eh?”
“Nay, nay, do not be so cruel! Could ye not lay him down gently, and tie something heavy to him?” She must have turned the thought over in her head a hundred times already, for new ideas never came quick to slow, soft Manon.

All was agreed on speedily, save the time of payment. The mail-clad men itched for their gold, and demanded it upfront. Manon demurred. What, did they doubt their word? Then let her come along with them, or watch from a distance to make sure the work was done. “Me?” Manon gasped in horror. “I would liever die than see that done with my own eyes.”
“Which yet you would have done for all that.”
“Ay, for sore is my need. Times are changed.” She had already forgotten her earlier instruction to Denys, that the men must never learn the request came from her.

An hour later, the unpleasant last relic of Manon’s old, disgraced life no longer hung there to canker her new status as a respectable matron, no longer did the grim dead eyes of the past glower down into the clover fields she walked past each day. After that, Manon went on to make the innkeeper a steady, average wife, a famously fierce guardian of his household, and outlived every last person who remembered her old, poorer self. The two soldiers, returning from executing their grim errand with the unthinking, matter-of-fact brutality of medieval folk, got a sharp shock: the market square, empty only an hour prior, was now black with crowds of chattering villagers. Conscience smote them at once — they were sure they had been caught desecrating the dead. But the bolder of the two, emboldened by the dark, stole forward alone to slip in amongst a group, and soon returned to his companion, his tone sharp with entirely unreasonable reproach: “Ye born fool, it is only a miracle.”

Letters of glowing fire blazed across the face of the town church wall that morning, their scrawled question bold as if scrawled by a hand from the clouds: *Why is no mass said for our good duke, in this hour of all our trouble?* A crowd of awestruck townsfolk gaped up at the writing for hours as it slowly faded, left frozen to the cobblestones too dumbfounded to move. The municipal council, determined not to be outdone in loyalty to their temporal ruler by a supposed angelic miracle, poured coin into a full schedule of special masses. The old cure, our long-time acquaintance, profited handsomely from the rush of pious spending, a windfall he enjoyed far more than he would ever admit. I would not have paused over such a commonplace local miracle at all, save that it lined his pockets just enough to let the rest of this tale unfold.

Shortly after, Denys was brought before the bastard Anthony of Burgundy. “Why break his heart *and* disgrace him?” his allies pleaded. “Make him swear on the cross hilt of his sword not to quit your service until this sedition is entirely put down.”
Denys had no choice but to agree. He loosed three roaring volleys of oaths to seal his vow, and walked away with his crossbow, his sword, and his liberty restored.
The troops halted for rest that afternoon at *The Three Fish* inn, and Marion the barmaid who knew Denys well shouted the moment she caught sight of him, “Bad luck to me! Who’d ever have thought to see your face back here again?” When she saw he did not laugh at the jest, but looked heavy-hearted and stung, she pressed him for the trouble weighing on him.
He told her how he had been forced to part ways with Gerard, bound for Rome alone while he was stuck serving the bastard’s campaign in Flanders. Marion brushed his fears aside with bright good sense. Gerard was too handsome, too gentle-mannered, ever to come to real harm, she argued. Every woman on the road would take his side, no matter what befell him. “It must go one of two ways for him,” she said, “either he falls in with a good party of pilgrims bound for Rome, or he turns for home and will be back in Holland before you are—what with all this fighting in Flanders they say you’ve got ahead of you.” She fetched out his gold pieces he had left in her keeping, and refused every coin he tried to press on her, no matter how much he urged her.
Denys half believed her, not least because her words lined up exactly with what he wanted to be true, and he was cheered no small bit by her stubborn honesty. It made him think better of the wide, lonely world his little friend Gerard was walking through all alone.

Small bands of foot soldiers, down to pairs and trios, were already tramping the roads toward Flanders, most of them penniless, passed from town to town by bailiffs who held writs ordering every innkeeper to feed and lodge them free of charge. Anthony of Burgundy overtook dozens of these wandering parties, gathered them under his standard, and crossed the Flemish frontier at the head of six hundred men. His brother Baldwyn met him there with fresh troops, arms, and cartloads of provisions, and the full force marched through town after town in formal battle array, met not with resistance, but with loud, cheering crowds. This unreserved loyalty from folk who were supposed to be in open rebellion drew bitter grumbles from the ranks.
“This so-called rebellion’s nothing but a fool’s joke,” growled Simon, a surly soldier who had unofficially appointed himself Denys’s constant comrade.
Denys said nothing, but he swore a quiet private vow to Saint Mars: if this sedition that had cost him Gerard turned out to be nothing but a petty squabble no one actually cared about, he would put a crossbow bolt straight through Anthony of Burgundy’s heart.

That same afternoon they caught sight of a heavily walled, fortified town, and a whisper rippled through the little army that this was the disaffected stronghold they had come to reduce. But as they drew near, they found the great main gate standing wide open, and each of the two flanking towers guarded by no more than a single sentinel. The advancing force relaxed their formation and marched careless, half expecting to be welcomed with cheers like every other town on the road.
When they were no more than a furlong from the walls, the drawbridge crossing the moat creaked slowly upward until it stood vertical, pressed flat against the outer fortifications. The very instant it locked into place, the portcullis at the gate rattled down with a deafening clang, and every tower stretch of curtain wall bristled with lances and crossbowmen. A low, angry hum ran through the front ranks and spread all the way to the rear.
“Halt!” the bastard shouted. The order echoed down the line, and the whole column froze. “Herald to the gate!”
A pursuivant spurred his horse out of the ranks, halted twenty yards from the walls, and blew a sharp summons on his bugle, his herald’s standard dangling from its end. A tall figure clad head to toe in glinting brass armour appeared on the battlements above the gate. A few sharp, fiery words passed between them, too far for anyone below to hear, but their meaning was plain: the herald blew a single fierce, warning note, and galloped back to the lines with his face set for battle. The bastard rode out to meet him, and their heads were barely together for two seconds before he turned in his saddle and roared, “Pioneers to the front!”
In an instant, roadside hedges were levelled flat, the force set up camp just out of arrow range from the walls, and mounted officers galloped off south, east, and west to every friendly nearby town, to drag back catapults, palisades, wheeled protective mantlets, raw hides, tar barrels, carpenters, provisions, and every supply needed for a full siege.
For the first time in weeks, Denys’s eyes brightened. The moment the portcullis clanged shut, the dull weight in his chest lifted, and he shouted loud enough for half the line to hear, “Courage, everyone! The devil of our bad luck is dead that day!”

The besiegers settled their camp a furlong from the walls, cut service roads, kept their pikemen at the ready for the eventual assault, and sent their sappers, pioneers, catapult crews, and crossbowmen to the front lines. They set to work filling the moat, digging mines under the walls, and preparing to breach the stone, all while taking constant fire from arrows, quarrels, bolts, and heavy stones hurled from the battlements. Every one of the siege crews needed a hundred eyes to stay alive, working with a vigilance, individual daring, and skill that made medieval sieges far more vivid and dramatic to watch than any modern battlefield shrouded in gunpowder smoke.
Their first move was to send carpenters rolling forward behind heavy wheeled mantlets, to build a tall, strong stockade right on the very edge of the moat. A handful of men lost their lives to defending archers there, but not many: Denys was part of a large force of crossbowmen who rolled their own mantlets forward, shooting over the workmen’s heads at every defender who dared show a face above the walls, every loophole and arrow slit that looked out over the work site. Protected by that concentrated, unrelenting fire, the carpenters soon finished the high palisade, blocking most ordinary missiles from reaching their work.

The defenders had expected exactly this, though. That same night, they rolled heavy wooden penthouses out over the top of the curtain walls, sliding the support beams into pre-cut square holes built into the masonry. From these elevated platforms, they could fire down at the besiegers with far more freedom and range than they could ever manage through the slanted, fixed loopholes cut into the stone below. The besiegers responded by dragging up their mangonels, and began hurling huge stone boulders at the woodworks, smashing them to splinters. At the same time, they built a tall triangular wooden assault tower, as high as the curtain walls itself, and parked it just out of the defenders’ maximum firing range.
The sight of that tower struck fear into the town’s garrison. These rolling wooden fortresses had taken dozens of towns before. The defenders immediately began digging a mine under the stretch of moat directly facing the tower, to lay explosives to blow it apart the moment it drew near. The besiegers were digging mines of their own, on the opposite side of the walls, their target the heavy square barbican gatehouse they planned to bring crashing down.

All this time, Denys stood behind his mantlet, paired with another arbalestrier, protecting the workmen and landing perfect shot after perfect shot at the defenders on the walls. His marksmanship soon earned him the respect of an unseen enemy archer, who kept sending feathered “compliments” quivering into the wood of Denys’s mantlet. One bolt buried itself an inch from the narrow slit Denys was squinting through at that exact moment.
“Peste!” Denys laughed out loud. “You shoot like a master, my friend! Come out and let me shake your hand! Talent like yours shouldn’t hide! Comrade, that’s one of those cursed Englishmen, with his half-ell long shafts. I won’t die till I’ve had a shot at London’s own walls!”

On the defenders’ side of the moat, a tall, commanding figure soon drew every eye. He paced the battlements unflinching under constant fire, clad in full polished brass armour, carrying a remarkably light but absurdly long lance he used to direct every movement of the garrison. Almost every setback the besiegers suffered that week could be traced back to that tall knight and his long lance.
Any reader will immediately ask, why didn’t Denys just shoot him? Denys did shoot him, every single day. Every other arbalestrier in the camp shot at him, every archer too. Every bolt went straight for that brass armour, and none of them seemed to do a single bit of harm. The knight walked his battlements as calmly as a veteran skipper paces his ship’s deck in a rainstorm, oblivious to the bolts bouncing off his plate. Eventually the besiegers grew so frustrated they stopped wasting good steel on him, and just shouted curses up at him instead. He did not even react to those.
Gunpowder has spoiled all the glory of war, Denys often thought. War has never done much for the solid peaceable interests of ordinary folk, but in the old days it had purpose: it painted bright pictures, sang great epics, gave the world its Iliads. Now all you get is invisible butchery under a thick pall of smoke a furlong wide, no heroism for a poet to record, no story to tell that doesn’t sound like a senseless, ugly racket. This siege was a small, petty affair, but any wandering minstrel could stand on a nearby rise and see every bit of it, make a honest penny singing of it to tavern crowds. It was fair sport, for the time.

The day was bright and crisp, almost but not quite frosty. All the besiegers’ efforts were concentrated on a 250-yard stretch of walls, holding two curtain sections and two towers: one the square barbican gate, the other capped with an overlapping pointed roof built over a stone machicolation, its row of angled crenels glowering down at the besiegers like the gaps between the teeth of some great stone beast. The penthouses on the curtains were already half shattered by the besiegers’ mangonels and trebuchets. The besiegers’ side of the moat looked like a teeming, chaotic giant arsenal, swarming with workmen hauling stones, bundles of fascines, mantlets, and rows of tar barrels. Hammers tapped nonstop all day, horses and carts rattled up in endless lines carrying fresh supplies. Only if you looked close could you see the constant hail of arrows flying back and forth, the great cranes that did not tenderly lower stones but hurled them through the air, and the occasional workman or soldier lying still on the ground, a feathered bolt sticking out of him, blood seeping slow into the mud.

A covered, sloped siege penthouse the men called a “cat” crept slowly toward the curtain across the moat, its crews filling the water beneath it with rubbish and fascines. The tall brass knight burned the first two cats by hurling blazing tar barrels down on them, so the besiegers built the next one with a steep roof covered in raw hides that the flaming pitch could not stick to. The knight ordered a small trebuchet on the walls to drop stones directly into the moat, and at last got the range right, sending a great boulder crashing straight through the new cat’s roof. Baldwyn of Burgundy lost his temper when he saw the damage, and ordered the huge main catapult that had been battering the curtain’s woodworks to be turned, aimed slantwise directly at that unkillable brass knight on the battlements.
Denys and his unseen English archer paused to take their dinner then, as they often did. The two rivals, who never laid eyes on each other, had struck up a quiet distant friendship across the moat, leaving little scraps of bread on the tops of their mantlets for the other to collect.

The big catapult was a marvel of medieval engineering. A whole fir tree was cut down, set to pivot on a horizontal axis between two tall posts, left deliberately unbalanced, with three quarters of its length on the besiegers’ side. The short, thick butt end was weighted with half a ton of lead. Before firing, crews used a powerful winch to pull the long, tapering arm all the way down to the ground, locked it in place with a bolt, and settled the fifty-pound stone into a sling fixed to the tip. When the bolt was released, gravity did all the rest: the heavy weighted butt end swung furiously downward, the long arm snapped upward with incredible force, and the stone was hurled high through the air.
This first shot missed the tall knight, but crashed straight through the roof of the defender’s penthouse, tearing a gaping hole through both wood and stone. Two bodies fell out through that gap: the stone, and the mangled corpse of a defending workman the boulder had struck, plunging down hundreds of feet into the dark sullen waters of the moat. They sunk together, and lay undiscovered there for two hundred years, until later cannon breached the old walls and civilization drained the moat dry.
“Aha! A fine shot!” Baldwyn shouted in delight. The tall brass knight disappeared from the battlements, and the besiegers hooted and jeered.
A few minutes later, he reappeared on the barbican’s platform, only the top of his helmet visible over the parapet. He called his crews to man an enormous Turkish catapult, its long arm hurling a twenty-pound sharp-edged stone two hundred and forty yards through the air. The first shot bounced and splattered mud straight in Anthony of Burgundy’s eye, making him curse loud enough for the whole camp to hear. The second shot struck a cart horse hauling a sheaf of arrows, bowling it over dead as a rabbit, spilling its load across the field. Next the Turk catapult was turned on the besiegers’ supposedly out-of-range wooden assault tower, smashing gaping holes in its side with every shot. The besiegers turned two smaller engines on the Turkish monster, killing two of its crew, but the great catapult did not waste time firing back. It hurled a forty-pound stone straight at the besiegers’ main catapult, striking its pivot axis, smashing the whole structure to splinters and sending its surviving engineers running for cover.

By late afternoon, Simon the grumbling soldier was running back to his mantlet from the palisade, when Denys, peeking through his slit, saw him freeze, stare, stretch his arms out, and collapse face first on the ground, a feathered arrow sticking straight out of his back. The English archer showed his face for a split second to enjoy his marksmanship, and Denys, already aiming, loosed his bolt. The archer staggered away wounded. But Simon was dead.
“I have cursed luck with my comrades,” Denys said quietly.

The next morning, the defenders woke to a unwelcome sight. The new “cat”, its roof padded with mattresses and raw hides, was steadily advancing across the moat, filling in the last stretches of water. The knight hurled stones at it, burning tar barrels, nothing worked. He personally lowered a sack of burning sulphur and pitch over the walls on a rope to smoke the crews out, but Baldwyn, clad head to toe in armour like a lobster, ran forward under fire and sliced the rope clean through, letting the work resume unharmed. The defenders’ miners finished their work that night, propped the mine tunnels with heavy wooden beams, and slathered every inch of the wood with grease and tar, ready to light the fuse.
At dawn, the moat was fully filled. The great wooden assault tower, its hidden internal levers turning its wheels without any visible crew pushing from the outside, began rolling slowly toward the curtain wall. Its top platform held the first storming party, protected by a vertical drawbridge that would lower directly onto the battlements the moment they reached the wall. The defenders hurled every stone and flaming barrel they had at the tower, but the hides and mattresses turned every shot aside. The moment the tower reached the edge of the moat, the tall knight gave the signal to fire the mine underneath it.

The Turkish catapult hurled a half-hundredweight stone straight into the group of knights standing on the assault tower’s platform, sweeping two of them off onto the plain below, one writhing in pain, the other dead. The besiegers’ remaining catapults hurled blazing tar barrels to fire the defender’s penthouses, clearing the walls, and the storming parties ran ladders up behind the tower, lowering the drawbridge across to the battered curtain. Led by Baldwyn, the armoured assailants poured across the narrow bridge. The tall brass knight met them head on with his men-at-arms, a brutal, desperate fight breaking out where men toppled screaming headlong off the narrow bridge down into the moat below. Fresh besiegers kept swarming up the tower behind, and the defenders were slowly driven back.
The town would have fallen in another minute, but the defenders’ mine had been perfectly timed. The tar-soaked wooden props holding up the mine burned through, and the whole stretch of ground under the assault tower gave way. The tower sank violently away from the walls, tearing its drawbridge clean free of the curtain, spilling all the men crossing it down onto the dry mud of the

A quiet, unlooked-for change settled over Margaret Brandt, soft as the mist that clings to Tergou’s cobblestones after dusk. She moved through her days of churning butter, carding wool, and tending the cottage hearth like a soul half lost in waking dreams. Even her old father Peter, slow and unobservant as he was, soon marked how she startled at the clink of a tankard or a sharp word from his lips, her great dark eyes flying wide with a terror that had no name. She visited her kind patroness Margaret Van Eyck far less often than of old, and when she did sit in that warm, tapestried chamber of the old painter’s home, she no longer leaned into the old woman’s caresses. She would stand passive, trembling, sometimes shrinking back as if the softest touch stung.

Strangest of all, she would not set foot outside her own threshold while the sun hung high. Any errand to the town of Tergou was made only after dark had wrapped the streets in shadow, and she slipped back home again long before the first rooster crowed at dawn. She would not even walk to the village church for the early matins. At last Peter, bewildered, asked her what ailed her. Her voice was thin as thread when she answered: “Methinks every soul I pass on the street stares right through my skin.”

One day Margaret Van Eyck drew her aside, gentle as she would handle a skittish fawn, and pressed her to speak of what grieved her. All the girl gave her was a wild, scared glance, then a flood of hot, unstopping tears. “What, sweetheart?” the old lady murmured, stroking her hair. “Are you afraid to lay your sorrows at my feet, who have loved you as my own?”
“I have no sorrows that I did not bring on myself,” Margaret whispered, shaking. “I am treated far kinder than I deserve—most of all in this house.”
“Then why do you not come see me more often, my dear?”
“I come far oftener than I deserve,” she sighed so deeply her whole frame shook, just as Reicht, the Van Eycks’ sharp but kind serving maid, called out for her from the yard. The old lady sent her off, and stood frowning softly, turning the puzzle over in her mind. At last she decided Margaret must be wounded that Gerard’s family, the hosier’s people, had treated her with cold contempt. “I will go speak to them,” she resolved, “call the women of that household to account for their churlishness.”

The very next morning she wrapped herself in her fur-lined cloak, pulled her hood low over her silver hair, and set out with Reicht at her heels for the hosier’s house. Catherine, Gerard’s mother, welcomed her with deep respect, wiping her hands on her apron and weeping as she thanked her for all the kindness she had shown her faraway son Gerard. But the moment Margaret Van Eyck turned the conversation to Margaret Brandt, Catherine’s tears dried up instantly, her lips pressed thin and stubborn as unworked clay, and her face set hard the way only ignorant, obstinate peasant women’s faces can set. You might as well try to argue with a brick wall as shift that look once it settled. Margaret Van Eyck pleaded with her, argued, tried every gentle persuasion she knew, and all to no avail. Proud and unused to being thwarted, she snapped at last, turned on her heel, and stormed out of the house, tossing a hasty, half-hearted curtsey over her shoulder that Catherine returned with a sharp, defiant nod, no obeisance in it at all.

Outside the door, Margaret Van Eyck found Reicht chatting with little Kate, Gerard’s gentle lame sister, perched on her crutches. The old painter was all flushed with anger, about to push past them with a scornful toss of her head meant for every last member of that stubborn family, when a small, soft hand slipped timidly into hers. She looked down, and saw the girl’s dove-like eyes swimming with tears, staring up at her, full of gratitude and a desperate, quiet plea all tangled together. The old woman’s anger melted away like snow in spring. She stopped, and kissed Kate’s soft forehead. “I see now,” she said, quiet. “Never fear, little one. I leave the matter to you.”
When she got back home, she sat down by her easel and sighed to Reicht: “I saw two things today, one very common, one very rare. I saw a stupid, stubborn woman as hard as any stone, and I saw an angel in the flesh. If I could paint that face of hers just right, I’d pick up my brushes again, old as I am, and never stop till I got it down on panel.”

Little Kate did not fail to live up to that good opinion. She waited a few quiet days, then told her mother everything she had heard from Reicht Heynes: how Margaret had spilled her own blood, cutting her arm open to drag the wounded, feverish Gerard out of the wolf-infested woods and save his life. “See, mother? No one on earth could love him more than she does.”
“Who wouldn’t love our Gerard?” Catherine said gruffly, but her voice was softening.
“Oh, mother, think what that must have cost her! The poor soul.”
“Ay, wench. She’s got her own troubles, sure enough, same as the rest of us. I can’t abide the sight of blood, let alone shed it for someone else.”
That was a small victory won, but the moment Kate tried to push her mother further on the subject, Catherine shut down hard and would not speak of it more.

About a month later, one evening, a soldier of the Dalgetty clan tramped up to the hosier’s door, just back from fighting in the Duke of Burgundy’s wars. He set a letter down on the supper table where Catherine and the rest of the family were seated, Peter being off on a business trip. He refused every penny they offered him as a reward for bringing it, tipped his cap, and tramped off for the tavern in Sevenbergen.
They spread the letter flat out on the table, and though none of them could read a word of writing, every one of them recognized Gerard’s scrawl at a single glance.
“And your father’s gone away, of all times!” Catherine wailed. “Are you all not ashamed? Not one of my brood can read a word of your own brother’s letter!”

But even though the inked words were hieroglyphics to them, there was something on that page they could read perfectly. Art has a tongue that needs no words, unshackled by the pen’s limits, that slips straight through the eye to the heart, for learned and unlearned alike. It crosses seas and borders, loses nothing on the way, needs no translator, for it speaks the one universal language all souls understand.
When they saw the little drawing Gerard had scribbled with his pencil, right between the two short paragraphs of his letter—two hands clasped tight together—they understood its meaning immediately, and it went straight to every heart in the room. Gerard was bidding them farewell. They stared at that simple sketch, every line of it so full of his old familiar way of drawing, that it felt like Gerard was standing right there in the candlelight, looking at them, saying goodbye. The women wept over it till their eyes were too blurred to make out the lines. Even Giles, the quietest of the boys, muttered “Poor Gerard!” in a softer voice than anyone had ever heard him use. Even Cornelis and Sybrandt, the two greedy brothers who had done their best to drive Gerard away, felt a sharp twinge of remorse, and sat silent and dark-faced, staring at the table.

But none of them dared bring a stranger in to read the letter out loud. They did not want anyone outside their family to see their ignorance, or see how broken-hearted they were.
“What if we go to Dame Margaret Van Eyck?” Kate suggested, small and timid.
“Ay, that’s a good thought, Kate,” Catherine said at once. “She’s got a kind heart, and she loves Gerard too. She’ll be glad to hear word from him. I was short with her when she came to the house, that’s the truth, but I’ll go apologize, and then she’ll read me every word my poor boy wrote to me.”

She was at the Van Eyck house in no time. Reicht led her into the parlour, and told her to wait a moment: the old dame was at her prayers. There was a young woman seated pensively by the stove, and she rose at once, moving politely out of the way so Catherine could warm her hands at the fire.
“Thank you, lass,” Catherine said, holding her palms out to the glowing coals. “Winter nights are cruel cold, and your stove here is a blessing.” She glanced the girl up and down, curious. The girl wore a plain linen wimple, but her gown was trimmed with soft sable fur, a sign of wealth and gentle birth in those days. But what struck Catherine most was the girl’s face, open, candid, and soft with a quiet modesty. She felt certain she would find sympathy there, and began to chatter.
“Do you know what brings me here, my dear? A letter! A letter from my poor boy, who’s off in some faraway savage land, God knows where. I’m shamed to say none of us in the family can read a word of it. I wonder if you can read writing?”
“Yes,” the young woman said, her voice trembling a little.
“Can you now? That’s such credit to you, lass. The old dame won’t be long, I’m sure—but every minute feels like an hour to a poor mother, pining to know what her boy says.”
“I will read it to you,” the girl said, holding out her hand for the letter.

Catherine was so eager, she did not notice the suppressed, wild eagerness in the girl’s slow outstretched hand, did not see the way her fingers shook as they closed around the crumpled paper. “Go on then, read it to me, for pity’s sake. I’m half wild waiting for it.”
“The first words are ‘To my honoured parents,’” the girl read, her voice thin and wobbly.
“Ay! He always was a good, respectful boy, the poor soul.”
“‘God and the saints have you in their holy keeping, and bless you by night and by day. Your one harsh deed is forgotten; your years of love remembered.’”
Catherine pressed a hand to her chest, and sank back in her chair, heaving one long, ragged sob.
“Then comes this,” the girl went on, “ ‘A long farewell.’”
“Ay, go on, bless you, lass. It’s sad comfort you give me, but it’s still comfort, all the same.”
“‘To my brothers Cornelis and Sybrandt—Be content; you will see me no more.’”
Catherine gasped. “What can that mean? Ah!”
“‘To my sister Kate. Little angel of my father’s house. Be kind to her—’” The girl’s voice broke.
“That’s Margaret Brandt,” Catherine said, tears running down her face. “His sweetheart, poor soul. I’ve not been kind to her, my dear. Forgive me, Gerard.”
“‘—for poor Gerard’s sake: since grief to her is death to me—’”

The girl could fight no more to keep her composure. All her strength gave way, and she slipped right off her chair, falling insensible to the floor, the letter still clutched tight in her hand, her head resting soft on Catherine’s knees.

Matrons who have tended households through fevers, frosts, and half a dozen labours of their own never screech at the sight of a fainting woman, nor leap to blame flighty whimsy for the fall. They know the body fails far faster than the mind, far more often, than any giddy fit of pique. So Catherine moved with brisk, unhurried purpose the second the young girl crumpled: she laid her flat on the cold earthen floor, no pillow under her head to choke her breath, threw the casement wide to let sharp autumn air pour in, and fumbled open the tight laces of her bodice before she even called for aid. Only when every sensible, proven remedy was applied did she step to the doorway, and call out loud enough for neighbours half a street away to catch the tone: “Come in here, if you please.”

Margaret Van Eyck and Reicht hurried through, to find the girl still laid flat, Catherine patting her wrists in steady, rhythmic little taps to rouse her. “Oh my poor girl! What harm have you done her?” the old painter cried, white with distress.
“Me?” Catherine glared, her hands never pausing. “Madam, I have done nothing but tend her. No harm befell her but what is natural to the state she is in.”

Margaret Van Eyck flushed bright with ire. “You speak very cool of it, when you are the very cause of that state! You and your husband schemed to tear the two apart, and now Gerard has run off all alone to Italy. You have broken this poor child’s heart between you.”
“That I have not,” Catherine answered blunt as a blacksmith’s hammer. “Nor any woman alive. Wait—you cannot mean this lass is my Gerard’s? That can’t be. The fur trim on her kirtle alone cost no less than five crowns an ell, and besides, this young gentlewoman is a wife, or by every right under God’s sky ought to be one.”
“Ought to be!” Margaret Van Eyck snapped. “And who is the reason she is not? Who stepped between them at the very altar to halt their vows?”
“God forgive whoever did that,” Catherine said gravely, “but it was not me, nor my man. Not a chance.”

The older woman softened a little, her anger seeping out of her shoulders. “Well, you have seen her laid low here now. Perhaps you will not bear her that bitter grudge any longer. Thank Heaven, she is fluttering back to her senses.”
“Me bear her a grudge?” Catherine blinked, bewildered. “That is long over and done with. Poor soul, she has trouble behind her, and worse still waiting ahead of her, and to think I made her, of all women in the world, read Gerard’s letter out loud to me! That’s what knocked her clean out, I’ll wager a silver penny on it. There now, sweetheart, don’t you be afraid. None but friends are here.”

They lifted her into a cushioned oak easy chair, the colour creeping slow and faint back to her pale lips. Catherine tugged Margaret Van Eyck aside by the sleeve. “She is not planning to trudge back to Sevenbergen tonight, is she?”
“She swears she will go, no matter what any of us say.”
“Then you will not let her. You are older and wiser than her, you can overrule her. Look, she is starting to notice our talk now.”

Catherine leaned in then, her mouth pressed so close to the old painter’s ear their warm breath mingled. It was barely a heartbeat, too little time to whisper a full word, let alone a whole sentence. But women who have shared the unspoken secrets of childbed, household illness, and quiet hardship speak that lightning-fast, wordless language of shared womanly knowledge in a single flash. Margaret Van Eyck reeled back, eyes wide and horrified, and whispered back:
“It is false! A calumny! Monstrous! Look at her face. It is blasphemy to lay such an accusation at the door of a girl with that look in her eyes.”
“Tut, tut, tut!” Catherine huffed. “You might as well argue this is not my own hand. I have borne seven children, I know what I see, and I tell you it is so.”

To Margaret Van Eyck’s utter shock, Catherine stepped right over to the girl, wrapped both arms around her, and kissed her warm and fierce on the forehead. “I grieved for Gerard these past months, and I hear you shed your own blood for him too. The very words you read out of my boy’s letter showed me how much wrong I did you. I held aloof from you all this time, but no more. From this hour, you are my own daughter.” Another tight, crushing embrace sealed that impulsive promise, and the warm, hot-tempered matron was gone off to rummage in her larder for spiced wine to heat for her new child.

Margaret sank back in the chair, a wobbly, faint smile stealing over her face. Gerard’s own mother had kissed her, and called her daughter. But the next moment she saw her old friend staring at her, her face tight with vexation.
“I cannot believe you let that woman kiss you.”
“His mother,” Margaret murmured, half reproachful.
“Mother or no mother, you would never have let her lay a finger on you if you heard the vile lie she whispered in my ear about you—you, whom she had never even laid eyes on before today.”

The old lady was just gathering her words, hesitant and careful, to make Margaret share her indignation, when an unlooked-for interruption closed her lips. The young woman slid from her chair straight to her knees, and began to beg piteously for pardon, clinging to the hem of her old friend’s gown. From the ragged, broken words of her penitence, any onlooker would have sworn she had inflicted some cruel, unforgivable insult on the venerable woman who had cared for her all her life.

The small household gathered around the hosier’s scrubbed oak dining table, passing mugs of spiced ale and crusty rye bread as they chattered over the strange, troubling news that had come to the doorstep that day. No one had seen Catherine return, until the heavy door thudded shut behind her, and she cast a piercing, unblinking glance over every face in the little circle. She laid Gerard’s crumpled letter flat on the tabletop, and traced its lines with a calloused, work-worn finger as she recited every single word from memory — a small, stubborn ruse to fool herself, and the rest of them, into believing she could read the script that had come all the way from Italy.

Then she lifted her head, and her sharp gaze locked straight on Cornelis and Sybrandt. The two brothers flinched, and their eyes fell to their laps.

The storm that had been brewing, quiet and smoldering, for months, burst over their heads at last. Catherine swelled like an angry mother hen ruffling all her feathers to shield her chicks from harm, and a torrent of words poured from her lips — a rushing current of sharp wisdom, tangled trivialities, blistering invective that no man alive could ever have uttered in one unbroken stream, and very few women. The unbroken monologue ran on, breathless and unstopping:

“I’ve had my suspicions for months now, that you two were the ones stoking the strife between Gerard and your father, that you set that old rogue Ghysbrecht Van Swieten on him to do your dirty work. And now Gerard’s own words, written with his own hand, prove every last bit of it. You drove your own flesh and blood halfway across the world, to a foreign land full of strangers, and robbed the mother that bore you of her dearest darling — the pride of my eye, the joy of my heart.

And you two have always been of a piece, through and through. Back when you were all small boys together, the rest of my brood were a comfort to me, but you two were nothing but a curse: sly, mischievous, tearing your clothes to rags so bad it took me half a day’s mending to stitch them whole, for work wears cloth thin slow, but petty malice cuts right through it. You’ve grown beards now, but prudence never grew with them. Still the last to bed, the last to drag yourselves out of it at dawn — don’t you know honest folks turn in early, and industry rises with the sun? Two layabouts in one house make a pair of ne’er-do-wells, and no mistake. I’ve sat and watched your ways a hundred times, wondering where on earth you could have come from. You don’t take after your father, and you are no more like me than a wasp is like an ant. I swear you were swapped in the cradle, or a cuckoo dropped you on my doorstep, for you have none of our calloused, hardworking hands, and none of our soft hearts. No one else of all my blood ever mocked the folks God saw fit to afflict, but I’ve heard you, a hundred times when my back was turned, snickering at poor hunchbacked Giles for being smaller than the other boys, and teasing my sweet Kate for not being as strong as a Flanders work mare. After that, you may as well go rob a church! You can’t be any worse in the eyes of the God who made Kate and Giles, nor in mine, who suffered through every ache of their birth just as I did through yours, you paltry, unfeeling, traitorous curs.

Hush, now, Kate, don’t try to calm me. Their cup is full to overflowing. It takes a great deal to turn a mother’s heart against the sons she nursed at her own knee. For years I bit my tongue, I winked at their tricks, I pretended I didn’t see half of what they did, lest your father find out exactly how bad they are — he would have thrown them out on the street that very minute. But now they have gone too far. Where did you get all that money you’ve been rolling in for the last month? You never wrought a single hour’s honest work for it. I would rather die than hear the story of how you stole it from some other poor soul out of another mouth. It all started that night you stumbled home long after dark, Cornelis, your head all swelled up like you’d won some great prize. Sloth and greed make a wretched pair, my masters. A man who loves money too much will either sweat for it honestly, or steal it. And if you robbed anyone, I’ll wager it was some helpless woman — any man would have chased you off with his bare fists. No matter. That money showed me plain what you would do with this shop, this house, and all our gear if it ever fell into your hands. I’ve watched you today: the two of you spent a whole groat between you, while I scarce spend a groat a week to feed and keep a roof over all of you, good and bad.

I will not wait for the day you might walk behind my coffin to claim what is mine. This shop, this house, none of it will ever belong to you two. Gerard is our heir — poor Gerard, the boy you banished, the boy you tried your best to kill. You’ve made him ten times dearer to me than he ever was before. My poor lost boy! I will see him soon, hold him in my arms, set him on my knee just like when he was small. Aye, you may stare all you like. You thought you were so clever, but you were not clever enough. You cut the flowering stalk right off, but you left the seed — the seed that will outgrow you, outlive you, outshine you. Margaret Brandt is quick with child, and it is Gerard’s. What is Gerard’s is mine. I have prayed to the saints a hundred times that it will be a boy, and it will, it must. When I first found that news, my bowels ached for that unborn child as if it were my own flesh and blood. He is our heir. He will outlive all of us. You two will not — a wicked heart in a man’s breast is like a worm inside a nut, it eats the whole shell away to dust long before its time.

Kate, go take down Gerard’s old bibs and little linen tuckers from the drawer you know of, the one at the back of the chest. One of these fine days soon we will borrow Peter Buyskens’ cart, ride out to Sevenbergen, and go comfort Gerard’s wife through her confinement. She is his wife. Who is Ghysbrecht Van Swieten, to come between a man and a woman standing before the altar, to tear apart what God and the priest have bound as one? She is my daughter now, and I am as proud of her as I am of you, Kate, almost. And as for you two — keep out of my sight for as long as you can. You are as welcome to me as a black ill-omened dog on my hearth.”

Cornelis and Sybrandt did not wait to be told twice. They slunk out of the house at once, every inch of them stinging with a hot, jumbled mess of half-hearted remorse, stubborn impenitence, and a slow, burning hate. For days after that, they dodged her gaze whenever they could, and Catherine never spoke a single word to either of them — not good, not bad, not even to ask them to pass the bread. She had unburdened every last grief and rage from her soul at last.

Catherine was the most careful housewife in Tergou, who scarcely ever left her hearth for a full day—for every time she did, some mishap or other was sure to spring up in her absence. Keenly aware of this, she waited for a lull in all her domestic duties, and put off her planned visit to Sevenbergen to call on Margaret Brandt from one day to the next. Even the rare afternoon when all chores were done and she could have spared the time, Peter Buyskens’ mule was gone off on an errand somewhere, and no other transport could be found.

At last, one day Eli asked her bluntly, right in front of the whole family, if the rumor was true that she’d been meaning to go visit Margaret Brandt.
“Ay, my man,” she said, flushing a little.
“Then I forbid you to go.”
“Oh, do you now?”
“I do.”
“Then I suppose there’s no more to be said on the matter,” she replied, her cheeks hot with surprise.
“Not a word,” Eli answered, stern and unyielding.

When she was alone with her daughter Kate, she raged not against her husband, but against her own foolishness.
“Fool that I am! I should have snuck off there like a cat creeping up on a robin before anyone could stop me. That’s always my way—like a silly hen that can’t lay an egg without cackling loud enough to call the whole house to come steal it away. Next time you and I have a mind to do even the smallest harmless thing, let’s do it right then and there, no waiting, no talking it over with anyone else. That way, if anyone questions us, we can honestly say we never meant a bit of harm, and no one could fault us. For two pins I’d march over there right this minute, defiance to the whole household!”

Kate, gentle as ever, was startled by her mother’s wild outburst. “Nay, mother, be patient. Father will come around in time.”
“Ay, and Michaelmas will come round too—but who knows when? I was so set on you seeing the girl for yourself, so we could put our heads together and judge her fairly. You can never know a body, man or beast, till you’ve looked them in the eye. If I had fifty more sons, I’d never thwart a single one’s fancy before I’d seen the lass they loved for myself, and spotted if there were quicksands underfoot. People tell me I was wrong to condemn Gerard’s choice sight unseen, and they’re right. Life’s a long school, and the last lesson’s never learned—we kick out one fault, and pick up another, blundering here, blundering there, till we blunder straight into our graves and that’s the end of it.”

“Mother,” Kate said, timid and soft.
“What is it now? You look as if you’ve got bad news, poor thing, all white and scared.”
“I have an avowal to make,” Kate faltered, her voice barely above a whisper.
“Now there’s a fine grand word for you!” Catherine said, proud at once. “Our Gerard taught you that, I’ll wager. Go on, out with it.”
“Well, then, truth to tell: I have already seen her. And spoken with her, too.”
“And you never told me? After that, nothing in the world can surprise me ever again.”
“Mother, you were so sharp against her back then. I waited till I could tell you without making you angrier still.”
“Ay,” Catherine said, half sad, half bitter, “like mother, like daughter—cowardice is the curse of us both. I can snap and snarl at everyone else to keep this house running smooth, but Kate, did you ever get a harsh word or cross look from your poor old mother that made you fear to tell me the truth? Nay, don’t cry, lass. Ten to one you had your good reasons. Rise up now, brave heart, tell me the whole story—better late than never. First off: when and how did you hobble all the way to Sevenbergen on your poor crutches without me knowing?”
“I never set foot there in my life,” Kate said. “I won’t say I never wanted to see her, but I never went looking for her there.”
“There now,” Catherine said, nodding, “I knew my girl would never sneak off behind my back. Go on, I’m all ears, dying to hear.”

“Word came to me somehow—please, mother, I beg you on my knees, never ask me how I heard— that Gerard was locked up in the Stadthouse tower, a prisoner.”
“Ah!” Catherine gasped.
“Pretended to be by father’s orders, they said.” Catherine sighed so deep it was almost a moan, and whispered that things were far blacker than she’d ever guessed.
“So Giles and I snuck out after dark to go cheer him up. And there at the foot of the tower, there was a brave lass I’d never seen before, come on the very same errand. At first we scared each other half out of our wits, what with the tower’s bad reputation and our heads full of old tales of devils, and we both went as white as sheets in the moonlight. But the next moment, I said ‘You must be Margaret,’ and she said ‘And you are Kate.’ Think of that!”
“Did anyone ever hear the like? It was Gerard, of course—he’s been chattering about you to her, and about her to you, back and forth for months!”

Kate rewarded her mother’s quick guess with one of those soft, composite kisses pressed to her cheek that said all at once: You’re exactly right, you’re the cleverest mother alive, it’s so sweet we’re of one mind after never having been anything else, and a dozen other tender little things too soft for words.
“Now speak your mind, lass. Gerard’s not here—God only knows I wish he was—so we can talk freely.”
“She’s comely,” Kate said, “and her looks do her no wrong, no matter what anyone’s painted of her.”
“Eh, listen to young folk!” Catherine laughed. “I care more for good acts than good looks. Does she love my boy the way he deserves to be loved?”
“Sevenbergen is farther from the Stadthouse than our own house is,” Kate said thoughtfully, “and she got there before I did.” Catherine nodded, she understood perfectly.
“Nay, more—she’d already got him out before I even arrived. Climbed down from that captive’s tower, all the way.” Catherine shook her head, unbelieving. “That’s the highest tower for miles around! That can’t be done.”
“But it’s true,” Kate insisted. “She and an old man she’d brought with her figured out a way to run a rope up to his cell. There it was, dangling out his window when we got there, and Giles climbed right up it. At first I thought it must be magic. But then that frank sweet lass threw her arms around me, and her heart was beating hard against mine, and her cheeks were all wet with tears, and I knew it wasn’t glamour at all. It was love. She’s strong and hearty, not frail like me, but even I, poor weak thing that I am, know what it feels like to want to move the whole world just to help the people I love. And she loves Gerard, no doubt of it.”
“God bless her for it! God bless her!” Catherine cried.
“But—” Kate hesitated.
“But what, my lamb?”
“But is her love perfectly honest? It’s strange, but that very act that warmed your heart made mine cool a little. She’s not his wife, not really, mother. No matter what people say.”
“Humph. They stood at the altar together, everyone says.”
“Ay, but they left the church just as they came, maid and bachelor, no vows spoken.”
“The parson himself said that?” Catherine asked.
“No, I don’t know that for a fact.”
“Then I’ll take no man’s word for such a tangled skein but Gerard’s own.” She thought for a minute, then made up her mind. “Still, you’re right, lass. I’ll go to Sevenbergen alone. I’m a wife, not a slave. We’re all in the dark here, and she’s the one who holds the clue. I’ll question her with no one else around—least of all you. I won’t bring a good innocent lass like you into any house that’s got even a shadow of a spot on it, not even a palace made of solid gold.”

The more Catherine turned their conversation over in her head, the more drawn she felt to Margaret, and curiosity— that most potent of human passions, sharpened all the more by the fact Catherine never read books to slake it—was burning hot in her breast. At last, one fine sunny day right after dinner, she whispered to Kate: “Try to keep the house from falling to bits while I’m gone, won’t you?” She pulled on her very best kirtle and hood, her bright scarlet clocked hose, and her brand new shoes, and set off briskly down the road to Sevenbergen, not troubling anyone to lend her a mule.

When she got to the village, she asked the first person she saw where Margaret Brandt lived. The man shook his head, said the name was strange to him. She walked a little farther, and asked a girl of about fifteen who was lingering in a doorway. “Father!” the girl called into the house, “there’s another one come looking for that magician’s daughter!” The girl’s father came out, and told Catherine that Peter Brandt’s cottage was just outside the village on the east side. “You can see its chimney from here,” he said, pointing. “But you won’t find them there, neither father nor daughter. They moved out of town a whole week ago, bless you.”
“Say it’s not so, good man! I’ve walked all the way from Tergou.”
“From Tergou? Then you must have met that soldier on the road, didn’t you?”
“What soldier? Ay, I did pass a soldier on the way.”
“Well, that same soldier was here yesterday looking for that very Margaret Brandt.”
