“And he was mad as fire that she was gone, too!” the girl put in. “That long beard of his and her pretty cheek—they’re no strangers, I’ll wager.”
“Don’t speak slander of people you don’t know, little one,” Catherine said sharply. “You’re far too young to be spreading tales. Now tell me more about this soldier, good man.”
“I don’t know much more,” the man said. “He turned up looking for Margaret, I told him she and her father had run off in the middle of the night a week prior, and some folks say the devil flew away with them, seeing as they’re both magicians. ‘The devil fly away with you and your bad news,’ he shouts at me, that’s all the thanks I get. But then he says he doesn’t believe me, so off he storms to the cottage. Presently he comes back, singing a different tune. ‘You were right and I was wrong,’ he says, and shoves a silver coin in my hand to prove it. My wife still won’t believe I told the truth all day, till I show it her.”
Catherine pretended not to care, but she leaned in to glance at the coin anyway.
“And he was quiet and sad, wasn’t he, father?” the girl said warmly. “He was the handsomest man I ever saw. Cheeks like a rose, a shiny full beard, eyes as dark and bright as sloe berries.”
“I saw he had a fine beard,” Catherine said, “but at my age, I don’t go gawking at young men the way I did when I was young and foolish. He was very polite, though, doffed his hat to me like I was a queen, and I curtsied right back to him, for good manners breed good manners. I never dreamed he was her sweetheart, though. Where is the baker in this town?”

The man blinked at the sudden, sharp turn of her question, and told her there were two bakers on the street, John Bush and Eric Donaldson. Catherine bade them goodbye, and set off again—but her sprightly little step dragged now, no longer tapping the ground with her heel in quick, eager jerks. She asked the bakers if Peter Brandt had left town owing anyone money. Bush said they’d never been his customers. Donaldson said not a single stiver: Margaret had come round the very night they left and paid every penny they owed, and he didn’t believe they owed a copper to anyone in the whole village.
“Can you tell me what sort of lass Margaret was?” Catherine asked as she turned to leave.
“Well, a bit too quiet and reserved for my taste,” Donaldson said. “I like a customer who’ll stop and chat when I’m not busy. But everyone says she’s a very good, dutiful daughter.”
“That’s no small praise,” Catherine said. “And they say she’s very pretty?”
“Wherever have you come from, old dame?” he laughed.
“From Tergou.”
“Oh, that explains it. The local lads call her the Beauty of Sevenbergen. The lasses, though, all scoff at that, and tear her to pieces so thoroughly no two of them can even agree what her faults are.”
“That’s all the proof I need,” Catherine said. “The bakers of Sevenbergen aren’t fools, and the young girls here are no shallower than they are in every other town in the world.”

She bought a small loaf of manchet bread, partly out of fellow-feeling for another shopkeeper, partly to prove to her own household that the bread she baked for them every day was far better than what they sold in Sevenbergen, and trudged back home to Tergou, heavy and dejected.

Kate met her just outside the town, her eyes bright and hopeful.
“Well, Kate lass, it’s a good thing I went,” Catherine said, her voice hollow. “My heart’s broken. Our Gerard has been cruelly wronged. That girl is no kin of ours, not from this hour on.”
“Alas, mother, I don’t understand what you mean.”
“Ask me no more questions, lass. Never speak her name to me again. That’s all.” Kate sighed soft and humble, and the two of them walked home together.

When they stepped through their door, they found a soldier sitting calmly by their hearth. The moment they came in, he stood up and saluted them politely. They stared at him—Kate a little surprised, Catherine full of rising, boiling indignation.
“What are you doing in my house?” Catherine snapped at him.
“I came looking for Margaret.”
“Well, we know no such person.”
“Don’t say that, dame. You know very well who Margaret Brandt is.”
“We’ve heard of her, and all to our cost.”
“Come, dame, I beg you, just tell me where she lives, that’s all I ask.”
“I don’t know where she lives, and I don’t care.”

Denys could tell she was lying on purpose, and bit his lip in frustration. “I expected to find myself in enemy territory here in Tergou, but if you knew the whole truth, you wouldn’t be so harsh to me.”
“I do know the whole truth,” Catherine said bitterly. “This morning I knew nothing at all.” She planted her hands on her hips, voice raised and eyes flashing, and demanded to know what impudence he had to sit down by her hearth, the last hearth on earth he should ever darken.
“May the devil fly away with your hearth to the lake of fire and brimstone!” Denys roared back, fluent in the local Flemish tongue. “Your own servant bade me sit here and wait for you, else I never would have set foot in your house. A curse on this churlish roof that treats an innocent stranger so!” He turned, scowling, and stormed toward the door.

Catherine gasped, suddenly frightened and a little guilty, and the fiery virago sat straight down and burst into tears. Kate sat down beside her, crying quiet too, not a moment behind her.
There’s an old saying from a wise writer long lost to us: She says “I feel all the weakness of a woman,” and he replies “Then you are invincible.” Denys learned that truth that day, right there on their doorstep. He stood looking ruefully at the mess his angry outburst had made.
“Nay, good wife,” he said, softening at once. “Don’t cry over a fool’s hasty words. I don’t mean half what I shout. Your house is your own, I’ve no right to be here at all. I’ll go now.”

“What is all this commotion?” said a grave, steady man’s voice. It was Eli, just come in from his shop.
“Here’s a ruffian been shouting at your wife and daughter and making them cry,” Denys explained.
“Little Kate, tell me what really happened,” Eli said, sensible as ever. “Ruffians don’t usually call themselves ruffians.”
Before Kate could speak, Catherine cut in: “Hush, girl. Muriel bade him sit down, and I didn’t know it, and snapped at him for intruding. Then he started storming about laying a curse on our whole house, root and branch. I’ve never been so cursed in all my life!”
“You were both a little to blame, the two of you,” Eli said calmly. “But what my servant promises, I will stand to. We don’t keep an open house for every stranger, but we’re not so poor we can’t give a seat by the fire on a cold day to a wayfarer with an honest face. And I see you are wounded, man.”
“Wounded?” Catherine and Kate both cried out at once.
“Do you think a soldier slings his arm up in a sling for fun?”
“Nay, it’s only a little arrow wound,” Denys said cheerfully.
“Only an arrow?” Kate cried, horrified. “Mother, how did we not see it before?”
“Truly, it’s nothing at all. But let me use it as an excuse for my bad temper just now. These little silly trifling wounds are the ones that make a man fretful. Why, your Gerard— he’s the sweetest tempered soul that ever breathed, but once when a bear took a chunk no bigger than a crown out of his calf, he turned so hot and choleric you’d have sworn he wasn’t your son at all, but sired by Sir John Pepper on Dame Mustard, that fiery knight and his hot wife. Who’s this?

The very next day, Denys seized a quiet moment to pull Catherine and her daughter aside, and told them all the rest of Gerard’s adventures, excusing himself in his gruff, soldierly way for keeping Cornelis and Sybrandt in the dark. “It is not for me to blacken their names—they come of a good, honest stock. But Gerard counts them no friends in this matter, and I am his sworn comrade. Us soldiers live by a rule: we tell the enemy nothing but lies.”

Catherine sighed and said nothing more at first. The stories Denys recounted stirred such a tumult of grief and agitation in the pair that they wept freely at the tale of the two friends’ parting, a moment Denys himself could barely speak of without his voice faltering. By the end of it all, though, their sorrow softened into bright, eager hope that Gerard would soon be home. Denys shared their confidence, but reminded them that hope was no excuse to let Gerard’s last wishes go unfulfilled. “Why, if Gerard walks through that door next week and his Margaret is nowhere to be found, what sort of grief will he fall into?”

Catherine had never felt so tender toward the absent girl as she did now, and was just as anxious to find her and welcome her home before Gerard’s return as Denys was. But she refused to agree they ought to leave the neighborhood to hunt for her across the whole country. “She must have told someone where she was bound. This isn’t a pair of thieves fleeing justice—they owe not a single stiver to any soul in Sevenbergen. Dear heart, Denys, you cannot chase every last corner of Holland looking for her.”

“Can I not?” Denys said, grim and determined. “That we shall soon see.” After a moment’s thought, he outlined their plan: they would split their forces. Catherine would stay close to home, keep her ears pricked and her eyes wide open for any gossip of Margaret’s whereabouts, while he would ransack every town and village in Holland if need be. “She will not be more than a few leagues off, depend on it. Three people cannot flee half so fast, nor half so far, as one alone.”

“That is sensible enough,” Catherine agreed. But she insisted he pay a visit first to the demoiselle Van Eyck. “She and our Margaret were bosom friends. She must know where the girl has gone, if only she will tell us.” Denys was all for going that instant, so Catherine smoothed her gown and tidied her cap in two shakes, and the pair set off together.

The old painter received them graciously in her richly tapestried, sunlit parlor, but the second Catherine laid out their errand, the embroidery slipped right out of Margaret Van Eyck’s hands. “Gone? Left Sevenbergen without so much as a word to me? The thankless girl.”

The visitors were stunned. “You do not know where she went? When was she last here?”

“Mayhap ten days agone. I had dragged my old brushes out of storage, after years of laying them aside, to paint her portrait. I never did, though, for reasons of my own.”

Catherine protested how strange it was that Margaret would vanish bag and baggage without a by-your-leave, no explanation given. “Just when all our hearts are warm to her, too! Here is Gerard’s own comrade come from the ends of the earth with word from him, and we cannot find her, and Gerard himself is on his way home. Sure she did not leave without a reason. Prithee, good demoiselle, can you not give us the clue?”

“I have no clue to give you,” the elder lady said, a little peevish.

“Then I do.” Reicht Heynes stepped into the doorway, her cheeks bright pink.

“So you have been hearkening at the door this whole while, eh?” her mistress said.

“What use are my ears for if not that?” Reicht shot back. “There is no dark riddle here to puzzle over, if you ask me. The clue is a two-ply twine, and both ends are in this very room right now. Oh mistress, I cannot believe you sit there pretending you had no hand in this.”

Marry, the old lady’s cheeks flushed as red as her servant’s. “So I drove the foolish girl away, did I?”

“You did your full share. What sort of greeting did you give her the last time she called? She was all friendless then, you cannot think she missed how cold you were. You turned up your nose at her and said you’d altered your mind about painting her portrait.”

“I did not turn up my nose!” Van Eyck laughed, half indignant. “My nose is not shaped to point heavenward the way yours is.”

“All our noses point where our hearts lead them,” Reicht said, unrepentant. “The poor soul came into my kitchen after that, tears in her eyes, and said she wasn’t to be painted after all. I knew exactly what she meant. I’d seen how you looked at her work.”

Van Eyck sighed, and owned to as much, turning to Catherine to plead her case. “These young girls mimic every last thing their sweethearts do, you know, no thoughts of their own. Your Gerard is handy at the illuminator’s craft, and Margaret was his most diligent pupil—no marvel, with a woman’s eye for bright colour, and a lover to ape. But I have always despised that trick at heart: it takes the great, royal, aspiring art of colour, and chains it to the petty drudgery of writing and printing, shrinks it down to fit between the pages of tiny prayer books, to be stuffed in some rich fool’s pocket at church.
“Still, affection softens us all. When the girl would bring me her pages of little thorn leaves, lilies, ivy, dewberries, ladybirds, and butterfly grubs, all stuck flat in gold leaf like wasps in a honey pot, and show me her journal where she’d spent a hundred, a hundred and fifty, two hundred hours poring over every tiny page, I was wroth. An immortal soul, all that skill and labour, wasted on Nature’s tiniest scraps, barren letters and little bugs! But I held my tongue, and looked kindly at her work, and told her: if Heaven has doomed us to spend our hours painting great gilded letters and little beetles instead of saints and heroes and their grand passions, why not paint those scraps like they live? The grapes you see hanging in the woods hang in the air, not stuck flat to a wall. Those insects crawl and hover free, not wedged in a prison of gold like flies in glue.
“She said she saw what I meant, but that the gold ground was sacred—you could never shade it. All her teachers told her that, she said, even Gerard. So I told her ‘That for Gerard, and all the rest of the lot,’ grabbed my brush, and picked a colour that was false in nature, but true next to that garish glaring gold. In five minutes, I’d painted a bunch of raspberries so juicy you’d think you could reach out and bite them, and that butterfly grub she’d drawn so true it turned your stomach. The girl threw her arms right around my neck and cried out in delight!”

Denys finally wedged a word in. “The little love!” he said, grinning.

Van Eyck stared at him, then smiled, and went on to tell them how she’d been led step by step to promise she would take up her brushes again, the art she had laid aside mourning for her painter brothers, and paint a Madonna—with Margaret as her model. She even told them her trick for turning a living girl into a saint on canvas. “Your hair is adorable,” I told her. “Why, it’s red,” she said. Aye, I told her, but what a red! Brown, glossy, the very hue a painter would kill for. And your violet eyes, that now go languid pining for Gerard, now spark bright with hope of him? I will lift them heavenward, fixed in holy meditation. That resolute chin of yours? I will soften it a little, for a Madonna has no need of a chin that can stand up to the whole wicked world.”

“Softens her chin?” Catherine said, bewildered. “Well I never. A resolute chin, that little darling?” Denys added, soft and fond.

“And that was when the trouble came,” Van Eyck said, her voice falling. “When you told me the news that she was with child, unwed, it gave me such a shock I dropped my brushes. Was I, at my age, to turn a girl who could not keep herself chaste for her lover into the Virgin Mary? I love the silly girl still, but I adore our Blessed Lady. Most male painters would think nothing of it—their saints and virgins are no better than their mistresses, saving your presence, and they see no shame in painting street trollops as angels. But I am no man. My painting is half craft, half devotion. I could not do it. It was foolish, maybe, but I could not help it. I am sorry, though.” She ended despondently, the defiance she had started her speech with all melted away.

“Alas, but you must know that broke the poor girl’s heart,” Catherine said gently.

Reicht bit her lips, impatient, and rounded on Catherine next. “That was not the only reason Margaret and old Peter left Sevenbergen, you know. Nay. She left because Gerard’s own folk slighted her so cruelly. Who would bide among hard-hearted people who drove their own lad off to Italy, and then when he was gone, never once came near the girl he left behind, all alone?”

“Reicht, I was going—” Catherine stammered.

“Aye, going, and going, and going, for months on end!” Reicht cried. “You built her hopes up with soft words, and then let them drop flat with your deeds. The poor soul sighed to me that none of you had ever come to call. I know what that loneliness feels like. I am far from all my kith too, and when I first came to Holland I used to creep off and cry all by myself. Ten times rather be Reicht Heynes, separated from my family by leagues of sea, than be Margaret, right in the middle of the very folk who ought to love her, and yet lonelier than I am.”

“Alack, Reicht, I meant to call only yesterday, but one thing or another always hindered me—”

“Did anything ever hinder you from eating your dinner?” Reicht said, sharp as a tack. “If your heart had been half as set on seeing her as it was set on your meat, nothing would have stopped you. There she sat, day after day, watching the road for you, with your grandchild beating beneath her heart.”

Van Eyck, who had been nettled by Reicht’s frankness, chose that moment to strike. “Since you will be so disrespectful to my guests, you can seek another place to work at once!”

“With all my heart,” Reicht said, stout as anything.

“Nay, mistress,” Catherine put in, good natured as ever. “Truthful folk always speak their minds. Her tongue stings, but it is better she says what she thinks than let it fester in her heart. Do not send her away on my account. I have had my share of sharp, good servants. Once when I was young, I had one that hectoring me so hard I thought I would go mad. Then she married the baker, and I was my own mistress again. After that I only hired silly girls who did not know their left hand from their right, and taught them my ways, for at least a dunce cannot saucy me around. Though it is wearisome, teaching one fool after another—” She then rounded on Reicht, half cross. “And you think you are mistress here, do you?”

“I am no mistress here, and no longer a servant. You turned me off, remember,” Reicht said, indifferent.

“Then hear me!” Denys said, solemn as a judge. All heads turned to him at once. “Mistress Reicht—you are turned off. If a man who barely knows you might give counsel, I will say: now you are no servant, be a mistress. Be a queen.”

“Easier said than done,” Reicht replied, blunt.

“Not a jot,” Denys said, drawing himself up to his full height. “I am half an arbalestrier, still limping a little from that devil Englishman’s arrow, though I left my own bolt in his carcass for my trouble, which is a comfort. I have twenty gold pieces right here, and a strong right arm. In a week I will have twice that. Marriage is not a habit of mine, I will own—but I capitulate to so many virtues. You are beautiful, good-hearted, speak your mind plain, and above all, you stand up for my friend’s Margaret. Be an arbalestress. Be my wife, my mistress, my queen, Denys of Burgundy’s lady.”

A dead silence fell. It broke a moment later in a flood of indignant squawking. “Well did you ever?” Catherine gasped. “Never in all my born days!” Van Eyck cried. “Before our very faces! Of all the absurd, insolent, ridiculous—”

Denys cleared his throat, dry. “The lady I spoke to has not said a word. The rest of you, who had no part in the offer, are chattering overmuch.” The voices stopped, and every eye pivoted to Reicht. She glanced at Denys from under her lashes, half smiling. “I intend to take a good long look at any man before I leap into his arms.”

Denys drew himself up majestically. “Then look your fill. And leap away.”

That was all the spark Van Eyck needed. She pointed a long white finger straight at Denys, her voice breathless. “Stand there! In the name of all the saints, you are beautiful! You are inspired—with folly, but no matter, you are inspired. I must sketch your head at once!” She grabbed her pencil, and screamed at Reicht: “Hussy, come stand right in front of him, keep him looking inspired and handsome. Oh why did they give me that stupid brute of a centurion to paint before, with the low forehead and the shapeless beard, when I could have had this maniac?”

Catherine stood staring, half convinced the old painter had been a secret lunatic all this time. Reicht grumbled that her cauldron of stew was left boiling over on the fire, she had no time to waste playing fool and model both. Her mistress chided her for being rude to the art, so Reicht pouted and obeyed, glowering at Denys, who gazed back at her with unshaken admiration.
Van Eyck drew until her old, disused wrist cramped up, leaving a rough but noble sketch of the pair, and sighed that she could work no more that day.

“Then can I go tend my pot now?” Reicht demanded.

“Aye, go to your pot, get inside it, you will find your soul in there with it,” Van Eyck said, half laughing.

“Boo, that nonsense,” Reicht said, contemptuous. “You said you turned me off? When you want to get rid of me, you can turn yourself off and die—you are old enough for it, and I will not leave you. When that day comes, though, I will need a man to dry my eyes. If the soldier is still of the same mind then, he can say so. If not? It is all one to Reicht Heynes.” And off she went to her kitchen.

Catherine and Denys said their goodbyes not long after, both of them now certain Reicht had read Margaret Brandt aright: the girl had fled Sevenbergen broken hearted, crushed by loneliness. That very same afternoon, Denys set out on his quest. His plan was simple, like all great things: he would wander a hundred towns and villages, ask every burgomaster after new arrivals, inquire at every village fountain after an old physician with a fair young daughter and a longbow soldier. He tramped for months, roaming all of Holland, and never found a trace of her.
But his chivalrous quest was its own reward. For the first time in his life, he was half Spartan, half content: sober, prudent, vigilant, unshaken, happy even through constant disappointment, no time for reckless excess even when he flirted on the road, every step taken in service to his friend.
We leave him there now, tramping the muddy roads under the sun and stars, a pilgrim of friendship, just as Gerard had once been a pilgrim of love.

Catherine’s chest ached with quiet dismay as she counted the days: her son Gerard would be home within a month at the very farthest, far more likely within a week, and she had not kept the close, watchful eye on his betrothed Margaret that he’d begged her to before he left. That weight tangled with the gnawing, unanswerable uncertainty of what had become of the girl, and some days that fear curdled sick and sharp in her throat.
“Oh, Kate,” she groaned to her younger daughter, “what if she’s gone and done away with herself?”
“Mother, she would never be so wicked,” Kate soothed, soft and earnest.
“Ah, my lass, you know nothing of hasty young fools with no mother to steady their step,” Catherine sighed, twisting her worn hands in the hem of her linen apron. “They’ll fling themselves straight into a canal over a man, when the very next lad they meet on the road would cure them of their moping in a week. I’ve seen it: bold as brass one moment, leaping into the water, and screaming for help the next. They can’t even make up their minds about something that trivial, you see. And there are days their bodies ache queer, unlike any living creature I ever heard tell of, that strings their feelings so tight — their patience, which normally outlasts every living thing but a stubborn ass, vanishes in a breath, and in they go. That’s why I say men are monsters.”
“Mother!” Kate gasped, shocked.
“Monsters, no less!” Catherine insisted, stamping her foot light on the cottage earthen flags. “Building all these endless canals just to tempt poor women to their end! They know we’d never slit our own throats — we hate the sight of blood, and value our skin far more than our lives. And hanging? By the time you’ve hammered the nail in the beam and tied the noose, you’ve got time to change your mind a dozen times. But jumping in a canal? It’s as easy as climbing into bed. The water does all the rest, whether you want it to or no. Why, look at me — mother of nine bairns, and wasn’t I half mad to throw myself straight into our own village canal once?”
“Nay, mother,” Kate said, wide-eyed, “I’ll never believe that of you.”
“You can, though, it’s gospel truth,” Catherine huffed a small, bitter laugh. “It was our first year wed, me and your father Eli. He hadn’t learned all my soft, foolish weak spots then, nor I his. We pulled opposite on some petty thing, quarrelled so bitter I ran out the door crying, ready to spill my trouble to some silly gossip that had no business hearing it before the saints themselves. And right there on the path sat that cursed canal. D’they think we’re teal, to take to water like that? Oh, it looked so tempting! I thought to myself, ‘If he’s let me leave his door angry and wronged, he’ll find me drowned tomorrow. Then he’ll change his tune. He’ll sob his heart out, and I’ll look down from heaven’ — I clean forgot I’d likely be in the other place, fool that I was — ‘and watch him grieve, and won’t that be sweet?’ I was on tiptoe, ready to step into the water, when it hit me: my new gown was almost finished, the one I’d been saving linen for for months. So I turned right around and trundled home. And what was the first thing Eli said to me? ‘Let that flea stick to the wall, my lass,’ he says. ‘Not a single word I said to anger you was true, except this: I love thee.’ Those were his exact words, I’ve remembered them all these years, being our very first quarrel. I threw my arms around his neck and sobbed a bit, thought of that canal, and he was soft with me, same as I was with him — young, newly wed, you know. That was far better than lying cold in the water, spoiling my fine new kirtle and the pair of shoes old John Bush made, the man whose nephew runs the cobbler’s shop now. What’s a tiny quarrel like that, compared to the grief Margaret’s bearing now?”
Kate tried to soothe her, saying she was sure Margaret loved her aging father too much to leave him all alone, when he was all she had, both father and mother to her.
“Nay, Kate, they forget every single thing like that in a moment of despair, when the sky above looks like it’s turned solid black,” Catherine said, grim. “I’d trust an unborn bairn far more than a gray old man at death’s door to keep her out of harm. For it goes sore against a soul to die, when there’s a little innocent tugging at your heartstrings, feeding at your very veins, begging you to stay alive.”
“Then keep your heart up, mother,” Kate said, patting her arm. She added that all her fears were sure to be overblown, and then begged her very solemnly not to keep going on about Margaret’s baby being a boy — all the village gossips said it was terrible unlucky to name the child’s sex before it was born. “Dear heart, there are just as many girls born into the world as boys, after all!”
That reasonable remark made Catherine squawk in loud protest. “Have you the cruelty to threaten me with a girl?!” she cried. “I don’t want any more girls, I’ve already got you. What use would a lass be to me? Can I set her on my knee and see Gerard’s face in her, the way I could a boy? I tell you, it’s all settled already. It’s a boy.”
“How can you be so sure of that?” Kate asked, puzzled.
“Sure in my own mind,” Catherine said firmly. “And if I’m to be disappointed at the end, it’s not for you to disappoint me first, telling me it’s not going to be the boy I’m waiting for, but just another girl.”

Margaret Brandt had always kept herself apart from the close-knit, gossiping circle of Sevenbergen’s villagers, and her quiet reserve had long been misread as cold, haughty pride. Word of that judgment had reached her ears months before, and she knew full well how many hearts swelled with petty jealousy and hidden ill will toward her. What triumph they would take, she thought, when her condition could no longer be hidden from even the most casual passerby! That thought gnawed at her waking hours and haunted her sleep, driving her to shut herself inside their small cottage for days on end, shunning even the daylight on the rare occasions she dared step outdoors.

She did not mistake her own moral position, as many unlearned folk around her might have. Though she did not know the fine points of contemporary ecclesiastical law, she knew betrothal was a binding marriage contract, no more breakable by either party than a witnessed, signed legal deed. She knew that in past times, a marriage to a third party after a formal betrothal had been annulled by both Church and State, and that many betrothed couples had come together without further ceremony, their children recognized as fully legitimate. What weighed on her simple, earnest medieval mind was this: the physical paper of that betrothal contract was not in her keeping. Gerard had carried it away with him, and Gerard was leagues and leagues off, somewhere in distant Italy. She hated herself for that careless, fatal oversight that left her entirely at the mercy of cruel, false local opinion. Though she had never read Horace’s famous line about how firsthand visible harms strike deeper than words far away, her sharp, unclouded good sense saw the world exactly as it was. Her “marriage lines” hidden out of sight across the Alps would never balance the visible, unmissable proof of her pregnancy, and the child that would soon be born. What flimsy tale was that to still slanderous tongues? “I have my marriage contract, but I cannot show it to you.” What woman in all Sevenbergen would believe her, even pretend to? And as one of the most modest, soft-spoken girls in all Holland, it was the good opinion of other women she craved far more than that of men. Slander of that sort always strikes women with a cruel advantage, but here the slander would carry the whole visible weight of apparent truth behind it.

The “strong-minded woman” had not yet been invented in that age, and Margaret, though resolute and capable from having run her father’s household single-handed since she was sixteen, was soft as water in other matters, weakest of all when facing the threat of public shame. Like so many gentle, virtuous women of her station, she was a fragile little leaf trembling at every gust of public opinion, true or false. No pages of a man’s descriptive prose could ever fully paint the quiet, searing anguish of a virtuous woman who sees months of good reputation crumbling before her, and foresees herself paraded through the village as a fallen, frail thing. Had she been frail at heart, she might have brazened the gossip out. But she was pure as new-fallen snow, and she could feel the dark pitch of public shaming creeping closer, day by day.

She would sit listless for hours at a time, quiet moans of anguish catching in her throat, and when her old father spoke to her, she would answer mechanically, her mind miles away. More than once her cheeks would suddenly burn bright as fire mid-conversation, and Peter would stare, confused, wondering what harmless thing he had said to upset her. Nothing he said mattered at all. It was the ever-lurking dread of shame that sent heat flooding to her face, no matter what she pretended to talk or think about.

The fear and shame peaked the night she came home from Margaret Van Eyck’s. Her condition had been discovered, and by other women. The old reclusive artist might keep her secret, but Catherine — Gerard’s own mother — a lifelong gossip at the centre of a sprawling family and a crowded neighbourhood? Only one small spark of hope remained: Catherine had spoken to her that day with kindness, even warmth. There was no middle path for the woman who had raised the man she was betrothed to: she would either be her staunchest ally, or her worst enemy. Margaret waited in racking anxiety for days for word from her. No message came. She gave up all hope. Catherine would not stand by her. She would expose her, surely, when the natural love of chattering about a neighbour’s secret outweighed any faint kind feeling she might once have held.

That was when the wild, hungry urge to flee the neighbourhood took root in her, growing till it was a feverish, all-consuming passion. But how could she persuade her old, infirm father, who had lived in Sevenbergen his whole life, to pull up all his roots and move? The only choice left was to confide in him. It was far better than running away and leaving him behind. Trapped between her overwhelming need to hide, and her utter inability to speak of her condition out loud to any man, even her own father, she swung back and forth in torturous, endless suspense.

Then one fatal day, the terrible thought came to her: end it all. Many of the canals that laced the Low Countries were deep, dark, and still, that bogeyman Catherine had warned her of a hundred times, and for a moment they tempted her sorely. She stood on the bank one soft afternoon, staring down at the calm dark water that looked like perfect, endless rest. No more trouble. No more fear of shame. If Gerard had not loved her, she would surely have stepped into that water and ended it all there. As it was, she dropped to her knees on the bank, and prayed fervently to God to chase the wicked thought from her. “Oh, selfish wretch,” she whispered to herself, “to leave your poor old father all alone. Oh, wicked wretch, to kill your unborn child, and make Gerard lose every bit of that pain and peril he crossed the Alps through to come back to you. I will tell father all, ay, before this sun sets.”

She hurried home as fast as her feet could carry her, terrified her brave resolution would leak away before she got there. Wise old Peter, the scholar and healer, was as simple as a child in all domestic matters, and Margaret had ruled their household gently but absolutely since she was sixteen. It was a strange, unheard of sight in that little cottage, to see its steady, usually self-assured young mistress faltering, stammering, irresolute as she approached the quiet old man who held far less sway over the running of their home than the local blacksmith Martin Wittenhaagen, or even the little scullery maid who came each morning to wash their dishes for a pittance.

“Father,” she said, twisting her hands together, “I would speak to thee.”
“Speak on, girl,” he said, not looking up from his book of herbs.
“Wilt listen to me? And — and — not be angry? Wilt thou try to excuse my faults?”
“We all have our faults, Margaret. Thou hast no more than the rest of us, fewer still, unless a father’s fondness blinds me.”
“Alas, no, father,” she wept. “I am a poor foolish girl, that wanted only to do well, but have done ill — very ill, most unwisely — and now I must bear the shame. But father, I love you, in spite of all my faults. Will you not forgive my folly, and still love your motherless girl?”
“Thou mayest count on that, lass,” Peter said cheerfully.
“Oh, do not smile! How can I speak and make you sad if you smile at me so?”
“Why, what is all this coil about?” he asked, setting his book aside.
“Father, disgrace is coming to this house. It is at the very door. And I am the one at fault. Turn your head away, please. I — I — father, I let Gerard take away our marriage lines.”
“Is that all? ‘Twas only a silly oversight,” he said, relieved.
“‘Twas the act of a madwoman. But woe is me — that is not the worst.”
“The lad is honest, and loves you dearly,” Peter interrupted. “What is a year or two apart for two young folk? Gerard will come back, you may be sure, and keep his troth.”
“And meantime do you know what is coming?” Margaret wailed.
“Not I, except that I will be dead and gone long before any harm comes to you, at my age,” he said.
“It is worse than death. There is worse pain than dying. For pity’s sake, turn your head away, father.”
“Silly wench,” Peter muttered, but he turned his face away as she asked.

Margaret trembled so hard she could barely stand, her cheeks burning bright as embers. “I looked on Gerard as my husband, we being betrothed — and he was in such sore danger, and I thought I had killed him, and I — oh, if only you were my mother, I might find the courage to speak it out! You would ask me gentle questions, but you say not a word.”
“Why, Margaret, what is all this fuss about? Why are your cheeks bright crimson, speaking only to your own old father, no stranger in sight?”
“Why are my cheeks on fire? Because — because — father, kill me! Send me to heaven! Bid Martin shoot me through the heart with his arrow! Then the gossips will come and tell you why I blush so today. And when I am dead, I hope you will love your girl again for her mother’s sake.”
“Give me thy hand, mistress,” Peter said, his tone a little stern.

She put her trembling hand out to him. He took it gently, his face softening with quiet concern, and felt her racing, fluttering pulse.
“Alas, no,” she said, pulling away. “It is my soul that burns, not my body. I cannot, will not, stay in Sevenbergen another day.” She wrung her hands, impatient and distraught.
“Calm thyself, child,” the old man soothed her. “Do not torment thyself for nothing. You do not want to stay in Sevenbergen? There is no need to stay even a single day more if it vexes thee so and puts thee in a fever, for fevered thou art, deny it not.”
“What!” Margaret cried, staring at him in shock. “You would agree to leave this place, and — and ask no reason but that I long to be gone?” She threw herself on her knees beside him, clutching his sleeve, then his arm, then his shoulder in a fervour of desperate supplication, begging him to leave the village and never ask her why. “Alas, what need to tell you? You will see it soon enough. And I could never speak the words out loud. I would rather die.”
“Foolish child, who would pry into your girlish secrets? Not me. I have spent my whole life searching for the secrets of nature, not pestering my own daughter for hers. And as for leaving Sevenbergen? What is there to keep me here, if it makes thee miserable? Do the villagers respect me? Thank me? They call me quacksalver behind my back, and wizard to my face when they need me to heal their sick, and give all their praise and coin to the charlatans that kill them with their bad potions. Besides, what does it matter to me where we make our home? Choose wherever you wish, just as your mother did before you.”

Margaret hugged him tight, and wept against his shoulder. She was respited. Even as she cried in relief, she almost wished she had found the courage to tell him the full shameful secret. After a little while, he insisted she take a calming draught of poppy and lavender simples he had brewed. She took it submissively, to please him, and though he gave it in the mistaken belief that her upset was nothing but a nervous fever, it did her far more good than harm. She woke after a long, deep, restful sleep, calm at last, and began her preparations to leave that very day.

The next week, they left Sevenbergen bag and baggage, and took lodgings above a tailor’s shop on Brede-Kirk Straet in Rotterdam. Only one man in Tergou knew exactly where they had gone: the Burgomaster. He locked that secret tight in his own breast. The use he would make of it before long, not even he could guess yet. But time will show all things in the end.

Among strangers in the foreign city, Margaret Brandt found a quiet, comparative peace, and soon a new, unexpected stroke of good fortune seemed to light their path. A wealthy civic dignitary, ill and peevish as only a man of means with a stubborn fever can be, ran from one doctor to the next, bled and purged so thin he was nearly a shadow of himself, until he found himself at death’s door and sent in desperation for Peter Brandt.
Peter took one look at the wasted nobleman, heaved a whole battalion of his overzealous colleagues’ medicine bottles straight out the open window, beat fresh egg yolks smooth with neat Schiedam gin, dosed the patient in tiny gentle sips, then followed it with tender meat stewed in red wine and spring water, shredding in mild harmless febrifugal herbs that did no harm and nourished where the other doctors had only drained. Before long the dignitary was walking again, looking something between a living man and a limp pillowcase, and being a voluble, grateful sort, he spread Peter’s fame through every street in the city. The old healer, who had deserved a reputation for decades in vain, earned it overnight by pure luck. For a little while, things looked bright. Peter’s long-starved pride was stoked, his purse began to fill, and he spent almost every coin he earned on rare sovereign herbs and choice imported drugs – until Margaret, with her soft but firm wit, wheedled a good portion of his gains away to set aside for a rainy day.
That burst of happy excitement came too late. One evening, leaning in to bid her good night, Peter’s voice came thick and slurred, almost unintelligible. The next morning, Margaret found him motionless in his bed, speechless, only barely conscious. She, who had been his attentive student for years, saw at once he had suffered a paralytic stroke. Still, she did not trust her own judgment fully, and ran for a doctor – one of the very men Peter had once stopped from bleeding the dignitary to death – who cheerfully confirmed her fears. He immediately proposed bleeding the half-paralyzed old man, but Margaret refused flat. “He always said never to bleed the old and weak,” she told him.
Peter lived, but he was never the same man again. His memory was frayed to ribbons, he could not be trusted to write a single prescription, and the line of patients who had waited eagerly to see the famous new healer all melted away. Misery stared her straight in the face. With no income, two helpless men to house and feed, and her own pregnancy fast approaching, she swallowed her pride and decided to go for aid and comfort to her cousin William Johnson, a relation she had avoided out of shame for her own poverty until now.
She arrived to find him and his supposed servant sitting in the same room, neither of them sober. Margaret mastered her surprise, gave them her greetings, and said she had come to speak of private family business, glancing pointedly at the woman to hint for a moment of privacy. The woman took the hint, but not as Margaret expected.
“Oh, speak free before me, can’t she, old man?” she cackled, slapping William on the shoulder.
Margaret’s face burned scarlet. “I crave your pardon, mistress. I did not know my cousin had fallen into this town’s loose customs. I shall come back at a fitter hour,” she said, rising to leave.
“I know not what you mean by the town’s customs,” the woman snapped, bouncing to her feet. “But I know this: a faithful servant’s duty is to keep her master from being preyed on by his beggarly kin.”
“You do yourself too little credit, mistress,” Margaret retorted sharply. “You are no servant. Your own tongue betrays you. It is only when the ape climbs a tree that she shows her tail so plain. There sits the real servant, poor soul! And as long as things stand so, never fear his kin will be so poor in spirit as to come begging where the likes of you can flout their sorrow.” She cast one look of mute, stinging reproach at her cousin, who had sat passive and silent through the whole exchange, too cowardly to speak up for her, and swept haughtily out of the house. She did not shed a single tear until she got home, and realized how completely alone she was.
Yet even in that dark hour, the coming child proved to be her greatest strength. The wild, stubborn maternal instinct that makes every bird, every beast, every lowly insect cunning in providing food and shelter for their unborn young woke strong in Margaret Brandt. She sat brooding for hours, turning every possible scheme over in her head, determined to outrun destitution. Even with five gold pieces still left from their journey from Sevenbergen, she could see starvation creeping closer, step by inevitable step.
When a woman thinks with the sharp, focused intensity usually reserved for men, her plans are as practical and unflinching as any man’s. Margaret rose, bade Martin carry the half-paralyzed Peter to a back room, tidied her own front parlor spotless, polished her father’s old glass alchemy globe until it glowed, hung it from the ceiling, dusted the stuffed crocodile Peter had nailed to the wall years before, and fixed it to the outer front of their house. She gave Martin careful instructions, then set him to loitering like a casual sentinel by the street door, to tell every curious passerby that a great, ancient, learned alchemist dwelt within, who in his rare moments of rest from searching for the fabled elixir of life, deigned to amuse himself by curing mortal ills.
Patients began to trickle in almost immediately. Margaret received them all, and told them no one could see the great alchemist, for not even princes were allowed to disturb his studies. They must tell her their symptoms, and return in two hours. When they came back, their medicine was always waiting for them. For wealthier, more worshipful patients, she would scan their faces, take their pulse, listen long to their complaints, then slip quietly back to Peter’s room, sit and puzzle out how her father, whose every method she had studied for years, would have treated the case. Then she would scrawl an illegible, cabalistic-looking note, bring it down reverently, and show it to the patient, asking if they could read the sacred prescription. None could. “Aye, but I can,” she would tell them. “It is sovereign. You may look on yourself as cured.” If she had the herbs and simples in stock, she would even let the patient watch her mix the medicine, glancing every few moments at the scribbled “prescription” as if afraid to make a mistake and offend the great alchemist’s science. They left with their purses light of coin, their pockets full of harmless, healing medicine, their heads full of faith, completely satisfied. The people wanted to be fooled, and Margaret gave them foolery that did far more good than harm.
After every patient left, she would take down the two little carved boxes Gerard had made her, one labeled *To-Day* and the other *To-Morrow*, tuck the small coins into the first for immediate expenses, and the larger coins and remaining gold pieces into the second, to save for the rainy day she knew was coming. Still, her conscience pricked her sore for running this little fraud, and every night after her last patient left, she knelt and prayed God to forgive her, for the sake of her unborn child. Then cure after cure was reported back to her, and her conscience softened, then hardened, as she saw she was doing more good than ill.
Old Martin Wittenhaagen had grown stiff and slow lately, after a lifetime of hard campaigning, but he was still as strong as an ox, and in this new strange business he showed all the qualities of a good soldier: unreasoning obedience, punctuality, speed, and a very bad weakness for strong drink. He fell in with a crowd of drinking “good fellows,” who plied him with Schiedam gin until he was babbling and bragging. He thought Margaret’s little scheme was not science at all, but pure brilliant strategy, and he boasted loud and long in a mixed tavern company how “me and my General, we are biting the burghers for their coin.”
Word of the joke spread through the city, and before long, Margaret found two constables at her door. They led her, trembling and begging for mercy, before the burgomaster, where a whole row of real licensed physicians in long robes and square caps stood waiting to accuse her of practising unlawfully on the bodies of the duke’s lieges. At first she was too frightened to speak, the very name of the law paralyzing her. But when they questioned her, not unkindly – for no man could be harsh to a pretty, tearful pregnant girl – she told them the whole truth. She was her father’s lifelong pupil, she had only followed his methods, she had cured dozens of people, and she was not doing it for profit for vanity. “Sirs, I have two poor helpless honest old men at home, and a child coming, and how else am I to feed them?” she pleaded. “You will not stop a poor girl from earning her bread honestly, but you wink at idleness and shame all around us. You are all husbands and fathers; you must see I have no other choice.” The moment the words left her lips, she would have given everything to take them back, covering her face with one hand while tears trickled down beneath her fingers.
The burgomaster was unmoved by her plea. “What have we to do with that?” he said. “If you will vow never to break this law again, I will spare you imprisonment, and only exact a fine.”
Margaret clutched her hands together, and vowed most penitently that she would never cure a man or beast again, and was dismissed with the constables to pay her fine. The trouble was, the fine could only be paid from the *To-Morrow* box, which she had nailed shut tight weeks before, to stop herself from dipping into the emergency savings on a trivial temptation. Now she could not pull the nails out. The constables grew impatient, and offered to break it open for her, but she refused. “You will break it worse than I shall.” She picked up a hammer, struck it too softly, lost all strength for a moment, and wept hysterically, until finally she brought the hammer down hard. A little broken cry bubbled from her throat as the carved wood split apart. The fine took every last coin of her “unlawful gains” and two of her precious gold pieces to boot. When the constables left, she gathered the broken splinters of Gerard’s hand-carved box and the few pitiful coins left to her on the table, wrapped her arms around them, let her long hair fall loose over the wreckage, and sobbed, “My love’s box is broken, and my heart with it.”
Martin came in to find her prostrate, and when he heard what had happened, he was not so sad as furious. Some traitor gossiper had betrayed him. He swore he would hunt the man down and run an arrow through his throat.
“Idle chat, idle chat!” Margaret moaned, not lifting her head from the table. “When you have slain every gossip in this town, can we eat them? Tell me how we are to keep the three of us fed, or hold your peace, and let the saints leave me a moment to think.” Martin held his tongue, and looked uneasily at his defeated little general.
Towards evening, Margaret washed her face, pinned her hair back up, and bade Martin take the stuffed crocodile down off the wall, and set out a wicker laundry basket in its place.
“I can do finer linen work than any washerwoman on this street,” she said, “and you will carry the basket of linen for me.”
“That I will, for your sake,” Martin said.
“Good Martin, forgive me for speaking sharp to you just now.”
Even as they spoke, a man who had come looking for the alchemist knocked at the door. Margaret told him the mayor had forbidden her to sell medicine. “But I will gladly iron and starch your linen for you, and come fetch it from your house myself.”
“Are you mad, young woman?” he huffed. “I came for a leech, and you offer me a washerwoman?” and he stormed out in a huff.
“Stupid creature,” Margaret said sadly.
Presently a woman came, to describe the symptoms of her sick little boy. Margaret stopped her before she could finish. “The bailiff has forbidden me to sell drugs. But I will wash, iron, and starch all your linen for you – and I will come fetch it from your house.”
“Oh, aye,” the woman said. “I have a pile of smocks and ruffs all foul. Come for them, and when you are at the house, you can look in on the boy for me.”
An introduction was an introduction. Two or three of the former patients who had come to her for medicine hired her as their washerwoman, soon after.
“Martin, you must help,” Margaret said. “I will not keep more cats than can catch mice.”
“Mistress, I have the stomach for the work, but not the knack, worst luck,” he said.
“Oh, I do not mean the starching and ironing, that takes a deft woman’s hand. But the scrubbing? Any man can manage that. Why, a mule has wit enough to scrub linen with his hooves, if you drove him to the tub. Come, off with your doublet, and try.”
“I am your man,” the old soldier said, stripping his sleeves up for the unwonted toil. “I’ll risk my arm in the soapsuds, if you’ll risk your good name as a washerwoman.”
“My what?”
“Your glory and honour as a washerwoman.”
“Gramercy! If you are man enough to bring me half-washed linen to iron, I am woman enough to fling it straight back in the suds.”
And so the brave girl and the brave old soldier worked side by side, cheerfully, and kept the wolf from their door. They could pay the rent every week, and keep a pot boiling over the fire, but nothing more. Margaret glued the broken *To-Morrow* box back together, and her tears fell into the glue as she worked, cementing her exiled lover’s broken little box with them. When it was whole again, it stood empty, for there was no spare coin left to tuck inside it.
Word of her good work spread, and eventually she was recommended as a washerwoman to the burgomaster himself. One day, as she brought his clean linen home to his kitchen, she heard the servants gossiping that his only daughter, eighteen years old, was stricken with a mysterious wasting illness, and not expected to live. Margaret cross-questioned them gently, gathered snippets of the girl’s symptoms from one servant and the next, and pondered every detail.
A few days later, she met the burgomaster on the street. He recognized her at once. “Why, you are the unlicensed doctor.”
“I was,” Margaret said. “Now I am your worship’s washerwoman.”
The dignitary coloured. “That is a sharp come-down.”
“I bear no malice,” Margaret said. “Your worship could have been far harsher to me. I would rather do you a kindness. Sir, you have a sick daughter. Let me see her.”
The burgomaster shook his head. “That cannot be. The law I enforce on others I cannot break myself.”
Margaret’s eyes went wide. “Alack, sir, I seek no payment for curing folk now! I am only a washerwoman. I think one may heal all the world, if the world will but let you starve in return.”
“That is no more than just,” the burgomaster said, and added, “If you do not trade on it, there is no offence in it.”
“Then let me see her.”
“What good would it do? The most learned leeches in Rotterdam have all tended her, and done her no good at all. Her illness is inscrutable. One says it is the spleen, one the liver, one the blood, one the stomach, and one says she is possessed of a demon. In truth, she acts like it: shuns all company, pines alone, eats no more than a sparrow, speaks to no one, and wastes thinner and paler every day, drawing closer to the grave.”
“Sir,” Margaret said, “if you took your velvet doublet to six different traders in Rotterdam, and asked each what it was worth, they would all give you the exact same answer, because they know their trade. But all your leeches give six different answers. That is because they do not know theirs. My father used to say every physician is infatuated with one particular ailment, and sees it in every patient, like a bat seeing only its own favourite prey. Most of them would have given you those same six diagnoses without ever laying eyes on your daughter. Let me see her. We are both women, and that counts for much.”
When he still hesitated, the frustration of her pregnancy broke through, and two violet eyes flashed fire. “Saints of heaven! Is this how men love their own flesh and blood? Her mother would have taken me by the arm and carried me straight to the sick room before now.”
“Come with me,” the burgomaster said hastily.
He stepped into his daughter’s room ahead of Margaret. “Mistress, I have brought you a new doctor.”
The pale, sullen eighteen-year-old girl wrenched her shoulder away in contempt, and turned even closer to the fire she was huddled over.
Margaret came in softly, and sat down beside her. “But this one will not torment you.”
“A woman!” the young lady exclaimed, half surprised, half scornful.
“Tell her your symptoms,” the burgomaster urged.
“What for? You will be no wiser.”
“You will be none the worse.”
“Very well. My food has no taste, and I have no heart for anything at all. Cure me now, and go.”
“Patience a little while longer,” Margaret said gently. “Is your food tasteless on your tongue, no matter what you eat?”
“Aye. How did you know that?”
“I did not, until you told me. I think you would be the better for a little good company.”
“I think not. What use is their silly chatter to me?” Margaret asked the father to leave them alone, and put a few more soft, practical questions, then sat and thought a minute.
“When you wake in the morning, do you find yourself trembling, as if for no reason at all?”
“Nay… aye. How knew you that?”
“Shall I dose you with medicine, or shall I just tease you a little with my

Anyone who knew the pair could guess how much they had to pour out to one another in the days that followed. For Margaret, it was a time stitched half of honey and half of wormwood: she had gained the truest rough-and-tumble friend she’d known in years, but the news Denys brought curdled her joy at once. She learned, for the very first time, that her Gerard was wandering all alone in that far, strange Italian land, no kinsman, no familiar comrade at his back. She could not bring herself to share Denys’s breezy certainty that he would soon turn for home—if that had ever been his plan, he would have crossed the Channel and stepped back onto Dutch soil long before now.

Denys was a constant soft balm to her frayed nerves. He took to calling her his she-comrade, and chivvied her out of every dark mood with his raucous old marching songs and absurd tales of the road. In turn, Margaret fussed over him, fed him, and hectored him as gently as she hectored old Martin the weariest of the day, forbidding him to eat a single meal at an inn, and clapping him down whenever a coarse oath slipped out. “It spoils you, Denys,” she would chide, mock-frowning. “Good lack, to hear such ugly words tumble out of so comely a head! Forbear, or I shall cross my arms and turn you out of doors, so be civil.” At that Denys would pull himself up straight and do his very best to behave, and the ludicrous little battle between his natural gentleman’s politeness and the rough, swaggering ruffian manners he’d picked up on the road was the best comedy in Margaret’s little cottage that season.

And as the old saying goes, misfortunes never come singly, nor friends for that matter: other folks soon began seeking out Margaret’s company, too. Some weeks prior, she had penned a humble, careful letter to Margaret Van Eyck, telling her she knew full well she was no longer the favored ward of old, and would keep her distance so as not to presume—but that she could never forget all the kindness her old benefactress had shown her in better days. She wrote briefly of all the backbreaking ways she had scraped a living to keep her and her child fed, and ended with one earnest plea: that Van Eyck never breathe a word of where she was living, least of all to Gerard’s family. “I hate them,” she had scrawled, her pen digging deep into the paper. “They drove him away from me. And even after he was gone, their hearts never turned soft to me, as they would have if they’d ever truly repented the cruelty they dealt him.”

Margaret Van Eyck was perplexed by the letter, and at last she confided the whole secret to Reicht. The secret passed through Reicht quick as an arrow through a hollow tube, straight to Gerard’s mother Catherine. “Ay, and has she turned that bitter against us?” the good woman huffed. “She stole our son from under our noses, and now she hates us for not running to greet her with open arms? Natheless, it is a blessing she is alive, and no farther away than Rotterdam.”

At that very time, the English princess, now Countess of Charolois, was making a stately royal progress through the northern states of the Duchy of Burgundy, accompanied by her young stepdaughter, Marie de Bourgogne, the great heiress of all Burgundy. Old Duke Philip, the most magnificent prince in all of Europe, turned out his full splendor to do them honor: crowds of dazzling knights in gilded armor, bevies of noble ladies draped in silk and gemstones thronged the retinue. Minstrels, jongleurs, bards, actors, tumblers, and every kind of traveling entertainer followed in their wake, and every town the royal party passed through buzzed with fencing matches, dances, feasting, and unbridled joy. Richart, Gerard’s brother, invited all the Tergou clan to meet him in Rotterdam to watch the grand pageant, and so they all traveled south together.

They had been settled in Rotterdam for several days when Denys ran straight into Catherine on the street. They greeted each other warm as old friends, and Denys bade her rejoice at once, crowing loud that he had found his she-comrade at last. But Catherine doused his glee at once, pointing out he would have found her far sooner if he’d stayed quietly at home in Tergou instead of vagabondizing all over Holland chasing her shadow. “And now we’ve found her, what good is it? Her heart is set dead against us.”

“Pah, let that flea stick to the wall!” Denys laughed. “Come on, I’ll take you straight to her house.”

Catherine shook her head. She would not go bursting in where she was sure of a cold, ill welcome. “Folks that come unbidden sit on thorns,” she said. No, Denys would have to be their mediator, smooth things over, bring the two sides to a good understanding.

Denys seized the office at once, full of pomp and brimming confidence. He trotted straight back to Margaret’s cottage. “She-comrade!” he announced. “I met a friend of thine today.”

“Thou must have leaned over the Rotterdam canal and seen thine own reflection, then,” Margaret teased back.

“Nay, ‘twas a woman, one that longs for thy goodwill,” Denys said. “It was Catherine—Gerard’s own mother.”

Margaret’s smile died on her face. “Oh, was it?” she said, quiet and sharp. “Then you may tell her she comes far too late. There was a time I ached and longed for her, when I needed her most. But she held herself aloof from me then, and so now we will go on as we always have, strangers.”

Denys tried to shake her resolution. He coaxed, he wheedled, but Margaret was bitter, sullen, and would not budge an inch. At last he lost patience and scolded her roundly for her stubbornness—at which she burst into hysterical sobs. Terrified that his well-meaning scolding had brought on such a fit, Denys let his guard slip, and she trapped him into a solemn, sacred promise never to bring the subject of her and Gerard’s family up ever again.

He trundled back to Catherine crestfallen, and told her the whole sorry tale. Catherine flared up at the news, and went straight home to tell all the rest of the family how their overtures had been spurned. They all flared up in turn, and a bitter little feud ignited, burning hotter with every passing day. Only little Kate, the youngest sister, tried to make soft excuses for Margaret’s anger.

The very next day, a visitor knocked at Margaret’s cottage door. He walked in to find the whole household’s military order mightily degraded: Martin was up to his elbows in soapsuds scrubbing pots, Denys was fumbling awkwardly with a hot iron pressing linen, and Margaret was plaiting fine ruffs, her sharp eye keeping watch over her two clumsy raw recruits. The visitor was an old man, seeming venerable at first glance, but on closer look sharp-faced, wizened, and hard.

Margaret cried out “Ah!” the moment she saw him, then spun around and hid her face, her whole body stiff with invincible repugnance. “Oh, that man! That man!”

“Nay, fear me not,” said Ghysbrecht, the old former scheming burgomaster of Tergou. “I come on a friend’s errand. I bring thee a letter from foreign parts.”

“Mock me not, old man,” Margaret whispered, slowly turning around.

“Nay, look, see for thyself,” Ghysbrecht said, and held out a great, thick, folded letter. Margaret darted forward and seized it, her hands trembling so hard she nearly dropped it, her eyes glistening bright. It was Gerard’s handwriting, plain as day.

“Oh, thank you, sir, bless you for this!” she gasped. “I forgive you every ill thing you ever did to me.” She pressed the letter tight to her bosom with one hand, and slipped swiftly out of the room, alone with her treasure. She did not come back for hours, and at last Ghysbrecht left, casting a sour scowl at old Martha as he shut the door behind him. Margaret spent all those hours shut away, reading and re-reading the letter that had come all the way from her Gerard.

When Margaret Brandt descended the stairs that afternoon, every line of her had softened. Her eyes glistened with recent tears, but they were steady, calm, all the hot rage and bitter hurt that had possessed her for days washed clean away.

“Denys,” she murmured softly, stepping to where the old soldier whittled by the hearth, “I have my orders now, from Gerard’s own hand. I am to read his letter aloud to his folk.”

The soldier gaped at her. “Nay, you will never do that—after all they have done to part you two?”
“Ay, will I.” A faint, tender smile touched her lips. “I see not a jot of kindness in that letter toward them, Denys, not a jot. But if I hated them as poison itself, I would not disobey my love. To obey him is so sweet—sweetest of all, to obey one who is a hundred leagues away across wild roads, who cannot force my duty with a harsh word or a hand, who only trusts my love to make me keep his command. Ah, my Gerard, my darling, if you stood before me now, I might have pouted and slighted your orders, still smarting from the ill will his folk have shown me. But now? If you bade me wade straight into the raging North Sea and read your sweet letter to the sharks, I would go. So go to his mother, Denys. Tell her I hold a letter from Gerard, and if she and hers would hear it, I am their servant. Let them name their hour, and I will seat them as best my small lodgings allow, and welcome them as warmly as I may.”

Denys wasted no time trundling off to Catherine’s cottage, where the whole family sat at their midday dinner. The news that a long, sure letter had arrived from their long-lost Gerard sent a buzz of joy round the table so loud the pewter mugs rattled. Before they could even cheer aloud, Denys added, “And her heart is softened. She will read every word of it to you herself, with her own pretty mouth. You have but to choose the time that suits you best.”

Catherine frowned, setting down her trencher hard. “What, does she think none of us can read but her? Let her send the letter over here, and we will read it ourselves.”
“Nay, mother,” little Kate put in gently, “mayhap she cannot bear to let it leave her hand. She loves him far too dearly.”
Cornelis snickered from the far end of the table. “Doubtless she thinks we will steal it. She means to wedge herself into this family for good, using that scrap of parchment as her key.”

Denys fixed the young man with a look of withering scorn. “There spoke a rotten heart. Let me tell you true: that girl hates all of you like wormwood. Do not mistake me, I do not defend her wild temper—but that is the plain truth. And yet, maugre all that spleen, at a single word from Gerard she proffers to read you his letter, and her voice is sweet as honey. That is a fair offer, and none of you should snarl at it.”

“Honest soldier speaks sense,” rumbled Eli, the patriarch of the house, thumping one calloused hand on the table. “It deserves a civil reply. Hold your tongues, all you squabbling women, and I will answer her. Go tell her that I, Gerard’s father, set aside every last old grudge for this grace of hers, and thank her heartily. If she would earn double that thanks, let her send my son’s letter back with your faithful hand. I will read it aloud to every one of his own flesh and blood, and I will return it to her as surely as my name is Eli, son of Dierich, son of William, son of Luke—free burgher of Tergou, same as all my forebears, and a man who keeps his word.”
“Ay, and a man who keeps it far better than most who swear to it,” Catherine put in fondly. “The only such man I ever met.”
“Hold your peace, wife,” Eli chided, not unkindly.

“Art a man of sense, Eli, a proper thing-em-bob,” Denys cheered, snapping his fingers. “That lass will be right glad to obey Gerard and not have to face the lot of you she hates, mark my words. She is all submission today, says obedience tastes like honey. And small wonder—she gets so little of it, what with her pretty face and soft tongue, and the way she flies into little fits that scare the wits out of us soldiers if we cross her, now chiding us sharp as a thorn, now petting us like lost lambs. She has turned two stout, swashbuckling lads into her most loyal slaves: I am the ironing ruffian these days, and the other fool does all the washing. Before long, when the little one comes into the world, I shall be rocking the cradle, and that knave will be scrubbing all the bibs and tuckers. So I will go fetch the letter from her right now. You will let me bide and hear it read, will you not?”
“Else our hearts would be black as Newcastle coal,” Catherine said warmly.

Denys left grinning, but he returned not long later, crestfallen, dragging his boots across the threshold. “She will not let that letter leave her hand. Not to me, not to any one of you, not to any man or woman alive.”
“I knew it,” Cornelis snickered.
“Whisht, man, whisht,” Eli waved him quiet. “Let Denys tell the whole of it.”

“I argued with her, to be sure,” Denys said. “Said, ‘Be ruled by me, lass.’ ‘Not I,’ says she. ‘Come now,’ says I, ‘what of that sweet honey obedience you spoke of?’ ‘You are a fool,’ she says, and laughs right in my face. ‘Obedience to Gerard is sweet. But who ever said obeying any other soul on God’s green earth was sweet?’ At the last, she softened a little, and gave me this scrap of written paper, to give to you folks.”

Eli took it, scanned the neat, looping handwriting, and read it out almost in a whisper, for the words were Gerard’s own:
“And sweetheart, if these lines travel safe to you, make trial of my people’s hearts. Maybe they are turned toward me, now that I am far away. If that is so, they will show it to you, for they cannot show it to me now. Read this letter aloud to them, then! But I strictly forbid you to let it leave your own hand. And if they still hold aloof from you, why, say nought of me, let them think me dead. Obey me in this, for if you slight my will here, you do not love me.”

A hush fell over the cottage. The little scrap of parchment was passed from hand to hand, every one leaning in to trace the ink, as if touching Gerard’s own words could bring him closer.
“Well,” Catherine said at last, huffing a little, “that changes matters. But still, methinks it should be them coming to us, not us trundling over to her lodgings.”
“Alas, mother, what difference does that make?” little Kate pleaded.
“Nay, it makes enough,” Eli said. “Tell her we are too many of us to traipse all the way to her small rooms. Bid her come here, the sooner the better.”

When Denys had left, Eli sighed, and admitted it rankled him. “When that lass crosses my threshold, all the mischief and misery she has sown in this house these past years will come pouring in after her, all at once. But what else could I do, wife? We have to hear news of our Gerard. I saw it in your eyes, I felt it in my own bones. She is backed by our undutiful but still well-loved son, and so she is stronger than us. She has brought our noses right down to the grindstone, the sly, sharp little jade. But never heed. We will hear that letter, and then she can go back out the door as unblessed as she came unwelcome.”
“Set your mind at rest,” Catherine said, though there was a faint, unmistakeable tone of regret in her voice. “She will not come at all.”

Not long after, Richart arrived, the family’s long-absent son, grave and dignified in his burgher’s velvet robe, gold chain glinting at his throat, starched ruff soft at his neck, furred cap set square on his head. They welcomed him not just with affection, but with deep respect—for he had climbed a rung higher on the social ladder than his parents, and such rises in medieval Holland were marked as clearly as the steps on a household’s staircase. When he was admitted to the family council, he made no secret, though he was far from rude, that his burgher pride was deeply wounded that they had even deigned to treat with Margaret Brandt. “I see the temptation,” he said, stiff. “But who among us has not, at times, had to wish one way and do quite another?” His words cast a cold chill over the old couple.
“Vex not yourself, dear Richart,” little Kate soothed him. “Mother says Margaret will not come at all.”
“All the better, then,” Richart said. “I fear that if she does cross this threshold, I will turn right around and hie me back to Amsterdam that very hour.”

Just then, Denys popped his head in through the doorway, grinning. “She will be here at three, by the great dial of the town clock.”

Not a soul spoke. They all stared at one another, the heavy, charged silence hanging thick as smoke in the low, raftered room.

“Nay, Richart,” Catherine said at last, her voice worn thin with the weeks of bickering, “for Heaven’s sake let not this one sorry wench set us all by the ears. Hath she not stirred up ill blood enough between us already?”
“In very deed she hath. Fear me not, good mother. We will show her no more than decent, constrained civility, as befits a guest beneath our roof, no favour, no softness. She may come and read the letter of our poor boy she hath bewitched by devil’s arts, and then she will go. Give me your word ye will not cross that line of bare courtesy, and I will say no more.” On that quiet, wary understanding, the whole household waited for their unwelcome foe.
For her part, Margaret had braced herself for the interview in a spirit little less tense than their own. When Denys brought word that the family would not call on her at the inn, but would receive her in their own home, her lip curled. She bade him mark how every petty burgher pride they nursed loomed larger in their hearts than love for their own lost Gerard. “Well,” she said, biting back her anger, “I have no such excuse. I will not mimic their stiff, unlettered burgher pride. I go to them for Gerard’s sake. Oh, how I loathe this!”
Poor good-natured Denys, who would not have known malice if it bit his boot, was thus unwittingly hauling the materials for a full explosion across the threshold of the Tergou household.
Margaret dressed for the meeting in the same spirit a knight of her day armed himself for battle: he to parce blows, she to parce glances—glances of contempt for her straitened purse, of irony for any care she might take over her appearance. Her kirtle was plain dark blue English broadcloth, her farthingale and hose the same sturdy material, dyed a rich glossy claret. Not an inch of pretentious fur trimmed her gown, only crisp snow-white linen wristbands, and curiously plaited linen that stretched from the neckline of her bodice up to the base of her throat, cut square to frame her face rather than circle her neck. Soft waves of her front hair peeked out across her forehead, a style Mary Queen of Scots would not popularize for another hundred years, and instead of a silver net that would have ill suited her reduced circumstances, the rest of her hair was tucked under a tiny, tight-fitting dark blue cloth hood, hemmed with thin silver thread. Her shoes were bright red, but the claret of her petticoat and hose softened the shock of the colour, drawing the eye instead to her arched instep and shapely foot.
Beauty knew its craft then as well as it does now.
Even so, she kept the whole household waiting long past the three o’clock mark on the town dial.
At last she set off, attended by Denys, her loyal comrade-at-arms. Halfway to the house, she stopped short, her face going pale. “Denys!”
“Aye, she-general?”
“I must go home,” she whispered pitifully.
“What, have ye left some trinket behind?”
“What? My courage. Oh, oh, oh!”
“Nay, nay, be brave, lass. I shall not leave your side,” Denys promised.
“Swear you will stay right close to me, the whole time I am in there?”
Denys swore, and she resumed her march, stepping gingerly as if the very cobblestones might burn her.
Back in the Eli’s house, the whole family sat waiting for her, tangled in a mess of conflicting feelings: mortification that their son had run off with a girl they now were forced to host, burning curiosity, panting, unextinguished love for the boy they had lost, sharp aversion to the woman who came to stand between them and their hope of Gerard’s return, and another, quieter curiosity to see what there was in her that could bewitch their son so thoroughly he had abandoned home and kin.
At last Denys slipped in alone, and whispered, “The she-comrade is standing outside the door.”
“Fetch her in,” Eli ordered. “Now whisht, all of ye. Not a one of you speaks to her but me.”
Every head turned to the door in dead silence.
A low murmur drifted from the hall: Denys’s rough, rumbling voice, and a woman’s soft, mellow reply. Then the muttering stopped. The door creaked slowly open, and Margaret Brandt stepped across the threshold, dressed as we have described, a little pale, but calm and lovely, her gaze fixed straight ahead of her.
Everyone in the room stood up but Kate, and they stayed mute, staring like folk turned to stone.
“Be seated, mistress,” Eli said gravely, gesturing to a hard wooden chair that had been set apart for her, well away from the rest of the family circle.
She inclined her head, and crossed the room slowly. In her walk, her condition was impossible to miss: not only in the soft roundness of her shape, but in the faint languor that weighted every step.
Cornelis and Sybrandt hated her for it on sight. Richart thought it spoiled whatever slender grace her beauty held. The women of the household softened, just a little.
She pulled Gerard’s letter out from the bosom of her gown, and kissed it as if she were entirely alone, then settled into her seat, with the quiet air of one who knew she had come for no purpose but to read that letter, and nothing more.
But as she began to speak, she noticed they had seated her apart from all of them, as if she were a leper. She darted a quick glance at Denys, and made a swift, furtive motion with her hand held down by her side, bidding him come stand beside her. He jumped to obey as if she had shouted “March”, and took his place at her shoulder like a sentry. The whole household saw at once he had been ordered there by her, and Margaret flushed bright with embarrassment before she lifted her voice again. She read Gerard’s words in a mellow, clear tone, so soft, so earnest, so thrumming with feeling, that her very soul seemed to cling to each precious sound. It was a voice that sounded as if it had been shaped by Heaven itself to carry the weight of a lover’s longing.
“I do nothing doubt, my Margaret, that long ere this letter meets thy beloved eyes, Denys, my most dear friend, will have sought thee out, and told thee the manner of our unlooked-for and most tearful parting.
