Therefore I will e’en begin at that most doleful day. What befell him after, poor faithful soul, fain, fain would I hear, but may not. But I pray for him day and night next after thee, dearest. Friend more stanch and loving had not David in Jonathan, than I in him. Be good to him, for poor Gerard’s sake.”
At those words, which came entirely unlooked for, Denys leaned his head on the high back of Margaret’s chair, and groaned aloud.
Margaret turned quickly in her seat, found his hand, and pressed it tight. So the two of them, sweetheart and loyal friend, held hands while the sweetheart read on.
“I went forward all dizzied, like one trapped in an ill dream, and presently a gentleman came riding up with his servants, all on horseback, and had liked to have ridden me right down under their hooves. He drew rein at the brow of the hill, and sent his armed men back to rob me. They robbed me civilly enough, took my purse and the last copper I owned, and rode gaily away. I wandered stupid on, a friendless pauper.
There was a soft general sigh, followed by an angry oath from Denys.
“Presently a strange dimness came o’er me; I lay down to sleep on the snow. ‘Twas ill done, and with packs of wolves hard by. Had I loved thee as thou dost deserve, I had shown more manhood. But oh, sweet love, the drowsiness that did crawl o’er me desolate, and benumb me, was more than nature. And so I slept; and but that God was better to us, than I to thee or to myself, from that sleep I ne’er had waked; so all the folk I met afterwards do say. I had slept an hour or two, as I suppose, but no more, when a hand did shake me rudely. I awoke to my troubles. And there stood a servant girl in her holiday suit. ‘Are ye mad,’ quoth she, in seeming choler, ‘to sleep in snow, and under wolves’ nosen? Art weary o’ life, and not long weaned? Come, now,’ said she, more kindly, ‘get up like a good lad;’ so I did rise up. ‘Are ye rich, or are ye poor?’ But I stared at her as one amazed. ‘Why, ‘tis easy of reply,’ quoth she. ‘Are ye rich, or are ye poor?’ Then I gave a great, loud cry; that she did start back. ‘Am I rich, or am I poor? Had ye asked me an hour agone, I had said I am rich. But now I am so poor as sure earth beareth on her bosom none poorer. An hour agone I was rich in a friend, rich in money, rich in hope and spirits of youth; but now the Bastard of Burgundy hath taken my friend, and another gentleman my purse; and I can neither go forward to Rome nor back to her I left in Holland. I am poorest of the poor.’ ‘Alack!’ said the wench. ‘Natheless, an ye had been rich ye might ha’ lain down again in the snow for any use I had for ye; and then I trow ye had soon fared out o’ this world as bare as ye came into it. But, being poor, you are our man: so come wi’ me.’ Then I went because she bade me, and because I recked not now whither I went. And she took me to a fine house hard by, and into a noble dining-hall hung with black; and there was set a table with many dishes, and but one plate and one chair. ‘Fall to!’ said she, in a whisper. ‘What, alone?’ said I. ‘Alone? And which of us, think ye, would eat out of the same dish with ye? Are we robbers o’ the dead?’ Then she speered where I was born. ‘At Tergou,’ said I. Says she, ‘And when a gentleman dies in that country, serve they not the dead man’s dinner up as usual, till he be in the ground, and set some poor man to it?’ I told her, ‘nay.’ She blushed for us then. Here they were better Christians. So I behoved to sit down. But small was my heart for meat. Then this kind lass sat by me and poured me out wine; and tasting it, it cut me to the heart Denys was not there to drink with me. He doth so love good wine, and women good, bad, or indifferent. The rich, strong wine curled round my sick heart; and that day first I did seem to glimpse why folk in trouble run to drink so. She made me eat of every dish. ‘Twas unlucky to pass one. Nought was here but her master’s daily dinner. ‘He had a good stomach, then,’ said I. ‘Ay, lad, and a good heart. Leastways, so we all say now he is dead; but, being alive, no word on’t e’er heard I.’ So I did eat as a bird, nibbling of every dish. And she hearing me sigh, and seeing me like to choke at the food, took pity and bade me be of good cheer. I should sup and lie there that night. And she went to the hind, and he gave me a right good bed; and I told him all, and asked him would the law give me back my purse. ‘Law!’ quoth he; ‘law there was none for the poor in Burgundy. Why, ‘twas the cousin of the Lady of the Manor, he that had robbed me. He knew the wild spark. The matter must be judged before the lady; and she was quite young, and far more like to hang me for slandering her cousin, and a gentleman, and a handsome man, than to make him give me back my own. Inside the liberties of a town a poor man might now and then see the face of justice; but out among the grand seigneurs and dames—never.’ So I said, ‘I’ll sit down robbed rather than seek justice and find gallows.’ They were all most kind to me next day; and the girl proffered me money from her small wage to help me towards Rhine.”
“Oh, then, he is coming home! he is coming home!” shouted Denys, interrupting the reader. Margaret shook her head gently at him, a soft rebuke.
“I beg pardon, all the company,” Denys said stiffly, falling silent.
“‘Twas a sore temptation; but being a servant, my stomach rose against it. ‘Nay, nay,’ said I. She told me I was wrong. ‘Twas pride out o’ place; poor folk should help one another; or who on earth would?’ I said if I could do aught in return ‘twere well; but for a free gift, nay: I was overmuch beholden already. Should I write a letter for her? ‘Nay, he is in the house at present,’ said she. ‘Should I draw her picture, and so earn my money?’ ‘What, can ye?’ said she. I told her I could try; and her habit would well become a picture. So she was agog to be limned, and give it her lad. And I set her to stand in a good light, and soon made sketches two, whereof I send thee one, coloured at odd hours. The other I did most hastily, and with little conscience daub, for which may Heaven forgive me; but time was short. They, poor things, knew no better, and were most proud and joyous; and both kissing me after their country fashion, ‘twas the hind that was her sweetheart, they did bid me God-speed; and I towards Rhine.”
Margaret paused here, and gave Denys the coloured drawing to pass around the room. The women crowded in to examine it eagerly, curious about the foreign Burgundian peasant costume that differed in small ways from Dutch domestic dress: the girl’s hair tucked in a tight linen bag, a yellow half-kerchief crossed her head from ear to ear, throwing out a rectangular point that hung down the centre of her forehead, and two more points that met over her bosom. She wore a red kirtle with long sleeves, kilted very high in front to show a green farthingale, and a great red leather purse hanging down over it, red stockings, yellow leathern shoes cut low-quartered and square-toed, secured by a strap buckling over the instep, a simple style that was the rough early germ of the jewelled diamond buckle that would come a century later.
Margaret continued reading:
“But oh! how I missed my Denys at every step! Often I sat down on the road and groaned. And in the afternoon it chanced that I did so set me down where two roads met, and with heavy head in hand, and heavy heart, did think of thee, my poor sweetheart, and of my lost friend, and of the little house at Tergou, where they all loved me once; though now it is turned to hate.”
“Alas! that he will think so,” Catherine whispered, her voice breaking.
“Whisht, wife!” Eli hissed.
“And I did sigh loud, and often. And me sighing so, one came carolling like a bird adown t’ other road. ‘Ay, chirp and chirp,’ cried I bitterly. ‘Thou hast not lost sweetheart, and friend, thy father’s hearth, thy mother’s smile, and every penny in the world.’ And at last he did so carol, and carol, I jumped up in ire to get away from his most jarring mirth. But ere I fled from it, I looked down the path to see what could make a man so lighthearted in this weary world; and lo! the songster was a humpbacked cripple, with a bloody bandage o’er his eye, and both legs gone at the knee.”
“He! he! he! he! he!” cackled Sybrandt, doubling over laughing.
Margaret’s eyes flashed, and she began to fold the letter up, ready to march for the door.
“Nay, lass,” Eli barked, “heed him not! Thou unmannerly cur, open thy mouth to gibe once more and I’ll drag thee out and put thee to the door.”
“Why, what was there to laugh at, Sybrandt?” Catherine remonstrated more mildly. “Is not our Kate afflicted? and is she not the most content of us all, and singeth like a merle at times between her pains? But I am as bad as thou for chattering, prithee read on, lass, and stop our gabble with something worth the hearkening.”
“‘Then,’ said I, ‘may this thing be?’ And I took myself to task. ‘Gerard, son of Eli, dost thou well to bemoan thy lot, thou hast youth and health; and here comes the wreck of nature on crutches, praising God’s goodness with singing like a mavis?’”
“There you see,” Catherine murmured.
“Whisht, dame, whisht!” Eli muttered.
“And whenever he saw me, he left carolling and presently hobbled up and chanted, ‘Charity, for love of Heaven, sweet master, charity,’ with a whine as piteous as wind whistling through a keyhole. ‘Alack, poor soul,’ said I, ‘charity is in my heart, but not my purse; I am poor as thou.’ Then he believed me none, and to melt me undid his sleeve, and showed a sore wound on his arm, and said he, ‘Poor cripple though I be, I am like to lose this eye to boot, look else.’ I saw and groaned for him, and to excuse myself let him wot how I had been robbed of my last copper. Thereat he left whining all in a moment, and said, in a big manly voice, ‘Then I’ll e’en take a rest. Here, youngster, pull thou this strap: nay, fear not!’ I pulled, and down came a stout pair of legs out of his back; and half his hump had melted away, and the wound in his eye no deeper than the bandage.”
“Oh!” every

When Margaret stirred back to full consciousness, her head rested heavy on Catherine's broad, warm arm. The honest, unfeuding half of the household that had once greeted her as a hostile interloper crowded round her, uttering rough, homely words of comfort—none louder than Giles, who roared at her to stop carrying on so piteously. "Gerard’s alive and well, isn’t he? Else he could never have penned this letter, the biggest any man alive has ever laid eyes on—well, no, the beautifullest, most moving, smallest scrawl ever stitched onto paper, that’s what it is."

"Aye, good Master Giles," Margaret sighed feebly, "he was alive when he wrote it. But how am I to know what harm has befallen him since? Oh, why did he ever leave Holland to wander among strangers fierce as lions? And why did I not drive him away from me sooner, rather than tear him from his own flesh and blood? Forgive me, you that are his mother!"

She shifted gently to pull free of Catherine’s arm, and made a wobbly attempt to slide off the chair onto her knees—though after a brief, lopsided tussle with Catherine’s far sturdier frame, she found herself pulled tight to the older woman’s bosom instead. Margaret held the letter out to Eli then, her voice faint but soft as clover honey. "I will trust it from my hands now. Truth to tell, I am far too worn to read another line—and loth to leave this comfort," she finished, looping her free arm around Catherine’s neck.

"Read it, Richart," Eli said, pushing the letter toward his eldest son. "Your eyes are younger than mine."

Richart took the sheet, and whistled low. "I never saw writing like this. Looks as if he drew every line with a needle’s point, and clear as a bell too. What in heaven’s name is he doing vagabonding out there in the wide world, when he could be making his fortune in my Amsterdam counting house?"

The letter picked up in Gerard’s own voice:
*"When I came to myself, I was seated in the litter, and that kind merchant holding fast to my hand. I babbled I know not what nonsense for a while, then shuddered silent. He pressed a horn of spiced wine to my lips."*

"Bless him! Bless that good man!" Catherine cried.
"Whisht, woman," Eli chided gently.

*"And I told him all that had befallen. He insisted on seeing my leg: it was sprained so sore the ankle was swollen tight, and all the laces of my hose had snapped, so I could scarce hold them up. 'Sir,' I told him, 'I fear I shall be nothing but a burden to you now, and I can make no sweet music for you either—my poor psaltery, that has been my companion over so many weary leagues, is broken.' And I grieved so over that shattered music box I could barely speak. But he patted my cheek, bade me not fret, propped my leg up soft on a pillow, and tended me like my own good father ever could."*

"January 19. I sit in the litter all day, for we push forward with all haste, and each night that kind merchant tucks me straight into bed and will not let me turn a hand to work. How strange it is! No sooner do I stumble upon men that are no better than fiends, than God sends some kind soul to cross my path, lest I turn my heart from all humankind. Oh Margaret, how strangely mixed all people are! I feel a hundred years older than I was only three months ago. And would you believe it? Good Master Fugger has gone and bought me a brand new psaltery!"

"Eli, my man," Catherine declared, leaning forward, "if that merchant ever comes within ten miles of Tergou, we will buy a hundred ells of cloth from him, and not haggle over a single penny."
"That I will," Eli swore.

While Richart paused to lick his thumb and turn the page, Kate glanced at her mother, blushed faint, and pulled a half-finished piece of needlework from under her apron, bending low over it to sew. Catherine followed suit, drawing her own half-done work from her pocket and stitching in silence. Both of the surreptitious little pieces they had hidden were baby caps, more than half complete, soft and delicate and shaped like tiny monks’ cowls, and the two women never spoke a word of what they meant.

Richart cleared his throat and resumed.
*"January 20. Laid up in the litter, almost as good as blind from the throb of my ankle, but when we halted to bait the horses, the plains of Lombardy burst full into view. Oh Margaret! It is a land flowing with milk and honey: sloping green meadows, stately rivers, laughing orchards and blooming gardens. It is midwinter here, but the air feels warmer than beloved Holland at the height of midsummer, and the sight of such soft, smiling earth makes the wanderer’s face glow and his heart leap for joy. Here are vines, cedars, olive trees, and cattle in plenty, though you will see three goats to every sheep. The draught oxen wear little white linen wrappings about their necks, and standing beside the dark green olive trees, every one of them looks like a painted picture. The folk, especially the women, wear fine straw hats trimmed with silk flowers and leaves mixed with threads of silver, so cleverly wrought you can scarce tell them from the real thing. Today we crossed a river on a chained ferry boat: there was a windlass on either bank, and one single man turned the handle to pull our whole party across the water. I stared in wonder, never having seen the like before. Some country folk crossed with us, and an old woman, spying a pretty young maiden, hid her face behind her hand and held out her crucifix as a knight would hold his sword in a tourney, fearing the evil eye."*

*"January 25. Safe at last in Venice. You have heard our mariners talk of its strange, surpassing beauty a hundred times, you and I. Do you remember how Peter would rattle on about it for hours while we snuck treats under the tavern table, telling us of this peerless sea-throned city shaped like a bow, its great grand canal, palaces built on wooden piles, its waterways crowded with gilded boats, and that market place for all the nations—orbis, non urbis, forum, St Mark’s Square? And the statue of the saint with jewels glowing in his eyes, and the great lion at his gate? But here I lie at my window with my aching leg, and have seen none of these wonders yet, only a dull paved street and houses patched with oiled paper and linen instead of glass, the passersby with all their strange gestures and odd habits. So instead of staring out the window, I turn my eyes inward, and bind up all the wisdoms I have gleaned from my travels in this letter, to share with you. For I love you so well that no treasure pleases me if I cannot share it, and no treasure is half so lasting or good as knowledge. This, then, I have learned, footsore traveler that I am: every nation has its own wisdom, and its own folly. If only a great king or duke could tramp the roads as I do, and see all with his own eyes, he could pluck the flowers of every land and cast the weeds aside, and lead his own people up the hill of true Wisdom.
The Germans in the north are churlish, but frank and honest; those in the south are kindly and honest too. Their great flaw is drunkenness: they carry it so far they mock and despise any man who stays sober. They have a common saying: 'If you cannot eat and drink your fill, you can never serve your master well.' In England, the common folk drink just as deep, but the gentry think excess a shame: they raise a health or two for courtesy, not gluttony, and always sweeten their wine. The Germans drink in silence, no mirth, no talk, just crying 'Be merry!' as they ply each other with cups. The best of their drunken games is 'Kurlemurlehuff', a drinking ritual where you tap your glass, your beard, and the table in perfect turn, punctuated with whistles and clicks of the fingers, so cleverly choreographed it is a labour of Hercules, but a sight to make any onlooker laugh until their sides ache. Their topers, on the advice of local leeches, sleep with pebbles in their mouths: they say a boiling pot must have its lid ajar to let off steam, and so do these walking wine casks, to vent the heat in their bellies. Even so, many drop dead suddenly from drink—but it is a point of custom to gloss over it, and blame some innocent small ailment for their death. Yet this is more custom than nature: their women walk among the drinkers, but only pause a moment to press their lips to the cup, and are the most temperate, modest, virtuous women in the world, true spouses and true friends to their husbands—far better than our Holland lasses, who will propose to the man themselves when they are maids, and lord over their husbands the moment they are wed. Why, there is a wife right here in Tergou, not far from our door: a man came looking for her husband one afternoon, and she said 'You will not find him. He asked my permission to go out, and I gave it to him.'"

"Truth! Every word of it!" Catherine burst out. "That was Beck Hulse, Jonah's wife. That comes of a woman wedding a boy too young for her."

*"In the south where wine grows, the gentry will drink themselves right out of their fortunes—but not in the north: with beer in their cups, a nobleman will sooner burst his own body than sell a single acre of his land. They are quarrelsome, but only because of the liquor, not their nature: they hold no grudges, and if they make a foolish bargain drunk, they will stand to it honour bright when sober. They keep their windows polished bright, and judge a man by the clothes he wears. Any fruit or grain or herb growing by the roadside, you may pluck and eat, and the owner will greet you with a welcome. But if you pluck a wayside grape, your very life is in danger: that is fruit Heaven made to make men drunk, not to eat. The French speak far fairer than the Germans, but are not half so true of heart. Sweet words cost them nothing. They call it 'paying in blank.'"*

"The rogues! Ha ha!" Denys laughed, slapping his thigh.

*"Yet courtesy runs in their very blood. They say to every stranger 'Pray do me the favour of sitting down.' Those small turns of speech show you exactly what the land is like. If you are at a public show and wish to leave your seat but keep it for your return, all you need do is tie your napkin around the bench, and no man or woman in France will dare sit there. They will guard the spot for you."*

"Gramercy! That is proper manners. France for me!" Catherine said approvingly. Denys stood and placed his hand gracefully over the gorget of his breastplate in a little mocking bow.

*"Yet they shout shocking, unkind things in jest: 'The devil take you!' 'Go to the devil!' and the like, though I do not believe they ever mean such dreadful curses—no doubt it is nothing but empty custom. They are temperate in their drinking, mix water with their wine, and sing and dance over their cups, so that they are enchanting company. They will never drink from another man’s cup. In war, the English beat them on the open field, but the French outdo them all in attacking and defending cities: witness Orleans, where they besieged their besiegers and cut them to pieces with double and triple culverines, and a hundred other sieges this century. More than any other nation, the French flatter their women, and despise them behind their backs—even if a woman is their sovereign ruler, they hang their female criminals instead of drowning them decently, as other nations do. The furniture in their inns is carved walnut, while in Germany you will only get plain deal planks. French windows are absurd: the lower half is wood that opens, the upper half is fixed glass, so the servant can never reach it to wipe it clean. The German windows are all glass, and moveable, so they gleam like diamonds from far off. Many humble houses in France have no glass at all. Once I saw a Frenchman walk right past a church without doffing his cap. I never saw that in Holland, Germany, or Italy. At most French inns, the host will show you your sheets before you get into bed to prove they are clean, and warm them at the fire right in front of you: a very laudable custom. They greet you kindly as a guest, then most of the time they cheat you, and sometimes cut your throat. They say their cruel, tyrannous laws are to blame for it—and it is true, their laws stick their nose into every platter and their fingers into every pie. In France, noblemen wear their hats and furs indoors, and go out lightly clad. In Germany, they wrap their furs and don their hats to go outside, but sit bareheaded and in thin linen around their indoor stoves.

The French never mix men and women together in assemblies, as we Hollanders do. At their church services, the women sit in rows on their heels, and the men stand behind them. Their harvests are rye, flax, and wine. You will see three mules to every horse, and whole flocks of sheep as black as coal. In Germany, the snails are red. I do not lie. The French pay for minstrelsy, but make their own jests and their own mirth. The Germans keep hired fools in ear-caps, who make them laugh by pretending to be mad—though madness is a thing that deserves pity, not laughter. In that, the lighter French nation is far wiser than the grave German, what say you? Alas, you cannot answer me now.

In Germany, the petty local laws are wondrous wise and just. The laws against criminals are bloody. In France they are bloodier still, and carried out just a little more cruelly. The breaking wheel is common there, and the fiery stake, and under their present king they drown men by the score in the Seine river. But the English are just as quick to hang and drown folk for small offences, as all travellers report. At the end of it all, a true-hearted Frenchman, when you find one, is as near perfect a man as you will find on all the earth—and that is my Denys, for all his foul mouth."*

"Foul mouth? Is that what it says there, Master Richart?" Denys asked, leaning over his shoulder.
"Aye, true enough, see for yourself." Denys inspected the letter gravely. "I do not read it that way."
"How then?"
"Humph! Ahem. Why, it reads just the opposite." He shrugged, grinning. "Tricky work, reading these black scratches men agree to call words. I reckon you clerks are still guessing half the time, eh? My foul mouth! That is the first I ever heard of it. Eh, ladies?" The women did not rush to reassure him loudly. Margaret blushed and said nothing, while Kate and Catherine bent their heads over their sewing, hiding sly little smiles. Denys studied their faces for a long, careful moment, and appeared fully satisfied. He turned back, huffing with the air of a man wronged but patiently forgiving, and bade Richart read on.

*"The Italians are a polished, subtle people. They judge a man not by his habits, but by his speech and gestures. A rough country boor can never pass as a noble gentleman there, as I did in Germany when I wore my fine servant’s clothes. They are the wisest of all nations in their extreme temperance with food and drink. They are the most foolish, though, for stopping strangers at their borders to search their bags and forbid them bringing much coin into the country. They ought to invite money in, instead of stopping travellers from bringing it. And here in Venice, the ladies dye their black hair yellow with sun and art, to think themselves wiser than He who made them. You cannot enter any Italian town without showing a bill of health, even though there is no plague anywhere in Europe now. All that fuss is nothing but a trick to wring extra coin out of strangers. Innkeepers fawn and cringe and cheat you, and in the countryside they will murder you in your beds. But they will give you clean sheets if you pay them well enough. They are very dainty eaters, and hate to dip their hands in the shared plate: they will use a crust of bread or a scrap of food to pick up a morsel, rather than touch it. They even tell of a cardinal in Rome who gives his guests a little two-pronged dagger for the left hand to hold their meat steady, while they cut it with their knife. And that, too, is men thinking themselves wiser than the God who made the human hand so supple and perfect.

Everyone here suffers from the itch, and salve for it, unguento per la rogna, is cried for sale on every street corner in Venice. From my window I saw one ragged urchin sell it to three fine ladies in silk gowns, and to two knights in velvet cloaks. Their bread is lovely white, but they ruin every meat dish by sprinkling cheese all over it—oh, perversity! Their salt is black, I swear it is. In trade, the Venetians are masters of land and sea, and govern their territories very wisely. They have only one great flaw, that I once heard a learned friar point out against Plato’s perfect republic: they openly encourage sin, and make the sex workers pay a tax to the state. Not content with honest, profitable cargoes of silk and spice, they trade in vice. There are twenty thousand of these women in Venice and Candia alone, pampered and honoured for drawing foreign visitors to the city, many living in their own princely palaces. I think the wise signors of Venice have forgotten what King David said: 'Except the Lord keep the city, the watchman waketh but in vain.' In matters of religion, they shift their sails with every wind, siding now with the Pope, now with the Turk, but always bowing to the god of traders, Mammon. Can a flower so cankered bloom forever? But speaking of flowers, no one can deny they are cleverest of all at

Some two months before the quiet scene unfolding in Eli’s cottage hearth, the inhabitants of a tiny coastal hamlet tucked between Naples and Rome flocked to the shingle beach, every eye fixed seaward on a merchant vessel fighting for its life against a gale blowing straight for the shore. At moments, she clawed far enough off the coast that the crowd cheered her aloud, certain she would outrun the danger; at others, wind and waves drove her visibly closer, and the onlookers nursed a quiet, unacknowledged thrill they would never admit even to their own hearts. It is not that the torment of others brings joy, but that to stand safe while watching perils you yourself are spared feels a soft, sweet pleasure all its own.
The ill-fated craft, never built for sharp sailing, was almost perfectly engineered to run aground: her absurdly tall, overhanging poop caught every gust like a sail, and her hull lines curved like a cocked hat flipped upside down. To the watchers on the beach, her battered, labouring frame seemed almost alive, a panting thing fighting tooth and nail against death. Had they stepped aboard her deck, though, they would have seen a score of beating hearts, and a dozen different natures laid bare in the terror of that hour.
Sailors stumbled wildly across the tilting planks, hauling at ropes as each saw fit, cursing and crying for mercy in the same breath. Passengers huddled in a trembling mass around the main mast: some sitting, some kneeling, some flat on their bellies clinging to the bulwarks as the ship rolled and pitched through mountainous seas. A comely young man, his cheeks ash pale but his lips clamped tight to hold back any whimper of fear, stood a little apart, white-knuckled on a thick shroud, flinching every time a wall of green water crashed over the rails. It was Gerard, luckless and far from home.
Vows and desperate prayers rose from the huddled throng, so many different names of the divine called out it seemed there were nearly as many gods on deck as there were men and women. The sailors at least clung to one goddess, though they called her by every title they knew: Queen of Heaven, Star of the Sea, Mistress of the World, Haven of Safety. The landsmen, though, ran wild with their devotions: an English merchant swore a mountain of gold to Our Lady of Walsingham, a Genoese trader vowed a four-pound silver collar to Our Lady of Loretto, a Tuscan noble promised ten pounds of beeswax candles to Our Lady of Ravenna. Not a one of them swore on the fragment of the true cross itself, but on the fragment of the true cross housed in this city, that town, the other market square across the sea.
A sudden, brutal gust caught their remaining sail at a bad angle, the rotten shrouds snapped with a crack like thunder, and the canvas tore free to go cartwheeling down the wind, shrinking smaller and blacker until it fluttered into the waves half a mile off like a scrap of charred paper. Before the helmsman could swing the ship’s head to run before the gale, a great wave slammed into her quarter and drenched every soul aboard to the bone, a cold foretaste of the death waiting to swallow them. One man screamed a vow to become a Carthusian monk if St. Thomas spared him. Another swore to walk barefoot, bareheaded, clad only in a coat of mail, all the way to Compostella if St. James would see him safe to shore. Others called on Dominic, Denys, and above all Catherine of Sienna.
Two shivering Neapolitan traders huddled side by side. The first shouted at the top of his lungs, “I vow to St. Christopher of Paris a wax statue the exact weight of the saint, if I win to dry land!” His companion nudged him sharply. “Brother, have a care what you swear! You could sell every last thing you own at public auction and never raise enough wax for that.” “Shut your fool mouth,” the first snapped, then whispered, “You think I’m in earnest? Let me step foot on shore, and I won’t even give him a single rush-dip candle.”
Some lay flat on the deck, flattering the sea itself like a petty, cruel king. “Oh most merciful sea, oh most generous sea, oh bountiful, beautiful sea, be kind, spare us in this hour!” Others wailed and moaned in raw animal terror every time the ship lurched harder than the last, now little more than a plaything in the arms of the storm.
A humble Roman woman sat half-bared at the mast, her baby at her breast, silent amid the screaming throng. Her cheeks were ash pale, but her eyes were calm, her lips moving only in quiet, unspoken prayer. She did not weep, did not lament, did not bargain with any saint for her life. Every time the ship sank so far under a wave that bearded men squeaked like children, she only kissed her child. That was all. She sat there patient, nursing him even in the jaws of death: why should he lose any small joy she could give him, even as they both might die? There, unmistakeably, sat the old blood of Antiquity, running untainted through her veins 1600 years after the fall of Rome, an instinct to die with quiet dignity most of the medieval passengers around her could not fathom.
A gigantic Dominican friar stood on the poop, feet spread apart like the Colossus of Rhodes, not defying the storm so much as simply ignoring it. He chanted verses from the Canticles in a loud, unwavering voice, inviting all passengers to confess their sins to him. A handful knelt in the sloshing seawater at his feet; he heard their confessions, laid his hands on their heads, and absolved them as calmly as if he stood in a dry, snug sacristy rather than on a ship breaking apart under his feet. Drawn by instinct to the only steady, unshaken man aboard, Gerard drifted slowly closer, and the courage of any warrior facing mortal men would have paled next to the friar’s gigantic, unshakable composure. Even here, two souls upheld the dignity of the human race: the tender, heroic Roman mother, and the monk steeled by his faith against every mortal fear.
With the sail gone, the sailors hewed down the useless mast a foot above the deck, its remaining tangled rigging falling over the side to drag in the waves. For a few moments, it lightened the ship’s labour a little. But now the hull, no longer pushed by canvas, could not outrun the following seas, which crashed over the poop again and again, blows so heavy they felt like the impact of a rocky mountain, not water.
The captain left the helm, his face as white as death. “Lighten her!” he roared. “Throw everything overboard, or we’ll founder before we ever hit the reef, and lose the only small chance we have to live.” As the sailors scrambled to obey, the captain turned to the crowd of pale, staring passengers, and spoke in a tone no English skipper in the same peril would ever have used. “Friends, last night when the sea was calm, too calm, alas, a globe of fire hovered right beside the ship. When two of those fiery globes appear, sailors call them Castor and Pollux, and no ship can drown that voyage. But if only one comes, no Castor with no Pollux? The ship is doomed. Make your peace, good Christians, for we have no long time left.”
A great wail went up at his words. To a trembling question of how long they had to prepare, he replied, “She might last half an hour, no longer. She leaks like a sieve. Hurry, men, lighten her.”
The passengers seized every loose object on deck and heaved it over the rails. Before long, they grabbed a heavy sack an old man had been lying on, seasick, and dragged it out from under him. It rattled. Two men hauled it to the gunwale, until its owner leaped up with an unearthly shriek and threw himself on top of it. “Holy Moses, what do you think you’re doing? That’s all I have! The whole profit of my journey! Silver candlesticks, silver plates, brooches, goblets-”
“Let go, you grey old villain,” the rest roared. “Do you want all our lives lost for your ill-gotten gains?” “Throw him in with it,” one man yelled. “It’s this Hebrew that’s drowning all us Christians!” They wrenched the sack out of his arms and heaved it over the side. It vanished under the waves with a soft splash. Its owner gave one cry of unutterable anguish, stood staring out at the water, his white hair streaming in the gale, and would have leaped after it if the sack had floated. Instead it sank, gone forever. He staggered back and forth, tearing at his hair, cursing the passengers, the ship, the sea, and every power in heaven and hell alike.
“Look!” the captain shouted. “There’s a church in sight. Steer for that church, mate! And all of you, pray to whatever saint it’s named after.”
They turned the ship’s last bit of steerage towards the shoreline church, and prayed to whatever unknown saint watched over it. A giant sea crashed over the stern, snapped the rudder clean off and jammed it immovable, flooding the entire deck waist-deep. Wild with superstitious terror, a crowd of passengers swarmed around Gerard. “This is the cause of all our ruin!” they screamed. “He never called on a single saint! He’s a heathen, a pagan, right here on our ship!”
“Alas, good friends, do not say so,” Gerard stammered, his teeth chattering with cold and fear. “Call those who pray to the sea heathens, not me. Friends, I honour the saints, but I dare not waste time going through them now. Dominic, Thomas, Catherine- what use are they to me? St. Peter sits closer to God’s throne than all of them, and I’d drown before he had time to plead my cause. I must go straight to the One who made the sea, and the saints, and me. Our Father which art in heaven, save these poor souls and me that cry for bare life! Oh sweet Jesus, pitiful Jesus, who walked the waves of Genezaret when Peter sank, who wept for Lazarus when the apostles were still dry-eyed, save poor Gerard- for dear Margaret’s sake!”
At that very moment, the sailors were seen clambering into the tiny jolly-boat every ship carried, ready to desert the sinking hull. A rush of selfish, desperate men followed, and thirty souls crammed themselves into the tiny craft, pushing off for shore. Left behind were three souls too dazed to move, two paralyzed with terror, sat like heaps of wet rags on the sloshing deck. One man crawled on his knees after the full-sized wooden statue of the Virgin Mary the sailors had pried reverently from the mast, clinging to it and praying aloud as the statue washed back and forth across the deck in the rising seawater. The Jew sat cross-legged, past even the petty passion of fear, wailing over his lost bag of silver, shaking his fist at every spray that lashed his face and cursing the Nazarenes, their gods, their devils, their ships, and their seas for all eternity. The giant Dominican, having shriven every soul left aboard, stood calmly communing with his own spirit. The Roman woman sat pale and unflinching, only drawing her baby closer to her bosom as death crept nearer.
Gerard saw her, and the sight woke his manhood. “See, see!” he cried. “They took the boat and left this poor woman and her child to drown.” His mind raced, searching for something that would float. There were no loose casks, no spare planks. His eyes fell on the wooden Virgin. He caught it up in his arms, ignoring the wail that burst from the praying man like a child robbed of his favourite toy, and ran aft with it. “Come, wife,” he called to the Roman woman. “I’ll lash you and the child to this. It’s worm-eaten, but it will hold long enough.”
She turned her great dark eyes on him, and asked one single word, soft, full of tenderness: “Thyself?”
“I am a man,” he replied, “with no small child to care for.”
“Ah,” she said, and the spark of hope lit her face, chasing away a little of her calm resignation. He tied the statue tight to her side, and the hope of life made her tremble a little, though her eyes never wavered. The ship sat so low in the water now that Gerard could lever her over the gunwale with an oar, easing her into the waves. “Go,” he said, “while there is still time.”
She turned her Roman eyes, now wet with tears, to him. “Poor youth! God forgive me! My child!” He pushed her out into the surf, guiding her away from the hull with his oar so she would not be dashed against it.
A heavy hand fell on his shoulder. A deep, booming voice sounded in his ear. “It is well done. Now come with me.” It was the giant friar. Gerard turned, and the friar took two long strides, grabbed the broken stump of the mast, and Gerard obeyed by instinct, laying hold of the other end. With one enormous, straining effort, they hoisted the heavy timber and heaved it over the side. One of the dazed passengers had run after them, and leaped first, landing on one end of the mast. Gerard seized the other end, and the friar settled himself in the middle.
It was a terrible ride. The mast bucked and plunged like a kicking horse with every wave, spray lashing their faces so hard it blinded them, threatening to knock them off and under the water. Presently a long, grinding grating sound echoed ahead: the ship had struck the reef. A moment later, their mast was hurled against the stationary hull with tremendous force. The bewildered passenger’s head struck the jagged broken rudder with a sickening crack, smashed like a coconut under a sledgehammer. He sank immediately, leaving nothing but a red stain on the water, a clump of white matter on the rudder, and his dying cry ringing in their ears as their mast drifted clear under the lee of the black hull. The friar uttered a short Latin prayer for his soul, then settled back calmly on the spar.
They rolled along the troughs of the waves, one moment sunk so low they saw nothing but water all around them, the next catching glimpses of the shore lined with cheering villagers waving their arms in wild Italian gestures to encourage them. The jolly-boat the thirty men had crammed into drifted past them, bottom upwards. Not far off, the Roman woman rose and fell on the waves, holding a stray paddle she had found, her baby tucked tight under her left arm as she paddled gallantly with her right.
After what felt like an eternity, the friar spoke quietly. “I touched the ground.”
“Impossible, father,” Gerard gasped. “We are still a hundred yards from shore. Do not leave our mast, I beg you.”
“My son, you speak prudently,” the friar replied. “But I have business for the Holy Church waiting for me in Rome, and I will not waste time floating when I can walk in her service. There, I felt the sand under my toes again! The advantage of wearing sandals, not heavy shoes. The water here is shallow. You are shorter than I am: stay with the mast as long as you need to. I walk.”
He stepped off the spar, spreading his great powerful arms, and charged through the surf. Gerard followed close behind him. At every huge breaking wave, the friar stood like a stone tower, mouth closed, head thrown back to meet the wall of water, vanishing entirely under it for a heartbeat before emerging again, ploughing steadily onward. At last they were almost to the shore, but the outward drag of the surf foiled every attempt to wade to dry land. The villagers waded out to meet them, stout fishermen linked arm in arm in a triple chain holding long spears, and dragged them all to safety.
The friar shook the seawater off his robes, gave the gathered crowd a short paternal benediction, and set off on the road to Rome, his eyes bent to the ground as his order required, never pausing, never glancing back at the sea that had nearly swallowed him whole, but had no power to harm him without his Master’s leave.
While he stalks onward alone, I am not bound by the rules of the Dominican order to march straight on unseeing. The crowd left Gerard to dry himself beside their enormous bonfire, with a delicacy he would never have met in the cold north, and it was only then that he pulled two precious parchments from the breast of his tunic, laying them out carefully to dry before he even thought of stripping off his soaked clothes. Only once they were fully dry did he consent to change into a spare fisherman’s tunic, leaving his own waterlogged garments by the fire, and walk down to the shoreline to watch the rest of the wreck wash in.
The captain had stayed aboard his ship, not out of gallantry, but convinced it was useless to fight the fate the fiery single Castor had marked for him. Even so, the sea tore the poop section free of the rest of the hull, and swept him safe ashore, still clinging to the timbers. Gerard helped haul him out of the surf. The disconsolate Hebrew landed on another chunk of floating wreckage, and the moment his feet touched dry land he offered a large reward for his lost bag of silver, a plea that won no sympathy from the villagers, only a little amusement. Two more passengers survived, washed in on other pieces of the broken hull. The thirty men who had crammed into the jolly-boat came ashore too, but one at a time, all dead. One still drew breath when they pulled him out, and the villagers, acting with the very best intentions, dragged him too close to the roaring bonfire to warm him. He, too, soon breathed his last.
As Gerard stood at the edge of the waves, half horrified half curious to see the bodies of his late shipmates washed onto the shingle, a soft hand touched his shoulder. He turned. It was the Roman matron, glowing with unspoken gratitude. She lifted his hand gently, raised it to her lips, and kissed it- a gesture so noble, it felt less like a show of thanks than an honour conferred on a man who had earned it. Then, her face bright with tears, she held her baby up and made the little boy kiss his preserver’s cheek. Gerard kissed the child again

Gerard settled into a humble, sun-warmed garret lodging on the west bank of the Tiber, its small window framing a distant glint of the river through tangled laundry lines strung between terracotta rooftops. Each dawn he set out with a rolled specimen of his script tucked under his arm, calling at every scribe and manuscript shop in the city he could track down.
The reception was uniformly cold. “Our lettering runs far slimmer than this,” one tradesman sniffed, prodding his work with a grubby finger. “Your ink is far too heavy and dark,” another complained. But the refrain he heard most often stung worst of all: “What use is fine Latin here these days? Can you not write Greek?”
“Ay, but not half so well as I can turn Latin script,” Gerard admitted.
“Then you will never earn a crust in Rome.”
Undeterred, he borrowed a precious, beautifully illuminated Greek manuscript from a collector at a steep price, trundling home with a gaping hole in his purse but not a flicker of diminished courage. In a fortnight he had mastered the Greek character far beyond the standard the local shops turned out, and thereafter arranged his days to grind at the new script until noon, then hunt for commissions the rest of the afternoon. But when he returned to the traders with Greek specimens finer than any they had on their own shelves, they only shrugged: Greek and Latin alike were unsaleable now, the city was flooded with imported manuscripts from every corner of Europe. He ought to have come the year before.
Not ready to surrender, Gerard bought a small psaltery to teach himself lay songs for spare coin, and began practicing the art of colouring playing cards to eke out a little side income. His kind Siennese landlady, who had taken a liking to his mild manners and fair, gold-streaked hair, stopped by his rooms one evening, pressed him to dine at her own table, and gently pried the story of his misfortunes out of him. She laughed and shook her head at his naivety.
“Those sly booksellers,” she declared, “keep their own underpaid scribes on payroll, sell their work to nobles for a king’s ransom, and pay the poor wretches pennies. Of course they blow cold on you. Your script is far too good for them. I have seen it, you know—you never lock your door like that surly Florentine Pietro across the hall, and women are curious by nature. Your fine work would make their shoddy overpriced manuscripts look like garbage, and ruin their grift.”
Gerard sighed. “Alas, dame, you think the worst of folk, and you so frank and kind yourself.”
“My dear boy, the Romans are a devious lot. *I* am Siennese, praise the Virgin, and we do not lie for sport. You think leaving Augsburg was your mistake? Pah! Augsburg is a hick town no one of consequence in Rome has ever heard of. You will make your fortune here in spite of those rogue booksellers. Everyone knows our great nobles have been bitten by the writing bug for years, they pour out gold like water to fill their chests with fine copied manuscripts, and it has even cut down on the faction stabbings and the old custom of roasting their enemies’ livers for supper. Cardinal Bassarion and the Holy Father himself alone could keep a dozen scribes like you working night and day. I will speak to my maid Teresa—she hears every scrap of court gossip, and will dig up names of patrons who are actually looking for fine work.”
The next day she returned to him with a list of five highborn signors all obsessed with manuscript collecting. Gerard copied out new, flawless specimens, left a copy with his name and address at each noble’s door, and waited hopefully.
Weeks passed. No replies came. Day after day slipped by, leaving him heartsick, and by a cruel twist of fate this was the exact same stretch of time that Margaret, hundreds of miles away in Rotterdam, fought tooth and nail to keep their household fed, only to be arrested by the guild for healing the sick without a license, rather than bleeding them or maiming them according to the approved rules of the surgeons.
Ruin stared Gerard full in the face. He cut his meals down to one a day to stretch his last remaining coins thin, but his sharp-eyed landlady caught him at once. She rounded on him, brusque but gentle, scolding him for being a fool to try to outrun poverty on an empty stomach. “Patienza, my lad! Times will mend. Meantime I will feed you for the love of heaven, no payment required.”
Gerard protested that he could not let an honest woman lose her due on his account, but she brushed him off and began to tell him of his reclusive neighbour Pietro. The Florentine painter had arrived in Rome some months prior with a full purse and a half-finished masterpiece, rented an unfurnished room across the hall from Gerard, and furnished it neatly. When he finished his painting, he had turned down every offer for it so disdainfully he had turned all his would-be patrons into enemies. Month by month he had sold every stick of furniture, and now he owned only one set of clothes, and slept at night on a great oak chest. He locked his door every time he stepped out, too proud to let anyone see his poverty.
Gerard’s heart ached. The man’s fate was his own. He tried to waylay Pietro in the hall to offer help, but the painter always slipped past him, until one afternoon he heard a low groan drift through the wall. He knocked, and a surly voice bade him enter.
The room was all but bare: one rickety chair, an iron basin, an easel, a great oak chest, and a massive large painting propped against the far wall, face turned inward. Coiled on the chest was a haggard young man with dark, sour features and glittering, sharp eyes, who looked for all the world like a cobra coiled to strike the first unwary comer.
“Good Signor Pietro,” Gerard said softly, “forgive me for intruding on your solitude. I am your nearest neighbour, and methinks your brother in misfortune. I too am an artist.”
Pietro jumped off the chest, brightening at once, and waved him to sit on the chest. “You are a painter? Welcome.”
Gerard smiled and shook his head. “I am a caligrapher, I copy Greek and Latin manuscripts for hire. I dabbled a little in paint in my youth, but I am no master of the craft.”
Pietro’s face fell a little. “A caligrapher? That is no art, that is only copying the thoughts of other men. An artist thinks, and paints his own thought onto the panel.”
Gerard laughed gently. “You are not wrong. But a scribe can preserve the words of the great ancients, the pure reason no brush could ever paint, the thoughts of God no angel could render. Let that pass, though. I wanted to befriend you, for we are both fallen on hard times here.”
At that moment the landlady’s step sounded on the stair. “Ah, the good dame brings my dinner!” Gerard called. “Hostess! I am here visiting Signor Pietro, I will eat my meal in his company.”
She set the smoking, savoury ragout down on the chest without a word and withdrew. Gerard dipped his spoon in, then paused. “I never eat well alone. For Our Lady’s sake, share this with me, there is more than enough for two.”
Pietro’s glittering eyes locked on his. What he saw was not kindness, but the insult of patronizing alms. He reached out, seized the dish, and hurled the entire contents out the garret window. He turned back, shaking with rage and mortification. “Let that teach you to offer charity to an artist you do not know, master scribe.”
Gerard’s face flushed hot, and he had to fight hard to resist boxing the proud fool’s ears. He thought of his mother, who had taught him never to waste good food, and pity softened his anger. “That was no alms,” he said coldly. “I offered you half my dinner, and you threw the whole thing away. You had every right to destroy your own share, but mine you stole. Pride is a fine thing, but justice is finer.”
Pietro stared, then hung his head. “I took you for a fool, transparent in your pity. Forgive me. The world has soured me, I hate all men. Go now, and leave me to my misery.”
But Gerard stopped at the door. “We Dutchmen are hard bargainers. We would shave an egg to save a penny. For my lost dinner, I claim a forfeit: let me look at your painting, the one you keep turned to the wall.”
Pietro went white. “No. Do not ask that. I have sworn a solemn vow to drive my dagger through the next man who flouts my painting, my whole heart and soul made manifest on panel. If you mock it, I will kill you.”
“I will say nothing unkind,” Gerard promised. “I will not mock it. Let me see it.”
Pietro hesitated, then turned the great canvas to face the room, dragging it into the slant golden Roman afternoon light. He coiled back onto his chest, hand resting on the hilt of his stiletto, and waited.
Gerard stood silent. He stepped close, studied the brushstrokes, then backed all the way across the tiny room to take in the whole composition. For half an hour he moved slowly back and forth, never speaking a word.
At last Pietro snapped, irritable and impatient: “Well? Have you not a single word to say?”
Gerard started, and drew his short sword from his belt. Pietro jumped up with a shriek, convinced he meant to stab the painting. “Calm yourself,” Gerard laughed, pointing the tip of his blade at the painter instead of the canvas. “I am only defending myself against your stiletto, so we may have a fair fight if you take against my criticism. Now sit down. First: your oil paint recipes are far inferior to those used by the Van Eycks in Flanders, and I will teach you every secret of their craft if you will let me. But that is a small thing. You Italians are the sons of the sun—we Flemings have colour, but you have imagination. You have poured your whole immortal soul onto this panel. The drapery of the Virgin is a little stiff and short, true, but the rest? That vast sprawling landscape, forty miles wide, where every distant tree and cottage fades so gently into haze you feel you could walk straight into it, the floating cloud of cherub faces around the holy pair, that deep purple sunset sky hanging over the whole wide world? It makes every tiny cramped landscape I ever painted or admired look like cheap dross. In Ghent or Bruges, or even Rotterdam, patrons would tear this painting out of your hands for a fortune. You are no starving fool, Pietro Vanucci. You are a king of your craft. Viva il maestro! Long live the master!”
Pietro burst into tears, and threw his arms around Gerard’s neck. Everyone had called his work a madman’s useless dream, he sobbed, but Gerard had seen it. “I was a monster to throw your dinner away! I will never hate mankind again, not now that I have found a friend who sees what I made. Come, let us go and order the finest supper in the whole quarter. We will bring the painting with us, and make it our third guest.”
Gerard laughed, and followed him out into the golden Roman dusk, and for the first time in months, neither man felt his poverty weigh heavy at all.

Barely seven days had slipped by, and the two friends sat side by side at their workbench in their cramped, sun-warmed Roman garret, though their spirits could not have been more unalike. Pietro dashed at his half-finished fine art panel in fitful bursts, turning out strokes of breathtaking genius in the space of a few breathless minutes, only to fling down his brush a moment later and curse the very canvas he had just blessed. Then, white-hot with creative fury, he would snatch up his tools again, labour like one possessed for an hour, and finally collapse back in his chair with a guttural groan of despair. All the while, the steady, canny Dutchman beside him worked on, calm as a millpond, a faint, constant smile playing about his lips.

To put it plainly, Gerard – who had never yet made a friend he could not gently steer to shared purpose – had harnessed Pietro’s wild, unruly talent to a far more practical end. The two were painting custom playing cards to put bread on the table and keep their landlord from the door.

When the last of the stack was finished, the indignant Pietro swept up his own masterpiece to set out on his daily, fruitless round of calls on wealthy Roman patrons. Gerard pressed him to take the newly finished cards along too, and try to sell them for whatever they could get. Pietro’s face tightened, coiled as a rattlesnake ready to strike, but after a long, hot moment he softened, embraced Gerard in the warm, quick Italian fashion, and tucked the deck under his arm – first laying the still slightly damp top cards out to crisp in the strong, golden Roman sun that gilded the window sills that season.

Left to his own devices, Gerard scribbled a pair of elegant Greek calligraphy strokes for a small commission he was picking at, then fetched a needle and thread to mend a tiny rent in his wool hose. His landlady found him thus occupied, and leant in the doorway to tease him, irony lacing her tone: “Have we no women left in the whole house, that a fine young man must stoop to mending his own clothes? Once you’re done patching that, come down and speak to Teresa – the friend I told you of a while back, the one married to a good-for-nothing lout who never stops boasting of his acquaintance with every great lord in the city.”

Gerard trundled down the stairs after her, and when he stepped into the parlour, who should be sitting there waiting but the Roman matron whose small son he had saved from drowning not long before. “Ah, madama!” he exclaimed, delight flooding his face. “It is you! The good dame never told me it was you I was to meet. And the little fair-haired lad – is he well? Did he take no lasting harm from that dreadful adventure in the drifting boat?”

“He is perfectly well,” Teresa said, her throat tight with unspoken gratitude.

“What in the world are you two on about?” the landlady cut in, staring from one to the other in frank bewilderment. “And why are you trembling so hard, my dear Teresa mia?”

“He saved my child’s life,” Teresa said, forcing herself to steady her voice.

“What? My quiet little lodger? And he never breathed a single word of it to me?” The landlady rounded on Gerard, half mock-indignant. “Art thou not ashamed to look me in the face and keep such a grand, kind deed hidden?”

“Oh, do not speak harshly to him,” Teresa pleaded, turning to her friend and pouring out a glowing, vivid account of the day Gerard had dragged her boy from the Tiber. Gerard stood blushing like a shy schoolgirl the whole time, hardly able to recognise his own small act of kindness when the matron’s fond gratitude painted it in such glowing colours.

“To think I once asked you to put in a good word for this young man,” the landlady laughed, turning to Gerard. “I knew nothing of him save that you spoke well of him, Fiammina – and that was enough for me. Dear boy, helping you succeed will feel like paying back a debt I never even knew I owed.”

For the next hour, the two women chattered eagerly, plotting every possible way to help Gerard break through the thick, tangled wall of bribes, hidden fees, and petty chicanery that stood between unknown young artists and the wealthy art patrons of the Eternal City. Teresa smiled a sad, knowing smile when Gerard told her he had left samples of his work propped on the doorsteps of great men’s palaces. “What, no promise to share a cut of the sale with the doormen? Not even a single coin to slip the servants so they will actually show your work to the masters of the house?” she said, shaking her head. “You might as well have tossed every sketch straight into the Tiber. They will use them to stoke the kitchen fires before their masters ever lay eyes on them.”

“Alas, what is a poor artist to do then?” Gerard sighed, dismayed. “We are not rich men, we cannot afford to scatter bribes at every gate.”

“Then you ought to go to a noble city that is not half so greedy as this one,” Teresa said. “The Roman court will not take a sheep that does not come already shorn of every last coin it has.” She sank into quiet thought, then told him she would come back to see him again at the same time the next day.

The moment Teresa had stepped out the door, Pietro stormed back up the steps, his face black as a thunderstorm. Gerard exchanged a quick, worried glance with his landlady, then hurried upstairs to comfort his friend. “What, did none of them buy your masterpiece?” he asked gently.

“Same as every other day,” Pietro growled.

“Fools, all of them,” Gerard said.

“That is not the worst of it,” Pietro snarled.

“What on earth has gone wrong, then?”

“They bought the cards!” Pietro yelled, flailing his fists wildly at the empty air.

“All the better!” Gerard said, brightening.

“They practically pounced on me the second I laid them out,” Pietro ranted. “They were utterly enraptured, could not hide how badly they wanted them even when they tried. I saw the longing in their eyes, played the hard-to-get fool, and picked their pockets clean – curse those witless boobies!” He flung a dozen small silver coins clattering across the floor, then danced on them, his eyes blazing like a serpent’s, kicking them across the garret until they skittered under every last stick of furniture.

Gerard dropped straight to his knees, chasing the poor maltreated coins across the floor, tucking every last one tenderly into his purse. “You ought to smile at their foolishness, my friend, and turn it to good profit,” he said.

“Oh, I will turn it to profit,” Pietro said, his voice thick with simmering indignation. “The brutes! We will paint a full pack of cards every single day, we will have the whole city gambling and ruining their households, and we will live like princes off their vices and their stupidity. Though there was one queen in that last pack I almost could not bear to sell. You painted her, brother – the one with the red-brown hair like ripe chestnuts, and eyes as blue as sapphires, and more than that, a soul you could see shining right through the paint.”

“Pietro,” Gerard said softly, “I painted that one straight from my heart.” The quick-witted Italian nodded, his eyes twinkling with understanding. “You love her that much, and yet you left her behind?”

“Pietro, it is because I love her more than anything in the world that I have wandered all this long, weary road so far from home.”

Their quiet conversation was cut short by the landlady shouting up the stairs from the bottom of the landing: “Gerard! Come down at once, you are wanted!” He hurried down the steps, to find Teresa waiting for him by the door, holding her shawl. “Come with me, Ser Gerard,” she said, and held out her hand.

Gerard walked silent at Teresa’s side, his artist’s mind turning over and over to puzzle out what fate she was steering him toward rather than simply asking, as a plainer soul would have done. At last she spoke unprompted, explaining that a friend had tipped her off a goldsmith’s wife nearby was seeking a scribe. They reached the shop within minutes, and Teresa made her plea: “Madama, Leonora told me you have need of a writer. I have brought you the finest one there is—he snatched my child from the waves at sea, and for Our Lady’s grace, I beg you look on him with favour.”
The goldsmith’s wife, Olympia, complied in one sense: her eyes fixed on Gerard’s comely, earnest face and she could barely tear them away. But her answer was no. “I have no use for a scribe myself,” she said, suddenly recalling. “Ah, but my gossip Claelia, the sausage-maker, was asking for one but three days past.”
Teresa bowed politely and withdrew. Claelia’s house was some distance off, and when they arrived, she was out. Teresa seated herself on a stone step, still and statuesque, so calm that Gerard was halfway pulling a charcoal sketch of her from his pocket when the sausage-maker rounded the corner. She repeated her plea, leading Gerard forward by the hand, but Claelia shook her head. “I’ve no need of a writer—though my friend Appia Claudia the tailor, who lives on Via Lepida, was badgering me for a lead to one no later than yesterday.”
Gerard protested that he did not want to drag her on a wild goose chase all across Rome, but Teresa only blinked at him, mild but firm. “What good thing ever was done without a little patience? I will knock on every door in this city before you go without the work you have earned.”
It was then Gerard noted the man shadowing them, sometimes far off, sometimes drawing near enough that his footsteps echoed theirs. “We are followed,” he warned.
Teresa’s cheek flushed faintly, but her tone was cool. “I saw him long ago. It is my poor Lodovico.” She stopped, turned, and crooked her finger. The man approached sheepishly, and she bade him greet the young scribe who had plucked his wife and infant from the stormy sea. The forced grin fell off Lodovico’s face at that, and he embraced Gerard with genuine, tearful gratitude—though there remained something furtive about the way he had trailed them that left Gerard ill at ease. He refused to cross the Tiber with them, however, and turned back toward their home, leaving the pair to walk on, Teresa’s mood turning quiet and somber.
Appia Claudia sent them no farther than a hundred yards down the lane to Lucretia, the merry little glove-seller, who laughed and admitted she kept all her shop’s accounts in her head, and had no use for a scribe. “It is for my confessor, Fra Colonna, of the Colonna house, that I asked after one,” she explained. “He is mad for good writers, and illuminators, and all learned folk. He would turn away a duke mid-audience if a Greek scholar was closeted with him pouring over an ancient parchment. And he has coin enough, never fear—any of his noble kinsmen would pour a thousand crowns into his lap if he but asked.”
She then told them the famous story of the time she’d tried to rouse him from his perpetual reverie by confessing she’d murdered her lodger’s little girl and baked her into a pie, and he had only blinked awake to assign her three Paternosters, three Aves, and no butter or eggs the following Wednesday before wandering off again, half in a world of old texts. “But mind this,” she warned, suddenly serious. “Hate bunglers worse than poison. A man brought him a clumsily carved crucifix last week, and he raged so loud at the fellow for shoddy work made in mockery of the Christ’s agony that the whole street heard him. If you cannot prove your skill, do not go near him.”
Teresa drew herself up proudly. “I will answer for his skill. He saved my child.”
Gerard, however, was nervous. The friar had seen the work of every great scribe in Italy, he pointed out, and he would far rather spend a day crafting a perfect sample of his work than walk in blind. He begged for a single day’s grace, and Teresa consented at once, cutting off Lucretia’s quip that he was a coward to defend him: “He is not a coward. He is modest.”
As they walked back toward Gerard’s lodging, his eye caught a flawless, creamy white vellum skin in a shop window. He ached to buy it, but had not the coin, and hurried past before he could linger too long. He was halfway resolved to take the old family deed he had carried all the way from Sevenbergen, his last precious link to his father’s land claims, and erase the old writing to make his sample, when he sat down and pored over the faded, cramped script. To destroy it would be reckless, he realized. He would decipher every word at his leisure, not waste it on a single scribe’s test.
He trundled downstairs, resolved to buy a small scrap of cheaper vellum with his last few coins, only to find Teresa chatting with his landlady. The woman pulled something from under her apron: the very perfect vellum skin he had longed for. Teresa had seen the way his gaze had lingered on it through the shop window, seen the quiet sigh he’d let out when he turned away, and bought it for him, no questions asked. Before he could stammer out thanks or offer to pay her, the Roman matron bade him goodbye and slipped away down the street.
The next afternoon, Lucretia’s son led Gerard to Fra Colonna’s lodgings. He tipped the friar’s housekeeper Onesta, and she ushered him into a large chamber heaped high with manuscripts, carved ivory, half-finished paintings, and odd antiquities from every corner of the known world. The friar himself sat in the middle of that glorious, loving chaos, poring over an Arabian manuscript, and looked up peevishly at the interruption.
Gerard’s hands shook too hard to write a fresh sample on the spot, he admitted, but he had brought a finished vellum page, with Greek text illuminated in cobalt and gold, and its Latin translation penned neatly beneath. He laid it in the friar’s outstretched hand and waited, heart in his throat. The verdict staggered him: the Dominican jumped to his feet and threw his arms around Gerard’s neck, laughing out loud with joy.
Across the sea, in Holland, an event unfolded that no man then living, no reader even now, could have guessed would twist Gerard’s fate so far off its path. A procession came tramping up the road to Eli’s cottage, a strange centaur of a sight: a man mounted on a horse so absurdly over-decorated you could barely see a single inch of honest horseflesh. Its ears were sheathed in linen tipped with blue and silver, its body swaddled in stiff brocade that hung all the way to the ground, its tail tucked so far out of sight it might as well have never existed. Only its eyes gleamed through two cut holes in the fabric, and its tiny front hoofs peeped out like rats as it minced along.
This absurd, over-gilded creature bore the will of the duke, straight from his progress at the nearby tournament. The man on its back hailed Eli and his wife Catherine, who appeared in the doorway, and announced he had come to collect their dwarf son Giles for the court.
Catherine shrieked that there was no dwarf in their house, but Eli sighed and corrected her. “He means our Giles, who is small of stature. There is no gainsaying the duke’s messengers.”
The emissary confirmed it: their last court dwarf had tumbled down an unlatched well only days before, and the duke had sent for Giles to fill the post. When Catherine raged that she would never let her son go to a household so careless it let its wells lie open like wolf traps, the messenger’s face turned hard. Obey, he told them, and Giles would be fed like a bishop and clothed in cloth of gold. Refuse, and all three of their heads would be stuck on poles, the bellman crying out that they were traitors who hoarded the duke’s rightful property.
Before the dispute could drag on, the object of it stepped out the door on his own, and sided with the crown. “My folk are daft, but I am not,” he roared. “I’ll go with you, right now.”
He brushed off his mother’s tears, telling her he was sick of moping around the cottage ever since Gerard had left, he would never be farther than Rotterdam, and no duke alive could keep him there if he did not like it. He refused the tiny stunted dwarf mule they had brought for him, saying he hated all small things, and demanded he be given the highest, biggest horse in the whole retinue. When the servants warned him the big horse kicked and would not let a little man mount him, Giles dashed back inside, climbed to an upper window, fastened a rope to the frame, and slid down as smooth as an oiled bolt of lightning, landing square astride the big horse’s back without the beast even noticing he was there.
Catherine fussed over him, crying, and mended the tiny tear in his sleeve he had made climbing out the window, her tears dripping onto his arm as she stitched. Then Giles rode off, laughing and jocund, while his parents wept over his virtues back at the cottage, blind to every one of his rough edges. He arrived at court and became an immediate favorite, and soon won a privilege no other soul in the realm dared claim: he was allowed to speak nothing but the unvarnished truth, and he bawled it loud enough for the whole palace to hear, to the utter horror of every courtier who crossed his path.

Happy is the man who has two strong cables to pull him through life: merit, and the favour of women. Oh, that I, like our Gerard, possessed such a "chain of ladies" to hoist me upward! I should be prose laureate, or professor of the then-fashionable spasmodic school of writing, or some such distinguished post, in no time. While I wait for that good fortune, let me sketch for you the singular Fra Colonna.

The true revivers of ancient learning and philosophy were two writers of fiction themselves: Petrarch and Boccaccio. Their work did not win great, public, immediate success in their own lifetimes, but they sowed good seed that never perished, quickening in the soil for generations while it waited for sunshine. From their day onward, Italy never lacked at least one native scholar fluent in Greek, and every learned Greek who landed on her shores was welcomed as a brother. By the end of the 14th century, Poggio, Valla, and the elder Guarino were born; and early in the 15th century, Florence under Cosmo de Medici hummed as a nest of Platonists. These scholars, led by the Greek-born Gemistus Pletho, began writing in the 1440s to argue Aristotle out of his place of honour: for few minds are broad enough to do full justice to great A without dealing great B a slanderous injustice. Theodore Gaza defended Aristotle with moderation; George of Trebizond attacked him with ferocious bitterness, and struck back at Plato in turn. Then Cardinal Bessarion, another Greek by birth, stepped in to oppose George and his Aristotelian idol in a treatise titled *Against the Slanderer of Plato*. Pugnacity, wise or unwise, is always a mark of vitality.

Born with no taste for petty controversy in that zealous age, Francesco Colonna, a young Florentine noble, lived only for the arts. At twenty he took Dominican orders, seeking nothing but quiet study. He withdrew from idle company, faction fights, and the humming, stinging chaos of the human hive, to find refuge with Saint Dominic and the Nine Muses. An eager student of languages, paintings, statues, chronology, coins, and monumental inscriptions, these last artefacts slowly loosened his faith in the popular myths peddled as official history. He travelled the East for many years, returning home laden with treasures: master of several rare manuscripts, fluent in Greek and Latin, Hebrew and Syriac.

He found his country had not stood still. Other lettered princes besides Cosmo de Medici had risen: Alfonso, King of Naples, Nicolas d'Este, Lionel d'Este, and many more. Above all, his old friend Thomas of Sarzana had been elected Pope, and had lent enormous new force to the spread of letters: he amassed 5000 manuscripts in the Vatican Library, and commissioned Poggio to translate Diodorus Siculus and Xenophon's *Cyropaedia*, Laurentius Valla to translate Herodotus and Thucydides, Theodore Gaza to translate Theophrastus, George of Trebizond to translate Eusebius and several treatises of Plato, and dozens of other similar projects. The friar found Plato and Aristotle had called a truce to their quarrel, but Poggio and Valla were at daggers drawn over tiny points of grammar, burning with that bitter *odium philologicum* that makes the lives of true book lovers feel like paradise. He settled back in his native land, his days passing as a rosy, unbroken dream.

No one is happier than the man of versatile tastes, so long as he does not have to earn his bread by his hobbies -- and Fra Colonna was versatility incarnate. He knew seven or eight languages, a little mathematics, could write verse passably, paint a little, model clay, sing a little, pluck a lute passably well, and best of all, could recognise and genuinely enjoy true excellence in every one of those fields. For that last trait alone, he deserved all the happiness he had. Gauge the intellects of your own acquaintances, and you will find precious few whose minds are not deaf, blind, or completely dead to at least one great art or science, so that "wisdom at one entrance quite shut out." Worse still, the conceited fools who lack that breadth of taste will often parade the holes in their intellects as badges of pride instead of blushing for them.

A zealot for art, the friar was a naïve sceptic in matters of religion. In every age, a small handful of men hold opinions that belong to a different era, past or future. His doubt was as simple and unassuming as his artistic enthusiasm: he looked on the religious ceremonies of his own day much the way his idols, the pagan philosophers, looked on public worship of gods and dead heroes -- harmless mummeries, good for keeping the populace content. And he drew a droll, unplanned distinction here: any Christian ceremony he traced back to purely pagan origins he respected, out of sheer reverence for antiquity, even though had he lived in the days of that original pagan rite, he would have scorned it from the heights of his own philosophy.

Fra Colonna was utterly charmed by his new scribe Gerard, and with free run of half the noble palaces in Rome, he sang his praises so loudly that patrons soon came knocking to poach the young Dutchman away. "But I am so happy with you, father," Gerard protested.

"Fiddlestick about being happy tucked away with me," Fra Colonna waved him off. "You cannot afford to be happy. You must learn to be a man of the world -- that is the great lesson I drum into all the young. The Montesini family can pay you three times what I can, and they shall too -- by Jupiter!" And the friar set a very steep price on Gerard's pen work, which the Montesini accepted without a single murmur. Manuscript copying fetched far higher rates back then than printed authors would earn for centuries after the invention of the press. Gerard received three hundred crowns just for transcribing Aristotle's treatise on rhetoric.

The great are endlessly affectionate to their pets, for as long as the fancy lasts, and in the height of the craze for Greek manuscripts, the handsome, careful scribe soon became the favourite of Roman high society: nobles of both sexes caressed him like a pampered lapdog. It would have turned a vain man's head, but the shrewd Dutchman saw the steel hand beneath the velvet glove, and never presumed on their favour. Even so, it was a proud day for him when he and Fra Colonna found themselves seated at the table of his current patron, Cardinal Bessarion. They sat nearly a mile down from the head of the table, but no matter: there Gerard saw roast pheasants dished up still covered in their feathers, as if they had just flown out of a coppice instead of off the spit, and chickens cooked sealed inside glass bottles, so tender they melted like peaches.
