But the greatest novelty that electrified Gerard far more than any modern reader could imagine were the napkins, surpassingly fine, folded into cocked hats, birds' wings, and fluttering fans instead of lying flat on the table.

After dinner, the tables were taken apart and carried away, and lo, under each one was a second table set out heaped high with sweetmeats. The Roman signoras and signorinas fell on them and gormandised, while the men eyed the sugar confections with reasonable suspicion. "But dear father," Gerard objected, "I do not see those two-pronged daggers men say his excellency puts in every guest's left hand."

"Nay, that is Cardinal Orsini's silly invention, that peevish little instrument for his guests to fumble their meat withal," Colonna snorted. "I hear one man, in a great hurry, skewered his tongue to his own palate with it. O tempora, O mores! The ancients, reclining godlike at their feasts, would have spurned such pedantries instantly."

As soon as the ladies had tired themselves playing among the sugarplums, those tables too were swept away, and all the guests sat lined up against the wall. Then two clerics entered, ducking and scraping, carrying lutes, knelt at the cardinal's feet, and sang the daily office, then retired with deep obeisance. The cardinal answered their respect by fingering his skullcap the way the later Iron Duke of Wellington used to tip his hat, and the whole company dispersed. Gerard had just dined with a cardinal who had thrice come within a hair's breadth of being elected Pope.

But greater honour was still in store for him. One day the cardinal sent for him, praised the flawless beauty of his script, and took him in his own coach to the Vatican, up a private stair to a luxurious little chamber with a great oriel window. It was fitted out with inkstands, slanted writing frames, and every tool of a scribe's trade. The cardinal whispered a word to a courtier, and soon the Pope's private secretary arrived carrying a glorious, grimy old manuscript of Plutarch's Lives. Soon Gerard was seated alone copying it, awe-struck, half-delighted at the thought that his Holiness would one day hold his work and read it. The papal inkstands were all gilded and glorious on the outside, but the ink inside was thin, vile rubbish. But Gerard always carried good homemade ink in a dirty little inkhorn slung at his belt; he knelt for a moment to pray for a firm, skilful hand, and set to work.

One whole side of his room was almost occupied by a massive heavy curtain, divided down the centre, its ample folds overlapping. For a long while Gerard resisted the growing impulse to peep through the gap, but at last it overpowered him. He left Plutarch half-written, stole across the matted floor, gathered up the folds of the curtain gently with his fingers, and poked his nose through the chink -- right against the cold steel of a halbert. Two fully armed soldiers were standing behind the curtain, their glittering weapons crossed in a triangle. Gerard drew swiftly back, but in that instant he heard the soft murmur of voices, and caught a glimpse of a whole group of people cringing before some hidden figure on the other side. He never repeated the attempt to pry through that guarded curtain, though he found his eyes drawn to it again and again. Every hour or so an ecclesiastic would peep in, stare hard at him, chill his blood, and leave without a word. It was all gloomy, mechanical, lifeless.

The next day a gentleman, richly armed, bounced in and glared at him. "What is going on here?" he demanded. Gerard told him he was writing out Plutarch, with the help of the saints. The spark said he did not know any Signor of that name. Gerard explained the circumstances of time and space that had deprived Signor Plutarch of the honour of the young noble's acquaintance. "Oh! One of those old dead Greeks they make such a coil over."

"Ay, signor, one of them who, being dead, yet live."

"I understand you not, young man," the noble said, drawing himself up with all the dignity of complete ignorance. "What did the old fellow write? Love stories? Merry tales, like Boccaccio?"

"Nay, lives of heroes and sages."

"Soldiers and popes?"

"Soldiers and princes."

"Will you read me of them some day?"

"And willingly, signor. But what would my employers say, were I to break off work?"

"Oh never heed that! Know you not who I am? I am Jacques Bonaventura, nephew to his Holiness the Pope, and captain of his guards. I came here to look after my fellows. I trow they have turned them out of their own room to make space for you." He hurried away after that.

This lively companion soon got into the habit of running in on the little chamber, and finding Gerard excellent company, he popped in constantly, chattering trivial court gossip while Gerard wrote the immortal lives. One day he came in a changed, moody man, threw himself into a chair, and cried, "Ah, traitress! traitress!" Gerard inquired after his ill, but only got the same reply: "Traitress! traitress!" So Gerard went back to writing Plutarch. After a minute Bonaventura sighed, "I am melancholy, and for Our Lady's sake read me a story out of Ser Plutarcho, to soothe my bile. In all that Greek is there nought about lovers betrayed?" Gerard read him the life of Alexander. He got so excited he marched up and down the room, threw his arms around the scribe, and vowed to shun "soft delights," that bed of nettles, and follow glory forever.

Who so happy now as Gerard? His art was honoured, fabulous prices were paid for it; in a year or two he would return by sea to Holland, his pockets heavy with good store of gold, and set up with his beloved Margaret in Bruges, or Antwerp, or dear Augsburg, and end their days in peace, and love, and healthy, happy labour. His heart never strayed an instant from her. In his prosperity he did not forget poor Pietro. He took Fra Colonna to see his friend's masterpiece. The friar inspected it severely and closely, fell on the artist's neck, and carried the painting to one of the noble Colonna family, who gave a noble price for it. Pietro moved down to the first floor, and lived like a gentleman. But Gerard remained in his garret. To increase his expenses would have been to postpone his return to Margaret. Luxury had no charms for that single-hearted young man, when set against the joy of seeing his love again.

Jacques Bonaventura made him acquainted with crowds of other gay young fellows of the papal court. They loved him, and sought to entice him into vice and reckless spending. But he begged humbly to be excused, and escaped that temptation. But a far greater trial was waiting for him just around the corner.

Fra Colonna had free run of the Pope’s vast, cobwebbed library, and often wrapped up his work at the same hour as Gerard, so the two would wander the sun-warmed streets of Rome together. For the young Dutch artist, every step was glowing: the great domes of the churches, the carved marble facades of palaces, the half-buried relics of ancient glory all stretched before him like a page of living legend, wrapped in the soft gold Roman light.

The friar would grant the ruins their grandeur, but pour cold common sense over the rest of Gerard’s starry-eyed wonder.
“This place you see as Rome? It is no more than the tomb of the true, mighty Rome of old.” He pointed out how twenty or thirty feet of the famous triumphal arches lay buried under muck and later construction, how the noisy modern streets ran straight over the tops of broken columns and the foundations of palaces that had stood tall a thousand years prior. Comparing the cramped, small bounds of the current city to the scattered, gargantuan traces of the old civilization peeking through the cobblestones here and there, he offered a sharp, memorable simile: “I tell you, this little village they call Rome is no different from one of those swallows’ nests you must have seen built tucked under the eaves of a long-decayed abbey.”

“Then old Rome must have been beyond beautiful,” Gerard breathed.
“Judge for yourself, my son. Look at the great Cloaca Maxima, the sewer the Romans built when their civilization was still in its infancy – that will outlast Vesuvius itself. Look at the broken fragments of the Temple of Peace. What do you think you would feel if you could see the old Capitol with its full twenty-five temples? This Monte Savello hill? It is nothing but the crumbled ruins of Marcellus’s ancient theatre. And Testacio, one of the highest hills in modern Rome? It is nothing more than an old rubbish heap: the women of old Rome tossed their shattered pots and pans there for generations, and lo – a mountain. *Ex pede Herculem; ex ungue leonem* – judge Hercules by his foot, the lion by his claw.”

Gerard listened respectfully, but when the friar drifted into claiming that the pagan Romans had been proportionally morally superior to their modern descendants, Gerard pushed back hard. “Then do you mean the world lost something when Christ came to us?” He blushed the second he said it, ashamed to speak so sharply to his benefactor.

“Saints forbid!” Colonna said at once. “That would be rank heresy to say so.” But after that quick, formal concession, he wandered off into winding, subtle circumlocution, creeping towards that forbidden idea of pagan virtue via a spiral back staircase of classical references. Mid-debate, they rounded a corner to find a small church porch crammed with onlookers: a demon was being exorcised inside.

Fra Colonna had a curious habit of letting out a soft, quiet moan whenever he was presented with claims no philosopher like Zeno or Epicurus would ever have accepted as fact. The sound, for those who knew him well, carried equal parts unmistakeable dissent and gentle pity for human credulity, ignorance, and error – especially when that error blinded people to the merits of the old pagan world. He moaned now. “Come away, then.”
“Nay, father, please, please,” Gerard begged. “I have never seen a devil cast out in my life.”

The friar sighed, shrugged heavily, and followed Gerard inside. They found the man said to be possessed forced to his knees before the altar, a scarf tied tight around his neck so the officiating priest could hold him fast like a chained dog. Not many onlookers had dared turn up: word had spread that the last demon cast out of that very church had not fled far at all, but hopped straight into one of the onlookers gathered there, the way a ferreted rabbit bolts from one burrow straight into the next.

By the time Gerard and Colonna arrived, the priest decided he had just enough spectators, and began. He turned to the struggling demoniac, breviary in hand, and started calling out names to identify the spirit he was chasing:
“Come out, Ashtaroth. Oho, not you, then. Come out, Belial. Come out, Tatzi. Come out, Eza. No, he does not tremble. Come out, Azymoth. Come out, Feriander. Come out, Foletho. Come out, Astyma. Come out, Nebul. Aha! I have found you, you crawling reptile, back to your old tricks. Let us pray!
“O Lord, we pray you drive the foul fiend Nebul out of this your creature: out of his hair, and his eyes, out of his nose, out of his mouth, out of his ears, out of his gums, out of his teeth, out of his shoulders, out of his arms, legs, loins, stomach, bowels, thighs, knees, calves, feet, ankles, fingernails, toenails, and soul. Amen.”

The priest rose from his knees, turned to the gathered crowd, and said genially, “Good folks, this is as stubborn a devil as you will see on any summer’s day.” He rounded back on his captive, addressing first the man, then the demon that supposedly spoke through his mouth: one minute the voice screamed hatred for the holy names he kept shouting, the next the demon whined that it felt dreadfully cramped and miserable inside the man’s body.
First the priest blurred the line between the possessed victim and the supposed demon, cuffing the man soundly, kicking him, and spitting repeatedly in his face. Then he lit a candle, held it upside down to burn the flame against his own fingers until he yelped and dropped it. Next he showed the man the ciborium holding the Consecrated Host, then lit another candle to burn his fingers a little more cautiously. At last he spoke gently to the man’s human self, dismissed him, and accepted the warm compliments of the crowd.

“Good father,” Gerard said, wide-eyed, “How well you know all their names. Priests back in my northern Holland have no such exact knowledge of the ranks of hell.”
“Ay, young man, here we know all their names, and all their tricks, the vile reptiles. This Nebul is one of the hardest fiends to ever hunt out.” The priest went on to tell the crowd a string of his exorcism stories, ending with his feat the day before, when he had driven a huge, hulking fiend out of a woman’s mouth. The demon had left behind a mess of nails, pins, and a tuft of its own hair, and shrieked in anguish as it fled: “It is not you that has conquered me. Look at that stone on the window sill! The Archangel Gabriel once landed on that very stone when he came down to earth – it is that that defeated me!”

Fra Colonna moaned again. “And you all believed that story?”
“Of course! Who but an infidel would doubt a revelation that precise?”
“What, believe the father of lies? That is stretching credulity past all reasonable bounds.”
“Oh, a liar does not lie every single time.”
“He does when he tells you an absurd story first, then waves a supposed holy relic at you to arm you against his own kind. If demons existed, they would never be that stupid. You should have answered him with a line from the ancients: *Timeo Danaos et dona ferentes* – I fear the Greeks, even when they bring gifts. Some scoundrel murdered his wife on that window sill stone, young man, mark my words.” He herded Gerard quickly out of the church.

“Alas, father, I fear you embarrassed that good priest,” Gerard said.
“Ay, by Pollux!” Colonna chuckled. “I pricked him all over with a single jab of Socratic interrogation. What modern man can parry the weapons of the ancient world?”

One afternoon, when Gerard had finished his day’s work, a liveried, fine-dressed lackey arrived to summon him to the Cesarini Palace. He went, and was led into a grand, high-ceilinged apartment where a young girl sat working at a tapestry. She rose at once, excused herself, and said she would go alert her mistress.

Gerard cooled his heels there for a full hour, and soon grew fretful. “These nobles think nothing of wasting a poor man’s time.” Just as he had decided to slip out and go back to his work, the door swung open, and a strikingly beautiful young woman entered, followed by two maids. It was the young princess of the house of Cesarini. She had been talking loudly and haughtily to her servants as she came in, but the second she spotted Gerard, she softened her voice to a gentle, feminine lilt. “Are you the scribe, messer?”
“I am, signora.”
“Good.” She sat down, leaving Gerard and her maids standing. “What is your name, good youth?”
“Gerard, signora.”
“Gerard? By Bacchus’s body, is that even a proper name for a human being?”
“It is a Dutch name, signora. I was born in Tergou, in Holland.”
“Such a harsh name for such a handsome young man, girls,” she laughed to her servants, who nodded eagerly in agreement. “Why did I send for him, again?” she said, leaning back on her throne-like armchair in lazy hauteur. “Ah, I remember. Sit down, Ser Gerardo, and write a letter to Ercole Orsini, my lover – at least, that is what he claims he is.”

Gerard sat, pulled out his paper and ink, and looked up for her instructions. She looked down at him from her high chair, her eyes just as puzzled as his.
“Well, Gerardo.”
“I am ready, your excellence.”
“Then write.”
“I am only waiting for your words to write down.”
“And who, pray, do you think is supposed to give them to me?”
“Who but your grace, since the letter belongs to you?”
“Mercy on us! You scribes can’t even find the words yourselves? What is the point of your craft if you can’t think of the words for me? I think you might be an impostor, Gerardo.”
“Nay, signora, I am no impostor. I could easily put all your highness’s speech into proper grammar, as well as write it down. But I cannot read your silence. Speak whatever is in your heart, and I will set it down on paper before your very eyes.”
“But there is nothing in my heart. Sometimes I think I have no heart at all.”
“What is in your mind, then?”
“Nothing there, either. Nor in my head, for that matter.”
“Then why write the letter at all?”
“Now that is the first sensible thing either of us has said all afternoon, Gerardo. A pox on that man! Why did he not write to me first? Then I could have replied saying nay to this and ay to that without all this headache. And besides, it is not a lady’s place to say the first word in such matters, is it?”
“No, signora – only the last.”
“Very well spoken, Gerardo. Ha ha! You get a gold coin for that wit. Hand me my purse!” She paid him on the spot, quick as was the custom of the Middle Ages. Gold in his hand only made Gerard eager to help her out of her difficulty. “Signorina,” he said, “these tasks only feel hard because people try too hard, are too fancy, and labor over flowery phrases. Just imagine that the gentleman you love –”
“I do not love him.”
“Very well, the gentleman you do not love, is sitting right at this table, and tell me exactly what you would say to his face.”
“If he sat there, I would tell him, ‘Go away.’”
Gerard, who had been flourishing his pen in preparation, set it down with a groan.
“And once he was gone,” one of her maids Floretta put in, “your highness would say, ‘Come back.’”
“Likely enough, you little minx. Now all of you be quiet, let me think. He pestered me to write, and I promised, so my honour is at stake. What lie can I give Gerardo to pass along to that fool?” She turned her head away, rested her noble chin on her half-clenched white hand, and sank into deep thought.

She was so lovely, statuesque, looking almost like some divine figure lost in lofty meditation, that Gerard forgot everything but his artist’s eye. He picked up his pen and began rapidly sketching that perfect profile on a spare sheet of paper. He was nearly done when the fair “statue” snapped her head around and caught him in the act.
“Nay, Signora,” he said, a little peevishly. “For heaven’s sake, do not shift your posture – it was perfect. See, you are almost finished.”

All eyes turned at once to the drawing, and everyone began chattering at once.
“How lifelike! And done in a minute – wait, I think her highness’s chin is just a little softer than that.”
“Oh, one small touch will fix that.”
“What a shame it is not coloured! I adore colour, nothing beats it. Black and white is so dull. And her highness has such lovely skin – take that away, and half her beauty is gone.”
“Quiet. Can you colour this, Ser Gerardo?”
“Ay, signorina. I am not very skilled at oils, that is where my friend Pietro shines, but in this small scale I can tint it so you would swear it was alive, if you have time to spare for such vanity.”
“Call this vanity? And as for time, it hangs on me like lead. Go get your colours right now – this instant, for the love of all the saints.”
“Nay, signorina, I need time to prepare them. I can come back tomorrow at this same hour.”
“So be it. And you, Floretta, see that he is let in at any hour. Oh! Wait, do not finish her head right now, leave it just as it is!”
“Forgive me, Signora, I was only going to prep the lines at home before I tint it. But I will leave it be. Now let us finish that letter.”
“What letter?”
“The one to Signor Orsini.”
“And do you think I will waste my time writing silly letters to that empty fool, who cares for me no more than he cares for the moon? Nay, not no care – I have just realised my true feelings. I hate him and despise him. Girls, I forbid you ever to mention that man’s name to me again, or I will whip you until the blood runs. You all know how hard I can hit when I am roused.”
“We do, we do,” they said, bobbing curtsies.
“Then do not tempt me.” Her eyes flashed for a second like a sharpened blade, before she turned back to Gerard all soft honey warmth. “Addio, Gerardo.” Gerard bowed and backed out of what he could not help but think of as a velvet tiger’s den.

He returned the next day to colour the portrait, and soon after that the princess commissioned a half-length portrait, then a full-length one. He found himself forced to set aside two hours every afternoon to draw and paint the famously beautiful, famously vain young noblewoman, who had a whole line of suitors begging for portraits of her. Suddenly Gerard’s income was growing steadily, and Margaret felt closer than ever, waiting for him back home.

It was Holy Thursday, and no work was permitted for the day. Fra Colonna and Gerard sat at a high window watching the religious processions wind past below. Their numbers, and the glowing pious ardour of the crowds, thrilled Gerard: the whole city, recently given over to ordinary worldly joys, seemed transformed by that deep devotion.

Before long, the Pope himself paced majestically past at the head of his cardinals, wearing a red hat, white cloak, and a capuchin of red velvet, riding a stunning white Neapolitan barb draped in red velvet fringed and tasselled with gold. A hundred fully armed horsemen rode behind him, lances held upright, the butts resting on their thighs. The cardinals all rode bareheaded – all but one, de Medicis, who rode right beside the Pope chatting to him like an equal. Every fifteen steps the Pope paused for one brief moment, raised his hand to bless the crowd, then moved on again.

Gerard and Colonna climbed down from their window, wound their way through side streets, and reached the portico of one of Rome’s seven great basilicas. The whole facade was hung with black cloth, and soon the Pope and his cardinals, who had entered the church by a different door, stepped out onto the steps holding torches, separated from the crowd by wooden barriers. A canon then read out a Latin papal bull, excommunicating several named people – most notably any princes who were keeping the Church from any of its temporal lands.
The awed ceremony made Gerard tremble, and the rest of the crowd trembled right along with him – but two of the cardinals ruined the whole effect, laughing openly and unreservedly the entire time.

Once the reading was done, the black cloth was stripped away to reveal bright, richly coloured hangings. The Pope blessed the assembled crowd, then tossed his torch down into their midst – and two of his cardinals did the same. Immediately a wild scramble broke out over the burning torches: people fought over them, tore them to pieces, competing so fiercely for small fragments of the sacred flame that many walked away with black eyes, bloody noses, and burnt fingers. While the crowd was caught up in that chaos, the Pope and his entire retinue withdrew peacefully.

Then a cry went up, and the crowd surged towards a square where a large open stage had been set up, with a group of priests praying on top. They rose, and with great ceremony pulled on bright red gloves. One of them knelt, and with every sign of deep reverence drew a square frame like a mirror out of a shrine. Inside was what looked like the faint impression of a human face.
It was the Verum Icon, the true image of Our Saviour’s face, taken at the very moment of His most terrible mortal agony. Received by every Christian there without a single grain of doubt, the sight moved every heart in the crowd. People threw themselves face down on the ground the second the priest held it high, cries of pity burst from every mouth, and tears stood in almost every eye. After a little while, the crowd rose, and the priest carried

Princess Claelia had ordered a full-length portrait of herself, and Gerard had gently suggested she commission his dear friend Pietro Vanucci to paint it.

But she waved the suggestion off at once. “There will be time enough to slight our Gerardo when his own work fails to content me.” Gerard, who knew full well his gifts lay in line and draughtsmanship far more than in rich colour mixing, then pitched her a different concept: he would render her not in oils, but as a Roman marble statue, laying on vellum such careful graduated tones no onlooker could fail to mistake the drawing for polished Carrara stone. She was curious at first, but demurred sharply when the enthusiast explained she would need to sit for him draped in the full tunic, toga, and leather sandals of antiquity.

“Why, I’d as lief sit for you in my smock,” she said, with unvarnished medieval frankness.

“Alas, signorina,” Gerard protested, “you have surely never marked the beauty of that ancient habit: so free, so ample, so simple, yet so noble, and made to suit your highness’s Roman features as no modern gown can. It will show off the shapely arm and hand Heaven gave you, that modern tight sleeves hide away from every eye.”

“So you can flatter just like all the rest, Gerardo? Very well. Give me time to think on it. Come on Saturday, and I will tell you yes or no.”

The week of respite she gained was spent in secret in her private chambers, stitching together the tunic and toga from soft, fine white linen, twisting this way and that before her full-length mirror to judge if the thousand-year-old garb suited her beauty well enough to justify its oddity.

Gerard was hurrying to that Saturday meeting when he stopped dead, rooted to the cobblestones by a bookshop window. His sharp calligrapher’s eye fell on an open copy of Lactantius laid out on the display. “That script is perfectly wrought, at any rate,” he thought. He stared a moment longer, and his blood ran cold. It was not written by hand at all. It was printed.

Gerard groaned out loud. “I am lost. My enemy is at the door. The printing press has come to Rome.”

He stepped into the shop, affecting casual indifference, and asked how long the new printing press had been in the city. The shopkeeper shook his head, laughing. “There is no such thing in Rome itself, messer. That Lactantius? It was printed up on the slopes of the Apennines.”

“What, did the printing press fall there out of the moon?” Gerard asked, bewildered.

“Nay, messer, it rose there from Germany,” the trader chuckled, pointing to the title page. Gerard leaned in eagerly, and read the fine print: *Opera et impensis Sweynheim et Pannartz Alumnorum Joannis Fust. Impressum Subiacis. A.D. 1465.*

“Will you buy it, messer?” the shopkeeper pressed. “See how even and fair the letters are. Few scribes left alive can match that hand, and it costs barely a quarter the price of a hand-copied manuscript.”

“I would take it gladly,” Gerard said sadly, “but my heart will not let me. Know that I am a calligrapher, and these pupils of Fust chase me across the whole world, snatching the bread out of my mouth. Yet I wish no ill to them. Heaven forbid.” He hurried out of the shop, his mind flying straight to Margaret. “Dear Margaret, we must lose no time. We must make our hay while the sun shines. One month more, and an avalanche of printed type will roll down those Apennine slopes to Rome, and lay waste every scribe who earns his living by his pen.” He broke into a near-run for the princess’s palace.

He was ushered into an apartment he had never entered before: small, but luxuriously furnished, with a little fountain splashing soft in its centre, and floors laid with panther skins tanned with their fur still on, so no footfall could make a sound. No door broke the opposite wall, only a heavy, draped tapestry of gold and crimson thread that marked the entrance to the princess’s private boudoir. He was left alone there so long he began to fidget, wondering if the maid had mistakenly shown him to a stranger’s chambers.

His doubts dissolved swiftly. A light step hurried behind the tapestry; it parted in the middle, and there stood a figure the old pagans would have knelt to worship. She was not quite Venus, nor quite Minerva: nobler than the goddess of love, softer and more womanly than Jupiter’s warrior daughter. Toga, tunic, sandals, not a single modern stitch on her, and her beauty, that was timeless, took Gerard’s breath away. He jumped to his feet, every inch the artist glowing with unfeigned delight. “Oh!” he cried, innocent in his rapture, and stared as if spellbound.

That unforced, unflattering admiration was the sweetest compliment Claelia had ever received. A soft rose blush tinted her cheeks, her eyes brightened, and her mouth curved in delicious, unguarded pleasure. When they had stood gazing at one another for several long moments, and she saw Gerard could do nothing but gape and gasp in awe, she spoke. “Well, Gerardo, you see I have turned myself into an antique monster for you.”

“A monster? I doubt old Fra Colonna would fall straight to his knees and adore your highness if he saw you thus attired.”

“Nay, I do not care to be adored by an old man. I would far rather be loved by a young one, of my own choosing.”

Gerard pulled out his pencils, laid a sheet of thick, sturdy paper over his canvas, and set to work. He was so absorbed in catching every perfect line of her drapery and the soft curve of her cheek that he had no mercy on his model, making her stand in one unbroken pose for nearly an hour. At last she spoke, faint and trembling. “Gerardo, I cannot stand thus a moment longer, not even for you.”

“Then sit and rest awhile, signora,” he said, immediately penitent.

“I thank you,” she sighed, sinking into a chair, her face going pale. Gerard was alarmed at his own thoughtlessness, scooped a handful of water from the fountain to dash on her face, but she lifted a white hand to stop him. “Nay, do not fling it at me. Press your wet palm to my brow, prithee.”

Gerard laid his damp hand timidly to her forehead, and she sighed in relief. “That is reviving. Again.” He did as she bade, then she asked him to ring the small hand bell on the table. A maid came, was sent to fetch a large fan from Floretta.

Floretta returned with the fan immediately, and no sooner had she stepped close to the princess than Claelia’s highbred nostrils flared wide, like a thoroughbred horse scenting a strange rival. “Wretch!” she cried, leaping up with a sudden burst of vigour. She seized Floretta’s hair in her left hand, and boxed her ears hard three times. The bare, strong arm left free by her loose toga rose and fell like a piston, heavy slaps resounding one after another on Floretta’s shoulders, until the last blow drove the sobbing, screaming maid stumbling out through the tapestry. Her wails echoed long after she was gone.

“Saints of Heaven!” Gerard cried, bewildered. “What harm has she done?”

“She knows full well. It is not the first time. The nasty toad! I will teach her to come near me stinking of musk-cat perfume.”

“Alas, signora, that seems but a small fault, methinks.”

“A small fault? Nay, it was a foul fault.” Then her whole demeanour shifted, melting into sudden humility and soft sweetness. “Are you wroth with me for beating her, Gerar-do?”

“Signora, it ill becomes me to lecture you. But methinks those whom Heaven appoints to rule others should first learn to rule themselves.”

“That is true, Gerardo. How wise you are, for being so young.” She called her other maid, pressed a small purse of coins into her hand, and bade her give it to Floretta, tell her Gerardo had interceded for her, and so she must be forgiven. Gerard blushed bright at her trust, and offered to resume work on the portrait.

“Not yet,” she said. “Beating that hussy has left me breathless. I will sit awhile, and you shall talk to me. I know you can talk, when it pleases you, as beautifully as you draw.”

“That would be easy enough,” Gerard said, fumbling for words.

“Then do it, Gerardo.”

Gerard was taken aback. “But signora, I know not what to say. This is most sudden.”

“Say your real mind. Say you wish you were anywhere but here.”

“Nay, signora, that would not be true. But I do wish one thing.”

“Ay? And what is that?” she asked, soft as a breeze.

“I wish I could have drawn you as you were beating that poor lass. You were awful, yet lovely. Oh, what a subject for a portrait of a Pythoness!”

“Alas! he thinks of nothing but his art.” She laughed, a little bitter. “And why do you make such a fuss over my beauty, Gerardo? You are far fairer than I am. You are more like Apollo than I to Venus. You have lovely hair, and lovely eyes—yet you do not know what to do with them.”

“Ay, but I do. To draw you, signora.”

“Ah, yes, you see my features clearly with them. But you cannot see what any Roman gallant would have seen in your place, long ago. Yet surely you have marked how very welcome you are to me, Gerardo?”

“I can see your highness is always far kinder to me than I deserve, a poor stranger in your land.”

“No, I am not kind, Gerardo. I have been cold to you, even rude, many times. And you are so simple you never saw the cause. Alas! I feared for my own heart. I feared I would become your slave, I who have always made others my slaves. Ah, Gerardo, I am unhappy. Ever since you came here, I have lived only for your visits. The day you are to come, I am bright and light. All the other days, I am listless, and long for them to end. You are not like the Roman gallants. You make me hate all of them. You are ten times braver to my eye, and wise, and scholarly, and you never flatter, never lie. I scorn any man who lies. Gerar-do, teach me your magic. Teach me to make you as happy at my side as I am at yours.”

Her voice dropped to a trembling whisper, half smothered with passion, and her white hand stole soft down his arm, resting on his wrist as light as a bird that might take flight at a single word. Gerard, who had no vanity, no experience of courtly love, wrapped up wholly in Margaret and his art, had never seen this confession coming, though it had built slowly before his eyes for months. He blushed from his hairline to his collar, and not for a single moment did his admiration for the regal beauty before him push the absent Margaret’s image from his mind. But this was a princess, wooing him with a grace and tenderness he had never dared imagine. How to reject her without wounding her, or worse? He trembled and stammered.

The siren saw his hesitation, and leaned in to soothe him. “Poor Gerardo, fear not. No harm will ever come to you under my protection. Will you not speak to me, Gerar-do mio?”

“Signora,” he muttered, trying to deprecate her. At that moment his eye, fallen in confusion, caught the shapely white arm coiled around his elbow, and he remembered exactly what that same lovely, powerful limb had done to Floretta only minutes before. He shivered.

“Alas!” the princess sighed. “I scare him. Am I so very terrible? Is it my Roman robe? I will take it off, and dress as I did when you first came to me. Do you remember? That was the day you came to write a letter to that barren fool Ercole d’Orsini. I hated him the very second I laid eyes on you, your pretty ways, your wise words. I thought I liked him well enough before that. Do you know how many times you have come to me since then? You do not, I see. You do not love me half as I love you. Eighteen times, Gerardo. And each time you are dearer. The day you do not come, it is night, not day, for Claelia. Speak to me, cruel boy. Have you a princess kneeling at your feet every day?”

“Signora,” Gerard faltered, “what can I say that is not better left unsaid? Oh, evil day that ever I came to this palace.”

“Nay, do not say that. It was the brightest day that ever shone on me, or even on you. I will make you confess that, before long, ungrateful one.”

“Your highness,” Gerard began, in a low, pleading voice.

“Call me Claelia, Gerar-do.”

“Signora, I am too young and too little wise to know how to speak to you without seeming blind, or ungrateful. But this I know: I would be both false and ungrateful, and the worst enemy you ever had, if I took advantage of this passing, mad fancy. Some ill spirit must have been allowed to afflict you with it. It is all unnatural, that a princess adorned with every grace should abase her affections on a poor churl like me.”

The princess drew her hand slowly back from his wrist, lingering for one soft, parting moment against his sleeve. “You fear my kinsmen’s daggers,” she said, half sad, half contemptuous.

“I no more fear their daggers than your maids’ bodkins,” Gerard said haughtily. “But I fear God and the saints, and my own conscience.”

“Truth, Gerardo, the truth. Hypocrisy sits ill on you. Princesses, while they are young, are not scorned for love of God, but for some other woman. Tell me who it is you love. If she is worthy of you, I will forgive you.”

“There is no such woman in Italy, on my soul.”

“Ah, so there is someone somewhere. Where?”

“In Holland, my native land.”

“Marie de Bourgoyne is fair, they say, but she is still but a child.”

“Princess, she I love is no noble. She is as common as I am. She is not so fair as you. But she is fair, and she is linked to my heart for ever by her virtues, by all the dangers and griefs we have borne together, for one another. Forgive me, but I would not wrong my Margaret for all the highest dames in Italy.”

Claelia leaped to her feet, standing over him, far more terrible than she had been when she beat Floretta: then her cheeks had been flushed red with anger, now they were pale as bone, and her eyes blazed with concentrated, noble fury. “You dare say that to my face, unmannered wretch!” she cried. “Was I born to be both insulted and scorned by the likes of you? Beware. We nobles brook no rivals. Choose now: the love of a Cesarini, or her hate. After all I have said and done to you, it must be one or the other, between us, to the death. Choose.”

Gerard looked up at her, towering over him in her flowing Roman toga, and felt like a puny mortal who had affronted an ancient goddess. He sighed deep, and said nothing. Perhaps that soft, patient sigh struck a tender chord in her unruly heart; or perhaps the tide of her fury ebbed as fast as it had risen. She sank languidly back into her seat, and hot tears began to stream fast down her cheeks.

“Alas! alas!” Gerard cried. “Weep not, sweet lady. Your tears accuse me, and I will soon weep for company. My kind patron, be yourself again. You will live to see how much better a friend I was to you than I seemed.”

“I see it now, Gerardo,” the princess said, wiping her eyes. “Friend is the right word. The only word that can ever pass between us. I was mad. Any other man would have taken advantage of my folly. You must teach me to be your friend, and nothing more.”

Gerard hailed that promise with joy, and quoted Cicero to her, telling her how godlike true friendship was, far rarer, truer, and more lasting than any romantic love, and even told her tales of his old friend Denys to prove he knew what real friendship was. She listened with her eyes half lidded, watching his face to read every corner of his character, to find his weak spot. At last she spoke, calm and collected. “Leave me now, Gerardo. Come back to me tomorrow, as you always do. You will find your lesson well bestowed.” She held out her hand to him; he kissed it, and left, pondering every strange turn of the interview, wondering if he had acted wisely.

The next day he was received with marked, cold distance. The princess stood before him as still and rigid as the marble statue he had first proposed to draw, and after a very short sitting, excused herself and dismissed him. Gerard felt the sharp chill, but told himself she was acting sensibly. The day after that, he found her surrounded by a crowd of vain young Roman nobles, all fawning over her and flattering her to the skies. They treated Gerard like a performing dog that could do a trick none of them could, and picked apart his portrait with a perfect mix of ignorance and insolence that made his cheeks burn bright red. Claelia watched his face, half lidded, demure, at every sharp little jab they threw, and the moment they left, she barred all of their names from her palace rolls, never to be received again.

The day after that, she met him alone, cold and silent. After standing as his model for a few minutes, she said, “You treated my guests with far less respect than was proper.”

“Did I,

Gerard dragged himself back to consciousness and to raw, unvarnished despair before his eyes even fluttered open. The acrid tang of fever herbs and leech’s poppy draught clung to his tongue, and every thud of his pulse sent a white-hot lancing pain through his skull. By the second day, he was raving, brain on fire, thrashing so hard the neighbors could hear his broken cries for Margaret through the thin oak walls. On the table hard by his bed, coiled like a stray pelt, lay his rich auburn hair, long as a woman’s, shorn off by the leech while he thrashed unaware.
Worse symptoms stacked on each other fast: the cold sweats, the glassy unseeing stare, the rattle in his chest that made the gossips huddle on the landing and cross themselves. On the fifth day, the leech snapped his satchel shut, shook his head at the landlady, and bade her make ready for the end. But the very same sunset, Gerard fell slack into a deep, unyielding sleep so still the maids thought he’d already drawn his last breath.
Most of the town said he would wake only to die. But an old gossip whose opinion carried weight — she’d nursed plague victims and battlefield wounded for thirty years — declared his young, hard-worn body might yet pull through, if only he could sleep twelve unbroken hours.
His old landlady cleared every last soul out of the room that instant, barred the door, and settled herself in the chair by his bedside. She vowed a wax candle to the Virgin for every hour he should sleep, lit the first, and watched.
He slept twelve hours. The good soul fell to her knees, weeping, and thanked Our Lady out loud.
He slept twenty-four hours. She began to fidget, checking his even breath every ten minutes, the little pile of burnt candle stubs piling up by the statue in the corner.
At the thirtieth hour, she sent a runner for the old nurse. “Thirty hours! Shall we wake him?”
The woman leaned over Gerard, inspected his half-parted lips, his soft damp palm, and shook her head. “Learned leeches would rouse him to prod at his tongue and scribble nonsense on their parchments, and be none the wiser. But we that be women know better than to meddle when bon Nature is doing the healing. When did sleep ever harm a racked brain or a torn heart?”
By the forty-eighth hour, word of the man who slept two full days straight leaked out, and they had to bar the stairwell to keep the gawking neighbors from crowding the sickroom. They let only two visitors pass: Fra Colonna, the gentle humanist friar, and his friend the gigantic, stolid Fra Jerome, who had sailed through a hundred North Sea storms at Gerard’s side. The two relieved the exhausted women, sitting silent by the bed: Colonna’s eyes glistened with tears as he gazed at his young friend, while Jerome, his rosary wrapped tight in his big calloused hand, watched Gerard as calmly as he had watched the towering waves the day they nearly drowned together.
At last, as the first pale streaks of dawn seeped through the room’s leaded window, the landlady nudged Fra Colonna’s elbow. He looked up. Gerard had opened his eyes, soft and slow, as if he had only been dozing by a cottage fire.
He stared, bewildered, for a long minute. He drew himself up a little in the bed, lifted a shaking hand to his head, and found his hair was gone, cropped close to his scalp. He spotted Colonna, and a flicker of old warmth crossed his face, a smile of quiet pleasure at seeing a friend. But halfway through the smile, the memory of Margaret’s death, of the cruel weeks he’d spent wandering before the news found him, crashed over him all at once. His face convulsed with anguish so sharp it looked like it might tear him apart. He gave a great, raw cry that rattled the window panes, and twisted to shove his face hard against the rough plaster wall.
His landlady wept aloud at the sight. She had been widowed young, she knew what it felt like to wake and remember the person you loved most would never walk through the door again. Fra Jerome began reciting canticles and prayers from his breviary, his deep voice low and steady. Gerard rolled himself tight in the bedclothes, as if he could hide from the world.
Fra Colonna stepped to his bedside, sniffling, and reminded him all was not lost. The divine Muses were immortal, he said. He must turn his affection to them; they would never betray him nor fail him like creatures of clay. The simple, good father could not finish his plea before his own emotion overcame him, and he hurried out of the room to compose himself.
Fra Jerome remained, his broad frame filling the doorway. “Young man,” he said, solemn as a judgment, “the Muses exist only in the brains of pagans and idle visionaries. The Church alone gives repose to the heart on earth, and happiness to the soul hereafter. Hath earth deceived thee, hath passion torn thy heart to rags? The Church opens her arms: consecrate thy gifts to her! The Church is peace of mind.”
He spoke the words and turned to leave before Gerard could reply.
“The Church!” Gerard screamed, leaping barefoot out of bed and shaking his fist at the friar’s retreating back. “Malediction on the Church! But for the Church I should not lie broken here, and she lie cold, cold, cold in the dirt of Holland. Oh, my Margaret! Oh, my darling! My darling! And I ran from thee the very last months thou hadst to live. Cruel! Cruel! The monsters around thee, they let thee die. Death never comes without signs. Those blind, selfish wretches saw not, or recked not — but I would have seen them, I that loved thee. Oh, had I been there, I had saved thee! I had saved thee! Idiot! Idiot, to leave her for a moment!”
He wept bitter, heaving sobs for a long time. Then all that grief curdled into white-hot rage, and he cried out so loud the rafters trembled: “The Church! For whose sake I was driven from her! My malison be on the Church, and the hypocrites that name it to my broken heart. Accursed be the world! Ghysbrecht the thief lives, and Margaret dies. Murderers, harlots, thieves thrive to grey old age. Only angels die. Curse life! Curse death! And whosoever made them what they are!”
Fra Jerome never heard the heretical words, only the roar of raw rage that echoed down the stairwell. It was a mercy. If he had heard them, he would have dragged his old shipmate to the forum stake to be burned with no more hesitation than he would have roasted a kid for his supper.
The landlady, who had followed Colonna down to the landing, heard the raised voice and hurried back up, frightened. She found Gerard yanking his best velvet doublet over his shoulders, tears still streaming down his face. She remonstrated with him.
“What avails my lying here?” he said, his voice hollow and bleak. “Can I find that which I seek beneath these sheets?”
“Saints preserve us! Art distraught again? What is it you seek, my poor lad?”
“Oblivion.”
“Oblivion, my little heart? Thou art far too young to talk of that.”
“Young or old, what else have I to live for?” He buckled on his fine leather belt. The good dame fussed, trying to stop him. “My pretty Gerard, know that it is Tuesday, not Sunday. Thou never wearest thy brave clothes on working days. Bethink thee.”
“What I did when she lived, I did. Now I shall do whatever erst I did not. The past is dead. There lies my hair, and with it my whole old way of life. I served one Master as well as I could. You see my reward. Now I’ll serve another, and give him a fair trial too.”
“Alas!” the woman gasped, turning pale. “What dark words are these? What new master is this whose service thou wouldst try?”
And with that horrible declaration on his lips, the miserable creature walked out of the house, his cap and feather set jauntily lopsided on his head, his fever-weak limbs wobbling under him, his face pale as ashes, all drawn and lined as if he had lived sixty years in the space of a few weeks.

A heavy, unrelenting dark cloud settled over Gerard’s once noble, bright spirit. His pure, unmatched love for Margaret had long been his guiding polar star across every hardship and strange land; now that star had been snuffed out, and he drifted adrift on a sunless, hopeless sea.

He did not only suffer despair: he burned with sharp, biting exasperation that every bit of his self-denial, fortitude, years of peril, and steadfast virtue had been not just wasted, but counterproductive. It gnawed at him ceaselessly that if he had stayed home lazy, selfish, and unadventurous, he would never have left Margaret unprotected, and she would still be alive. The two poisons of grief and fury raged together in his young blood, maddening him and eroding every moral boundary he had ever held. He threw himself fiercely into every available pleasure, and in 15th century Rome, pleasure of the kind that numbs pain was almost indistinguishable from vice. He chased wine, gambling, and loose company, anything that could grant him an hour of fevered excitement and a single moment of escape from his thoughts, flinging himself into these excesses the way a man tired of life might run headlong into enemy musket fire. The large sum of money he had saved carefully for Margaret’s future gave him endless means for debauchery, and he soon became the leader of the very band of reckless rakes he had once kept strictly at arm’s length.

His heart rotted alongside his morals. He snapped at his kind old landlady when she tried to offer gentle, well-meaning warnings to pull him back from the edge, and finally moved to a distant, unfamiliar quarter of the city entirely to escape all remonstrance and every last reminder of his old, diligent life. Weeks of this debauchery left his hand too unsteady to produce the fine, precise calligraphy he had once prided himself on, and his patience for quiet craft vanished as his lazy, indulgent habits took root. He abandoned writing entirely, and took to painting portraits instead – though he neglected that work too, the second his idle rakish companions knocked on his door to drag him out drinking. He waded deeper and deeper into foul, mirey waters, chasing the sorry, empty prize of total oblivion.

It serves no purpose to lay out every coarse, vice-ridden scene Gerard took part in at this lowest point. What matters is to state the plain, unvarnished truth: he had become a rake, a drunkard, one of the wildest, most unmoored young men in all Rome. Those who soften or slur the wickedness of the formerly good do no favours to truth, or to struggling sinners who deserve no false, sugar-coated fables to rob them of their chance at redemption. Gerard never did anything by halves, and he was not half-hearted in his self-destruction either.

His old well-meaning acquaintances gossiped about his downfall constantly. His former landlady begged Teresa, her friend, to help track him down, and Teresa passed the story on to her husband Lodovico, the streetwise swordsman, asking him to keep an eye out for the lost young painter. “You would remember his face, Lodovico mio?” she asked. “A man in my line of work never forgets a face,” he told her, “least of all a benefactor’s. But you know I almost never leave the house by daylight.” Teresa sighed. “How long will that go on?” “Till some rich hot-headed cavalier runs his sword through me,” he said grimly. “They will never let a poor man like me turn to an honest trade.”

Pietro Vanucci, the painter who had never handled prosperity well, had been kicked out of his old lodgings a short while prior for coming home at all hours of the night. He ran into Gerard on the street, greeted him like an old friend, and soon moved into Gerard’s new house of loose company. He brought with him a sharp, stunningly beautiful teenage apprentice named Andrea, who ground his colours, served as his model, and was as quick-witted as a needle. Pietro feigned great warmth and friendship for Gerard, who – every last trace of old gentle sentiment burnt out of him – accepted the affection coldly. Pietro was not just a libertine, but a bitter misanthrope and open atheist, and the two men moved through the city in a strange, mismatched pair.

One day, after Gerard had all but ruined his health, stripped the bloom off his once famous good looks, and run through most of his savings, Pietro organized a grand, absurd day trip: a cruise up the Tiber in a galley pulled by buffaloes. Lorenzo de’ Medici had imported these massive beasts to Florence only three years prior, and they were a total novelty in Rome. Nothing would satisfy Pietro, the newly wealthy beggar-on-horseback, but to be towed upriver by the strange brutes. Their rules for the party were simple: every rake must bring a handsome woman as his guest, and anyone who failed to bring a pretty companion would pay a fine. The man who brought the loveliest guest of all would be crowned with laurel and named a public benefactor.

The whole wild crowd gathered at the embarkation point – all except Gerard. They waited, first patiently, then with growing irritation. Pietro laughed it off. “I heard him say he forgot to find a fardingale for his lady,” he joked. “The good lad is hunting for a beauty fine enough to hold her own among all these peerless dames. Be patient, ladies, he has a hard task ahead of him!”

At last they spotted Gerard in the distance, walking arm in arm with a tall, striking woman. “She is certainly long enough,” one of the assembled ladies snarked, squinting at her from afar. “Mercy, look how big her strides are,” added another. “Of course she hurries,” Pietro excused her. “She is eager to join such fine company.” But the second the pair drew close, every taunt died on their lips. Gerard’s companion was a peerless beauty, who outshone the entire boatload the way the rising sun snuffs out all the stars. She was tall but perfectly proportioned, straight as an arrow yet supple as a young panther, her face a perfect oval, her forehead pale, her cheeks rich olive with warm blood glowing just under the surface, and her glorious eyes framed by thick, silken long eyelashes that looked capable of sweeping men’s hearts away by the handful. She had saucy, full red lips and teeth polished white as ivory.

All the women on the boat were visibly deflated by the sight of her, while the men went wild with delight, cheering and waving their caps. One over-excited man even knelt on the boat’s gunwale and swore she must be divine. His girlfriend promptly grabbed his hair and wrenched it, while the “goddess” gave him a playful little kick, and he toppled backwards flat onto his back. She stepped right over him without deigning to glance his way, and took the best seat right at the prow. Pietro Vanucci sat frozen, gawking at her with his mouth hanging open like a dead codfish.

The drover shouted commands to the buffaloes, the ropes tightened, and the galley lurched upriver. The women grumbled about the strange beasts, complaining their horns were terrifying, their nostrils were ugly gaping holes. One hot-headed young gallant jumped ashore, drew his sword, and began goading the buffaloes to make them run faster, ignoring the drovers’ shouts of protest. The big beasts only snorted and flicked their tails, no faster than before, making the whole boatload roar with laughter – until he jabbed the patriarch old lead bull. The massive beast spun instantly, ran its two long horns straight through the man’s doublet, and tossed him 20 feet through the air in a great parabola, until he splashed sitting upright, still waving his sword blindly, into the yellow murk of the Tiber.

The women screamed in shock, all except Gerard’s beautiful companion, who swore under her breath, seized the helm, and steered the galley out to pull the sputtering man back into the boat, dripping and confused. He stared around, peevish and bewildered. “I cannot make head nor tail of that,” he muttered, which set the whole party laughing harder than before. Gerard’s lady teased him that he was enjoying his natural element, and advised him to go back to pricking the buffaloes until his wits caught up, to work the riddle out as slowly as lawyers climb to heaven, and buffaloes climb the Tiber.

The assembled cavaliers praised her wit as loudly as they praised her beauty – all except Pietro, who now sat coiled up in the corner, his face half covered, two bright eyes twinkling with barely contained mirth as he never took his gaze off her. She did not spare him so much as a glance, except a casual, unremarking sweep of her lashes now and then, as if he was no more notable than the wooden benches under them.

The fun broke apart when the humiliated ladies, furious that every man’s attention was fixed on the new arrival, began muttering insults about her under their breath. The beautiful girl had none of the quiet tact to rise above it, and she snapped back openly. “Not a single one of you wears beauty that was given by Nature,” she announced, pointing rudely in one lady’s face. “All that paint you wear is sold in every shop: cerussa white lead for your skin, stibium kohl for your eyes, purpurissum red for your cheeks. I use those things too, bless you – but I never paint my face with them.” She went on to mock their dyed horse-tail hair, their padded bosoms, their absurdly tall wooden chopine platform shoes that turned little stunted dwarfs into apparent giants, and rattled off the crude local rhyme about them: “tall of wood, fat of rags, red of dye, white of lime.”

The ladies shrieked back insults, calling her rude and vulgar, saying her figure was shaped like a coal shovel. Gerard, woken out of his dark, brooding reverie, told his companion sharply to hold her tongue, and stop being insolent. “The grave will close over your beauty just as it has over far fairer women than you,” he said. She pouted, and whispered back that she had only done it to make him laugh, that she saw how sad and distracted he was, and if she was really the great lady everyone took her for, she would do anything to chase his grief away. Gerard sighed, shook his head, and stroked her jet black hair as one might pat the head of an affectionate loyal dog.

Just then, a large galley drifting down the river got tangled in their tow ropes. Seated under a rich canopy on that passing vessel was Princess Claelia, attended by a whole retinue of gallants and servants. Gerard looked up, saw her, and his face flushed bright red with shame as he snatched his hand away from Andrea’s head. He remembered, not three months prior, he had turned down her passionate, refined, illicit offer of love – a temptation so great it might have melted an anchorite – just to stay loyal to Margaret. Now here he was, wallowing in this gutter of vice, ashamed to be seen by her.

Two of the Roman ladies, who had long suspected “the beauty” was no woman, seized a lapful of almonds and tossed the whole handful into her lap on a whim. She clamped her knees tightly shut by instinct, to catch the nuts before they fell through her legs. A woman, after all, would spread her knees wide to catch nuts in her apron. “Got you!” the lady who threw the nuts cried. “You are a man, or a boy! Confess it!” Andrea only casually cracked an almond between his teeth and said calmly, “They have found me out, Ser Gerard.”

Pietro burst into roaring, uncontrollable laughter. He announced that the “goddess” was none other than his 17-year-old apprentice Andrea, who ground his colours and posed for his paintings. All the men were furious they had been pranked, but the women swarmed around the beautiful boy, cooing over his eyes, his eyelashes, his perfect teeth, his rosy cheeks, vowing no one would harm a hair on his head – lavishing all their adoration on him to get revenge on their men for gawking at him all afternoon.

But Gerard was not laughing. The sight of Princess Claelia had torn his old, half-healed wound wide open. The brief, numbing fumes of his weeks of vice cleared away entirely. His health was broken, his savings almost gone, his old diligence, his innocence, his piety, all the balms that might have soothed his grief were thrown away forever. The gulf between him and the Margaret he loved was wider than any grave. The hot, wild fit of despair wore off, and the cold, heavy, empty despair settled in. He turned his back on all his rakish companions, wandered the streets alone, drank wine alone to paralyze the dark, gnawing remorse eating at his chest, and lay for hours stony-eyed and woebegone among the crumbling ruins of old Roman temples – more broken, more ruined, than any of the ancient stones around him.

At last, solitude, that dark, siren foe of diseased minds, pushed him to the final terrible edge. He wandered the banks of the dark Tiber at night, staring down at the slow, quiet black water, his disgust for the idea of slipping beneath its surface fading more with every passing day. There, he thought, was peace. There was escape. His old landlady, Teresa, Lodovico – all the people who cared for him – had no idea where he was, no idea how close he was to that final, fatal madness. There was no friendly voice, no kind smile, to step between him and the dark choice he was weighing.

But there was a pair of eyes fixed on him. Every step he took, every wandering hour, every return to his hovel, was tracked. It was not the eye of a friend. It was the eye of a mortal enemy, who meant to destroy him for good.

Beneath tapestries stitched with silver and gold thread, in a chamber draped with heavy crimson velvet, the polished stone floor was thickly strewn with striped wolf pelts and dappled leopard furs. A noble lady sat there, arms stretched out stiff before her, hands half clenched, every line of her face matching the restlessness of her posture: her cheeks flamed then blanched in sharp turns, one foot tapping a rapid, agitated rhythm against the soft fur at her feet.

At last the heavy velvet curtain over the doorway was drawn aside by a trembling domestic. The lady’s brow flushed hot at the sight. The maid leaned in, voice a whisper thick with awe: “Your Highness, the man you sent for has come.”

The lady bade her admit him, then snatched up a small black velvet mask and fixed it to her face. In a single heartbeat all colour drained from her cheeks, and the stark, uncanny contrast between the black mask and her marble-pale skin seemed ghostly, heavy with unspoken threat.

A man stepped inside, bowing and scraping so low his forehead nearly brushed the floor. He was the sort of unremarkable figure that vanished in any crowd: close-cropped hair, a round unmemorable head, plain but well-kept wool clothes, features neither handsome nor harsh enough to draw a second glance. Nothing about him stood out at all, save for a pair of singularly restless, sharp eyes that darted over every corner of the room in an instant. After a dozen more profuse bows, he planted himself opposite the lady and waited, silent, for her to speak.

“They have told you why you are summoned?” she said, low and tight.
“Yes, Signora.”
“And those who negotiated with you agreed on the full sum you are to receive?”
“Aye, Signora. The full price buys the greater vendetta, unless of your grace you choose to settle for the lesser.”
“I do not follow your meaning,” the lady said.
“Ah! This must be the Signora’s first time, then. The lesser vendetta, my lady, is the death of the body only. We track our mark as he leaves church, or catch him unawares in some innocent quiet hour, and strike clean. The greater vendetta? We lie in wait, seize him hot from some unconfessed, unrepented sin, and so slay his soul as well as his flesh. Though that kind is less in demand these days than it was a few years back.”

“Man,” she said, her voice sharpening, “silence his tongue for good. Let his treasonous, lying heart beat no more. His soul is no affair of mine, I have no grudge against it.”

“So it shall be, Signora. Those who sent word to me knew neither the man’s name, nor his face, nor where he lodges. From whom am I to learn these things?”
“From my own lips.”

At that, the bravo showed the first flicker of true anxiety he had yet betrayed, and entreated her to speak with great care and perfect exactness on this part of the business.
“Fear not for me,” she said. “Listen close. He is a young man, tall of stature, with auburn hair and dark blue eyes, and an honest face so guileless it would deceive a saint. He lodges in Via Claudia, at the corner house belonging to the glover. There are only three men lodging under that roof: him, a short, dark-visaged painter, and a slim young boy. The man who betrayed me is a stranger here, fair of face, and taller even than you are.”

The bravo drank down every word. “That is all I need,” he said.
“Stay,” she cut in. “Does he haunt any secret, out-of-the-way place where you might strike without being seen? My spies report he has taken to wandering the banks of the Tiber after dusk of late, no doubt to meet his light-o’-love, the girl who dares call me her rival. Slay him even there! Let that smooth, heartless, insolent traitor’s little paramour stumble across his corpse, and learn what it means to cross a princess.”

“Calm yourself, Signora. He will never betray another lady again.”
“I do not count on that,” she snapped. “He wears a sword, and he can wield it. He is young, and stubborn, and resolute.”
“Neither of those will save him.”
“You are so sure of your skill? What weapons do you carry for such work?”

The bravo held up a heavy steel gauntlet. “We strike with such force we must guard our own hand, lest we break our bones. That is our mallet, to stun our mark before he can cry out.” Then he undid the laces of his doublet, and showed her the glint of fine chain mail sewn into the lining beneath. Finally he laid a long, glittering stiletto down on the oak table with a flourish.

The lady shuddered at first, but then she reached out with her white soft hand, lifted the blade, and tested its sharp point against the tip of her finger.
“Beware, madam,” the bravo warned.
“What, is the edge poisoned?”
“Saints forbid! We do not steal lives like cowards. We take them with steel, not drugs or potions. But the blade is newly ground, and I feared for the softness of your Highness’s fair skin.”

“His skin is as white as mine,” she murmured, a sudden flicker of pity crossing her face. It died out as quickly as it had come. “But his heart is black as soot. Tell me, am I not right to rid the world of a traitor who slanders me, who spurns my favour for common trash?”
“The Signora may settle that account with her confessor,” the bravo said, with a small deferential shrug. “I am no more than a tool in noble hands, same as my stiletto there.”

The princess did not seem to hear him. “Oh, how I could have loved him! Loved him to the death, as fiercely as I hate him now. Fool! He will learn what it means to trifle with princes, to spurn their favour then fawn for it, to prefer the dregs of the town to one of royal blood, to make me a laughingstock for gossips.” She lifted her head sharply. “Why loiter here? Go! Avenge me at once.”

“By custom, Signora, half the sum is paid beforehand.”
“Ah, I forgot,” she said, pushing a heavy leather purse across the table at him. “Your revenge is bought. This is more than half. When the blow is struck, return for the rest.”
“I shall see you again very soon, Signora.” He bowed himself out, scraping and bobbing, until the curtain fell shut behind him.

Left alone, the princess burned with the heat of unspent jealousy, mortified pride, and the gnawing terror of public exposure—for no blemish had ever stained her reputation before she set eyes on Gerard. She sat exactly where the bravo had left her, mask still fixed to her face, arms held straight out before her, the nails of her clenched hands digging deep into the oak tabletop. So sat the fabled Sphinx of old, silent and terrible; so sits a tigress robbed of her cub.

Yet as soon as the assassin was gone, a cold chill crept over her. Moody, heavy misgivings swelled in her chest, the first faint precursors of a remorse that would come too late to do any good.

Gerard and Margaret were souls born far ahead of their time. The princess before us was the true unalloyed medieval noble: proud, amorous, vindictive, quick to give charity, quick to act the fool, sharp-witted when she wished, impulsive, unprincipled, and ignorant as the dirt beneath her shoes. Power is the curse of such a creature. If she had been forced to carry out her own crimes, the weakness of her frayed nerves would have balanced the violence of her passions, and her threats would have rung far louder than any blow she could ever have struck. But power puts the tools of violence into the hands of weak, furious women: male agents, trained for murder. The effect is as terrible as that combination is unnatural. And in this very moment, that combination was sharpening an assassin’s dagger for a poor, forsaken wretch who was even then standing on the riverbank, meditating his own suicide.

Two days after the harrowing scene we have already recounted, Gerard wandered listlessly through one of Rome’s filthiest, most ramshackle back streets, its cobblestones slick with stale runoff and its overhanging eaves draped with tattered laundry. A sudden, roiling thunderstorm burst overhead, great booming cracks of thunder shaking the facades of the mean little houses, and he ducked for shelter in a low-ceilinged, smoke-choked tavern that reeked of sour wine and tallow fumes. He called for a cup of rough local red, and as the rain lashed the windows hard enough to rattle their wobbly panes, he drank cup after cup until his thoughts blurred into a thick, dull haze, and he dozed off with his elbows propped on the scarred pine table, his head pillowed on his arms.

In time the room filled with more patrons, their raucous banter, clinking tankards, and shouts for more wine slowly rousing him from his stupor. That was when he caught the low murmur of two men huddled at the table directly beside him, speaking so quietly no other guest could pick out their words. One was clearly a pardoner, his tunic pinned with a cheap tin papal seal and his satchel bulging with supposed relics on his hip. The other, by his neat, modest, mended clothing, might easily have passed for an honest small tradesman—but he had slouched his broad felt hat so far down over his brows that no one could see a scrap of his face save for his coarse, unkempt beard: the classic telltale mark of a man who shuns the gaze of both upright citizens and the city watch.

The pair were haggling openly in the unholy market of pre-forgiven sin, a common transaction of the era that saw men purchase signed indulgences in advance, guaranteed to wipe clean any crime they chose to commit later, no penance, no judgment required. The man in the slouched hat grumbled loudly that the price of pardons had risen so high soon poor, working men would be locked out of heaven entirely. The pardoner flatly denied the claim. “Indulgences have never been cheaper for sensible folk who sin by the market, like reasonable creatures. If you are fool enough to pick out some crime the Pope has publicly denounced, blame your own stubbornness, not me!”

To prove that every man but the absolute dregs of society could afford some form of pre-purchased absolution, he unfurled a crumpled parchment list of official prices, reading the figures off in a low, quick murmur. It is a shocking, unflinching document that cannot be reproduced fully here, nor could any truncated version do justice to its warped priorities: any scholar may find the full text in any major archival library of the era. Suffice it to say that the pardon for murdering an ordinary layman cost a tiny fraction of the price tagged for many petty, trivial offenses most modern readers would never dream of ranking as a greater sin than taking an innocent man’s life.

The haggling wrapped up shortly after a few tiny concessions from both sides: silver changed hands, the man in the hat tucked the crumpled indulgence into the lining of his tunic, and he walked away holding guaranteed pre-forgiveness for the “removal” of one unspecified layman. Neither of them ever once spoke the word assassination, framing the whole sordid transaction as mundanely as one might haggle over a sack of grain.

All of it buzzed in Gerard’s muzzy ears, but he never lifted his head from the table, listening stupidly, too numbed by grief and wine to feel anything but faint, distant disgust. Only when the pair rose and separated to leave did he half-raise his head, glowering at the retreating back of the man who had bought his pre-pardon for murder. “If Margaret was alive,” he muttered thickly under his breath, “I’d seize you by the throat and throttle you where you stand, you cowardly stabber. But she is dead. Dead. Dead. Let the whole world rot and die. It is nothing to me, so long as I am the first to go.”

When he stumbled back to his lodgings later that night, soaked through to the bone, he barely registered the figure in the slouched hat pacing briskly back and forth on the opposite side of the road, keeping a careful eye on his doorway. His grief had hollowed him out so completely that not even a clear, lurking threat could pierce the fog of numb despair that had wrapped itself around his whole being.

Two nights after those events, Pietro Vanucci and Andrea lingered at the supper table, waiting for Gerard. The trencher of warm spiced bread and roasted chestnuts had gone cold, the light red wine in their cups had turned flat, and Pietro’s patience frayed thin as the edge of an old vellum manuscript when the bell in the piazza tolled past nine o’clock. At last he snapped at Andrea to trudge up to Gerard’s chamber, desperate for the slim chance the younger man had slipped in unobserved and curled up asleep without announcing himself.

Andrea shrugged his broad shoulders, huffed under his breath, and obeyed. He returned empty of Gerard, but clutching a crumpled scrap of paper. Andrea could not read in the formal, scholar’s sense the men of their trade were trained in, but his eye was sharp as a point of a stylus: he had seen Gerard scrawl Pietro Vanucci’s name at the foot of so many small notes left on their shared workbench that he spotted the familiar looping script at once. “That’s for you, I trow,” he said, puffing out his chest proud of his clever guess.

Pietro snatched the scrap and read it out loud to Andrea, lacing every line at first with his usual dry, sardonic tone:
“‘Dear Pietro, dear Andrea, life is too great a burden.’
‘So ’tis, my lad,’” Pietro jested, “‘but that is no reason to tarry abroad past supper time. Supper is not a burden.’
‘Wear my habits!’
‘Said the poplar to the juniper bush, take my cast-offs when I’m gone,’” he chuckled, before his grin began to falter.
“‘And thou, Andrea, mine amethyst ring; and me in both your hearts a month or two.’
‘Why, Andrea?’” he said, quieting now, as a cold prickle ran down his spine.
“‘For my body, ere this ye read, it will lie in Tiber. Trouble not to look for it. ’Tis not worth the pains. Oh unhappy day that it was born oh happy night that rids me of it.
Adieu! adieu!
The broken-hearted Gerard.’”

“It’s nothing but a sorry jest from that peevish rogue,” Pietro blustered, but his cheeks were pale as unmarked parchment, and his teeth chattered so hard his words nearly rattled apart. Andrea wasted no time on pretense: he wailed so loud the whole household echoed with his cries, startling apprentice boys from their benches and maids from the kitchen fire. “O, miserable day! O, calamity of calamities! Gerard, my friend, my sweet patron! Help! help! He is killing himself! Oh, good people, help me save him!” He tore out the front door bareheaded, screaming his plea to every passerby on the cobblestone street, begging every good Christian to stop and lend a hand.

A small crowd gathered fast, but none would move. Trudge down to the Tiber after dark? No, that was no one’s business. No one could name exactly where he might have waded in. It was a fool’s errand, and worse: everyone knew the river banks after sundown were thick with ghosts of all the poor souls who had drowned themselves there, and to walk them after dark was to call ill luck down on your own head. Only a lackey who had loitered across the street for hours, unseen, stepped forward and said he would go with Andrea. That small show of courage shamed three or four of the younger idlers in the crowd to tag along.

The small band set off for the river. The lackey, who was a secret spy for Princess Claelia, plied Andrea with questions as they walked, and Andrea, sobbing so hard his words stumbled, told him of Gerard’s quiet, brooding moods of late, how he would stare out the window at the Tiber for hours on end without speaking a single word. The moment they rounded the last street corner and hit the river’s cold, sharp breeze, thick with the smell of mud and moving water, every voice went dead silent. The moon hung high and clear in a cloudless sky, silvering the ripples of the Tiber, and the crunch of their boots on the gravel bank sounded loud and ominous against the still, quiet night.

Presently they hurried around a sharp river bend and nearly ran straight into a man. He stopped, irresolute, at the sight of them. His hair was bare, dripping, glistening like strands of glass in the moonlight, and every step he took left a dark wet puddle on the stones: his clothes were soaked through to the skin. “Here he is!” one of the young men cried, who had never seen Gerard before. The stranger panicked instantly, turned on his heel, and fled as fast as his water-heavy legs could carry him.

They gave chase at full tilt, Andrea leading the pack, the princess’s lackey right at his heels. Andrea was fast gaining on the fugitive, but the man twisted sharp up a narrow, alley so small Andrea could not check his own momentum and skidded right past its mouth. By the time the rest of the party skidded to a halt behind him, the stranger had vanished into the labyrinth of twisting, unmarked lanes that crisscrossed that quarter, known only to people who lived every inch of them. It was useless to chase further.

They trundled back to the spot where they had first encountered the dripping man, to find Pietro waiting there, shaking his head. “That was not Gerard,” he told them plainly. “Wrong height, wrong face, I never laid eyes on that man in my life.”

“Are ye verily sure?” the others protested. “He was soaked through from the river. Why, in the saints’ names, did he flee at our approach?”

But the lackey cut in before they could bicker further. “See the wet prints he left all down the path,” he said. “Let us track them back to the water’s edge, to make certain Gerard is not there.” The group agreed, and followed the dark wet marks easily for fifty yards, only to find they veered sharp away from the river, straight for the heavy oak gates of a grim, shadow-shrouded monastery, its stone walls towering high overhead like a dark secret. Andrea spotted a second set of wet prints branching off the path, however, leading straight back toward the Tiber, and they followed those until they reached the very edge of the bank, where a whole bucketful of river water had evidently dripped off the fugitive’s clothes.
