They found a fisherman who lived in a hut not far off, paid him liberally with copper coins, and promised him a purse full of gold if he dragged every stretch of the Tiber up and down that bank with his nets, searching for Gerard’s body. The rest of the party ran up and down the shore screaming his name, but the river flowed on calm and voiceless, holding Gerard’s fate and a thousand other strange, dark secrets tight behind its glassy surface. Suddenly Andrea gave a sharp cry of hope, and sprinted back to the house, only to return half an hour later, wringing his hands, his face streaked with tears. He had checked every tavern, every friend’s house, every shadowed nook Gerard was known to frequent, and found nothing.

“What is the hour?” the lackey asked, his voice grave.

“Four hours past midnight,” someone answered.

“My pretty lad,” the lackey said solemnly to Andrea, “go say a mass for thy friend’s soul. For he is not among living men.”

Dawn broke pink over the distant hills, and Andrea and Pietro dragged their exhausted, aching bodies back home, heartsick and hollow. The days rolled on after that, as silent and unyielding as the Tiber itself, and never once yielded a single clue as to what had become of Gerard.

It would have been far stranger still if the local men lingering on the riverbank that evening, armed with nothing but vague guesses and the faint, half-erased smudges of footprints in the damp grass, had ever guessed what had unfolded there. The event that had just played out on that very spot was, taken all together, something almost without parallel in the whole recorded history of mankind—perhaps to remain unmatched for all ages to come. It shall be told plainly, a few words from me first, and then the rest straight from the mouth of one who stood in the thick of it.

When Gerard had finished scrawling his brief, bitter final adieu to his friends Pietro and Andrea, he slipped away down to the river as dusk bled purple over the water. He had gone about his errand with that cold, dogged resolution common to people who have set their hearts on self-destruction and will not be turned aside. He stuffed every last silver groat and copper farthing he owned into the pockets of his tunic, heavy weights to drag him straight down to the riverbed, no chance of floating back to the world he hated. Thus laden, he hurried to the stretch of stream he had marked out days before: a lonely, untrafficked bend, far from the washerwomen’s stepping stones and the fishermen’s mooring posts.

There are people, especially women, who hover on riverbanks half-hoping someone will spot them and step in to save them. But Gerard scanned every shadow only to make sure no one was there to stop him. To his sharp irritation, he spotted a single figure leaning against the mouth of a dark alley, watching him. He affected to stroll idly away, waited a few minutes, then circled back to his intended spot. Lo, the same man had drifted out of a side street, loitering casually right between him and the water.

“Is he watching me? Can he possibly know what I came here for?” Gerard thought. “Impossible. I have no enemy alive who would care what I do.” He strode briskly off, walked two blocks over, made a wide detour and came back a second time. The man had vanished. But when Gerard turned in a full circle to confirm he was truly alone, there he was, a few yards behind him, pretending to kneel and fasten his bootlace. The moonlight glinted cold off a steel gauntlet peeking out from the edge of the stranger’s cloak. This is an assassin, Gerard realized.

Strangely, it never once crossed his mind that he was the man’s intended target. He had no idea he had made a foe in the world. He walked straight up to the waiting bravo, face tight with desperate eagerness.
“Good friend,” he cried, clutching the man’s wrist, “sell me the use of thy arm! One single stroke, that is all I ask. Look—here is every coin I own, take all of it!” He forced the crumpled, heavy handful of silver and copper into the assassin’s free palm. “I beg of thee, do one act of mercy tonight, and rid me of this hateful, worthless life!” Even as he spoke, he fumbled open the laces of his doublet and bared his gaunt, pale breast to the blade he expected to meet.

The bravo stared back at him, frozen, as if stunned into immobility.
“Why do ye hesitate?” Gerard shrieked, his despair curdling into rage. “Hast no pity at all? Is it such a great labor to lift thine arm and strike? Is it because I have no gold to give thee, only this paltry change? Coward! Thou art only fit to stab men in the back, never face one eye to eye and strike! Go on then—turn thy head, hold thy tongue, and I will do the work myself!” With a snarl of pure contempt, he turned and ran full tilt for the dark current, throwing himself headfirst into the cold, churning water before the other man could move. The last sound on his lips as he went under was a single soft cry: “Margaret!”

The heavy, resounding splash jolted the bravo out of his stupor. He let out a sharp, strangled cry of his own, ran to the edge of the bank, and plunged straight into the icy river after the man he had been sent to kill.
What follows will be told in the assassin’s own words.

A woman carries her own quiet, unspoken troubles, just as a man does—and we male scribes rarely ever do more than trace the barest outline of the griefs that belong to the other sex. We must trust the sharp, gentle intuition of women readers to step in and fill the soft, raw, unwritten spaces between our cold sparse lines. So too have I marked, rather than fully described, every hardship Margaret Brandt endured up to that fateful day when she stepped over Eli’s threshold as an enemy, read her sweetheart’s long-lost letter, and left it bound to their household as a friend. Now the hardest trial a woman can face drew near, and Gerard was leagues away, across the Alps, no word of him reaching her for months.

She rarely leaned into Eli’s sudden new favour, always ready with a gentle, plausible excuse to turn down his invitations to stay long in his home. She never breathed a word of the true reason: two men lodged under that roof, whose faces made her blood run cold the moment they came into sight. She had read unmasked wickedness and smouldering hatred in their stares, caught furtive, secret signals they passed between each other when they thought no one was watching. She preferred to receive Catherine and her daughter in her own small cottage, where no ill wish could seep through the walls. Catherine came to visit her every single day, her whole world wrapped up in the coming birth. She was one of those sturdy, warm Dutch women whose whole calling seems to be bearing and rearing children, the sort who, once their own brood is half-grown, hover around every young expectant mother they know clucking like a mother hen, as if they can multiply their care for little ones by proxy. It was that very instinct that made her badger Eli until he agreed to return to his work in Tergou, leaving her behind in Rotterdam to tend Margaret.
“The poor lass hasn’t a single soul around her who knows the first thing about tending a lying-in woman,” she argued. “What use are those two rough soldiers you leave hanging around the house? Why, that sort of folk ought to be shown the door the second a time like this comes round.”

That arrangement was the greatest comfort Margaret could have asked for. Poor girl, as the days drew near, her anxiety grew sharp: she was half-convinced she would die in childbed, and Gerard would not be there to hold her hand.

But life balances its weights, does it not? The grinding poverty, the burden of tending her helpless blind father that had cost her so many sleepless, weary nights of struggle, now served her well. Adversity’s hard iron hand had forced her to fight off the heavy, weak lassitude that fell on wealthier women of her station when they carried a child, keeping her on her feet spinning, tending the cottage, working right up to the very end, just as Catherine had advised her to.

And so, one soft golden evening, as the sun dipped low over the Rotterdam rooftops and gilded the surface of the canals, she lay weak as water, spent but whole, a tiny warm face tucked at her side, the bright, soft heaven of new motherhood opening up before her.

Catherine noticed tears rolling down her cheek. “Why ever are you weeping, my sweet lass? All of a sudden, when all is well?”
“He is not here to see it,” Margaret whispered.
“Ah, well, never you mind,” Catherine soothed her. “He’ll be home long before that little one is weaned. The good Lord has been kinder to you than any woman alive, hasn’t he? And think, it could have been a girl — why, my own Kate swore she was carrying a girl the whole time she was in labour, and out popped the bonniest, heaviest bouncing boy in all Holland! Praise the saints for that, eh?”

“Ay, mother,” Margaret said, wiping at her eyes with a tired smile. “I’m a selfish, ungrateful wretch to cry. I bore it well enough, him being gone through all my hard, sad days. But oh — it feels so cruel, that he cannot share this joy. Gerard! My dear, dear Gerard, come to me, I beg you!” She stretched out her thin, feeble arms towards the empty air, as if she could reach him across hundreds of miles.

Catherine bustled around the room adjusting blankets, sorting the swaddling clothes, turning her face away from Margaret so the girl wouldn’t see her own tears, pricked raw by the tenderness of that cry that echoed exactly how she had once called out to her own absent son years before.

When she turned back a moment later, she found Margaret staring at her, eyes wide and strange.
“Did you not hear that?” Margaret asked, quiet.
“No, my lamb. Hear what?”
“I called out to Gerard, just now.”
“Ay, ay, I heard you do that, lass.”
“Well. He answered me.”

Catherine tsked softly, coming over to smooth her hair. “Hush, now, don’t say such things. You’re tired, your wits are wandering a little after your labour.”
“Mother, as sure as I lie here with his boy at my breast,” Margaret said, earnest, no trace of delirium in her voice, “I heard his voice, clear as day, call ‘Margaret!’ It wasn’t his happy laugh, though, the way he usually says my name. But that must just be the distance, right? All voices sound sad, stretched thin across miles and miles. Why are you not smiling, my sweet? I have never felt so happy in all my life, I think. It feels like I never knew pain or care at all, before this night.” She turned her soft gaze back to the little sleeping face beside her, drinking in every tiny feature in silent rapture.

That very same night, half across Europe, Gerard threw himself into the cold, dark waters of the Tiber. And at the exact hour that Margaret heard his voice call her name, he cried out loud in the grip of death and utter despair: “Margaret!”

Let those who can explain that strange, unbreakable bond between two souls make sense of it. I cannot.

Within the rough-hewn stone guest chamber of a Dominican convent lay a lone stranger, his frame wracked by successive, violent bouts of nausea that had finally ebbed, leaving him so weak he could barely lift his lids—just as Margaret had lain, helpless and fevered, that terrible night back in the Dutch lowlands. A massive oak fire blazed on the wide hearth, and beside its glowing embers hung the patient’s water-soaked clothing. A giant of a friar sat by his bedside, reading pious collects aloud from his breviary, the soft rolling Latin cutting through the crackle of flame. The stranger, Gerard, eyed him fitfully, seeming to listen at intervals, while at others he would squeeze his eyes shut and let out faint, ragged moans.

The monk knelt then, pressing his forehead flat to the cold stone floor, and prayed long and earnestly for the man on the cot. When he rose, he bade him farewell. “Day breaks over the city walls,” he said. “I must go prepare for matins.”
“Good Father Jerome, before you leave—how came I to be here?”
“By the hand of Heaven. You flung away God’s precious gift of life, and He reached out to give it back to you. Mark this: you have tested the world, and found only its bitter gall. Now test the Church. The Church is peace. Pax vobiscum.”
He was gone. Gerard lay back, drifting through confused, wondering thoughts, until his exhausted frame gave way and he slipped into a shallow doze.

When he woke, a new nurse sat beside his bed: a layman, whose small, restless eyes were a world away from Friar Jerome’s calm, majestic gaze. The man leaned in, eager to ask after his health.
“Very, very weak,” Gerard whispered. “Messer, have I not seen you somewhere before?”
“I hope you hold no grudge for my gauntlet blow!” the other replied, with no small measure of anxiety. “I had no choice but to strike you, or the both of us would be fathoms deep in the Tiber right now.”

Gerard stared at him, bewildered. “You are the one who saved me? How?”
“Ah, signor, I was on the Tiber banks that night on an errand I need not name. You came straight up to me, begging me drive my dagger through your heart. But before I could oblige you—ay, even as you spoke—I recognized you for the young gentleman who dived into a wild North Sea storm to save my wife Teresa and our baby from drowning.”
“Teresa’s husband?” Gerard breathed, his face draining of color. “And you are an assassin?”
“At your service,” the man shrugged. “Now, Ser Gerard, the next thing I knew you’d hurled yourself straight into the Tiber, screaming at me to keep back. Any other man on God’s earth, I’d have let him drown. I hold no love for the rest of the world, let them all hang on one rope or sink in the same river for all I care. But when you went under, crying out the name ‘Margaret’? My own heart screamed ‘Teresa’ right back. How could I ever look my wife in the face again if I let the man who saved her die the very same death she almost perished in? So I dived in after you, and lucky for both of us I swim as easy as a duck. You, determined to meet your end, grabbed at me to drag us both down, so I swam clear, and—forgive me for the rudeness—clouted you hard on the nape of the neck with my steel gauntlet till you lost your senses. The current was strong, and it was all I could do to drag your limp, water-heavy body to the bank. I slung you over my back, heading for my own hovel, thinking Teresa would nurse you back and be pleased I’d done a good turn for once. But not far from this monastery, that giant holy friar met us, asked what had befallen you, and recognized your face straight away. Said his brethren had heard tales of the young clerk from Holland, that the convent had far better warmth, food and care than my cottage could ever offer. We struck a deal: I get to come visit you once a day, no questions asked. That is how you came to be here.”

The man the world called a cutthroat fixed Gerard with a strange, soft look of sincere affection and interest. Gerard did not meet his gaze. He felt a cold prickle down his spine, as if a venomous snake had curled up at the foot of his bed. He shut his eyes tight.
“Ah, you would sleep,” the assassin said eagerly, taking the hint. He tiptoed for the door, promising to return every day.

Gerard lay still, eyes closed, not sleeping, his mind reeling. He had tried to throw his life away, and Heaven had sent a hired killer to fish him out of the river? He had cursed God, spat at the world, defied every holy truth he had ever been raised to believe, and instead of striking him down, the Almighty had snatched him back from the brink. He shuddered, thinking of all his recent blasphemies. He tried to pray, and found the words would form on his tongue, but they could not reach his heart. “I am doomed eternally,” he sobbed to himself. “Doomed, doomed.”

Then the rich, solemn harmony of the convent’s organ burst through the stone walls, followed by the voices of the choir lifting in full chant. One voice rose above all the rest, clear and pure, a boy’s tone so sweet and angelic it seemed to climb straight to the heavens. He closed his eyes and listened, and all the soft, unburdened days of his own boyhood came flooding back to him. No earthly rot there, no fierce, tearing passion that rends and corrupts the soul. Only peace: soft, balmy, gentle peace. “It is true,” he sighed, tears spilling down his cheeks. “The Church is peace of mind. Till I left her bosom I never knew sorrow, nor sin.”

And through the blur of his tears, a familiar face leaned over him: one he had never thought to see again in Rome. It was Father Anselm, the old friar who had tended his wounded body back to health in Juliers. The good father had only arrived at this convent two nights prior. Gerard cried out, reaching for him.
“Oh, Father Anselm! You cured my broken body in Juliers—now cure my hurt soul in Rome! Alas, I fear you cannot.”
Anselm sat beside the cot, laying a gentle hand on his fevered head, and calmed him with soft, soothing words. He already knew the full story of how Gerard had been pulled from the Tiber, and spoke to him with kind but steady gravity, helping him see the weight of his despairing act, urging him to turn to repentance, and give thanks to the Divine Power that had thwarted his suicidal will to save his soul.
“Come, my son,” he said. “Purge the load from your breast.”
“Ah father,” Gerard wept. “In Juliers I could confess, for then I was innocent. Now, I am an impious monster, I dare not speak my sins aloud to you.”
“Why not, my son? Do you think I have not sinned deeply against Heaven in my own youth? Oh, how deeply! Come, poor laden soul, pour out your grief, pour out all your faults, hold nothing back. Do not let hidden sins oppress and crush you.”

Before long, Gerard was kneeling at Father Anselm’s feet, confessing every last one of his sins, heaving with sobs and groans of unfeigned penitence.
“Your sins are great,” Anselm said gently, when he had finished. “But your temptation was far greater, terribly, cruelly great. I must go consult our good prior on a fitting penance for you.” He kissed Gerard’s forehead, and left the room.

And lo—Gerard could pray now. He prayed with all his heart. The phase his tormented mind now passed through could be summed in a single word: Penitence. He turned away from the thought of the world with terror and deep aversion, begging passionately to be allowed to stay within the convent walls. To him, raised in the shelter of the Church from boyhood, it felt like a wounded, worn bird flying back to its soft, safe nest. He entered his novitiate, and spent his days in prayer, quiet mortification, pious reading, and meditation.

Meanwhile, Princess Claelia’s spy returned to her palace, and reported that Gerard was most certainly dead, drowned in the Tiber, his body yet to be recovered. She went utterly still, stunned, as if the words had struck her a physical blow. When she finally found breath to speak, it was to bemoan her own cursed luck, to have been served by such overzealous brutes. “So soon,” she sighed. “See how swiftly these monsters rush to do ill deeds. They creep to us in our hot blood, tempt us with their venal daggers, then carry out the very mortal acts we would never have dreamed of on our own.”

Within hours, her pity for Gerard and her burning hatred for his killer Lodovico had risen to a fever pitch. “Poor soul, I cannot call you back to life. But the traitor who slew you shall not live another day.” She posted armed men hidden in the antechamber of her palace, ordering them to wait for Lodovico to arrive to collect his payment, then fall on him and hack him to pieces. “Strike for his head,” she commanded. “He wears a secret coat of mail beneath his tunic, and if he leaves that room alive, your own heads will answer for it.” And so she sat, weeping for the young man she had wronged, pulling the strings of her vengeance to shed a second man’s blood for having been the unwitting tool of her cruel, foolish whim.

One of the young novice Gerard’s self-imposed penances was to greet Lodovico with open kindness each time they met, even as every instinct in him recoiled as if he were hosting a cold, slimy serpent dragged from the river mud. Never was an act of self-denial more wisely chosen; and like all thoughtful, purposeful penance, it soon ceased to feel like a burden at all.

At first, the pride and self-satisfied complacency the erstwhile assassin bore as he looked upon the one life he had been paid to take, and spared, was as absurd as it was pathetic. But to pry open a crack for goodness in a hardened heart is no small feat: one good act soon tugs another through that open door. Lodovico discovered that the sweetness of saving a life far outstripped the thrill of taking one, and the miscreant grew first averse to spilling blood, then racked by remorse, until at last he drew near to full, heartfelt penitence. Teresa aided this shift immeasurably: she had threatened to leave him a dozen times before, and now renewed her ultimatum that he must at last consent to live an honest, peaceful life. The good fathers of the convent lent their support, and soon Lodovico and Teresa were sent by sea to Leghorn, where Teresa had long-standing family ties. There the former assassin settled down and took work as a porter.

He complained loudly at first that the slow, plodding drudgery of hauling heavy loads all day was miserably dull work. But that unglamorous, quiet life of honest labor was far kinder to him than the short, sharp excitement of being hewn limb from limb by Princess Claelia’s vengeful myrmidons would have been. His quiet exile saved the unaware penitent from that brutal fate.

Balked of the revenge she had hungered for, the princess sank into brooding, and soon fell into a deep, consuming melancholy. She dismissed her old confessor, and sought out a new one famed across Italy for his unflinching, uncompromising piety. That new confessor was none other than Fra Jerome, and she could not have fallen into better hands.

He heard her pour out what she called her “griefs” with grim, unsmiling attention, then took her by the shoulders and shook every last trace of her self-serving delusion out of her as roughly as he would rouse a napping kitchen maid. To do this harsh, unyielding monk justice, he feared the wrath of princes no more than he feared a storm at sea when he walked the path of his duty. In a few short, thunderous, lightning-sharp words he laid bare that she was the guiltiest sinner of all.
“Thou art no better than the devil’s proxy: thou hast used thy gold to tempt a man to slay his fellow, and then, blinded by thine own selfish vanity, thou refusest to blame and punish thyself, and now thou thirstest after more blood—the blood of a guilty man, but one a hundred times less guilty than thou.”

At first she resisted, snapping that no confessor had ever dared rebuke her so, that she was a princess unused to such rough treatment. But he overpowered every excuse she made, threatened her unflinchingly with the Church’s curse on earth and in the afterlife, tore the scales clean from her eyes, thundered at her until her pride crumbled to dust, and she sank grovelling at the feet of that giant, fiery Boanerges, wracked with remorse and terror.
“Oh holy father, have pity on a poor weak woman, help me save my guilty soul! I wandered in total darkness for want of true ghostly counsel such as thine, good father. I wake now as from a terrible, long dream.”

“Doff thy jewels,” Fra Jerome said sternly.
“I will. I will.”
“Doff thy silk and velvet. Clothe thyself in raiment plainer than that worn by the meanest servant in thy household, and wend thou instantly to Loretto.”
“I will,” the princess whispered faintly.
“No shoes. Thou shalt wear nothing but a single rough sandal on thy feet.”
“Yes father.”
“Thou shalt wash the feet of every pilgrim thou meetest, both going and coming on the road. And to every holy friar thou dost encounter, thou shalt lay bare thy sin, and abide humbly by their admonition.”
“Oh holy father, let me wear my mask!”
“Hmph.”
“Oh mercy! Bethink thee! My features are known through every corner of Italy.”
“Aye. Beauty is a curse to the lot of you vain souls. Well then: thou mayst mask thine eyes, and no more.”

Grateful for even that small concession, she reached to take his hand to kiss it, but he snatched it rudely away.
“What would ye do? That very hand handled the Eucharist but an hour agone. Is it fit for a sinner such as thou to defile it with thy touch?”
“Ah no. But oh, go not without granting thy penitent daughter thy blessing.”
“Time enow to ask for it when thou comest back from Loretto, truly penitent.”

That strange, fateful scene on the banks of the Tiber left its indelible mark on every soul it touched, as great prodigies are said to do. The assassin, softened by the life he had been paid to kill and chose to spare, laid his stiletto down forever and took up the heavy porter’s knot. The proud princess walked barefoot all the way to Loretto, weeping over her crime as she washed the calloused feet of base-born pilgrims. And Gerard, who had been carried half-suicidal out of the Tiber and into the convent, was soon regarded within its walls as a young living saint.

Loving, experienced eyes watched over his progress, and his probation was cut far shorter than custom dictated before he was admitted to priest’s orders. Not long after, he took his final monastic vows, and became a friar of St. Dominic. Dying to all the world, the monk parted with the very name he had borne in his old earthly life, snapping the last lingering link that bound him to worldly memories and attachments. The man Gerard was gone. Brother Clement had begun.

As goes the race of leaves, so too goes the race of men. That year, two fates played out on 15th century soil: one great life budded completely unnoticed in a tailor’s cramped, sunlit cottage in Rotterdam, while another grand, world-renowned figure fell to earth amid all the blare of court trumpets and public ceremony.

Philip, Duke of Burgundy, Earl of Holland, and half a dozen other titled honours besides, lay sick in Bruges. In that rough age, paupers sickened and recovered or died as Nature pleased, but woe betide the wealthy: for every one patient illness managed to kill, three were finished off by the bloodthirsty, untested tomfoolery of court physicians. The Duke’s complaint, nameless to 15th century healers, we now know as diphtheria. It was, and is, a terribly weakening malady, and the Duke was already well advanced in years. Taken together, the attending doctor saw fit to bleed him until the old man turned icy cold, his breath coming in shallow, faint gasps.

The physician then reached for the hidden, arcane secrets of his craft. “This is grave,” he announced. “Flay an ape incontinent, and press its warm pelt straight to the Duke’s breast to draw the sickness out!” Officers of state scattered seven different ways across the Bruges court and grounds, hunting high and low for an ape to counteract this reckless folly of their own species. To their utter fury, the duke’s menagerie held no apes at all: there were buffaloes, lizards, captured Turks, spotted leopards, every strange and unreasonable beast under the sun but the exact one they needed.
“Why, there used to be an ape about just last week,” one officer protested. “I saw him standing right where you are.” There had been, sure enough — but the castle mastiff had mangled the sprightly little creature for stealing his supper, and so perfectly fulfilled the unspoken human precept, “Be of your own century!”

In this emergency, the seneschal cast his despairing gaze around the crowd of panicking courtiers, and his eyes lit up. A hopeful gleam shot through them. “Here is this,” he murmured sotto voce, nodding at a figure strutting unawares across the tiles. “Surely this will serve: he is altogether apelike, doublet and hose apart.”
“Nay,” the Chancellor snapped peevishly. “Princess Marie would hang us all. She dotes on that fool.” That fool was none other than our old friend Giles, preening in a new suit of cloth of gold, entirely ignorant of the fate that had nearly befallen him.

The doctor grew impatient at the delay, and bade them flay a dog instead. “A dog is next best to an ape — only it must be a dog of one solid, uniform colour.” So they flayed a liver-coloured hound, and clapped its still palpitating warm skin to their sovereign’s chest. Philip the Good died beneath it.

Thus scientifically disposed of, the Duke left thirty-one children behind him: of that number, exactly one, somehow, was legitimate, and took the throne in his stead. The good Duke made provisions for nineteen of the other thirty; the remaining eleven were left to shift for themselves as best they could. Flemish chroniclers of the time claimed the deceased prince traced his line all the way back to the kings of Troy, through Thierry of Aquitaine, Chilperic, Pharamond, and all the old kings of Franconia. But that was no special distinction at all. Not a single prince of that era has the narrator ever been able to discover who did not claim descent from Troy. “Priam” was medieval shorthand for “Adam.”

The good Duke’s body was carried all the way to Burgundy, and laid in a grand black marble mausoleum at Dijon. All Holland rang with the news of his death, not one soul there guessing that a figure far more lasting in fame had been born on their own territory that very same year. That judgment has long since been reversed. Men now travel to gaze at the humble tailor’s cottage in Rotterdam, where the greatest birth of the 15th century took place. As the old song says, what house the good Duke died in “no one knows and no one cares.”

And why? Dukes Philip the Good come and go, and leave mankind not a halfpenny wiser, nor better, nor altered in the slightest than they found it. But when, once in three hundred years, such a child is born to the world as Margaret’s son, lo! a human torch lit by fire from heaven blazes forth, and *Fiat Lux* — “Let there be light” — thunders out from pole to pole.

Once the most feared, most powerful order across all of Christendom, the Dominican friars – known far and wide as the Black Friars – were in slow, sharp decline by the 15th century. Their bitter rivals the Franciscans, with their raucous, populist preachers and humble, appealing vows of poverty, were outstripping them everywhere: even in wealthy, devout England, where the Black Friars had once been so powerful no noble would dare turn them away empty-handed from their gates.

So the order’s shrewd leadership, who guarded the Dominicans’ waning influence like smoldering embers they would not let die, grew desperate to recruit sharp, zealous new sons, hone them to a fine edge, and send them out to win back the flocks slipping from their grasp.

Brother Clement – the former scribe Gerard, living hidden under his new religious name – soon drew their notice. His rare gift for tongues, that allowed him to speak polished Latin for scholars, lyrical Italian for Roman crowds, formal French for northern courts, and both high Dutch for merchants and rough low dialect for peasant farmers, was a skill no other novice could match. The leadership set their plans: they would send him to travel and preach across England, reporting directly back to the Roman curia.

But Jerome, the gruff, battle-hardened senior friar who had the prior’s full confidence, blocked the order’s plan before it could move forward.
“Clement still carries the milk of the world in his veins,” he argued. “All its soft attachments, its untested weaknesses. Do not let his bright new-born zeal and gentle humility trick you into abandoning our old, tried wisdom. Test him first, temper him in the fire, lest one day we find ourselves leaning on a gilded reed for a staff, and it snaps clean in two.”
“Good counsel,” the prior agreed. “Take him in hand yourself, then, and prove his mettle.”

Jerome set to work, following centuries of Dominican custom. One day he led Clement to a public green where young men of the city played the popular games of the era: he knew this was a haunt of Clement’s old worldly friends. Sure enough, before long Pietro Vanucci and Andrea wandered past them, tossing a careless glance at the two shaven friars. They did not recognize their old lost friend, the scribe they thought dead, under the tonsure and black habit.
Clement flinched only for half a heartbeat, then cast his eyes firmly to the ground and murmured a quiet Paternoster.
“Will you not step forward and greet them, brother?” Jerome prodded, testing him.
“No, brother. Yet it does me good to see them. They remind me of the worldly sins I can never atone for deeply enough.”
“It is well,” Jerome said, and submitted a short, unenthusiastic but favourable report on Clement’s progress.

Next Jerome took Clement to a dozen plague-ridden deathbeds, and then down into Rome’s worst noisome dungeons: places where the dark was so thick you could not see your own hand in front of your face, the stench of sewage and rot so loathsome it made the stomach turn, where men who had been abandoned there rotted half-mad, coiled in rags and filth like feral beasts, all hope long dead. The work wore Clement’s body raw, but his soul gathered all its strength to lean close, hold their shaking hands, and speak to them of God’s unmerited mercy. He shone through the trial, and Jerome reported back: “His spirit is willing, but his flesh is weak.”
“Perfect,” the prior smiled. “A man whose flesh is weak but his spirit willing is far more reliable than the brute who never feels weariness or revulsion at all.”

But a far harsher trial still waited for Clement. It was witnessed by hundreds of onlookers on a crowded Roman main street, as described below:
One morning the principal thoroughfare leading out to the scaffold was packed shoulder to shoulder, side avenues blocked with heads craning to see. It was no ordinary execution. The crime had been unthinkable, the victim no common man: the governor of Rome had been found hacked to death in his bed at dawn. One hand, raised to fend off the blow, had been severed clean at the wrist and lay by his side, his throat slit ear to ear, his temples bashed in with a blunt club. The murder had been traced to his own household servant, and the sentence decreed retribution equal to the crime.
Italian executions were rarely gratuitously cruel in that era, but this butchery had enraged the whole city, and the crowd bayed for matching blood. The killer was first tied to the outer wall of the murdered governor’s house for half an hour, to taste the first bite of vengeance. Then his left hand was lopped off, just like his victim’s. A newly slaughtered fowl was cut open and bound around his bleeding stump, a bizarre folk remedy favoured by local doctors no one could quite explain the logic of, and the mutilated, bandaged man was hurried to the scaffold.
There, a young friar – Clement – knelt by his side, praying fiercely, speaking soft words of comfort, holding a crucifix pressed close to the condemned man’s eyes. Before long the executioner roughly shoved Clement out of the way, bashed the prisoner’s skull in with a heavy mallet, and fell on him to slit his throat. A collective cry of horror burst from the crowd. Clement swayed, and fainted dead away. The gigantic Jerome strode forward, slung him over his shoulder like a fainting child, and carried him back to the convent.
Clement returned to the cloister heavy with shame, weeping as he confessed his failure to the prior.
“Courage, son Clement,” the prior soothed him. “A Dominican is not forged in a single day. You shall have another trial, and I forbid you to go to it fasting.”
He did not have long to wait. A notorious robber was dragged to the scaffold, a monster of cruelty who had waylaid travellers, robbed them, and butchered them for sport, no provocation needed. Clement spent the last night with him in his prison cell, walked with him to the scaffold, and prayed so earnestly by his side that the hardened ruffian burst into tears, and threw his arms around the friar’s neck. Clement hugged him back, even as his flesh quivered with revulsion, and held the crucifix steady before his eyes. The man was garrotted, his soul leaving his body, and Clement drowned out the noise of the crowd with his own loud, passionate prayers. No sooner was the man dead than the hangman pulled out his axe, and quartered the corpse right there on the scaffold. The same crowd that had watched the robber die with indifference, almost satisfaction, wailed piteously at every stroke of the axe on the corpse that could feel no pain. Clement shuddered, but stood firm, like a rock that vibrates under a storm but cannot be toppled.
Then Jerome’s voice snapped in his ear: “Brother Clement, climb up on that cart and preach to the people. Quick! Strike while their hearts are hot, while there are souls here ripe for saving.”
Clement’s face flushed pale then red, he breathed hard, his hands shaking. But he obeyed, stumbled up the cart’s wobbly steps, and faced the largest crowd he had ever seen in his life: a sea of upturned heads. His throat was parched, his heart thudded against his ribs, his voice trembled as he began.
Slowly, the magnitude of the moment, the sight of all those faces hungry for words, and his own heart brimming with zeal lit a fire in him. He told them the robber’s own story, the small, trivial first sins that had led him step by slow step down the fatal ladder to murder, warned them all to never take that first tiny, seemingly harmless step off the path of virtue. One moment he thundered against the sin of bloodshed, the next he moved the crowd to soft pity and charity, and soon all his tremors fell away. He felt strung tight as a lute string, gifted with a power he never knew he had: he could feel the crowd’s very pulse, play on their hearts like he once played his psaltery. Sobs and groans rippled through the crowd, already raw from the tragedy they had just watched. Jerome stared, dumbfounded, like a man who strikes a tinder stick expecting a small flame, and accidentally sets off a rocket.
Clement caught Jerome’s shocked, unsmiling glance, broke off his sermon abruptly, and stepped down to join him.
“It was my first try,” he said apologetically. “Your command came on me like a thunderbolt. Did I do wrong? Tell me, correct me, lend me the benefit of your wisdom, Brother Jerome.”
“Humph,” Jerome grumbled, frowning thoughtfully for a long minute. Then he said, sullen and half-reluctant, “Give the glory to God, Brother Clement. My judgement is that you were born an orator.” He reported the same back to the order’s leadership, even though it galled him a little – for he was an honest friar, even if he was a dour one.

The next trial that came Clement’s way was the ordeal of Julio Antonelli, a man accused of sacrilege. Three witnesses swore on their lives they had seen him leaving the church the very night the golden candlesticks were stolen. Three other witnesses swore just as firmly he had been across the city at the time, with an unassailable alibi. No testimony could be shaken, so the court ruled he would submit to trial by ordeal: he could choose to plunge his bare arm to a depth of fourteen inches into boiling water to retrieve a pebble, or be bound hand and foot and lowered eight feet down into the Tiber. The clergy who believed him innocent pushed him to choose the hot water trial, which they secretly rigged to be far less painful for those they favoured. But the poor man was terrified of scalding, and picked the cold water ordeal – giving Jerome another chance to temper Clement’s nerve.
Antonelli took the sacrament, was stripped naked on the banks of the Tiber, and tied hand and foot to stop him thrashing, which would lift his torso above the water and falsely mark him guilty. He was lowered gently into the stream, floated for a split second with only his hair sticking above the surface, and a roar went up from the crowds on both banks: guilty! Then the new wet ropes slipped, and he sank entirely under the water. Another roar burst out: innocent! They left him at the bottom for the ordained half-minute, then hauled him up, gurgling, gasping, screaming for mercy. After the set prayers were recited, he was set free, formally cleared of all charges.
Clement had prayed earnestly on the riverbank the whole time. When it was over, he thanked God in a loud, only slightly trembling voice. After a while he turned to Jerome, and asked: “Should he not be compensated, brother? For the pain, the terror, the suffocation. He lives, but he tasted every drop of the bitterness of death, and he had done no wrong at all.”
“He is rewarded enough to have been cleared of the false charge,” Jerome said.
“But he was innocent of that fault, and yet he drank of death’s cup, even if he did not drain it. And his accusers, who bear far more guilt than he, suffer nothing at all.”
Jerome replied sternly, “The real punishment and reward of men is not meted out in this world, Brother Clement. Unhappy are they who sin and suffer no ill for it. Happy are the ones who bear the small ills this earth can inflict: all of it will be counted to them in heaven, a hundredfold over.”
Clement bowed his head, submissive. “May your good words take root in my heart, and never fall to the ground, Brother Jerome.”

But the severest trial Clement ever underwent at Jerome’s hands was entirely unplanned. It came to pass when Jerome, in a rare moment of good humour, brought Clement along to visit the scholar Fra Colonna. On Colonna’s table lay the brand new, perfectly fair copy he had just finished of his *The Dream of Polifilo*. The proud author was eager to show off his masterwork.
“For ages,” he ranted, “fools have lavished all their most poetic, amorous compliments on mortal women – mere creatures of earth, reeking of their fleshly origins. Roman women stand at their windows, carefully learned over a lifetime to show you their one good feature, be it a single ear or a fluttering eyelash, and hide all the rest. They are sirens at the window, magpies at the door, angels in the street, and devils in their own homes. But I? I ransack every line of the old minstrels’ love verses, not forgetting all the pretty lines Petrarch wasted on that little French coquette Laura, the slyest of them all – and I lay all that heap of sweet, amorous spice at the feet of the only females worthy of such devotion: the Nine Muses!”
“By that clever trick,” Jerome huffed, flipping roughly through the pages, “you, a Dominican friar, have written an obscene book.” He slammed *Polifilo* hard down on the table.
“Obscene? You discourteous monk!” Colonna ran around the table, snatched his manuscript away, locked it fast in a chest, trembled with mortification, and spluttered: “My Gerard – pshaw, what’s-his-name, the friar who was here before – never found *Polifilo* obscene. To the pure, all things are pure.”
“All those who read your *Polifilo* – heaven grant there are few of them – will find it exactly what I find it,” Jerome retorted.
Poor Colonna had to swallow the bitter insult. If he had not been in his own lodgings, a high-born gentleman as well as a famed scholar, a vulgar brawl would have broken out. Instead, he fought to steady himself, turned the conversation to a beautiful chrysolite the Cardinal Colonna had lent him, and as Clement turned it over in his fingers, he waxed lyrical on the supposed moral virtues of precious stones, a superstition his whole age devoutly believed in.
Jerome would have none of it, and argued against the folly of believing a dead stone could grant a man valour, chastity, immunity from poison, or temperance.
“Centuries of experience prove they do,” Colonna insisted. “As for that last virtue you named, there sits a living proof. This Gerard – I beg your pardon, Brother Thingemy – comes from the north, where men drink like fishes, and yet he was always the most abstemious soul alive. Why? Because he carried an amethyst, the clearest, richest coloured one I ever saw, on any hand but a noble’s. Where in heaven’s name is your amethyst now? Show it to this unbeliever!”
“And you think that little stone made the boy temperate?” Jerome asked, sneering.
“Of course! What is the very meaning of the word amethyst? *a-*, not, and *methuo*, to get drunk. Names are not assigned things for two thousand years for no reason at all.”
He went on to list all the great jewels, illustrating their powers with anecdotes from respected ancient historians.
“These are nothing but old wives’ fables,” Jerome said contemptuously. “Was there ever such credulity as yours?”
Colonna smarted under the jibe, and the insulted scholar, the man who had written the Dream of Polifilo, turned the full force of his vast, unruly learning on Jerome. He launched into a long, roaring tirade, of which only fragments are recorded here:
“The heathen blotted out? Why, they hold four fifths of the whole world. What have we Christians invented that they did not do first? Painting? Sculpture? These are heathen arts, and we are but pygmies beside them. What modern man can carve forms half so godlike as the great Athenian sculptors, or Dinocrates of Macedon, or the masters who carved the Laocoon out of a single block of marble? What prince has the genius to carve an entire mountain into a statue, as was done at Bagistan, and once planned for Mount Athos? What city has the soul to raise a colossus of brass in the sea, so tall the largest sailing ships could pass between its legs?
“Architecture? We are but children at it. Can any modern building match the pure perfect lines of the Parthenon? The grandeur of the Greek and Roman theatres, or the monstrous Egyptian temples that men walked to down a mile-long avenue of sphinxes, each as big as a Venetian palace? Their porphyry monuments are polished like crystal, not rough-hewn like our own shoddy structures. Even now their broken pillars lie overgrown with acanthus and myrtle, still sparkling, mocking the sloppy work of our modern masons. Roads? Aqueducts? Sewers? We have forgotten how to build a good road even with all the Roman models under our very feet. Tombs? No Christian nation has ever raised a tomb that does not make a learned scholar laugh when he sees it. Think of the Mausoleum, the Pyramids, the giant mountain tombs along the Indus and Ganges, stuffed inside with mines of precious stones. You have never seen the East, Jerome, or you would never dare decry the heathen.
“Even in the world of the mind, what have we invented? Geometry? Logic? We are all pupils of Euclid and Aristotle. Written letters? We did not invent them any more than Cadmus did. Poetry? No Christian has ever come close to Homer, or Virgil, or Horace. Tragedy? Comedy? The poets, the actors, the marble theatres all turned to dust at our touch, and we could never revive them. Would you compare our silly little morality plays, with their frigid personifications and dog Latin, to a Greek tragedy performed in a marble amphitheatre before a whole city of audience, written by Sophocles?
“Monotheism? The learned philosophers of Greece and Rome were monotheists. Their vulgar people worshipped many gods, and so do ours. We did not even invent that. Our saints are exactly their deified daemones, their lesser gods that people prayed to to intercede with the high god – and the uneducated mob, too stupid to understand the distinction, worshipped those lesser saints instead of the Almighty. The pagan mariners worshipped Venus, called her *Stella Maris*, Star of the Sea, and *Regina Coelorum*, Queen of Heaven. Our Christian mariners worship the Virgin Mary, and call her exactly the same names. Call that an invention? An old doub

A Catherine is no unalloyed blessing in a strange house. The urge to order and govern hums strong in her bones. She has scarcely stepped across the threshold before the pewter pots on the dresser shine brighter of their own accord, the hearth sweeps itself free of ash, the cottage windows glow with twice as much light, and the whole little home thrums with the tireless energy of some giant, ever-busy cricket. But this cricket is a relentless meddler, a busybody of the most uncompromising sort, and that is no small character trait. She makes no distinctions: every pot, every chair, every person gets hauled into line to suit her sense of order.
Many things do improve for being tidied. But not everything. Nothing on earth resents being forced into perfect order more than the messy, breathing lives of human beings — save, of course, the quiet, unchanging peace of the grave.
Catherine shifted every chair and table in Margaret’s home, likely for the better, but she would not stop at inanimate furniture. When Margaret’s time to give birth drew near, Catherine decided no bumbling men could be allowed underfoot. She tricked the two good, simple wanderers Denys and Martin, first telling them a short stroll would do them good, then hinting that if their walk stretched on until the middle of the next week, all the better.
The two burly men, who had faced bandits and blizzards without flinching, had no defence against a sharp-tongued woman who ordered them out of their own borrowed home. They crept out at daybreak each morning, slipped back after dark like thieves, and if they ever accidentally lingered indoors, they moved as carefully as cats treading a wall lined with broken glass, their faces wide with awestruck submission, looking as dejected as scolded hounds. Even that was not enough for Catherine. Their very presence jangled on her nerves; surely two big hardy wanderers had no business cluttering up a house where a new life was about to arrive, she thought. No breastplate or sword could deflect the tiny, stinging pinpricks of her sharp, snappish remarks, until at last when Margaret came down the stairs after her confinement, the kitchen was entirely swept clear of heroes.
Martin, stiff with old age, had not wandered far. He dragged out his favourite three-legged stool as his “baggage of war” and perched placidly on it right in the street, baking in the sun like a contented tortoise. Margaret laughed when she spotted him there, not realising he had settled there full-time, and asked where Denys was. “Good, kind Denys,” she said softly, “he must be so pleased to see me up and about again.”
Catherine was wiping an earthen bowl so hard she nearly wore a hole through the wood, and told her dismissively that Denys had set off for his family home in Burgundy. “High time, too — he hasn’t been back to see his folks in three years, by all accounts.”
“What? Gone without saying goodbye to me?” Margaret’s violet-soft eyes filled with tears. Catherine coloured hot, the pricks of conscience stabbing her for the first time. She tossed her head, though, and made excuse that Margaret had been fast asleep when he left, and she had not wanted to wake her.
“Poor Denys,” Margaret whispered, and the tears welled over and rolled down her cheeks. Catherine, seeing that, slipped quietly outside to coddle the remaining displaced wanderer, Martin, with a sudden burst of warmth and hospitality. But old Martin was stubborn, set in his ways. “No thank you, mistress,” he said gruffly. “I’m used to being out of doors now. I never cared for constant changes. I don’t bother anyone here, and no one bothers me.”
“You horrid, grumpy old thing!” Catherine shrieked, flipping instantly from honeyed softness to sharp vinegar, and flounced back into the house.
Later, when she had calmed down, she had a little private cry, then soothed her own guilt by vowing she would be so kind to Margaret and the new baby that the young mother would never miss her two wandering friends. Still a little restive, she washed all her regrets away the simplest, surest way she knew: she gave the new baby a full, proper bath, head to toe, in warm soapy water, and all thoughts of wronged, displaced heroes dissolved into nothing, lost in the lather.
Margaret could not stand still the whole ceremony, hovering round Catherine like an eager little sparrow, desperate to have even a small part in tending her son. She dipped a finger into the bath water first, for form’s sake, not fooling anyone that she was checking the temperature — Catherine would never have let her near it to mess it up anyway. She knelt across from little baby Gerard, chattering to him nonstop, deliberately lisping and using baby talk, for what possible sense could a cherubic newborn make of the ridiculous, formal grown-up way of speaking?
“I wish you could wash that off,” Margaret said suddenly, staring at the baby’s tiny little finger.
“What?” Catherine peered closer.
“Don’t you see? That little brown mole there on his finger.”
Old Catherine leaned in for a good look, and her face lit up. “Why, that’s the strangest thing!” she cried. “Nature is a stubborn, meddlesome old thing, isn’t she? Haven’t you seen that exact same mark on someone else before? Tell me the truth now, lass.”
“On him? No, mother, I never did,” Margaret said, confused.
“Well, it’s there on his father, on the very same spot! You never noticed that, did you? But of course, you never knew your Gerard from a tiny babe up to man’s height the way I did. I had him on my knees a hundred times, just like this little one, washing him top to toe in warm water.” She puffed out her chest a little, proud of her years of knowing the boy Margaret loved, and Margaret looked up at her meekly, as if she were the wisest woman alive.
Catherine paused, reflecting, as busybodies sometimes do (not very deeply, of course, or we would not dare write it down). “Life is a whirligig, spinning round and back on itself,” she mused. “Us women, our lives are all cut from the same cloth, aren’t they? When my Gerard was a tiny babe just like this, I tried to scrub that very mole right off his finger! ‘Fie, what an ugly little blot,’ I said to myself, and scrubbed so hard I made the poor little wail. Only then I stopped, thought I was being silly. And now here you are, telling me to try and wash that same mark off your baby’s finger, too! Think of how the world turns!”
“Wash it off?” Margaret gasped, horrified. “I wouldn’t do that for all the gold in the world. Why, that’s the sweetest, dearest little thing about my baby! I’ll kiss that mole every morning and every night, until the man who first had it comes back to join the three of us.” She leaned down and kissed that tiny brown mark, then before she knew it she had the baby sprawled across her lap, kissing his soft little back over and over, nuzzling him like a mother wolf fawning over her lamb, while Catherine smiled on. She’d seen many a young mother get this same giddy, overjoyed bout of affection in her long days.
For months after that, Margaret’s whole life was summed up in one single, radiant, blissful word: motherhood. You who know all that that word holds can fill in the rest of the picture: the young mother nursing her babe, bathing him, dressing him, singing silly little rhymes, laughing as he coos and gambols on the cottage floor. Now, faster than a lightning strike, dart across the Alps all the way to Italy, to a cold stone cloister. The monks drift past like pale ghosts, their eyes cast down, their hands folded meekly across their chests, their hearts long since dead to all earthly joy and longing. One of those cowled ghosts is Gerard — the man Margaret waits for, who she thinks will one day come back to her, full of youth and love and happiness.
In the Grindelwald valley, the traveller sees on one side the sheer, towering Alps, nothing but rock, ice, and everlasting snow, piercing through the clouds to touch the sky. On the other side are gentle, ordinary green slopes, as bright as emerald, dotted with grazing cows, tiny thatched cottages, and warm, everyday life. Those great mountain peaks are all bare, lifeless, inhuman, and sublime, while the little green lower slopes hum with soft, ordinary joy. Wherever else you go, those soft common things of life pass unnoticed, but set against the grim grandeur of the ice mountains, they soothe the heart, they strike you with their gentle sweetness, all the brighter for the contrast.
That is exactly what these two halves of our story are, seen rightly: on the Italian side, rough adventure, burning passion, despair, vice, penitence, all pure ice and holy snow, soaring straight up towards heaven. On the Dutch side, everything small, soft, womanly, and ever green. And just as a narrow footpath separates those towering ice spires of Grindelwald from the little sunny green hills below, so only this one page lies between the Cloister, and the Hearth.

The newly elected pope held the Dominican order in special favour, and soon a messenger arrived at the convent from the Vatican, calling for a learned, capable friar to take up a teaching post at the University of Basle. Brother Clement was the very man for the task: fluent in half a dozen languages, and long ago, in his worldly life, he had sat in the lecture halls of Guarini the younger. His planned visit to England was put on hold, though not abandoned, and he was dispatched towards Basle – with three months to fill before his post began, tasked with preaching in every village and town along his road.

He passed out of the northern gate with his eyes cast low, his whole being wrapped in quiet, pious contemplation. If we could paint the full story of a man’s soul as a living, breathing work of art, what a walking fresco this barefoot friar made! Hopeful, bright young love, shattering bereavement, bottomless despair, blasphemy, reckless vice, a suicide attempt, gnawing remorse, religious terror, penitence, a total death to worldly ties, and at last soft resignation. All of that, crammed into twelve short months. Now he was a traveller on foot again – but everything had changed. There were no more perilous adventures waiting for him on the road. Even common thieves and robbers bowed low to the ground when they spotted him, and instead of robbing him, they forced their stolen coins into his hands and begged him to pray for their souls. His journey thus held almost no grand, melodramatic incidents. But for the readers who care less for swashbuckling plots and more for the quiet, unspoken movements of a man’s heart, these undramatic moments speak volumes, marking the slow, steady growth of his soul.

The first Sunday of his journey brought a quiet, profound milestone: he prayed openly for the soul of Margaret. He had never dared do that before. It was not that her eternal welfare was not dearer to him than anything else on earth – it was his own crushing humility. The terrible blasphemies he had screamed in his frenzy when he heard news of her death horrified his pious readers, yes, but they horrified him far more, as he turned them over again and again in his thoughts. For months during his novitiate, he was crushed by religious despair, convinced he had committed the sin against the Holy Spirit that dooms a soul forever. Slowly, under the gentle guidance of old Anselm, that dark cloud lifted, but a deep, searing sense of his own unworthiness remained. He feared his own salvation was far from secure, and that it would be a mocking insult to Heaven for a man so stained with sin to pray for a soul as innocent, comparatively, as Margaret’s. So he had coaxed good Anselm and other kindly, soft-hearted old monks to pray for her in his stead, and they did it with all their heart. The older friars of the convent, for all their flaws, bore a pure, tender love for their younger brethren that could never have sprung from the world.

That Sunday, after he had preached to a rapt crowd in a small Italian town and felt his spirit carried high on the power of his own words, a balmy, soft sense of God’s forgiveness and loving kindness settled over him. He prayed for Margaret’s soul then, and from that day forward, it became his daily habit – the last, purified tie that bound his heart to the earth. All ties to his own blood family had faded as if they had never existed: the Church would not share a man’s devotion with the world, and even the Church could not cure the pain of his great, lifelong love for Margaret without erasing all smaller earthly attachments along with it.

For most of his journey, Clement rarely felt any flicker of warm life stir in him except when he stood in the pulpit. The only other exceptions came when he stopped to relieve the suffering of some fellow traveller. Once, he found a young man in the grip of what the villagers said was tarantula bite – or what might equally well have been a ferocious hysterical delusion. For two days, the boy had not slept, thrashing, leaping, and beating the walls of his cottage in convulsions, with the village musicians only making his agony worse by blaring loud, wild tunes. Left to run its course, the illness would end in exhaustion and death. Clement sent for a psaltery and tried soft, soothing melodies at first, but instead of calming him, the notes crushed the boy into groaning, huddling on the dirt floor. Then Clement noticed his lips moving in a constant, quiet whisper. He leaned in, and found the boy was murmuring a strange, unwritten tune no one else had ever heard. He learned the melody, and began to play it. The boy’s face brightened instantly, and he began to dance lightly about the room in perfect contentment. By the time Clement’s fingers ached so badly he could barely pluck the strings, the young man sank down peacefully into a deep, healing sleep that saved his life. After teaching the strange tune to the village musician for future use, Clement went on his way, his heart a little warmer than it had been.

On another occasion, he found a mob dragging a well-dressed stranger down the street, the man struggling and shouting in a language no one in the crowd could understand. He had walked into the town sweltering in the Italian heat, holding a mulberry bough over his head for shade, and the villagers had stared stupidly, uncomprehending, before pouncing on him to drag him before the podesta. Clement followed, trying every language he knew – Italian, French, German, Dutch – until the stranger replied back in tolerable, sharp-accented Latin. He was an Englishman, a Kentish squire named Rolfe, of Betshanger, educated at Cambridge. He had plucked the nearest leafy bough to shade his head, he said, because in England anyone was welcome to take fruit and branches that grew by the public highway. He would happily pay for the twig, he protested, he could not fathom why the whole town was up in arms over a handful of leaves. The stubborn podesta was ready to throw the islander in jail, until Clement mediated, carefully explaining that mulberry leaves were sacred property, for they fed the silkworms that were the Duke of Italy’s most valuable source of income. Rolfe, unapologetic, pulled out a long purse and declared the whole matter simply mercantile: “What damages?” he said. “Name the sum, and I will pay it at once.” The podesta’s eyes lit up at the glint of gold, fined him a single ducat – worth far more than the entire mulberry tree – and pocketed the coin.

Free at last, Rolfe laughed off his anger immediately and shook his head at the absurdity of the whole situation. He was deeply grateful to Clement, and pressed him to come back to England with him. “You are too good for this fool’s country, father,” he said. “England is the only place worth living. I was a fool to leave it to wander among mulberry trees and idiots. My house is always open to you. We sit forty people down to dinner every day at Betshanger – one more guest will never be missed. You can end your days with me and my heirs, if you wish. What an Englishman says, he means.” Clement promised he would visit one day, not to overstay his welcome. Rolfe then begged Clement to hear his confession, saying he had lived like a heathen ever since he left England. While he knelt on the roadside to confess, Clement asked if the rumours were true that England was overrun with Lollards and Wycliffites. Rolfe flushed a little, then spoke gravely. “There are black sheep in every land, holy father. But the English love their own ways, and above all their own mother tongue. The Normans conquered our weapons, but they never conquered our speech – they tried for a hundred years to stamp it out by law and proclamation, and failed. Foreign priests come to us and preach the word of God in mangled Latin or bad French, that sounds no more sense to a plain English farmer than the bleat of a sheep. Then Wycliffe and his men come and read the scripture out of its own book, in plain, simple English, that speaks straight to every man’s heart. Who could resist that? I swear the English would turn deaf ears to St. Peter himself, if he did not speak to them in the tongue their mothers lulled them with, along with their kisses.” He hastily added that this was for the common folk, not himself, who had been educated at Cambridge and knew Latin well. “The key to the English heart is the mother tongue, father.”

Rolfe offered his dual-language English and Latin Book of Hours to Clement, to help him learn the language, and the two men swapped books: Clement gave him his own Latin and Italian devotional manuscript, refusing to “sell” his promised daily prayers for Rolfe’s soul, saying he would offer them freely. The delighted Englishman then stuffed a heavy purse of coins into Clement’s hands, refusing to listen when Clement protested his vow of poverty. “Lay it out for the good of the Church and the good of my soul,” he insisted. “You do not have to keep it for yourself, but you will take it.” The two men embraced, blessed each other, and went their separate ways.

A mile down the road, Clement found two tired German workmen resting in the deep shade of a great chestnut tree beside their cart, which carried a rough, clumsy printing press no bigger than a wine press, drawn by a jaded, half-dead mule. He stared at the machine, the old bitter hatred he had once felt for the craft of printing fading into a faint, distant dream. “Sweynheim!” he called softly.

The two men jumped to their feet, panicked, and scuttled off into the trees, thinking a sorcerer had called their names out of nowhere. Clement laughed, and called to them to come out, explaining he had seen their printed copy of *Lactantius* in Rome, and knew they were the disciples of Johann Fust, the first printers. The two men came forward sheepishly, and complained that their mule was too tired to make it to the next town, and they had no money left to pay for his food or their own. Clement freed the mule of all its harness but a thin halter, and the creature immediately rolled happily in the dust, refreshing himself. He then handed them the purse Rolfe had given him, telling them it was a gift from a charitable English stranger, to pass the kindness on to some other traveller in need someday. The two workmen’s eyes filled with tears. Before they parted, they dragged their press out of the cart, and in a few moments, pulled a fresh printed sheet of eight pages – already set type for Augustine’s *City of God* – for Clement to keep. He stared in wonder at the words, fixed fast to the paper, and warned them never to abuse their great craft, never to print wicked books, for those would spread across the world like locusts to devour men’s souls. They promised they would sooner lay their own hands under the press screw than do that, and the three parted as friends.

Later, at an inn in Tuscany, Clement had a strange, sudden encounter with his past. He was sitting alone in a corner of the big barn the inn had lent to a crowd of travelling pilgrims, poring over his new Book of Hours and working out the English words with the help of his old Dutch, when a servant set a bucket of water at his feet, and a masked lady of high rank – performing public penance – knelt down without a word, rolled up her sleeves, and began to wash his feet. Her mask was barely an inch wide, but it completely hid her face, and she handled his bare feet with a soft, gentle touch no servant could match. When he gently asked if he could do anything to help her soul, she broke down, and confessed her terrible secret.

She had loved a handsome young Dutch stranger named Gerard once, she said, and when he rejected her for a poor girl back in his homeland, she had flown into a jealous rage, hired a bravo to kill him, and then lied to his sweetheart that he had died unfaithful. She had thought him dead for years, his body never found, and her soul was crushed under the weight of the murder. Clement slowly, gently revealed the truth: the bravo she had hired was the very man whose life Gerard had saved at sea, along with his wife and infant child. The assassin had not killed Gerard – he had dragged him out of the Tiber, after Gerard had thrown himself in to die in his grief over Margaret’s supposed death. Gerard had renounced the world then, to become a Dominican friar.

The lady froze. She raised her head slowly, peering through the tiny slit in her mask at Clement’s face. She recognized his voice. The next moment, she let out a faint, soft shriek, and collapsed forward, her brow pressed to his bare feet, weeping so hard her whole body shook.

Clement drew a slow, heavy sigh. He began to wonder if he had chosen the wisest path with this fiery, unruly soul laid bare at his feet. Young as he was, though, he had already drunk deep of the hard-won wisdom of the Church: one of the first lessons he had been taught was the grace of pause. When tangled difficulties arose, to do or say nothing at all, hold his tongue, and pray for clarity, until the knots of the matter softened and unspooled a little on their own.

So he kept his peace, knelt quietly a while, and prayed for wisdom to guide her. The only small movement he made was to gently try to withdraw his foot from where it rested near her. But the distraught penitent flung her arms tight around it with a piteous, half-sobbing cry, clinging to it convulsively, hot tears dripping down onto his worn leather sandal. The full agony of her tangled shame and true penance revealed itself then, as a bright, burning crimson crept all the way up her throat, where she lay quivering on the cold stone at his feet.

“My daughter,” Clement said, his voice soft and steady, “take courage. Torment yourself no more over this Gerard who lives only as a ghost of your own fancies now. As for me, I am Brother Clement, sent to you by Heaven this very day to comfort you, and help you save your soul. You have made me your confessor, and so I claim your obedience, as is my right.”

“Oh yes, anything,” she sobbed.

“Leave this pilgrimage at once, and turn straight back for Rome. Penance done wandering foreign roads, far from the people and places that know you, is worth very little. The temptations we are called to defeat, lest we perish, lie right where we have built our lives. We do not run from them to hunt down newer, showier trials that never cut close to the quick. It is easy to wash the feet of strangers when our own faces are hidden behind masks. It is far, far harder to practice quiet meekness and charity with the people we live beside every day.”

“I will never, never lift a hand to harm her again,” she gasped.

“Nay, I speak not only of your servants,” he corrected her, “but of all your household dependents, your kinsmen, your friends. This shall be your penance: the very last thought before you sleep each night, and the first after matins at dawn, call to mind your sin, and the boundless goodness of God. From that remembrance, learn to be humble and gentle when those around you stumble and err. The whole world courts the rich and powerful, but you shall seek out the poor—not the common beggars at the crossroads, who for the most part are neither honest nor truly destitute. Seek instead those worthy souls who blush to beg for aid, yet are in dire need of help you can give. To give to them is to lay up treasure in Heaven, to lend directly to God. And you shall marry a good, faithful son of the Church.”

“Me? I will never marry,” she cried, shocked.

“You will marry within the year,” he said firmly, gentle but unshakable. “I entreat you, and command you, to take for your husband a man who fears the Lord. For you are soft, unshaped clay. Mismatched to a cruel or godless man, you will crumble to nothing. But wedded to a worthy husband, by the grace of God, you may live as a pious, charitable princess—ay, and die a saint, one day.”

“Me?” she whispered, disbelieving.

“You,” he said.

He bade her rise then, and set off to begin the good work he had laid out for her. She pushed herself up to her knees, pulled off her mask, and cast one long, eloquent, tearful look up at him, before dropping her eyes meekly to the ground.

“I will obey you as if you were an angel sent straight from Heaven. I am so happy, and yet so unhappy—for my heart tells me I will never look upon your face again. I will not leave until I have washed and dried your feet.”

“That is unnecessary,” he told her. “I have already excused you this bootless, unnecessary penance.”

“It is no penance to me,” she wept. “Ah, you do not truly forgive me if you will not let me tend to your poor, tired feet.”

“Then so be it,” Clement said, resigned, and thought to himself with a faint, amused softness that truly, women will cling fast to the smallest, most trivial small acts of piety. These weak-seeming creatures, who gravitate toward tiny, tender gestures as the stars are drawn to the great central light of the heavens, hold flashes of angelic intelligence no man can match, though. When the princess had finished drying his feet, she looked up at him with tears glistening in her beautiful eyes, and murmured with a singular tenderness and goodness he had not expected from her:

“I will have masses said for her soul. May I?” she added, timid, as if afraid to overstep.

The words caught him entirely off guard, and a faint warm blush rose to the monk’s cheek, and softened the cold, clear blue of his eyes. It was such a gentle, gracious thought, coming from a soul he had just moments before judged so shallow and flighty.

“It is a gracious, blessed thought,” he told her. “Do as you will. Oftentimes such kind acts fall back on the one who gives them like blessed dew. But I am your confessor, not hers. It is your soul I must bend all my strength to save now, or woe will fall on my own. My daughter, my dear daughter, I see good angels and ill angels fighting for your soul this very day, this very moment—oh, fight on the side of good, for your own sake. Do you remember every word I bade you do?”

“Remember?” the princess echoed. “Sweet saint, every syllable that has fallen from your lips is carved deep into my heart.”

“Then one last word, before we part. Pray much to Christ our Lord, and little to his saints.”

“I will,” she promised.

“That is the best, truest word I have the light to give you. So we part on it. You will return to the place that becomes you best, your father’s house. I go back to the work of my holy order, the work of God.”

“Farewell,” the princess faltered. “Farewell, you whom I have loved too well, hated too bitterly, known and revered too late. Forgiving angel, farewell—for ever.”

The monk caught those faint, sighing words, even half-breathed.

“For ever?” he cried aloud, sudden ardor lighting his whole face. “Christians live for ever, and love for ever—they never part for ever! They part as the earth parts from the sun at dusk, only to meet far brighter a little while later. You and I part here for the span of a single human life. And what is that life? One short line in the great, endless story of the Church, whose son and daughter we are. One handful of sand in the endless dunes of time, one single drop in the ocean of eternity. Farewell—for this little, fleeting moment we call a life! We part now in trouble and sorrow, but we shall meet in perfect peace. We part now as creatures of clay, but we shall meet as immortal spirits. We part in a world full of sin and grief, but we shall meet where all is purity and divine love, where no ill passions can ever touch us, where Christ reigns, and all His saints stand around Him clad in white. There, in the turn of an hourglass, in the burst of a bubble on the water, in the passing of a single wisp of cloud, she, and you, and I, shall meet again. We shall sit at the feet of angels and archangels, apostles and saints, and glow with unutterable joy, bathed in the light that streams from the shadow of God upon His throne, for ever— and ever— and ever.”

And so they parted. The monk stood erect, his eyes turned heavenward, glowing with the sacred fire of holy zeal. The princess walked slowly away, turning again and again to cast one lingering glance of awe and soft, tender regret back on that inspired, glowing figure.

She returned home subdued, her heart purged and made soft. Clement, in the fullness of time, reached Basle, and took up his new duties: he taught at the university, and preached to the crowds of the town and all the surrounding villages. The life he led could be summed up in just two words: unceasing deep study, and rigorous, devout self-mortification. The reader has already been given a small glimpse of his soul. At Basle, he grew ever deeper in holy zeal and sacred knowledge. The other brethren of his order soon began to recognize in him a true heir to the saints and martyrs of the early Church.

Little Gerard was barely three months old when a messenger came spurring hot from Tergou, mud splattered up to his knees, to fetch Catherine home. "Go back at once," she told him shortly, wiping flour from her wrists. "Tell them I will not stir—they have Kate to tend to all their silly needs."

The man departed, and Catherine turned back to Margaret, her face softening as she rested a calloused hand on the young mother’s shoulder. "There, lass, I *must* go after all. The house is all at sixes and sevens, this is the third time they’ve sent begging me to come back, and if I delay till the morrow, my old man will trudge over himself and drag me home by the ear, with a sharp flea in it for good measure."

She rattled off every trick she had learned across forty years of tending fussy infants, warned Margaret of colic, of teething fevers, of the strange little ills that creep up on a babe unlooked for, and pressed a heavy purse of silver into her palm. Margaret thanked her but refused the money. Catherine insisted, then grew sharp with frustration when Margaret would not budge. Every excuse Margaret made was so gentle, so reasonable, that Catherine rejected them out of hand—they felt thin, unwomanly, to her no-nonsense mind.

"Come now, out with your real heart, when we’re parting like this, and mayhap we’ll never see one another’s faces again," she said.

"Oh mother, do not say that!" Margaret protested.

"Alack, lass, I’ve seen too many partings that never met again. It creeps into my head every time now. When I was your age, I never thought of such things—we all thought we’d live forever, back then. So out with it."

Margaret sighed. "Well then, I would not have told you otherwise. Your Cornelis looked at me the day you first brought me to Tergou, and said plain as day, ‘So you’ve come to share with us, eh mistress?’ I told him I would never do such a thing. But mother, I will take no grudged bounty from any household. Not unless I saw my child starving, and heaven alone knows what I might do then.
