Give me only your love—for that I prize above all silver, and they do not grudge me that, as far as I can tell. Not one stiver of your coin will I carry out of your house."

"You foolish lass," Catherine huffed. "If it were me, I’d take it just to spite him."

"No you would not," Margaret smiled. "We are apples off the very same tree."

Catherine yielded with good grace, but when the final moment of parting came, they clung to each other, tears running down both their faces.

No sooner had Catherine’s boots vanished down the lane than the baby began to wail, sharp and inconsolable. Margaret bounced him, sang to him, rocked him, and could not hush him, till she suspected a stray pin. She stripped off his swaddling and searched between his clothes and his soft skin, and found a fine gold angel coin digging into his backbone.

"There now, little Gerard," she laughed through her tears. "I thought granny gave in far too sudden." She wrapped the coin in a scrap of fine linen, tucked it at the very bottom of her strongbox, and told the wide-eyed baby that she could be just as stubborn and clever as his granny, when she chose.

When Catherine got back to Tergou, she told Eli all about Margaret’s stubborn pride, and how she had outwitted it by hiding the coin. Eli only nodded, and said Margaret was right, and Catherine was wrong. Catherine tossed her head, but Eli sat quiet for a long time, turning the thought over in his mind.

Margaret had no shortage of small domestic anxieties. She still had two old men to feed, and could no longer work the long hours at her ironing and illumination that she had before the baby came. It was all she could do to keep the house clean, tend to little Gerard, and cook hot meals for all three of them. But she had a little sum of coin laid by, and she would lean over the cradle every evening and whisper to her boy that his father would be home to help them long before that money ran out. With that bright hope, and the sweet treasure of her son in her arms, she spent several soft, happy months.

But time wore on, and Gerard did not come. Stranger still, there was no letter, no word, no rumor of him at all. Her mind grew heavy with disquiet. Contrary to her usual practical, steady nature, she would sink into long sad reveries, sighing silent to herself while she stitched or stirred the pot. All the while, her little store of coin was melting away, little by little. One day she opened her cupboard and found it bare, and looked across at the two old men sitting by her hearth. Her heart swelled with pity for them, and she leaned down to the baby in his cradle and asked him how she could ever let grandfather and poor old Martin go without a hot meal. She went to her strongbox and pulled out Catherine’s hidden gold angel, and a tear of gentle, mortified shame fell right on the bright face of the coin as she unfolded the linen.

She sent Martin out to change it for smaller coin. While he was gone, a French gentleman came to her door with one of the art dealers who had offered her a pittance for her illumination work some months prior. The Frenchman told her he was sent by his sovereign, the Duchess of Burgundy, to collect the very finest masterpieces of local craft for her private Book of Hours. Margaret showed him her two best small works, and he fell utterly in love with the tiny panel she had painted of wild strawberries, creeping clover, and little wood violets, the very piece Margaret Van Eyck herself had taught her to shade. He offered her a sum of gold so large she could scarce believe her ears.

"Do not mock my need, good stranger," she said, shaking her head. "There are three mouths in this house, and none but me to fill them."

"I do not mock you, fair mistress," he said warmly. "My princess gave me strict charge: ‘Seek out the best craftsfolk, do not drive hard bargains, make them content with you, and you content with them.’ I pay you what your work is worth, no less."

A moment later Margaret was on her knees, kissing little Gerard all over his soft face, showering the four new gold pieces over his swaddling chest again and again, chattering the whole story out to him in her broken, giddy Dutch. "Oh, what a good princess, isn’t she? We will pray for her, won’t we my little lambkin, when you are old enough to say your prayers?"

Just then Martin trundled in the door, furious. "They would not change that gold angel! I swear they think I stole it off some poor traveler."

"I am beholden to you for trying," Margaret said hastily, snatching the coin from his hand, wrapping it back in its linen scrap, and tucking it away in the bottom of her strongbox once more, safe and secret.

Before that unexpected windfall ran out, Margaret was back at her ironing and starching again. But right in the middle of her busy work, Martin fell sick. He lay ill for nine days, then died. Nearly all her new gold went to bury him properly, decently, no pauper’s grave for the old man who had sat by her hearth every day.

He was gone, and his empty wooden chair sat by the fireside, for he had always preferred the warmth of her hearth to the sun outdoors once the meddlesome old busybodies left them be. Margaret would not let anyone else sit in that chair. Every time she let her gaze linger on its empty seat, it cost her a hot, quiet tear.

Now there was no one to carry her heavy bundles of laundered linen home from the great houses across town. To do it herself, she would have to leave little Gerard in the care of a neighbor. But she would not trust her most precious treasure to any mortal, and she could not bear to be parted from him for hours at a stretch. So she put out word that she was looking for a boy to carry her laundry basket every Saturday and Monday.

A plump, fresh-cheeked youth named Luke Peterson turned up at her door, blushing so hard his ears were pink, twisting his wool bonnet between his fingers. He looked no older than fifteen, though he was already eighteen. "Would a man not serve your turn just as well as a boy?" he asked.

Before he spoke, Margaret had been thinking to herself that this boy would do perfectly. But she laughed, and took his cue. "Nay, a man might ask for more coin than I can afford to pay."

"Not I!" Luke said warmly. "Mistress Margaret, I’m your neighbor, and I make a fine wage at the coopering trade. I can carry your basket before or after my day’s work, and welcome. You don’t need to pay me anything at all. We aren’t strangers, you know."

"Why, Master Luke, I know your face, but I cannot recall that we ever exchanged a single word before today," Margaret said, puzzled.

"Oh but we did!" he said. "Don’t you remember? One day you were trying to carry your heavy baby and a full pail of water all at once, and I said ‘Give me the baby to carry.’ And you said ‘Nay, I’ll give you the pitcher, and keep my bairn myself.’ So I carried the full pail all the way back to your door, and you took it from me right here, and you said ‘I’m muckle obliged to you, young man,’ in that soft sweet voice you have, not sharp the way everyone else on this street speaks to a body."

"I do remember that now, Master Luke. And it was the very least I could say," Margaret smiled.

"If you will say as much every time I carry your basket, I won’t care how far I bear it, or how heavy it is," he said.

"Nay, nay," Margaret said, coloring faintly. "I will not impose on your good nature. You are young, and you are very kind. What say I give you your supper every Saturday night when you bring the linen home, and a warm dawn breakfast every Monday morning? Will that make us even, a little?"

"As you please," Luke mumbled, red as a cherry. "Only don’t go telling people I asked for two measly meals just to carry a basket."

With chubby, good-hearted Luke’s timely help, and the strength Heaven lent the hardworking young mother to balance all her many troubles, the household ran smooth for a little while. But Margaret’s heart grew heavier and heavier with every week of Gerard’s long, strange silence. Suspense, that cruel mental torturer, began to tear at her heart with its hot pincers, till she cried out, loud and vehement, "Oh that I could only know the worst!"

While she was in that state, one day she heard a heavy, unfamiliar step climbing the stairs. She started, trembling. That’s no step I know, she thought. Ill tidings.

The door opened, and Eli stood there, grave and gentle, an unexpected visitor. Margaret stared at him in silence, her agitation rising by the second.

"Girl," he said, "the skipper is home from Rome."

Margaret gasped, clutching the edge of the table. "One word. Is he alive?"

"Surely I hope so. No one has seen him dead."

"Then someone must have seen him alive!" she cried.

"No, girl. No one has seen him, dead or alive, these many past months in Rome. My daughter Kate thinks he has wandered off to some other city, far away. She bade me tell you that thought."

"Ay, like enough," Margaret said gloomily, staring over at the cradle. "Like enough. My poor babe."

The old man, his voice thin and tired, asked her for a morsel to eat—he had walked all the way from Tergou fasting. Margaret pitied him even through the fog of her own agitation, and she cooked him a hot meal, trembling the whole time, hardly knowing what she stirred. Before he left, he laid his hand soft on her head.

"Be he alive, or be he dead," he said, "I look on you as my own daughter. Is there nothing I can do for you today? Think hard, lass."

"Ay, old man," Margaret whispered. "Pray for him. And pray for me."

Eli sighed, and trundled slowly, heavily down the stairs. Margaret listened half-stupidly to his footsteps, till the last sound of them faded away. Then she sank down moaning beside the cradle, and drew little Gerard tight to her bosom.

"Oh my poor fatherless boy," she sobbed. "My fatherless boy."

The small hosier’s household at Tergou were gathered over their midday rye bread and pottage, the hearth glowing soft against the crisp autumn chill, when Luke Peterson burst through the door, dust caked thick on his boots and wool tunic, his breath ragged from riding nonstop. “Good people, Mistress Catherine is wanted instantly at Rotterdam.”

Eli the hosier paused mid-bite, and his wife Catherine wiped grease from her fingers on her apron, frowning. “My name is Catherine, young man. Kate, that will be Margaret, sure.”

“Ay, dame,” Luke nodded, still catching his breath. “She said to me, ‘Good Luke, hie thee to Tergou, and ask for Eli the hosier, and pray his wife Catherine to come to me, for God His love.’ I didn’t wait for daylight to set out.”

“Holy saints!” Catherine clapped a hand to her chest. “Has Gerard come home, then? Nay, she would have said so at once. What on earth can have befallen her?” She tumbled over wild guesses one after another, till Kate, her stepdaughter, ventured timidly that perhaps the young messenger knew the truth of it.

“That I do,” Luke said gravely. “Her babe is a-dying. And she was so wrapped up in the little lad, it has all but broken her.”

A quick, furtive glint of satisfaction passed between Eli’s two ne’er-do-well sons, Cornelis and Sybrandt. Luckily for them, Catherine never saw it, her face turned straight to her husband. “Now Eli,” she cried fiercely, “if you say a single word against me going to her, we shall quarrel after all these years of peace.”

“Who gainsays thee, foolish woman?” Eli grunted, already pushing back his bench to stand. “Quarrel with your own shadow while I run and borrow Peter’s mule for ye.”

“Bless thee, my good man!” Catherine’s face softened. “Thou never yet failed me at a pinch. Eat your dinners who can, while I go make ready.”

She brought Luke back with her in their cart, cross-questioning him so sharply then wheedling him so gently by turns that before they had even cleared the edge of Tergou, she had every last scrap of information he possessed dragged out into the open. Margaret met her at her Rotterdam cottage door, pale as linen, her eyes hollow with weeping, and threw her arms around Catherine’s neck, her look full of desperate pleading.

“Come, he is alive, thank God,” Catherine said, scanning her face keenly, and stepped past her to the cradle where the babe lay listless, his little cheeks sunken. She looked from the wasting child to the hollow-eyed mother, back and again, and said plainly: “Lucky you sent for me. The child is poisoned.”

“Poisoned! By whom?” Margaret gasped.

“By you. You have been fretting yourself to skin and bone over Gerard.”

“Nay, indeed, mother! How can I help fretting?”

“Don’t tell me that. A nursing mother has no business to grieve so. She must turn her mind away from her sorrow to the comfort that lies in her lap. Know you not the child pines if the mother vexes herself? This comes of all your reading and writing – those idle crafts befit a man, but they drive all useful, plain sense out of a woman’s head. The child must be weaned at once.”

“Oh, you cruel woman!” Margaret burst out vehemently. “I am sorry I sent for you. Would you rob me of the only bit of comfort I have left in all the world? When I nurse my Gerard, I forget I am the most unhappy creature beneath the sun.”

“That you do not,” Catherine retorted staunchly, “or he would not be wasting away this way.”

“Mother!” Margaret begged, tears spilling over.

“’Tis hard, I know,” Catherine relented, softening a little. “But bethink thee: would it not be far harder to look down and see his lovely wee face looking up at you out of a little coffin?”

“Oh Jesu, no!” Margaret shuddered.

“And how could you face all your other troubles with your heart aye full of grief and your lap empty of your boy?”

“Oh, mother, I consent to anything. Only save my son.”

“That is a good lass. Trust to me! I stand outside your grief, and see clearer than you can.”

Unfortunately, there was another consent to be gained: the babe’s, and he was far more refractory than his mother. “There,” Margaret said, trying to sound like she was scolding his misbehavior, “he loves me too well to give up my milk easy.” But Catherine was a match for them both. On her walk through the village that morning, she had spotted a hale, young woman sitting outside her own door with a fat rosy infant of her own, and now she went to her, explained the case, and asked if she would nurse the pining little lad temporarily, till Margaret could wean him proper.

The young woman agreed with a smile, popped her own babe into his cradle, and came straight into Margaret’s house. She dropped a curtsey, and Catherine put the ailing child into her arms. The woman examined him, pitied him, cooed over him, and proceeded to nurse him as naturally as if he had been her own flesh and blood. Margaret, paralyzed at her ease, cast a rueful glance at Catherine and burst out sobbing.

The visitor looked up. “What is to do? Wife, ye told me not the mother was unwilling.”

“She is not,” Catherine said. “She is only a fool. Never heed her; and you, Margaret, I am ashamed of you.”

“You are a cruel, hard-hearted woman,” Margaret sobbed.

“Them as take in hand to guide the weak need be hardish,” Catherine replied bluntly. “And you will excuse me; but you are not my flesh and blood – and your boy is.” She let that plain speech sink in a moment before she added, “Come now, this good wife is robbing her own babe to save yours, and you can think of nothing better than blubbering right in her face. Out fie, for shame!”

“Nay, dame,” the nurse put in gently. “Thank Heaven, I have enough milk for my own and for hers to boot. Prithee wyte not on her! Maybe the troubles o’ life have soured her own milk.”

“And her heart into the bargain,” the remorseless Catherine said, but not unkindly.

Margaret looked her full in the face, then dropped her gaze. “I know I ought to be very grateful to you,” she sobbed to the nurse, then turned her head away over the back of a chair, so she would not have to witness the intolerable sight of another woman nursing her Gerard, and little Gerard making no distinction between this new stranger and the mother he had known his whole short life.

“You are very welcome, my poor woman,” the nurse said softly. “And so are you, Mistress Catherine, which are my townswoman, and know it not.”

“What, are ye from Tergou? All the better, but I cannot call your face to mind.”

“Oh, you know not me: my husband and me, we are very humble folk by your standard. But true Eli and his wife are known and respected all through the town. So I am at your call, dame; at yours, wife; and yours, my pretty poppet, night or day.”

“There’s a woman of the right old sort,” Catherine declared as the door closed behind her.

“I HATE her. I HATE her. I HATE her,” Margaret burst out, fierce with the fervor of raw grief. Catherine only laughed. “That is right. Better say it out loud than sit sly and brood over it. It is very natural, after all. Come, here is your bundle o’ comfort. Take and hate that, if ye can,” and she put the now drowsy little Gerard into her lap.

“No, no,” Margaret said, turning her head half away from him – she could not for her life turn the other half. “He is not my child now; he is hers. I know not why she left him here, for my part. It was very good of her not to take him to her house, cradle and all; oh! oh! oh! Like father, like son – some other woman has got him away from me, oh! oh!” Catherine let her cry it out in peace, sorry for her pain.

After that, whenever Catherine wanted Joan’s help, she would take little Gerard out for a walk in the fresh air. Margaret never objected, never voiced the smallest bit of incredulity, but every time they returned, she was red-eyed and in tears. Before long, she was altogether as eager as Catherine to get the boy weaned. It was done at last, and soon Gerard recovered his health and vigour – only to fall to the next trial of teething. Here Catherine’s long years of motherhood made her wisdom invaluable, and even in the thick of her grief and anxiety over the missing Gerard, Margaret had moments of pure bliss, watching tiny new teeth peep through her son’s soft red gums. “Teeth, mother?” she would cry. “I call them not teeth, but pearls of pearls.” Each little white nub that sparkled into view was to her the greatest feat Nature had ever achieved. Catherine shared the illusion entirely: had a stranger told them that fields of standing corn were equally admirable, Margaret would have stared at him like a wounded gazelle, and Catherine would have marched him straight out the door. Every new pearl’s arrival was announced with a shriek of triumph by whichever of them spotted it first.

Catherine gossiped often with Joan, and learned she was the wife of Jorian Ketel, a man from Tergou who had once been servant to Ghysbrecht Van Swieten, the powerful burgomaster, before he had fallen out of favour and returned to his native Rotterdam. His friends had got him the post of parish sexton, and between that and his carpentering work, he did very well for a humble man. Catherine told Joan in turn whose child she had nursed, all about Margaret and her lost Gerard, and the deep, gnawing anxiety his total silence had plunged them all into. “Ay,” Joan sighed, “the world is full of trouble.”

One day Joan leaned in close to Catherine, and whispered: “It’s my belief my man knows more about your Gerard than anybody in these parts; but he has grown closer than an oyster of late. Drop in some day just afore sunset, and set him talking. And for our Lady’s sake say not I set you on. The only hiding he ever gave me was for babbling his business, and I do not want another. Gramercy! I married a man for the comfort of the thing, not to be beat for every word I say.”

Catherine dropped round to their cottage that evening. Jorian was ready enough to tell her how he had once befriended her son, and even perhaps saved his life – but that was no news to Catherine. The moment she began to cross-question him, to ask if he could guess why her lost boy neither came home nor wrote, he cast a grim glare at his wife, who met it with a look of perfect, stolid innocence, and his answers turned short and sullen. “What should he know more than any other man?” he grunted, and after a long pause added, “Think you the burgomaster takes such as me into his secrets?”

“Oh, then the burgomaster knows something?” Catherine said sharply.

“Likely. Who else should?”

“I’ll go ask him.”

“I would. Go make him mine enemy. That is what a poor fellow always gets if he says a single word to you women.” From that moment Jorian shrunk inwards, as impenetrable as a hedgehog, and almost as prickly.

His conduct left the two poor women writhing in agony of mind, wracked with alarm and irritated curiosity. They knew Ghysbrecht was Gerard’s mortal enemy: he had stopped their marriage, imprisoned him, hunted him across the country. And here his old servant had hinted, almost against his will, that this same enemy held the secret to Gerard’s silence. They sifted every word, every look of Jorian’s, but the truth stayed dark and mysterious. Finally Catherine told Margaret to go and speak to him herself. “You are young, you are fair. You will maybe get more out of him than I could.”

The guess was a reasonable one. Margaret tucked little Gerard into her arms, and tapped timidly at Jorian’s door just before sunset. “Come in,” called a sturdy voice. She stepped inside, and there sat Jorian huddled by the fireside. At the sight of her, he rose, snorted, and stormed straight out of the house.

“Is that for me, wife?” Margaret said, turning bright red.

“You must excuse him,” Joan replied, a little coldly. “He lays it to your door that he is a poor man instead of a rich one. It is something about a piece of parchment that went amissing. He got not a penny from the burgomaster all along of that one.”

“Alas! Gerard took it,” Margaret said, wincing.

“Likely. But my man says you should not have let him – you were pledged to him to keep them all safe. And sooth to say, I blame not my Jorian for being wroth. ‘Tis hard for a poor man to be so near fortune and lose it by those he has befriended. However, I tell him another story. Says I, ‘Folk that are out o’ trouble like you and me didn’t ought to be too hard on folk that are in trouble; and she has plenty.’ Going already? What is all your hurry, mistress?”

“Oh, it is not for me to drive the goodman out of his own house,” Margaret said, already making for the door.

“Well, let me kiss the bairn afore ye go. He is not in fault anyway, poor innocent.”

Stung by that cruel rebuff, Margaret came to a secret resolution she did not confide even to Catherine. Six weeks after she had arrived, the good old woman from Tergou packed her bags and headed home. On little Gerard’s first birthday that soon followed, Margaret did no work at all, but put on her finest Sunday gown, tucked her boy in her arms, and went to the village church, where she prayed long and fervently for Gerard’s safe return.

That very same day and hour, half a continent away in the minster church at Basle, Father Clement celebrated a mass for Margaret’s departed soul, in the full and pious belief that she was long dead.

As the rogue Sybrandt once slurred, a lie is not like a blow from a curtal axe. The consequences of any strike with a physical weapon can be guessed, more or less, but a lie knows no bounds at all: by its very nature it ramifies far beyond any human ability to calculate. In ordinary life, a single lie has cost a man his life, or laid waste the homes of two or three. In this tale, that one heartless falsehood wove such tremendous, unforeseen harm the traitors who spun it reaped barely a scrap of the gain they’d chased.
The two brothers who invented the lie only to cut Gerard out as a claimant to their father’s property found their scheme backfiring the moment little Gerard, the orphaned son of their dead sibling, stole their mother’s entire affection. Worse still, Eli openly proclaimed one day that with Gerard lost and presumed dead, he had drafted a new will that provided handsomely for little Gerard and Margaret, his poor son’s widow. The look that passed between the two black sheep of the family was a warning to every traitor who thinks their plots will turn out as planned. Cornelis had the words “Gerard is most likely still alive” on the tip of his tongue, but caught his mother’s sharp, suspicious eye and bit his tongue in time.
Ghysbrecht Van Swieten, the other co-conspirator in that lie, was now a frail, failing old man. He could see his end fast approaching, when all his hoarded wealth would slip from his cold fingers, and all his misdeeds would cling to his soul for eternity. Too shrewd to fool himself entirely, he had never been free of sudden, sharp gusts of remorse. When he intercepted Gerard’s letter to Margaret, he struck a petty, cowardly compromise: his ravenous Avarice insisted “I will not give up the land and the money I stole from her,” while his tiny, cowering Conscience added “But I will cause her no unnecessary pain.” He pried open the seal first, found no mention of the stolen deed anywhere in the text, then hand-delivered the letter to Margaret, patting himself on the back for the small decency – a self-assigned offset to his treachery, measured on the lopsided scale of a man who acts as judge of his own crimes.
The birth of Margaret’s child shocked him to his core, and cast his old treachery in a horrifying new light. If his lie held, he would be the one to bring public dishonour to the daughter of one old friend, the granddaughter of another, all while he continued to hoard her stolen land. These thoughts gnawed at him at a time of life when the body’s strength ebbs, and the memory of long-dead loved ones rises sharp and vivid, filling him with gloomy, waking horrors. Still he dared not confess: the local cure was an honest man, who would have forced him to disgorge every stolen penny. For him, Avarice was a habit rooted deep in his bones, while Penitence was no more than a passing, weak sentiment.
Things stood thus, when one day he returned from the town hall to his home, and found a veiled woman waiting in his vestibule, holding a small child in her arms. He assumed she was there to beg indulgence for some shameful affair, and addressed her magisterially – until she dropped her veil and looked him full in the face. It was Margaret Brandt.
Her sudden appearance and blazing earnestness startled him so thoroughly he could not hide his confusion.
“Where is my Gerard?” she cried, her bosom heaving. “Is he alive?”
“For aught I know,” he stammered. “I hope so, for your sake. Prithee, step into this room – the servants will hear us.”
“Not a step,” Margaret said, and she grabbed his shoulder, holding him fast with all the raw, fiery energy of a heartbroken, desperate woman. “You hold the secret that is breaking my heart. Why has not my Gerard come home, nor sent a single line these many months? Answer me, or I will shout it loud enough for every soul in this town to hear, let alone your servants. My misery is too great to be played with as a trivial jest.”
He persisted in claiming he knew nothing of Gerard, but Margaret told him the people who had sent her to him had told her a very different tale. “You do know why he neither comes nor sends,” she said, steady as a rock.
At this Ghysbrecht turned paler and paler, but he summoned all his remaining dignity and snapped, “Would you believe those two knaves against a man of worship?”
“What two knaves?” Margaret shot back, sharp as a needle.
He stammered and floundered. “Said ye not –? There I am a poor old broken man, whose memory is all shaken. You confuse me so, I know not what I say.”
“Ay sir, your memory is shaken right enough, or you would never be my enemy. My father dragged you out of the plague ward when no other soul would come within an arm’s length of you, and was your loyal friend all his days. My grandfather Floris pulled you out of early poverty, and loved you from boyhood to manhood. Three generations of us you have known. This is the fourth.” She held the child up to him. “This is your old friend Peter’s grandchild, and your old friend Floris’s great-grandchild. Look down on his innocent face, and think of theirs!”
“Woman, you torture me,” Ghysbrecht sighed, sinking heavily onto a stone bench.
Margaret saw her advantage at once. She knelt before him, and set the little boy right on his knees. “This fatherless babe is poor Margaret Brandt’s, who never did you ill, and comes of a race that loved you. Nay, look at his face. It will melt you more than any word of mine. Saints of heaven, what can a poor desolate girl and her babe have done to wipe out all memory of your own young days, when you were as guiltless as he is, now looking up in your face and imploring you to give him back his father?” She held the child up higher and higher, the little one gurgling soft under the old man’s gaze.
Ghysbrecht cast one wild, anguished look at the child, then another at the kneeling mother, and leaped up shrieking, “Avaunt, ye pair of adders!” The sting of his guilty soul lent his frail old limbs a burst of unnatural vigour, and he paced rapidly back and forth, wringing his hands, tearing at his own white hair. “Forget those days? I forget all else. Oh, woman, woman, sleeping or waking I see nothing but the faces of the dead, hear nothing but the voices of the dead, and soon I shall be among the dead myself. There, there, what is done is done. I am in hell. I am in hell.”
That unnatural force drained out of him as quickly as it came. He staggered, and would have fallen flat if Margaret had not caught him with her one free arm, crying out for help. A pair of servants came running, and carried him away half-swooning. The last Margaret saw of him was his old furrowed face, white and helpless as the white hair that hung loose over the servant’s elbow.
“Heaven forgive me,” she whispered. “I doubt I have killed the poor old man.”
Her attempt to pierce the mystery had left it as dark as ever, if not darker. When she pondered every word he had spoken, her suspicion only hardened that Ghysbrecht did know Gerard’s secret. “And those two knaves he thought had let slip the truth to me?” she murmured. “Oh, my Gerard, my poor deserted babe, you and I are wading in waters far deeper than we ever dreamed.”
The journey to Tergou had cost her more money than she could spare, and a customer who owed her a large sum ran off without paying his debt. Once more, she was forced to fetch Catherine’s gold angel out of its hiding place. But strange to say, when she came down the stairs clutching it in her hand, she found loose silver scattered across the table, with a scrap of writing laid atop: For Gerard his wife.
She fell on the note with a cry of shock that swelled, moments later, into a cry of wild joy. “He is alive! He sends me this by some friendly hand!” She kissed the scrap of paper over and over, and tucked it deep in her bodice, next to her heart.
Time rolled on, and still no news of Gerard. But roughly every two months, a small sum of silver found its way into her home. Sometimes it lay on the kitchen table. Once it was flung through her bedroom window, tucked in a small leather purse. Once it was tucked at the bottom of Luke the peddler’s basket, after he had stopped off at the public house to chat with a friend. The giver, or his agent, was never caught. Catherine disclaimed all knowledge of it. Margaret Van Eyck swore she had no hand in the gifts. So did Eli. Every time the money arrived, Margaret would turn to little Gerard and murmur, “Oh, my poor deserted child, you and I are still wading in deep waters.” She poured at least half of that modest but useful supply into dressing the little boy far neater than most children of their station. “If this money does come from Gerard, he shall find his boy spotless the moment he steps through the door.” Soon all the other mothers on the street began to sneer at her, especially the ones whose own brats ran around in rags, elbows poking through their tattered sleeves.
The months rolled on, and the sharp, burning agony of anxious waiting faded into a cold, dead numbness in her heart. She returned to her first darkest fear: Gerard must be dead. She would never see her boy’s father again, never lay eyes on their marriage lines. This last grief, which had been softened for a time by Eli and Catherine’s open recognition of their betrothal, now revived in full force: strangers would never look so favourably on her story. Often she moaned over the fear of her boy being marked as illegitimate. “Is it not enough that we are bereaved of all we love? Must we be dishonoured too? Oh, that we had ne’er been born.”
A change came over Peter Brandt then. His mind, clouded for nearly two years after his paralytic stroke, seemed to clear at last. He had long intervals of full lucidity, where he and Margaret would sit and talk of Gerard, until the fog drifted back over his wits. But one day, when Margaret returned home after a few hours’ absence, she found him conversing easily with Catherine, a thing he had not managed since the stroke first fell.
“Eh, lass, why did you have to wander out?” Catherine said. “I told him every last thing, and we sat and cried together over thy troubles.”
Margaret stood silent, joy glowing in her face, looking back and forth between the two. Peter smiled softly at her, and held out his hand. “Come, let me bless thee.”
She knelt at his feet, and he blessed her most eloquently, telling her she was the most loving, truest, most obedient daughter Heaven had ever sent to a poor old widowed man. “May thy son be to thee what thou hast been to me!”
He dozed off shortly after that, and the two women whispered together. Catherine said, “All our talk just now was of Gerard. It lies heavy on his mind. His poor foggy head must have been listening to us all the months he seemed completely senseless. Margaret, he is a very sharp man, and thought of all kinds of things: ‘He may be in prison,’ he said, ‘or forced to go fighting for some foreign king, or sent to Constantinople to copy old manuscripts there, or gone into the Church after all.’ He always had a strong leaning that way.”
“Ah, mother,” Margaret whispered sadly in reply, “he only deceives himself, the same as we do.”
Ere she could finish the sentence, a strange, loud interruption burst out. A great voice cried, “I SEE HIM, I SEE HIM.” The old man’s eyes were wide and dilated, as if he were staring straight through the cottage walls. “IN A BOAT, ON A GREAT RIVER, COMING THIS WAY. His face is sore disfigured – but I knew him. Gone! Gone! All dark now.”
He sank back weakly, fumbling. “Where is Margaret?”
“Dear father, I am by thy side,” Margaret sobbed. “Oh, mother! Mother, what is this?”
“I cannot see thee now,” he whispered feebly, “but a moment agone I saw every corner of the whole world. Aye, aye. I am ready. Is this thy hand? Bless thee, my child, bless thee. Weep not! The tree is ripe.”
The old physician had read the signs aright. Those calm, soft words were his last. The next moment, he drooped his head, and gently, placidly, drifted away from earth, as soft as an infant sinking off to sleep. The torch of his life had flared bright one last time, before it went out for good.

Margaret, who had wept so freely for the sad, slow decline of old Martin, could no more bear his final parting with cold stoicism than a tender sapling can bear the felling of the oak it has leaned on for years. Catherine, her betrothed mother-in-law, did her best to soothe her with well-worn platitudes: she told Martin had gone happy, that he himself had said his life was fully ripe, ready to fall from the bough. But her words curdled to bitterness when she added that now there were fewer mouths to feed, and one heavy burden off Margaret’s shoulders.

“Burden?” Margaret gasped, her face streaked with fresh tears. “Such ‘burdens’ were the only joys I had left. They filled this desolate heart of mine, and now it is not just desolate – it is hollow, empty as that oak chair pulled up to the hearth. Oh, that empty chair! My chest aches so to look at it. Poor old man, how could I have loved him by halves? I used to sit and watch him drowse, and think but for me, you would have starved in your old age, once so learned and sharp, till you grew as helpless as my own sweet babe. I loved him more like my child than my father. Oh, empty chair! Oh, empty heart! Woe is me, woe is me!”

No words of comfort would stem the tide of her pious grief, and at last Catherine fell silent, hanging her head in shame. A day later she spoke her true thought out loud: “I’ve been talking at you out of my head, not my heart. You are right to turn a deaf ear to such empty words. If I was in your shoes, I would mourn the old man just as hard as you do.” Margaret hugged her tight, and that flash of unvarnished sympathy did her more good than a month of pious platitudes.

Catherine’s heart ached for the girl she had come to love as her own daughter. “My poor lass, you were never made to live all alone. Stop wasting your youth pining for my son Gerard. Either he died out on that mad pilgrimage of his to Rome, or he has proven a traitor and forgotten you. It cuts my own heart to say it, but who can deny the plain truth? Your father is gone, and I cannot linger at your side every hour of every day. There is an honest lad who has loved you well these many years – take him, take the comfort he offers. Heaven sends us these souls to torment us and cheer us, for we are nothing at all in the world without someone to lean on.”

When Margaret stared back at her, bewildered, Catherine huffed a laugh. “Surely you are not so blind you have never seen it?”
“Seen what? Who?”
“Why, Luke Peterson, of course.”
“Our Luke? The boy who carries my market basket on market days?”
“Nay, he is turned nineteen, and a fine strapping healthy lad, not a child. I asked around, and every soul in Rotterdam says he is a steady, capable workman, and never touches a drop of strong drink – a rare thing for a Rotterdam lad, most of whom are half man, half drunkard’s sponge.”

Margaret smiled for the first time in days. “Luke loves dried suet puddings more than anything else in the world,” she said. “I make them just the way he likes, I do believe that is the only reason he comes a-courting round here.” Then she flushed bright red. “But if I thought he was daring to come after the wife of your son – the wife that is, and ought to be – I would show him the door so fast his boots would spin.”
“Nay, nay, do not go making mischief for nothing,” Catherine said quickly. “Poor lad! I wormed his secret out of him near on a twelvemonth ago.”
“Oh, mother, and you let him keep coming?”
“I did think of you,” Catherine defended herself. “I said to myself, if the fool is daft enough to be her willing slave for nothing, all the better for her. A lone woman is lost without a man about to fetch and carry her little errands. But now my mind is changed, and I think the best use you can put him to is marry him.”

“So you would wed me off to the first lout that looks my way, even against my own heart?” Margaret said, her voice sharp with hurt. “Gerard has no one in all the world but me. I will not believe he is dead till I see his gravestone with my own eyes, nor that he is false till I see him standing hand in hand with another lover. Foolish boy – I will not be civil to him ever again.”

The poor unsuspecting Luke, used to warm welcomes and extra slices of pudding at Margaret’s hearth, walked straight into a wall of cold shortness. At first he was hardly spoken to, then spoken to sharply, till the big soft-hearted fellow started whimpering like a lost hound, and asked Margaret plain what he had ever done to offend her.
“Nothing. It is all my fault. I am cursed,” Margaret said. “If you take my advice, you will keep out of my way for a good long while.”
“It was all my doing, Luke,” Catherine cut in, before he could spiral further.
“Dame Catherine?” Luke blinked at her, bewildered. “What did I ever do to you, to set her against me?”
“Nay, I meant all for the best. I told her I had seen you were looking at her through a wedding ring, and she will not hear a word of it.”
“There was no need to tell her that,” Luke said, plainspoken. “She knows I have been courting her this twelvemonth.”
“Not I,” Margaret said, wide-eyed. “Else I would never have opened my door to you.”
“Why, I come here every Saturday night,” Luke said, confused. “That is how lads in Rotterdam do court. If you sup with a lass on a Saturday, that is official wooing, everyone knows that.”

“Oh, that is Rotterdam’s custom, is it?” Margaret said, a faint glint of amusement in her tear-reddened eyes. “Next time you come, make it Thursday or Friday. For my part, I was fully convinced you only hung around for my puddings, boy.”
“I do like your puddings well enough,” Luke said tenderly. “You make them far better than my own mother does. But I like you far better than any pudding.”

Margaret’s smile faded, and her voice turned soft but firm as iron. “Then you have seen the last of those puddings. How dare you speak so to another man’s promised wife, when he is far away on his travels? You need not trouble to come back here any more, Luke. I can carry my own market basket well enough.”
“Oh, very well,” Luke moped. He sat stupid and silent for a little while, then rose and said sadly to Catherine, “Dame, I reckon I got the sack,” and trundled out the door.

But the very next Saturday, Catherine found him huddled on their doorstep, blubbering so hard his shoulders shook. He said he had gotten so used to walking the path to their cottage every Saturday night, every other street in Rotterdam felt strange and cold to him. She went inside and told Margaret, who sighed, and relented a little. “Poor Luke. He can come in again, if he will only know his place, and treat me like a wedded wife waiting for her husband, no foolish talk of wooing.”

Catherine ran back to relay the news, then nudged the hesitating Luke hard in the ribs. “Pshaw, boy! Promises are only pie-crust, made to be bent. Promise her all the world, sooner than sit outside on the step like a fool, when one word will get you inside. Humour her every little whim, run all her errands, wait it out. A lone woman is never one to hold out forever. If my poor Gerard never comes home to claim her, you will be sure to win her in time.”

For more than a twelvemonth, Brother Clement had tended Basle’s souls: teaching catechism to the town’s children, preaching under the vaulted arches of the Dominican chapel, and dividing his remaining hours between prayer and quiet study of a new language he had long suspected he would soon be called to use. Then one blustery spring afternoon, a travel-worn figure stumbled through the priory door, cloak caked in Rhine mud, scrip bulging, a triumphant fire dancing in his eyes. It was Brother Jerome.

“Give all glory to God, Brother Clement,” he gasped, brushing dust from his tonsure. “The way is clear. You may ride for England at my side, at last.”

Clement, who had long awaited this day, did not even pause to rise from his stool. “I am ready,” he said softly. “These months, between homilies and vigil hours, I have pored over the English tongue, till I can speak to their folk as one of their own, not a foreigner mouthing stilted Latin phrases.”

“That was wise forethought,” Jerome nodded, leaning against the stone wall to catch his breath. He explained his long delay: he had traveled all the way to Rome, and secured extraordinary papal bulls granting them two rare privileges: full authority to collect alms across every parish in England for the Church’s charitable works, and leave to hear confession in every secular monastery on the isle, no prior abbot’s approval required. “So gird up your frock, brother,” he finished, clapping Clement on the shoulder. “We go forth to strike a strong blow for Holy Mother Church, and root out the mischief the Franciscans have sown across those northern parishes.”

The two friars set off down the Rhine, preaching their way toward the coast that would carry them across the Channel. In large market towns, they shared the pulpit, speaking in turn to packed congregations. In the tiny riverside hamlets, they split paths, one taking the east bank, one the west, agreeing to meet at the next ferry crossing a day’s march ahead. Both were preachers of rare skill, but their styles could not have been more different. Jerome’s oratory was grand, stately, weighted with solemn reverence for sacred text – though some unkind souls might have called it a touch rigid, its focus narrowed to only the strictest theological topics, its measured cadence a little too unchanging for crowds used to livelier roadside sermons. Clement, by contrast, was fire and flexibility all at once. He wove colloquial turns of phrase into his homilies, soft as a lullaby one moment, curling around the listener’s heart and nudging their reason to see their own sins without sting. But when the spirit moved him, he soared far higher than Jerome’s most solemn grandeur, rising to heights of passion that matched the tales of ancient inspired prophets, or the greatest heathen orators of old: vehement as a gale, rushing as a mountain torrent, blazing as lightning, he thundered, flashed, and swept all before him on waves of rushing eloquence that left crowds breathless.

The narrator pauses here, noting he would transcribe full passages of those fiery sermons, but five small barriers stand in the way: the task is difficult, time is short, he has recreated them elsewhere in his work, a later skilled imitator has done the job even better, and while identical peas are a mark of quality, identical passages in a book are nothing but vice.

What he will reveal, though, is Clement’s quiet secret: before every stop, he would slip a few pence to the local baker or tavern maid, to learn the recent troubles of the town, and the particular sin that clung thickest to its inhabitants. Jerome, unbending and uncompromising, would never stoop to such a trick – he preached the same unchanging truth to every crowd, tailored to no man’s weaknesses.

At one large market town a few leagues back from the Rhine, they climbed the same stone pulpit in the central church, one after the other. Jerome went first, preaching against the sin of vanity in dress, a favourite theme of his. His words were sharp, satirical, eloquent – and the crowd listened with perfect, unperturbed complacency. It was a vice none of them were much guilty of.

Then Clement stepped up, and preached against drunkenness. It was the town’s besetting sin, and one no local priest ever dared speak against: the entire secular clergy was drunk on spiced ale most nights, and popular prejudice had long wrapped the vice in a sacred, untouchable cloak. Clement did not hold back. He rained blows on it from every page of Holy Writ, and from every known tale of worldly woe. Drunkenness was no mere small fault, he thundered: it was the nursing mother of almost every other crime, the root of theft, of brawling, of murder. He reminded them of the recent parricide committed on their own streets, by an honest, hardworking man who had been blind drunk when he struck his father down. He told them of the neighbouring village where a gang of drunkards had roasted one of their own comrades alive over a tavern fire, in a stupid, witless frolic they could not even remember the next morning.

“Your late prince,” he called out, his voice ringing off the rafters, “they say he died of an apoplexy, but every man of you knows in his heart he drank himself to death. Last month, one of your own aldermen perished in the gutter, so deep in his cups he suffocated in a puddle of mud. Your children go bare-backed in cold weather, your wives go hungry at the end of every week, so you may fill your bellies with ale that turns you into worse beasts than the swine you herd: silly as calves, raging as wild boars, driving your families to ruin and your souls straight to hell. I tell you, your town, your very whole nation, would sink to the very dregs of mankind if your women drank as deep as you do. How long do you think they will stay temperate? How long will they resist the example of their own husbands and fathers? Vice never stands still. You will mend your ways, or you will live to see them sink down to your level – it has already happened in Bohemia, where women drink alongside men now. What think you? Would you love to see your wives drunken? Your own mothers, rolling drunk in the gutters?”

A great shout of horror burst from the crowd – medieval congregations did not sit silent and passive while a sermon moved them. “Ah, that strikes home, does it not?” Clement cried. “What madmen you are! You think it shocks your sinful, unreasoning selves to see a woman made a beast of drink – yet you think the all-pure God is less shocked, when man, His noblest creation, debases himself to that very same state?”

He closed the sermon with two vivid, unflinching pictures, laid out in sharp detail: the ragged, hungry home of a drunkard, his children crying for bread, his wife in rags; and the warm, peaceful home of a sober man, his table full, his family safe at his side. They were so true to life that the women in the congregation began to murmur aloud, “Eh, that is the very truth, that word.”

The sermon set the whole town abuzz. Crowds clustered in knots on the streets: the men grumbled and fumed at the preacher for daring to rebuke their favourite pastime, while the women at first made a great show of standing with their husbands, declaring a working man had every right to his ale after a long day’s labour, that they would never trade their men for lily-livered milksops. The very next evening, though, nearly a hundred of those same women swarmed around Brother Clement in the market square, stuffing his alms wallet full of the finest bread and cheese and honey the town had to offer, plucking the roses right out of their hair to lay at his feet, kissing the hem of his coarse Dominican frock and blessing him for daring to rebuke their drunken, sot husbands at last.

Jerome, for his part, had thought the sermon far too focused on earthly, worldly matters. “Drunkenness is no heresy, Clement,” he had protested. “There is no cause to devote an entire sermon to it.” But as they traveled further down the Rhine, he was forced to admit he was surprised: Clement’s sermons sank deeper into their hearers’ hearts than his own ever did, making men stop and think, weep, and even amend their wicked ways. “He has the gift of stooping to the level their souls are at,” Jerome mused. “Yet he can soar high enough when the need calls for it.”

It puzzled Jerome, who had long felt a quiet, secret sense of superiority to his softer, more tender brother. Two hundred miles into their journey, the puzzlement curdled into quiet displeasure – but he reined that feeling in, judging it petty and unworthy. “Souls are like the locks on a door,” he told himself. “Preachers must be like their keys, each shaped differently, or the Church will never open those doors for God to step through. And for certain, this novice holds the right key for these northern souls, for he is a northern man himself, born and raised among them.”

And so they traveled slowly down the Rhine, sometimes drifting a few miles downstream on a passing barge, but more often walking the muddy banks, preaching at every village crossroads, teaching the children, hearing the confessions of thousands of sinners, until at last they stepped onto the quay of Dusseldorf. It was the very same small quay where long ago, Gerard and Denys had climbed aboard a boat to sail up the Rhine. The friars set foot on that same worn stone. The streets were unchanged. The old Silver Lion tavern still hung its familiar sign over the door. Nothing had altered at all – save for the barefoot friar walking slowly through its lanes, his heart calm, his old passions long stilled, hands folded across his breast, eyes meekly bent on the ground, a true, devoted son of Saint Dominic and Holy Church.

The peat fire glowed soft and golden on the cottage hearth, gilding the edges of Eli’s ale tankard and the frayed cuffs of his two layabout sons, Cornelis and Sybrandt, who skulked idly in the shadowed corner, listless as lost hounds since they’d received word they believed confirmed Gerard’s death far from home.

Eli looked up when Catherine nudged his elbow. “Eli,” she said, sharp but not unkind, “answer me straight as a man, and I’ll ask no more of you today. What is wormwood?”

Caught off guard mid-sip, Eli blinked, fumbled for a moment for his wits, then offered a slow, sheepish reply: “Why, that’s something that tastes main bitter, is it not?”

“That’s a fair guess, my man, but not the answer I’m after,” Catherine said, tapping the hearthstone with her wooden shoe. “I’ll tell you what it is. Wormwood is having two grown men in this house doing nought but loitering, waiting for thy shoes and mine, waiting for the best friend they ever had’s coffin to be nailed shut, with no work and no purpose to fill their days. It warps folks worse than Nature ever meant them to be. Why not set them up with a trade somewhere, give them a fair chance to turn right?”

Eli groaned, the barb sinking deep. “I’d not be against it,” he said, “but I misdoubt they’d drink and gamble away the very shelves of their shop before the first week was out.”

“Nay, think me no fool,” Catherine huffed. “I’ll watch them close at the start, steer them with a loose rein as the saying goes, so they cannot slip off the path easy.”

“Where would you set ’em up? Not here, that would split our own custom to bits.”

“Not likely!” Catherine scoffed. “Rotterdam’s the place, against the whole world. I’ll go see them settled myself.” She would never admit, even to her own heart, that the real reason she chose Rotterdam was to be close to little Gerard, her lost grandson, the son of the son she still refused to believe was dead.

After a dozen long evenings of haggling and Cornelis and Sybrandt swearing eager, earnest promises of better behaviour, Catherine packed her bags for Rotterdam, and brought gentle, lame Kate along for a change of air. They found a small shopfront right on a busy merchant thoroughfare, shabby and long neglected, its walls streaked with grime and its shelves rotting through, so they haggled the rent down to a fraction of what it would have cost new. The two women set to work at once: scrubbing the floors until the wood shone, hewing sturdy new oak shelves for the shop, whitewashing the walls bright, and kitting out the tiny upstairs dwelling space with warm blankets and a crackling hearth of its own.

All the while, Luke Peterson, that broad, soft-hearted young man who adored Margaret, was forever pestering her to name some task he might do to lighten her heavy, grief-laden days. Again and again she shook her head, her voice soft and sad: “Nothing, Luke. Nothing at all.”

“What, a woman so clever and quick as you, cannot think of one small thing I might do to help you?” he would press, and each time she gave him the same quiet answer. Until at last, weary of his gentle importuning, she varied the reply: “If you could make something to help my sweet sister Kate get about easier, that would be a kindness.”

Luke’s face lit up like a sunrise. The slave to his quiet, unspoken love set to work that very day, and soon fashioned a little light wooden cart, lined it with soft wool cushions, fixed a sturdy leather harness to its front, and yoked himself to it. Each evening at twilight, he would pull Kate out of the city gates and along the tree-lined, flower-dusted boulevard that ran beside the canal, Margaret and Catherine walking slow at his side, little Gerard curled safe and warm in Kate’s lap. The sight of them might have looked idyllic to a stranger’s eye, but there was a quiet weight of unspoken grief hanging over the little party that no passerby could see.

Kate, for her part, enjoyed every moment of the ride: little Gerard was hers to dote on, his soft curls brushing her cheek, and the two of them looked for all the world like a pale white lily cupping a tiny, blushing rosebud, a cherub resting in the lap of a gentle little angel. The coarsest of the town folk jeered at the sight, though: they called out taunts, asked Luke how thistle meat tasted, mocked him that his mistress could not afford a four-legged donkey to pull the cart. Luke did not heed their jeers one bit, but Kate’s tender heart ached for him.

“Good Luke, you made this cart for me, and that is far more than I ever deserved,” she said one evening, her voice trembling. “It was wrong of me to let you pull me yourself. We can easily pay some poor hardworking soul to do that work. I love my rides, and I love holding little Gerard, but I would far rather never ride again than see you mocked for my sake.”

“Little do I care for their foolish tongues,” Luke laughed, his big shoulders rolling. “If their jibes bothered me, I’d knock every last one of their empty heads together. I’ll draw you along this road every evening until my mistress Margaret tells me to stop.”

“Luke, if you will do as Kate bids you, you will oblige me very much,” Margaret said softly, and Luke agreed at once, without a moment’s hesitation.

Only one soul among the onlookers spoke a kind word. That was Joan, wife of Jorian Ketel, the wise old market woman who called out to them as they passed: “That is strength well spent, not wasted! To draw the weak along where their own feet cannot carry them. Her prayers will be your reward, that lass – she carries her pain so gentle, with a smile always on her face, she will not be long in this world.”

Simple, single-minded Luke only shook his head at that, and called back: “I do not need the poor lass’s prayers! I do all this to please my mistress Margaret.”

After that, Luke kept on pestering Margaret week after week, begging her to name some other task he might do for her, and again and again she turned him away. Until one afternoon, he pressed her so hard that she finally turned on him, her eyes glistening, her voice thick with a longing she had kept locked in her breast for years, too deep for words to ever fully capture.

“Find me my boy’s father.”

“Mistress, everyone in the village is saying he is dead.”
Margaret’s head snapped up. “Not so. They still feed me soft hope to my face.”
“Ay, to your face, but behind your back every last one of them swears Gerard Eliassoen will never walk these streets again.”

The dam of Margaret’s control broke, and hot tears streamed down her cheeks. Beside her, Luke whimpered in sympathy: big as a ploughman, broad-shouldered and strong, he had the soft, tender heart of a girl who could not bear to see anyone grieve.
“Prithee, do not weep so, sweet mistress,” he stammered. “I would drag him back from the grave itself before I’d see you sob so sore.”
Margaret wiped her eyes, swearing she was crying only out of anger at their two-faced lies, then laid a steady hand on his shoulder. “Luke, he is not dead. You know the old tales that dying men are given sight beyond what we living folk can see? Listen to me. My own father, when he was on his deathbed — I was such a fool, I was humming making a sleeve, convinced he would get completely well — he sat in that very chair you are in right now, and all at once he was bright as a flame, not a dying man at all. He cried out, ‘I see him! Sore disfigured, on a great river, coming this way.’”
Her voice cracked. “Ah, Luke, if you were a woman, and cared for me half as much as you think you do, you would pity me, and go find him. He is the father of my child.”
“Alack, I would if I knew how!” Luke protested. “But how?”
“Nay, of course you cannot,” she said, shaking herself. “I am mad to even speak of it. I only know that if anyone truly cared for me, they would find a way.”

Luke fell quiet, turning the idea over slow in his head, for his thoughts could never gallop the way Margaret’s did. “The old folk do say dying men see more than the rest of us. A great river… the Maas is great, but if he were on the Maas coming this way he would have reached Delfshaven long ago. The Rhine is greater, far longer, stretching all the way up to the German lands. That must be the one.”
“I think so too,” Margaret said, her eyes lighting. “Denys told Gerard he would make his way home down the Rhine. But what if he turns off before he reaches his birthplace? He does not pine for me half as much as I pine for him, that is plain. Luke, do you not think he has deserted me?”
She waited for him to contradict her, but he said bluntly, “It looks very like it. What a fool that man must be.”
“Nay, we know nothing for certain!” she implored him.

“Let me think again,” Luke said, frowning. At last he had it: there was a river station sixty miles up the Rhine, he said, where every public trading boat put in to resupply. He would travel there, linger at the docks, and ask every passenger that stepped off if a man named Gerard Eliassoen was aboard. “I do not know his face, but if you give me a little letter to hand him, no one will doubt I have a real errand from someone who knows him.”
“Good, kind, thoughtful Luke!” Margaret breathed, tears of relief stinging her eyes. “How little I have valued you all these months! Give me until supper, and I will write it.”

At supper she pressed a long, silk-tied, sealed letter into his palm, her cheeks burning bright. Luke weighed it in his hand, his face growing grave. “Tell me, mistress: if your father’s vision was true, if I find this man, if he turns out better than I think him, and comes home to you straight away — what will become of me?”
Margaret’s face flushed all the way to her brow. “Oh, Luke, Heaven will reward you. I will fall on my knees and bless you, and I will love you all my days as a mother loves her son. Trouble ages the heart, and I feel years older than you. You need not go, it is selfish of me — love makes us all think only of ourselves.”
“Humph,” Luke said, not satisfied. “And what if that scapegrace reads your letter, hears me tell him how you are pining away, and is still a traitor, or too much of an idiot to come home? Must I die an old bachelor, and you waste away lonely into your grave, neither maid, wife, nor widow?”

Margaret panted, shaken by his plain, unflinching good sense. At last she faltered out, “If — and may our Lady be merciful and forbid it — if he refuses to come back, then he shall give me our marriage lines, and I shall be an honest woman, even if I am wretched, and our little boy will not be a bastard. And I swear to you, for all the good you have done me this day, I will never be so ungrateful as to walk past your door to another man’s.”
“Ay, but will you walk in at mine?” Luke pressed.
“Oh, do not ask me that! Not yet. Someday, perhaps, when my wounds stop bleeding. I will try. I will try not to throw myself and my child into the Maas. Do not go, Luke! Do not think of this! It is all madness, from first to last.”

But Luke was as slow to abandon an idea as he was to form it. “Madness is better than nothing,” he said. “I am tired of sitting around doing nothing for you. I leave at peep of day. Only — I have no money. My mother keeps all my wages locked away, and I never see a penny of it.”
Margaret pulled out Catherine’s gold angel, the one that had escaped every narrow scrape for months, and pressed it into his hand. At dawn he set off on his wild errand, and in that superstitious age, guided by a dying man’s vision, it did not feel half so mad to him as it does to us.

When Catherine heard what Margaret had done, she was furious. “Sending that poor boy on such a wild-goose chase! You are just like every other girl, mark my words: you will wear that Luke out, make him sick of you as a whipped dog, and then you will suddenly be as fond of him as a cow is of her calf, and by then it will be too late.”

---

Twelve hours after Luke set off up the Rhine, two friars crossed the southern border into Holland. The wild-goose chase, for all its absurdity, was drawing the two parties closer every hour. Jerome, unable to preach to the Low Dutch-speaking villagers, was desperate to push on to the coast and catch a ship for England as fast as possible, and with the current carrying their boat downstream, they would have slipped right past Luke’s river station without ever seeing him — if not for one small, fateful detour.

Twenty miles above the docks Luke was headed for, Clement (the young friar who was once Gerard Eliassoen) stopped to preach in a large village. Halfway through his sermon, he noticed a grey Franciscan nun weeping openly in the crowd. After the service he went to her gently, and asked what grieved her.
“It is not my own grief that makes me weep,” she told him. “I weep for my dearest friend. Your words reminded me of the sweet girl she was before she was lured away from her vows. You are a Dominican, and I am of St. Francis’s order — but I cannot keep it to myself any longer.”
She told him that the convent’s favourite young nun, Mary, had been tricked into running away, and after a long spiral of sin, was now trapped working in a roadside inn, forced to act as a decoy for wealthy customers. The innkeeper, she said, was a former servant of the local fierce baron, and had the lord’s full protection; if the nuns tried to storm the inn and drag her back, he would burn their convent to the ground.
“Brute force will never save a soul,” Clement said quietly.

He convinced Jerome to stop for the night at the Franciscan convent, but when he announced the next morning that he had promised the abbess he would try to win Mary back, Jerome threw up his hands. It was not their business, he argued, a waste of precious time they could spend making their way to England. But Clement was no longer a docile, obedient pupil. He stood his ground, and at last they struck a deal: Jerome would push ahead to the coast, book their passage on the next outbound English ship, and give Clement a few days to try his well-meaning, seemingly futile experiment.

By ten o’clock that morning, a tall figure in a rough horseman’s cloak, heavy riding boots, and a drooping wide-brimmed felt hat stood frozen outside the roadside inn where Mary was trapped. Clement’s heart was sick with dread, his body cold with sweat; these fiery, ardent souls dream of grand acts of piety, but falter when they come face to face with the ugly, messy reality of sin. He prayed for courage long at the door, then stepped inside, called loudly for a cup of wine, and made a show of drinking it.
“Landlord,” he said, dangling a heavy gold chain across the table, “I hear you have the prettiest chambermaid for miles around.”
The landlord’s eyes lit up at the sight of the gold. He laughed and yelled, “Janet! Come out here, there’s a fine young lover for you, who’d bind you in chains of gold!”
A voice trilled from the back: “Send him in, then. I’m in double luck today.”

Clement rose, shuddering, and followed her into the private back parlour where she was half-heartedly mending a piece of sewing, breaking off every minute to sing a ragged, half-remembered tavern song. He asked if they could go somewhere more private, and she led him to a small, locked back room. Clement softly closed and latched the window shutters.
“What on earth are you doing that for?” Janet asked, frowning.
“Sweetheart,” he whispered, putting on a mysterious air, “so that God may not see us.”
“Madman,” she scoffed. “Do you think a wooden shutter can block His eye? The only way to get through this life is to stop thinking of Him entirely — if you don’t, it poisons every cup you drink.”
Clement waved the heavy gold chain before her. “Feel this. It is pure virgin gold. I will cut two of these heavy links off for you, all yours.”
“Ah, now you are speaking sense,” she said, grabbing for it greedily. “Why, it’s as heavy as the chain around the Virgin’s neck at the conv—”
She cut herself off, horrified.
“Whisht,” Clement breathed. “It *is* the Virgin’s chain. And you shall have your share — if you do not betray me.”
“Monster!” she yelped, jerking back from him. “Rob the Blessed Virgin of her chain to give to a —”
“You are no sinner beyond saving,” he cried triumphantly, dropping his disguise. “Mary!”

She screamed and lunged for the window, fumbling with the shutters. Before she could get them open, Clement kicked off his heavy boots, pulled off his felt hat, and let his horseman’s cloak fall to the floor. He stood before her in his plain black Dominican robes, holding his crucifix aloft, his face calm and solemn, no trace of the roguish horseman left. The sight did not fill her with fear of harm, but crushed her under the weight of long-buried remorse. She cowered back against the wall.
“Mary,” he said gently. “One word. Are you happy?”
“As happy as I will be in hell,” she whimpered.
“The nuns at your convent are not happy, either. They weep for you day and night — most of all, your Sister Ursula.”
“Poor Ursula,” she sobbed, the tears breaking through.
“The angels weep for you too. Will you not dry all their tears, on earth and in heaven, and save your own soul?”
“I would,” she gasped. “But it is too late.”
“Avaunt, Satan!” Clement thundered. “That is your favourite lie! Listen not to him, Mary — I who come to save you am a far greater sinner than you. Sin is not half so sweet as you thought it would be, is it? Eternity is waiting for you, and you do not have to burn for the choices you made.”

He convinced her the convent would welcome her back, that the abbess and the sisters cared far more about her than they did about the Virgin’s golden chain, that he had broken his order’s rules by entering an inn and wearing lay clothes just to come rescue her. When she hesitated, he showed her plainly the dark end of the life she was living, and stoked the long-forgotten, gentle piety she had buried deep months before. At last she knelt sobbing at his feet, swearing she had never known a moment of peace since she broke her vows, that she would come back with him only if he walked beside her — she could never face the abbess and the sisters alone.

As they prepared to leave, a hundred small, silly little obstacles cropped up, silken nets tangled around her resolve, but Clement swept every one aside. He had brought a spare grey Franciscan habit and cowl for her to change into, to hide her fine tavern clothes. When she gathered up all her stolen trinkets and jewels to take back to the convent and sell for the poor, he told her their source was too impure, and bade her fix her eyes on his crucifix and trample them under her feet. She obeyed, then flung the glittering heap out the window onto the nearby dunghill, casting off the wages of sin forever.

They had barely stepped into the kitchen before the landlord realised what was happening. He roared for his men to stop them: “Reuben! Carl! Gavin! Here is a false friar spiriting away our Janet!”
The farmhands ran in, fists raised. Clement strode at them, crucifix held high, and roared in a voice like thunder: “Forbear! She is a holy nun returning to her vows. The first man who lays a hand on her cowl shall have his arm wither, his body lie unburied, cursed by Rome, and his soul shall roast in eternal fire!”
They shrank back as if they had been burned by flame. Clement grabbed the innkeeper by the neck, strong as a lion in his righteous fury, and hurled him across the room, pitching him headfirst onto the stone floor. He wrenched the front door open, and led the trembling nun out onto the high road.
“Mary,” he said, gasping for breath as they walked, “my choler is ungovernable, a wild beast lurks beneath this black gown. If those men had laid a finger on you, I would have beaten their brains out with this crucifix. I know I am a flawed man.”
“Alas, father,” she said, clinging to his arm, “if you had been any less fierce, I would still be trapped in that place. To save me, you needed to be wary as a fox, and bold as a lion.”
Clement crossed himself. “God chooses imperfect instruments to do His perfect work. Glory be to Him.”

When they neared the convent gate, Mary stopped short, too afraid to go in. Clement left her sitting on a stone to calm herself, and went in to tell the abbess her lost nun was waiting outside. The joy of the sisters was boundless. They arranged a gentle welcome for her, no harsh penance on her first day back. When Clement led her around to the side postern, they heard the whole convent singing, music floating out over the garden.
“It is a feast day,” Mary said, confused. “I have come to spoil it.”
“Hardly,” Clement smiled. “You are the queen of the feast. There is more joy in heaven over one sinner who repents than over ninety-nine just people who need no repentance — and today that joy is here, too.”
The postern flew open, and Sister Ursula flung herself at Mary, sobbing and kissing her on the cheek, clinging to her neck as if she would never let go. The abbess followed, tears running down her face. They begged Clement to stay for the celebrations, but he told them he could not. He had already kept Jerome waiting too long, and had to hurry back to the Rhine, to catch the next boat for England. He bade them farewell, and strode briskly down the road towards the river, entirely unaware he was less than a day’s travel from Luke, the man Margaret had sent to find him.

---

Margaret’s letter, the one she had given Luke to carry, was the kind of soft, tender, utterly unresentful letter only a woman who loves deeply can write. She told him of the birth of their little boy, named Gerard for his father, the comfort he had been through all the long months of silence. She described his every feature, down to the tiny mole on his little finger. “All the mothers on our street envy me my boy, but I envy the wives, for you are not home to us,” she wrote. “Some say you are dead. But if you were dead, how could I still breathe? Others say you are false — but I will believe that from no lips but yours. My father, as he lay dying, said he saw you on a great river, face turned towards me, sore disfigured. If cruel men have scarred your face, if you have lost a limb — why, then you have all the more need of me. My love is not light as a man’s, my dearest Gerard: I will love you more, not less, than I did the day I pricked my arm and shed those few drops of blood for you, remember? I do not reproach you. I only wait.”

She had said nothing of her doubts, nothing of the pain of waiting alone, for fear that if he was still alive, still hurt, her anger would scare him away. She was no angel, she was only a woman in love, and she had sent soft, loyal Luke to carry that letter to him.

Luke had mingled with passengers from two full river boats, and heard no word of Gerard Eliassoen. He was

Waiting for a letter freighted with all your dearest hopes never leaves the mind still, not for long. Margaret, in the letter she had sent off with young Luke, had poured out every last scrap of her energy and hard-won faith in her dying father’s final vision, the strange sight he had sworn to see of Gerard alive and well. But once Luke had vanished down the road, she quickly stared at her own impulsiveness, wondering how she could have been so foolishly credulous, and her conscience pricked her for dragging the kind-hearted boy on such a long, fruitless errand. Old Catherine fussed and scolded her for chasing wild fancies, and the sharp come-down from her brief, bright surge of hope dragged her into a far deeper despondency than any she had known before.

That was the state in which Joan Ketel, the loyal new friend she had made only weeks prior, found her. Joan bustled in, face bright with a new idea.
“Margaret, lass, I know the cure for this black mood of yours. The hermit of Gouda! A wondrous holy man, he is, and when the spirit moves him, he can tell you exactly what the future holds.”
“Ay, I’ve heard the tales,” Margaret replied listlessly, with no spark of hope left.
Joan wore her down at last, persuading her to walk the miles to Gouda to consult the hermit, and they tucked a pat of fresh butter and a clutch of new-laid eggs into a wicker basket to bring as an offering.

The two women had grown so fast and firm a friend over Jorian Ketel’s near-death illness six weeks prior. A brutal bowel pain had seized him first, and when that ebbed, an awful symptom settled in: no food or drink, not even a sip of water, would stay in his stomach for more than a minute. The village doctor had declared he would be dead before sundown, and ordered Joan to boil a chicken with a golden angel coin steeped in the broth to try to draw the sickness out. That gilded chicken broth came right back up, same as all the humble porridge and water that had come before it. Next the local curate steeped the relic of St. Sergius’s thumb in beef tea, to no better effect. At last Joan had run to Margaret sobbing, to beg for a scrap of good linen to sew her husband’s shroud.
“Let me see him first,” Margaret had said, and she walked straight to the sickbed, felt Jorian’s racing pulse, and ordered the stifling room’s windows thrown wide open, every scrap of damp, overheated linen stripped off him and changed. Joan had protested that it was waste to use good linen on a dying man, but Margaret had insisted, and Joan had found herself obeying. Margaret returned moments later with her apron heaped with flowering feverfew she had spotted growing wild right below the sickroom window. She brewed a strong decoction, sipped a spoonful first to prove it was harmless, and coaxed the half-dead man into swallowing the rest, bit by bit, slipping a single drop of schiedam gin into the third spoonful and a little beaten egg yolk into the seventh. By slow, steady degrees, she dragged him out of Death’s grip, until his body settled and he began to heal. She made the pair of them swear never to tell a soul who had cured him, for the village would accuse her of witchcraft and lock her away, far from her little boy.

When Margaret and Joan reached the hermit’s cave, they set their basket of offerings on the rough stone ledge at its mouth. Margaret leaned close to the speaking hole carved into the rock, and called out, “Holy hermit, we bring thee the best butter and eggs from our larders, and I, a poor deserted girl who is a wife yet no wife, and mother to the sweetest babe alive, beg thee tell me if my Gerard is quick or dead, true to his vows or false.”
A faint, rattling voice drifted out of the dark cave: “Trouble me not with the trivial things of earth. Send me a holy friar. I am dying.”
“Alas, poor soul!” Margaret cried. “Is it so? Let us come in and tend to thee.”
“Saints forbid!” the voice gasped. “Thine is a woman’s voice. Send me a holy friar, and do not draw near.”

They trundled home heavy-hearted. Joan huffed all the way that the notion women were imps of darkness forbidden a dying man’s bed was utter nonsense, but Margaret was too sunk in gloom to speak. Joan’s rough consolation fell on deaf ears until she mentioned Jorian’s unspoken secret.
“Jorian’s half ready to spill everything, you know. He’s that grateful to you he can scarce keep it in. Though he grumbles he can’t believe a man of his inches was cured of death’s door by no more than common feverfew — he was half minded to pull all the feverfew out of his own garden before he fell ill! He says he doesn’t want to stir up strife between Gerard’s kin and your friends for no good, that spilling what little he knows won’t bring Gerard back. He’s all twisted up about it, doesn’t know what to do.”
