Margaret only shook her head softly. “Ay, we are wading in very deep waters, my little babe and me.”

Saturday came, and there was no sign of Luke. “Poor Luke,” Margaret murmured. “It was so good of him to go on such a fool’s errand for me.”
“Luke’s one in a hundred,” Catherine said warmly. “He’d never be anything but kind to your little Gerard.”
Margaret smiled. “Then I shall be extra kind to him, for all the trouble I’ve put him through, when he comes home.”

---

Brother Clement, once known to the world as Gerard Eliassoen, followed the directions the nuns had given him to skip a sharp, dangerous bend in the river, and strode fast and steady until he reached a staging post far closer to the coast than the spot where unsuspecting Luke lay waiting for him on the road. He set out before dawn the next day, and stepped onto the Rotterdam quay by noon, hurrying to meet Jerome so he would not keep his fellow Dominican waiting. He spotted a cluster of his order’s friars gathered at the water’s edge, but Jerome was not among them. When he asked after his companion, one of the monks pointed to a billowing white sail far out on the North Sea, already shrinking toward the horizon.
“Jerome? He sailed for England on that very ship, an hour past. He said he could not bear to lose a single day.”
Clement cried out in sharp, wordless anguish, and the rest of the monks turned, recognized him as the famous young preacher Jerome had spoken of, greeted him with brotherly warmth, and pressed a crumpled, hasty note Jerome had left behind into his hand. The note was cold, almost dismissive. Jerome wrote that he had not wished to waste the rare chance of a fair wind to England, that Clement was far too soft and tender a soul to win over the haughty islanders, that he would do far better to stay in his native Holland and preach to his own countryfolk, where his gift for speaking to Dutch hearts would shine. He warned Clement that a stranger had already asked after him by his old worldly name of Gerard, and bade him be on his guard, never to let the world snare him again with silken nets. Solitude, fasting, and prayer, he wrote, were the sword, spear, and shield of the soul. Farewell.

Clement was cut to the quick. They had been shipwrecked together, clinging to the same splinter of wreckage to stay alive. He had been Jerome’s pupil, his penitent, his spiritual son, and they had traveled four hundred miles together in the service of the Church — and Jerome had shaken him off like a bit of unwanted dirt at the first chance, with no kindness, no second thought. Even worldly hearts, he thought bitterly, had never been so cold and untrustworthy. The only soul that had ever truly loved him lay buried in the churchyard at Sevenbergen. He bade the monks farewell, promising he would stay at their convent and preach wherever their prior appointed, and turned his feet toward Sevenbergen.

Three hours later he passed Peter’s old cottage. It had been fully repaired, a new outhouse built on, and a crowd of noisy, rosy-cheeked children chased each other around the door. He turned his head hastily away, not to mar the soft, tender memory he carried of the place, and walked straight to the little village churchyard. He searched every grave for Margaret Brandt’s headstone, and could not find it anywhere. He could not believe they would grudge her a marker, and his heart ached at the thought that grim poverty had left no one alive who cared enough to put a name to her resting place. He stepped into the empty church, knelt, and prayed long and earnestly for the soul of the woman he had loved better than life itself.

When he came back out, he spotted an ancient man of eighty-two leaning on the churchyard gate, looking out over the graves. Clement asked if he knew where Margaret Brandt lay buried.
“Margaret Brandt? As if I didn’t know her,” the old man said, a little testy at first, then softening. “She doesn’t lie here, lad. Her whole family packed up and left ages ago, moved to Rotterdam, so I heard. I’d wager she died there, poor lass. She was a May rose of a thing, that one, blooming and sweet, with the softest smile you ever saw. No one expected to see her cut down so young, leaving old weeds like me standing here still.”

Clement bade the old man farewell, and hurried back to the Rotterdam convent as the sun dipped below the horizon. He spent the rest of the night in the chapel, keeping vigil, praying for the soul of Jerome who had abandoned him, and for the soul of Margaret he thought was buried in some unknown grave far away, until the small hours of the morning, and his frayed, aching soul settled back into the cold, calm stillness of his monastic life.

The next day, Sunday, after mass, Catherine’s home on the Hoog Straet hummed with quiet, bright bustle. The new shop out front was fully kitted out at last, and Cornelis and Sybrandt were set to open its doors at dawn the next morning. Their names were painted in bold, gilded lettering above the lintel, alongside their trade sign: a spotless white lamb nuzzling a gilded ewe. Old Eli had trundled over earlier that day, bringing extra stock from his own warehouse to give the two boys a solid head start, no risk of falling short their first week of trade. The lads’ parents glowed with quiet pride to see their wastrel sons turn to honest work at last, while Cornelis and Sybrandt paced the back garden side by side, vowing they were sick to death of their old lazy, profligate days. Turning an honest guilder, they agreed, was a hundred times sweeter than squandering coin on drink and idle mischief, and they swore to stick to their business like wax to a candle, no slipping back. Catherine, ever sharp and watchful, overheard their resolution through the open parlour window, and slipped off to tell Eli, her heart light as thistledown.

The family supper planned that evening would include Margaret and her little boy, serving as an inaugural feast of sorts: the elders would pass on all their hard-earned trade wisdom, and spiced wine would flow freely to toast the two lads who had renounced the unprofitable vagrancy of their "wild oats" days. Margaret had come over early to help her mother-in-law with the cooking, half to shake off the heavy, listless languor that had clung to her for months, and both their cheeks were flushed as rosy as the glow from the great hearth fire.

Presently, Joan bustled in carrying a crisp, dewy salad fresh from Jorian’s vegetable plot. “He cut it special for you, Margaret! You’re all he chatters about these days, I’ll soon turn green with jealousy. Told him we’re laying a feast today, and he wouldn’t hear of you going without the freshest greens. But oh lass, that sermon in the new church just now? I’ve never heard preaching like that in all my born days.”

“Ah, I wish I’d been there,” Margaret said softly. “My soul’s been parched for want of that heavenly dew these past weeks.”

“He’s preaching again this very afternoon,” Joan told her. “Though I thought you’d be needed here, like enough.”

“Needed nowhere but where she wants to be,” Catherine cut in at once. “Off you go, lass, if your heart’s set on hearing him.”

“Truth be told,” Margaret smiled, “I think I won’t be such a damp squib at the supper table if I sit down to it warm from a good sermon, my heart lightened.”

“Then you’d best be quick,” Joan nodded to the street outside, where crowds of burghers were already making their way toward the church. “And look there, if it isn’t that holy hermit friar everyone’s been talking about. Bless us, Margaret—we almost forgot! I want a closer look at him.” The sprightly woman bounded out the door, darting across the high road to stop the friar before he could pass, and was back in the house before you could blink.

“There,” she panted. “I told him there’s a sick man waiting for his visit, and he said ‘My daughter, please God I will come to him before the sun sets.’ Sweetest voice I ever heard in my life. But oh, mistresses—he’s so young, and his cheeks are all thin and worn, and those great dark eyes? They’re almost the exact colour of yours, Margaret.”

“I’ve half a mind to go hear him,” Margaret said, fidgeting a little. “But my cap’s not as clean as it ought to be, and everyone else will be there in their spotless white mutches.”

“Here, take my linen handkerchief out of that basket, tuck it round your hairline,” Catherine said at once. “You can’t bring the little one with you, though—I need him to sit with poor Kate, it’s one of her bad pain days.”

Margaret didn’t argue, just carried the little boy up the stairs to Kate’s chamber. The poor girl was propped up in bed, her face tight with unspoken agony. “How fares my sweetheart?” Margaret said, not bothering to wait for an answer. “Nay, I don’t need to ask—you’re in sore pain, aren’t you? Look, I’ve brought someone you love.”

“Two, if you ask me,” Kate said, with that soft, angelic smile she wore even through the worst of her spasms. A wave of wrenched her then that would make a strong man roar, but she did not make a sound. “I love him far too dearly to ever feel his weight,” she said, when Margaret moved to set the toddler beside her on the covers.

Margaret set the boy down carefully, then tidied her hair and smoothed her skirt by the dresser looking glass. “I’m off to the church to hear that wonderful new preacher everyone’s gushing about,” she told Kate.

Kate sighed, a little wistful. “Only a minute ago I was all eager to go too,” Margaret added, “that’s how I’ve been these past months, up and down like the waves on the Zuyder Zee. I’d just as soon stay right here beside you, say the word and I’ll not step foot out the door.”

“Nay,” Kate said, soft. “Go on, please, and come back and tell me every single word he says. I wish more than anything I could go myself.” Tears glistened in the sick girl’s eyes, and that settled it for Margaret. She kissed Kate’s forehead, glanced down at the little boy, and heaved a soft little sigh. “I daren’t kiss him goodbye, not even a peck,” she said. “My father always said never wake a sleeping child, day or night. When he wakes up of his own accord, you can teach Aunt Kate those two new little words he’s just learned, eh?” She slipped out of the room, looking back over her shoulder at the pair of them with eyes full of love, and shut the door so softly it did not make a sound.

“Joan, will you give me a hand peeling these turnips and apples?” Catherine called from the kitchen below.

“Of course I will, dame,” Joan said, and the two set to work on the feast, quiet and steady, no idle chatter.

“Now Joan,” Catherine half-laughed, “the rule in this house is, those who help me cook and serve the feast get a full share of it too, no exceptions.”

“There’s far worse laws in all of Holland than that one,” Joan replied, grinning. “I’m happy to do it—my Luke’s out earning his supper digging ditches today, lucky for him the ground’s soft after last night’s rain.”

Just then Margaret came down the stairs, all fresh and tidy. “Eh, lass, look at you!” Catherine exclaimed. “You washed your face, smoothed your hair, and now there’s no one in all Rotterdam half as pretty as you!” She snapped her fingers playfully at the mention of the big city. “Come here, give me a kiss! And mind, Eli won’t wait supper for the Duke of Burgundy himself, so don’t you go lingering after the service ends.”

Joan and Catherine followed her to the front door, and stood there watching her walk down the Hoog Straet until she was almost out of sight. For these homely burgher housewives, a walk out to church on a Sunday afternoon was a small, special event all its own.

“Look at her go,” Catherine said softly to Joan, as they leaned in the doorway. “It feels almost like I’m seeing my own daughter off to church, same as I’ve done a hundred times before. Joan, that lass will not hear a single word said against our Gerard, not one. Even if he is alive right now, he’s treated her cruel as anything—and that’s why my bowels ache for the poor wench. I’m older, wiser than her, and I’ve made up my mind: I’ll wed her to that good, simple Luke, and that’ll be the end of all her heartache. What’s one grandchild, after all? Plenty of folk have bigger families, and she’ll have a good, steady roof over her head for the rest of her days.”

Margaret stepped through the heavy oak doors of St. Laurens just as the sermon began. The great church was far from done, as most grand churches of the era were—no building of such scale rose in a single generation. Its side aisles were fully roofed, but the central nave and chancel gaped open to the sky, their rafters bare above scattered workmen’s piles of hewn stone and lime. The pillars and rounded arches were mostly complete, many freshly whitewashed, but only one single window in the entire sprawling structure held glass; all the rest were jagged, rough-hewn openings cut into the outer stone walls.

On that golden summer afternoon, every one of those half-finished flaws turned to magic. Bright sunlight spilled through the uneven gaps in the walls and rafters, breaking into streaks of dazzling gold that lanced through the cool dim of the side aisles like rivers of molten light, glowing warm against the whitewashed pillars. The whole length of the vast central nave was chequered with shifting patterns of light and shadow, the dark patches soft and cool as well water, the sunlit spots glowing like shards of amber lit from within by some quiet heavenly fire. Overhead, stretching unbroken from west to east, the summer blue of the sky curved like a living vault, so close and bright it felt you could reach up and touch it. The sea of white linen coifs perched on the heads of the packed congregation winked like foam beneath that wide blue sky, and for all the thousands of people crammed shoulder to shoulder in the unroofed nave, not a sound broke the hush but the low, mellow, earnest voice of the preacher, holding every last soul spellbound.

Margaret stood frozen a moment, caught fast by the beauty of the place, the quiet devotion, the thick soft calm that hung over the whole crowd. She slipped behind a thick stone pillar in the north aisle, and though she could barely make out a word the preacher said, a soft, drowsy devotional languor stole over her, smoothing all the sharp, frayed edges of the worries she’d carried with her that day. It felt like warm, scented oil seeping into every line of her tense, overworked heart, and she leaned her weight against the stone, eyes half-lidded, every sensation soft and dreamlike. It felt nothing short of holy to be there.

Presently she spotted a well-dressed woman a little ways across the aisle get up to move, fleeing the direct sunlight that was pouring straight down on her head from the only glazed window in the church. Margaret slipped quick and silent across the gap, and claimed the empty spot before anyone else could take it. Now she stood beside a pillar in the south aisle, less than fifty feet from the pulpit, just a little behind the preacher’s shoulder, where she could catch every single word he spoke.

Her focus drifted for a minute, though, caught by the bobbing shadow of a man’s head and shoulders dancing oddly against the stone at her feet. She bit her lip to keep from giggling, until she glanced over her shoulder through the unglazed window and spotted Jorian Ketel the sexton, digging a new grave in the churchyard just outside, his movements the source of that droll bobbing shadow.

Just then, a single cadence of the preacher’s voice hit her ear so sharp and clear it felt like a physical blow, thrumming right through every bone in her body. She clapped a hand to her bosom, gasping a little at the sudden, shocking thrill, and spun around to look up at the pulpit. The preacher’s back was turned to her, and all she could see was the smooth shaved circle of his tonsure glinting in the sun. She sighed, disappointed—what could a stray friar from no place she knew have a voice that familiar? But the sound of him wrapped around her anyway, rising and falling as he warmed to his subject, waking faint, half-buried echoes of a thousand happy memories she’d thought long buried. She didn’t dare look up again to shatter that soft, melancholy pleasure, her eyes fixed on the floor.

Then, mid-flow of a soaring, eloquent sentence, the preacher stopped dead.

Margaret almost sighed out loud, as if a sweet song had been cut short mid-note. Could the sermon be over already? She glanced around, and no one was moving—instead, dozens of faces were turning sharply in her direction. She spun around, terrified, thinking some terrible thing stood behind her, but there was nothing there at all.

Nearby, other parishioners were staring up at the pulpit, their faces white with shock. Margaret followed their gaze, and her blood turned to ice. The friar stood frozen in the pulpit, his face as pale and still as a corpse just risen from the grave. His eyes, already large beneath his thick brows, were blown wide open to an unnatural size, bulging straight at her, fixed unblinking.

The whole church erupted into chaos. People leapt to their feet all across the nave, craning their necks to stare first at the friar, then at Margaret, then back at the friar again. The rustle of hundreds of turned coifs rose to a loud, rushing roar, women shrieked, men muttered and buzzed in confused agitation. Margaret, every eye locked on her, cringed back behind the nearest pillar, one single scared, fleeting glance darting back up to the pulpit.

That glance was enough. She saw the look on his ashen face, and it made her quiver from head to toe. Her knees gave out, and she sank down onto a heap of wood chips the workmen had left piled by the wall, burying her face in her hands.

The preacher recovered himself a moment later, and the sermon resumed. She could hear the hum of his voice, but not a single word of what he said. Her mind spun too fast to think, whirling around one single, unshakable thought: that look seared onto his face, that wide, wild, disbelieving stare, had not been confusion, or fright.

It was recognition.

The sermon wavered for a few minutes, then built up into a soaring, feverish peak of fiery eloquence that swept over the crowd, leaving most of them chattering excitedly as they dispersed, the strange, frozen pause in the pulpit half-forgotten in the wake of that rousing close. Margaret slipped into the throng and followed them out the doors, but instead of turning for her cottage, she veered off into the churchyard, straight for her father Peter’s grave. Poor as she was, she’d scraped together every spare penny to buy him a proper stone slab and carved headstone. She sank down onto the cold slab, pressed a soft kiss to the weathered stone, then pulled her linen apron up over her head to hide her face, so no passing parishioner would spot her tear-streaked face or her bright red hair.

“Father,” she whispered, quiet enough that only the breeze could hear, “you heard me say many times I was wading out in deep waters, but now I know the bottom of them is deeper than any of us ever guessed. I’ll follow that friar round the whole wide world if I have to, but I will get close enough to see his face. He’s going to tell me why he looked at me like a dead man woken from his grave, when there was no soul standing behind me at all. Oh father, you always believed in me, when others said hard things. Speak one good word for me up there, won’t you? Because I’ve wandered far past my depth now.”

Her father’s tomb sat where it had a clear side view of the church’s main door. There she sat, face covered, hidden in the shadow of the old yew tree that grew at the stone’s foot, lying in wait for the holy preacher.

The ancient stone church, its walls dappled with shifting sunbeams and its vaulted ceiling streaked with the deep heavenly purple of stained glass, wrapped around Father Clement like a soft, cooling blanket, soothed him exactly as it soothed Margaret lingering at the edges of the congregation. More than that, it lifted his mind straight to the Creator who made every good, pure delight in the world. His gaze drifted to the broad main aisle, packed wall to wall with his country folk, a thousand crisp white linen caps stitched with fine gold filigree bobbing in the pews. In all the hundreds of leagues he had wandered across foreign lands, he had never seen anything that looked quite like them—nothing but fresh fallen snow, drifting soft across field and roof.

That morning, he had mounted the pulpit and thundered of sin and judgment, but this warm drowsy golden afternoon felt entirely out of step with threats. His chest ached with tender yearning for the crowd before him; he had to speak to them of God's quiet, abiding love. For these simple souls heard almost no mention of that gentle love from most pulpits of the day, no more than far-off heathen people who had never heard the name of Christ at all. He told them the glad, soft tidings of salvation, and every last man, woman, and child leaned in, hanging on every word of his earnest, unhurried voice. He was never the sort of preacher who gyrated across the pulpit like a weathercock spinning on a steeple: he stirred hearts far more than he stirred his own body.

Warmed through by the theme, determined that not a single soul in that multitude would miss the joyful news of Christ's love, he turned to face the south aisle. There, framed in a broad slant of sunlight spilling through the high arched window, was the radiant face of Margaret Brandt.

For a long beat he gazed at it without conscious feeling, numb from the crown of his head to the soles of his feet, soul and body both locked in ice. Soon the words died in his throat, and he trembled, fixed fast on that sight. There she stood, her auburn hair bathed in sunbeams, glittering like the halo of a saint, her face glowing doubly bright with her own soft beauty and the golden light that gilded her skin. She leaned very lightly against a smooth white marble column, her lashes fallen tenderly, listening exactly as he had seen her listen to him a hundred times back in Sevenbergen. There was no change in her: this was the blooming Margaret he had left, only a shade riper, sweeter, lovelier than the memory he had carried like a relic across all his years of wandering. He stared at her with wide, unblinking eyes, his cheeks drained of every drop of blood. The thousand people in the pews vanished out of his sight. He heard a faint rustle, the sound of hundreds of parishioners shifting in their seats, as if filtered through a mile of thick wool, but he could not tear his gaze off that warm, living face, that wondrous copper hair glistening gloriously in the sun. He waited for her to vanish, for it to be some trick of the light or ghostly vision. She did not move.

All at once, she lifted her head and looked full at him, straight into his very own soul through those famous violet eyes he had dreamed of every night. He was beside himself, his lips parting to shriek her name across the whole church, when she turned her head swiftly, and slipped back out of the sunbeam. She did not disappear completely before she darted one more glance at him, quick as lightning, that locked with his: a startled, inquiring, nameless, indescribable look, the very last split second before full recognition hits. She staggered, reeling, her mind a whirl of unnameable confusion, while he panted, clutching the edge of the pulpit convulsively so hard his knuckles went white.

He summoned all his strength to mutter a few words no one in the congregation could possibly make sense of, then feebly stumbled back into his sermon. He stammered and babbled on for a while, forcing himself, now that she was out of sight, to frame the sight as a vision from the other world. A strange, unnatural fire of excitement rose in him, and he finished the sermon in a wild flow of eloquence bordering on rhapsody, that electrified every simple soul listening.

When the sermon ended, he sank down onto the little stool inside the pulpit, badly shaken from head to toe. Then a thought, typical of the pious certainties of that age, took hold of him: he had searched Sevenbergen high and low for Margaret's grave in vain. She had been permitted to appear to him now, to show him she was buried here, right by the very pillar where her spirit had revealed itself. That idea settled in his mind as solid and unshakable as a proven fact. He knew he had only to speak to the sexton—whom he had spotted digging in the churchyard mid-sermon, much to his mild displeasure—to learn the exact spot where she was laid to rest.

The church was soon empty of all worshipers. He climbed down from the pulpit, stepped through a low opening in the south wall onto the soft sun-warmed grass, and walked straight over to the sexton. He recognized Jorian in an instant. But Jorian never suspected that the wild young lad whose life he had saved years ago stood before him in the robes of this holy friar. The loss of Gerard's full, shapely beard had altered the whole outline of his face far more than his tonsure, his cropped hair streaked with premature grey, or his cheeks thinned and paled by years of fasts and midnight vigils.

"My son," said Friar Clement softly, "if you keep any memory of the souls you lay in the earth, prithee tell me: is any Christian buried inside the church, near one of the pillars?"

"Nay, father," said Jorian, leaning on his spade, "all who rest here are buried in the churchyard, not under the church stones. Why do you ask?"

"No matter for that," Clement said. "Prithee tell me then where lieth Margaret Brandt."

"Margaret Brandt?" Jorian stared stupidly up at him. "She died some three years ago, aye, and was buried here."

"Oh, that is another matter," said Jorian, shrugging. "That was long before my time. The vicar could tell you, likely—if she was a gentlewoman, or at least rich enough to pay him his grave fee."

"Alas, my son, she was poor," Clement whispered, his head sinking onto his breast, "and paid a heavy penalty for it. But she came of decent folk. Her father Peter was a learned physician; she came hither all the way from Sevenbergen to die." The words barely left his mouth before he went still, no strength or will left to question Jorian further. He was lost entirely in the past, and I doubt he even knew where he stood.

Jorian set his spade down, planted his fists on his hips, and said sulkily, "Are you making a fool of me, holy sir, or has some wag been making a fool of you?" He turned back to digging, flinging dirt with sharp, irritable vigor that made it clear his temper was ruffled.

Clement gazed at him with a puzzled, gently reproachful eye; the tone was rude, and the words made no sense to his foggy, grief-addled mind. Crusty as he was, Jorian was good-natured at heart. He had barely thrown up three spadefuls of earth before he grew ashamed of his outburst. "What a base churl am I to speak thus to thee, holy father, and thee standing there looking at me as mild as a lamb! Aha! I have it. 'Tis Peter Brandt's grave you would fain see, not Margaret's. He does lie here, hard by the west door. There, I'll show you." He laid down his spade, pulled on his doublet and jerkin, and prepared to walk the friar over to the tomb.

He had no idea there was anyone sitting on top of Peter Brandt's grave, still less that she was watching for this very holy friar. Pietro Vanucci and Andrea had not recognized him without his beard, either. The truth is, a beard that has never known a razor grows to become such a distinct, defining feature of a man's face that shaving it off can act as an almost perfect disguise.

As Jorian tugged his coarse linen doublet smooth and settled his thick wool jerkin over it, ready to lead the visitor to Peter Brandt’s grave, his rough, good-humoured tongue did not idle.
“Folks out Sevenbergen way used to call old Peter a bit of a magician, you know. And they swear he left them with a parting taste of his craft: told them he saw Margaret’s lad coming down the Rhine in fine velvet clothes and a purse heavy with coin, but his face scarred by a foreign sword, and short a limb or two from what he left with. But dear heart, none of it ever came to pass. Margaret still wears herself thin waiting for her Gerard, and old Peter lies as quiet in the clay as any of his neighbours—though she did pay to put a carved stone slab over him, to keep him settled where he belongs, as you shall soon see.”
He braced both hands on the edge of the open grave to heave himself up out of the dirt, but the friar laid a trembling, ice-cold hand on his shoulder, and spoke in a strange, hoarse whisper.
“How long has Peter Brandt been dead?”
“Some two months now. Why?”
“And his daughter buried him, you say?”
“Nay, I dug the grave for him, but she paid all the church dues and had that stone raised to mark the spot. He never had more than the one daughter, Margaret, leastways none he ever owned to.”
“Then—you think Margaret is still alive?”
“Think? Man, I’d be dead in her place else. Riddle that one, will you? She saved my life not six weeks back. I’d come down with a wasting sickness, couldn’t keep a crumb on my stomach, and all the town doctors couldn’t do a thing for me. My Joan was already measuring me for a shroud, and then Margaret—who folks round here said died three years back, mark you—turned up, threw open my stuffy windows, had them move me out of my damp bed, and cured me in the blink of an eye. And what d’you think she used? The scurviest little weed growing wild in my very own garden: feverfew! I used to call it a nuisance, but now every time I pass that patch I doff my cap and give it a civil nod.” Jorian stopped short, staring at the friar as the man’s face flushed bright then drained ashen pale in quick succession. “What ails you, father? You look like you’ve seen a ghost.”
“Surprise—joy—wonder—terror,” gasped Clement, his chest heaving. “I knew a man who loved her so deeply the false news of her death nearly tore his soul clean from his body. You say she lives? I believe you.”
Jorian stared long and hard, then spoke very gravely. “By Our Lady, answer me this: did you truly know the lad that loved poor Margaret? Where?”
Clement nearly threw off his friar’s cowl right there to reveal his own face, but he remembered Jerome’s warning letter, and shrank back from the old name he had left behind in the secular world. “I knew him in Italy. His name was Gerard Eliassoen. I was with him when a letter arrived from Margaret Van Eyck, telling him the woman he loved was dead and buried. Let me sit down, my strength fails me. Foul play. Foul, cruel play.”
“Father, Heaven itself must have sent you here to me.” Jorian guided the staggering friar to a half-rotted grave marker to rest on, then spat on his palms and drove his spade furiously into the loose grave dirt, grinding his teeth. “I’ve held the riddle of that lie locked in my head for years, sick at heart for the both of them. Two knaves in this town I’d gladly bash sense into right this minute if I had the chance. You say you want to know who tricked your Gerard? It was Ghysbrecht van Swieten, the old burgomaster of Tergou, and those two worthless hounds Cornelis and Sybrandt, Gerard’s own blood brothers.
“I was doing carpentry work up in the burgomaster’s upper chamber once, patching the floor, and I’d lain flat on my stomach to sneak my tools away before they saw me loiter, when I heard the whole plot. They planned to swap the true letter that painter Hans Memling was carrying out to Gerard in Italy, for a forged one that said Margaret was dead. The old man was nervous they wouldn’t go through with it, so he opened a drawer brim full of silver, and said if they pulled the trick off they could each plunge a hand in and keep every coin they could hold.
“Next dawn I spotted those two rascals slinking out of their house, each sporting a fresh black eye. I followed them to the burgomaster’s, and hid in the rafters. I saw them open that drawer, every silver piece glinting, and you never saw two fools strain so hard to hold more coins than their fists were meant for. Sybrandt had even daubed the back of his hand in glue to stick extra pennies to his skin, the greedy lout! They did the foul deed, swapped the letters, and ran off—so giddy they even left their own silver rings behind in the drawer, the devil got the better end of that bargain.
“They’ve got a fancy new shop in the Hoog Straet now, sign hanging out front all gilded: a sheep and a lambkin. A pair of wolves sucking their dam would be closer to the mark. The whole family’s feasting there today, celebrating their wicked little victory. All these years Margaret’s sat by her window staring down the street, crying her eyes out for Gerard, never once guessing he’d been tricked into thinking she was rotting in the ground. If it weren’t for those two cowards, the lad whose life I fished out of the river would be here beside her now, the happiest man in all Holland, instead of wasting away in a foreign country, and she’d have her head on his shoulder instead of pining alone day after day—”
The rest of his rant died unspoken. The friar had sprung to his feet, livid with unchained, wordless fury, fists clenched high over his head, and tore headlong out of the churchyard as if the hounds of hell were at his heels. Jorian’s own anger fizzled out to nothing at the sight of that raw, unhuman tempest of grief, and he stood gaping after him, bewildered, until a small, trembling hand closed around his arm.
It was Margaret Brandt. She had waited for the friar on old Peter’s tombstone for so long she’d wandered into the church to look for him, only to see his enormous shadow tear across the south aisle floor and brush right past her, spurring her after him into the yard. She stared after the vanishing wild figure down the lane, then turned to Jorian, white-lipped.
“What did he say to you? He spoke to you, do not deny it.”
“Girl, he asked me where you were buried in this churchyard. I told him nowhere, thank the Lord, that you were alive and going about saving fools like me from the grave. Then he told me he knew your Gerard in Italy, and got a letter that said you were dead. I told him the truth: that letter was a forgery, those two knaves Cornelis and Sybrandt swapped it, I saw the whole thing.”
Margaret gasped, half laughing through tears. “He lives! The worst fear of all is gone, thank God.” But her face blanched again a heartbeat later. “Oh, Jorian—what have you done? That friar is no stranger. That is Gerard. Himself! You do not know him like I do. He once struck the burgomaster Ghysbrecht so hard the man dropped senseless to the ground. He’s heading straight for that shop on Hoog Straet. Quick! Help me run, before there is bloodshed.”
Jorian’s blood turned to ice. The tonsured friar’s sunken, fasting face snapped into place in his memory, that was the lad he’d dragged out of the Rhine all those years ago. He scrambled out of the grave, yanking his jerkin on as he ran beside her, their boots thudding down the cobblestones.
They rounded the corner onto Hoog Straet, and spotted the gilded sheep sign swinging over the new shop barely twenty yards ahead, when a roar like a wounded wild beast burst out from inside the house. The door flew off its latch, and the friar burst out, still white with unspent rage, fists raised high, deaf to Jorian’s shouts to stop, and tore down the far end of the street before they could even call his name.
Margaret screamed, and fainted dead away against Jorian’s chest. A moment later she stirred, her face calm and cold as winter frost.
“Help me inside, Jorian. Let me see what horror lies there. Let me know the worst, and die if I must.”
He supported her shaking limbs across the threshold, the house unnaturally, deathly still around them. No sound of shouting, no cry of pain. He pushed the unlatched inner door open softly with his palm, and the two of them stood frozen, side by side, on the threshold of the great back chamber. What they saw there, you shall soon know.

Supper time had fallen soft over Eli’s cottage, the hearth fire spitting golden light across the scrubbed oak table heaped with smoking earthen dishes. Every soul of the household was gathered round the board save Margaret, and to Catherine’s utter surprise, Eli leaned back in his oaken settle and announced he would wait a while for her.
“Why, I told you not to linger for the duke himself, no less,” Catherine fussed, tucking a stray strand of hair back under her cap.
“Ah, she is no duke,” Eli rumbled. “She is a good lass, poor thing, that hath waited not mere minutes, but long years, for that graceless son of mine. You can set all the meat out just the same—then we may fall to without wasting a second more the moment she steps through the door.”
The savour of spiced barley stew and roasted pork wrapped in herbs drifted thick across the room, and at last Eli’s good intentions crumbled. “She will come running the moment we set knives to board, you mark my word—they always do,” he said, waving a hand to their guest. “Come, sit ye down, Mistress Joan! You are no servant here, but an honoured guest. There—hark, that’s a quick step on the cobbles! Off with the covers, and fall to.”
The silver lids were whisked off the dishes, every man’s knife raised to carve, and the figure that burst through the door was no soft-faced Margaret. It was a Dominican friar, his black habit flapping, his face livid with unholy rage.
He cleared the distance to the table in one long stride, leaned his tall frame across its narrow width, and hovered both hands over the cowering heads of Cornelis and Sybrandt like eagles swooping down on a trapped quarry. He cursed them by name, soul and body, in this world and the world to come. That was an age when men wove curses as vivid as any sermon, but this one was so full, so minute, so blighting and searing in its wrath, no full transcript could be set to paper without turning the reader’s blood cold.
“Cursed be the lips,” he shrieked, “that spoke the lie that Margaret was dead! May they rot on your faces before the grave claims you, and burn on kisses of white-hot iron in hell for all eternity! Doubly cursed be the hands that tampered with my letters, that hid the truth from two hearts that loved true—may the hangman’s knife strike them off at the wrist, that they may handle nothing but hell’s unquenchable fire forever! Thrice accursed be the cruel, coward hearts that conceived that damned lie to tear true love apart! May you sicken and wither on this earth, joyless, loveless, hopeless, waste away to dust long before your allotted years, and burn for all time in the fires below!”
He cursed the food at their very mouths, cursed every hair on their heads, every bone, every drop of blood, down to the soles of their trembling feet. The two brothers cringed so far down they were half hidden beneath the table, and the friar tore a crumpled letter from the bosom of his habit and flung it hard at Eli’s chest.
“Read that, hard old man—you that locked your own son away, read it and see what monsters you have reared under your own roof! The memory of my wrongs, and hers, shall hang heavy on all of you for every day you draw breath. I will meet you all again on judgment day. On this earth, you shall never see my face again.”
He was gone as swiftly as he had come, vanishing out the door and down the lane before a single person could move to speak, leaving the whole family stiff and cold and white as carved statues huddled around their untouched, smoking supper.
It was this frozen, eerie sight that greeted Margaret and Jorian as they stepped over the threshold. Pale, motionless figures clustered around untasted food, exactly as old Eastern poets wrote of folks turned to stone mid-meal by a curse. Margaret’s eyes darted round the room, and she gasped, pressing a hand to her chest.
“Oh joy! All are whole, no blood has been spilled. Oh, you cruel, cruel men! I thank God he did not strike you dead.”
Catherine let out a sharp, sobbing scream the moment she saw her, then turned her face away. But Eli had just scanned the false, tampered letter the friar had thrown down, every thread of the long, cruel deceit clicking sharp in his mind. Seeing Margaret, the other wronged victim, standing there pale and weary with all her years of grief written on her face, he roared out in a white heat of rage.
“Stand clear! Let me get at those traitors. I will hang for them, I swear I will!”
He whipped out the short iron sword he kept at his belt, and lunged for the two brothers.
“Fly!” Margaret shrieked. “Fly for your lives!”
Cornelis and Sybrandt scrambled howling across the floor, slipped under the table, and crawled out the far side. But before they could reach the door, the furious old man circled the table and cut off their escape. Catherine could only scream and wring her hands, quite useless in the face of such violence, and blood would surely have spilled that night if Margaret and Jorian had not thrown their full weight against Eli’s arms, holding him fast till the two rascals stumbled out the open door and fled down the lane. Only then did they release him, and he stormed out after them, raging and shaking his sword at the dark empty street long after they had vanished over the horizon.
When he trundled back home, he hacked down the wooden board nailed to his outer wall that bore the two sons’ names, and flung it straight into the roaring hearth. Catherine sat huddled in her chair, rocking back and forth, her apron pulled over her face. Joan had hurried to her husband’s side. Margaret had her arms wrapped tight round Catherine’s neck, pale and panting, doing all she could to soothe her.
But there was no soothing her that night. “Oh, my poor, lost children!” Catherine wailed between sobs. “Oh, miserable mother that I am! It is a mercy our Kate is laid ill upstairs. I thank God for that now, for it would have killed her to see all this. He would have done far better to stay in Italy, than come home to curse his own flesh and blood and turn this whole house upside down.”
“Hold your silly chatter, woman!” Eli snapped at her, sharp with anger. “You still take the side of the evil-doers! You got exactly what you deserved—your soft foolishness is what made those rogues what they are. I was all for correcting them hard when they were lads: sore ills need sharp remedies, but you always took their part, undermined me, and baffled all my wise severity. And you, Margaret, leave off comforting her—she ought to be comforting you, for what is her hurt compared to yours? She never had a grain of true justice in her bones, and never will. Come to me now. From this hour, I am your father.”
It was no request, it was a gentle command. Margaret kissed Catherine’s wet cheek, tottered over to him, and he set her down on a chair right beside his own. She laid her weary, feeble head on his broad, honest breast, and not a tear fell—her grief was too deep, too long held back, for tears. “Poor lamb,” he murmured, stroking her hair.
After a little while, Eli cleared his throat, and spoke in a rough, broken voice to Jorian and Joan. “Good folks, you can see we are in a bit of trouble here. But that is no reason you should go hungry. For our Lady’s sake, sit and fall to your supper! Do not add to my grief the shame of being thought a churlish host.” He gave a sudden, ghastly attempt at a hearty laugh. “The more knaves I have the luck to be rid of, the more I need good, true folk like you to help me clear these dishes, and cheer my eyes with honest faces where there ought to be nothing but gaps. Fall to, I entreat you.”
Catherine, still sobbing, added her own plea to his. These were poor, simple, hospitable old souls, and Jorian—whose appetite had been ravenous ever since his recent illness—was all ready to tuck in, till Joan leaned over and whispered a word in his ear. He drew back at once.
“Nay,” he said, shaking his head. “I will touch no meat that a man of Holy Church has laid his curse upon.”
“Ah, that is right, I forgot,” Eli said, apologetic. “My own son, that was reared at my very table, has cursed my victuals. A strange thing, that. Well, what God wills, man must bow to.”
The whole untouched supper was carried out and dumped in the yard for the strays and the pigs. Jorian and Joan walked home through the gathering dark, and heavy, unbroken sadness hung over Eli’s cottage for the rest of that night.
Where was Clement, meanwhile? He lay stretched full length on the cold stone floor of the convent church, his lips pressed to the lowest step of the altar, caught in a tangle of terror, utter misery, penitence, and self-abasement—with tiny, bright threads of joy shining through it all, the knowledge that Margaret was alive, after all those years of grief.
Night fell, and found him still lying there, weeping and praying. Morning would have found him there too, if he had not jolted suddenly awake, horrified to realise that in the heat of his own rage, and his own grief, he had committed yet another sin: he had neglected a dying parishioner that had sent for him hours earlier.
He stumbled to his feet, groaning at his own accumulated wickedness, and set out at once to repair his mistake. The weather had turned, rain lashing hard at his face, and when he had left the town behind him, he heard the wolves baying, out hunting on the moor. But Clement was himself again, almost whole, and he thought little of danger or discomfort. He had a shameful omission of his priestly duty to make amends for, and he tramped steadily forward through the rain and the dark, beating his breast again and again, crying out over and over:

No pen, no matter how deft, could ever fully trace the searing, twisting agony that tore through Clement’s sensitive mind, soft conscience, loving heart, and devout religious soul in the first few shocking, tremendous hours after his world upended. To feel it at all, you must step into his boots, stand where he stood, and taste that same gale that ripped every last one of his certainties to shreds. I could spin a whole volume recounting every lurch and tremor of that inner tempest, and still end no closer to the truth than if I’d asked you to imagine it for yourself.

So instead, I will tell you only of his next two deliberate acts, each a clear window into the man he was, once that first wild hurricane of emotion had ebbed to a steady, smoldering resolve.

He’d spent the whole prior night at the dying hermit’s side, trading holy consolations, sharing prayer, tending to the old man’s last breaths. When he set out at dawn, he did not turn his feet toward Rotterdam as he’d once planned. He walked instead for Tergou. There he meant to confront his old, bitter enemy the burgomaster, and use the long-lost parchment—whose own winding history was a tale full of adventure all its own—to force the man to disgorge what he had stolen, and give Margaret Brandt back what was rightfully hers.

Sweaty, dust-caked, his boots crusted with miles of rutted country road, he stopped at a village fountain just outside Tergou, pulled a crust of black rye bread from his scrip, and knelt to sip cold water straight from the spout. He was halfway through his simple meal when a breathless female servant came running toward him, white-faced, begging him to come shrive her dying master at once. Without a single word of protest, he tucked the half-eaten bread back into his wallet and followed her.

She led him straight to the Stadthouse. A small, involuntary shudder ran through him when she pushed open its heavy oak doors, but he mastered himself in an instant, stepping across the threshold and following her up the wide, creaking staircase.

There in the great bed, propped high on a mountain of down pillows, lay the man who had been his deadliest enemy for years—Ghysbrecht the burgomaster, his face waxen, already looking more like a corpse than a living man. Clement stood in the doorway for a long moment, his eyes fixed on him, and all the old wrongs rose unbidden: the prison tower, the ambush in the woods, the forged letter that had torn Margaret and him apart for years. Then he spoke, his voice low and soft, though he trembled a little as he did: “Pax vobiscum.”

The dying man greeted him with all the eagerness his failing strength could muster. “Thank the Good Lord you’ve come in time, father,” he gasped. “Absolve me of my sins, pray for my soul, you and your brother friars, before it is too late.”

“My son,” Clement said, steady as he could, “absolution can only come after true, full confession. Hide nothing, if you value the salvation of your immortal soul. Think long now, of the wrongs you have done most grievously against God and His Church, while I kneel to pray for the wisdom to guide you.”

He knelt then, and prayed. When he stood again, his face was calm, his voice even. “Confess your sins, my son.”

“Ah, father,” Ghysbrecht whimpered, “they are many, and they are great.”

“Then let your penitence be great, my son, and you shall find God’s mercy great in turn.”

Ghysbrecht clasped his trembling hands, and began to recite his sins with every show of deep contrition. He owned he had eaten meat in the middle of Lent. He admitted he had skipped Mass on Sundays and feast days far too often, and trifled with all manner of small religious observances, listing every minor lapse with scrupulous, exact care.

When he finished, Clement spoke quiet and sharp. “That is all well, my son. These are small faults. Now tell me of your crimes. You would have done far better to start with those.”

“Why father?” the old man bleated, feigning shock. “What crimes could I have committed, if these are not counted as sin?”

“Who is here to be confessed to whom?” Clement said, a little sternly.

“Forgive me, father! I confess to you, of course. But I do not know what it is you name as crimes of me.”

“Are you free of the seven deadly sins?”

“Heaven forbid I should be guilty of them! I do not even know all their names!”

“Many a man commits every last one of them without ever being able to recite their names off by heart,” Clement said. “Start with the sin that begets lying, theft, and murder.”

“I am innocent of that one, no matter what it is called!” Ghysbrecht protested.

“It is called Avarice, my son.”

“Avarice?” The burgomaster blinked, all wide-eyed innocence. “Oh, that! Why, I’ve been a careful, saving man all my days, but I kept a good table for my household, and I never turned the poor away empty handed, not entirely. But I am a great sinner, no doubt—maybe the next sin you name will be mine. What is it?”

“We have not yet finished with this one,” Clement said, unshaken. “You will not trifle with Holy Church.”

“Alas! A man at death’s door has no power to trifle with anyone now!” Ghysbrecht moaned. “Avarice? Avarice?” He wore a look of perfect, puzzled confusion.

“Have you ever robbed the fatherless?” Clement asked, blunt and unflinching.

“Me? Robbed the fatherless?” Ghysbrecht gasped. “Not that I recall, no.”

“Once more, my son, I must tell you that you are trifling with the Church,” Clement said, his voice cold as winter stone. “Miserable man! One more evasion, and I will turn and leave this bed at once. Fiends are already gathering at your bedside, waiting to drag you straight down to the bottomless pit.”

“No! Do not leave me, holy man, do not leave me!” Ghysbrecht shrieked, terrified out of his wits. “The Church knows all, I will confess! I must have robbed the fatherless, I admit it! What names? My memory is all shaken, I can’t call them to mind!”

Clement had no time for this clever dodge. “Have you forgotten Floris Brandt?” he said, flat as a hammer striking iron.

The dying man reared straight up in bed, rigid with terror. “How did you know that?” he yelped.

“The Church sees many things,” Clement said, icy calm. “Paths are open to her that you, in your small worldly cunning, can never fathom. Miserable, unrepentant wretch! You called for a friar to shrive you, thinking to pick some stranger who knew nothing of your secret sins. You thought you would cheat the Church on your deathbed, lie to the priest, and die as you had lived, unpunished. But God, kinder to you than you ever were to yourself, sent the one man to your side that you cannot deceive. He has borne with you, He has warned you not to mock Holy Church—but you cannot bring yourself to confess, for your heart is hard as a stone. Go then, and die as you have lived. I see the fiends crowding at the foot of your bed, their claws out, waiting only for me to step away. And I will go.”

He turned his back to the bed, but Ghysbrecht threw himself forward, clutching tight to the hem of Clement’s friar’s frock. “Mercy! Stay! I will tell you everything, every last secret! I robbed my old friend Floris Brandt! Oh, I wish that was the worst of it—he lost almost nothing to me, at first. But then I seized his lands, and kept them from his son Peter, and from Peter’s daughter Margaret. I always meant to give them back, truly I did! But I could not bear to part with the gold, I could not, I could not!”

“Avarice, my son, plain and simple avarice,” Clement said, softening a little. “It is a mercy you have not waited too late to turn from it.”

“I will leave all her lands to her in my will!” Ghysbrecht babbled. “She will not have long to wait, you see! I will be dead in a month or two at the very most!”

“You fool,” Clement said, sharp and pitying. “You would damn your immortal soul for the sake of a single month’s hoarded possession of land that will rot beneath you before the year is out?”

Ghysbrecht groaned, begged the friar to be reasonable, to have pity on his age and his weakness. But Clement was firm, gentle, endlessly patient, and little by little he pried the dying miser’s grip loose from stolen property. There were moments when his own temper frayed thin, when he almost reached inside his robe to pull out the long-hidden parchment he had carried all the way to Tergou to force the issue. But after the wild, passionate grief that had overtaken him the day before, he was on his guard against anger. He conquered his impatience. He conquered the deep, visceral loathing he felt for this man, so strong it made his flesh crawl every moment he spent leaning over that deathbed, fighting for the man’s very soul. And in the end, without ever mentioning the hidden deed, he won. Ghysbrecht agreed to make full, immediate restitution, no delays, no wills, no waiting for his own death.

The exact details of that restitution, the strange, curious shifts that came over Ghysbrecht once he had done it, and the terms on which the burgomaster and Clement parted ways, will be told elsewhere in good time.

I promised to tell you of two acts of Clement’s that laid bare the state of his mind after that great storm of the soul. The first you have just heard. The second can be told in two short words.

The very moment he was certain Margaret Brandt had every last inch of her land back, and was secure, and rich, and well provided for?

He vanished.

The day after that shattering, terrible quarrel, the small cottage on Hoog Straet lay as still and silent as a fresh grave. Even Catherine, who was by nature the sprightliest, busiest soul in the parish, moved through the rooms listless and hollow-eyed, her cheeks streaked with the traces of hours of weeping. Once the dinner dishes were cleared, she slipped off to the convent, determined at the very least to speak to Gerard, to lay the first small stone that might one day mend the rift between them. It took her a long while to make the doddery old porter understand exactly which brother she was inquiring after; when he did, he broke the news gently that Gerard had left the convent grounds late the night before, and no one knew when he would return.

Sighing heavy, she trundled off to bring the news to Margaret, and found her sunk in a chair, her hands idle, as if life had lost all its salt for her. She clutched her little boy so tight to her chest it almost hurt, as if he was the last scrap of everything she had left, and half-convinced someone would creep in and tear him away too. Catherine begged her to come back to the Hoog Straet house, but Margaret only drew a weary breath. “What for?” she sighed. “You must all think, in your hearts, that I am the cause of every last bit of this ruin.”
“Nay, nay,” Catherine hurried to reassure her, “we are not so hard-hearted. Eli dotes on you, you know; maybe you will be the one to soften his temper enough to make things right.”
“If you think I can do any good at all, I’ll come,” Margaret said, and rose slowly, no fight left in her limbs.

When they stepped over the threshold of the house, they found Eli standing beside a carpenter, nailing a new name plaque over the spot where Cornelis and Sybrandt’s had once hung. The name carved into the wood, plain and bold, was Margaret Brandt’s. For all her love for the girl, the sight drove a knife straight through Catherine’s heart. “One man’s bane is another’s meat, that’s the truth of it,” she murmured.
“You cannot force me to spend that coin unjustly,” Margaret said, cold and steady.
“You are a good soul,” Catherine conceded. “And best to make peace with it, sith Eli is master of this house, after all.”

The next day, Giles dropped by for a visit. Catherine poured out the whole sorry tale, framing the two wayward sons as poor, cursed creatures cast out onto the wide world by their own father, and begged him to take pity on them. But Giles’s sympathies ran entirely the other way: he heard her out, then said bluntly the two knaves had got off far lighter than they deserved, and ought to have been hanged right outside Margaret’s door for all the harm they had done. He dismissed them with a snort of contempt, then brightened, crowing with delight at the thought of his favourite Gerard soon coming home. “I’ll show him,” he swore, “what it is to have a brother in court who has the heart to serve his friend, and the wits to point him straight to the best possible place.”
“Bless thee, Giles,” Margaret whispered soft.
“Thou wast ever his truest friend, dear Giles,” little Kate added, “but alack, I cannot see what thou canst do for him now, after all that has befallen.”

Once Giles had left and the house settled back into its heavy, sad quiet, a well-dressed man pushed the door open softly, and asked if Margaret Brandt lived there. Catherine perked right up, her old gossipy, curious self peeking through her gloom immediately. “D’ye hear, lass? You’ve a visitor,” she called.
“Well, mother,” Margaret said listlessly, “here I am.”
Shuffling feet sounded at the threshold, and a colourless, gaunt old man was helped into the room. It was Ghysbrecht Van Swieten. Catherine shrieked, and threw her apron over her head. Margaret shuddered so hard her whole body jolted, and twisted her head sharply away so she would not have to look at the man.
A thin, wobbly voice drifted from his lips. “Good people, a dying man has come to beg your forgiveness.”
“Come to gloat over the work of your own hands, you mean,” Catherine said, yanking her apron down and bursting into sobs. “There, look – she’s fainting! Eli, quick, tend to her.”
“Nay,” Margaret said, her voice faint, “the sight of him gave me a turn, that is all. Prithee, let him say his piece and go. For he is the man who murdered every good thing in me and mine.”
“Alas,” Ghysbrecht breathed, “I am far too feeble to say all this standing, and not one of you has bidden me sit.”
Eli, who had followed him in, spoke up half sullen, half ashamed. “Well, burgomaster, it is not our custom to leave a guest standing while we sit. But man, man – you have wrought us too much ill.” His honest voice shook with the rage he fought hard to contain, for this was his own hearth.

Then little Kate, the quiet one whose words seldom fell on deaf ears in that family, spoke. “Father, mother, I owe you all duty, but this is not right. Death squares every debt. And can you not see the reaper standing at his shoulder? I shall not live long, good friends – and his time is shorter than mine.”
Eli hurried to drag a chair over for their dying enemy with his own two hands. Ghysbrecht’s attendants settled him into it, then carried in two heavy oak boxes and withdrew, leaving their master alone with the family he had tormented for so long. Every eye was fixed on him save Margaret’s. His fingers trembled as he undid the latches, and pulled from the first box the full set of title deeds to every house and acre of land in Tergou that had once belonged to Floris Brandt.
“This land was yours by right, as his granddaughter,” he rasped. “I seized it over a debt that was paid off, long ago, with interest. I kept it out of greed, but I restore it now, with penitent tears.” He opened the second box, and it glinted with three hundred and forty golden angels, stacked neat. “This is all the rent and fines I collected from that land, every penny over and above the debt Floris owed me. I kept count all these years, always telling myself I would make it right one day – but Avarice held me back. I was not born a thief, as you all know.”
“Well, will you look at that!” Catherine gasped. “And you the burgomaster, who whipped more thieves in the town square than I can count! Still, better late than never. Margaret, what ails you, lass? The man has brought you back what is yours. You are a rich woman now – alack, what a mountain of gold!”
“Bid him keep the land and the gold,” Margaret said, still not turning her head, “and give me back my Gerard, that he stole from me with his lies and his treason.”
“Alas,” Ghysbrecht sighed, “would that I could. All that was in my power to do, I have done. I dragged myself from my deathbed to bring this myself, lest some clerk or greedy kin steal it from you before it reaches your hands.”
“Old man,” Margaret said, “since you, who worshipped pelf all your life, have done this, I pray God and the saints will forgive you. But I am no saint, no angel – only a poor woman whose heart you broke. Speak for me, Kate. I feel half dead.”
Kate’s soft, silvery voice fell over the room like cool rain. “My poor sister has a grief no amount of gold can mend. Give her time, Ghysbrecht. It is not in nature for her to forgive you all at once. Her boy is fatherless, and she is neither maid, wife, nor widow – the wound was torn open only two days past, and it bleeds still. Give her time. Ere you die, she will forgive you all, even to please me – for I shall not be long behind you, Ghysbrecht. The rest of us, whose wounds are sore but not half so deep, forgive you, a penitent dying man. I, for one, will pray for you from this hour. Go in peace.”
Eli even invited him to stay to break a crust of manchet bread and drink a stoup of spiced wine to strengthen him for the journey home, but Ghysbrecht declined. “All that land I clung to for decades was nothing but a bed of nettles to me,” he said. “Now it is gone, and I feel lighter, livelier, than I have in years.” His attendants lifted him into his litter, and he was gone.

Catherine immediately fell to poring over the golden coins, she had never seen so much wealth piled in one place in her life, and grew almost cross with Margaret for sitting there like a wooden statue. She gushed on and on about all the good things they could do with the money, nagging Margaret until she finally consented to come and look at it.
“Better leave her be, mother,” Kate pleaded. “How can she relish gold, when her heart in her bosom is liker lead?”
But Catherine would not be put off. Margaret looked down at all her glinting new wealth, her eyes wide and uncomprehending. Then suddenly she wrung her hands, and a piercing cry tore out of her that echoed off the cottage walls:
She collapsed into ragged, heaving hysterics, sobbing over the fortune that had arrived far too late to share with the man she loved. A fraction of that gold, a single plot of that land, even a year or two prior – and Gerard would have never left her side, never run off for Italy chasing fortune.
Too late. Too late.

Barely a handful of quiet days slipped past before the tidings came: Margaret Van Eyck was dead and laid in her grave. A will she had drawn up a full year prior left all her property, after covering funeral costs and a handful of small personal gifts to her loyal maidservant Reicht Heynes, to her beloved adopted daughter Margaret Brandt, with a gentle request that Margaret keep Reicht in her household for as long as the older woman remained unwed.

Margaret thus inherited a fully furnished house, plus a collection of paintings and sketches that would count as a princely fortune in the modern day. Chief among them was a piece she valued more than an entire royal gallery of works: *The Betrothal*, a scene where the quiet solemnity of the ceremony glowed on the grave, earnest face of the groom and the soft demure complacency of the bride. The elder Margaret Van Eyck had painted almost all of the central figures, with Jan Van Eyck finishing the intricate accessories that remained a marvel of master craft centuries later. Margaret sent word back to Reicht begging her to stay on in the Van Eyck home for the time being; she could not yet bear to cross its threshold, to walk halls that no longer hummed with the old painter's voice and warm greeting. She charged Reicht to guard the little picture in the "small cubboord" above all others — the tiny hand-painted diptych that had been Margaret Van Eyck's most cherished possession.

The very next week Luke Peterson returned home, and learned the news that Gerard had taken holy orders as a monk. He was nearly mad with joy, and burst straight to Margaret's cottage.
"Hear me, mistress," he cried. "If he cannot marry you, I can."
"You?" Margaret blinked at him. "I have already seen him."
"But he's a friar now."
"He was my husband, and my boy's father, long before he ever put on a friar's robes." Margaret's voice was steady, though her hands twisted tight in her apron. "I have seen him, I tell you, I have seen him."
Luke was thoroughly flummoxed. "I have a cousin who is a lawyer," he said. "I'll go ask him straight if you are legally married or still free to wed."
"Nay, I do not need a lawyer to tell me what my own heart already knows." Margaret shook her head, sharp with quiet disappointment. "And you would make me the talk of the whole town over this? Fie on you, that is no mark of respect for me. If you so much as breathe a word of this to any soul outside this room, you will never come near me again."
Luke sighed heavy as lead. "You are soft as a dove to every other soul in the parish, but a hard-hearted tyrant to me."
"That is your own fault, dear Luke, for wooing me." Margaret's tone softened. "I cannot be the kind to you that I want to be, so long as you carry that hope in your heart. I am rich now, you see — I cannot make myself happy, but I can make my dearest friends happy. Look out at the street, look around at all the lasses who live here: twice as fair as I, and never worn thin with years of weeping. Pick one, speak to her yourself, and I will go speak to her mother on your behalf. They will not turn you down, mark my words."
Luke turned bright red. "I see what you mean. But if I cannot have your liking, I will have none of your charity. I was your servant back when you were poorer than I was, and hungrier too. If you would rather be a friar's secret companion than an honest man's wife, then you are not the woman I took you for. So we part without malice: you seek your comfort on that road no woman ever found joy on, and I will live and die a bachelor. Good even, mistress."
"Farewell, dear Luke." Margaret's eyes glistened. "May God forgive you for saying that to me."

For days after that, Margaret waited for the meeting with Gerard, torn between dread and desperate longing. She told herself it was only natural he needed a little time to work through his grief and his vows. Surely he would soon hear he was a father, and the urge to see their little boy would overcome every other restraint. "If that meeting does not kill me," she whispered to her reflection, "I know I will heal after it."
But day after day slipped by, and there was no word of him. A cold, creeping doubt seeped through her bones. What if his absence was intentional? What if he had run back to his cold, hard fellow monks, and they had convinced him he must never set eyes on her again? The cloister had already proven itself as merciless to true lovers as the grave itself. At that thought, the life felt to drain out of her. For the first time, sharp indignation began to mingle with her grief. Could he ever have truly loved her, to run from her and his own child without a single word? Even the foolish, stubborn Luke cared more for her than that.

While her mind was twisted in that dark spiral, the dwarf Giles came roaring into the house, banging his fists on the table. "I have hit the mark! Our Gerard is the Vicar of Gouda!"
A quick sketch of Giles's time at court will explain how he pulled off that feat. Some months before he joined the Burgundian royal household, his wits had suddenly bloomed: he himself dated the shift to the 8th of June, when he was swinging one-handed from a tight clothesline strung across the drying green, a week's worth of washing strung beside him, and something gave a soft crack inside his head. All at once his sharp intelligence was unchained. At court, his shrewd blunt speech, booming giant's voice and tiny frame made him an unignorable power — without that small stature, he would no doubt have been hauled straight to the gallows for his cheek. The young Duchess of Burgundy and the heiress apparent Marie doted on him, as great ladies have always petted clever dwarves, and the court poets fawned over him so thoroughly they could have stewed Goliath in all the buttered praise they poured over his head. They even versified and watered down rough, pithy lines he dictated, churning out long flowery verses that Giles sent to his father Eli, titled *The High and Puissant Princess Marie of Bourgogne her Lytel Jantilman Hys Complaynt of ye Coort, and Praise of a Rusticall Lyfe, Versificated and Empapyred by me the Lytel Jantilman's right lovynge and obsequious servitor*.
Giles reached the peak of his fame at a grand court joust, the day before the main events, when he challenged the Duke's personal giant to a trial of strength. He had a tall smooth pole planted ready, and at the appointed hour he shinnied up it like a squirrel, held his body perfectly horizontal by nothing but the strength of his arms, then slid down so fast the princess squeaked and hid her face in her hands, sure her tiny pocket Hercules would dash his brains out on the stone. The giant only managed to climb ten feet before he was sweating through his tunic, clambering back down to grumble that it was Giles's small body, not his greater strength, that won the contest. The crowd hooted that excuse down at once.
"Fine," Giles said, grinning. "If you will argue that, I'll wrestle you, and I will even blindfold you first."
The smarting giant jumped at the chance to win back his pride.
"Ladies and gentlemen," Giles called out to the crowd. "Watch yon blind Samson. At a single signal from me, he will bow low to me, and doff his bonnet."
Wagers flew left and right, and at the exact moment the bets were all laid, Giles popped a sharp, light punch right into the giant's gut. The giant doubled over in a perfect bow, his bonnet tumbling off his head, and the whole court roared with laughter. Giles took off at a sprint, ducking through a tiny hidden door in the wall he had pre-prepped that no giant could ever fit through, and left a little rhyme painted on the far side of the trick door:
After that, Giles was an untouchable force at court.
Now he told Margaret the full story of how he secured the living for Gerard.
"When the princess sent for me to her bedchambers as she always did, to chase away her boredom, I came not full of my usual jests and country proverbs, but dull as lead," Giles recounted. "She asked what ailed me, if I was sick, and the hussies they call her maids of honour tittered that I must be in love. I told them I could not be half that mad, not after all the foolery I'd seen at court. The princess sent the ladies off to stand apart, and bade me speak my mind without fear. I reminded her of five years past, when a tall, fair young boy came to her chambers with a letter from painter Margaret Van Eyck — that boy was my brother Gerard. I told her how she and her mother the late Countess of Charolois had promised Gerard a good church living, once he was old enough to take orders. She burst straight into tears, saying she had not forgotten, that her mother on her deathbed had charged her to make sure that promise was kept. I told her the old Vicar of Gouda had died the week before, and she declared on the spot that Gerard would be the new Vicar of Gouda, no delays, no questions asked. She cried for her mother, I cried for my poor brother, and that is how it was done."
Margaret could not contain herself. She caught the tiny dwarf up in her arms, hugging him tight and kissing his cheek. "Oh Giles, your body is so small, but your heart is bigger than any man's twice your size. You are his truest friend. Bless you, bless you, a hundred times bless you! Now we will see him again, after that terrible day we lost sight of him."
Giles had the town criers shout the news that Friar Clement, now the new Vicar of Gouda, was wanted to take up his post across Rotterdam and all the neighbouring towns, to Margaret's secret delight. But days rolled on, and Gerard never came. Giles was mortified, Margaret indignant and wretched, convinced he had run all the way back to Italy, that he hated her for not being dead.
Joan suggested she consult the famous hermit of Gouda, but Margaret laughed the thought off. "What does a man shut up in a cave know of where Gerard has gone? Less than I, no doubt."

Not long after, a messenger arrived from Tergou, saying old Ghysbrecht Van Swieten had seen Gerard more recently than any other soul alive. Margaret set off for Tergou at once, and found the old burgomaster sitting in his wheeled chair in his garden, old and feeble, but glad to greet her. He told her he had not met Gerard Brandt, but Friar Clement, and that the day the friar crossed his threshold had been the most blessed of his whole life. He recounted how the friar had arrived, made him give back all the land he had stolen from Margaret years before, then gently tricked him into confessing the evil letter he had written to tear the two lovers apart. Ghysbrecht had sobbed that he could never be forgiven for that wicked act — and then the friar had leaned in, soft and tremulous, and said "Ghysbrecht, look at me closer. I am Gerard, son of Eli." The old burgomaster broke down weeping as he told Margaret how he had tried to fall at Gerard's feet in contrition, but Gerard would not let him. He said those three days he had spent praying under Ghysbrecht's roof had let him find the strength to forgive the man who had ruined his life. Then he had taken his leave, without waiting for anything more.
Margaret wept with him, told Ghysbrecht she forgave him too, and begged him to help her find Gerard before the Church gave the Gouda living to a stranger. The old man summoned his servants, dictated letters to every burgomaster in every major town across Holland, and sent trusted couriers as far away as Basle in Switzerland to spread the news that the new Vicar of Gouda was needed to take up his post. Margaret went home glowing with fresh hope, and swore to herself she would never judge Gerard again until she heard his side of the story straight from his own lips.

But soon a new, terrible disaster struck. Sybrandt, the wastrel son of Eli and Catherine, had been given gold Margaret had lent his mother to keep him fed, and he drank every penny of it away. Drunk out of his mind one afternoon, he climbed the stable roof of the inn he was carousing at, slipped, and fell straight onto a wooden paling, then toppled to the ground. His drunken friends carried him, helpless and unable to stand, to Margaret's door. She looked at his pale, streaky face, and knew at once his spine was broken — he would never walk again. The curse he had joked about for years had fallen on him at last. Margaret, remembering how Gerard had forgiven even his worst enemy Ghysbrecht, tended the helpless, injured man no matter all the wrongs he had done her.
Catherine arrived from Tergou almost mad with grief, blaming herself for sneaking her worthless son money to feed his drinking binges. Streaks of grey turned her hair white within weeks, and she was never the bright, bustling singing woman she had been before. Sybrandt wailed day and night for Gerard, begging Margaret to find him and lift the curse that had left him paralyzed. Luke Peterson appeared soon after, thin and haggard, saying he would rather be her loyal brother than stay away from her entirely, and would do any work she asked of him. Margaret sent him off to search every corner of the country, then the continent, for their lost marriage banns and Gerard himself.

Months slipped by: Sybrandt's body never healed, and he remained Margaret's helpless pensioner for life. Catherine moved into Margaret's cottage in Rotterdam, with Eli's quiet permission, saying little Gerard — Margaret's son, the spitting image of his father — was the only thing that could soothe her heavy, fearful heart, now that she lived in constant dread that the same curse that had struck Sybrandt would fall on her other rogue son Cornelis. The people of Gouda sent a second formal petition to the Duke of Burgundy, complaining they had gone six whole months without a vicar: their children were dying unbaptised, their dead were buried by chance travellers passing through, and no one could tend to their souls. Even with all of Giles's influence, there was no way to hold them off for much longer. Margaret's last sliver of hope was fraying thin, and the race to find Gerard before his living was given away to a stranger was nearly at its end.

The hermit of Gouda, that quiet, unseen soul the villagers brought offerings of bread and herbs to, was none other than the long-lost vicar of Gouda himself—so absolute had his decades-long seclusion been, that neither his old parishioners nor even he himself had ever stumbled on the truth.

Any reader who knows Clement will recall that the second the white-hot frenzy of his recent passion and rage burned away, he was seized by a remorse so sharp it left him reeling. But only those who have climbed as high the ladder of spiritual devotion as he had, only to slip and fall hard from that peak, can grasp the icy terror that took hold of him then. He felt as if his own misplaced self-confidence had lured him right to the lip of a sheer precipice, one misstep from eternal ruin. “Ah, good Jerome,” he gasped, chest heaving, “how far better you knew my weakness than I knew it myself! How bitter, how wholesome, was that warning you spoke to me long ago.”

Trained his whole adult life to dissect his own heart, he spotted the root of his fury at once: it was all for Margaret. “That means I love her more than God,” he realized, hollow with despair. “More than I love the Church. What good can ever come of such a love, for her or for me?” He shuddered at the thought. “Let the strong stand and fight temptation. The weak? The weak run. And what have I just proven myself to be, if not weak? All my years of penance, all my carefully built piety?
