It was nothing more than a house of cards, stacked slowly over months and years by my own hands, and one single breath of earthly love blew the whole thing to dust. I must start again. This time, I will build my faith on ground so firm no passion can shake it.”

He resolved to flee Holland at once, to spend years hidden away in a distant, foreign convent before he ever dared set foot on Dutch soil again. By then, he reasoned, the fire of his earthly passion would have long since burned to ash; as an older, wiser monk, he would have full mastery over his human affections, and Margaret, abandoned and free of him, would marry a good, steady man and build a life with someone who would never risk her soul the way he had. The sharp, twisting pain that thought wrenched from him was proof, to his relentlessly self-scrutinizing mind, that he was finally walking the hard path of true religious duty.

Even so, he would not abandon her to poverty while he saved his own soul. The sweet, steady comfort of knowing he could secure her a lifetime of modest comfort, of worldly plenty that she was never bound to reject, carried him through the bitter agony of turning his back on her without a single kind word, a single gentle look. “What will she think of me?” he groaned to himself. “She will surely see me as the most heartless, inhuman wretch alive. But that is for the best. It is far better that she hate this miserable, broken thing I am. Heaven is merciful— it leaves me this small comfort. I can force that villain who robbed her to return every penny that is hers, so she will never lose another true lover because of grinding poverty. Another? Ah me. Ah me. God and all the saints, lend me your aid.”

The outcome of that errand has already been told. First, as you may remember, he snuck out by night to hear the dying confession of that old hermit of Gouda. He found the old man drawing his last breaths, and never left his side until he had closed his eyes, and buried him in the dirt floor of the tiny oratory attached to his cell. It was the peaceful end to a long, stormy life: the hermit had been a brutal soldier in his youth, and still wore a steel corselet against his skin, saying he was Christ’s soldier now just as he had once been Satan’s.

After Clement had shriven him and knelt praying at his deathbed, the dying man turned and urged him to take his place as the new keeper of that small, peaceful retreat. “I fought a hard battle against the world, the flesh, and the devil,” he whispered, “and I never truly defeated any of them until I locked myself away in this citadel of solitude.”

Those words, and the quiet, pious death that followed moments later, stamping them with the weight of eternal truth, sank deep into Clement’s soul. They met no resistance in his heart, for the solitary recluse was still held in profound reverence across the whole medieval Church, whether an anchorite walled into a cave or cell belonging to a monastery, or a hermit living independent, hidden away in the wild woods. Clement knew more about the lives of these holy solitaries than most clergymen half his senior: he had pored over their stories in the monastery near Tergou, devoured their hagiographies in Vatican manuscripts, and debated their lives for hours with mendicant friars from half a dozen nations. Before the invention of printing, these wandering friars were the great messengers who carried local annals and biographies from convent to convent, across every border in Christendom.

His old teacher Jerome, too, had spent three years as an anchorite on the heights of Camaldoli, where the ancient piety of the Thebaid desert had been kept alive for four hundred years. Cold, curt, and dismissive of most casual religious talk, Jerome had lit up with bright enthusiasm when he spoke of those hermits. He had studied the annals of St. John Baptist’s abbey, scattered with hermit caves, and told Clement story after story of noble knights and famous warriors who laid down their swords to die as hermits, of bishops and archbishops who left their wealthy sees for bare stone cells, or left their hermitages only to take the throne of St. Peter. He spoke of the Archbishop of Ravenna who left his archiepiscopal palace for a cave, of Pope Victor the Ninth who had left a cave to take the papal crown. He described their brutal, deliberate austerities: how every hermit hunted down his own weakest spot, and attacked himself without mercy, day after day, until even there, he was strongest. How seven times in every twenty-four hours, through thunder, rain, and snow, by starlight, twilight, or torchlight, the solitaries tramped miles over rough, precipitous paths to worship in the abbey church, at matins, prime, tierce, sexte, nones, vespers, and compline. He even described the famous anchorites he had sung the psalter beside: the Duke of Moncata, who left all the pomp of the Spanish court in the flower of his youth to live alone on the mountain; Father John Baptist of Novara, who had once led armies to battle before becoming a private soldier of Christ; and the aged Sylvanus, who had met the great Duchess de’ Medici at the first wooden cross leading up the holy mountain, and persuaded her so firmly not to be the first woman in centuries to profane that sacred ground that she turned her entire retinue of courtiers, soldiers, and pages around and retreated without setting foot further up the path.

In Basle, Clement had found still more stories of German and English anchorites, and had even compiled a *Catena Eremitarum* — a Chain of Hermits — tracing their history from 250 AD, when Paul of Thebes began his ninety years of total solitude, right up to 1470. He called them *Angelorum amici et animalium*: Friends of Angels and Animals.

Back then, he never dreamed he would ever become a recluse himself, but the road had been paved for him, every step of it. When the dying hermit of Gouda blessed the citadel of solitude he had won his victory in, and invited Clement to pick up the breastplate of faith that was slipping off his shrunken, dying body, Clement thought to himself: Heaven itself led my feet here for this very end. It struck him as no small sign that his own patron saint, Bavon, had been a hermit too, a hardened cuirassier of the solitary cell.

No sooner had he made his peace with Ghysbrecht Van Swieten than he hurried eagerly toward the hermitage, praying all the while that no one had claimed it in the three days since the old hermit died. His fear was far from foolish: these famous holy cells never stayed empty for long. He found the rough, unbarred stone door ajar, and his heart sank. He pushed it open and stepped softly inside. No — the cell was empty. The old hermit’s great ivory crucifix stood on the stone shelf, his pens and ink, his seed packets, the carved skull memento mori, his hair cilice, his bristle cilice, his worn sheepskin pelisse and hood, his hammer, chisel, and psaltery, all exactly where he had left them. Dozens of villagers had passed that door in the last three days, but none had dared intrude, let alone steal. Simple faith and reverence had guarded that keyless cell far more securely than any layman’s house, with its gates built like modern prisons and iron bars nailed over every window, or any noble’s estate, ringed with moats, bastions, chevaux-de-frise, and portcullises.

The second Clement stepped fully inside, there was a loud flap of wings, a flurry of movement, and a great brown owl swooped down from a high corner and whirled out the window, brushing cold air against his face. He started, shuddering. Was the owl some diabolical spirit, come to scare him away from the work of saving his soul? On second thought, might it not be a good spirit the old hermit had left to guard the cell, even the old hermit’s own soul? In the end, he decided it was only an owl, and he would be kind to it and try to make it his friend. He knelt down, and began his new life in a long, earnest prayer.

Clement had far more than his earthly love for Margaret to subdue, a passion so powerful it still made him tremble for his eternal soul: he had to do penance for the violent, ungodly rage that had made him curse his own brothers in the monastery. He glanced around the roomy, comparatively comfortable cell, and compared it in his mind to the horrific, brutal dwellings of the great saints of the desert: the *eremus in eremo*, the desert within a desert, where Saint Jerome had wrestled with sickness, temptation, and despair for four mortal years; the narrow, thorny little hole in the face of a precipice where the boy hermit Benedict had hidden himself, living for three years on the scraps of bread the kind monk Romanus could spare him from his own scanty rations, splitting every single mouthful with his friend, a raven; the hollow tree where his patron Saint Bavon had made his home; the earthly purgatory in Fribourg where an unnamed saint lived in a horrid cavern, his eyes perpetually chilled by total gloom, his ears stunned nonstop by the roar of a waterfall; the pillar that Saint Simeon Stylites stood on for forty-five years; the narrow stone box, the *destina*, where Saint Dunstan lived, barely big enough for him to sit, stand, or lie down in, a tomb more than a home; the lead-sealed living tombs of Thais, Christina, and so many other holy recluses; the damp, dark dungeon cell of Saint Alred. Scores of these miserable, bare dens, where true hermits wore out their wasted bodies on cold rock, the same rock that had been their bed as they slept, their kneeler as they prayed, flooded his mind. “This gentle, easy retreat is enough to keep my soul safe,” he thought, “but it is not enough penance. Jesus, aid me against the sins I will commit in the years to come. For the sin I already rue, I vow that no living human being shall see my face for a full twelvemonth and a day.” He had famous, well-documented precedents for this severe, unusual vow: the original hermit who had built this cell had clearly been bound by the same oath, which was why he had left two narrow slits in the stone wall, one to speak through, one to hear through, so he could converse with visitors without ever showing his face.

For the rest of his rule, he followed the ancient, uniform customs of hermits and anchorites. He divided his whole day into the seven monastic offices, ignoring the petty accidents of light and dark, both creations of the God he prayed to unceasingly. He memorized the entire psalter by heart, and every moment not spent in devotion or broken, short sleep he spent working hard with his hands. No rule of the hermits was more ancient or more strictly enforced than that: a hermit could not be idle. His new vow of invisibility complicated this, though: what work could he do, unseen, that would benefit his neighbors, rather than only sustain his own meager life? He would only labor for his own food if no one else supplied it, and the villagers of Gouda were already more than happy to bring him all the bread and water he needed. So on moonlit nights, he slipped out of the cell like a thief in the dark, and dug over the vegetable gardens of the poorest villagers on the edge of town. He wove wicker baskets, and left them quietly on the doorsteps of humble cottages. And since he could do nothing for the good of the people who passed his cell in broad daylight, he snuck out in the dead of the night, hammer and chisel in hand, and carved short moral and religious sentences from the Gospels into the soft sandstone rocks that lined the road. “Who knows?” he thought. “Even a chance, random word can strike straight home to a heart that needs it.” Oh, his sore, aching heart — he comforted the poor and bereaved with holy words written in their native Dutch, because he said to himself, “The common tongue is the key that unlocks the common people’s hearts.” He remembered, too, the learned Colonna telling him of the “written mountains” in the east, where kings had carved their great military victories into the rock. “Those eastern monarchs are wise enough to engrave their fleeting, bloody glory on stone, so that a bubble of war can last as long as the earth itself,” he reasoned. “Shall I leave the rocks all around me silent about the King of Glory, at whose very word the mountains were made, and at whose breath they will crumble to dust? No. These stones will speak to every tired, footsore wayfarer who passes of eternal peace, and of the Lamb of God, whose frail, afflicted, happy servant is at work carving them here among you.”

At that time, the holy words of the Gospels that have consoled the poor and suffering for ages had not yet been printed in Dutch. To the illiterate villagers and travelers of the region, these golden sentences carved into the rocks seemed like fresh oracles straight from heaven, like dew falling on parched summer flowers. The hermit’s words softened hard hearts here and there, and sent heavy-laden, grieving people back on their way singing for joy.
(1) It takes a strong act of imagination for modern readers to grasp how deeply these simple sentences — “Blessed are the poor in spirit”, “Come unto me all ye that labor and are heavy laden” — moved people who had never read the Gospels, never seen the words written out, before.

These holy oracles that seemed to spring up out of nowhere along the roadsides, the gentle, wise counsel he gave visitors through his narrow window, and above all his total invisibility, soon won him a massive, widespread reputation for sanctity. His fame only grew when the villagers begged him, tears in their eyes, to give them medical advice for their sick loved ones, and he complied reluctantly. If their patients recovered, they gave all the credit to the holy invisible hermit. If their patients died? They blamed the devil entirely. He never killed anyone, for his remedies were all gentle and mild: sage, wormwood, hyssop, borage, spikenard, dog’s-tongue, lady’s mantle, feverfew, and above all, faith, all in small, careful doses.

His strict abstinence only added to his saintly reputation. The eggs and milk the villagers first brought him he refused with horror. Did they not know the ancient hermit’s rule was no more than bread, herbs, and pure water? Eggs were unhatched birds in disguise, he told them, and milk was little better than white blood. When they brought him far more bread than he could eat, he refused the excess. They would press it on him, saying, “Holy father, give the extra bread to the poor!” “You who go among the poor every day can do that far better than I,” he would reply. “Is bread something you fling carelessly out a hermit’s window?” When they kept on insisting, he would quote a line of Latin to shut their protests down: *Occasio avaritiae nomen pauperum* — Avarice often hides behind the name of the poor — and the good simple souls would immediately relent, just as they did when he quoted a line of Virgil’s *Aeneid*.

All that reputation for sanctity was only on the outside, though. Inside his small cell, Clement held himself as far from sainthood as dirt is far from gold. “I cannot deceive myself,” he muttered. “I cannot deceive God’s creatures, either. Look at the little birds: how shy they are! I leave out seed for them every day, and long for their friendship, but not one of them will come close enough to the cell to perch on my hand. Why? Because this cell does not hold a Paul, a Benedict, no Hugh of Lincoln, no Columba, no Guthlac. No hunted doe will flee here for shelter, for there is no Fructuosus, no Aventine, no Albert of Suabia living here. Not even a little squirrel from the woods nearby will come to eat the acorns I have hoarded for it, for there is no Columban here. Even the owl that used to roost here flew away. The animals cannot be fooled. I remember a Pope wrote once that wild creatures could spot a hypocrite from a mile away, and Heaven rest his soul, he was right.”

Clement did have one great advantage over Margaret, the image he was still fighting to tear out of his heart. He had already survived the searing pain of bereavement once, and the human mind can never relive that exact same peak of anguish again. He had spent so long training himself to think of Margaret as dead to him, that after the shocking scene in the church and graveyard of St. Laurens had shattered that habit like a thunderbolt striking a stone house, there were still more than enough stones left standing

One bitter winter day, the hermit Clement lay huddled in his cave, sighing, groaning, his spirit so broken he could no longer bring himself to pray, no longer hum the old sacred chants, every flicker of hope snuffed out. Then a thought flashed through his dark despair like a stray spark: what he had once done for wandering paupers and wayfarers, he would do for his own tormented soul. He would line his den of grief with the holy name of God, the living magic words of scripture, and the soft, consoling prayers of the Church. Like Christian scrambling to grab his sword at Apollyon’s feet, he lunged out and seized his own humbler weapon of peaceful labour: his chisel. He carved as if his very soul hung on the strength of his arm.

The generation ahead, they say, Michaelangelo would carve marble statues not by laboriously modelling clay first and hiring a mechanic to hew out the rough form, but by seizing the cold block, conceiving the full image in his mind’s eye, and swinging mallet and steel until marble chips flew thick and fast and the stone burst into life. Even so, Clement drew no guiding lines on his walls. He pulled every gracious phrase straight from his memory, then threw himself at the soft cave stone, graving the words deep into it, his work half labour, half desperate spiritual combat.
He begged every visitor who passed his cave for discarded candle ends and rancid cooking oil. “Anything is good enough for me,” he told them, “if only it will burn.” By night, the cave glowed far off like a blacksmith’s forge, light seeping through the small window and the wide cracks in his rough stone door. Local rustics, seeing the eerie glow, crossed themselves and muttered rumours of devilish sorcery. But inside, sacred talismans bloomed on the walls one after another: chips of stone flew day and night, night and day, as the lone soldier of solitude and the Church plied his bloodless weapon, wrenched between hard work and harder fighting.
*Kyrie Eleison.* Lord have mercy.
*Christe Eleison.* Christ have mercy.
*Satanan suntripson upo tous pothas ymwn.* Beat down Satan under our feet.
*Sursum Corda.* Lift up your hearts.
*Deus Refugium nostrum et virtus.* O God, our refuge and our strength.
*Agnus Dei, qui tollis peccata mundi miserere mihi.* O Lamb of God that takest away the sins of the world, have mercy upon me.
*Sancta Trinitas unus Deus, miserere nobis.* O Holy Trinity, one God, have mercy upon us.
*Ab infestationibus Daemonum, a ventura ira, a damnatione perpetua. Libera nos Domine.* From the assaults of demons, from the wrath to come, from everlasting damnation: deliver us, O Lord.
He carved the full collect for the feast of St. Michael and All Angels next, then the ancient cry:
*Quem quaerimus adjutorem nisi te Domine qui pro peccatis nostris juste irascaris?* Of whom may we seek succour but of Thee, O Lord, who for our sins art justly displeased?
*Sancte Deus, Sancte fortis, Sancte et misericors Salvator, amarae morti ne tradas nos.* Holy God, Holy Strong One, Holy and merciful Saviour, deliver us not over to bitter death.
Beneath the great wooden crucifix he had nailed to the cave wall, he graved a passage from St. Augustine:
> O anima Christiana, respice vulnera patientis, sanguinem morientis, pretium redemptionis. Haec quanta sint cogitate, et in statera mentis vestrae appendite, ut totus vobis figatur in corde, qui pro vobis totus fixus est in cruce. Nam si passio Christi ad memoriam revocetur, nihil est tam durum quod non aequo animo toleretur.

Translated in plain words, it read: O Christian soul, look on the wounds of the suffering One, the blood of the dying One, the price paid for our redemption! Think how great these things are, and weigh them in the balance of your mind, so that He may be wholly nailed to your heart, who for you was all nailed to the cross. For call but the sufferings of Christ to mind, and no hardship on earth will be too heavy to bear with calm composure.

Soothed only a very little by the pious words he had raised all around him, and worn thin from days and nights of nonstop work, Clement collapsed one morning in a heap from total exhaustion, and fell into a deep, unbroken sleep that lasted for hours.
He woke soft and quiet, to the faint cheep of a small bird. He opened his eyes, and there perched on his breviary, laid on the low stool at his feet, was a plump robin redbreast. It ruffled all its feathers in one sharp tug, smoothed them just as fast, and tilted its little bill this way and that with a vast show of cunning that was entirely imaginary.
Clement held his breath, half-lidded his eyes so he would not frighten his tiny winged guest. The robin hopped down to the dirt floor, went through its silly pantomime of pretended cleverness, then pim, pim, pim, three stiff little hops that made it look like a woolen ball strung on vertical wires, and it landed right on the hermit’s bare foot. It swelled and shrank again there, feathers ebbing and flowing, but Clement shut his eyes tight altogether, barely daring to breathe, terrified he would scare it away. He was content just to feel the weight of its tiny claws on his skin, so faint he could only sense it at all because he knew it was there.
A minute later, a flutter of two small wings, and the busy little creature was back on the breviary. Clement determined to feed his pretty new visitor without startling it. It was no easy task. He had a piece of bread within arm’s reach, but how to reach it without scaring the bird? It took him five full minutes to creep his hand across the floor to the bread, and once there he did not dare move his arm an inch. He slyly pinched a crumb between his finger and thumb and flicked it like a boy shooting a marble, keeping his hand perfectly still. The robin saw it fall nearby, pretended to be very wise and cautious, and did not move. When he flicked a second crumb, then a third, the little redbreast hopped down and snatched one up, and flew for safety to a new high perch: the hermit’s knee. Their little game went on like that until a much bigger crumb than usual rolled across the stone. That was a prize. The robin pounced on it, bore it aloft, and fled so swiftly out of the cave the air buffeted and hummed with its passage.
“God bless you, sweet little bird,” sighed the stricken, solitary man. “Your wings are music, and you are a feathered ray of sunlight that has come to light my darkened soul.”
He turned back to his prayers then, and then to his chisel, with a spark of new courage, and spent the rest of the day carving the ancient hymn Veni, Creator Spiritus deep into the wall.
The days rolled on, the air grew colder, and Clement’s heart grew warmer. The thick cloud of despondency that had wrapped him tight began to drift away, until at last it vanished entirely, like fog burning off at sunrise. He had outlived it. Everything was reversed now: his small cave glowed with quiet joy. The work of his hands pleased him, his prayers flowed full of unction, his psalms burst free in unforced praise. Whole flocks of small birds followed their crimson leader, flying from the coming snow and the cruelty of the local villagers to make fast friends with the gentle hermit they called Abel.
One sharp, frosty night, as he sang the praises of God to his little psaltery, the hollow cave ringing with his psalmody as if it were David’s harp itself, he heard a clear, low whine, not unmelodious. It grew louder, less tuneful. He peeked through the cracks in his rough door, and there sat a great shaggy red wolf, moaning melodiously with its nose lifted high to the moon.
Clement was overjoyed. “My sins are falling away from me!” he cried. “All the creatures of God are recognising me, one after another.” Bursting into enthusiasm he struck up the Laudate Dominum: “Praise Him all ye creatures of His! Let everything that hath breath praise the Lord.” And all the while he sang, the wolf bayed in response, soft and low.
He thought now he was drawing near to that celestial, holy communion that was the mark and bliss of every true hermit: his dreams of saints and angels grew so vivid they were almost visions. He saw bright figures clad in woven snow, their eyes lovelier than the antelope’s eyes he had seen once in Rome, their wings broad and dyed like rainbows, and their gentle voices bade him walk straight on his chosen path.
He had not long enjoyed this gentle bliss when his dreams took a strange, new turn. He wandered with Fra Colonna through the ruins of ancient nations, the friar lame and leaning on a staff. Colonna waved that staff over the broken stones, and whether the ruins were Egyptian, Greek, or Roman, the temples and palaces rose again like mist from the ground, thronged with their long-dead famous inhabitants. Singers who might have outshone both Apollo and his rival poured out their lays, women as godlike in form as Minerva drifted through marble courts in soft, graceful dances. Sculptors carved away surrounded by admiring pupils, forms of supernatural beauty blooming out of Parian marble in a quarter of an hour, grave philosophers talked of high and subtle matters while young listeners knelt reverently at their feet. But all the while, a quiet, uneasy suspicion lurked in Clement’s dreaming mind: this was only a prologue, a show, there was something hidden behind it, something that meant him no good, something mysterious and awful.
One night, when the wizard Colonna had outdone even his own magic, he pointed his staff and all those great ancient cities sank back into the earth. The two of them stood on a vast, empty sandy plain, a huge crimson sun sinking low on the horizon. Great palm trees dotted the landscape, and little bulrush huts barely as tall as a man stretched out all the way to the edge of the sand, glowing red in the sunset.
“These are the anchorites of the Theban desert,” Colonna said calmly. “Followers not of Christ and his apostles, and the great Church fathers, but of Greek pupils of Egyptian pupils of the old Brahmins and naked philosophers.”
Clement burned to run to them, embrace the holy men, tell them all his troubles and beg their advice. But his feet were tied fast, he could not move. The crimson sun sank, dusk fell, and the little huts grew almost invisible. Colonna’s figure grew shadowy, shapeless, only his eyes glowed ten times brighter. That shapeless thing all eyes spoke: “Nay, leave them be. A pack of fools. I see how dismal all this is.” Then he perked up suddenly, bright and sprightly: “But I hear one of them keeps a manuscript of Petronius written on papyrus. I am going to buy it. Farewell for ever, for ever, for ever.”
The dark turned pitch black, then a light like a soft stroke of warmth bloomed at Clement’s back: a glorious roseate light, that warmed as well as brightened. It loosened the chains around his feet. He turned around, and there stood Margaret Brandt, her face lit as if by sunshine, her hair glittering like the halo of a saint. She blushed, smiled, and cast a look of ineffable tenderness at him. “Gerard,” she murmured, “be whose thou wilt by day, but at night be mine!”
The shock of seeing her so suddenly jolted him awake. He lay trembling from head to foot. That radiant figure and soft, mellow voice seemed to have set the keynote for all his nights to come.
Awake, he was master of himself: he could pray, praise, worship God unhindered. But the moment he closed his eyes to sleep, Margaret, or Satan in her shape, beset him, a seeming angel of light. He might dream of a thousand different things, as far apart as the poles, but before he woke that imperial, glowing figure was sure to appear, snuffing all other visions out in an instant, as the rising sun extinguishes every star. She glowed with two beauties that could never belong to a heavenly angel: an angel’s radiance, and a woman’s soft blushes. Angels cannot blush. So he knew it was a fiend.
He was alarmed, though hardly surprised at this latest artifice of the demon. From St. Anthony to Nicholas of the Rock, there was scarcely a hermit who had not been beset this way: sometimes with wild voluptuous visions, sometimes with lovely phantoms, warm, tangible, womanly on the outside, demons hidden within, that many a saint had failed to drive away. Everyone knew the tale of that “angel form with a devil’s heart” that came weeping to St. Macarius, hanging its lovely head like a bruised flower, telling a feigned tale of woe, weeping until it first beguiled the saint out of his tears, and then out of half his virtue.
But alongside those tales of Satanic cunning were the long, copious records of the hermits’ triumphs, and the weapons they had used to conquer. *Domandum est Corpus:* the body must be tamed. That had been the watchword of the desert saints for twelve hundred years. It was a tremendous war cry: they counted earthly affections as well as base appetites as part of the “body,” and crushed the whole heart through the medium of suffering, mortified flesh.
Clement told himself that the great enemy of man had only retreated to spring all the harder, had granted him a few days of pure joy and peace only to lull him off his guard against the soft, honeyed temptations he now poured over a soul that had already survived so many of his cruel blows. He set himself to tame his body: he shortened his hours of sleep, lengthened his prayers, pushed his usual strict temperance into total abstinence. Before, he had eaten only once a day, at sunset, in line with the ordinary hermit’s rule. Now he ate but once every forty-eight hours, drinking only a little water each day.
The visions grew even clearer. Then he turned to the famous antidote, the great febrifuge of all old anchorites: cold water. He found the deepest pool in the stream that ran past his cave, its source a little ways up at a holy well. He cleared all the large stones from the bottom, so he could stand in the water up to his chin. Fortified by the tales of a hundred saints who had gone before him, the next time the demon harassed him he sprang from his rough bed and plunged straight into the icy water. It made him gasp, almost shriek with the cold. It froze his marrow. “I shall die,” he cried, “I shall die, but better this than the eternal fires of hell.”
The next day his joints were so stiff he could not move. He felt like one great throbbing ache. Even in sleep his very bones felt like a row of raging, aching teeth — until the phantom he dreaded stepped close, gave him one pitying smile, and all his pain vanished at once.
Afraid that to plunge back into icy water again, weak and wasted as he was, would amount to suicide, he scourged himself with a whip of knotted cords until the blood ran, and then lay down smarting. When exhaustion blunted the sharp sting of the blows down to a soft, throbbing ache, the present faded, and the past came smiling back. He sat with Margaret at the duke’s feast, minstrels playing divinely, fountains gushing purple wine. Youth and love reigned in every heart, the very air perfumed with sweetness. Then the scene shifted: they stood at the altar together, man and wife, no one interrupting, and they wandered hand in hand, telling each other all their terrible dreams. He told her he had dreamed she was dead, and he was a monk, and that the dream had been so vivid, full of so many tiny, specific details, that only his own eyesight now could convince him it was only a dream, and they were truly one.
Once that new keynote was struck, every tune his mind played turned on it. Awake he was Clement the hermit, risen from unearthly night visions as dangerous as they were sweet. Asleep he was Gerard Eliassoen, the happy husband of the loveliest, best, truest girl in all Holland, all the happier for having spent so long trapped in hideous dreams where he had lost her.
His constant fasts, coupled with other austerities and the deep mental strain of fighting a supernatural foe, had reduced him nearly to a skeleton. But over those aching, thin bones hung flesh still unsubdued, quivering with earthly passion, or so he told himself. Why else would evil spirits hold such power over him?
His opinion was confirmed one day, when he caught himself sinking to sleep with a quiet feeling of complacency, because soon Margaret would come, and all his pain would be gone, and the unreal would feel real, and the real world would fade to nothing, for an hour.
He sprang up with a cry of dismay, stripped himself to the skin, climbed the bank of brambles above his cave, and threw himself down on them, rolling back and forth, writhing with the stabbing pain. He stumbled back into his den a mass of cuts and gore, and lay moaning for hours, until he fell into a deep, completely dreamless sleep from total exhaustion.
He woke to throbbing bodily pain, and bright mental exultation. He had broken the fatal spell. Yes, it was broken. Day after day passed, and her image no longer molested him. But he caught himself sighing a little, at his own victory.
The birds grew tamer and tamer, they perched on his hand. Two of the smallest let him gild their tiny claws. Eating only once every two days left him more bread crumbs to share with them.
His tranquility did not last long. A woman’s voice drifted in from outside the cave, told him his own full life story in a very few words, and asked him if he knew where

Her posture would have roused pity far more than terror in any eye unclouded by fixed, fanatical suspicion. Her chest fluttered like a trapped bird’s, red and white chasing across her cheeks in shifting waves, and one hand pressed flat to the rough stone wall by the instinct of all timid things, for she trembled so violently she could barely stand. The purple gaze she turned on the gaunt, glaring hermit was stitched through with equal parts of adoring love, pious awe, tender shared memory, and quiet pity: a sight no unpoisoned heart could have misread.

“Aha!” he cried, snatching up his small wooden crucifix. “Thou art come at last in flesh and blood, as thou didst come to tempt Saint Anthony. But I see through thy wiles. I am armed.” He held the crucifix out trembling at her, the other hand clutching a guttering candle that shook so hard its hot wax dripped onto his bare wrist. *“Exorcizo te.”*

“Ah no!” Margaret cried, putting out two soft, deprecating palms. “Work me no ill. It is Margaret.”

“Liar!” he shouted, his voice cracking. “Margaret was fair, but not supernaturally fair as thou art. Thou didst flinch at that sacred name, thou subtle hypocrite. *In Nomine Dei exorcizo vos.*”

“Ah, Jesu!” Margaret gasped, half mad with terror. “Curse me not! I will go home. I thought I might come. For pity’s sake, do not banish me with Latin prayers! Oh, Gerard, is this how we meet at last, after all the long years apart?” She sank almost to her knees, sobbing with equal parts superstitious fear and lacerated affection.

Saturated as he was with months of unbroken Satanophobia, Clement might still have doubted whether this soft, distraught, entirely human creature was fiend in disguise, but her spontaneous cry of his old, beloved name dissolved all his fevered delusions. He saw clearly with his own eyes, heard truly with his own ears, and uttered a cry of bitter self-reproach. He tried to lift her to her feet, but six months of fasts and the overwhelming shock of having his long solitude broken left his legs too weak to hold his weight. “What,” he gasped, hunching over her trembling form, “is it truly thee? And did I greet thee with harsh, cruel words? Alas!” They were both choked with emotion, and could not speak for a long, quiet minute.

“I do not mind it overmuch,” Margaret said bravely, fighting back her sobs. “Thou didst take me for another: for a devil. Oh, oh, oh!”

“Forgive me, sweet soul!” he managed, as soon as he could force more than one word past his tight throat. “The evil one has beset me constantly since I came to this cell.”

Margaret shuddered, glancing over the dark, reeking cave. “That I can well believe. Then take my hand, and let me lead thee out of this foul place at once.”

He stared at her in uncomprehending astonishment. “What? Desert my cell, and go back into the world? Is that why thou hast come to me?” he said, his voice sharp with sad, reproachful hurt.

“Ay, Gerard! I am come to take thee to thy very own vicarage at Gouda. Thanks to Heaven and thy good brother Giles, thou art appointed its vicar, and thy mother and I have made it all so neat and sweet for thee. It is warm and snug enough in winter, I promise thee, and wait but a little: when the hawthorn blooms, the walls will wear a kirtle of bright roses and sweet woodbine. Did we ever forget thee, or the foolish little things thou dost love? And dear Gerard, thy mother waits for us by the path, it is far past her bedtime. Prithee, prithee, come away! The moment we step outside this dark hole I will show thee a treasure thou hast earned, and know nothing of, or thou wouldst never have fled from us so.” She broke off, confused, when he drew himself tight into a rigid huddle, his face twisted with a strange mix of fear and suspicion.

“Unhappy girl,” he said solemnly, his whole frame shaking with repressed agitation, “wouldst have me risk thy soul and mine for a mere vicarage and the flowers that grow on its walls? This is not thy doing. The bowelless fiend sent thee, poor simple girl, to bait me with this temptation. But oh, cunning fiend, I will unmask thee even to thy innocent pawn, and she shall see thee, and abhor thee as I do. Margaret, my lost love, why am I here? Because I love thee.”

“Oh no, Gerard, thou dost not love me, or thou wouldst never have hidden from me. There was never any need for all this.”

“Let there be no deceit between us two, who loved so true once, and after this night shall meet no more on earth.”

“Now God forbid that!” Margaret cried.

“I love thee still. Thou hast not forgotten me, or thou wouldst have married long ago, and never been the one to find me buried here, hidden from all mortal sight. I am a priest, a monk now. What but folly or sin can come of us living as neighbours, feeding a passion that was once innocent, but which Heaven has now deemed unholy and impious? No, though my heart break in two, I must be firm. I am the man, and I am the priest. We must meet no more, until I have been schooled by long solitude, and thou art wedded to another man.”

“I would accept my own doom, but never thine. I would ten times rather die than see thee rot in this foul, dismal cave, while that sweet warm manse waits for thee.” Clement groaned. With every word she spoke, his duty grew clearer, and the searing agony of fulfilling it cut deeper.

“My beloved,” he said, his voice tender and yet unyielding with dogged resolution, “I bless thee for giving me one more sight of thy sweet face. And may God forgive thee, and bless thee, for destroying in a single minute the holy peace it took six months of solitude to build. No matter. A year of penance will, Dei gratia, restore me to my calm. My poor Margaret, I seem cruel, yet I am kind. It is best we part. Ay, this very moment.”

“Part, Gerard? Never. We have seen what comes of parting. Thou hast not heard half my story, no, not a tenth part. It is not just for thy own comfort that I am bringing thee to Gouda. Hear me out!”

“I may not. Thy very voice is a temptation, all music and sweet memory.”

“But I say thou shalt hear me, Gerard. I will not leave this place unheard.”

“Then I must flee this temptation by other means,” Clement said, sadly.

“Alack, what other means? Wilt thou push me out the door, being the stronger?”

“Nay, Margaret, thou knowest full well I would suffer a thousand deaths before I would force thy sweet body. But our two immortal souls are a million times dearer to me than our mortal flesh. I have withstood this direst of all temptations long enough. Now I must run from it. Farewell! Farewell!”

He stumbled for the door, wrenched it open, and half stepped outside, when Margaret darted after him and caught him hard by the arm. “Nay, then another must speak for me. I thought to reward thee for yielding to me, but unkind as thou art, I find I need his help now. Turn but this way one moment.”

“Nay, nay.”

“But I say ay! Turn away from us then, if thou canst.” She loosened her grip a little, sure he would not deny her such a small favour, and in that instant he saw his chance. “Fly, Clement, fly!” he shrieked. His religious frenzy lent him the strength of his old youth for a moment, and he tore free of her hold so wildly he threw her full onto the stony ground. He bounded a few paces to the little icy stream, splashed halfway across it, then stopped and looked back. She lay face down on the earth, her hands spread out before her.

He groaned, and took one step back toward her, his resolve crumbling, before a wilder impulse seized him, and he flung himself neck-deep into the freezing water instead. “There,” he cried, his teeth chattering, “kill my mortal flesh, but save our souls!”

He stood half submerged in the liquid ice, and saw Margaret rise slowly to her knees, her face pale, her eyes glistening with tears. In the quiet dark night, he heard her voice, thin and breaking: “Oh God, who knowest all things, Thou seest how I am used. Forgive me, then. I will not live another day.” She sprang to her feet, and ran past his hiding place like a wild, mortally wounded creature, shrieking four times at the top of her lungs: *“CRUEL!—CRUEL!—CRUEL!—CRUEL!”*

All human agony was packed into that single word: wounded love, trampled pride, utter despair, the first flicker of coming madness. It froze his heart far worse than the icy water chilled the marrow of his bones. In his moment of grim, supposed triumph over temptation, he felt an almost uncontrollable urge to curse the Church, curse religion itself, for demanding such savage cruelty of mortal flesh. He crawled half dead out of the stream at last, and staggered back into his dark cave. “I am safe here,” he groaned. “She will never come near me again. Unmanly, ungrateful wretch that I am.” He threw his emaciated, frozen body down on the dirt floor, half hoping he would never rise again.

But soon he saw by his hourglass that it was past midnight. He dragged himself up slowly, stripped off his soaking clothes, and moaning all the while at the pain he had caused the woman he loved, he pulled on the old hermit’s bristling hair cilice, and over that the heavy iron breastplate he had never dared wear before, doubting he was worthy of the arms of such a tried, pious soldier. Now he needed every aid he could find: the bristles of the cilice might distract his earthly remorse with physical pain, and the breastplate might hold some holy protective virtue. He knelt and prayed humbly that God would release him from the burden of his flesh that very night. Then he lit all his candles, and began reciting his psalter doggedly, every word heavy as a lump of lead, every breath wrenched out of his leaden heart.

Midway through the office, he spotted a small soft bundle in the corner he had not noticed before in the dimmer light, with something that looked like spun gold peeking out of its wrappings. He stumbled over to see what it was, and the moment he looked closer he threw up his hands in rapture. “It is a seraph,” he whispered. “A lovely seraph. Heaven has seen my bitter trial, and approves my resolve, and has sent this flower of the skies to cheer me as I faint under my burden.” He fell to his knees, gazing in ecstasy at the golden hair, the soft tender skin, the cheeks blushed like a ripe peach. “Let me feast my sad eyes on thee before thou fliest back to thy blessed abode, leaving my cell dark again, as it went dark when she left.”

His quiet reverie woke the little visitor. Two wide eyes the colour of a summer sky blinked open, saw the strange wild figure kneeling over him, and he cried piteously, “MUMMA! MUM-MA!” Big tears began rolling down his round little cheeks.

Clement, who had not seen a human face other than his own for more than six months, had always been fond of children, and the monastic life fostered that softness. The innocent distress on the cherubic face, the tears streaming from those violet-blue eyes, the plaintive cry for his mother, went straight through his broken heart. He used every bit of his gentle skill to soothe the child, and soon the boy stopped crying, wide-eyed wonder replacing his fear, scanning the strange wild man who spoke so softly even though he wore armour, who did not hurt little boys but cooed over them.

Clement was bewildered how this little glowing human flower had ended up in his gloomy cave, until he remembered he had left the cave door wide open when he ran out. He concluded some desperate soul had seized the chance to abandon her unwanted child (1). His heart ached so fiercely for the poor little abandoned cherub that tears of pure tenderness stood in his eyes, and he saw God’s divine goodness working even through the mother’s heartlessness, to comfort his own breaking heart. “Bless thee, bless thee, sweet innocent. I would not trade thee even for a cherub in heaven.”

“At’s pooty,” the infant replied, ignoring all uninteresting remarks as all infants do, pointing straight at his breastplate.

“What is pretty here besides thee, my love?”

“Ookum-gars,” (2) the boy lisped, his little finger still outstretched.

Clement laughed. “So many children, so many strange little phrases! Hector’s own babe screamed at his father’s glittering helmet, and here a medieval babe is charmed by a polished cuirass, and my griefs are assuaged.” He told the little boy his storks scared him, that he hated the big flapping birds who were far bigger than he was, and promised him he had tiny pretty birds the boy would not be afraid of. Soon the two were chattering like old friends, and when Clement asked if he had a daddy as well as a mammy, we step back a little, to watch through Margaret’s eyes.

When Margaret ran past Gerard in the dark, she was almost mad. It was that fevered state of mind that has driven affectionate mothers to kill their children, and themselves, in moments of utter despair. She ran straight to Reicht Heynes, pale and trembling, and clung to her neck. “Oh Reicht, oh Reicht!” She showed Reicht her hands, scraped raw and bleeding from the stony ground, told her he had thrown her down, thought she was a devil sent to tempt his soul, that he would not even look at the treasure she had brought him. “I will fling myself and him into the Rotter this night.”

Reicht talked her down, but in her frenzy, Margaret suddenly realized she had left the baby, her own child, the treasure she had hidden so carefully, all alone in the hermit’s dark cave. They set off back at once, Margaret’s courage failing her as they drew near, until she sent Reicht ahead to fetch the child, too heartsick to face Gerard herself. Reicht ran back, wide-eyed, to tell her the cave was lit up bright, and there were two voices inside, not one: a man’s, and a little child’s, talking as pleasantly as two old friends. Margaret crept on all fours to the crack in the cave wall, and peered through.

Inside, she heard the little boy say, when pressed about his daddy, “Dad-da ill man. Run away and left poor mum-ma.” She winced, for that cruel tale had never come from her lips. Then she heard Gerard curse that imaginary coward who would abandon his own child, swear he would be both father and mother to the little boy, feed him soft eggs and warm milk, teach him to read, sing him old lullabies from their home town of Tergou, the same lullabies Gerard’s own mother had sung to him as a babe. He took off his heavy breastplate, took off the bristling cilice that would prick the child’s soft skin, sat the little boy on his knee, and chanted old fairy stories to him, until the child’s eyelids grew heavy, and he sank fast asleep in his arms. Gerard stopped singing, gazed down at the little golden-haired face, and sighed, thinking of all the joy he had thrown away over a single false piece of paper.

The next moment, moonlight poured through the cave mouth, and Margaret stepped forward, sinking to her knees at his knee, her soft trembling hand resting light on his shoulder.

---
(1) More than one medieval hermit received such unasked-for gifts of unwanted children in this era.
(2) The child’s lisp almost certainly means “looking glass,” mistaking the polished metal breastplate for a mirror.
(3) The word “craft” here means trade or profession.

The hermit, Clement, started so violently he nearly dropped the sleeping child from his left arm, his gaze darting from the small warm face pressed to his tunic to Margaret kneeling at his right knee, and back again. His astonishment was only matched by the sharp, jarring jolt of seeing her here, when he had long convinced himself she was dead. Gone was the pale, breathless, frightened girl he had wrestled down barely an hour before; before him stood a woman glowing with quiet, unassailable majesty, cheeks flushed bright pink from the crisp autumn air, eyes sparkling, lips parted in a soft triumphant smile, her whole face lit with a look he had never seen before: unshakable maternal pride.

He stared, breath catching, the child stirring faintly in his hold.
“Us?” he gasped at last, his wonder-stricken eyes still flicking back and forth between the two of them.

Margaret laughed, low and warm. This was an age of instinct over cold fact, and she could not fathom his confusion. “What? Doth a father not know his own flesh and blood? And a man of God, at that? Fie, Gerard, do not pretend! You are far too wise, far too good to have missed it. I watched you, these past days. Look at the two of you side by side! That is your own child you hold pressed to your heart.”

Clement shook so hard his shoulders trembled. “What words are these?” he stammered. “This angel, mine?”
“Whose else, when he is mine too?” Margaret said.

Clement turned his gaze back to the sleeping boy, a look so tender, so raw with newly uncovered love no pen could ever capture it, and he quaked all over, as if he was memorizing every line of the little face seared into his memory. Margaret’s eyes softened, following his.
“He is not a bit like me,” she said proudly. “But oh, some days he is your very image, shrunk down small. Look at that golden hair! Yours was exactly that shade when you were his age — ask your own mother, if you doubt it. And see this tiny mole on his little pinky? Now look at yours, there! Your mother told me you carried that mark from infancy, long before this little one was born. That was how I found you! I stood outside your cell window, watching you feed the birds, and spotted that same mole on your finger, and knew at once you were his father.”
She seized the child’s small hand, pressing eager kisses to the knuckles, half the little fist vanishing into her mouth as she laughed through tears. “Ah, my blessing on you, little one! You found your poor daddy for me, and now you have mended our little quarrel — our first, our last. You were so cruel to me just now, my poor Gerard, but I forgive you, all for the love of your child.”

Clement could not speak. He sobbed in great heaving gasps, half-choking, weakened by months of fasting, unhinged by years of total solitude. The once strong young man was overcome with hysterics, slumping forward nearly fainting. Margaret was alarmed, but her years of hardship had taught her steady kindness, and her pity far outstripped her fear.
“There, there, do not take on so,” she murmured, smoothing the hair back from his brow. “Be brave! No man is the first to come home from wandering richer for a lovely little new life than he set out. You are a man of God now, take courage. He sent this little one to comfort you for what you thought you lost in me — and that loss is not so very great, my lamb. The better part of my love for you will never cool, not even here, though it ought to, now you are a priest, and parson of Gouda.”

“I? Parson of Gouda? Never,” Clement mumbled faint, his voice thin as thread. “I am a friar of St. Dominic. But speak on, sweet voice. Tell me all that has befallen you, before we must part again.”

Any other woman might have raged against the very idea of parting, dragged up all the old arguments right then. But Margaret was not any other woman. She did not make the same mistake twice, and once her heart was set on something, no one could outmaneuver her. She nodded, setting the thought of the Gouda manse aside for the moment, and told him her whole long tale, pausing often to speak of the great kindness his parents had shown her through all her troubles. As she spoke, his hand crept to hers, and she felt him wince with rage at every hardship she described, squeeze her hand tight in wordless sympathy, as if he felt every bruise and every sorrow right along with her.
“O, what a piteous tale, a true heart battling alone against such cruel odds,” he said at last.

“It all feels so small now, when I have found you again, and see you nursing my boy,” she said. “True friends like us are so rare — it is madness to tear ourselves apart before death does it for us.”
“That is true,” Clement said, off his guard.

Then she asked him to tell her what he had suffered for her sake. He begged to be excused, and she agreed — only to gently press question after quiet question, until every peril he had survived, every lonely night, every ache of grief, was laid bare between them. She sighed over and over, more than once hiding her face in her hands, terror still thrumming through her at the dangers he had escaped, even now they were past. To comfort him, she knelt down, slipped her arms under the sleeping boy, and lifted him gently up to press him into Clement’s arms again.
“Kiss him softly,” she whispered. “Again, and again — kiss your fill, he is fast asleep. This is all I can do to comfort you, until you leave this foul den and come to your sweet manse, just over the hill.”

Clement shook his head.
“Very well,” she said. “Let that pass. You must know, I have been sorely affronted these past weeks, all because I could not find our marriage lines.”
“Who dared affront you?”
“Never mind. They will do it again if you have lost them — and the saints forbid that.”
“Lose them? They are right there, close to your hand.”
“Where, where, oh where?”

Clement hung his head. “Look in the Vulgate. Heaven forgive me: I thought you were dead, a saint in heaven, and had no use for them any more.”
She opened the old, tattered book, and found their marriage papers on the blank end leaves. “Thank God!” she cried. “Thank God! O, bless you, Gerard, bless you! Why — what is all this?”
On every spare blank page, tucked between the lines of scripture, was every scrap of paper she had ever sent him: the slip where they had scrawled their two names together for a lark, the lock of her chestnut hair she had given him the night he left, the half of a broken silver coin they had split between them, even the single straw she had sipped her soup from the very first day they met.
When Margaret saw all these quiet, tender proofs of his grief and his love, her joy at finding the marriage lines was swallowed up in a gush of tears. She staggered a little, pressing a hand to her bosom, and leaned her forehead against the cold stone wall of the cell, weeping so silently he did not notice. She would not let him see her break, for she knew she had to be the strong one now — weakness would ruin everything.

“Gerard,” she said, steadying her voice, “I know you are wise and good. You must have a reason for hiding yourself away like this, no matter how unreasonable it seems. Let us talk like old friends. Why have you buried yourself alive in this hole?”
“To escape temptation,” he said quietly. “My anger at the men who wronged us grew from the ache in my heart, so I must deaden that heart, Dei gratia, by degrees. Am I a servant of Christ, to court temptation? To pray every day to be led away from sin, and then walk straight into it with my eyes wide open?”
“That is sensible enough, for a start,” Margaret said, with perfect, gentle candour.
“’Tis unanswerable,” Clement sighed.
“We shall see. Tell me: have you escaped temptation here? I ask because when I am alone, my thoughts run far more wild and foolish than when I am with other folk. Come now, speak the truth.”
“I must own I have been tormented here with evil imaginations far worse than I ever was in the world outside.”
“There now.”
“Ay, but so were St. Anthony, St. Jerome, Macarius, Hilarion, Benedict, Bernard — all the saints. It will wear off in time.”
“How do you know?”
“I feel sure of it.”
“Guessing, pitted against what you have already seen. Men are so much sillier than us women, it is a wonder. Wise in their own conceits, they will not let themselves see what is right before their eyes, too proud to learn from their own experience. If a woman went to hide in a hole in a bank to escape temptation, and found it waiting for her there, she would just hitch up her farthingale and march right out, and never even realize how clever she was until she saw a man making the exact same fool of himself.”

Clement smiled faintly. “I grant you humility and a teachable spirit are the roads to wisdom. But even so, here I only wrestle with my own imagination. At Gouda, you — whom I love far more than any priest or monk dare love any but the angels — you would tempt my weak soul, even if you did not mean to.”
“And what exactly would I tempt you to, in God’s name?” Margaret said, her eyes flashing. “Speak for yourself, my lad. You must be thinking of some other Margaret, not Margaret Peter. Has my mind ever once turned to folly or frailty? Wait — is it because you were my husband once, as these lines prove? Do you think the road to sin is more beaten for you than any other man? O, how shallow the wise are! You cannot even read me, when I can read you top to toe. Learn your A B C. If a stranger came to me with unchaste offers, I would flinch, of course, defend myself without making a whole great fuss — for I know men are so, even the best of them, sometimes. But if you, my own husband, the father of my child, ever dared speak to me so, to humble me in my own eyes, and yours, and our son’s? I would spit in your face, Gerard — or, since I am no vulgar woman, I would snatch the nearest weapon to hand and strike you dead.”
No one looking at her, eyes blazing, nostrils flared, could have doubted a single word she said.

“I never had the sense to see that,” Gerard said, quiet, and he sat pondering, his brow furrowed.
Margaret let the silence stretch a little while, until her temper cooled, then spoke soft again. “Let us not quarrel. Tell me of your family. Your father?”
“He is well, and grows warmer every day to the thought of you and me,” she said. “Poor soul, he drew his glaive on those two knaves who wronged you that day, but Jorian Ketel and I held him back, and he drove them out of his house forever.”
“He cannot do that. He must take them back.”
“He never will, for us. You know the man — dour as iron. But he would do it at once for one word from the man who will not speak it.”
“Who?”
“The vicar of Gouda. I hear he will be waiting for you at the manse tomorrow.”
“You keep circling back to that,” he said, half laughing.
“Forgive me! I am but a woman, born to nag. You must distract me with questions, so I do not get carried away. What of your sister Kate?”
“Alas!”
“O no, no harm has befallen her! Far from it,” Margaret hurried to soothe him, then took a slow, steadying breath, and spoke soft and low. “My poor Gerard. Kate left all her troubles behind her. She saw more joy and more sorrow in her short life than most folk will ever see, and she smiled even when she was in pain. She fell into a soft languor, all her aches and pains fading away. Your mother tried to fool herself, said it might be a turn for the better, but Joan Ketel, who is a sensible woman, looked at her and said ‘Down sun, down wind!’ The gossips told your mother to be brave, for Kate was half way to sainthood. But Kate would not let her mother weep, and one very old woman said she would die as easy as she had lived hard. She lay painless for three whole days, sipping heaven before she ever got there. When she was just slipping away, she asked for Gerard’s little boy. I brought him, set him on the bed, and he sat there as quiet as a lamb. She was past speaking by then, but she pointed to a drawer, and her mother pulled out the two gold angels you gave her years ago, as a child. She nodded at the little boy, all anxious, so we put the coins in his small hands, and when his fingers closed around them she smiled, content. She gave her little earthly treasures to her favourite’s son — for you were always her favourite — and her immortal soul to God. She passed so sweetly none of us even noticed the exact moment she left us.”

Gerard wept. “There will never be another like her on this earth,” he sobbed. “O how softly the old affections of this world curl around my heart! I cannot help it. God made them, after all. Speak on, Margaret. The sound of your voice rolls the old tides of memory back over me, all the old loves and hopes of youth come drifting into my dark cell, and my darker heart, on waves of music.”
“Gerard, I hate to grieve you, but Kate cried a little, when she first grew sick, that you were not there to close her eyes.”
Gerard sighed. “You were less than a league away, but you hid your face from her.”
He groaned.
“Forgive me for nagging! I am but a woman. You would never have been cruel to your own flesh and blood on purpose, would you?”
“O no, never.”
“Well then. Your brother Sybrandt is in my care, with a broken back — the fruit of your curse.”
“Mea culpa! Mea culpa!”
“He is so penitent. Forgive him, tonight, for your own peace.”
“I forgave him long ago.”
“Do you think he can believe that from any mouth but yours? He is not far from here, you know — only two butts’ length away.”
“So near? Where?”
“At Gouda manse. I brought him there last night. I knew you: your curse was hardly cold on your lips before you regretted it,” Margaret said, and Gerard nodded, agreeing. “I told myself, Gerard will thank me for taking Sybrandt to die under his own roof. He will beat his breast and cry mea culpa, but never begrudge three small footsteps to comfort his withered brother on his last bed. He may have a bee in his bonnet, but he is no hypocrite, no man full of pious words and no charity.”

Gerard staggered where he sat, stung right to the core.
“Forgive me for nagging,” she said, smiling soft. “Your mother too is waiting for you. Is it kind to keep her in such torment? She will not sleep a wink all night. Think, Gerard: she is everything to you that I am to this little boy. She suffered for you, nursed you, tended you from a babe to a man. Hermit, monk, priest — call yourself whatever you like, to her you are only one thing: her child.”
“Where is she?” Gerard whispered, his voice shaking.
“At Gouda manse, pacing the night through, praying and worrying for you.”

Margaret knew the moment had come. She had softened him with kindness, with memory, with love, and now she brought out the full weight of her argument, plain and steady, the way a smith heats iron hot before he brings the sledge down. She told him, in plain homely Dutch, that his life in the cave was nothing but a higher form of selfishness, spiritual egotism. A priest had no more right to care only for his own soul than he had to care only for his own body. That was no path to heaven.
“Who ever lost their soul by saving the souls of other people?” she said. “The Almighty loves the man who thinks of others. When he sees you caring for the flock the duke has put into your hands, he will care ten times more for your soul than he ever could here, all alone in the dark.”

Gerard blinked, struck by her words. “You are very shrewd in an argument,” he said.
“Far from it,” she replied. “Only my eyes are not bandaged up with conceit. As long as Satan walks the whole earth, tempting men, and the sons of Belial never lock themselves in caves but run back and forth corrupting others, the good man who skulks apart is playing the devil’s game, giving him every advantage. You call yourself a soldier of Christ? Ask your old comrade Denys, who is only a soldier of the duke — ask him if he ever skulked in a hole to avoid battle, just because battle holds danger as well as glory and duty. Our kings and dukes never had such cowardly soldiers as Christ has. What was that you preached in the Rotterdam church, about the man in the parable who buried his talent in the earth, and angered the Lord? Your great gift for preaching — is that not a talent, a gift from your Creator?”
“Such as it is, yes,” Gerard said.
“And have you used it? Or buried it? Who have you preached to these seven months? Bats, and owls? You have buried your gift right here in this hole, along with yourself and all your once good wits. The Dominicans are the friars preachers. You were founded to preach the word of God, and so you are false to St. Dominic, as well as to his Master.
“Do you remember, when we were young, walking hand in hand in the fields? If you saw a sheep stuck on its back, three fields off, you would

Margaret slipped back to Rotterdam long before Gerard roused from the deep, healing sleep that followed his rescue, and left their little boy behind at the Gouda parsonage. No sooner was she home than she dispatched Reicht, that stout, loyal soul she trusted with every secret, straight to Gouda, bearing the plain vicar’s grey frock and wide soft felt hat she had prepared, with word-for-word instructions on how to care for her new master.

Next she sought out Jorian Ketel, the closest-mouthed man she had ever met, the only one in Rotterdam she could count on to keep silent, and the pair hatched two sly, unspoken schemes she would carry to her grave. I shall not name them here: if a woman as frank and good as Margaret kept them hidden till her dying breath, I, a mere man, *verbum non amplius addam* — no more words will I add.

For days she refused to step foot near the Gouda parsonage. The sharp words exchanged in the heat of their last argument had rankled long after the emotion of the moment faded, and she burned at the thought that Gerard could ever doubt she would see the priest in him no less than the man she had loved since girlhood. “What did he take me for?” she had wondered, stung, and her innocent pride tangled with modesty to whisper that she ought not go back uninvited. She had left little Gerard there on purpose, after all: not to win his father over with her own words, but to let the boy’s bright, uncomplicated love anchor the man forever to the living world, far from the cold darkness of his hermit’s cave.

But the separation cost her more than she had ever guessed. She had not spent a single hour apart from her son in his whole young life, and the empty quiet of her home grew unbearable by the day. By the third night, she crept through the dark all the way to the parsonage, skulking around the premises like a thief until she spotted Reicht alone in the kitchen. She tapped softly on the window pane, and begged her, for pity’s sake, to slip the boy out to her unseen. Reicht soon found an errand to take him out into the lane, and mother and child clung to each other in giddy, tearful joy before they had to part again. They struck a deal there and then: every afternoon, at the same set hour, Reicht would walk little Gerard halfway to Rotterdam, and Margaret would meet them. After the wild, gambolling play — the pair tumbling and laughing like a young cat and her first kitten — the boy would sometimes wander off to amuse himself at their feet, and the two women would huddle close to plot over poor Luke Peterson.

“Reicht,” Margaret murmured once, “I as good as promised him I would wed Luke. Told him all he had to do was say the word.”
“Poor Luke,” Reicht sighed at once.
“Why poor Luke?”
“To be tossed back and forth between yes and no like that, no mind of his own in the matter.”
“Wait — you haven’t gone and fallen soft on the boy yourself, that you take his part?” Margaret teased.
“Me?” Reicht tossed her head so hard her cap slid askew.
“Pardon me, then. You can do me a good turn, all the same.”
“Whisht! Hush! That little darling’s staring at us, eyes big as saucers, listening to every word.”
Both women ducked their heads under the same wide wool cap to muffle their voices, two quiet schemers conspiring against one unsuspecting boy.

When these secret, stolen meetings had run five days, Margaret began to chafe at the injustice of hiding like a criminal, and was sobbing over the loneliness of it when a rickety cart rumbled up to her front door. There sat Gerard, clean as a newly minted penny, his beard freshly shaved, his pale hands soft and white as snow, a faint healthy flush back in his cheeks, clad in exactly the grey frock and broad felt hat she had sent him.

She ran straight upstairs, scrubbed the traces of tears from her face, and swapped her worn everyday cap for a crisp one she had only just pulled fresh from the drawer before hurrying back down to him. He seized both her hands and kissed them, and a hot tear fell upon her knuckles. She turned her head away fast to hide the tears that had sprung to her own eyes.
“Sweet Margaret,” he said, soft, “why do you hold aloof from the good deed you yourself did? We have waited for you at the parsonage every single day, and no Margaret came.”
“You said things,” she told him, stiff, not looking at him.
“What? Things my mad hermit self babbled, back when I was nothing but a stubborn donkey?”
“Aye, but you said them all the same. And you had no cause to think so little of me.”
“Forget every word I ranted that day. No one heeds the ravings of a maniac, and I know now I was only weeks from turning into a gibbering idiot, locked alone in that cave. Not a soul on earth but you could have dragged me away. What wit, what kindness you lavished on me! I cannot thank you properly here in this street. No — I will thank you properly in the parsonage you have given me, among my flock, the people you made me shepherd. I love them already, and there I will call you what you are: the truest friend a man ever had. So now I say to you what you once said to me: come to Gouda manse.”
“Humph. We shall see about that,” she said, pretending to be cool and unhurried, though every inch of her burned to go at once.
“Margaret, do you think I would have kept our dear boy from you all these days if I had not been certain you would come back to him any hour? He has curled right around my heartstrings, but what claim have I on him next to yours? Confess now — you have thought hard, unkind thoughts of me for keeping him from you.”
“Nay, nay, never,” she said, softening. “Ah, you are yourself again, you who always thought of everyone before yourself. I have half a mind to come back to Gouda with you, just for saying that.”
“Come then with half a mind — that is worth more than the whole mind of any other man alive.”
“Well, I dare say I will. But there is no such mighty rush,” she said, forcing her face into a neutral line. “Tell me first how you get on with your new parishioners.”
“Why, my poor folk have already taken root in my heart,” he told her, smiling. “Simple, rough, a touch superstitious, but the kindest souls alive.”
“I knew you would find a grain of good in even a bushel of trouble,” she said.
“Whisht, hush — and Margaret, two men of the parish who feuded for four years straight came to the parsonage each trying to win me over to their side. But praise God, I won them over to each other instead, and now they laugh at their own old foolish quarrel.”
“But are you truly their vicar?” she pressed him. “Answer me that.”
“Certes! Have I not gone before the bishop, taken my oaths, rung the church bell, and touched the altar, the missal, and the holy chalice right there before the churchwardens? They handed me the parish seal, look, here it is tucked in my pocket. A real, duly sworn vicar, inviting his dearest friend home to Gouda manse.”
“Then my mind is at ease. Tell me everything else.”
“Well, sweet one, the soul dearest to me in all the parish is a poor cripple my guardian angel — that is you, you know, I saw you turn your head away — put right under my roof. Sybrandt and I are closer than brothers now, we forgave each other long ago. It would make you glad, and sad too, to hear how we wept and hugged. He speaks of nothing but your goodness, and is more pious and content now in his pain than he ever was in the days he was whole and strong. He will never leave my house, I swear, until he goes straight to heaven.”
“Tell me something that happened to you, not to everyone else,” she said, laughing. “I do not need to be told what a good man Sybrandt is, I have known you since we were children.”
“Let me think. At first the sun dazzled me so bad I could barely step outside, like some silly old owl just pulled from its tree — but that is all past now. And good Reicht Heynes — humph.”
“What of her?”
“Nothing but this, that she is a diamond of a woman. Her voice cuts through me like a knife, still, after all those months of silence, every voice but yours sounds harsh and loud. Oh, and I have news you will smile at. I spoke yesterday with an old man in the parish who fancies himself a terrible ill-tempered fellow, and works hard to play the part for everyone else — but his gruff act is threadbare, and the softest, kindest heart beats under it.”
“Sounds like the whole parish is full of angels,” Margaret said, dryly ironic.
“Then why do you stay away from them?” Gerard retorted. “He told me no parish in all Holland is more plagued by the devil than Gouda. And he gave me this example: ‘We had the holiest hermit in all the country, right here — but Gouda being Gouda, the devil came for him this week, bag and baggage. Not a scrap of him left but a patch of skin as prickly as a hedgehog, and a scrap of old rusted iron.’”
Margaret smiled.
“Aye — and the strangest part is, that very cave the hermit lived in has caved in entirely. If I had been stubborn enough to resist you, it would have buried me dead right where I chose to bury myself alive. I see the hand of Providence in that, Margaret. It condemns that mad, wasted life I led, and approves the new one you gave me. What say you to that?”
“Nay, I cannot pierce such mysteries,” she said, shaking her head. “I am but a woman.”
“More than that, I think. This very tale proves you are my guardian angel, nothing less. So come home to Gouda manse with me now.”
“You go on ahead,” she said. “I will follow.”
“Nay, ride back in the cart with me.”
“Not so.”
“Why ever not?”
“Can I tell you why and wherefore, being a woman? All I know is I feel — I wish — I must come alone.”
“Be it so then. I will leave the cart for you, for as you say, you are a woman who will have her way, and I will walk ahead on my own two feet, a man again, to carry the joyful news of your coming to the whole house.”

When Margaret reached the parsonage, the first thing she saw was the two Gerards together: the little boy doing wild, giddy somersaults on the patch of lawn, the father slouched in a chair in his big broad hat, pencil in hand, trying with endless patience to sketch his wiggling, fast-moving son. He showed her his rough sketches, frustrated. “I cannot fix him on the page no matter how hard I try,” he sighed. “He is pure quicksilver. Look at how he moves, a thousand different poses, none of them ungraceful, melting from one to the next like water.” He laughed a moment later. “Woe to all the old illuminators! Looking at this little rascal, I see what lumpy, lopsided, awkward toads they used to paint in missals, and call them cherubs and seraphs!” He crumpled the paper in despair and threw it away, and Margaret quietly picked it up and tucked it into the neck of her bodice.

That night, all four of them sat around the glowing peat fire, and Gerard bade them look at how the brass candlesticks and other metal trinkets glowed soft and warm in the hearthlight. “And the linen sheets I sleep in,” he said, half laughing, half earnest. “My conscience pricks me every night. ‘Who are you,’ it says, ‘to lie in linen white as spiderweb? Dives himself never had sheets so fine.’ And to think there are folk in the world who own all these nice things and still are not content. Let any one of them spend six months locked alone in a dark hermit’s cell, never seeing another human face, and they will learn how lovely this wicked world is, how fair and good ordinary men and women are. Margaret, you were always fair, but never half so bright to my eyes as you are now.” Margaret shook her head, disbelieving. “And my mother, here,” he went on, turning to Catherine, “I never noticed how exceeding comely you are until I came out of that cave.”
“Nor I neither,” Catherine said, smiling. “A score of years ago I might have passed unremarked in a crowd, but not now. I am old.”
“Every age has its own beauty,” Gerard told her, soft. “Look at that mild grey eye of yours, that has looked on nothing but motherly love for all these years — all that love has left its shadow on your face, and that shadow is a beauty no time can touch. Look at that soft lip, those pure white teeth, that brow where youth’s comeliness melts right into reverence. You are beautiful to me, mother dear.”
“That is all I need to hear, my darling,” Catherine said, wiping a happy tear from her eye. “It is past time you were in bed. You have to preach tomorrow morning.”
Reicht and Catherine exchanged a quiet, amused glance, that said plain as day: We have an amiable maniac on our hands, who thinks every last thing on God’s green earth is beautiful.

Sunday came, and they sat in the packed church to hear him preach. The pews were crammed full of people who had only come out of curiosity to gawk at the mad former hermit who had been made their vicar — and every last one of them left devout. Never had his great gift for speaking shone more bright. His own heart was so full the first time he looked out over the flock he had neglected for so many years, he poured his whole soul into the two-hour sermon that flew by so fast it felt to the crowd like barely twenty minutes. He terrified the impenitent and the careless, comforted the grieving and the afflicted, lifted the hearts of the poor, and when he finished the whole congregation stood still, rapt, unwilling to believe the rich, divine music of his voice had fallen silent.

Two poor women huddled in the back corner, crying so hard their shoulders shook.
“Wherever did he learn all that?” Catherine whispered, holding her apron to her eyes. “By Our Lady, he did not get it from me.”
As soon as they were back in the quiet parsonage, Margaret threw her arms around Catherine’s neck and kissed her. “Mother, mother,” she sobbed, “I am not quite a fully happy woman, but oh — I am so proud.” And she knelt there on the floor, and swore a solemn vow that no word or deed of hers would ever let their old love come between this young, holy priest and his Heaven.

Have you ever stood on the seashore after a great storm, when the wind dies suddenly?
