The waves do not stop the moment the wind that drove them fades — for a little while they lash the shore even harder than they did in the height of the gale. But you know, deep down, that the inevitable calm has come, and it is only rocking the last of the wild waves gently to sleep. That was the life of those two tempest-tossed lovers from that night, when they walked hand in hand under the stars back from the old hermit’s cave to the warm lights of the Gouda manse. Now and then a loud, roaring wave would rise up, but it was nothing more than memory’s echo of the old storm that had swept their lives for years. The gale itself was over, and the churning, boiling waters of their old pain began to sink, slow and soft and inevitable, into quiet.

That image takes the place of all the small, tedious, trivial details of the long, gentle years that followed. What matters most is their strange, unheard-of situation — one that history, bold as it is, rarely matches for oddity. Gerard and Margaret were bound tight by old affection, by years of shared familiarity, by a marriage that had been irregular but fully legal in its day. But they were separated now by the Holy Church they both loved deeply, and by their own consciences that sided unreservedly with that Church. They lived only a few miles apart, Margaret called Gerard’s own mother her own mother, and every Sunday she brought little Gerard out to Gouda, returning only after dark. No matter when she came, the parsonage was a feast day, and she was welcomed like a little queen. Catherine and Eli grew so tired of the quiet little town of Tergou, with nothing to draw them there compared to Rotterdam and Gouda, that they left it entirely and set up their new home in the city.

The years glided by, so empty of great dramatic incidents, so free of towering hope and terrible fear, so identical to one another, that I could barely mark the passage of time without dates to guide me.

Early the next year, 1471, the Duchess of Burgundy — with the Duke’s public dissent but secret connivance — raised an army to send her deposed brother Edward IV back to England to take back his crown. Our old friend Denys the soldier enlisted, and passed through Rotterdam on his way to the ships. He heard on the road that Gerard had become a priest, and Margaret was living alone. He found her at her shop, and told her he had never been the sort of man to settle down and marry — but since his old comrade Gerard had put it out of his own power to keep the troth he had sworn to her, Denys felt bound to keep it for him. “A comrade’s honour is as dear to me as my own,” he said.
Margaret stared at him, then laughed out loud. “I would rather stay your she-comrade,” she told him. “If we were to marry, we might find we do not get on half so well.” And in that role of his loyal she-comrade, she outfitted him with a fine new sword forged in Antwerp, and a double handful of silver coins.

There is no moment a priest wears his sacred calling more fully than when he stands in the chamber of the newly dead. Gerard performed every last rite the Church ordains for the departed, every prayer, every anointing, exactly as he would have done for the humblest cottager in his Gouda parish. His movements were automatic, his mind reeling under the weight of the sudden, cataclysmic blow that had fallen on him before he could even brace for it; the raw, gnawing pangs of true bereavement had not yet had time to sink in through the stunned numbness. Then, caught up in a sharp, fiery rush of religious devotion, he dropped to his knees and thanked Heaven she had been granted so gentle, pious a Christian end.

No sooner had that prayer left his lips than every thought in his head narrowed to a single purpose: he would not leave her buried among strangers, far from the land she knew. He would bring her home, to lay her in the hallowed ground of his own parish churchyard.

That very same dusk, a single-horse cart draped in heavy black cloth set out on the road to Gouda. Inside the cart rested a plain lead coffin, and beside it Gerard lay huddled, his arms slung tight over its cold surface, his chin propped on the lid. The short, fierce burst of energy that had carried him through all the hasty, necessary preparations for the journey had burned out entirely, leaving him crushed, clinging to the only piece of her he had left.

The carter who had hired out the cart walked at the horse’s head the whole miles, never speaking a word to the huddled mourner behind him. Even when he stopped to bait the beast, he spoke only in a soft whisper, his voice unconsciously hushed out of reverence for that quiet, searing agony unfolding behind him. When they halted for the night at a roadside inn, he and the landlord tried gently, out of simple kindness, to draw Gerard away from the coffin to eat a crust of bread and stretch out for a few hours of rest. But Gerard beat them back, and when they pressed their plea, he almost snarled at them like a loyal hound guarding its dead master, clinging to the cold lead lid through the whole long night. The two men said no more after that, laid a thick wool cloak over his huddled shoulders, and left him to his vigil.

By noon the next day, the sorrow-laden cart rumbled up the drive of Gerard’s manse. A full score of his parishioners had gathered there, each with some small, trivial trouble to bring to their parson—they had already felt the gap left by his absence, and had come seeking his counsel. When they saw the black draped cart, and their gentle, steadfast healer bowed almost to breaking point beneath his grief, they lifted a loud, unfeigned wail of sorrow. The sound cut through the thick, numb lethargy of Gerard’s mourning, and he blinked, saw the familiar faces of his flock all clustered around him, and tried to speak. “Oh, my children! My children!” he cried, but the words choked in his throat, thick with anguish, and he could say nothing more.

The next day, despite every protest and plea from his parishioners that he rest and let another priest lead the service, Gerard insisted on burying her himself. He read the full burial rite over the open grave, his voice only trembling now and then, steady in its devotion. A hundred hot tears fell on the dark earth piled beside her resting place. When the last words of the service were spoken, he did not move. He stood there like a marble statue, rooted to the spot, until the crowd of mourners slipped quietly out of the churchyard, out of respect for his private grief.

He stood lost in a waking dream for what felt like hours, until the sexton—an ordinarily decent man, but as unthinking as most folk who work with death day in and day out—picked up his spade and began shoveling earth down into the grave, no warning given. At the first heavy thud of soil landing on the lid of her coffin, Gerard let out a high, piercing scream that split the quiet of the churchyard.

The sexton froze mid-motion, his spade hanging in the air. Gerard staggered, one hand flying up to press hard against his chest. The sexton caught him before he could fall, shouting for help. Jorian Ketel, who had lingered at the edge of the churchyard mourning the benefactress who had been so kind to him, ran over at once, and the two men half-carried, half-supported the reeling Gerard back to the manse.

“Ah, Jorian! Good, faithful Jorian!” gasped Gerard, his voice thin and shaking. “Something snapped inside me. I felt it. I heard it, right here, Jorian—right here.” He pressed his palm hard against his breast, his face ashen white.

A fortnight slipped by, sharp with the first frosty bite of late autumn, when a pale, stooped figure in a threadbare cleric’s cloak limped through the heavy oak gates of the Dominican convent huddled on Gouda’s mist-fringed suburban edge. He asked the porter for audience with Brother Ambrose, the convent’s acting head: the old prior had died only weeks prior, and the prelate appointed to succeed him had not yet arrived to take up his post.
That ailing visitor was Gerard. He had come full circle, to lay down what remained of his days in the quiet order he had once dreamed of as a boy, long before years of wandering, loss, and grief wore him thin. He formally presented himself to enter as a novice on standard probation, but no one who looked at his sunken cheeks, or the tight hollow cough that shook him unannounced, could miss the hard truth: he was a failing man, and he knew it. He had come here to die in peace, within reach of the kind, gentle Ambrose his oldest friend, and the rest of the monks who had been welcome at his hearth, his larder, and his open heart for decades. The empty vicarage he had left behind was a torture he could bear no longer—every beam, every windowsill, every climbing rose by the threshold was stitched through with memories of her.
Ambrose, who knew full well both Gerard’s worth and the quiet, unshakable sorrow that was eroding him faster than any bodily ailment, clung to a soft, secret hope that he might nurse his friend back to strength and restore him to the parish that loved him. To that end, he assigned Gerard a bright, draft-free cell set above the convent’s main arched gateway, with a clear view over the flat green meadows stretching down to the river, and strictly forbade him from joining the other novices in fasts or harsh bodily austerities, ordering the lay brothers to bring him rich broth, warm buttered bread, and spiced cider each day.
But barely a handful of days later, the new prior arrived, and he proved a hard, unyielding man of the sort that prized rigid discipline above all mercy. For the first weeks he threw himself entirely into rooting out small, long-tolerated laxities in the convent’s routines, tightening rules for every brother under his roof, until word reached him that the former vicar of Gouda had joined the house as a novice. His lip curled. “That will not do. Let him first formally renounce his vicar’s post, or leave these walls. I will not have soft, overfed parsons lingering in my house taking ease no other brother is permitted.”
He sent a lay brother to summon Gerard to his quarters at once, and Gerard came, his steps slow, leaning a little on a gnarled oak staff. The moment the two men crossed the threshold and laid eyes on one another, both froze, their faces blanching with unnameable shock.
“Clement!”
“Jerome!”

Jerome remained as dour and unyielding in his general temperament as he had always been, yet a soft spot had grown in his stern heart for Gerard. All the months he spent in England, he had found he missed the quiet, frail young monk far more than he had ever expected he would, and in the years since, he had often wondered what had become of him. The stories he heard of Gerard in Gouda – above all, the account of his standing firm against the Pope and the Minorites to denounce what Jerome himself called “the infernal heresy of the Immaculate Conception” – had raised the young brother high in his esteem. But when a tearful young novice came to him to reveal that Gerard was wasting away not from bodily ailment, but from grief for a woman, all his old sharp contempt flared back.
He was determined to stamp out this unseemly scandal. He visited Clement (Gerard’s monastic name) twice each day in his cell, bringing all his old authority, all his fiery, persuasive eloquence, to rouse the young man from his unspiritual despondency, to stop him robbing the Church of such rare piety and such a gifted preacher at so critical a time. Gerard heard every word, nodded, agreed his reasoning was sound, admired Jerome’s iron strength, confessed his own weakness – and still visibly faded, day by day, toward the land of the faithful departed.
One day Jerome told him he had learned the full story of Gerard’s life, and heard it with great pride. “But now,” he said, “you spoil it all, Clement. This is no noble end, it is the triumph of earthly passion. Better to have yielded to your love while she lived and repented after, than to resist it all her days, only to succumb to it now, body and soul.”
“Dear Jerome,” Gerard replied, his tone so soft and sweet it stripped the rebuke from Jerome’s remonstrance, “you do me an injustice here. There is no raging passion left in me, only a deep, quiet affection I will not blush for here, for I will never blush for it in heaven. Bethink you, Jerome: the poor hound that dies of grief on his master’s grave – no one calls that sinful passion, do they? Neither am I guilty of it. Passion would have saved my life and lost my soul. She was my good angel. She sustained me in my duties and my works of charity, her face gave me courage in the pulpit, her lips soothed me when the people I served turned ungrateful. She wove herself into every good part of my life, and after leaning on her so long, I could not bear to walk the rest of the road alone. And dear Jerome, believe me, I am no rebel against Heaven. It is God’s own will to release me. When they threw the first spadeful of earth onto her poor coffin, something snapped right here in my bosom that no man can mend. I heard it, I felt it. Ever since that hour, no food I put in my mouth has any savour. Blindfolded, I could not tell you bread from meat by the taste.”
“Holy saints!” Jerome gasped.
“And from that very same hour, my heavy dark despair left me, and I smile again. I know why. The Lord who holds life and death in his hands gave me my great summons that minute: some last thin cord of mortal life snapped within me. He is very pitiful. I would have lived a long, miserable empty life, but He said, ‘No; enough is done, enough is suffered, poor feeble loving servant. Thy shortcomings are forgiven, thy sorrows draw to an end. Come thou to thy rest.’ I come, Lord! I come!”
Jerome groaned. “The Church has ever had her holy but feeble servants. I would give ten years of my own life to save yours. But I see it may not be. Die in peace.”
And so, a few days later, Gerard lay dying in a frame of mind so holy and bright that more than one aged, long-proven saintly monk lingered by his cell to garner his dying words. That evening, he had seen his brother Giles, and begged him not to let poor old Jack starve, to see that little Gerard’s trustees did their duty, to kiss his elderly parents for him, and to send his old comrade Denys safely to his family in Burgundy: “Poor thing, he will feel so strange here without his old companion.”
After that, he spoke alone with Jerome. What passed between them was never distinctly known, but it must have been a profound, remarkable meeting, for Jerome stepped out of the cell with his arms crossed over his breast, his proud high head bowed low, sighing softly as he walked.
The two monks who kept watch over him through the night till matins reported that he broke out every little while in pious ejaculations, praises, and quiet thanksgivings. Only once, they said, he wandered a little, and cried that he saw Margaret walking in green meadows among other spirits clad all in white, all of them smiling and beckoning him to come. Both the monks swore (though it may well have been fancy) that just before dawn, three soft, slow taps sounded on the cell wall, one after another. The dying man heard them, and whispered, “I come, love, I come.”
This much is certain: Gerard spoke those words, and made ready for his departure. He sent for all the monks who were keeping their vigils at that hour, and they came, hovering like gentle spirits round him with words of holy comfort. Some knelt in silence, their faces pressed to the cold stone floor to pray for him; others tenderly supported his head. When one of them began to speak of his life of self-denial and charity, Gerard stopped him, and addressed them all clearly:
“My dear brethren, take note that he who dies here so happy does not hold to these new-fangled doctrines of man’s own merit. Oh, what a miserable hour this would be for me if I did! Nay, I hold, with the Apostles, and their pupils the ancient Church fathers, that we are justified not by our own wisdom, or piety, or the works we have done in holiness of heart, but by faith.”(1)
Silence fell, and the monks glanced at one another significantly.
“Please you sweep the floor,” the dying Christian said, his voice suddenly restored to all its old clarity and force. They obeyed at once, awed and curious. “Make me a great cross with wood ashes.” They strewed the ashes across the stone floor in the shape of a wide, great cross. “Now lay me down on it, for so will I die.” They lifted him gently from his bed, and laid him soft upon the ash cross.
“Shall we spread out thine arms, dear brother?” one asked.
“Now God forbid! Am I worthy of that?”
He lay silent, his eyes raised in ecstasy. Presently he spoke half to them, half to himself: “Oh, it feels buoyant. It lifts me, floating up to the sky, whence my own merits would have sunk me like lead.”
Day broke, and its light fell on his face cast upward in silent rapture, his hands folded tight together, just as Margaret’s had been. Around the very same hour she had breathed her last, he spoke his final word in this world: “Jesu.” And even with that word on his lips – he fell asleep.
They laid him out for his last resting place. Under his linen robe, they found his horsehair shirt. “Ah!” the young monks cried, “behold a saint!” But under the rough hair cloth, they found a long, thick tress of auburn hair. They recoiled, horrified, a babel of voices breaking out, some condemning him, some excusing him.
Right in the midst of the uproar, Jerome walked in, heard the dispute, and turned to the ardent young monk Basil, who was shouting scandal the loudest. “Basil,” he said, “is the woman who owned this hair alive or dead?”
“How may I know, father?”
“Then for aught you know, it may be the relic of a saint?”
“Certes it may be,” Basil replied sceptically.
“Then you have broken our rule,” Jerome told him, “which saith, ‘Put no ill construction on an act done by a brother which may be construed innocently.’ Who are you to judge such a man as this was? Go to your cell, and stir not out for a week by way of penance.”
He carried the lock of hair away himself. When the coffin was to be closed, he cleared all the other monks out of the cell, and laid the tress soft on the dead man’s bosom. “There, Clement,” he whispered to the still face. He set himself a private penance for the act, and nailed the coffin shut with his own hands.
The next day Gerard was buried in Gouda churchyard. The monks followed him in procession from the convent, and Jerome, carrying out the unspoken wishes of the deceased, read the full burial service. The grave was dug extra deep, and at its bottom rested Margaret’s lead coffin. Gerard’s own little coffin, light as a feather he was so wasted away, was lowered down and placed gently by its side.
After the service, Jerome spoke a few words to the crowd of parishioners who had gathered to take one last look at their best friend. When he spoke of the departed’s gentle virtues, loud wailing and weeping burst forth, and tears fell on the coffin like rain.
The monks returned to the convent, and Jerome gathered them all in the refectory to speak to them. “We have this day laid a saint in the earth,” he said. “The convent will keep his trentals, but we will feast, not fast; for our good brother is freed from the burden of the flesh. His labours are over, and he has entered into his joyful rest. I alone shall fast, and do penance; for to my shame I say it, I was unjust to him, and knew not his true worth till it was too late. And you, young monks, do not be curious to inquire whether the lock he bore on his bosom was a token of pure earthly affection or the relic of a saint. Remember only the heart that beat beneath it. Most of all, fix your eyes upon his life and conversation, and follow them an ye may: for he was a holy man.”
Thus after all life’s fitful fever, these two true lovers were at peace. The grave, kinder to them than the Church ever was, united them for ever; and now a man of another age and nation, touched deeply by their fate, has laboured to raise their tombstone, to rescue them from long and unmerited oblivion. He asks for your sympathy, but not your pity. Put this story to a wholesome use. So much fiction peddles false views of life and death: here, curbed by history, it gives you true ones. Let the cruel barriers that kept these two apart prepare you to accept that on this earth, there will nearly always be some obstacle or other to your perfect happiness. To their early death, apply your Reason and your Faith, by way of exercise and preparation. For if you cannot bear to be told that these two died young – who had they lived a hundred years would still be dead – how shall you bear to see the gentle, the loving, and the true glide from your own bosom to the grave, and fly from your house to heaven? Yet this is in store for you. In every age, the Master of life and death, who is kinder as well as wiser than we are, has transplanted to heaven, young, earth’s sweetest flowers. I ask your sympathy, then, for their rare constancy and pure affection, and their cruel separation by a vile heresy(2) in the bosom of the Church; but not your pity for their early but happy end.
(1) He was citing from Clement of Rome – *οὐ δι ἑαυτῶν δικαιούμεθα οὐδὲ διὰ τῆς ὑμετέρας σοφίας, ἢ εὐσεβείας ἢ ἔργων ὧν κατειργασάμεθα ἐν ὁσιότητι καρδίας, ἀλλὰ διὰ τῆς πίστεως*. – *Epist. ad Corinth.* i. 32.
(2) Celibacy of the clergy, an invention truly fiendish.

I yield to a custom I have long despised, yet lack the stubborn spirit to resist, lingering on the final stage of this tale to gather up the small, scattered fragments of human life I wove through the story: not all of them, for the passing wayfarers who crossed Gerard’s path along his journey have no further claim on me. Their purpose was served the moment they convinced you that the young pilgrim traveled from Holland to Rome through a world of breathing, contradictory real people, not a population of stiff, lifeless dolls.

Eli and Catherine lived to a remarkably great old age, so long that even the memory of their son Gerard and his beloved Margaret softened and dimmed to faint, hazy echoes in the twilight of their years. Giles too was long-lived: he journeyed to take service at the court of Bavaria, and was still living there at ninety, though by then he had weathered down to little more than bone and tanned, leathery skin, his voice still blaring out loud and brassy as a military trumpet.

Cornelis, meanwhile, had no rivals left standing between him and the family shop, and was long ago fully forgiven by his mother, who clung to him all the tighter now that every other one of her children had scattered to far-flung corners of the world. He waited, and waited, and waited for his elderly parents to draw their last breath. But Catherine’s old shrewd prediction came true long before the two of them wore out their days: this man, who had done nothing but loiter and covet what was not yet his, rusted away himself first. At sixty-five, he lay dying of creeping old age in the arms of his mother, still hale and sharp at eighty-six. He drifted unconscious for a while, then woke clear in the very last moments before death, saw her leaning over him, and babbled eagerly of all the grand renovations he would make to the shop and the whole premises the very second they became his. “Yes, my dearest boy,” the poor old woman soothed him gently, and a minute later he was still as clay, and that clay was borne to his grave by every pair of feet whose shoes he had spent decades idly waiting for.

Denys, brokenhearted by the death of his dearest comrade Gerard, was glad to turn his face for home to Burgundy. A small royal pension the court granted him kept him housed and fed for years, until he unexpectedly came into a sizable inheritance left by a distant relation. For decades after that, he was a well-known fixture in his hometown: a crusty, gruff old soldier who could spin rousing, vivid tales of war and foreign roads when he chose, and who railed against the whole fairer sex with a bitter, unshakable edge no one could ever talk him out of.

Jerome, disgusted by the loose, lax morals he’d seen across the northern lands, retired to Italy, and thanks to his powerful high-placed connections, rose to become a mitred abbot by the time he was seventy. He clamped down hard on discipline in his abbey, turning the screw of monastic rule tight until his monks both revered and resented him. He ruled his community with an iron rod for ten full years. Then one night he died, all alone—for he had spent his whole life carving rules and enforcing order, and had never once found the way to unlock a single human heart. The Vulgate Bible rested on his pillow, a crucifix was clasped tight in his hand, and on his lips was a faint soft smile no one had ever seen grace his face while he lived. So I like to think, in that terrible, solemn hour, he was not quite as alone as he seemed. May he rest in peace. The Master he served has many servants, and they carry many different natures; even the faithful ones can be gruff and unyielding, as is often the case in our mortal lives.

The yellow-haired little laddie, Gerard Gerardson, belongs not to fiction, but to recorded history. History has written of his birth in far grander terms than mine. Carved over the doorway of the tailor’s house on Brede Kirk Straet are the words: *“HAEC EST PARVA DOMUS NATUS QUA MAGNUS ERASMUS”* — This is the little house that gave birth to great Erasmus. The world has written dozens of biographies of him in the centuries since, but there is still work left for history to do. No scholar has ever truly comprehended the great Erasmus, not any more than a pygmy can wrap his mind around a giant, or a biased partisan can fairly judge a man of perfect impartiality. He was the foremost scholar and divine of his entire age, and he was also a heaven-born dramatist, unmatched across his century. Some of the brightest, most memorable scenes in this very tale are drawn directly from his medieval pen, and they shine bright wherever they appear on our pages. For the words of a genius as towering as his are never born to die. Once their immediate work on their own generation is done, they may seem to slumber, forgotten in dark library stacks—but with every fresh wave of intelligence Time pours over the generations that study him, they prove their immortal nature. They rise again, spring up from the dust of old great libraries, bud, bloom, bear fruit, and scatter seed, generation after generation, age after uncounted age.
